preparation.text: The leaves have a pleasant acid flavour and make a pleasant addition to salads. Use the leaves in moderation. In South Africa it is a traditional ingredient in dishes such as waterblommetjiebredie ('water flower stew').

recipes.method: For the filling: about 680 g leafy greens (spinach, Swiss chard leaves, nettles, lamb's quarters, amaranth or quickweed); 3 egg yolks; 1 egg; 250 ml (1 cup) crème fraîche or sour cream; 125 ml (½ cup) whipping cream; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt, plus more if needed; plenty of black pepper; 45 ml (3 tbsp) chopped Bermuda buttercup stems. For the pastry: 560 ml (2¼ cups) plain flour; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt; 125 ml (½ cup) extra virgin olive oil; 125 ml (½ cup) tepid water. Make the filling first; the pastry needs no resting. Bring 2.5 cm of water to the boil in a large pot, pack in about 680 g of leafy greens (spinach, Swiss chard leaves, nettles, lamb's quarters, amaranth or quickweed), cover and cook on high for 2 minutes, stir, then cook 2 minutes more until just tender but still bright green. If you use nettles, cover them in boiling water instead and cook about 5 minutes. Drain, refresh in cold water, squeeze as dry as you can, roll in a clean tea towel to press out the rest, and chop roughly. Beat 3 egg yolks and 1 egg with 250 ml (1 cup) crème fraîche or sour cream, 125 ml (½ cup) whipping cream, 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt and plenty of black pepper, then stir in the greens and 45 ml (3 tbsp) chopped Bermuda buttercup stems, adding more salt if needed. For the pastry, stir 560 ml (2¼ cups) plain flour, 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt, 125 ml (½ cup) extra virgin olive oil and 125 ml (½ cup) tepid water together and form a ball. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Roll the pastry into a disc about 30 cm across on an oiled or lined baking tray, turn up and crimp the edge into a lip, spread in the filling and bake 40–45 minutes, until the pastry is crisp and the centre is set.
recipes.title: Leafy green tart with Bermuda buttercup

recipes.method: Pasta of your choice; olive oil or butter; shredded parmesan (or any cheese); a couple of handfuls of Bermuda buttercup leaves; salt and pepper. Cook pasta of your choice as the packet directs, drain and return it to the pot. Stir in olive oil or butter until melted, then add shredded parmesan (or any cheese), a couple of handfuls of Bermuda buttercup leaves, and salt and pepper to taste. Toss and serve.

Retrieved 10/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxalis_pes-caprae — quoted verbatim. The warning is two sentences from the Hazards section, which Wikipedia tags 'Original research' (November 2012); those two sentences cite Bown 1995, Sturtevant 1972 and Chai & Liebman 2005. The runners-eaten-raw-or-boiled sentence cites Watt & Breyer-Brandwijk 1962; the waterblommetjiebredie sentence cites de Villiers 2010. Not used: the raw bulbs used against tapeworm and the plant used as a diuretic ('possibly hazardously'), which are medicinal; and the Hazards paragraphs on livestock deaths, which concern stock and carry 'citation needed' tags.

Facts read, not written into the page: NZPCN (all rights reserved; https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/oxalis-pes-caprae/) gives biostatus Exotic, naturalised 1883, origin South Africa, reproducing by bulbils. Flora of New Zealand Online (CC BY 3.0 NZ) gives flowering Jan.–Dec. and cites Connor 1977, The Poisonous Plants in New Zealand; its Weed-tab URL redirects to the Taxon profile, which has no habitat line. Weeds Australia (Centre for Invasive Species Solutions, all rights reserved; https://weeds.org.au/profiles/soursob-bermuda-buttercup/) says it is poisonous to stock because of oxalate in all its parts and mildly toxic to humans especially if eaten in large quantities; that it can be mistaken for clover when not in flower or for other weedy Oxalis species; that hand removal after bulbil formation spreads the bulbils; and that in Australia it flowers June to October. Plants of the World Online was behind Cloudflare and was not read.

Months not changed, 10/10/2026. The iNaturalist New Zealand month histogram (place 6803, research grade, n=696) peaks in September (198) and at a quarter of the peak admits June to October; the entry's months also include November (3 records). Weeds Australia says rising temperatures kill the aerial growth after flowering, and the Pacific Bulb Society describes a dry summer dormancy, so the leaves are above ground over much the same months the records fall in.

summary.text:
Oxalis pes-caprae is a species of tristylous yellow-flowering plant in the wood sorrel family Oxalidaceae. Some of the most common names for the plant reference its sour taste owing to oxalic acid present in its tissues. Indigenous to South Africa, the plant has become a pest plant in different parts of the world that is difficult to eradicate because of how it propagates through underground bulbs. In the non-native range the plants largely reproduce vegetatively and many populations have only one style length and the plants never produce seed.
In New Zealand: North Island: a common to abundant weed in lowland areas; South Island: Marlborough, Nelson, less common in coastal Canterbury. Naturalised from South Africa, first recorded in 1883.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

All parts contain oxalate, and eaten in quantity the plant poisons livestock: sheep grazing it have died of oxalate poisoning in Australia and Italy, and miniature horses with access to it have been poisoned. It has not been reported poisoning livestock in New Zealand. It is mildly toxic to people, especially eaten in large quantities.

identification.text: Cap 5–11 cm across, brownish grey to dark brown, rounded, finely velvety and dry. Underneath there are pores, not gills: greyish white, with the pore surface sunken around the top of the stem. Stem 5–13 cm long, greyish white and covered in dark grey scales, tapering upwards, with no ring. Flesh white. Some New Zealand collections stain blue in the cut stem; a New Zealand mycologist has suggested these may be a second, unnamed Leccinum species.

lookalikes.howToTell: Porcini looks similar to birch bolete, with a rounded stem and a similar brown cap. Look at the stem: porcini's is pale brown with a fine white net over at least the top third and no scales; birch bolete's is greyish white and covered in dark grey scales. Birch bolete grows only under silver birch, but porcini can grow there too, so the tree alone does not settle it.

preparation.text: Cook thoroughly. Use young, firm caps; older ones go soft and hold water, and are better sliced and dried. In older ones, remove the pores, and peel the stem if its outer layer is tough. The flesh darkens almost to black when cooked, which does not affect eating.

recipes.method: 450 g birch boletes, cleaned and sliced; water to cover; 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter or olive oil; a shallot, chopped; 30 ml Riesling. Cover the mushrooms with water, bring to a rolling boil and boil for 15–20 minutes, then drain them well. Heat a large frying pan over medium-high heat with the butter or oil, add the mushrooms and shallot and pour in the Riesling. Cook, stirring now and then, until all the liquid has gone, then keep cooking about 5 minutes more until browned.
recipes.title: Sautéed birch boletes with Riesling

summary.text: An introduced bolete that in New Zealand grows only under silver birch. It looks similar to porcini, but its white stem is covered in dark scales.

warnings: Leccinum boletes have caused stomach upsets, mostly when eaten raw or undercooked. Cook them thoroughly.
Some people react badly even to edible mushrooms, so eat only a small amount the first time you try one.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): A very common weed of open, disturbed sites, in arable land, waste ground, roadsides, dry riverbeds, and pastures. Recorded elevations range from 0 to 1525 m.
Veronica persica is a common ruderal and arable weed associated with disturbed habitats such as cultivated fields, gardens, lawns and roadsides. The plant prefers moist conditions and grows well in loamy, nutrient-rich soil.
In New Zealand it is a common weed of crops, gardens and pasture, quick to colonise bare soil (Massey, Yates). In lawns, mowing tends to keep it down (Yates).

identification.text:
Annual herb to 0.1 m tall. Stems prostrate to decumbent and rooting at nodes, eglandular-pubescent; hairs uniform. Leaf bud indistinct; leaves separating while very small, opposite-decussate, erecto-patent to spreading; lamina thin, ovate to broad ovate, sometimes deltoid, 6–35 mm long, 5–30 mm wide, dull green above, paler beneath, midrib and palmate secondary veins evident; surfaces eglandular-hairy; margin pubescent, serrate; teeth in 3–8 pairs; apex rounded to sub-acute; base truncate; petiole 0.5–7.0 mm long. Inflorescence a terminal raceme, 200–500 mm long; flowers distant, 12–50, all bisexual; bracts alternate, leaf-like; pedicels spreading, 5–15 mm long, up to 40 mm long and incurved at fruiting, with short, antrorse, eglandular hairs and scattered longer eglandular or occasionally glandular hairs. Calyx lobes 4, tapered to narrow obtuse apex, sub-equal, 5–7 mm long, with short, antrorse hairs on margins and a few longer ones on calyx tube. Corolla 8–12 mm diameter; tube white and yellow, about 1 mm long, much shorter than calyx, eglandular-hairy inside; lobes 4, usually sky-blue, rarely white, erecto-patent to spreading, unequal, orbicular to broadly elliptical, 5–8 mm long, rounded; nectar guides dark blue or purple, rarely absent. Stamen filaments white or pale blue, 2–3 mm long; anthers dark blue. Style glabrous, 1.5–3.0 mm long. Capsules angustiseptate, didymous with prominent veins, diverging obtuse lobes and broad sinus between, eglandular- and glandular-hairy in distal half, 3.5–4.0 mm long, 6–7 mm at widest point. Seeds ellipsoid, smooth and concave on funicle side, wrinkled and convex on back, straw-yellow to brown, 1.5–1.8 mm long.
Veronica persica is distinctive among the common weedy speedwells in New Zealand. Plants can be identified by their coarsely toothed leaves, lax terminal inflorescences of alternate leaf-like bracts and pedicellate blue flowers, and distinctive capsules, which are broader than long, with widely spreading lobes, shallow sinus, and ciliate margins. The anterior corolla lobe is usually, but not always, paler than the other three lobes, and the short stamens are curved and more or less erect alongside the style.
The stems are round, and the whole plant is quite hairy, on stems and leaves (Massey). The flowers fall off very easily once the plant is picked (Massey).
Other speedwells grow in the same places. Field speedwell (Veronica arvensis), the commonest speedwell in lawns, is very similar but a bit smaller, with tiny pale blue flowers that are not on stalks (Massey, Yates). Creeping speedwell (Veronica filiformis) is a perennial with runners and small, oval, hairy leaves; turf speedwell (Veronica serpyllifolia) is a perennial with runners, smooth thyme-like leaves and small white flowers (Massey, Yates).

lookalikes.howToTell: Ground-ivy's leaves are round to kidney-shaped, 1–3.5 cm long, with a heart-shaped base and scalloped edges, and its flowers are tubular and two-lipped, 1–1.5 cm long, blue or blue-violet with purple spots on the lower lip. Bird's-eye speedwell's leaves are ovate, 6–35 mm long, with 3–8 pairs of coarse teeth and a squared-off base; its flowers are flat, 8–12 mm across, with four sky-blue lobes striped dark, each alone on a long, slender stalk, and its seed capsules are two-lobed and broader than long. Both creep and root at the joints and both have blue flowers, so neither tells them apart. Ground-ivy grows mostly in shade below trees and around buildings, speedwell in open, disturbed ground. Ground-ivy's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked; they are bitter.
lookalikes.name: Ground-ivy

lookalikes.howToTell: Field woundwort's flowers are two-lipped, 6–7 mm long, pink or lilac, and grow in clusters around the stem up a leafy spike; bird's-eye speedwell's are flat, 8–12 mm across, with four sky-blue lobes (rarely white) striped dark, each alone on a long, slender stalk. Field woundwort's stem is square; speedwell's is round. Both are hairy, sprawl across the ground, have paired, toothed leaves of much the same size, flower all year, and grow in gardens, fields, waste places, roadsides and river beds, so none of these tells them apart. Field woundwort poisons livestock (staggers); no record of it being eaten by people has been found, so do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Field woundwort

lookalikes.howToTell: Field speedwell's flowers are tiny, 2–3 mm across, and sit almost stalkless (stalks 0–2 mm) among small bracts at the stem tips; bird's-eye speedwell's are 8–12 mm across, each alone on a long, slender stalk (5–15 mm, longer in fruit). Field speedwell's leaves are 5–20 mm long with 3–6 pairs of teeth; bird's-eye speedwell's are 6–35 mm with 3–8 pairs. Out of flower they look much the same: both are hairy, with paired, toothed leaves of similar shape, and both grow in gardens, crops, lawns and waste ground. Size alone does not separate them, as field speedwell can grow large in gardens. No record of field speedwell being eaten has been found.
lookalikes.name: Field speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Turf speedwell's flowers are pale blue fading to whitish, 3–5 mm across, on short stalks (1–3 mm) up a spike at the stem tips; bird's-eye speedwell's are sky-blue, 8–12 mm across, each alone on a long, slender stalk. Turf speedwell's leaves are almost hairless, 5–17 mm long, with shallow, rounded teeth; bird's-eye speedwell's are hairy, 6–35 mm long and coarsely toothed. Turf speedwell is a perennial that stays below the mower in lawns and damp pasture; bird's-eye speedwell is seldom in mown turf and is commoner in gardens and crops. Both creep and can root at the joints, and both have paired leaves and dark-striped flowers, so neither tells them apart. The older Flora (1988) gives turf speedwell's flowers as c. 8 mm across on stalks 2–6 mm long, which overlaps bird's-eye speedwell's at the edges, so go by colour and layout: turf speedwell's are white or very pale blue and sit in a long spike at the stem tips, bird's-eye speedwell's are bright blue and sit singly in the leaf joints. Turf speedwell's record as food is thin, so it is not given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Turf speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the petals: scarlet pimpernel's flowers have five lobes, (2–)6–15 mm across, orange or orange-red; bird's-eye speedwell's have four, 8–12 mm across, usually sky-blue (rarely white) with dark stripes. Scarlet pimpernel's leaves have no stalk, smooth edges and often faint black dots underneath; bird's-eye speedwell's have a short stalk and 3–8 pairs of coarse teeth. Scarlet pimpernel's stem is square and hairless; speedwell's is round and hairy. Both sprawl across the ground, carry their flowers singly on long, slender stalks, have leaves of overlapping size, flower all year and grow in gardens and crops, so none of these tells them apart. Blue-flowered plants are blue pimpernel (see that card). Scarlet pimpernel is poisonous: eating it can cause nausea, headache and bodily pain.
lookalikes.name: Scarlet pimpernel

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the petals: blue pimpernel's flowers have five lobes, 6–15 mm across, blue, with finely scalloped edges; bird's-eye speedwell's have four, 8–12 mm across, usually sky-blue (rarely white) with dark stripes. Blue pimpernel's leaves have no stalk, smooth edges and often faint black dots underneath; speedwell's have a short stalk and 3–8 pairs of coarse teeth. Blue pimpernel's stem is square and hairless; speedwell's is round and hairy. Both sprawl, carry blue flowers singly on long, slender stalks, have leaves of overlapping size and grow in cultivated land and waste places, so none of these tells them apart. Do not eat blue pimpernel: it was long treated as a blue form of scarlet pimpernel, which is poisonous.
lookalikes.name: Blue pimpernel

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping speedwell's leaves are round to kidney-shaped, 3–8 mm long and 5–12 mm wide, with rounded teeth and a squared-off to slightly heart-shaped base; bird's-eye speedwell's are generally slightly narrower than long, ovate, 6–35 mm long, coarsely toothed, with a squared-off base. Leaf size overlaps at 6–8 mm long, so look at the shape. Both have flat, four-lobed blue flowers of much the same size (8–10 mm across in creeping speedwell, 8–12 mm in bird's-eye speedwell), each alone on a slender stalk, so the flower alone does not separate them. Creeping speedwell's flower stalks are thread-like, 15–40 mm long; bird's-eye speedwell's are stouter and shorter (5–15 mm in flower, up to 40 mm in fruit), and its front lobe is usually distinctly paler than the other three. Creeping speedwell sets no fruit in New Zealand; bird's-eye speedwell sets two-lobed seed capsules, broader than long. Creeping speedwell is a perennial that forms dense mats in lawns; bird's-eye speedwell is an annual seldom found in mown turf. Both creep and root at the joints. No food use of creeping speedwell has been confirmed; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Creeping speedwell

preparation.text: Add the young leafy stems to salads, pesto or smoothies, or cook them in soups and casseroles. In Udhampur district, India, the young leaves and shoots are made into a vegetable dish with yogurt. For tea, bring a handful to the boil and let it steep. The flowers make a pretty decoration, if you have the patience to pick them. They fall off very easily once the plant is picked.

summary.text:
Veronica persica is a flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae.
Veronica persica is native to central and southern Europe and west Asia, but it has become widely naturalised elsewhere. It now has a near cosmopolitan distribution, having been introduced to Europe, North Africa, the Americas, East Asia, Australia and New Zealand.
The species was first recorded in Britain in 1825. It rapidly extended its range during the 1800s and was ubiquitous throughout lowland Britain and Ireland by 1960.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: widespread in all districts. South Island: widespread but not yet recorded in Western Nelson and Fiordland. Kermadec Islands, Chatham Islands, Stewart Island, Campbell Island, local.
Other names in New Zealand (NZPCN, Massey): scrambling speedwell, Persian speedwell. In New Zealand 'field speedwell' is Veronica arvensis, although some overseas pages use that name for this species. Naturalised in New Zealand by 1867 (NZPCN).

warnings: Its record as food is thin: young leaves and shoots cooked with yogurt in one district of northern India, and a handful of foraging pages, two of them from New Zealand.
Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed. It survives many common lawn weedkillers (MCPA, 2,4-D, clopyralid), so a healthy-looking patch may still have been sprayed. Pick from ground you know.

associations.note: Slippery jack has been recorded under bishop pine.
Poisonous. Fly agaric has been recorded with bishop pine.
Porcini has been recorded with bishop pine.

identification.text:
A small to medium-sized, wide-spreading, often dense pine with deeply fissured bark, dark grey on the surface and reddish brown beneath. The needles come in pairs (very rarely threes or fours), 7–15 cm long, slightly curved, greyish green or bluish green, rather stiff and sharp-pointed. The cones sit close to the branch, mostly in clusters of 4–5, pointing backwards; they are 6–9 cm, egg-shaped and lopsided, chestnut brown when ripe, armed with stout, rigid prickles, and stay closed on the tree for many years. Needles in pairs together with these large, very prickly, long-lasting cones set it apart. Radiata pine, its close relative, has needles in threes, which is the most reliable way to tell them apart.
Shoots greenish brown or brown, somewhat shining, hairless. Buds cylindrical or conical-cylindrical, purplish, resinous; scales usually pressed tight. Needles usually 2 per bundle, 7–15 cm × about 1–1.5 mm, curved except on vigorous upright leading shoots; resin canals midway; the sheath up to about 2 cm long at first, becoming much shorter. Male cones broadly cylindrical or nearly round, 5–15 mm long. Young female cones almost stalkless, the scales with long prickly points. Mature cones stalkless or nearly so, (5–)6–9 × (3.5–)4–6 cm when closed; prickles best developed on the large, swollen scale ends of the lower upper side. Seed wing lopsided, roughly oblong, 1–2 cm long. Two forms are grown in New Zealand, one with green and one with blue foliage; the blue form is the one known to grow wild.

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the needles in a bundle: the most reliable test. Radiata pine has needles in threes, 6–15 cm, deep or dark green; its cones are 6–13 cm, in clusters of 1–6, and the scale ends are usually without prickles when ripe. Bishop pine has needles in pairs, 7–15 cm, greyish or bluish green, stiff and sharp; its cones are 6–9 cm, mostly in clusters of 4–5, with stout rigid prickles. Both keep their lopsided cones on the tree for years. Radiata pine's seeds are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Monterey pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have needles in pairs and keep their prickly cones closed on the tree for years. Contorta pine's needles are short, 3.5–6.5 cm, often twisted and yellowish green; its cones are small, 3–6 cm, with a short slender prickle on each scale. Bishop pine's needles are 7–15 cm, greyish or bluish green; its cones are 6–9 cm, mostly in clusters of 4–5, with stout rigid prickles. Contorta pine's seeds and spring inner bark are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Contorta pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have long needles in pairs; look at the cones. Corsican pine's cones are symmetrical, 4–9 cm, with at most a tiny prickle, and fall at or soon after ripening; its needles are light green, fairly flexible and not very sharp. Bishop pine's cones are lopsided, 6–9 cm, with stout rigid prickles, mostly in clusters of 4–5, and stay closed on the tree for many years; its needles are greyish or bluish green, stiff and sharp. Corsican pine's seeds, needles and young cones are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Corsican pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have stiff, sharp needles in pairs; look at the cones. Austrian pine's cones are symmetrical, 4–9 cm, with at most a tiny prickle, and are shed each year; its needles are dark green. Bishop pine's cones are lopsided, 6–9 cm, with stout rigid prickles, mostly in clusters of 4–5, and stay closed on the tree for many years; its needles are greyish or bluish green. Austrian pine's seeds, needles and young cones are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Austrian pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have needles in pairs; look at the cones. Scots pine's needles are 2.5–7 cm, twisted and bluish or grey-green, often looking silvery; its cones are small, 3–6 cm, on a short stalk that curves back, with no prickles, and fall whole each year; high on the trunk the bark turns orange-brown and flaky. Bishop pine's cones are 6–9 cm, lopsided, stalkless, with stout rigid prickles, mostly in clusters of 4–5, and stay closed on the tree for many years; its needles are 7–15 cm, stiff and sharp. Scots pine's young needles, male cones, seeds and inner bark are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Scots pine

preparation.text: Pick cones while they are still green and soft enough to cut through with a knife; brown, woody or opened cones will not do. Young bishop pine cones have long prickly points on the scales, and green cones ooze sticky resin, so wear gloves. Look the cones over and throw out any with holes or insects. Smaller cones give a stronger flavour; large ones can be cut up so more fit in the jar.

recipes.method: Pack 225 g (about 500 ml) young green bishop pine cones and 450 g brown sugar into a 1 litre jar. Leave in a warm, sunny place for 30 days, shaking it now and then. For the first few weeks open the jar occasionally to let out gas, as the mixture may ferment. Scrape the cones and sugar slush into a pot, add 30 ml water, and bring to a brisk simmer for 5–10 minutes, just until the sugar melts (reducing it further makes it crystallise as it cools). Strain, discard the cones and bottle the hot syrup. It keeps best in the fridge once opened. Use it like maple syrup: on pancakes, fresh fruit or soft cheese, or a little in desserts and dressings.
recipes.title: Mugolio (young pine cone syrup)

recipes.method: Put 10 young green bishop pine cones in a jar and top up with 500 g brown sugar, shaking so the sugar settles round the cones. Close the jar and leave it for about 2 weeks, until all the sugar has turned to syrup. Pass it through a sieve and bottle. Add it to marinades or pour it over pancakes.

summary.text:
Bishop pine (Pinus muricata) is an evergreen pine of the pine family (Pinaceae) from the coast of California and north-west Baja California. Its young green cones can be steeped in sugar to make a pine syrup.
In New Zealand: It was first recorded wild in 1940. It is planted in state forests, though not on a large scale, and has been used as a coastal windbreak tree in many places; it tolerates considerable cold, drought and exposure to salt winds. It grows wild mainly near plantations and state forests in Taranaki, Nelson, Marlborough and Canterbury. Its regeneration is sometimes prolific, as at Kaingaroa in the central North Island, especially after fire, which often opens the cones that otherwise stay closed on the tree. Two forms are grown, with green or blue foliage, and the blue form is the one known to grow wild. It may occasionally hybridise with radiata pine, its close relative.
It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds and in regional pest plans from Northland to Southland and the Chatham Islands.

method.text: Needles: simmered, not boiled, in a covered pot of water until the water has coloured, then lifted out; wet fabric is kept in the bath at a gentle heat for about an hour, longer for a stronger colour. Scoured hemp with no mordant, dyed in an aluminium pot, came out a soft mauve-clay, and one bath coloured several pieces. The needles are also listed as giving a tan or green dye. Cones: soaked in water for a day to soften, cut into pieces, boiled for up to four hours (a lower heat loses less dye) and strained through muslin; cotton dyed for an hour and left to cool in the bath came out beige to light brown, mordanted or not, and the bath was used again the next day. On cotton and silk, cone tannins give beiges with orange and pink hues.

recipes.method: A box of pine needles about 30 × 20 cm; a 20-litre aluminium pot of cool water; a piece of hemp fabric about 1 × 1.5 m. Scour the fabric in a 40 °C wash with fragrance-free powder and about 250 ml (a cup) of baking soda, no fabric softener, then soak it in water for about an hour. Put the needles in the pot of water, cover, and bring to a simmer without boiling; turn the heat down a little and keep it there until the water has the colour you want. Lift out the needles with a fine sieve (straining through muslin gives a more even colour). Add the wet fabric, push out the air bubbles with a wooden spoon so it is all under, and keep it at a gentle heat for about an hour, stirring now and then; leave it longer for a stronger colour. Wring it out, wash and rinse it with fragrance-free powder and no softener, and dry it out of direct sun. The same bath dyes several pieces in turn.
recipes.title: Mauve-clay hemp dye

method.text: Tinder: needles left to dry for a season, or dry ones from the forest floor, catch fire easily, more so with a little pitch. Fatwood, the dense amber wood soaked with resin in the stumps and lower branches of dead pines, is shaved into thin slivers and lit with a spark or flame, and still lights when damp. Glue: resin that has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground is gathered rather than cut from the tree, melted (on a hot rock beside a fire, for example), mixed with finely ground ash or powdered charcoal and left to cool; it is reheated to use. A little water softens old pitch into a soft glue, and pine shavings or sawdust worked into it make a wood filler. Oil or strong alcohol takes pitch off your hands. Incense: needles tied into a bundle with natural twine and dried for about two weeks. Cleaner: chopped needles covered with vinegar in a glass jar, with baking paper under the lid so it does not corrode, left for two weeks and strained; the vinegar is mixed with baking soda and castile soap for cleaning.

method.text: Resin is gathered from what has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground rather than cut from the tree, at any time of year. It sticks to everything, so keep a knife and jar just for it; oil, then soap, takes it off your hands, and rubbing alcohol off clothes. Large lumps melt faster if frozen and broken up with a hammer inside a thick paper bag. Warmed with an equal amount of beeswax, mixed and left to set in its container, it makes a simple balm; melted into an oil, strained and firmed with beeswax it makes a balm for dry or cracked skin, lips and hands.

recipes.method: 60 ml (¼ cup) pine resin; 125 ml (½ cup) oil such as olive or almond; 15–30 g grated beeswax. Melt the resin in the oil in a double boiler over a low heat. Strain through a coffee filter or a strainer, return to the double boiler, add the beeswax and heat gently until it has melted. Pour into tins or jars and store somewhere cool and dark.
recipes.title: Pine resin balm

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) pine resin; 250 ml (1 cup) olive oil, or another oil safe for skin; 125–190 ml (½–¾ cup) grated beeswax; 35 drops rosemary essential oil. Put the resin and oil in a glass jar in the top of a double boiler and simmer, stirring, until the resin melts; this can take several hours. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine sieve and return it to the double boiler. For every 250 ml of resin and oil add 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) grated beeswax (more gives a firmer balm) and heat gently until it melts. Pour into jars or tins, stir 5 drops of the essential oil into each, and put the lids on straight away so the scent stays in. Leave to cool and set, and store somewhere cool and dark. Use it on dry or cracked skin, as a lip or hand balm, or overnight on the face.
recipes.title: Pine resin and olive oil balm

identification.text:
Open thicket-forming with rhizomes running extensively. Culm 4–7 m (often much taller in cultivation), green, remaining so or becoming black or heavily blotched black in 2nd year, erect, with white waxy ring beneath nodes when young; nodes all more or less evenly spaced. Culm-sheaths uniformly purple or purple-flushed, sometimes dark blotched above; auricles on main shoots prominent, dark; oral bristles long, caducous; sheath-blade linear, undulate. Branches green or black, spreading widely (giving an open network). Leaf-sheath with very short auricles. Oral bristles present. Leaf-blade usually 5–9–(13)× 0.5–2–(3) cm, lanceolate, abaxially glaucescent, adaxially moderately shining, acuminate.
[From: Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Arrow bamboo's canes are 3–5 m and dark green, with a white band just below each node; black bamboo has a white waxy ring there on young canes too, so the band does not separate them. Arrow bamboo's internodes are round, not notched; black bamboo's are flattened or grooved on alternate sides above each node, though usually round below the lowest branches. Arrow bamboo has 1 branch per node, sometimes 2–3 at upper nodes; black bamboo usually has 3, with the middle one small or missing. Arrow bamboo's leaf-blades reach 25 cm (up to 30 cm) and are shining dark green above; black bamboo's are usually 5–9 cm (up to 13 cm). Arrow bamboo's cane sheaths stay on and hide most of the lower and middle internodes; black bamboo's fall away. Arrow bamboo forms dense thickets, black bamboo open ones. Arrow bamboo's young shoots, cooked, have a rather bitter flavour.
lookalikes.name: Arrow bamboo

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the lower part of several canes. On some of fishpole bamboo's canes the lower nodes are crowded together and sometimes zigzag, with swollen, often lopsided internodes; black bamboo's nodes are all more or less evenly spaced. Not every fishpole cane shows the crowding, so check more than one. Fishpole's canes are green in their first year and yellow afterwards; black bamboo's are green and either stay green or turn black or heavily black-blotched in their second year. The cane sheaths differ: fishpole's are light mauve-brown or pinkish brown mottled dark purple, with no auricles or bristles; black bamboo's are uniformly purple or purple-flushed, with prominent dark auricles on the main shoots. Height does not separate them (fishpole usually 3–6 m, black bamboo 4–7 m), and both have a white waxy ring below the nodes on young canes. Both have edible young shoots, cooked.
lookalikes.name: Fishpole bamboo

preparation.text: Somewhat acrid when raw, they are prepared for eating by boiling in one change of water, the water being changed after 8 - 10 minutes. Do not eat the shoots raw. Cut a fresh shoot in half lengthwise, peel away the outer leaves and trim off any fibrous tissue at the base. Slice it thinly into strips and boil in lightly salted water for 8–10 minutes, then throw the cooking water away before using the shoots in other dishes.

recipes.method: Cut the shoots at about 8 cm above the ground, 5 cm below the soil. Handle the husk with care: it is many overlapping brown layers covered in fine, sharp hairs. Run a knife up the side of the shoot to slit it, then unwrap and throw away the layers until you reach the pale core; cut off the pointed tip and the fibrous base. The shoots are wide — about 5 cm across — so slice them before boiling if you want the leaching to reach the middle. They are somewhat acrid raw: cover with water, boil, and change the water once after 8–10 minutes, then simmer until tender. They keep a distinct taste and smell of their own.
recipes.title: Preparing fresh shoots

recipes.method: For two: 200 g of shoots already boiled, 1 chicken thigh (about 200 g), 3 snow peas and 15 ml oil; for the seasoning, 15 ml sake, 30 ml mirin, 5 ml sugar, 22.5 ml soy sauce, 2.5 ml granulated dashi and 200 ml water. Cut the tips into 4–5 cm lengths and halve them lengthways; slice the rest 7 mm thick. Cut the chicken into bite-sized pieces and fry it in the oil over a medium heat until it changes colour. Add the seasoning and the shoots, bring to the boil, cover and simmer on a low heat for 10–15 minutes. Top with the snow peas, blanched. Written for hachiku, the green-caned var. henonis, which is naturalised here.
recipes.title: Hachiku simmered with chicken

recipes.method: Written for hachiku, the green-caned var. henonis, which is naturalised here. About 3 shoots, boiled as in 'Preparing fresh shoots'; 200 ml dashi, 22.5 ml sugar, 22.5 ml light (usukuchi) soy sauce, 15 ml mirin, a pinch of salt and a handful of katsuobushi (dried bonito flakes). Cut the shoots to any size you like. Put them in a pan with the dashi, sugar, soy sauce, mirin and salt, cover with a drop lid and bring to the boil, then simmer on a low heat for 10–15 minutes. Turn off the heat and stir in the bonito flakes. It tastes better left to cool, as the flavour soaks in.
recipes.title: Simmered hachiku with bonito flakes

recipes.method: Written for hachiku, the green-caned var. henonis, which is naturalised here. About 300 g of shoots, boiled as in 'Preparing fresh shoots'; 15 ml sesame oil; 200 ml Chinese-style chicken stock, 22.5 ml soy sauce, 15 ml sake and 7.5 ml sugar; 7.5 ml mirin. Cut the shoots into wedges about 5 cm long. Fry them lightly in the sesame oil, add the stock, soy sauce, sake and sugar and simmer until the liquid has almost gone; add the mirin and cook until it has evaporated. Use on ramen, with rice, or chopped and mixed into hot rice.

summary.text: Phyllostachys nigra, commonly known as black bamboo or purple bamboo (Chinese: 紫竹), is a species of bamboo, native to Hunan Province of China, and is widely cultivated elsewhere. Two forms have naturalised in New Zealand: var. nigra since 1991 and the green-caned var. henonis since 1993.

warnings: Fresh bamboo shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides, which can break down to release hydrogen cyanide. They must be fully cooked before eating; do not eat them raw.

habitat.text: Lowland to montane forest, from sea level to 914 m but mostly below 600 m, in mixed forest with podocarps, broadleaved trees and, in the North Island and the north-west of the South Island, hard beech. Dominant on slopes and in gullies in the drier country east of the main ranges; in the south-west of its range confined to ridges and glacial outwash surfaces. Suits moderately fertile, well-drained soils and is hardy to wind and frost, but seedlings are tender to drought and hard frost and establish best in partial shade.

identification.text: Tree 20–25 m tall, sometimes to 30 m; trunk straight, 0.6–1 m across; crown spreading. Bark smooth, thin and light grey on young trees; fibrous, fissured and dark to almost black on old trees, often sooty. Leaves leathery, 8–20 × 3.5–11 mm, on stalks 0.5–2.5 mm long, oblong-elliptic to ovate, tapering evenly to the base, with a rounded tip that often ends in a tiny point and an untoothed margin; glossy green above, grey-green and thinly felted below; veins indistinct. No fringed pits (domatia). Young plants have broadly ovate, oval or almost round leaves with rounded tips, sometimes red or bronze, and saplings are often half-divaricating. Nuts 5–7 × 3–4.5 mm, three-sided or lens-shaped, hairy, red-brown or brown. Very like mountain beech, whose leaves are ovate to triangular-ovate with an oblique base and a pointed or nearly pointed tip; the two hybridise, and trees between about 300 and 600 m are often intermediate and hard to name.

lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain beech's leaves are ovate to triangular-ovate, tapering to an oblique base, with a pointed or nearly pointed tip, and are often more thickly white-felted below; black beech's are oblong-elliptic to ovate, tapering evenly to the base, with a rounded tip. Mountain beech grows higher, up to the treeline, but the two often grow together and hybridise, and many trees are intermediate.

summary.text: Black beech (Fuscospora solandri), tāwhairauriki, is a forest tree of the southern beech family (Nothofagaceae), endemic to New Zealand. In the North Island it is very rare north of the Volcanic Plateau and East Cape, with Little Barrier Island its northern limit, and grows in the ranges of the central North Island, Gisborne, Taranaki and Wellington; in the South Island it grows in Nelson, Marlborough, Westland south to the upper Inangahua and Maruia valleys, and Canterbury south to Staveley and Banks Peninsula. It seeds heavily in mast years. It is assessed Not Threatened (2023), but Regionally Critical in Auckland (2025). It was long known as Nothofagus solandri. Scale insects in the bark exude honeydew, which feeds native birds and bees, and introduced German wasps, and grows the sooty mould that blackens the trunk. Yellow mistletoe and red mistletoe grow on it. It is commonly grown by nurseries and planted for native timber, as it grows fast for a native tree. It is here as a root partner of the fungi that grow with it.

warnings: No record of black beech as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

identification.text:
a medium-sized tree, up to 15 m high, deciduous, with a tall trunk and erect or spreading branches. its leaves are alternate, thin, green, about 10 cm long, and have toothed margins. its white flowers (about 1 cm across) are spreading and borne in dense terminal racemes.. its fleshy black-purple fruit (up to 1.5 cm long) have a stony centre and resemble a cherry.

Flora of New Zealand: leaf blades broadly elliptic to obovate, 50–80 × 30–45 mm, shortly pointed, flat and glossy deep green above, hairless except for hairs along the midrib beneath, finely toothed with the teeth curved strongly inwards so they look rounded; the leaves fall late. Flowers many, in open, more or less hanging racemes 120–150 mm long; petals about 4 mm long. Fruit small, round and black.
For about its first decade the bark of a black cherry tree is thin, smooth, and banded, resembling a birch. A mature tree has very broken, dark grey to black bark. An almond-like odour is released when a young twig is scratched and held close to the nose, revealing minute amounts of cyanide compounds produced and stored by the plant as a defence mechanism against herbivores.

preparation.text: It must be fully ripe or else it will have a bitter flavour. The fruit can taste sweet or bitter. The better fruits have a thin skin and a juicy flesh with a pleasant vinous flavour. The fruit can also be used as a flavouring in liquors.

recipes.method: 5 cups fully ripe cherries; 15 cups cold water; 5 cups raw cane sugar; 2 tsp citric acid (or 8 tbsp lemon juice). Use fully ripe cherries, so dark purple they look black; red ones are under-ripe. If they need cleaning, float 5 cups of cherries in a large pot of cold water, pour off whatever rises, and drain. In a large glass jar (about 7.5 L) crush the raw cherries by hand to break every skin — hands are gentler on the stones than a masher. Add 15 cups cold water, 5 cups raw cane sugar and 2 tsp citric acid (or 8 tbsp lemon juice) and stir until the sugar dissolves; any left will dissolve over the next day. Cover with cheesecloth or a linen towel tied on with string, so it can breathe but fruit flies cannot get in, and keep it in a cool spot out of direct sun, such as a kitchen counter. Stir vigorously with a clean spoon about once every 12 hours (at least once a day) and taste a teaspoon after each stir. After 2–3 days it should be bubbly; fewer days give a sweeter, less fizzy drink, more days a drier, fizzier one — the recipe's authors bottle theirs after 5–7 days. Strain out the stones, skins and pulp, finishing through a fine-mesh strainer, pour into swing-top bottles or jars (not plastic or metal) and refrigerate at once. Never store the bottles at room temperature: the fermentation keeps building pressure and they can burst. It keeps in the fridge for months, and is lightly alcoholic, probably about 1–2.5%.

summary.text:
Black cherry, Prunus serotina, also called rum cherry and wild black cherry, is a deciduous tree or shrub of the rose family (Rosaceae), native to North and Central America.
In New Zealand it was first recorded as a casual at Takahue, near Kaitaia, in 1956 (Flora of New Zealand). It is a National Pest Plant Accord species, so it must not be sold or distributed anywhere in the country, and it is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. Animals spread its seeds, and Auckland Council says it reduces plant diversity and may feed invasive mammals.

warnings: Like apricots and apples, the seeds of black cherries contain cyanogenic glycosides (compounds that can be converted into cyanide), such as amygdalin. These compounds release hydrogen cyanide when the seed is ground or minced, which releases enzymes that break down the compounds.
The foliage, particularly when wilted, also contains cyanogenic glycosides, which convert to hydrogen cyanide if eaten by animals.

The plant (especially the seed and young shoots) contains cyanogenic glycosides, especially amygdalin and prunasin. When ingested, these compounds break down in the digestive tract to release cyanide.

identification.text:
Deciduous tree, to 25 m high; twigs puberulent when young, angled, usually with stout scattered stipular spines up to about 1 cm long. Leaves glabrous to puberulent particularly below, petiolate; leaflets ovate to elliptic, acute or obtuse, sometimes shortly mucronate, in 4–10 more or less opposite pairs, (10)–20–40–(50) mm long, stipellate; petiolules 2–5 mm long. Raceme with numerous flowers; pedicels 5–10 mm long. Calyx puberulent; calyx teeth unequal, broadly triangular. Corolla white with the base of standard greenish or yellowish, 15–23 mm long. Pod glabrous, irregularly oblong, 2–8-seeded, 35–80 mm long; seeds smooth, brown- spotted, oblong. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers, the pods and the leaves. Black locust's flowers are white, 15–23 mm long, many to a cluster; honey locust's are small, greenish or creamy-yellow, with petals 4–6 mm long, in golden-hairy spikes 5–10 cm long. Black locust's pods are 35–80 mm long with 2–8 seeds; honey locust's are 15–40 cm long and 3–4 cm wide, dark brown when ripe, with 15–25 seeds set in pulp. Black locust's leaves are once divided, with 4–10 pairs of leaflets; honey locust's are more often twice divided, though some are once divided with 5–15 pairs. Black locust's spines are up to about 1 cm long, scattered on the twigs; honey locust's are 2–10 cm long or more, often branched, on the trunk and branches. Both are planted in forms without spines and in golden-leaved forms, so missing spines or leaf colour do not tell them apart. Honey locust's pod pulp is eaten (see its page).

preparation.text: Pick the flower clusters when the flowers have just opened. The flowers are dipped in batter and fried as fritters, made into jam, cakes or pancakes, or made into a drink. They have also been eaten raw, mostly by children for the nectar.

recipes.method: Makes about 20–25 fritters. 250 g plain flour, 2 eggs, 200 ml milk, 150 ml beer, 50 g granulated sugar, 1 tsp vanilla extract, 1 tbsp rum (optional), ½ tsp fine salt, 625 ml vegetable oil for frying, icing sugar to dust, and black locust flower clusters picked when just open. If you rinse the flowers, dry them well before frying. Mix everything except the flowers into a smooth batter, cover and rest for 30 minutes to an hour. Heat oil 2.5–4 cm deep in a saucepan; it is ready when a few drops of batter sizzle and turn golden within seconds. Dip the flowers in the batter, drain slightly and fry about 3 at a time for 2–3 minutes a side, until golden brown. Drain on paper towel and dust lightly with icing sugar.
recipes.title: Black locust flower fritters

recipes.method: Makes about 30. 350 g plain flour, 250 ml (1 cup) milk, 2 eggs, 80 g sugar, 1 sachet baking powder, 2 tbsp sunflower oil, more sunflower oil for frying, icing sugar to dust, and 2 cups (500 ml) black locust flowers. Clean the flowers and strip them from the central stalk. Mix the flour with the sifted baking powder, the sugar, eggs, milk and the 2 tbsp oil into a batter, stir in the flowers and let it rest while the frying oil heats. Fry until well browned, drain on paper towel and dust with icing sugar. Best freshly made, but also good cold. For a vegan batter use sparkling water instead of the milk and aquafaba instead of the eggs; for a savoury one leave out the sugar, add 1 tsp salt and salt the fritters when they come out.
recipes.title: Black locust flower fritters, Italian style

recipes.method: Makes 10–12 fritters, for 2. 60 g (½ cup) plain flour, ½ tsp baking powder (optional; more makes the fritters bitter), 120 ml (½ cup) light-coloured or non-alcoholic beer, 10–12 freshly picked black locust flower clusters, 1 tbsp brown sugar, ½ lemon, and vegetable oil for frying. Shake and look over the flowers to remove dirt and insects. Whisk the flour, the baking powder if using, and the beer into a smooth batter, slightly thick but still runny. Holding each cluster by its stalk, dip it in the batter and let the excess run off. Heat enough oil to cover the base of a large frying pan; it is ready when a drip of batter fizzes and starts to brown. Fry over medium-high heat until golden underneath, turn and brown the other side, adding oil between batches. Eat soon after cooking, sprinkled with the brown sugar and a squeeze of lemon. Pull the stalks out as you eat; they are not eaten.
recipes.title: Beer-batter black locust fritters (vegan)

recipes.method: For 20–25 flower clusters. 250 g sifted plain flour, 5 g salt, 2 tbsp melted butter, 150 ml beer, 200 ml lukewarm water, 1 tbsp brandy plus a little more for the flowers, 2 egg whites, vegetable oil for deep-frying, caster sugar, and 20–25 black locust flower clusters picked young. Sprinkle the clusters with caster sugar and a little brandy and leave them for 30 minutes. Put the flour, salt and melted butter in a bowl, mix in the beer and water without working the batter too much, and add the 1 tbsp brandy. Beat the egg whites until stiff and fold them in last. Holding each cluster by its stalk, dip it in the batter and deep-fry in hot oil until golden; a small saucepan works, frying two at a time, as long as the oil is hot enough. Drain, sprinkle with caster sugar and eat straight away. Halve the recipe for fewer fritters.
recipes.title: Escoffier's black locust fritters

recipes.method: Serves 2. 50 g black locust flowers, 3 strawberries, 4 tbsp Korean green plum syrup (maesil-cheong, often sold as plum extract), 1 tbsp honey, 1 tbsp olive oil, and a little salt and ground pepper. Wash the flowers by swishing them gently in water with a little salt and vinegar, then drain. Strip the flowers from their stalks. Cut the strawberries into 6–8 pieces each, depending on size. Mix the plum syrup, honey, olive oil, salt and pepper into a dressing, toss the flowers in it, then add the strawberries and mix. Other fruit can stand in for the strawberries.
recipes.title: Black locust flower and strawberry salad

summary.text: Black locust or false acacia, a deciduous tree of the pea family (Fabaceae) from central and eastern North America, naturalised in New Zealand by 1870. In the North Island it is locally common throughout; in the South Island it is occasional in Nelson, Marlborough, Westland, Canterbury and Otago. False acacia is used in soil conservation, and grown as an ornamental tree. The species suckers freely and forms small thickets from plantings; it has become a problem in some reserves and parks in the North Island. Cultivars include forms with golden or gold-green leaves, and forms without spines, but almost all naturalised material is green-leaved and spiny. New Zealand nurseries sell the golden-leaved cultivar 'Frisia' as a street tree, tolerant of heat, drought and pollution. It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds in New Zealand.

warnings: The bark, leaves and seeds are poisonous. They contain toxalbumins (robin and phasin) and can cause nausea, weakness, flushing, lethargy and vomiting; larger amounts or more chewing can bring a weak or irregular pulse, fever, seizures, and in bigger doses paralysis and coma, with possible gut bleeding and liver and kidney damage.
Children have been poisoned after chewing the bark or eating the seeds.
Only the flowers are eaten. Every other part of the tree, especially the bark, should be treated as toxic.
Twigs usually carry stout spines up to about 1 cm long. Punctures from them can cause pain, swelling and rash, and a few reports describe worse outcomes.

identification.text:
Procumbent or ascending, annual or short-lived perennial herb; stems moderately to densely hairy in upper part. Leaves moderately to densely hairy on petiole and undersurface of leaflets, almost glabrous or sparsely hairy above; petioles about 2–15–(40) mm long; leaflets narrowly to broadly obovate, acute to emarginate, mucronate, obtuse at base, finely or irregularly serrate in upper half, uniform in colour, about 4–20 mm long; terminal petiolule (1)–2–3–(7) mm long; lateral petiolules less than 1 mm long; stipules narrowly to broadly ovate, acuminate, entire or irregularly serrate. Inflorescence with (5)–10–numerous flowers; peduncles more or less glabrous to moderately hairy, much longer than petioles; pedicels longer than calyx tube. Calyx hairy; calyx teeth narrowly triangular, usually with linear apex, longer than tube. Corolla yellow, 2–3 mm long. Pod moderately hairy, but more or less glabrous and black when mature, reniform, coiled in about 1 complete turn without a hole in the centre, distinctly reticulately veined but otherwise smooth, 2–3 mm diameter, 1-seeded; seeds yellow to brown, about 2 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Its small, spineless, one-seeded pods set it apart from the other naturalised medicks (bur medicks have prickly burs). It is sometimes confused with suckling clover, which keeps its dried florets on the head and has straight pods and leaflets that are usually notched rather than pointed.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small yellow-flowered plants of lawns, pasture and waste places, with three small leaflets, the middle one on a longer stalk than the other two, and heads of tiny yellow pea-type florets on stalks well above the leaves, so the leaves and the head shape do not separate them. Look at the leaflet tips: black medick's end in a distinct short point (sometimes in a notch with a point in it); suckling clover's are usually notched and only rarely have a short point. Look at the florets after flowering: suckling clover's dried florets stay on the head around the pods; black medick's fall off. Look at the pods: black medick's are kidney-shaped, coiled in about one full turn, net-veined and black when ripe, 2–3 mm across; suckling clover's are straight, hairless and 2–3 mm long, hidden by the old florets. Sizes overlap — black medick's leaflets are about 4–20 mm, suckling clover's 3–12 mm; black medick's corolla is 2–3 mm, suckling clover's 2.5–4 mm; and both have hairy stems. Neither has a confirmed food use here; see each page.
lookalikes.name: Suckling clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small sprawling or upright plants of dry waste places and grassland, with three small toothed leaflets, the middle one on a longer stalk than the other two, and heads of tiny yellow pea-type florets on stalks well above the leaves, so the leaves and the head shape alone do not separate them. Look at the florets: hop trefoil's are 3.5–5 mm long, 20–40 to a head, and stay on the head as it ages, hiding the small straight pods; black medick's are 2–3 mm long and fall off, leaving bare kidney-shaped pods coiled in about one full turn, net-veined and black when ripe, 2–3 mm across. Look at the leaflet tips: black medick's end in a distinct short point; hop trefoil's are rounded or notched and only occasionally have a short point. Sizes overlap — hop trefoil's leaflets are about 4–15 mm, black medick's about 4–20 mm. Neither has a confirmed food use here; see each page.
lookalikes.name: Hop trefoil

lookalikes.howToTell: Black medick: its yellow florets, 2–3 mm long, come 5–10 or more together in a small head on a stalk well above the leaves; the florets fall after flowering, leaving kidney-shaped pods coiled in about one full turn that turn black when ripe. Its stems lie along the ground or rise a little and are hairy in the upper part. Its leaflets, about 4–20 mm long, end in a distinct short point and are the same green all over. White clover: its florets, 8–12 mm long, are usually white, occasionally pink to reddish, many together in a round head; its hairless stems creep and root at the nodes. Its leaflets, about 5–25 mm long, are rounded or notched at the tip and often carry light or dark markings. Out of flower, look at the leaflet stalks: black medick's middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (usually 2–3 mm) than the two side leaflets (under 1 mm); white clover's three are about equal. White clover is eaten (see its own entry); black medick has no confirmed food use here, so do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: White clover

summary.text:
Black medick (Medicago lupulina) is a small, yellow-flowered annual or short-lived perennial of the pea family (Fabaceae), native from southern Europe to western Asia and North Africa and naturalised in New Zealand since 1867.
In New Zealand it is locally common throughout the North Island but has not been collected from Taranaki; in the South Island it grows in Nelson City and in the east from the Marlborough Sounds to Southland; it is also at Halfmoon Bay on Stewart Island and on the Kermadec and Chatham Islands. It is listed as an environmental weed in New Zealand.
Other English names recorded for it in New Zealand are hop clover, nonsuch and yellow trefoil.

warnings: Do not eat it. Its food use is not confirmed here: the records are hedged, and plants of its genus contain compounds such as canavanine whose risks in black medick are not well established.

Its small yellow flower heads and three leaflets look like suckling clover's and hop trefoil's, and it is confused with both and with white clover. Check the leaflet tips, the old florets and the pods (see Lookalikes).

sources: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
Gardens, cultivated ground, compost heaps, disturbed soil.
Generally abundant, especially in open places such as arable land, waste places, dry riverbeds and roadsides, particularly much-disturbed areas.

identification.text: An annual or short-lived perennial herb to about 75 cm tall, usually hairy, sometimes nearly glabrous, with oval, slightly wavy leaves. Small white five-pointed star flowers with a yellow centre, in small, usually few-flowered clusters, then berries in clusters, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow.

lookalikes.howToTell: Poroporo is a hairless, soft-wooded shrub to about 3 m; black nightshade is a herb to about 75 cm, usually hairy. Poroporo's flowers are usually 4–5 cm across and violet, though white ones are recorded; black nightshade's are 10–13 mm across, usually white, sometimes pale mauve. The other native poroporo, Solanum aviculare, has flowers 10–40 mm across in white, lavender or dark blue, so flower size and colour alone do not settle it. Poroporo's berries are 23–30 mm long, egg-shaped to ellipsoid and hanging, usually yellow or pale orange; black nightshade's are 7–10 mm across and round, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow. Poroporo is poisonous too: its green and yellow berries and its leaves are poisonous, and ripe orange berries lose much of their toxicity; the fruit can be eaten when ripe, orange and with its skin bursting.
lookalikes.name: Poroporo

lookalikes.howToTell: Before flowers or fruit appear, the only character here is the coating: fat hen's leaves may be green or grey-mealy, the meal denser underneath when present, and very rarely a plant is bright green, while no mealy coating is recorded on black nightshade, whose leaves usually carry scattered short hairs. Leaf shape and toothing overlap and do not separate them. In flower they differ: black nightshade has flowers 10–13 mm across, often star-shaped, usually white (sometimes pale mauve) around a yellow cone of anthers, in small, usually few-flowered clusters, then round berries 7–10 mm across, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow. Fat hen's flowers are tiny and green with no petals, usually packed in dense spikes and panicles, and it forms no berry: its fruit stays wrapped in the flower parts around a glossy black seed (1.0–)1.1–1.4(–1.6) mm across.
lookalikes.name: Fat hen

lookalikes.howToTell: Field mustard's flowers are bright yellow with four petals 6–10 mm long, and its fruit are long, thin pods, not berries; black nightshade's flowers are usually white with yellow anthers, followed by clusters of round berries. Field mustard's lower leaves have a large end lobe and 1–3 pairs of side lobes and are bristly; black nightshade's are oval to lance-oval, entire to coarsely toothed, only sometimes slightly lobed. Field mustard starts as a rosette at ground level; black nightshade is a tall, upright, usually much-branched plant.
lookalikes.name: Field mustard

lookalikes.howToTell: Both can have white flowers. Wild radish's have four petals 13–20 mm long, usually veined with mauve, and its fruit are pods pinched between the seeds, not berries; black nightshade's flowers are 10–13 mm across with yellow anthers in the centre, followed by round berries 7–10 mm across. Wild radish's rosette and lower leaves are divided into an end leaflet and 1–8 pairs of side leaflets, and are bristly; black nightshade's are oval to lance-oval, entire to coarsely toothed, only sometimes slightly lobed.
lookalikes.name: Wild radish

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaves and shoots: black nightshade's hairs are usually scattered, short and simple, and the plant is sometimes nearly hairless; velvety nightshade is greyish and velvety-hairy, a dense soft felt of hairs above and below, so the leaves feel like velvet. Look at the berries: black nightshade's are 7–10 mm across and usually rather dull black, sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow; velvety nightshade's are 5–7 mm across and dull purplish black or purple, so size and colour overlap and neither settles it alone. Black nightshade is an annual or short-lived perennial herb recorded to about 75 cm; velvety nightshade is a perennial herb or subshrub recorded to about 1.5 m, with mature stems that have 2 ridges. Flowers, leaf size and place do not separate them: black nightshade's white flowers are 10–13 mm across and velvety nightshade's 8–13 mm, their leaf blades overlap in size (2–12 cm against 2.5–11 cm long), and both grow in gardens and orchards. No source records whether velvety nightshade is edible; like every Solanum, it is poisonous to some extent, particularly in the green parts.
lookalikes.name: Velvety nightshade

Wikipedia contributors. 'Solanum nigrum', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solanum_nigrum Corroborates the solanine and adds the delay. Symptoms may follow eating raw immature green fruit or mature leaves, with 'typically a delay of 6 to 12 hours after ingestion for symptoms to occur', beginning with fever, sweating, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, confusion and drowsiness; death from large amounts comes through cardiac arrhythmia and respiratory failure, though the plant 'is rarely fatal'. Most suspected poisonings involve leaves or unripe fruit. Solanine is practically insoluble in water and can be destroyed by boiling but not by baking, though 'S. nigrum's leaves may be different from this perspective'; there are ethnobotanical accounts of the young leaves and shoots being boiled as a vegetable with the water discarded and replaced several times. Livestock have also been poisoned by nitrate from grazing the mature leaves and green berries.

The confusion this page does not currently card, and the test for it. Solanum nigrum is sometimes mistaken for the far more toxic deadly nightshade, Atropa belladonna, which is a different genus. Two differences: black nightshade berries grow in bunches while deadly nightshade's grow individually, and black nightshade's flowers have white petals. Wikipedia contributors. summary.text:
A common garden weed with white star flowers and black berries. Its green parts are poisonous, and it is too easily confused with poroporo and fat hen to treat as food.
Native to Eurasia, it was first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1853 and now grows throughout the North and South Islands and on the Kermadec, Chatham and Campbell Islands.

warnings: Leaves and green berries contain solanine: vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness. Fully ripe berries are eaten in some cuisines, but telling ripe from nearly ripe in the field is not a bet this guide makes.
Keep children away from the black berries — they look like tiny blackcurrants.

identification.text:
Vigorous vine, glabrous except for pistil and stamens. Shoots slightly angular. Leaves deeply 3-lobed, but entire on young plants; petiole 1–3 cm long, with 2 sessile glands near apex; stipules 10–15 mm long, linear-subulate, entire; lamina lobes more or less elliptic, submembranous, deep shining green above, rounded at base; middle lobe largest, 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm, serrate or serrulate, obtuse to acute. Flowers ☿, solitary. Pedicels 4–6 cm long at flowering. Bracts 1.5–2 cm long, ovate, free, coarsely serrate. Hypanthium inconspicuous. Sepals 2.5–3 cm long, oblong, green on reverse, white inside; petals white, similar to sepals; corona threads 2–2.5 cm long, white with purple base. Filaments puckered, purple towards base, otherwise white; anthers 8–10 mm long, longer than filaments. Ovary puberulent. Fruit 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broad-ellipsoid or subglobose, dull purple; pulp orange, sweet. Seed about 5 mm long, ovate, black, pitted. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. The fruit separates them too: black passionfruit's is dull purple and nearly round; the fruit of banana passionfruit (P. tripartita) is yellow or orange when ripe and elongated. Blue passionflower, which has no entry here, has a flower much like black passionfruit's, but its leaves are 5-lobed almost to the base and its pulp is scanty and inedible. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia's leaves are undivided and leathery and its flowers under 2 cm across, while black passionfruit's leaves are 3-lobed. A young black passionfruit's leaves are undivided too, so on a young plant go by texture: kōhia's are leathery, black passionfruit's thin. Kōhia is dioecious: only female plants bear fruit, and only after pollen reaches them from a male plant, so a vine without fruit can still be kōhia; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Kōhia

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube about 6–8 cm long (published figures run from up to 6 cm to 8 cm), with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and published lengths run from up to 9 cm to 14 cm. Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. The fruit separates them too: black passionfruit's is dull purple and nearly round; the fruit of banana passionfruit (P. tarminiana) is yellow or orange when ripe and elongated. Blue passionflower, which has no entry here, has a flower much like black passionfruit's, but its leaves are 5-lobed almost to the base and its pulp is scanty and inedible. Both are edible.

preparation.text:
The ripe aromatic fruit is allowed to wrinkle and develop its sweetness, it is then eaten raw, juiced, made into a syrup or used in sauces, cakes, ice creams, sherbets etc.
In Australia and New Zealand, it is available commercially both fresh and tinned. It is added to fruit salads, and fresh fruit pulp or passion fruit sauce is commonly used in desserts, including as a topping for pavlova (a regional meringue cake) and ice cream, a flavouring for cheesecake, and in the icing of vanilla slices.

recipes.method: The pulp of about 12 passionfruit (250 ml), 125 g unsalted butter, 165 g caster sugar, 5 eggs and 2 extra yolks. Whisk the pulp to loosen it and push it through a sieve, then stir half the seeds back into the juice. Put the juice, butter and sugar in a heatproof bowl over a pan of simmering water, keeping the bowl clear of the water, and stir until the butter melts. Beat the eggs and yolks lightly, whisk them in gently, and keep stirring for 20–25 minutes until it thickens: it is ready when a finger drawn across the curd on the back of a spoon leaves a line that holds. Pour into warm sterilised jars, seal, cool, and keep in the fridge for up to 8 weeks.
recipes.title: Passionfruit curd

recipes.method: 880 g caster sugar, 500 ml water, 250 ml passionfruit pulp, 1 teaspoon citric acid. Put everything in a saucepan over medium heat and stir until the sugar dissolves, bring to the boil, take off the heat and let it cool. Keep it in the fridge for up to 4 weeks. Serve over crushed ice, topped up with water or soda water. Makes about 1.25 litres.

scientificName: corrected from 'Passiflora edulis f' to 'Passiflora edulis', 08/10/2026. The old value was a truncation of 'Passiflora edulis f. edulis' at the interior full stop, and it failed the lookalike-name test against banana-passionfruit's card, which names the species correctly. Species rank is what the other three Passiflora entries use, and the catalogue has no golden passionfruit (f. flavicarpa) entry for the form epithet to distinguish it from, so the rank buys nothing and the interior full stop is a known hazard here. This is the third time the value has been truncated (490d638, restored in 9357667, truncated again in f4c406e). summary.text:
Black passionfruit, Passiflora edulis, also called purple passionfruit and purple granadilla, is a vigorous vine of the passionflower family (Passifloraceae), native to tropical America. It was brought to New Zealand as a crop and was recorded naturalised in 1950.
This sp. is the black passionfruit of commerce and is widely cultivated in warmer parts of the country. All wild and virtually all cultivated plants in N.Z. belong to f. edulis, and not the less hardy, yellow-fruited f. flavicarpa Degener which is the usual form grown in tropical Polynesia.
N.: N. Auckland (plantations at Waitangi and Silverdale), near Auckland (Waitakere Range), Great Barrier Id; K.: well-established on Raoul Id where it grows so abundantly on and near the forest margin in some places that attempts have been made to eliminate it.

habitat.text:
It occurs primarily in coastal and lowland forest, extending locally into montane forest, from sea level to 650 m.
Cyathea medullaris is a tall emergent species that occurs mostly in broadleaved forest, but also in podocarp, beech and kānuka forest and under introduced conifers and Salix species. It can be abundant in the initial forest formed on slips and other disturbed sites undergoing regeneration. It is a frost-tender species, and prefers damp habitats.

identification.text:
In the field Cyathea medullaris is readily distinguished by its tall trunk with black hexagonal stipe scars, and large arching fronds with thick black stipes. The lamina and stipe scales have dark red setae along both margins, which distinguishes this species from all other native species. Even very young plants of Cyathea medullaris can be positively identified by this character. The naturalised Cyathea cooperi has similar scales but is distinguished by its pale brown stipes and exindusiate sori. Plants of Cyathea cunninghamii are superficially similar to Cyathea medullaris but have more slender trunks covered in appressed stipe bases, shorter and more lacy fronds, and thinner stipes. Cyathea cunninghamii also has scales that lack the marginal setae, and indusia that open to form a hood-shape, rather than splitting open irregularly.
Rhizomes erect, forming a woody trunk up to about 20 m tall, 150–300 mm in diameter, covered in black, hexagonal stipe scars; bearing scales near the apex. Rhizome scales conform, acicular, bearing dark-coloured setae on margins, blackish-brown, shining. Fronds 3000–5000 mm long, arching upwards from the crown; dead fronds usually falling, but up to 5 occasionally persistent. Stipes 160–1650 mm long, 40–95 mm wide and 40–60 mm deep at the base, black, sometimes becoming dark brown distally, weakly tuberculate and slightly rough; blackish-brown or dark brown scales with dark-coloured setae on margins densely covering base of stipe, up to 50 mm long and 2 mm wide, becoming pale brown, smaller and more scattered distally. Laminae deeply 2-pinnate-pinnatifid to 3-pinnate-pinnatifid, elliptic or obovate, 3000–4000 mm long, 600–2000 mm wide, dark green on adaxial surface, pale green on abaxial surface, coriaceous; adaxial surfaces of rachis and primary pinna midribs abundantly covered in fine, acicular, colourless or pale brown hairs up to 1 mm long, more scattered on secondary pinna midribs and tertiary pinnae; abaxial surfaces bearing ovate scales with attenuate apices and dark red marginal and apical setae, up to 2 mm long and 1 mm wide on the pinna midribs, and acicular scales up to 5 mm long and 0.5 mm wide on the rachis; rachis blackish-brown on abaxial surface, becoming yellow-brown or pale brown distally, often yellow-brown or yellow-green or green on adaxial surface especially when young, tuberculate. Primary pinnae in 20–25 pairs, ovate, narrowly ovate or narrowly triangular; the longest at or above the middle, 350–950 mm long, 125–300 mm wide, short to long-stalked, abaxial surfaces of costae tuberculate. Secondary pinnae narrowly ovate or narrowly triangular, the longest 65–185 mm long, 12–37 mm wide, short-stalked or sessile. Longest tertiary pinnae 7–20 mm long, 2–4 mm wide, adnate to decurrent; apices acute; margins serrate or divided up to half way to costa. Sori 0.7–1.1 mm in diameter; paraphyses as long as sporangia; indusia completely covering sori before maturity, splitting irregularly at maturity.

preparation.text: The pith is slimy when first cut. Strip the outer layers of the trunk so the slime can drain or dry, then cook the pith slowly, traditionally for a long time in a hāngī or umu; baking separates the stringy fibres from the flesh. Cooked, it is bland to slightly sweet. Thin slices can be threaded on flax and dried in the sun, and the young shoots can be hung to dry. The young shoots can be boiled, made into a soup or relish, or steamed in a hāngī; cooked, they taste a little like turnip or marrow.

summary.text:
Mamaku, the black tree fern, has a trunk up to about 20 m tall covered in black, hexagonal frond scars, and arching fronds 3–5 m long on thick black stalks. It is Cyathea medullaris in the Flora of New Zealand and Sphaeropteris medullaris in the New Zealand Threat Classification System; medullaris (Latin, pithy) refers to the pith that Māori baked and ate.
It grows throughout much of the North Island; in the South Island it is found in coastal and lowland north-west Nelson and the Marlborough Sounds, sporadically down the west coast to Fiordland and Southland and on the east coast to Banks Peninsula, but not in inland Canterbury or Marlborough. The Flora records it as absent from Otago, while Otago's 2025 regional assessment ranks it Regionally Critical. It also grows on the Three Kings and Chatham Islands, rarely on Stewart Island, and in Fiji, Samoa, Tahiti and other Pacific islands. Nationally Not Threatened (2023).
In gardens it grows from fresh spores, though slowly; young plants transplant easily, and a freshly felled trunk will usually resprout if planted and carefully watered. Once established it copes with a variety of conditions. Do not take plants from the wild without the landowner's permission.

warnings: Taking the trunk pith means cutting down the whole tree fern, which kills it. The pith of young frond stalks can be taken without killing the tree.
Only about seven of New Zealand's roughly 200 ferns are edible. Eat only a tree fern you are sure is mamaku.
