identification.text: A large tree, 30–40 m tall in its native range; grown in the open it has a short trunk and a broad crown. Bark grey-black, deeply furrowed into thin ridges in a diamond pattern. Twigs with chambered, light brown pith. Leaves 30–60 cm long, with 15–23 leaflets, the largest in the middle of the leaf and the end leaflet usually missing or small; leaflets 7–10 × 2–3 cm, with a rounded base, a long pointed tip and toothed edges; dark green and usually hairy underneath. Leaves, stems and fruit husks have a pungent, spicy smell; the nut itself does not. Male catkins 8–10 cm long, drooping; female flowers 2–5 together at the shoot tips. Fruits round, 3–4 cm across, one to a few together, with a brownish-green, semi-fleshy husk around a brown nut whose very hard shell is irregularly and sharply ridged.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both edible; this is about which you have. Look at the fruit: black walnut's are round, 3–4 cm across, one to a few together (the female flowers are only 2–5 per cluster), with a brownish-green husk; Japanese walnut's hang 10–22 together in long strings and are egg-shaped, beaked, sticky and rusty-hairy. In spring, black walnut's female flowers sit 2–5 together at the shoot tips; Japanese walnut's spikes carry 9–22. Check the tip of a leaf: black walnut usually has no end leaflet, or a small one, with the largest leaflets in the middle; Japanese walnut has an end leaflet about the size of the side ones. Black walnut also usually has more leaflets, 15–23 against Japanese walnut's 9–17; the counts overlap, so let the fruit decide.
lookalikes.name: Japanese walnut

lookalikes.howToTell: Both edible; this is about which you have. Count and feel the leaflets: black walnut has 15–23, toothed, the largest in the middle of the leaf and the end leaflet usually missing or small; walnut has 5–9 with smooth (untoothed) edges, the end leaflet the largest and the lowest pair much smaller. Seedling walnuts can have toothed leaflets, so check an adult tree. Walnut's fruit is 3.5–5 cm, smooth and green with gland dots; black walnut's is 3–4 cm with a brownish-green husk. Crack one: walnut's shell splits easily in half along its seams when ripe; black walnut's is very hard and sharply ridged, and the kernel is hard to get out.
lookalikes.name: Walnut

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree of heaven is not food. Look at the edge of a leaflet: black walnut's is toothed all the way along; tree of heaven's is smooth apart from 1–3 coarse teeth or small lobes near the base, each tipped with a gland. Crush a leaf: tree of heaven's smells strongly, likened to peanuts or cashews; black walnut's has a pungent, spicy smell of its own. Black walnut's fruit is a round nut 3–4 cm across in a brownish-green husk; tree of heaven's seeds sit in flat, twisted, papery wings 3–5 cm long, often hanging on the tree for a long time. The leaflet counts overlap (black walnut 15–23, tree of heaven 11–25) and both often lack an end leaflet, so don't use either.
lookalikes.name: Tree of heaven

lookalikes.howToTell: Horse chestnut is poisonous. Look at the leaves: black walnut's are long, with 15–23 leaflets set in pairs along a central stalk; horse chestnut's have five to seven leaflets spreading like fingers from one point. Then the fruit: black walnut's husk is round, 3–4 cm across, smooth and brownish-green, around one nut with a very hard, sharply ridged shell; horse chestnut's case is up to 6 cm and covered in short spines, and holds one or two smooth, glossy, dark brown seeds with a large pale scar.
lookalikes.name: Horse chestnut

preparation.text: Gather the nuts once they fall in autumn, when the husk dents under a thumb, or when the husks start to discolour on the tree. Wear gloves: the husks stain skin, and the stain on clothing can be permanent. Left on the ground for a while the husks soften, often with fly larvae in them that don't reach the kernel, and can be rolled off under a boot. Wash off the black residue in several changes of water, throw out any nuts that float, and don't leave them soaking. Dry the nuts in the shell somewhere cool and airy, with air moving over them, for about three weeks until bone dry; they then keep for years. The shell is far thicker and harder than a common walnut's: on a hard surface or in a vice, crack each nut on its flat side, then on the seam, and use tin snips to free the pieces. Soaking the dried nuts in water for one to three days before cracking makes the shells less brittle, so fewer fragments fly and the kernels come out in bigger pieces. To sort kernels from shell, swirl the pieces in a bowl of water: both sink, but the kernels stay suspended longer. Rinse and dry the kernels and pick out any shell fragments left, which can crack teeth. Once shelled, the oily kernels go rancid quickly. For pickling, pick the fruit green, before the shell forms inside: a metal skewer should pass straight through. The whole fruit, husk and all, is used; after several months in brine it is sliced thin and eaten with cheese and cold meats. Pickled black walnuts have a strong, sharp flavour but a dry, grainy texture; blending them into a sauce keeps the flavour without the texture.

recipes.method: Makes about 250 ml. 2 cups (500 ml) tightly packed basil leaves; ⅓ cup (80 ml) black walnut kernels; 1 garlic clove; ½ cup (125 ml) sunflower or extra virgin olive oil; ¼ tsp ground black pepper; ½ cup (125 ml) grated parmesan or grana padano. Toast the walnuts at 180 °C for about 15 minutes until fragrant but not dark, rub them in a tea towel to remove the bitter skins and cool completely. Pick the basil leaves off their stems, blanch in boiling salted water until just wilted, cool in iced water, drain and chop roughly. Blend the basil, cheese, nuts, garlic and pepper to a rough purée, then drizzle in the oil until smooth. Press cling film onto the surface and keep in the fridge, or freeze.
recipes.title: Black walnut and basil pesto

recipes.method: Makes about 750 ml. 2 cups (500 ml) untoasted black walnut kernels, skins gently rubbed off; ½ cup (about 100 g) white sugar; ¼ tsp flaky salt, plus more to taste. Read through first and have a tray lined with a non-stick mat ready. In a heavy saucepan (not thin aluminium), heat the nuts and sugar over medium-high heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon; the sugar clumps at first, then after about 5 minutes starts to melt and colour. Keep stirring until it has fully melted to a dark amber and the nuts smell toasted but not burnt, then take it off the heat at once. Tip onto the tray, spread in an even layer and sprinkle with salt while hot, without stirring it in. Cool completely, break into bite-sized pieces and store airtight in a cool, dark place for a few weeks. For a spicy version, add ¼ tsp cayenne pepper just before taking the pan off the heat.
recipes.title: Salted candied black walnuts

recipes.method: 4 white fish fillets; 1 cup (250 ml) finely chopped black walnut kernels; flour for coating, seasoned with salt and pepper (rice flour for gluten-free); seasoning of your choice; 1 egg, beaten; olive oil; lemon. Set out the nuts and the seasoned flour on separate plates. Season the fish, dip it in the flour, then the egg, then press it into the nuts. Heat a teaspoon of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat and fry the fish until browned on each side, about 3 minutes, watching that the nuts don't burn. Squeeze lemon juice over and serve at once.
recipes.title: Black walnut-crusted fish

recipes.method: Written for black walnuts by Hammons Black Walnuts (Missouri). 4 large eggs; 250 ml packed brown sugar; finely grated zest of 1 lemon; 2.5 ml flaky salt; 340 g black walnut pieces. Line a 23 cm round cake tin (or springform) with baking paper or buttered foil. Separate the eggs and beat the whites to stiff peaks. Pulse the walnuts in a food processor to a coarse, sand-like meal. Beat the yolks with the sugar until pale and creamy, add the zest and salt, then stir in the walnut meal in 3–4 lots; the batter is very thick. Work in the egg whites in 3–4 lots; it comes together by the last lot. Bake in the middle of the oven at 180 °C for about 40 minutes, until the top is firm and well browned, lowering the heat a little and turning the cake if it browns too fast; dark edges are fine. Cool 10 minutes in the tin, lift out on the paper and cool completely on a rack, then wrap and chill; bring back to room temperature for 1 hour before serving. It is better the next day. Dust with icing sugar or serve with fruit or whipped cream.
recipes.title: Calabrian black walnut cake

recipes.method: Serves 6. 500 ml half-and-half (equal parts milk and cream); 250 ml cream; 125 ml maple syrup; 60 ml corn syrup or glucose syrup; 5 large egg yolks, or 30 ml cornflour; 2.5 ml salt; 2.5 ml vanilla extract (optional); a generous 125 ml black walnuts, roughly chopped. If you cracked the nuts yourself, drop them in a bowl of cool water so stray bits of shell sink, then lift them out and dry them. Egg version: whisk the half-and-half, cream, yolks, vanilla and salt. In a small saucepan bring the maple syrup to the boil and boil 4–5 minutes, until the bubbles start to climb the sides, add the corn syrup and boil 2 minutes more. Cool the pan a few minutes so it will not scramble the eggs (the syrup sets firm), then add the walnuts and the cream mixture and cook on medium-low, stirring often with a wooden spoon (not a whisk), until it just coats the back of a spoon, about 20 minutes. Pour into a metal bowl, stirring out any lumps, cover, cool and chill overnight. Cornflour version: whisk the cornflour into the half-and-half, cream and vanilla; boil the maple and corn syrups down the same way, add the cornflour liquid (the syrup will stiffen) and the walnuts, bring slowly back to a simmer, stirring and whisking only gently, and cook until it thickens; strain out any clumps and chill overnight. Churn in an ice-cream maker (about 30 minutes, to soft-serve), then pack into a lidded container and freeze about 12 hours to set. The flavour comes from cooking raw black walnuts in the base; roasted ones taste more like ordinary walnuts.
recipes.title: Maple black walnut ice cream

recipes.method: Makes about 20; needs a small silicone cookie or brownie-bite mould, as without one the dough spreads into thin discs. 200 g black walnuts, plus 20 g to garnish; 110 g sugar; 2.5 ml ground cinnamon; 60 ml (about 35 g) rolled oats or flour; 2.5 ml flaky salt; zest of half a lemon; 1 large egg. Toast the garnish walnuts lightly in a dry pan until golden and set aside. Pulse the sugar a few times in a spice grinder (it should stay coarse). Grind the 200 g walnuts as fine as you can, about 2 tablespoons at a time (a little chunky is fine), or grind them with the sugar in a food processor. Grind the oats to a fine flour and mix with the sugar, cinnamon and salt. Stir the ground walnuts, oat mixture and egg together, grate in the zest and mix well; the dough is sticky. Oil the mould lightly, press in 20 g pieces of dough (a generous tablespoon each), top with the toasted walnuts and press them in. Chill 10 minutes, then bake at 175 °C for 22 minutes, turning the mould halfway. Cool 10 minutes before unmoulding; they should be lightly golden and crisp at the edges and chewy inside. If they seem soft, crisp them a few minutes on a lined tray in a 150 °C oven. They keep a week airtight.
recipes.title: Black walnut oat cookies

recipes.method: 1 unbaked pastry case for a 23 cm pie dish; 3 eggs; 250 ml dark corn syrup; 250 ml sugar; 30 ml melted butter; 2.5 ml vanilla extract; 250 ml chopped black walnuts (chopped rather than whole, as the flavour is strong). Heat the oven to 180 °C. Grease the pie dish, as the filling is very sticky, line it with the pastry, crimp the edge and chill until needed. Mix the eggs, corn syrup, sugar, butter and vanilla with a fork. Spread the walnuts over the bottom of the chilled case and pour the filling over; the nuts float to the top as it bakes. Bake 25 minutes, then cover the crust edge with strips of foil if it is already brown, and bake 35 minutes more. The centre may still bubble when it comes out; let it cool for 1–2 hours to firm up. Serve with whipped cream or vanilla ice cream.
recipes.title: Black walnut pie

recipes.method: 250 ml sugar; 60 ml solid coconut oil or butter; 2 eggs; 5 ml vanilla extract; 125 ml plain flour; 30 ml finely ground carob powder; 2.5 ml salt; 125 ml finely chopped black walnuts. Heat the oven to 180 °C and line a 20 cm square tin with baking paper (the bars stick even to a greased tin). Cream the sugar and coconut oil, add the eggs and vanilla and beat for another minute. Mix the flour, carob and salt in another bowl and add them to the egg mixture in a few lots, mixing to a smooth, stiff batter, then stir in the walnuts. Spread in the tin and bake 30–35 minutes, until a skewer in the centre comes out clean. Cool, lift out by the paper, peel it off and cut into bars.
recipes.title: Black walnut and carob bars

recipes.method: Written for black walnuts by Hammons Black Walnuts (Missouri). Cake: 125 ml butter, softened; 125 ml vegetable shortening; 500 ml sugar; 5 eggs, separated; 250 ml buttermilk; 5 ml baking soda; 500 ml plain flour; 5 ml vanilla extract; 375 ml black walnuts; 30–85 g flaked coconut; 2.5 ml cream of tartar. Frosting: 225 g cream cheese, softened; 115 g butter at room temperature; 5 ml vanilla extract; about 450 g (1 litre) icing sugar; 250 ml ground black walnuts. Heat the oven to 180 °C and grease and flour three 23 cm cake tins. Cream the butter and shortening, then beat in the sugar a little at a time until light and fluffy. Beat in the egg yolks. Stir the baking soda into the buttermilk until dissolved. Add the flour to the creamed mixture alternately with the buttermilk, starting and ending with flour, then stir in the vanilla, walnuts and coconut. Beat the egg whites (at room temperature) with the cream of tartar to stiff peaks and fold them in. Divide between the tins and bake about 30 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean. Cool 10 minutes in the tins, then turn out to cool completely. For the frosting, beat the cream cheese, butter and vanilla until smooth, beat in the icing sugar slowly, then fold in the ground walnuts. Fill and cover the cake.
recipes.title: Black walnut layer cake

recipes.method: Written for black walnuts by Hammons Black Walnuts (Missouri). 450 g cream cheese at room temperature; 250 ml grated cheddar; 2.5 ml Worcestershire sauce; 60 ml finely diced green capsicum; 60 ml finely diced pimento (roasted red pepper); 15 ml finely diced onion; 1 ml garlic salt; 250 ml chopped black walnuts. Mix everything except the walnuts thoroughly, roll into a ball and chill until firm. Roll the ball in the walnuts, pressing them into the surface, and chill until serving.
recipes.title: Black walnut cheese ball

summary.text:
Black walnut (Juglans nigra), also called eastern black walnut, is a large deciduous tree of the walnut family (Juglandaceae) from eastern North America.
In New Zealand it is planted mainly for its dark, highly valued timber, and as a specimen tree in parks, school grounds and arboreta. Its nuts are edible, with a stronger, earthier flavour than common walnut, but the kernel is hard to extract, and one New Zealand tree farmer notes it is not a good nut tree and takes about 100 years to reach milling height.
It sometimes grows wild: herbarium sheets record escapes at Hobsonville, beside State Highway 43 at Te Wera and on Frenchmans Cap in the Hauraki Gulf, and seedlings come up under planted trees, for example at Massey University in Palmerston North, and in Oamaru, Rotorua and the western Bay of Plenty.

warnings: Walnuts are tree nuts, one of the commonest causes of food allergy in New Zealand, and can cause life-threatening allergic reactions in some people.

habitat.text:
Roadsides, riverbanks, gullies, forest margins, abandoned farmland. Forms impenetrable thickets.
Coast and lowlands, especially in high-rainfall country: pasture that is only lightly grazed, orchards and forestry blocks, hedgerows, roadsides and waste ground, scrub, forest edges and clearings, riverbeds, stream banks, swamps, sand dunes and gardens (NZPCN, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Raspberry's leaves are pinnate, with side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk, where blackberry's are palmate, all leaflets spreading from one point; raspberry's are densely white-felted underneath. A ripe raspberry comes away from its core when picked and is hollow; a blackberry keeps its core.
lookalikes.name: Red raspberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. The flowers separate them: blackberry's are 15–60 mm across and have stamens and carpels together, while bush lawyer's are 8–15 mm across, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Ripe blackberry is black and bush lawyer's yellow to orange or red, but blackberry is red before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit. The native lawyers lack the long, glandular, bristly hairs some introduced brambles carry on their young stems; not every blackberry has them, so their absence does not rule blackberry out.
lookalikes.name: Bush lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. The flowers separate them: blackberry's are 15–60 mm across and have stamens and carpels together, while white-leaved lawyer's are 8–15 mm across, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Ripe blackberry is black and white-leaved lawyer's yellow to orange or red, but blackberry is red before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit. The native lawyers lack the long, glandular, bristly hairs some introduced brambles carry on their young stems; not every blackberry has them, so their absence does not rule blackberry out.
lookalikes.name: White-leaved lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet, where blackberry's have (3–)5(–7); creeping lawyer creeps along the ground, blackberry arches and scrambles. Ripe creeping lawyer fruit is red, but blackberry is red too before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit.

preparation.text: Raw, or into jam, crumble, cordial and vinegar. Fully black and pulling away from the plant with no effort means ripe.

recipes.method: Written for blackberries; the page names no species. Makes about 8 jars. 1.8 kg blackberries, 1.5 kg jam sugar (sugar with added pectin), the juice and pips of 1 lemon, and a fingertip-sized knob of butter (optional). The night before, layer the berries and sugar in a very large bowl, cover and leave at room temperature so the sugar starts to dissolve; stir once in the morning. Put a small saucer in the freezer. Tip everything into a preserving pan or a large, wide pan and stir in the lemon juice; tie the lemon pips in muslin or a tea strainer and add them, because they give up pectin and help the set. Warm gently until all the sugar has dissolved, then bring to the boil and simmer for 5 minutes. Take off the heat and put a little on the cold saucer: once it is cool, push it with a finger, and if it wrinkles it has set. If not, boil 2–3 minutes more and test again, until it wrinkles. Skim, stir in the butter if using, and leave 15 minutes so the fruit settles before ladling into sterilised jars (wash them in hot soapy water and dry them in an oven at 170 °C, 150 °C fan, for at least 10 minutes). Keeps at least 6 months somewhere cool and dark; refrigerate once open.
recipes.title: Blackberry jam

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries. Makes about 200 ml. 350 g blackberries, 115 g caster sugar, 3 strips of pared lemon rind, 2 slices of ginger each about 0.5 cm thick, and 125 ml water. Wash and drain the berries and put them in a non-reactive pan with the sugar, lemon rind and ginger, then pour over the water. Bring gently to the boil and simmer for 15–20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the fruit is completely soft and the juice is starting to thicken. Take out the rind and ginger and press the pulp through a sieve with a wooden spoon (or use a mouli) to remove the seeds. Pour into a small sterilised bottle or jar, close it and leave to cool. Keeps up to a month in the fridge. Use it as a cordial with sparkling water, over ice cream, or folded into yoghurt or whipped cream.
recipes.title: Blackberry syrup

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the author notes many roadside patches are sprayed, so pick only where you know they aren't, or use frozen. Serves 10. Dough: 200 g softened butter, 200 g caster sugar, 4 eggs, ½ teaspoon vanilla essence, 400 g plain flour and ¼ teaspoon baking powder. Filling: 4 medium cooking apples (Granny Smith will do), peeled and cored, 200 g blackberries, 80 g caster sugar, the zest of a lemon, 50 g butter, plus caster sugar for sprinkling. Butter a pie dish about 24 cm across and 4 cm deep and swirl caster sugar round to coat it. Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla; sift in the flour and baking powder and stir until just combined. Cover and chill for at least an hour. Heat the oven to 190 °C (170 °C fan). Roll two-thirds of the dough between sheets of baking paper and line the base and sides of the dish; roll the rest for the lid and keep it chilled. Cut the apples into thick slices, toss with the 80 g sugar, the blackberries and the lemon zest, and fill the case. Dot with the butter, lay on the lid, press the edges to seal, cut a slit in the top and dust with caster sugar. Bake in the middle of the oven for 40–50 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean. Cool before serving with whipped cream or vanilla ice cream.
recipes.title: Apple and blackberry shortcake

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. 500 g blackberries, 250 g plain or wholemeal flour (or 200 g flour and 50 g rolled oats), 150 g soft brown sugar and 180 g cold unsalted butter, cubed. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan). Put the berries in a lightly buttered ovenproof dish, with a sprinkle of sugar if they are sharp. Rub the flour and butter together with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs, then stir in the sugar (and the oats). Spread the topping evenly over the fruit and bake on the middle shelf for about 30 minutes, until golden. Serve with cream or custard.
recipes.title: Blackberry crumble

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. Makes 12. 150 g blackberries, 2 eating apples, 50 g caster sugar plus extra for sprinkling, 2 tablespoons water, 1 beaten egg and 500 g shortcrust pastry. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan) and line a baking tray with baking paper. Peel and chop the apples small and cook them with the sugar and water over medium heat for 5 minutes; add the blackberries and cook 5 minutes more on low, then tip into a bowl to cool. Roll the pastry 5 mm thick on a floured surface and cut 12 equal rectangles. Lay 6 on the tray, brush the edges with egg, spoon the fruit into the middle, cover with the other 6 and press the edges firmly with a fork. Cut a few slits in each, brush with egg, sprinkle with sugar and bake for 20 minutes, until golden and bubbling.
recipes.title: Blackberry and apple hand pies

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. Makes 12. 100 g blackberries, 250 g jumbo rolled oats, 125 g unsalted butter, 125 g light brown sugar and 2 tablespoons golden syrup. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan) and line a 20 × 20 cm tin with baking paper. Melt the butter, sugar and syrup in a pan over low heat, stir in the oats until coated, and press the mixture into the tin. Scatter the blackberries on top and press down firmly so it is level. Bake for 20–25 minutes, until golden, then cool before cutting into 12.
recipes.title: Blackberry flapjacks

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. Blackberries alone or mixed with other summer fruit (raspberries, blackcurrants, redcurrants; frozen is fine) — enough to fill your pudding basin one and a half times — plus about 3 tablespoons caster sugar, sliced day-old white bread and a little butter. Butter the basin. Cut the crusts off the bread and line the basin with it, pressed firmly with no gaps, keeping a couple of slices for the lid. Heat the fruit and sugar gently in a pan until it simmers and runs with syrupy juice; taste carefully (it is very hot) and add sugar if it is sharp. Fill the basin with the fruit, keeping back some syrup and fruit. Put on the bread lid, press a plate on top and weigh it down with a can. Once cool, refrigerate overnight so the juice soaks into the bread. Turn out onto a plate, pour over the rest of the syrup and decorate with the leftover fruit.
recipes.title: Summer pudding

recipes.method: Written for wild brambles in Essex, England; the page names no species. Serves 1. A handful of young blackberry leaves; freshly boiled water; honey, to taste. Wash the leaves well, watching for insects. Chop them roughly, or scrunch them in your hands to bruise them. Put about 2 tablespoons (30 ml) of the chopped leaves in a tea infuser, pour over freshly boiled water and cover the cup. Steep for 5 minutes, taste, and give it another 5 minutes if you want it stronger. Stir in a teaspoon of honey if you like. To keep leaves for later, remove any stems, lay the leaves flat on a baking sheet and dry them in the oven at its lowest setting until brittle, then store them in a clean jar in a dark cupboard. Use 1 teaspoon of dried leaf per cup and taste after 2–3 minutes, because dried leaf infuses faster than fresh. The author finds the fresh tea grassy and slightly citrusy, like a green tea, and more tannic the longer it brews.
recipes.title: Blackberry leaf tea

sources: Langlands, Peter. Foraging New Zealand (Penguin Random House NZ, 2024), 'Blackberry' entry.

Its actual legal status, which 'declared pest' summarises. Blackberry is a Sustained Control pest in regional pest management plans rather than an eradication target, because it is too widespread to contain — Hawke's Bay, Bay of Plenty, Auckland and Tasman–Nelson all list it that way, with the occupier responsible for control and rules commonly requiring destruction within 10 m of a boundary where the neighbour is also controlling it. Breeding, distributing, releasing or selling it is an offence under the Biosecurity Act 1993. It is **not** a National Pest Plant Accord species. Hawke's Bay Regional Council, pest hub: 'Blackberry'. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.hbrc.govt.nz/environment/pest-control/pest-hub/pests/pest/21

What it is sprayed with and when, which is what the spray warning is really about. Hawke's Bay Regional Council's guidance for large patches is to spray in summer to autumn, before the leaves go brittle, with metsulfuron-methyl, Tordon Brushkiller or triclopyr 600 EC. Small patches are dug out year-round. Goats control it effectively where they are confined with it. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.hbrc.govt.nz/environment/pest-control/pest-hub/pests/pest/21

Why the scientific name carries 'agg.' — Rubus fruticosus L. is an ambiguous name that has been applied in several ways, which is why the European blackberries are treated as an aggregate rather than a species. identification.text:
Unarmed, deciduous shrub to 1.5–(2.5) m high, with a characteristic strong odour when bruised; branches and shoots more or less erect, glabrous except when young. Leaves plicately folded in bud with petioles to about 8 cm long, slightly clasping at base; lamina broadly deltoid, 6–11 × 8–13 cm, often smaller on upper part of flowering stems, palmately lobed, with 3 more or less triangular lobes; lower surface glabrate with fairly numerous prominent yellow glandular scales; upper surface slightly shining, somewhat rugose; margins crenate to coarsely serrate; base cordate. Racemes pendent, 5–15-flowered; flowers more or less fragrant. Hypanthium 2–4 mm diam., broadly campanulate to orbicular, green or reddish green, glabrous or hairy, with sessile, yellow, glandular scales. Sepals 3–5 mm long, triangular to oblong-elliptic, green or reddish green, more or less villous inside, reflexed at anthesis. Petals 2.5–4 mm long, oblong to broadly ovate or broadly elliptic, white or greenish white. Filaments 2–4 mm long. Fruit 7–10 mm diam. (to 15 mm in cultivation), globose, black, opaque, lacking bloom, glabrous; flesh very aromatic and moderately sweet.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In plain terms: a shrub up to 1.5 m high, sometimes 2.5 m, whose bruised leaves give off a strong blackcurrant smell. Each leaf has small yellow dots (glandular scales) on its underside, which separate it from redcurrant when there is no fruit. Small greenish-white flowers hang in short clusters of 5 to 15 in spring (September to November). The round berries, 7–10 mm across, ripen black from December to February; they are opaque with no whitish bloom, very aromatic and moderately sweet. It differs from flowering currant in its small greenish flowers and its yellow glandular scales (see the lookalikes).

lookalikes.howToTell: Flowering currant has pink to deep red flowers, 15 to many in each hanging cluster, with a long narrow tube behind the petals (white ageing pink to rose); blackcurrant's flowers are small, greenish white, 5 to 15 in a cluster, with a short round green or reddish-green cup. Flowering currant's leaves are only moderately aromatic and their glandular scales are small and almost colourless; blackcurrant's leaves have prominent yellow glandular scales underneath and a strong smell. Both shrubs have aromatic leaves, so smell alone does not separate them. Flowering currant's berries are smaller (5–7 mm), black, usually with a whitish bloom and little taste; blackcurrant's are 7–10 mm, black, with no bloom, aromatic and moderately sweet. Both berries are edible; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Flowering currant

preparation.text: The berries are strongly tart and aromatic raw, so they are usually cooked with sugar into purée, jam, jelly, syrup, cordial or juice; their high pectin and acid content makes jams and jellies set readily. The strong flavour can be softened by combining them with milder fruit such as apple, raspberry or strawberry. The young leaves are brewed as a tea, like raspberry leaves, or used to flavour tea, preserves and pickles, and sometimes alcohol.

recipes.method: 1 kg fresh or frozen blackcurrants; 375–500 ml water (the smaller amount for frozen fruit); 1.35 kg white sugar. Makes about 1 litre. Simmer the fruit in the water in a large pan until soft. Stir in the sugar until it dissolves, then boil hard for about 15 minutes, until a drop on a cold saucer wrinkles when pushed; if it doesn't, boil 1–2 minutes more and test again. Ladle into warm sterilised jars and seal. Keep somewhere cool and dark, and in the fridge once opened.
recipes.title: Blackcurrant jam

recipes.method: 750 g ripe blackcurrants; 1.5 litres water; 1.75 kg sugar. Boil the berries in the water for 10 minutes, then strain through muslin. Add the sugar to the juice, boil for 3 minutes more and bottle. It is a concentrate: dilute it to taste with water or tonic.
recipes.title: Blackcurrant cordial

recipes.method: 110 g sugar; 110 g flour; 70 g butter; 1 large egg, beaten; 180 g blackcurrants; whipped cream, to serve. Serves 4–6. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Blitz the sugar briefly to make it finer (or use caster sugar). Rub the butter into the sugar and flour until crumbly, mix in the egg, then gently fold in the berries. Tip into a lightly greased glass or china ovenproof dish (not metal) and bake for 40–45 minutes. Serve with whipped cream.
recipes.title: Blackcurrant deep-dish crumble

recipes.method: 2 litres loosely packed fresh blackcurrant leaves, washed; 2.5 litres water; 13 g citric acid; 250 g sugar. Put the leaves in a large pot. Pour the boiling water over them, stir in the citric acid, cover and leave to steep for 12 hours. Strain out the leaves and stir in the sugar until it dissolves. Freeze it to keep it longer. Dilute with chilled water as a cordial, or use it in sodas and cocktails.
recipes.title: Blackcurrant leaf syrup

recipes.method: 380 g blackcurrants; 4–5 blackcurrant leaves; 300 ml whole milk; 250 ml double cream; 175 g caster sugar; 4 egg yolks; juice of ½ lemon; a good pinch of sea salt; 3 tbsp water. Serves 8. Heat the milk, cream and salt to just below a simmer, add the leaves, turn off the heat and steep for 30–60 minutes; remove the leaves. Cook the berries with the water until tender. Blend about 300 g of them smooth and sieve; stir 25 g of the sugar into the remaining whole berries for a ripple and chill both. Bring the milk back to a simmer, pour it over the yolks whisked with the rest of the sugar, return to the pan and stir over low heat to 82 °C. Cool over iced water and chill for at least 6 hours. Whisk the purée and lemon juice into the custard, churn for about 20 minutes, swirl through the whole-berry ripple and freeze. Without a machine, freeze it in a bowl and whisk it every 90 minutes or so, three times.
recipes.title: Blackcurrant ripple ice cream

recipes.method: For one cup: 250 ml boiling water; 2–3 tsp cut fresh blackcurrant leaves (or 2–3 large whole leaves), or 1–2 tsp crushed dried leaves. Pick clean, undamaged leaves once the dew has dried. Pour the boiling water over the leaves, cover and steep 10–20 minutes for fresh leaves or 5–15 minutes for dried. Strain and sweeten if you like. Leaves can be dried, or frozen in a bag, for use out of season.
recipes.title: Blackcurrant leaf tea

recipes.method: 500 g blackcurrants; 170 g caster or white sugar; 500 ml brandy (or vodka). Wash, dry and pick over the berries. Crush them gently in a large glass jar, add the sugar and brandy, and stir. Keep it covered on a sunny windowsill for about a week, stirring every day until the sugar dissolves, then move it somewhere cool and dark. After about six weeks, strain it through muslin in a sieve for a couple of hours and pour into sterilised bottles. Frozen berries work if thawed and drained.
recipes.title: Blackcurrant cassis

recipes.method: 500 g blackcurrants; 100 g golden caster sugar; juice of ½ lemon; 2 tbsp water. Makes about one 455 ml jar. Bring the water and lemon juice to the boil in a large pan, add the blackcurrants and simmer until they break down. Add the sugar and boil to 105 °C on a thermometer. Pour into sterilised jars and cool. Keeps in the fridge for up to 3 weeks; spoon it over yoghurt, porridge or ice cream.
recipes.title: Blackcurrant compote

recipes.method: 200 g blackcurrants; 250 ml red wine vinegar; 100 g golden granulated sugar; ½ cinnamon stick. Fills about three 140 ml bottles. Put everything in a sterilised glass jar with a non-corrosive lid and shake well. Leave to macerate for a month or more, shaking every other day. Strain through a fine sieve (or muslin) into sterilised bottles. Kept cool and dark it lasts at least a year; refrigerate once opened. Use in dressings and sauces, with beetroot, or diluted with water as a drink.
recipes.title: Blackcurrant vinegar

recipes.method: 300 g fresh blackcurrants; zest and juice of ½ lemon; 50 g butter; 100 g caster sugar; 2 medium eggs. Makes one medium jar. Cook the berries gently with a splash of water for 5–10 minutes until they release their juice. In a heatproof bowl over barely simmering water, melt the butter with the sugar, lemon zest and juice. Whisk the eggs, sieve them into the bowl, add the fruit and stir for 30–40 minutes until the curd coats the back of a spoon. Sieve out the fruit skins and pour into a sterilised jar. Keep in the fridge and use within about 2 weeks, or freeze in small pots.
recipes.title: Blackcurrant curd

summary.text:
The blackcurrant (Ribes nigrum), also called black currant or cassis, is a deciduous shrub in the gooseberry family (Grossulariaceae), grown for its edible berries. It is native to temperate Europe and Asia and was naturalised in New Zealand by 1922.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) blackcurrants are abundantly cultivated, especially in colder areas, and wild plants are sporadic escapes from cultivation. The Flora records them in Canterbury (scattered in lowland areas and near Mt Cook) and in Otago (upper Taieri River), and says they are probably wild elsewhere in the south. Recent iNaturalist NZ records of wild plants (32 research-grade) are mostly from Canterbury, Otago and Southland. Herbarium sheets record wild plants in Canterbury, and in 1997 a large thicket in the understorey of a native forest remnant at Otahu Reserve, between Monowai and Tuatapere in Southland. Nurseries sell named cultivars such as 'Sefton', which needs fewer winter chilling hours than 'Magnus'; currants need a winter chill, and Auckland gives enough. Many cultivars are grown, and wild plants cannot be named to cultivar.
It is not a pest plant: it is not on DOC's list of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand: waste places, often coastal, especially near plantations. Herbarium sheets record it established on roadsides near Palmerston North (1953) and in the Hutt Valley (1985).
Planted, it tolerates poor, shallow soils and exposure, but grows best for timber in shelter on deep, moist soils; planted in waterlogged ground it dies from root rot.
Wetland status (NZPCN, from the national wetland plant list, Clarkson et al. 2021): facultative upland — occasionally in wetlands, but usually on dry ground.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree; twigs ribbed, glabrous to densely hairy. Leaves reduced to phyllodes, alternate; phyllodes glabrous, narrowly obovate, elliptic and symmetric or falcate, usually obtuse, sometimes shortly mucronate, entire, (40)–60–100 × 8–20 mm, with 3–4 prominent veins; stipules triangular, 1–2 mm long, conspicuous in young plants only. Inflorescence of few to numerous, many-flowered, pale creamy yellow, globose heads; heads solitary or in axillary racemes usually longer than the leaves. Flowers 5-merous, sessile. Pod glabrous, twisted or spiralled, 8–10 cm long (up to 4 cm diameter), 5–8 mm wide; aril pink to crimson or red, encircling seed. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Racosperma melanoxylon (R.Br.) Mart.]
Flowers August–November. Young plants may have feathery, twice-divided (bipinnate) leaves, and some leaves are intermediate, with bipinnate leaflets on a well-developed phyllode.
It is easily told from the other naturalised wattles with large phyllodes by its 5-parted flowers in round heads and the large aril enfolding the seed. Told from Sydney golden wattle (Acacia longifolia) by its flowers in round heads (Sydney golden wattle's are in cylindrical spikes) and, at fruiting, by the large red aril enfolding the seed (Sydney golden wattle's aril is slightly folded and cup-shaped).

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers: blackwood's are pale creamy yellow, in round heads; Sydney golden wattle's are pale to golden yellow, in cylindrical spikes. At fruiting, look at the seed: blackwood's has a large pink to crimson or red aril encircling and enfolding it; Sydney golden wattle's aril is not much folded, thickened and cup-shaped below the seed. Blackwood's pods are twisted or spiralled; Sydney golden wattle's are straight or slightly curved, but its coastal subspecies sophorae has extremely contorted pods, so pod shape does not always separate them. The leaves do not separate them: both have narrow, flat phyllodes with several prominent veins, blackwood's (40)–60–100 × 8–20 mm with 3–4 veins, Sydney golden wattle's (60)–80–130 × 6–22 mm with 2–4. Both grow in waste places, often near the coast. Sydney golden wattle's seeds are eaten (see its page).

IV (Webb, Sykes & Garnock-Jones 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series, 'Racosperma Mart.' genus treatment and key (https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/ebe2f180-bf00-4020-815f-10f78d912a69, retrieved 10/11/2026): key couplets 10–11, 'Many wattles are considered poisonous (Connor 1977).', 'Naturalised spp. 13.'. Habitat tags: coastal ('often coastal'), disturbed ('waste places'); 'near plantations' is not tagged forest.

Flowers, cooked — Plants For A Future, 'Acacia melanoxylon' (https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Acacia+melanoxylon, retrieved 10/11/2026; one source with Useful Temperate Plants; facts restated) ('Flowers - cooked', 'Rich in pollen, they are often used in fritters') and Bungalook Nursery (above): two records. summary.text:
Blackwood (Acacia melanoxylon), also called Tasmanian blackwood, is a shrub or tree, growing up to 40 m tall on favourable sites, of the pea family (Fabaceae), native to eastern Australia and Tasmania and naturalised in New Zealand.
In New Zealand: North Island: Northland, established in the vicinity of Auckland City, Hauraki Plains, the vicinity of Whakarewarewa and Rotorua, at Halcombe (Manawatū) and near Palmerston North; South Island: Christchurch and coastal North Canterbury, Otago Peninsula, also collected once from Te Waewae Bay, Southland. A herbarium sheet also records a self-sown seedling on a roadside at Taita in the Hutt Valley (1985). Naturalised from eastern Australia and Tasmania, first recorded in 1918.
It is used in forestry and for soil conservation, so it can be expected to spread further. Its hard, dark timber is used for furniture, boats and musical instruments, and it is increasingly planted in New Zealand for it. It is also planted for erosion control in gullies and on steep slopes, where its spreading roots sucker into new trees; it fixes nitrogen and becomes resistant to stock after 4–5 years. Because it spreads by seed and root suckers, it is not suited to planting beside streams. It is grown as shelter and trims into a tall hedge, and its pale yellow late-winter flowers are good for bees.
It is on the Department of Conservation's list of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024, but is not in any regional pest management plan. The common names wattle and acacia are used for many species of its genus, 13 of which are naturalised in New Zealand.

warnings: Many wattles are considered poisonous, and 13 wattle species are naturalised in New Zealand. Be sure of the species before eating any wattle seed or flower: Sydney golden wattle (Acacia longifolia) has similar leaves (see the lookalikes).
Eat only the seeds and flowers. The bark and twigs were used to stupefy fish.
The wood can cause hand dermatitis, and its sawdust is a problem particularly for furniture makers; occupational asthma from blackwood has been reported.

habitat.text:
Waste land, roadsides, arable land, railway yards.
Herbarium specimens also record it growing wild in back dunes at Eastbourne and at Castlecliff by the Whanganui River mouth, and on a clay bank above a road near Totara Park.

identification.text:
Stems glabrous or rarely sparsely hairy, 30–80 cm tall; all shoots dying back during winter. Leaves glabrous, rarely hairy, sometimes scabrid on margin, shape variable, (1.5)–3–10 × (0.5)–1–2 cm. Inflorescence (3)–6–30–(40)-flowered; bracts scarious. Calyx contracted at mouth. Capsule narrow-mouthed; teeth erect to spreading.
Stoutly taprooted perennial. Stems ascending to erect, swollen at nodes. Leaves glaucous, ovate to linear-lanceolate to oblanceolate, acute, usually very shortly connate; lower leaves petiolate; upper leaves sessile. Inflorescence a lax dichasium; pedicels 5–15 mm; bracts ovate. Flowers hermaphrodite. Calyx glabrous, glaucous, inflated, ovoid, 13–17 mm long; veins 20, weak with fine network of secondary veins; teeth broadly triangular, acute, ciliolate. Petals white; limb deeply emarginate, sometimes with 2 small lateral lobes near base; claw lobed near base of limb; coronal scales scale-like or oblong, 0–1 mm long. Styles 3, erect, about 2 cm long. Capsule ovoid to spherical, included in calyx, dehiscing by 6 teeth; carpophore 2–3 mm long. Seeds dull brown, reniform, flattened, warty, 1–1.5 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Silene vulgaris subsp. vulgaris and Silene vulgaris]
The swollen, glabrous, bladder-like calyx distinguishes it from the other species of Silene and Lychnis in New Zealand. Sea campion, which grows on coastal stony ground, is smaller and has 1–(3)-flowered stems with green bracts (see Lookalikes).

lookalikes.howToTell: Sea campion is the smaller plant of coastal stony ground: its stems are 10–30 cm tall, some of its shoots stay leafy through winter, and its leaves are 1.5–3 × 0.5–1 cm; bladder campion's stems are 30–80 cm tall, all its shoots die back in winter, and its leaves are usually 3–10 × 1–2 cm (from 1.5 × 0.5 cm). Count the flowers on a stem: sea campion has 1, sometimes up to 3; bladder campion usually has 6–30 (3 to 40), so a 3-flowered stem does not tell them apart. Sea campion's bracts are green and its calyx is wide at the mouth; bladder campion's bracts are papery (scarious) and its calyx is narrowed at the mouth. In fruit, sea campion's capsule is wide-mouthed with its teeth curled back; bladder campion's is narrow-mouthed with erect to spreading teeth.
lookalikes.name: Sea campion

lookalikes.howToTell: White campion is softly hairy: its stems and leaves have soft hairs, with glandular hairs as well higher up, its leaves are green, and its calyx is hairy with long, narrow, tapering teeth; bladder campion's stems are hairless (rarely sparsely hairy), its leaves hairless (rarely hairy) and blue-grey (glaucous), and its swollen calyx is hairless apart from tiny hairs on the broadly triangular teeth. White campion has separate male plants (flowers with 10 stamens) and female plants (flowers with 5 styles), and its capsule opens by usually 10 teeth (8 to 12); every bladder campion flower has both stamens and 3 styles, and its capsule opens by 6 teeth. A female white campion's calyx is swollen too (ovoid, 17–25 mm long), so a swollen calyx alone does not tell them apart. White campion's bracts are green; bladder campion's are papery (scarious).
lookalikes.name: White campion

preparation.text: Young shoots and leaves are eaten raw or cooked. The young leaves are sweet and good in salads; use the leaves before the plant starts to flower. Pick it young: the stems toughen as they grow, and raw leaves turn more bitter with age. Keep the tender tips and discard the thicker stems. Cooked young shoots, picked at about 5 cm long, taste like green peas with a slight bitterness. The leaves and shoots are also blanched quickly in boiling salted water, fried in olive oil, cooked with eggs, or added to soups, stews and rice dishes.

recipes.method: Serves 4. 5 cups (about 1.25 litres, packed) bladder campion; about 1 litre (4¼ cups) hot vegetable stock, or a little more; 1 tbsp extra virgin olive oil; 1 spring onion, with some of its green; 1⅔ cups (400 ml) Vialone Nano, Arborio or Carnaroli rice; 3 tbsp butter; 4 tbsp grated Parmesan; white wine (optional). Wash the campion well in cold water and drain it. Chop the spring onion, white and some green, and soften it in a risotto pan with the oil and a little water or stock. Add the rice and toast it for a few minutes, deglazing with white wine if you like. Add the hot stock a little at a time, stirring and letting each addition be absorbed. Chop the campion and stir it in halfway through the cooking, so it keeps its flavour and texture. Cook the rice until done, adding stock as needed, then take it off the heat and beat in the butter and Parmesan. Rest briefly and serve hot. For a vegan version, finish with olive oil and nutritional yeast.
recipes.title: Creamy bladder campion risotto

recipes.method: Serves 4. 300 g bladder campion; ½ onion (about 85 g; optional, or 1 garlic clove); a drizzle of extra virgin olive oil; water; salt. Wash the campion well and chop it roughly. Slice the onion thinly and stew it in a pan with the oil and a little water for 5–10 minutes. Add the campion and salt, cover, and cook, stirring now and then and adding a little water if needed; dry off any excess liquid before serving. For a pasta sauce, cook the campion with garlic or onion, peeled tomatoes, olive oil, salt and seasoning, toss it through drained pasta and serve with grated cheese. It keeps 3 days in the fridge in an airtight container; to freeze it, cook it only partly.
recipes.title: Sautéed bladder campion, also a pasta sauce

recipes.method: A good handful of bladder campion; ½ garlic clove; 2 espresso cups of cashews, soaked for 3 hours in lukewarm water and drained; 3 g coarse salt; a pinch of pepper; 1 espresso cup of extra virgin olive oil. Wash the campion and peel the garlic. Blend them with the cashews, salt, pepper and oil until smooth and creamy, loosening with a couple of tablespoons of water if needed. Serve at room temperature or cold, to dress pasta, rice or other grains, or as a dip with chickpea pancakes or raw vegetables.
recipes.title: Raw bladder campion and cashew pesto

summary.text:
Bladder campion (Silene vulgaris), also called maidenstears and double sea campion, is a perennial of the pink family (Caryophyllaceae) from Europe, north-west Africa and temperate Asia, naturalised in New Zealand.
It was first recorded wild here in 1871. It grows around Auckland and Wellington in the North Island, in Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, Westland, Otago and Southland in the South Island, and on Stewart Island. It has also been known in New Zealand as Silene cucubalus, S. inflata and S. latifolia. All New Zealand plants belong to subspecies vulgaris; sea campion (Silene uniflora), which the 1988 Flora treated as another subspecies of S. vulgaris, has its own entry. Its swollen, hairless, bladder-like calyx sets it apart from the other campions in New Zealand.
Its young shoots and leaves are eaten around the Mediterranean: in Cyprus, as strouthouthkia or tsakrithkia, in Crete as agriopapoula, in Italy as sculpit or stridolo, and in La Mancha, Spain, as collejas.

warnings: It contains saponins. They are poorly absorbed by the body and are broken down by thorough cooking, but do not eat large amounts.

habitat.text:
Subtidal, anchored on rocky bottoms in water about 3–20 m deep, on open coasts sheltered from direct wave action and in calm bays, harbours and sheltered offshore waters, where it forms beds with floating canopies. It tolerates strong tidal currents. Smaller plants grow in shallow pools and channels.
In New Zealand it forms large forests in the deep sheltered waters of the south.

harvestEthics.text:
This species is at risk. If you harvest it, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.
Removing a plant's floating surface canopy sharply cuts the number of reproductive blades it makes and can leave it sterile for weeks.
Attached bladder kelp may not be taken from the East Otago taiāpure; kelp that is unattached and cast ashore is exempt. In the Kaikōura Marine Area (Te Whata Kai o Rakihouia i Te Tai o Marokura) it may be gathered by hand only, within a daily limit. Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.

identification.text: Huge: up to 45 m long in New Zealand. Long cylindrical stipes carry the blades up towards the surface, where the fronds form a floating canopy. Blades are long and leaf-like, wrinkled, with small teeth along the edges and a single oval gas bladder where each blade joins the stipe. New blades split off one after another from a growing point near the top of each frond. The holdfast is a massive dome of intertwined cylindrical haptera. Golden brown. Reproductive blades are smooth, have no bladders and sit in a cluster just above the holdfast, with darker patches where spores form. Blades from wave-exposed sites are thicker, narrower and corrugated; those from sheltered sites are smooth.

preparation.text: Chop fresh blades into roasted vegetables, marinate them for salads, or dry them and sprinkle them into soups and stews. Dried blades can be oven-baked and eaten like crisps, or ground into a seasoning. Cooked blades turn bright green and can be used to wrap seafood. Small slices soaked in light vegetable stock for a few hours can be blended into a purée for soups and stews. Dried and ground, it is made into kelp powder and kelp salt.

summary.text:
Bladder kelp, known as giant kelp elsewhere, is New Zealand's largest kelp — a native brown seaweed whose gas-filled floats hold its blades up to form floating canopies.
In New Zealand it grows around the southern North Island, the South Island, and Stewart, Chatham, Bounty, Antipodes, Auckland and Campbell Islands. Its current northern limit appears to be D'Urville Island in the western Marlborough Sounds, near Mana Island on the North Island's west coast and Palliser Bay on its east coast; it does not persist where the sea stays above 18–19 °C for several days. It is also widespread in cool southern hemisphere waters and in the Americas from Alaska to Mexico and from Peru to Argentina and Uruguay.
It is assessed as At Risk – Declining, with low confidence because the data are poor. Range retraction and declines are linked to warmer seas, reduced light and sediment from land runoff, and, in parts of its range, invasion by wakame (Undaria pinnatifida). Its beds along the Canterbury coast shrank after the 2017–18 marine heatwave and recovered quickly once the sea cooled. It has retreated in the Marlborough Sounds to cool-water refuges in Queen Charlotte Sound, and a forest that once stretched 20 km between Brighton and Taieri Mouth, south of Dunedin, has gone.
Attached bladder kelp has been in the Quota Management System since 01/10/2010 in the South East, where commercial cutting is limited to the top 1.2 m of water. In New Zealand it has been harvested to make kelp powder and kelp salt. It is hand-gathered commercially in Akaroa Harbour, then dried and milled for food products, supplements and gin distilling.

warnings: Bladder kelp is a brown seaweed, and brown seaweed can contain very high levels of iodine. High levels of iodine can cause thyroid problems, so eating it more than every once in a while may be unsafe, especially when pregnant or breastfeeding.
A single gram of dried bladder kelp can hold about 2.7 mg of iodine — about 18 times an adult's daily need of 0.15 mg, and more than twice the adult upper limit of 1.1 mg a day.
Harvest only from clean water — never near stormwater drains, in harbours, or where there is heavy boat traffic.
Seaweed absorbs pollutants as well as minerals and nutrients.
Cut blades with scissors — never pull seaweed up by its base; leave the holdfast in the water.

harvestEthics.text:
Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.
An Unwanted Organism and National Pest Plant Accord species: it must not be bred, distributed, released or sold anywhere in New Zealand. Cut pieces and slashed stems resprout, so if you remove it, take the plant material to a landfill or refuse transfer station. Do not leave cut stems lying on the ground, where they re-root.

identification.text:
High-climbing, fibrous-rooted, hairy perennial. Stems twining and running. Petioles about 2–20 cm long, often purplish, densely hairy, otherwise smooth. Lamina usually deeply 3-lobed, 5–18 × 5–16 cm, more or less silky hairy below; sinuses rounded; terminal lobe more or less ovate apart from the generally narrow base, acute to acuminate; lateral lobes broad and asymmetric. Inflorescence axillary, few-flowered. Peduncles long, often longer than the leaves, with retrorse hairs. Pedicels more or less densely clothed in retrorse hairs. Bracts and bracteoles longer than the pedicels, usually narrow-linear, but sometimes small, simple, foliose basal bracts present. Sepals 1.8–2.5 cm long, narrow-lanceolate, acuminate, hairy especially on margins and towards base. Corolla 8.5–10 × 9–10.5 cm, funnelform; tube pink except for narrow white base; limb usually deep blue or purple with pink mid-petaline bands on the outside, often withering by afternoon and turning completely pink. Stamens 2.3–4 cm long, included; fused basal part of filaments broad and white-bearded at top. Style slightly exceeding longest stamens; stigma capitate, alveolate. Fruit not seen.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
A vine that climbs to the top of tall trees, with tough, hairy, twining stems and tough fibrous roots but no rhizomes. Its leaves are usually deeply three-lobed and silky-hairy underneath. From late spring to early winter it carries groups of 3–12 deep blue-purple trumpet flowers, pink at the base, about 10 cm across, which wither and turn pink in the midday sun. Told from great bindweed by its blue or purple flowers in clusters, its lobed, hairy leaves and its single rounded stigma: great bindweed has single white flowers half-hidden by two large bracts, smooth unlobed leaves, a two-lobed stigma and creeping rhizomes.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flower first. Blue morning glory's is deep blue or purple with a pink tube, often turning wholly pink as it withers by the afternoon, and comes in few-flowered clusters; great bindweed's is usually pure white (very rarely pale pink) and borne singly. Then look under the flower: great bindweed has two large bracts that overlap and partly hide the sepals; blue morning glory's bracts are usually narrow and thread-like, and its narrow, pointed, hairy sepals (1.8–2.5 cm) are in plain view. Inside, blue morning glory has a single rounded stigma; great bindweed's stigma is two-lobed. Blue morning glory's flower is also larger, 9–10.5 cm across against great bindweed's 5.5–8 cm. The leaves: blue morning glory's are usually deeply three-lobed and silky-hairy underneath, on densely hairy, often purplish stalks, and its stems are hairy; great bindweed's leaves are triangular to arrow-shaped with a deeply notched base and are usually smooth, as are its stems. A few blue morning glory plants have unlobed or two-lobed leaves, so check the flower too. Underground, great bindweed spreads by far-creeping white rhizomes; blue morning glory has tough fibrous roots and no rhizomes. Both grow on forest margins and around gardens in the lowland North Island and northern South Island, so where they grow does not separate them. Neither is food: great bindweed is reported to be highly purgative, and the seeds of some morning glories contain powerful hallucinogens.
lookalikes.name: Great bindweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flower colour with care: pink bindweed's flowers are usually pink with white bands (rarely all white), and a blue morning glory flower withering in the afternoon also turns wholly pink, so check the fresh flowers and the rest of the plant. Fresh blue morning glory flowers are deep blue or purple with a pink tube. Look under the flower: pink bindweed has two broad, rounded bracts (1–1.5 cm wide) that partly hide the sepals; blue morning glory's bracts are usually narrow and thread-like and its narrow, pointed, hairy sepals are in plain view and longer (1.8–2.5 cm against 1.2–1.5 cm). Inside, blue morning glory has a single rounded stigma; pink bindweed's stigma is two-lobed. Pink bindweed's flowers are borne singly with a limb 4–6 cm across; blue morning glory's come in few-flowered clusters and are 9–10.5 cm across. The leaves: blue morning glory's are usually deeply three-lobed and silky-hairy underneath; pink bindweed's are triangular to arrow-shaped with a deep, rounded notch at the base and are not lobed (a few blue morning glory plants have unlobed leaves, so check the flower too). Both can have hairy leaf stalks and young stems, so hairiness does not separate them. Pink bindweed spreads by extensive rhizomes; blue morning glory has tough fibrous roots and no rhizomes. Both grow on forest margins, banks and roadsides in the North Island and in Nelson and Marlborough, so where they grow does not separate them. Neither is given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Pink bindweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaves first. Railway creeper's are cut almost to the base into five to seven narrow, finger-like lobes and are 2.5–10 cm long; blue morning glory's are usually three-lobed with broad lobes and 5–18 cm long (a few plants have unlobed or two-lobed leaves). Blue morning glory's stems and leaf stalks are hairy and its leaves silky-hairy underneath; railway creeper is hairless or almost so. Under the flower, blue morning glory's sepals are 1.8–2.5 cm, narrow, long-pointed and hairy; railway creeper's are short (4.5–10 mm), oval and blunt. Blue morning glory's flowers are deep blue or purple with a pink tube and 9–10.5 cm across; railway creeper's are mauve to purple with a darker throat and 5–8 cm across. Both grow around Auckland and Northland, in hedges, waste places and scrub, so where they grow does not separate them. Railway creeper's young leaves are eaten cooked, but it is an At Risk native (see its page).

summary.text:
Blue morning glory (Ipomoea indica), also called blue dawn flower, is a high-climbing vine of the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae) from the tropics, naturalised in New Zealand. It was brought in as a garden ornamental and has been naturalised since 1950. It grows in lowland areas of the North Island from North Auckland to around Wellington, and in the northern South Island; most New Zealand plants have deeply three-lobed leaves and large deep blue flowers.
It grows very fast, lives long and climbs to the top of a high canopy, smothering and finally killing what it covers; it can replace forest with a low weedy blanket, and is often the last species left where bush is overrun by weeds. It spreads by its creeping stems, which root at the nodes, and from broken pieces carried off in dumped garden waste, by animals or in weeding. Viable seed was long thought not to form in New Zealand, but a plant found in the Bay of Plenty in 1996 was setting large amounts of seed, with seedlings nearby.
It is an Unwanted Organism and a National Pest Plant Accord species, and DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds includes it. It is named in the Auckland (site-led and sustained control), Gisborne (site-led), West Coast (progressive containment), Hawke's Bay (organism of interest) and Bay of Plenty (advisory) regional pest management plans; Auckland's rules also bar planting it anywhere in the region.

warnings: Do not eat it. No record of blue morning glory as food was found. The seeds of some morning glories contain very powerful hallucinogenic drugs, which act if the seeds are crushed or chewed; blue morning glory seldom sets seed in New Zealand, but it can.

Great bindweed, which is also not food, climbs over the same hedges and forest margins and has similar trumpet flowers; around Auckland and Northland, railway creeper, an At Risk native, has similar purple flowers. See Lookalikes.

habitat.text: In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): grows with scarlet pimpernel in the same habitats — cultivated land, waste places and other open, disturbed sites, especially stony and sandy areas, depleted and open pastures, coastal cliffs and dry river beds — but is nearly always much less common.

identification.text:
Annual; stems trailing or prostrate, (2)–5–40 cm long, sometimes mat-forming. Leaves sessile, (2)–5–25 × (1.5)–3–18 mm, ovate, elliptic, or elliptic-ovate, sometimes very broad-ovate, often indistinctly dotted with sessile black glands beneath; base rounded or subcordate; apex more or less obtuse. Flowers solitary; pedicels (0.5)–1–2 cm long. Calyx (3)–3.5–4.5 mm long; lobes lanceolate, acuminate; margins scarious. Corolla (2)–6–15 mm diameter, conspicuous; lobes about 3–7 mm long, elliptic or obovate, with numerous minute red to black-tipped glandular hairs on margin. Stamens about (1)–2 mm long; filaments much longer than anthers, more or less purple except for white-hairy dilated base. Capsule (2.5)–3–5 mm diameter, more or less equal to calyx; style persistent. Seed 0.7–about 1.4 mm long, reticulate, flattened on 1 side, convex and keeled on the other.
Blue pimpernel (Flora of New Zealand): Corolla blue; margin distinctly crenulate.
It has a square, hairless stem, and its stalkless leaves grow in opposite pairs, often with small black dots underneath (Massey). Apart from the flower colour it is the same plant as scarlet pimpernel, whose flowers are orange or orange-red.

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the petals: bird's-eye speedwell's flowers have four lobes, 8–12 mm across, usually sky-blue (rarely white) with dark stripes; blue pimpernel's have five, 6–15 mm across, blue, with finely scalloped edges. Speedwell's leaves have a short stalk and 3–8 pairs of coarse teeth; blue pimpernel's have no stalk, smooth edges and often faint black dots underneath. Speedwell's stem is round and hairy; blue pimpernel's is square and hairless. Both sprawl, carry blue flowers singly on long, slender stalks, have leaves of overlapping size and grow in cultivated land and waste places, so none of these tells them apart. Bird's-eye speedwell's young leaves and shoots are eaten, but its record as food is thin.
lookalikes.name: Bird's-eye speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Chickweed's stems are round with a single line of hairs; blue pimpernel's are four-angled (square in section) and hairless. Chickweed's petals are white and divided almost to the base (rarely absent), in usually loose clusters at the stem tips; blue pimpernel's flowers are blue, with five lobes, borne singly in the leaf axils on stalks (0.5)–1–2 cm long. Chickweed's lower leaves have a stalk about as long as the blade; blue pimpernel's leaves are stalkless and often indistinctly dotted with black glands underneath. Leaf size and the sprawling habit overlap and do not separate them. Chickweed's leaves and tender stem tips are eaten.

summary.text:
Blue pimpernel was long treated as a blue-flowered variety of scarlet pimpernel (Anagallis arvensis var. coerulea); Flora of New Zealand Online now treats it as a separate species, Lysimachia loeflingii, described in 2022.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands, in coastal and lowland areas, at least as far south as Canterbury, but rare south of Nelson. Naturalised from Europe and Asia Minor, first recorded in 1904.

warnings: Do not eat it. It was long treated as a blue form of scarlet pimpernel, which is poisonous: its saponins cause nausea and diarrhoea, and handling can irritate skin. No separate study of the blue plant was found.
It grows through chickweed and speedwell mats and has blue flowers like speedwell's — check every stem before picking (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text: In New Zealand it grows on the ground, mostly under introduced trees — most often oak, and also cedar, lime, silver birch, European beech and pine.

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to pick this mushroom. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.

sources: Karaduman, Uzun, Yeşilyurt & Kaya (2024), 'First record of Xerocomellus cisalpinus for Turkish Mycobiota', Biological Diversity and Conservation 17(2) (CC BY 4.0)
identification.text:
Pileus 30-50 mm in diameter, at first hemispherical, then convex to almost plane, surface dry, velvety, somewhat areolate in age, blackish to dark brown when young, pale brown to ochraceous at maturity with a reddish tint at marginal zone. Flesh whitish to creamy, soft, slightly blueing when injured. Tubes creamy yellow to pale yellow, slightly blueing when bruised. Pores almost concolorous with the tubes to olivaceous yellow, slightly blueing when injured. Taste and smell not distinctive. Stem 3−6.6(−7) × 5−9 mm, cylindrical without a ring, some slightly tapering towards the base, some slightly curved at the base or bulbose, yellow to olivaceous yellow in the upper half, gradually becoming dull red to ocher brown downwards, white fuzzy at the base, Context fibrillose and brittle, blueing when cut or bruised especially towards the base.
Basidia 32–43 × 10–11.5 µm, clavate, 2-4 spored (mainly 4). Basidiospores (10.1−)10.4−12.5(−14.3) × (3.8−)3.9−4.8(−5) µm, subfusiform, thick walled, 1-3 guttulate.
This species may have similar morphological appearance with X. chrysenteron, but the smooth spore surface of X. chrysenteron differs it from this species. Xerocomellus pruinatus also have similar spore ornamentation with X. cisalpinus. But it lacks the ability of blueing.

lookalikes.howToTell: These two are hard to tell apart in the field: macroscopic characters such as colour and cap cracking tend to intergrade between species in this group, both caps often crack, both stain blue, and both have been collected in New Zealand under silver birch. Riverine bolete's cap is described as bright red, carmine, dark red or reddish brown, often fading with age to apricot or ochre with a reddish tint; bluefoot's is usually ochre to brown, grey-brown or blackish brown, but can have a reddish tint or be entirely red. Habitat may help: riverine bolete grows in wet woodland, and its New Zealand collections are under poplar, goat willow and silver birch; about half of bluefoot's New Zealand collections are under oak, and others under cedar, lime, beech, pine and silver birch.

First Nature, 'Xerocomellus cisalpinus' — yellow flesh bruising blue-green, most strongly in the stem base, which is what the common name records; cap soon cracking to show pinkish flesh; pores lemon yellow ageing green-yellow and slowly bruising blue; mycorrhizal with both broadleaves and conifers. Described as edible but poor eating. No licence statement on the page, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/xerocomellus-cisalpinus.php

Why this entry exists. It is the species the catalogue's former 'Red-pored boletes' rule would have condemned: that page told the reader to stop if the flesh blued, and this is a common New Zealand bolete whose flesh blues and which is eaten in Europe.

Nomenclature: Biota of New Zealand holds the accepted name Xerocomellus cisalpinus (Simonini, H. Ladurner & Peintner) Klofac 2011, family Boletaceae, biostatus exotic and present here, with collections from Auckland, Gisborne, Mid Canterbury, Nelson, Wairarapa and Wellington, and the basionym Xerocomus cisalpinus Simonini, H. Ladurner & Peintner 2003 as a synonym.
