identification.text:
Annual or short-lived, sprawling or spreading perennial, (15)–20–150–(200) cm tall, densely hairy. Leaves petiolate. Lamina 5–16–(20) × 3–10–(17) cm, usually broadly ovate, entire or slightly sinuate-dentate; base subcordate or cordate; apex acuminate. Flowers solitary. Calyx densely hairy outside; teeth 3–5 mm long, narrow-triangular, acuminate. Corolla 15–22 mm diameter, pale yellow with purplish patch towards base; teeth very shallow, more or less acute. Anthers 3–3.5 mm long, violet. Fruiting calyx 3–5 cm long, 10-ribbed, hairy. Berry 10–20 mm diameter, orange; flesh sweet. Seed 1.5–2 mm diameter, broadly oblong-ellipsoid. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Apple of Peru is thought to be poisonous in most parts, probably mildly, and no record of it as food was found, so do not eat any husked berry until you have checked it. Look at the flowers, the hairs and the husk. Cape gooseberry's flowers are 15–22 mm across and pale yellow with a purplish patch near the base; apple of Peru's are bell-shaped, 3–3.5 cm long and 2.5–4.5 cm across, white and purple-marked in the lower tube and blue above. Cape gooseberry is densely hairy, with a hairy calyx; apple of Peru is almost hairless, its leaves smooth except sometimes along the main veins underneath. Cape gooseberry's calyx has five teeth 3–5 mm long and its fruiting calyx is a single inflated husk, 3–5 cm long, 10-ribbed and hairy; apple of Peru's calyx is very deeply divided into five and becomes papery in fruit with five large ribs. Cape gooseberry's leaves are 5–16 cm long (to 20), usually broadly egg-shaped, nearly entire, with a heart-shaped base; apple of Peru's are 4–17 cm, often lobed or wavy-toothed, and narrow into the stalk. Cape gooseberry is annual or short-lived, sprawling or spreading; apple of Peru is an erect annual. Several things overlap, so do not rely on them: both can stand 15–200 cm tall, both have a round berry about 1–2 cm across inside a papery husk, both flower all year, and both are garden escapes in waste places.

preparation.text: Take off the husk (the papery calyx), then eat the berry raw or cook it in jam, chutney, crumble, pies, cakes, jellies or compotes. Raw berries go in salads and salsas, and in stews in place of tomatillos. Halved berries can be dried in a low oven or a dehydrator, and the dried fruit can be used as a raisin substitute.

recipes.method: 500 g cape gooseberries; 500 g white sugar. Take off all the lantern shells, rinse and weigh the cape gooseberries. Put them in a medium-sized saucepan with a dash of water over low heat and stir until soft. Add the sugar and stir until dissolved. Bring slowly to the boil, stirring continuously. After 13–15 minutes, test for setting (a skin forms on the jam when a little is taken out on a teaspoon). Pour into hot sterilised jars and seal. The jam can also be frozen.
recipes.title: Cape gooseberry jam

recipes.method: 6 cups chopped cape gooseberries; 2 tsp salt; 1 tsp Sids Crazy Salt; ½ tsp cayenne pepper; 250 g raisins; 500 g onions; 1 tbsp ground ginger; 1 tbsp dry mustard powder; 500 g white sugar; 5 cups malt vinegar. Combine all the ingredients in a large saucepan, then simmer for 1½–2 hours until thick. Seal in hot jars. Makes about 2.5 litres.
recipes.title: Cape gooseberry chutney

recipes.method: 2 cups cape gooseberries; 1 cup sliced mango (1 can); 1 cup sliced peaches (1 can); 4 tbsp sugar; 2 cups flour; 100 g butter. Put the cape gooseberries in a pot with 2 tbsp of the sugar and bring to a simmer until soft. Turn off the heat, add the peaches and mango, mix, and put into an oven dish. In a bowl put the flour, butter and sugar and rub in the butter with your fingers until nice and crumbly. Cover the fruit mixture with the crumble and bake at 180 °C for 30–35 minutes.
recipes.title: Cape gooseberry crumble

recipes.method: 250 g cape gooseberries, husks removed; ½ cup water; ½ cup sugar; ½ cup lemon juice (about 2 lemons). Rinse the berries, put them in a stainless steel pot with the water, bring to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes. Stir in the sugar until it dissolves, then add the lemon juice, bring back to the boil and lower to a simmer. After 20 minutes, test for set by dropping a little onto a plate chilled in the freezer: if it thickens and wrinkles when pushed with a spoon it is ready; if not, cook 5 minutes more and test again. Pour into a hot sterilised jar, filling to a few millimetres from the top, and seal once cool.
recipes.title: Cape gooseberry and lemon jam

recipes.method: 2 cups cape gooseberries, halved or quartered; ½ medium red onion, diced; 1 capsicum, diced; 1 jalapeño, diced; 1 clove garlic, minced; 1 tbsp olive oil; 1 tsp honey or sugar; juice of ½ lemon; ¼ cup chopped fresh coriander; salt and pepper. Chop everything and mix well. Serve with tortilla chips or grilled fish. Keeps 2–3 days in the fridge.
recipes.title: Cape gooseberry salsa

recipes.method: Cut husked cape gooseberries in half and lay them on a tray lined with baking paper. Dry in the oven on its lowest setting for 6–8 hours, or in a dehydrator for 8–12 hours, until dry but not crisp. Store in a jar at room temperature and eat as they are or add to baking, muesli or trail mix.
recipes.title: Dried cape gooseberries

recipes.method: 225 g burrata; 170 g cape gooseberries, husked and halved; 285 g yellow cherry tomatoes, halved; 2 tbsp olive oil; 1 tsp flaky sea salt; ½ tsp ground black pepper; ¼ cup chopped soft herbs (parsley, lemon thyme, chives or oregano). Put the burrata in the middle of a large plate and arrange the cape gooseberries and tomatoes around it. Pull the burrata open to show the creamy centre, then drizzle with the oil and sprinkle with the salt, pepper and herbs. Serve with crusty bread if you like. Serves 2 as a lunch or 4 as a starter.
recipes.title: Cape gooseberry and burrata salad

recipes.method: 50 g bacon or pork lardons, chopped; 1 onion, chopped; 1–2 heads garlic, minced; 150 g cape gooseberries, husked and halved; 150 g padrón or poblano peppers (about 15); 2–3 jalapeños, seeds and membranes removed, finely chopped; 900 g pork shoulder, cubed; ½ cup chopped coriander; 1 tbsp ground cumin; 2 tsp salt; 1.5 litres water. Grill the padrón peppers about 15 cm under the grill for 3–5 minutes until blistered, then chop. In a heavy pot, fry the bacon over medium-high heat until the fat runs, add the onion, garlic, cape gooseberries and jalapeños and cook 5 minutes over medium heat, then lift out. Brown the pork in the same pot, return the bacon and vegetables, and add the peppers, coriander, cumin, salt and water. Bring to the boil, cover and simmer on the lowest heat for 4–5 hours (or in the oven at 120 °C, or a slow cooker 8 hours on low). Thirty minutes before the end, lift out the pork, shred it with two forks and return it. Serve over rice with grated cheese, or in burritos and tacos.
recipes.title: Pork chile verde with cape gooseberries

sources: Langlands, Peter. Foraging New Zealand (Penguin Random House NZ, 2024), 'Cape gooseberry' entry.

summary.text:
Physalis peruviana, the cape gooseberry (kūpere), is an exotic species in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) from tropical South America.
In New Zealand it is scattered throughout warmer areas of the North Island and South Island, especially in the North Island where it is locally common, and on Raoul Island in the Kermadec Islands. It was an early escape from cultivation, as in many other countries, and is still widely cultivated; it was brought in as a crop and naturalised by 1843. Wild herbarium collections reach as far south as Ōkārito in South Westland, Peraki Bay on Banks Peninsula and Broad Bay on Otago Peninsula, where two plants came up from discarded fruit. The golden berries are eaten and dispersed by animals and people, and birds disperse the seed. It has been known as Physalis edulis and Physalis pubescens in New Zealand.

warnings: Eat only ripe fruit. Green (unripe) berries, leaves, stems and flowers contain solanine and related alkaloids and may cause poisoning.
Do not eat the papery husk around the berry.

edibleParts.text:
Young leaves; flower buds.
All parts of the catsear plant are edible; however, the leaves and roots are those most often harvested. The root can be roasted and ground to form a coffee substitute.

habitat.text:
Lawns, paddocks, roadsides, dry banks.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Pasture, grassland, lawns, sand dunes, roadsides, riverbeds, waste ground, stony ground, railway ballast, scrub and damaged forest, swamps, up to 1400 m.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
A flat rosette like dandelion, but the leaves are rough with stiff hairs, where dandelion's are hairless and jaggedly toothed. Flower stalks are solid, wiry and branch into several yellow flowers; dandelion's are hollow, unbranched and carry one flower each.
Perennial. Stems ascending to erect, usually branched, glabrous or with a few sparse hairs below, 4–60–(150) cm tall. Leaves all basal, oblanceolate to linear-oblanceolate, usually shallowly to deeply pinnatifid, rarely simple and toothed, (2)–4–20–(40) × (0.5)–0.8–4–(9) cm, with moderately dense pale strigose hairs. Stem bracts few, minute. Capitula turbinate to campanulate. Involucral bracts linear-lanceolate with narrowly acute apex, 6–15 mm long at flowering, up to 20 mm long at fruiting, glabrous except for a row of strigose hairs on midrib (the distal hairs dark), herbaceous or with narrow scarious border. Florets yellow, about 1½× length of involucre. Achenes dark brown, scabrid, fusiform, beaked, 8–16 mm long, sometimes the outer achenes not or shortly beaked and then shorter. Pappus in 2 rows, the outer hairs short, slender, scabrid to plumose, the inner up to 12 mm long, plumose.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Beaked hawksbeard's flowering stems are ribbed to grooved and carry leaves of their own; catsear's leaves are all in the basal rosette and its stems carry only a few tiny bracts. Beaked hawksbeard's stems are hairy, with fine crinkly white hairs and stout, spreading, red-based ones; catsear's are hairless or have a few sparse hairs low down. Under the flower head, beaked hawksbeard's bracts have pale cobwebby hairs and often dark glandular hairs; catsear's are hairless except for a row of stiff hairs along the midrib. Beaked hawksbeard's seed parachute is of fine white bristles; catsear's is feathery. Leaf shape does not separate them: beaked hawksbeard's leaves are usually deeply lobed with lobes pointing back, and catsear's are usually shallowly to deeply lobed. Hairy leaves, branched stems and height do not separate them either.
lookalikes.name: Beaked hawksbeard

lookalikes.howToTell: A dandelion's flower stem is hollow, leafless and unbranched, with a single head; catsear's stems are usually branched, solid, carry a few tiny bracts and can carry several heads. A dandelion's leaves are hairless or carry sparse short hairs, mostly on the midrib above; catsear's have moderately dense, stiff, pale hairs. Both have a rosette of lobed leaves, yellow heads and milky sap, so none of those separates them. The dandelion's leaves, flowers and roots are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Dandelion

lookalikes.howToTell: Out of flower the two are strikingly similar. Use a hand lens on the leaf hairs: hawkbit's fork into two, sometimes three, at the tip; catsear's are simple. In flower, hawkbit's stem is unbranched, with a single head and at most a few tiny bracts; catsear's stems are usually branched and can carry several heads, so an unbranched stem alone does not settle it. Pulling a head apart also works: catsear has thin scales among the florets on the flower base, hawkbit has none. Both have hairy rosette leaves that are often lobed, yellow heads and milky sap. Hawkbit's leaves are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Hawkbit

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the bracts under the flower head. Catsear's carry a row of stiff hairs along the midrib — dark near the tip, usually pale near the base — like a miniature cock's comb; smooth cat's ear's are always hairless, the inner ones with broad papery margins. Catsear's florets stand about one and a half times as long as the bracts, smooth cat's ear's about as long, and smooth cat's ear's heads are narrowly cylindrical where catsear's are top-shaped to bell-shaped. Catsear's leaves have moderately dense stiff pale hairs; smooth cat's ear's are hairless or sometimes sparsely hairy, so leaf hair is a clue, not a test. Catsear is a perennial; smooth cat's ear is an annual, rarely perennial. Stems do not separate them: catsear's are usually branched, smooth cat's ear's sparingly branched or not. Catsear's heads are larger, 2–4 cm across against 0.5–1.5 cm (measured on British plants). The seeds differ: catsear's are beaked and 8–16 mm long, though the outer ones are sometimes short- or unbeaked; smooth cat's ear's outer seeds are never beaked and 4–5 mm long, and only the inner ones carry a beak, up to 8 mm long. The two hybridise, so a plant with mixed features may be neither. Both have yellow heads and milky sap. Smooth cat's ear's young leaves are eaten, though somewhat bitter (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Smooth cat's ear

lookalikes.howToTell: The surest test is inside the head: catsear has thin, tapering scales among the florets on the flower base, nearly transparent apart from their yellow tips and easily missed; autumn hawkbit has none. Autumn hawkbit's leaves are hairless or have sparse simple hairs, nowhere near as many or as stiff as catsear's. Its branched stems carry many small narrow bracts, especially near the top, where catsear's carry only a few minute ones, and its head tapers gradually into the stem, where catsear's narrows more abruptly. Both usually have branched stems with several yellow heads, rosettes of lobed leaves, and milky sap. Autumn hawkbit's leaves are used like dandelion and catsear leaves (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Autumn hawkbit

lookalikes.howToTell: Mouse-ear hawkweed's leaves are untoothed or very obscurely toothed, with a very dense coat of star-shaped hairs that makes the underside white, and the plant spreads by creeping runners; catsear's leaves are usually lobed, rarely just toothed, with moderately dense pale bristly hairs. Mouse-ear hawkweed has a single head on each stem; catsear's stems are usually branched. Catsear has thin scales among the florets on the flower base, mouse-ear hawkweed none. Catsear's achenes are 8–16 mm and mostly beaked with feathery inner pappus hairs; mouse-ear hawkweed's are about 2 mm, unbeaked, with simple bristles. Both form hairy rosettes with yellow heads and milky sap, and stem heights and leaf lengths overlap. No food use of mouse-ear hawkweed is recorded; its traditional uses are medicinal (see its page).

preparation.text:
Leaves are bitter and hairy raw — better wilted or in soup. Buds can be pickled. Treat it as a coarser dandelion.
In Spain the rosette leaves were eaten cooked: at El Atazar and Cervera (Madrid) they were stripped down to the midrib, which was boiled, then fried and eaten in scrambled eggs or stews. In the Serranía de Cuenca the plant was eaten in salads, and at Reinosa (Cantabria) the young leaves were eaten during the war.
Young leaves are slightly bitter to bland; older ones are stringy. Eat them raw in salads, steamed, or tossed in a pan with oil and garlic and finished with lemon and salt. Some Greek households use it as the green in hortopita. The flowers can be infused in honey or coated in flour for fritters, and the petals make a garnish.
Cooking reduces the bitterness but never removes it.

recipes.method: Dig up the roots, scrub them, roast them lightly in the oven, then grind them and brew to taste. No temperature, time or quantity is given; the dandelion root coffee on the dandelion page has them, for dandelion root.
recipes.title: Catsear root coffee

recipes.method: Flowering catsear stems with their buds and flowers; extra virgin olive oil; garlic salt, or whatever seasoning you like; petals from a fresh flower. Pick flowering stems with their buds and flowers; a good patch gives enough for dinner in a couple of minutes. Wash them and put them in a pot with a shallow layer of water, cover, and steam over medium heat until soft. Then fry them in extra virgin olive oil with garlic salt, or whatever seasoning you like, over medium-high heat until lightly golden. Scatter with petals from a fresh flower to serve.
recipes.title: Steamed and fried catsear buds

recipes.method: 300 g orecchiette; 225 g catsear leaves; 1–2 garlic cloves; a drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil; salt; freshly ground black pepper; 2–3 generous handfuls (more than 250 ml) of shredded Asiago. Cut the root off the catsear, keep the greenest leaves and wash them three or four times, more if the plants grew where dogs or cats go. Gently fry one garlic clove in a drizzle of olive oil in a wide pan, add the catsear with a splash of water and cook until the greens are tender and the water has gone; season with salt and pepper and take off the heat. Cook the orecchiette in salted boiling water until they float, drain, tip them into the pan and toss over the heat for a few minutes. Lift out the garlic, stir in the Asiago at the very end and serve at once.
recipes.title: Orecchiette with catsear greens and Asiago

recipes.method: Makes one thin omelette per egg: a fistful of boiled, squeezed catsear leaves (about a small handful once cooked); 1 egg; 1 tbsp grated Parmesan; a pinch of salt; olive oil for the pan. Wash the picked leaves well and boil them in water for a few minutes. Squeeze the greens dry, shape them into a ball a little larger than a walnut and chop it finely. Mix the chopped greens in a bowl with the egg, Parmesan and salt. Pour the mixture into a small oiled frying pan, cover and cook over a very low heat until set, then turn the omelette over to cook the other side.
recipes.title: Thin catsear omelettes (frittatine)

summary.text:
Flatweed. The dandelion lookalike with hairy leaves and branched, wiry flower stalks. It is edible too.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): throughout the North and South Islands; Stewart Island; Kermadec, Chatham and Campbell Islands. Naturalised from Europe and North Africa, first recorded in 1867.
Often more common than dandelion.

warnings: Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed. Pick from ground you know.

harvestEthics.text:
Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.
Exotic caulerpa is an unwanted organism: the Biosecurity Act forbids knowingly spreading it, and removing it from a site needs MPI's consent. If seaweed snags on your anchor, chain or gear, bag it so it can't get back into the sea and put it in a rubbish bin ashore; if you can't contain it securely at sea, put it back into the water it came from. It can survive out of water for a week or more if kept moist, as in an anchor locker or a bunched-up net, so check before moving on.
Legal rules on anchoring and fishing apply in MPI's controlled areas at Aotea Great Barrier Island, Ahuahu Great Mercury Island, Hauturu Little Barrier Island, Waiheke Island and Te Rawhiti Inlet in the Bay of Islands; report suspected exotic caulerpa to MPI on 0800 80 99 66.

identification.text: Bright green, flat blades shaped like oars, up to 10 cm long, rise from long horizontal runners (stolons). Established plants can cover large areas of seabed in dense mats. Caulerpa brachypus and Caulerpa parvifolia look identical and can be told apart only by genetic analysis; together they are known as exotic caulerpa. Native caulerpas, such as sea grapes, are sometimes mistaken for it, but their fronds are three-dimensional or bead-like rather than flat blades.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fronds. Exotic caulerpa has flat, bright green blades shaped like oars, up to 10 cm long, rising from long runners; sea grapes, a native seaweed, has glossy branchlets swollen like tiny grapes, in bunches on short upright stems, and grows on rock walls and in rock pools from low on the shore down to about 15 m. Native caulerpas like sea grapes are sometimes mistaken for exotic caulerpa, including when washed up after storms. If the fronds are flat blades, don't pick them: report them to MPI on 0800 80 99 66.
lookalikes.name: Sea grapes

lookalikes.howToTell: You can't tell them apart by eye: Caulerpa brachypus and Caulerpa parvifolia look identical and only genetic analysis separates them. Both are exotic caulerpa, an unwanted organism, so treat either the same way: don't take or move it, and report it to MPI on 0800 80 99 66.

summary.text:
Caulerpa brachypus is one of two introduced green seaweeds known together as exotic caulerpa; it comes from the Indo-Pacific, from Africa to Western Australia, the Pacific Islands and southern Japan.
Exotic caulerpa was first found in New Zealand in July 2021 at Aotea Great Barrier Island and has since been confirmed around the Hauraki Gulf, at Coromandel and in Northland, including the Bay of Islands and Whangārei Harbour; it is not known from the South Island. It probably arrived on a vessel from Australia or the Pacific.
It spreads fast, by growth from its runners and as fragments carried by storms, currents, boats and fishing and diving gear; even very small fragments can start new patches. It forms dense fields that smother native seagrass, seaweeds and shellfish beds, and grows over live scallops. It has been an unwanted organism since September 2021.

warnings: Do not eat, take or move it. Exotic caulerpa is an unwanted organism: the Biosecurity Act forbids knowingly spreading it, and removing it from a site needs MPI's consent. If you find it, note the place, take a photo and report it to MPI on 0800 80 99 66 or at report.mpi.govt.nz.
Sea grapes, a native seaweed that is eaten, grows on rocky shores in the same northern waters. Check the fronds before picking (see Lookalikes).

harvestEthics.text:
Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.
Exotic caulerpa is an unwanted organism: the Biosecurity Act forbids knowingly spreading it, and removing it from a site needs MPI's consent. If seaweed snags on your anchor, chain or gear, bag it so it can't get back into the sea and put it in a rubbish bin ashore; if you can't contain it securely at sea, put it back into the water it came from. It can survive out of water for a week or more if kept moist, as in an anchor locker or a bunched-up net, so check before moving on.
Legal rules on anchoring and fishing apply in MPI's controlled areas at Aotea Great Barrier Island, Ahuahu Great Mercury Island, Hauturu Little Barrier Island, Waiheke Island and Te Rawhiti Inlet in the Bay of Islands; report suspected exotic caulerpa to MPI on 0800 80 99 66.

identification.text: Bright green, flat blades shaped like oars, up to 10 cm long, rise from long horizontal runners (stolons). Established plants can cover large areas of seabed in dense mats. Caulerpa parvifolia and Caulerpa brachypus look identical and can be told apart only by genetic analysis; together they are known as exotic caulerpa. Native caulerpas, such as sea grapes, are sometimes mistaken for it, but their fronds are three-dimensional or bead-like rather than flat blades.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fronds. Exotic caulerpa has flat, bright green blades shaped like oars, up to 10 cm long, rising from long runners; sea grapes, a native seaweed, has glossy branchlets swollen like tiny grapes, in bunches on short upright stems, and grows on rock walls and in rock pools from low on the shore down to about 15 m. Native caulerpas like sea grapes are sometimes mistaken for exotic caulerpa, including when washed up after storms. If the fronds are flat blades, don't pick them: report them to MPI on 0800 80 99 66.
lookalikes.name: Sea grapes

lookalikes.howToTell: You can't tell them apart by eye: Caulerpa brachypus and Caulerpa parvifolia look identical and only genetic analysis separates them. Both are exotic caulerpa, an unwanted organism, so treat either the same way: don't take or move it, and report it to MPI on 0800 80 99 66.

Exotic caulerpa was first found in New Zealand in July 2021 at Aotea Great Barrier Island and has since been confirmed around the Hauraki Gulf, at Coromandel and in Northland, including the Bay of Islands and Whangārei Harbour; it is not known from the South Island. identification.text:
Erect terrestrial biennial, not rooting at nodes. Stems hollow, grooved, striate, up to 80–(100) cm high. Basal leaves 1–2-pinnate, with a leaf stalk; ultimate segments deltate or rhombic, lobed and crenate or dentate near apex, 2–4 cm long, more or less without a stalk; stem leaves similar to basal but often without a leaf stalk and becoming 1-pinnate or 3-foliolate with elliptic-obovate, entire or lobed segments. Umbels 2–5 cm in diameter, compound, more or less without a stalk and leaf-opposed, and so appearing bracteate; rays 4–15; bracts and bracteoles 0. Flowers numerous, greenish white, about 1 mm in diameter. Fruit broadly ovoid, dark brown, 1.5–2 mm long; ribs light brown, thread-thin.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
All parts of the plant smell strongly of celery. Descriptions differ on the stems: Flora of New Zealand gives them as hollow, British floras as solid, so do not lean on that.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand; all parts are poisonous if eaten. Look under the umbels: hemlock has about 4–8 narrow, pointed, down-turned bracts beneath each umbel and 3–6 bracteoles on the outer side of each small umbel; celery has none, though its umbels sit almost without a stalk opposite a leaf and so can look as if they had a bract. Hemlock grows up to 2–(3) m, its hollow stems usually purple spotted or blotched, though the spots can be missing or hard to see on young plants; celery reaches 80–(100) cm. Hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided into segments 5–40 mm long, celery's 1–2 times divided into lobed segments 2–4 cm long. Hemlock's flowers are white, about 2 mm across, and its fruit 2.5–3 mm long; celery's flowers are greenish white, about 1 mm across, and its fruit 1.5–2 mm long. Hemlock smells foetid when crushed and celery smells strongly of celery, but no source here treats smell as a reliable test on its own. Both grow in damp waste places, so place does not rule hemlock out.
lookalikes.name: Hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: Look under the small umbels: water celery always has 4–8 small bracteoles there, and celery has none. Water celery lies along the ground or rises from it and roots at its lower nodes; celery stands erect and does not root at the nodes. Water celery's leaves are once-pinnate, with 2–8 pairs of toothed leaflets 1–8 cm long (up to 12); celery's are 1–2-pinnate, with lobed segments 2–4 cm long. Both grow in wet ground, so place does not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Water celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Garden celery found wild can look very similar to sea celery, including on the Chatham Islands. Celery is an erect biennial up to 80–(100) cm tall; sea celery lies along the ground or rises from it. Celery has no bracts or bracteoles under its umbels, and sea celery usually has none (at most a single bract that soon falls), so that check does not separate them. The surest difference is the ripe fruit: celery's are dark brown with thread-thin ribs, sea celery's have broad, spongy ribs. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Sea celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Alexanders' flowers are yellowish; wild celery's are greenish white and about 1 mm across. Alexanders' umbels are 6–7 cm across, on rays 2–4 cm long; wild celery's are 2–5 cm across, almost stalkless and set opposite a leaf, with no bracts. Alexanders' leaves are divided in threes into flat, lobed, toothed leaflets, but wild celery's stem leaves can be in threes too, so leaf shape alone does not separate them. Alexanders' fruits are black and 6.5–8 mm long; wild celery's are dark brown and 1.5–2 mm. Both grow in waste places. Alexanders is eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Alexanders

lookalikes.howToTell: Celery-leaved buttercup is one of the most toxic buttercups; chewing it blisters the mouth and lips. Look at the flowers: celery's are greenish white, about 1 mm across, many together in compound umbels 2–5 cm across that sit almost without a stalk opposite a leaf; the buttercup's are pale yellow, 6–10 mm across, with 5 petals and 5 sepals bent back, each on its own stalk. In fruit, celery's are broadly ovoid, dark brown and 1.5–2 mm long; the buttercup has a cylindrical green head of hundreds of tiny seeds, each about 1 mm long. Look at the lower leaves: celery's are pinnate, divided into separate segments 2–4 cm long along the leaf stalk; the buttercup's are a single shiny, rounded blade with a heart-shaped base, mostly 3–5 cm long, deeply cut into 3 or sometimes 5 lobes with scalloped edges. Celery's stem leaves can be in threes, so check the lower leaves. Both stand erect (celery to 100 cm, the buttercup to 75 cm) and grow in wet ground, so height and place do not separate them. Celery-leaved buttercup is poisonous; do not eat any part of it.
lookalikes.name: Celery-leaved buttercup

preparation.text: Pull the tough strings off the stalks before cooking; a stalk separates readily into them. Chopped with onion and carrot, celery is the base of many soups and sauces. The stalks can be pickled: take off the leaves, boil the stalks in water, then add vinegar, salt and oil. Dry the leaves in a single layer in the oven at 180 °C for 5–7 minutes, or in a pan over medium-low heat, until crisp but not browned. Ground seeds mixed with salt, or crumbled dried leaves mixed with salt, make celery salt. It flowers from November to March, and the seeds follow the flowers.

recipes.method: Written for shop-bought celery. Makes about 240 ml, depending on the leaves. 1 bunch of celery, for its leaves; an equal volume of flaky sea salt. Pick the leaves off the stalks, outer and inner, leaving the stems behind. Rinse them in a sieve under cold water, shake off as much water as you can and pat them dry in a clean tea towel, so they toast rather than steam. Spread them in a single layer on a baking tray and bake at 180 °C for 5–7 minutes, or toast them in a large frying pan over medium-low heat, until dry and crisp but not browned. Let them cool completely, crumble them with your fingers, discarding any that aren't crisp, and mix with an equal amount of salt in a jar. The author prefers flaky salt, whose flakes match the crumbled leaves in size.
recipes.title: Homemade celery salt

recipes.method: Written for shop-bought celery. Serves 3–4. 30 ml (2 Tbsp) olive oil; 300 g celery, sliced, tough strings removed; 1 garlic clove, peeled; 200 g potatoes, peeled and cut into chunks; 500 ml vegetable stock; 100 ml milk; crusty bread, to serve. Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat, add the celery, garlic and potatoes and stir to coat. Add a splash of water and a big pinch of salt and cook for 15 minutes, stirring often and adding a little more water if the vegetables start to stick. Pour in the stock, bring to the boil, then simmer for 20 minutes until the potatoes fall apart and the celery is soft. Blend smooth with a stick blender, add the milk and blend again. Season and serve with crusty bread.
recipes.title: Celery soup

recipes.method: Written for shop-bought celery. Serves 6. 200 g bulgur wheat; 1 bunch celery, with its leaves; 1 apple; juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (4 Tbsp) olive oil; a handful of toasted hazelnuts, roughly chopped; 1 red chilli, deseeded and chopped; a large handful of pomegranate seeds; a small bunch each of parsley, mint and tarragon, chopped. Put the bulgur in a large bowl, just cover it with boiling water, cover the bowl and leave for 30 minutes to absorb the water. Meanwhile separate the celery stalks, set the leaves aside, slice the stalks very finely and roughly chop the leaves. Cut the apple into fine matchsticks and toss them in a little of the lemon juice. Whisk the rest of the lemon juice with the oil and some seasoning. Fluff the bulgur with a fork, then mix in the sliced celery and apple, then the nuts, chilli, pomegranate seeds and herbs. Pour over the dressing, toss gently and scatter with the celery leaves. It keeps in the fridge for a few days.
recipes.title: Celery and bulgur salad

recipes.method: Written for shop-bought celery; the recipe is by Ignacio Mattos. Serves 8 with grilled fish. 360 ml (1½ US cups) finely chopped parsley; 120 ml (½ US cup) finely chopped celery leaves; 1 garlic clove, finely grated; ½ lemon; ½ tsp mild red pepper flakes, such as Aleppo; 180 ml (¾ US cup) extra-virgin olive oil; salt and black pepper. Mix the parsley, celery leaves and garlic in a bowl. Finely zest the lemon into the bowl and squeeze in its juice. Add the pepper flakes, stir in the oil and season with salt and pepper. Leave for 10 minutes for the flavours to come together. The author serves it with whole turbot grilled in foil, and aioli.
recipes.title: Celery leaf salsa verde

recipes.method: Written for shop-bought celery; the recipe is by Najmieh Batmanglij, a vegetarian version of a stew traditionally made with lamb. Serves 6. 120 ml olive oil; 675 g cremini mushrooms, cleaned and thickly sliced; 8 celery stalks, washed and cut into sticks about 6 mm by 5 cm; 1 medium onion, thinly sliced; 2 garlic cloves, thinly sliced; 1 jalapeño, finely chopped, or ½ tsp red pepper flakes; 2 tsp sea salt; ½ tsp ground black pepper; 710 ml water; ½ tsp ground saffron dissolved in 30 ml water (optional); 45 ml (3 Tbsp) lime juice; 80 g chopped parsley; 40 g chopped mint, or 15 ml (1 Tbsp) dried mint; 45 ml (3 Tbsp) dried fenugreek leaves; Persian rice, to serve (optional). Heat the oil in a heavy pot over high heat and sauté the mushrooms for 5 minutes. Add the celery, onion, garlic and jalapeño and sauté 10 minutes more, then stir in the salt and pepper. Add the water, bring to the boil, then cover and simmer over medium heat for 40 minutes. Stir in the saffron, lime juice, parsley, mint and fenugreek, cover and simmer over medium-low heat for another 5 minutes, or until the celery is tender. Adjust the seasoning and keep warm until you serve it.
recipes.title: Persian celery stew with mushrooms (khoresh-e karafs)

recipes.method: Written for plantain and dandelion, with celery leaves and parsley (the page does not say which plantain). A small handful of celery leaves; 4 branches of parsley (go easy: it can take over); 4 leaves each of plantain, dandelion and kale. Blend the greens in 750 ml–1 litre (3–4 cups) water, then add 1 banana, 250 ml (1 cup) frozen blueberries, 1 kiwifruit and ½ avocado and blend again.
recipes.title: Thick and creamy green smoothie

Habitat tags checked 27/10/2026 (owner: 'double check' the coastal tag): `coastal` removed, `wetland` kept. No New Zealand source puts celery on the coast: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV gives 'Waste places, often palustral, not common.', and the coastal words in the habitat text are Wikipedia's native-range sentence (Britain and Europe). Flora's localities include islands and the west coast of Wellington Province, but name no shore habitat. On iNaturalist NZ, 4 of the 42 wild research-grade records are named after Horowhenua and Manawatū beaches (Hokio, Ōtaki, Kuku, Himatangi Beach; one observer, 2019); their photos show low plants among rushes and grass with no shore in view, one noted 'In a particularly wet location' — damp ground, with nothing to show the sea's edge as the `coastal` tag defines it (shore, dunes, estuary, saltmarsh). The rest are in towns, by a creek, in a ditch, and on Banks Peninsula and Lyttelton roadsides. `wetland` rests on Flora's 'often palustral'.

summary.text:
Apium graveolens, commonly known as celery, is an Old World species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae.
Wild celery is native to much of Eurasia, ranging from Ireland in the west, through Europe north to Scotland, Denmark and Poland, and east to the Caucasus and Central Asia, and as far as the western Himalayas, and also through Macaronesia and North Africa to West Asia and the Arabian Peninsula. It is widely naturalised outside this range, including in Scandinavia, North and South America, Africa, India, central, eastern and southern Asia, and New Zealand. The cultivar groups may also be naturalised.
In New Zealand it is an exotic from Eurasia, called wild celery, and not common. Flora of New Zealand (1988) records it in the North Island from the Three Kings Islands, Kaitaia and Kaitara in Northland, Rangitoto Island, Coromandel and the west coast of Wellington Province; in the South Island from the Marlborough Sounds and Christchurch; and on the Chatham Islands and Campbell Island. Its first New Zealand record, from 1832, was most probably native sea celery misidentified. The garden vegetable, grown for its leaf stalks, is a form of this species, and garden celery is reported growing wild.
In New Zealand it has escaped from vegetable gardens. The offspring of escaped cultivars soon go back to the wild form, leafier and less stalky, much like parsley; they grow in scattered places throughout the country but are not among the easiest wild plants to find (Knox 2013, restated).

warnings: Hemlock, one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand, also has white flowers in compound umbels and grows in the same damp waste places. Before you pick, check under the umbels and along the stems as described in Lookalikes.
Celery is a food allergen: in people allergic to it, it can cause a potentially fatal anaphylactic reaction, and it has caused skin rashes and cross-reactions with carrot and ragweed.

Celery sap on the skin followed by sunlight can cause phytophotodermatitis: 24–48 hours later the skin turns red and inflamed and often blisters, and dark marks can stay for several years. Vegetable pickers get it on their hands and fingers; gloves prevent it. Eating plants rich in the same chemicals can make the skin more sensitive to sunlight generally, and celery seeds have caused it.

identification.text:
Annual; roots all fibrous. Stems stout, erect, hairless or with sparse pressed-down hairs, (10)–30–60–(75) cm tall. Basal and lower stem leaves broadly ovate to kidney-shaped, heart-shaped at the base, deeply 3–(5)-lobed, hairless or with fine pressed-down hairs, (1)–3–5–(8) × (1.5)–4–6–(10) cm; lobes obovate-wedge-shaped, again shallowly 3-lobed and with scalloped margins; leaf stalks hairless, (2)–5–10–(30) cm long. Upper stem leaves similar; lobes becoming lanceolate, entire; uppermost leaves almost without a stalk, not lobed, becoming finely pressed-hairy. Flowers usually more than 30 per stem, 6–10 mm in diameter. Flower stalks erect, numerous, with sparse, fine hairs, grooved, 2.5–4–(6) cm long at fruiting. Sepals 5, hairy, bent back, acute, 3–4 mm long. Petals 5, pale yellow, broadly obovate, 3–4 × 2.5 mm; nectary single, 0.5 mm from petal base, pocket-like. Receptacle elongated, cylindrical, hairy. Achenes (100)–200–400–(700), in cylindrical heads, hairless, hardly flattened, weakly keeled, obovoid, weakly wrinkled; body about 1 × 0.8 mm; beak less than 0.5 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
A fleshy buttercup with shiny leaves that looks superficially like a young celery plant, but has small pale yellow five-petalled flowers, 0.5–1 cm across, and cylindrical green fruit heads on a much-branched flowering top to an upright leafy stem up to 60 cm tall. It is told from other buttercups by its hairless, deeply 3–5-lobed leaves, upright rather than creeping growth, sepals bent back and cylindrical rather than rounded fruit head.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers: celery-leaved buttercup's are pale yellow, 6–10 mm across, with 5 petals and 5 sepals bent back, each on its own stalk; celery's are greenish white, about 1 mm across, many together in compound umbels 2–5 cm across that sit almost without a stalk opposite a leaf. In fruit, the buttercup has a cylindrical green head of hundreds of tiny seeds, each about 1 mm long; celery's fruits are broadly ovoid, dark brown and 1.5–2 mm long. Look at the lower leaves: the buttercup's are a single shiny, rounded blade with a heart-shaped base, mostly 3–5 cm long, deeply cut into 3 or sometimes 5 lobes with scalloped edges; celery's are pinnate, divided into separate segments 2–4 cm long along the leaf stalk. Celery's stem leaves can be in threes, so check the lower leaves. Both stand erect (the buttercup to 75 cm, celery to 100 cm) and grow in wet ground, so height and place do not separate them. Celery is eaten (see its page).

Flora of New Zealand Online factsheet (https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/taxon/Ranunculus-sceleratus.html) — the Webb et al. 1988 description already used verbatim in identification; no change. Eat The Weeds tag page (https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/ranunculus-sceleratus/) — a second overseas food record ('leaves boiled and or fermented', in a genus-wide list of buttercups that have been eaten); recorded in edible-parts sources but not given: caution stays doNotEat on the New Zealand poisoning records (Sykes 2002 for the National Poisons Centre, Stewart 1971 for the Department of Health, NZPCN), as for redroot amaranth (NZ poisoning record over overseas food records); its '2.5% Protoanemonin (dry weight basis)' matches the Wikipedia figure already cited, not added; 'Extracts of R. sceleratus are good against plant fungus' is a second record of PFAF's fungicide line, now in docs/plans/useful-plants.md (the PFAF line said it was owed there and it was missing); its dye (light fawn with alum, green with chrome, yellow with tin) is written for buttercup flowers in general, not this species, not used. summary.text:
Celery-leaved buttercup (Ranunculus sceleratus), also called poison buttercup, is a poisonous annual of the buttercup family (Ranunculaceae) from Europe, south-western and central Asia and northern and tropical Africa, naturalised in New Zealand.
It is scattered throughout the North and South Islands and was first recorded wild in 1878, probably arriving as a seed or soil contaminant; its seed is spread by water, animals and contaminated machinery. It is one of the most toxic buttercups. Robust plants resemble celery, and it is sometimes eaten by mistake.

warnings: Do not eat any part of celery-leaved buttercup. It is one of the most toxic buttercups, and the fresh plant is poisonous, its leaves and flowers included.

Chewing it blisters the mouth and lips; the bitter, burning taste usually stops it being swallowed. Swallowed, it can cause abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and a slowed pulse, and eaten in quantity it can kill. If any has been eaten, phone the National Poisons Centre, 0800 POISON (0800 764 766).
Its acrid sap can blister the skin.

Its shiny, divided leaves resemble celery's, and it is sometimes eaten by mistake. Both grow in wet ground, so check the flowers and lower leaves before picking anything celery-like from a ditch or stream (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text: It is found growing by Nothofagaceae (beech).

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to harvest this mushroom, you can look at it and photograph it without disturbing.

identification.text: Cap is 3–5.5 cm in diameter. Golden yellow, apricot or occasionally reddish orange, dry and finely felted. Stalk is 2–3.5 cm long and 5–8 mm in diameter. It has no gills, the under part has dull red pores and looks spongy.

lookalikes.howToTell: Do not decide on the tree. This endemic grows under native beech, but the introduced peppery bolete, usually found with fly agaric under pines and introduced broadleaved trees, also turns up in beech forest where fly agaric has become naturalised. Cap colour helps but the ranges meet at orange. This one's cap is golden yellow, apricot or occasionally reddish orange, dry and finely felted. The peppery bolete's is fawn to light brown, brownish orange or cinnamon brown, and slightly slimy when wet. Look at the stem. The peppery bolete's stem is golden yellow at the base, with yellow flesh. This one's stem matches the cap or is reddish, pale yellow at the very top, with pale reddish-brown flesh. A crumb of the peppery bolete, chewed and spat out, is acrid and peppery; this one's taste is not distinctive.
lookalikes.name: Peppery bolete

sources: iNaturalist NZ. 22 of the world's 23 records are New Zealand ones, and iNaturalist lists it as endemic here. Checked 07/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/taxa/409342

Season: iNaturalist NZ month-of-year histogram — April 7, May 6, February 3, January 2, March 2. Too few records to read a season from with any confidence; set to the months that hold records at all, which is January to May. Checked 07/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/taxa/409342

New Zealand Plant Conservation Network, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus' — biostatus native; recorded from Nelson and Southland; gregarious or caespitose under Nothofagus; fruiting March and May. No common name is given. All rights reserved, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/chalciporus-aurantiacus/

Virtual Mycota, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus' — the McNabb description, in copyright, so the prose cannot be rendered and only its data is taken here. Cap 3–5.5 cm; tubes to 3 mm; pores 0.5–1 mm; stipe 2–3.5 cm long by 5–8 mm; spores 7.2–9 × 4.2–5.2 µm per McNabb and 7–9 × 4.2–6 µm per Pegler & Young; basidia 32–45 × 8–10 µm; cystidia 42–60 × 5.5–10 µm. Cap golden yellow, apricot or reddish orange; hymenophore dull red; stipe concolorous with the cap or reddish, pallid yellow at the apex; context sordid pallid fawn to yellowish fawn. Gregarious or caespitose under Nothofagus. The accounts are McNabb 1968, New Zealand Journal of Botany 6(2): 137–176, and Pegler & Young 1981, Transactions of the British Mycological Society 76(1): 103–146. The page's E. Horak photograph is Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial 3.0 New Zealand — a licence this project accepts — so it is the first real candidate for the photo this entry is blocked on. Checked 07/10/2026. https://virtualmycota.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/vM_Species_Details.aspx?pk=27591

New Zealand Organisms Register, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus (McNabb) Pegler & T.W.K. Young' — endemic; basionym Xerocomus aurantiacus McNabb. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.nzor.org.nz/names/169c81df-1fb4-4b19-9e3e-35ac5693f7c6

Conservation, global. IUCN/Global Fungal Red List assessment by J.A. Cooper, 26/07/2019 — Data Deficient, because the population size is uncertain and a decline is possible. Known from 23 records at 13 localities, with only 5 confirmed sightings since 2013 against 52 for the invasive C. piperatus in the same period; an estimate of up to 15,000 mature individuals across roughly 1,000 unrecorded sites. Recorded from both the North and South Islands, in beech forest. Ecology: likely a parasite on indigenous ectomycorrhizal fungi rather than mycorrhizal with the beech itself, host unknown, which may be what restricts it — so habitat prose should not say it partners with Nothofagus, only that it grows under it. Threat: displacement by the introduced C. piperatus and its host Amanita muscaria, which now occupy all but one recorded location of this species. No open licence on the page, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://redlist.info/iucn/species_view/112183/

Biota of New Zealand, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus (McNabb) Pegler & T.W.K. Young 1981' — endemic and present. A third synonym beyond the basionym: Boletus aurantiacus (McNabb) G. Stev. 1982. Hosts given as Nothofagus menziesii and N. truncata. Recorded from Buller, Fiordland, Marlborough Sounds, Nelson, Taupo, Wairarapa and Wellington, with historical records from Southland — a much wider range than the Nelson and Southland the NZPCN page gives, so the habitat text should not be written to the narrower claim. Images are under varying copyright and no blanket licence is stated, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/1cb1d0b5-36b9-11d5-9548-00d0592d548c

Landcare Research Fungal Guide, genus Chalciporus — the genus is characterised by reddish pores and bright yellow mycelium at the stipe base, with a viscid cap and a cinnamon to flesh-brown spore print. Two species here: C. aurantiacus, endemic, under native Nothofagus, with a golden yellow, apricot or reddish brown cap and a dull red pore surface; and C. piperatus, exotic, under pines and introduced broadleaves, usually close to Amanita muscaria. That contrast — native beech versus pine, and cap and pore colour — is the axis a person can write the lookalike guidance on. No licence statement, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://fungalguide.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/FG_Genus.aspx?Group=Chalciporus&pk=24737

Queensland Mycological Society, 'Queensland Fungal Record: Chalciporus aff. aurantiacus', P. Leonard, last updated 09/10/2017 — NOT this species. It is an Australian collection growing with Eucalyptus, and the record's own notes say the Queensland material is distinct from the New Zealand fungus: smaller, with pinkish red pores and narrower spores. Its measurements must not be used to describe the endemic. Recorded here only so the next person knows the near-relative exists and why it was set aside. © Queensland Mycological Society. Checked 07/10/2026. https://qldfungi.org.au/wp-content/uploads/FoQs/C-Misc/Chalciporus-aff-aurantiacus.pdf

Wikipedia contributors, 'Chalciporus' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — genus of Boletaceae, suborder Boletineae, about 25 species, erected by Frédéric Bataille in 1908. Boletoid fruit bodies with pores in shades of red to pink, stipes lacking reticulation, yellow mycelium and smooth oval spores. C. aurantiacus appears in the species list but the article carries no description of it and does not mention New Zealand at all. The genus prose is openly licensed and could be quoted verbatim as genus context if that is wanted, but there is no species prose here to render. Retrieved 07/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalciporus

Wikidata, Q10448162 — identifiers, for anyone chasing this further: GBIF 2524866, iNaturalist 409342, Index Fungorum 112183, NZOR 169c81df-1fb4-4b19-9e3e-35ac5693f7c6. Two of its claims are wrong or stale and are recorded here so they are not picked up again. It gives the basionym as Xerocomelus aurantiacus; Index Fungorum and NZOR both give Xerocomus aurantiacus McNabb, which is the one to use, with Boletus aurantiacus (McNabb) G. Stev. an illegitimate later name. And it reports an NZTCS status of Nationally Critical, which is the superseded Hitchmough 2002 listing — see the NZTCS 38 entry below. The four language Wikipedias linked (Cebuano, Swedish, Silesian, Waray-Waray) are bot-generated stubs; there is no English article for the species. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q10448162

Kaimai Bush, 'Chalciporus' — a small bolete, 30–60 mm across, dry, cap yellowish to apricot, pores dull red, yellow mycelium at the stipe base, under native beech. Gives the former name as Xerocomelus aurantiacus, agreeing with Wikidata against NZOR. Sets C. piperatus beside it as the introduced one under Pinus radiata, fawn to light brown, 40–70 mm, dull brown-red pores. No licence statement, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.kaimaibush.co.nz/Fungi/C/chalciporus.html

New Zealand Plant Conservation Network, factsheet PDF generated 05/06/2026 — the print version of the species page already cited above, with no facts beyond it. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/site/assets/files/0/20/990/chalciporus-aurantiacus.pdf

Conservation, national — THIS SETTLES IT. Cooper, Buchanan, Leonard, Allison-Cooper, Johnston, Padamsee, McKenzie & Michel, 'Conservation status of selected species of non-lichenised agarics, boletes and russuloid fungi in Aotearoa New Zealand, 2021', New Zealand Threat Classification Series 38, Department of Conservation, October 2022. ISSN 2324-1713, ISBN 978-1-99-116195-6. Licensed CC BY 4.0 — the only openly licensed source on this entry, so its text may be quoted verbatim with credit. Chalciporus aurantiacus is NOT THREATENED, listed with a status change of 'Better': it is one of nine taxa previously assessed as Threatened – Nationally Critical under Hitchmough 2002 whose status improved 'because of a better understanding of their potential distributions'. The Nationally Critical figure that Wikidata still carries is the 2002 listing and is twenty years out of date. Note the national and global assessments disagree in tone and that is not an error: Not Threatened here, Data Deficient globally in 2019. Retrieved 07/10/2026. https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/nztcs38entire.pdf

MOSTLY RESOLVED, and the resolution favours Cooper: whether this species has yellow mycelium at the stipe base. Cooper's IUCN assessment says C. aurantiacus 'has more persistent orange/red colours and lacks the yellow mycelium at the stipe base', making its absence the separator from C. piperatus. The Landcare Fungal Guide genus page says the genus is characterised by 'the base of the stipe with bright yellow mycelium', and Kaimai Bush gives this species yellow basal mycelium outright. The MycoKeys revision of the subfamily settles the genus-level half of it: across the Chalciporoideae species it describes, basal mycelium is white in five and yellowish in one, so yellow basal mycelium is NOT a genus character and the Fungal Guide's claim is a generalisation from New Zealand's two species. That leaves the specialist who assessed this species against an amateur site repeating a genus page. McNabb's description does not mention basal mycelium at all, so it cannot arbitrate. Cooper is the better authority, but the character has not been checked on a specimen, so the lookalike guidance is safer on cap colour and host tree — which every source agrees on. Checked 07/10/2026.

REJECTED, recorded so it is not used: The Hidden Forest, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus'. It calls the species 'Exotic (Introduced)' and 'Australasian' where NZOR, Biota NZ, the Fungal Guide and the IUCN assessment all have it endemic to New Zealand; gives a season of spring to summer against iNaturalist's January–May records; and gives a cap of 20–60 mm and a stipe of 30–70 mm against McNabb's 3–5.5 cm cap and 2–3.5 cm stipe. Its figures appear to describe something else. Nothing from it is used. It also repeats the yellow-basal-mycelium claim as a key Chalciporus trait, which the MycoKeys revision contradicts. No licence statement either. Checked 07/10/2026. http://hiddenforest.co.nz/fungi/family/boletaceae/bolet03.htm

Zhang, Li, Liang, Mu, Yu, Wu, Chen, Pu & Zeng (2025), 'The subfamily Chalciporoideae (Boletaceae, Boletales) in China', MycoKeys 124: 123–157, DOI 10.3897/mycokeys.124.165901, CC BY 4.0 — openly licensed and quotable, but it does not mention C. aurantiacus anywhere, so there is no description here to use. Two things it does give. Basal mycelium is white in five of the species it describes and yellowish in one, which is the evidence that yellow basal mycelium is not a genus character — see the mycelium note above. And on trophic mode: unlike most Boletaceae, Chalciporoideae species 'may adopt various nutritional strategies, including ectomycorrhizal, saprotrophic, or mycoparasitic modes', with C. piperatus now thought 'more likely a mycoparasitic or saprotrophic fungus' on isotopic and synthesis evidence. That independently supports Cooper's reading of this species as a parasite on other fungi rather than a beech partner. Retrieved 07/10/2026. https://mycokeys.pensoft.net/article/165901/

SEARCH EXHAUSTED for an openly licensed description, 07/10/2026 — recorded so it is not re-searched blind. Checked and came up empty: English Wikipedia (no species article; the CC BY-SA genus article carries no species text and never mentions New Zealand); the new-record-paper route that filled bluefoot-bolete (inapplicable — the species is endemic, so there is no 'first record for X' literature); the CC BY MycoKeys revision of the subfamily (does not include it); GBIF (no description attached to the species in any of its eight checklist datasets); Zenodo and the Biodiversity Literature Repository (no treatments); NZTCS 38 (CC BY 4.0 but a status assessment, no description). Everything descriptive that exists is all rights reserved — McNabb via the Virtual Mycota, NZPCN, Kaimai Bush — or wrong, as with The Hidden Forest. CONCLUSION: there is no openly licensed description of this species to copy. The summary, habitat and identification have to be written for this guide from the facts above, which README:267 permits with an empty sources array. The protologue itself is McNabb 1968, New Zealand Journal of Botany 6(2): 137–176, DOI 10.1080/0028825X.1968.10429056 — paywalled at Taylor & Francis, and the thing to read if the basal mycelium question is ever worth settling properly.

lookalikes.howToTell: written by the assistant on the owner's instruction, 07/10/2026. It restates facts from two all-rights-reserved sources — the Landcare Fungal Guide genus page (C. aurantiacus endemic under native Nothofagus, golden yellow to apricot or reddish brown cap, dull red pores; C. piperatus exotic under pines and introduced broadleaves, usually near Amanita muscaria) and Kaimai Bush (30–60 mm against 40–70 mm, apricot against fawn to light brown) — with no text reproduced. No openly licensed source separates these two species; the CC BY MycoKeys revision of the subfamily does not mention C. aurantiacus at all. Deliberately NOT written on yellow basal mycelium, which Cooper gives as the separator but the Fungal Guide and Kaimai Bush contradict — see the mycelium note on chalciporus-aurantiacus. Flagged here so it is greppable and reversible.

It is too peppery to eat in quantity' (McNabb 1968 via Virtual Mycota, Galloway Wild Foods, Wild Food UK, Foraging Course Company), so a picker who mistakes it for this endemic and cooks a serving gets a mushroom too hot to eat; 'unpalatable' states that, 'edible' would not. sourcingNote: An endemic species with no openly licensed description. The Virtual Mycota carries McNabb's account and it is in copyright; there is no English Wikipedia article, only a CC BY-SA genus article that never mentions the species or New Zealand; and the one openly licensed source here, NZTCS 38 (CC BY 4.0), is a status assessment with no description in it. So the summary, habitat and identification have to be written, from the facts gathered in the sources above. The conservation question is now settled and it went the permissive way: NZTCS 38 lists this species as Not Threatened, upgraded from the Nationally Critical of 2002 that Wikidata still shows, so harvesting guidance is not ruled out on status grounds. It still has to reckon with the IUCN picture behind that status — 5 confirmed sightings since 2013 against 52 for the introduced bolete that is displacing it, and now present at all but one of this species' recorded sites. The lookalike card to peppery-bolete has the material it needs in cap colour and host tree: apricot to reddish orange under native beech, against fawn under pine. It must NOT be written on yellow basal mycelium, which three sources contradict each other on — see the unresolved note in the sources. Photos are attached, so the only remaining blockers are prose: summary, habitat, identification, a warning or the lookalike card, and the harvesting and tikanga guidance. The lookalike card to the other Chalciporus is the assistant's restatement of the Fungal Guide and Kaimai Bush on the owner's instruction, not the owner's words.

habitat.text: On the Chatham Islands it grows on coastal cliffs, rocks and platforms, and on coastal gravels, often in very exposed sites. Planted, it does best in full sun in damp, well-drained, fertile soil.

identification.text:
Trailing herb. Stem flattened, 2-angled, glabrous. Leaves 3-angled, acute, tapering to connate base, (4)–10–15–(30) × 5–6 mm; margins papillate. Flowers 2–4 cm diameter. Petals uniformly white to purple, in 3–5 rows, 1–3 cm long. Stamens 5–6 mm long; inner filaments hairy at base. Stigmas 5–(6). Capsule valves with widely divergent expanding keels; placental tubercle present, 2-lobed or reduced to a ridge. Seeds yellowish brown to brown, obovoid, distinctly papillate, about 1 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Flowering: November–January; fruiting: December–April.
Told from the other New Zealand ice plants by its stems, which are papillate and 2-angled rather than smooth and terete, and by its distinctly papillate rather than wrinkled or smooth seeds.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stem: Chatham Island ice plant's is flattened, 2-angled and rough with tiny pimples (papillae); native ice plant's is round and smooth. Chatham Island ice plant's leaf edges are pimply too, where native ice plant's are usually smooth but rarely pimply, so go by the stem. Its leaves are mostly shorter, 10–15 mm long (4–30 mm) against mostly 20–30 mm (6–40 mm) on native ice plant, but the ranges overlap. Its seeds are yellowish brown to brown and distinctly pimply; native ice plant's are brown and wrinkled; both are about 1 mm long. Both are trailing succulents with 3-angled, pointed leaves and flowers 2–4 cm across with 3–5 rows of petals, white to purple here and white to deep pink on native ice plant, so flower colour does not separate them. Both grow on the coasts of the Chatham Islands, and Chatham Island ice plant grows nowhere else. On the Kermadec Islands native ice plant (subspecies stricticaule) also has pimply leaf edges, but its stem is round and smooth. Chatham Island ice plant was once counted as part of native ice plant. Native ice plant's leaves and fruit are eaten (see its page).

summary.text:
Disphyma papillatum, the Chatham Island ice plant, is a trailing succulent herb in the ice plant family Aizoaceae, endemic to the Chatham Islands.
It grows on Chatham, Pitt, South East, Mangere, Little Mangere, Rabbit and Castle Islands, the Forty Fours, the Star Keys, the Sisters and Western Reef. In the 2023 national assessment it is At Risk – Naturally Uncommon, as an island endemic with a restricted range.
Chinnock described it in 1971; before that it was counted as part of the normal variation of native ice plant, Disphyma australe, which also grows on the Chatham Islands.
Its fleshy capsules are spread by animals that eat them, and possibly by wind and water. It is grown as a groundcover in exposed coastal gardens, as it tolerates wind and salt spray. It is easily raised from rooted pieces and fresh seed.

warnings: No record of Chatham Island ice plant as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
It grows with native ice plant on the Chatham Islands and was once counted as part of that species, so any ice plant there may be either. Check the stem before picking (see the lookalikes).

edibleParts.text: Leaves - raw or cooked as a potherb. A mild pleasant flavour, they make a very acceptable alternative to lettuce in salads. Immature seeds - raw or cooked. They are used to make a creamed vegetable soup that resembles pea soup. A few leaves are also added for colouring. The seeds have a pleasant nutty flavour, though they are too small for most people to want to collect in quantity.

identification.text:
M. parviflora has a decumbent or erect habit, growing up to 50–80 cm in height.
Newly sprouted plants have hairless, heart-shaped cotyledons with long stalks. These cotyledons are 3–12 mm long and 3–8 mm wide. Stalks usually do have hairs. The first leaf is rounder and larger than the others. True leaves are round and weakly lobed with wavy, shallow-toothed edges and a red spot at the leaf base. The plant rapidly grows a deep taproot.
It is told from dwarf mallow by its petals, barely longer than the calyx, its calyx, greatly enlarged and spreading in fruit, and its strongly net-veined fruit segments with slightly winged edges.

Annual, procumbent to erect herb. Stems sparsely to moderately hairy with mostly stellate hairs. Leaves sparsely to densely clothed in mostly stellate hairs above, moderately clothed in mostly stellate hairs below, reniform to orbicular, cordate, shallowly or moderately 5–7-palmately lobed and crenate, 1–8 cm diameter; petioles 1.5–10 cm long; stipules ovate-triangular, 2–6 mm long. Flowers in axillary clusters of (1)–2–5; fruiting pedicels 2–10–(20) mm long; epicalyx segments linear, somewhat shorter than calyx; calyx teeth more or less orbicular with acute apex, glabrous or sparsely clothed in stellate hairs and ciliate, greatly enlarged and spreading at fruiting; petals white, pale mauve or pink towards tips, more or less equal to or only slightly longer than calyx, 3–5 mm long. Mericarps (9)–10–(11) per fruit, glabrous or hairy, strongly reticulately veined on back; edges slightly winged and sometimes toothed.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Both have strongly net-veined fruit segments, so the veining does not separate them; use the petal length, the calyx in fruit and the edges of the fruit segments. Leaf shape and size overlap (cheeseweed mallow 1–8 cm across, common mallow 1–15(–20) cm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. The two are separated by cheeseweed mallow's shorter petals, enlarged fruiting calyx and net-veined fruit segments with winged edges. Both are low herbs with round to kidney-shaped, lobed leaves of overlapping size (1–8 cm and 1–7(–8) cm across) and flowers in clusters in the leaf joints, so the leaves do not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. They are separated by the edges of the fruit segments (squared in French mallow, slightly winged in cheeseweed mallow) and French mallow's longer petals. Both have strongly net-veined fruit, so the veining does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and are unchanged in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Both have palmately lobed, toothed leaves whose sizes overlap (island mallow 2–15(–20) cm across, cheeseweed mallow 1–8 cm), so use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Both have round, palmately 5–7-lobed, round-toothed leaves, so the leaves do not separate them; use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Tree mallow

recipes.method: Written for mallow in general; the author says little mallow is the kind most eaten in Morocco. Serves 4. About 225 g mallow leaves and stems (about 2 litres, packed), 120 ml olive oil, about 120 ml chopped parsley and/or coriander leaves, 4 cloves garlic, pressed or finely chopped, 1½ tsp paprika, 1½ tsp ground cumin, ¼ tsp salt, ¼ tsp cayenne pepper (optional), 2 tbsp lemon juice, the chopped pulp of 1 preserved lemon, and preserved lemon rind and a handful of red olives to garnish. Wash the mallow thoroughly, drain, chop the leaves and stems and steam over simmering water for 15–20 minutes, until tender; it shrinks a lot and darkens. Press out the extra water against the side of the steamer basket. Meanwhile, fry the oil, garlic, herbs and spices over medium or medium-low heat for several minutes, until the herbs wilt and the garlic smells fragrant, without burning the garlic, then take off the heat. Add the mallow, preserved lemon pulp and lemon juice and cook over medium heat for 5–10 minutes. Taste and adjust the seasoning, and serve warm or at room temperature with the olives and preserved lemon rind, usually as a dip with bread. Without preserved lemon, use a little more lemon juice; the same method works with spinach, kale or purslane, with the steaming time adjusted.

recipes.method: Written for cheeseweed, which the author names as Malva parviflora, in the US Southwest. Several handfuls of cheeseweed leaves (about 1 litre once chopped), 1 large onion, diced, cooking oil (the author suggests bacon fat or butter), and salt and pepper, or lemon or vinegar. Strip the leaves from the main stem and wash them; the leaf stalks can stay but chop them small, as they can be tough (chopped stems add a celery-like crunch). Chop the leaves coarsely. Brown the onion in a large frying pan or wok as much as you like (spring onions or garlic chives also work), add the greens and cover with a lid so their own moisture steams them as they shrink. Season and serve as a side dish or on pasta.

summary.text:
Cheeseweed mallow, Malva parviflora, is an annual herb of the mallow family (Malvaceae), native from south-western Europe and the Mediterranean to western Asia. New Zealand floras call it small-flowered mallow or marshmallow.
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North Island, throughout the South Island except Westland and Fiordland, and on the Kermadec Islands. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1883.

warnings: M. parviflora accumulates pollutants such as cadmium and chromium. In nitrogen-rich soils, the plant's leaves and seeds can be toxic to cattle and poultry due to an accumulation of nitrates. If consumed in large amounts, the plant can damage energy homeostasis in horses, possibly due to its cyclopropene fatty acids.
It has often caused staggers in sheep, and less often in cattle and horses, in Australia and to a lesser extent South Africa; no cases have been confirmed in New Zealand.

harvestEthics.text:
An environmental weed that can invade intact native forest and reduces native recruitment. Harvest as much as you like, and do not spread the seed.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text:
Large shrub or small tree to 6 m high. Trunk smooth, pale brown. Shoots terete or subterete, puberulent when young. Petioles 7–10 mm long, puberulent. Lamina 4–8 × 2.5–4.5 cm, obovate, ciliolate toward base of margins and midrib, at least when young, otherwise glabrous, dotted with glands beneath, glossy and dark green above; lateral veins fairly conspicuous in dried material but not impressed or markedly raised; base cuneate, often narrowly so; apex usually obtuse, sometimes rounded. Flowers solitary, often produced in nearly all axils of upper leaves; pedicels 7–10 mm long, puberulent, jointed near apex with very small, caducous, ovate bracteoles. Hypanthium and calyx limb glandular-punctate; lobes usually 5, 3–4 mm long. Petals c. 5 mm long, elliptic, white, more or less glandular-punctate. Stamens longer than petals. Style c. 4 mm long, stout. Fruit more or less globose, c. 2 cm diameter, becoming dark purple, occasionally yellow; flesh usually purple, occasionally whitish, sweet. Seeds numerous.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Psidium cattleianum Sabine.]

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psidium_cattleyanum A small, highly branched tree usually 2–4 m and at most 13 m. Both the thin skin and the juicy interior are soft and edible, though the skin is often removed for a sweeter flavour; it also makes jam and juices, and the leaves can be brewed for tea. The seeds are small, white, high in vitamin C. On how aggressive it is, which is this entry's framing: it is considered the most invasive plant in Hawaii, and is among the worst on Réunion and Madagascar, where it threatens endemic forest — and it was introduced to most of the places it now invades precisely because people wanted the fruit.

On how fast the fruit goes over. Commercial products are not made from it partly for want of a market but also because of the heavy presence of fruit flies, which renders the fruit inedible soon after picking. summary.text:
Cherry guava, Psidium cattleyanum, also called strawberry guava, Cattley guava and purple guava, is a large shrub or small tree up to 6 m tall of the myrtle family (Myrtaceae), native to southern Brazil. It was brought to New Zealand as a fruit crop.
In New Zealand it was first recorded naturalised in 1977, as an escape from cultivation; by 1988 it was known wild near Whangārei, in Auckland and on Raoul Island. Auckland Council's regional pest plan lists it for sustained control across the whole region.
