identification.text:
Evergreen, wide spreading shrub or tree, up to about 10 m high when mature, not armed, glabrous or almost so; trunks often several, usually short, often forming large thickets. Leaf petiole 5–10–(12) mm long; blade coriaceous, oblanceolate to narrow-elliptic or narrow-oblong, (75)–90–150–(180) × (23)–30–50–(55) mm, acute to very short-acuminate but often splitting at tip and appearing emarginate, especially when dried, cuneate to rounded at base, shining above with prominent paler veins, less shining below; margin somewhat recurved, more or less entire toward base, with distant, short, acute teeth toward apex; stipules long-triangular, deciduous. Inflorescence an axillary or terminal, erect, dense raceme (80)–100–(120) mm long, with 20–30–(35) fragrant flowers; pedicels 2–2.5–(5) mm long, elongating slightly after anthesis. Hypanthium broad; sepals broadly triangular, about 1 mm long, acute, green, more or less erect. Petals 5, spreading, orbicular, 2.5–5 × 2–4 mm, rounded, greenish white to cream. Stamens longer than petals; filaments pale. Fruit about 10 mm long, ovoid, glabrous, dark purple, very bitter; stone smooth.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is told from other cherries and from Portugal laurel by being evergreen, by its flowers on long spikes rather than in small clusters, and by its leaves having only a few short, distantly spaced teeth, toward the tip. The fruits hang in grape-like clusters and look like dark purple to black cherries. The leaves can have the scent of almonds when crushed.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaf edge: cherry laurel's leaves have a few distant, short, sharp teeth toward the tip and are more or less smooth toward the base; bay's leaves are untoothed, on some leaves wavy. Cherry laurel's flowers are greenish white to cream, 20–35 on an erect, dense spike 80–120 mm long, and its fruits hang in grape-like clusters along the spike; bay's flowers are cream or whitish, 3–4 mm long, in small umbels in the upper leaf joints. Bay's leaves are aromatic; cherry laurel's can smell of almonds when crushed. Both are evergreen with shining leaves of overlapping length (bay 4–13 cm, cherry laurel 7.5–18 cm), and both have dark fruit, cherry laurel's dark purple and about 10 mm long, bay's glossy black and 1.3–1.5 cm long, so leaf size, shine and fruit colour do not tell them apart. Bay's leaves are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Bay tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Taiwan cherry is deciduous, with thin leaves finely and sharply toothed along the edge; cherry laurel is evergreen, with leathery leaves shining above and only a few distant, short teeth toward the tip. Taiwan cherry's flowers are bell-shaped, deep pink to rose-magenta, and hang in clusters of 1–5 (July–September); cherry laurel's are greenish white to cream, 20–35 on an erect spike 80–120 mm long (August–September). Taiwan cherry's fruit is glossy scarlet, up to 12 × 10 mm; cherry laurel's is dark purple, about 10 mm long, very bitter, and hangs in grape-like clusters along the spike. The fruits are of similar size, and cherry laurel fruits from November to January, when Taiwan cherry is also in fruit, so check the leaves and how the fruit is borne, not size. Taiwan cherry's fruit is eaten.

preparation.text: Pick only fully ripe fruit, nearly black and a little soft, and take out the stones. Taste one first and throw away any fruit that tastes very bitter. The fruit tastes like strong, somewhat bitter cherries, and is used for sauces, pies, jams, drinks, cordials and fruit leather, often mixed with sweeter fruit such as blackberries.

recipes.method: Ingredients: ripe cherry laurel fruit, stones removed; brandy or vodka. Half-fill a 1-litre jar with the pitted fruit, then fill it to the top with brandy or vodka. Cover and keep somewhere dark, such as a kitchen cupboard, for at least 6 weeks, shaking it now and then. Strain, and drink it on its own or topped up with sparkling water. The soaked fruit can be eaten too, for example over ice cream.
recipes.title: Cherry laurel cordial

recipes.method: Ingredients: 2 kg ripe cherry laurel fruit, stones removed; 1 kg raw sugar; 250 ml (1 cup) white vinegar; cloves, salt and pepper. Cover the pitted fruit with water and boil until soft, then mash. Add the sugar, vinegar, cloves, salt and pepper, boil hard for 20 minutes, then bottle.

summary.text:
Cherry laurel, Prunus laurocerasus, is an evergreen, wide-spreading shrub or tree up to about 10 m tall of the rose family (Rosaceae), native to south-eastern Europe. Its name comes from its likeness to bay laurel (Laurus nobilis), to which it is not closely related.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands. Naturalised from south-east Europe, first recorded in 1958. Flowering August to September, fruiting November to January. P. laurocerasus is frequently grown as a hedge plant for its dense, evergreen habit and relics of cultivation are very common in settled areas, especially around old homesteads, domains and parks.
Its seed is spread by birds, and it also spreads by suckers from the roots. It is named on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds and is an Organism of Interest in the Tasman-Nelson and Southland regional pest management plans. Its ripe fruit is eaten in the Black Sea region of Turkey, where it is grown as a fruit.

warnings: Eat only the fully ripe fruit flesh. The leaves and the seed inside the stone contain cyanogenic glycosides, including amygdalin, which release hydrogen cyanide. The leaves are poisonous to people and livestock; eating the leaves or seeds may cause severe discomfort, and in excess cyanide can cause breathing failure and death. Do not eat the leaves or the stones.

Unripe fruit is not safe: the cyanide-releasing glycoside is highest in young fruit and falls to an undetectable level only in mature fruit. Bitterness shows more cyanide, so do not eat any fruit that tastes bitter. The Flora of New Zealand describes the fruit of New Zealand plants as very bitter.
Its leaves look like bay leaves and its fruit like cherries. Check any 'bay tree' before using its leaves, and any wild cherry before eating it (see the lookalikes).

identification.text: Deciduous shrub or small tree up to 8 m high, with a short trunk and numerous spiny branches, mainly on the lower shoots. Young shoots hairless and shining. Leaves thin, narrowly obovate to broadly elliptic, (30)–40–80 × (13)–15–45 mm, usually green but sometimes purple or bronzy purple, somewhat shining, finely toothed, hairless except that the lower third of the midrib beneath is sometimes densely hairy. Flowers single (though usually closely spaced) or in clusters of 2–(4), not fragrant, in August–September; petals usually 5, round, 6–11 mm across, white or occasionally pink. Fruit (10)–15–30 mm long, usually roundish or broadly egg-shaped, slightly grooved, hairless, yellow to orange-red or scarlet, sometimes dark crimson, with a slight bloom; sweet; stone smooth.

lookalikes.howToTell: No single test settles it; most of these ranges overlap. Young shoots: cherry plum's are hairless and shining; the plum's are usually hairy and dull, though sometimes hairless, so a hairy shoot points to the plum. Size: a plum is 25–45 mm long, sometimes only 20 mm, and a cherry plum 15–30 mm, sometimes only 10 mm, so a fruit over 30 mm points to the plum, and anything smaller is not settled by size (the plum can be as small as 15 mm). Colour overlaps: plums are green, yellow, red or blackish purple, usually bloomed; cherry plums yellow to orange-red or scarlet, sometimes dark crimson, slightly bloomed. Do not use the midrib — cherry plum's can be densely hairy on its lower third underneath. Cherry plum fruits from November to January and the plum from January to February. Both flower in August and September, and their petals and flower stalks overlap in size.

preparation.text:
The fruits are edible. Some varieties have sweet fruits that can be eaten fresh, while others are sour and better for making jam. Cherry plums are a key ingredient in Georgian cuisine where they are used to produce tkemali sauce, as well as a number of popular dishes, such as kharcho soup and chakapuli stew.
In Middle Asia and Caucasus considerable quantities are processed to preserves, jam, pie and 'lavas' (fruit-flesh dried in thin layers).

recipes.method: 1.8 kg cherry plums, 1.8 kg brown cane sugar and about 285 ml water. Put everything in a large, flat-bottomed pan, stir, and bring to the boil. Boil until the skins start to come off and the fruit comes away from the stones. Pour the mixture into a large piece of muslin and squeeze the pulp through it back into the pan. Keep boiling until it reaches setting point, which can take as long as 30 minutes. To test, chill a couple of saucers in the fridge before you start; drip a little jam onto one, let it cool for a moment, then push it sideways with a finger — it is ready when it wrinkles and feels tacky. Pour into sterilised jars and screw on the lids. Makes about 7 jars.
recipes.title: Cherry plum jam

recipes.method: 2.8 kg cherry plums, 1.4 kg sugar, about 4 litres water, 1 sachet wine yeast (any red wine yeast will do), 1 tsp yeast nutrient and 1 tsp pectolase. Boil 1 litre of the water, pour it over the fruit and crush the fruit with the end of a rolling pin until no lumps are left. Leave it a few hours, then add the rest of the water and the pectolase — plums are rich in the pectin that sets jam and also clouds wine. Leave a couple of days, then strain through a fine sieve. Bring the juice quickly to the boil in a saucepan and turn off the heat straight away; the author once skipped this and lost the whole batch to acetobacter. Pour the hot juice over the sugar and stir until it dissolves, cool to room temperature, then add the yeast and yeast nutrient. Top up to 4.5 litres if necessary, funnel into a demijohn and fit an airlock. Rack into a clean demijohn after four to six weeks, and again a few weeks later if you want. Bottle when clear — or, if it will not clear completely, bottle it anyway.
recipes.title: Cherry plum wine

recipes.method: Written for plums in general rather than cherry plums. Makes a 1-litre jar. 250 g granulated sugar, 420 ml apple cider vinegar, ½ tsp crushed coriander, 1 tsp ground cardamom, 750 g plums, stoned and halved, 1 small cinnamon stick, 1 red chilli cut into quarters and 1 star anise. In a large saucepan, bring the sugar, vinegar, coriander and cardamom to a gentle simmer and cook for 5 minutes to infuse. Add the plums and cook for about 2 minutes, until just softened but still holding their shape. Put the cinnamon, chilli and star anise in a sterilised 1-litre jar (or two or three smaller ones), scoop in the plums and pack them tightly, leaving about 1.25 cm at the top, then pour the vinegar over until they are completely covered. Seal while still warm, leave to cool at room temperature, then refrigerate for 2 weeks before serving. They keep about a couple of weeks in the fridge; for longer storage they can be processed in a water bath. Good on toast with farmhouse cheese, on savoury porridge, in salads, or with pork chops, chicken or turkey.
recipes.title: Spiced pickled plums

recipes.method: Ingredients: 500 g cherry plums (weighed after stoning), chopped; 220 g long red chillies, ends removed, finely chopped; 1.1 litres (4½ cups) white wine vinegar; 1 kg (4½ cups) white sugar; 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) salt; 22 ml (1½ tbsp) grated fresh ginger; 5 garlic cloves, crushed; optionally 10 ml (2 tsp) cornflour mixed to a paste with 15 ml (1 tbsp) extra vinegar. Put everything except the cornflour paste in a saucepan and bring to the boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Boil over a medium heat for 40 minutes. If you want it thicker, stir in the cornflour paste and boil briefly. Bottle hot into sterilised bottles.
recipes.title: Cherry plum sweet chilli sauce

recipes.method: Ingredients: 3 kg cherry plums, washed and drained; 3 litres water; sugar (1 cup for each cup of strained juice); 10 ml (2 tsp) citric acid; 125 ml (½ cup) white or cider vinegar. Put the plums and water in a large pot, bring to the boil, then simmer for about 15 minutes until very tender. Drain through a colander, then pour the liquid through a muslin-lined sieve and leave a couple of hours to drip through. Measure the juice and add 1 cup of sugar for every cup. Bring to the boil, lower the heat, add the citric acid and vinegar and simmer 3 minutes more. Pour into sterilised bottles and seal; keeps up to 12 months somewhere cool and dark. Serve 1 part syrup to 4–5 parts chilled water or soda water.
recipes.title: Cherry plum cordial syrup

summary.text:
Cherry plum (Prunus cerasifera), also called myrobalan or purple-leaf plum, is known only as a cultivated or naturalised plant; the wild P. divaricata of south-east Europe and south-west Asia is often taken as the species it came from.
In New Zealand it is widespread in cultivation and as a relic, seeds freely and was first recorded naturalised in 1958. It grows wild in Manawatu (Bunnythorpe) and the Hutt Valley, is common from Nelson to south-east Otago, mostly east of the Main Divide, and is recorded at Tapanui, on Stewart Island and on the Chathams. Birds and people spread the seed. Purple-leaved forms with pink flowers and dark crimson fruit, mostly the cultivar 'Pissardii', are common garden trees, and their purple-leaved seedlings sometimes grow wild.

warnings: The plant (especially the seed and young shoots) contains cyanogenic glycosides, especially amygdalin and prunasin. When ingested, these compounds break down in the digestive tract to release cyanide.

habitat.text:
Damp shaded garden beds, under hedges, cultivated soil.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Grassland, waste land, roadsides, coastal sandy sites, damp sites, cultivated land, disturbed stony sites, riverbeds.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ; Webb et al. 1988 text), 'Stellaria media' (https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Stellaria-media.html) — description verbatim, abbreviations spelled out; the owner's lines above it are corroborated by the Flora (ovate opposite leaves, weak stems, 1 line of hairs; genus: petals 'divided almost to base') and Knox 2013, p. 69 (five split petals that look like ten; single row of hairs)
identification.text:
Small oval opposite leaves on a weak sprawling stem. The giveaway: a single line of fine hairs running along one side of the stem, switching sides at each node. Tiny white flowers with five deeply split petals that look like ten. Grows in dense low mats.
Annual. Stems weak, ascending, terete, (10)–15–40–(60) cm long, with 1 line of hairs. Leaves green, not connate, ovate to broadly lanceolate, acute to apiculate, narrowing abruptly at base, ciliate on proximal margins and midrib above, 5–40–(50) × 5–15–(25) mm; petiole ciliate, about equal to lamina in lower leaves, almost 0 in upper leaves; marginal vein distinct. Inflorescence terminal, cymose, usually lax, (1)–3–15–(50)-flowered. Bracts leaflike. Pedicels slender, patent, (5)–10–40 mm long, with 1 line of hairs. Sepals narrow-lanceolate, obtuse to subacute, not veined, (3)–4–6 mm long, hairy outside; margins scarious. Petals slightly shorter to slightly longer than sepals. Stamens (0)–3–5–(10). Capsule narrow-ovoid, equal to or slightly longer than calyx. Seeds dull brown, 0.9–1.2 mm long; tubercles triangular, sharp.

lookalikes.howToTell: Snap a stem: petty spurge bleeds white milky sap, and no milky sap is recorded for chickweed. Spurge sap irritates skin and has caused serious eye inflammation, so keep it away from your face. Petty spurge's stems are hairless, where chickweed's carry a line of hairs down one side; its leaves are alternate, where chickweed's are in opposite pairs; and its small green flower heads have no petals, where chickweed has white petals split almost to the base (rarely none). Both are weeds of gardens and cultivated ground.
lookalikes.name: Petty spurge

lookalikes.howToTell: Scarlet pimpernel's stems are four-angled (square in section) and hairless; chickweed's are round with a single line of hairs. Pimpernel's flowers are orange or orange-red, borne singly in the leaf axils on stalks (0.5)–1–2 cm long; chickweed's petals are white and divided almost to the base (rarely absent), in usually loose clusters at the stem tips. Pimpernel's leaves are stalkless and often indistinctly dotted with black glands underneath; chickweed's lower leaves have a stalk about as long as the blade. Leaf size and the sprawling habit overlap and do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Scarlet pimpernel

lookalikes.howToTell: Blue pimpernel's stems are four-angled (square in section) and hairless; chickweed's are round with a single line of hairs. Blue pimpernel's flowers are blue, with five lobes, borne singly in the leaf axils on stalks (0.5)–1–2 cm long; chickweed's petals are white and divided almost to the base (rarely absent), in usually loose clusters at the stem tips. Blue pimpernel's leaves are stalkless and often indistinctly dotted with black glands underneath; chickweed's lower leaves have a stalk about as long as the blade. Leaf size and the sprawling habit overlap and do not separate them. Do not eat blue pimpernel.
lookalikes.name: Blue pimpernel

lookalikes.howToTell: Chickweed's stem has a single line of hairs, and its leaves are hairy only on the lower edges and the midrib above; common mouse-ear chickweed's flowering stems have dense spreading hairs and its leaves are hairy. Chickweed's white petals are divided almost to the base; mouse-ear chickweed's are notched or divided only up to a third of the way. Chickweed has 3 styles and a narrow egg-shaped capsule as long as or slightly longer than the calyx, opening by 6 teeth; mouse-ear chickweeds have usually 5 styles and a cylindric capsule twice the length of the calyx, opening by twice as many teeth as styles. Common mouse-ear chickweed is a perennial, often with short tufted non-flowering side branches; chickweed is an annual. Both are eaten; mouse-ear chickweed's hairy texture is best hidden by pounding it into a pesto or chopping it short and cooking it.
lookalikes.name: Common mouse-ear chickweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Chickweed's stem has a single line of hairs, and its leaves are hairy only on the lower edges and the midrib above; sticky mouse-ear chickweed's stems have spreading hairs mixed with shorter glandular (gland-tipped) hairs, and its leaves are hairy. Chickweed's white petals are divided almost to the base; sticky mouse-ear chickweed's are notched or divided only up to a third of the way. Chickweed has 3 styles and a narrow egg-shaped capsule as long as or slightly longer than the calyx, opening by 6 teeth; mouse-ear chickweeds have usually 5 styles and a cylindric capsule twice the length of the calyx, opening by twice as many teeth as styles. Chickweed's flower stalks are usually 10–40 mm long; sticky mouse-ear chickweed's are no longer than the calyx, which is usually 4–5 mm long. Both are eaten; sticky mouse-ear chickweed's hairy texture is best hidden by pounding it into a pesto or chopping it short and cooking it.
lookalikes.name: Sticky mouse-ear chickweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Young white campion plants can look like chickweed from above. Chickweed's stem has a single line of hairs, and its leaves are hairy only on the lower edges and the midrib above; white campion's stems and leaves are softly hairy all over, with glandular hairs as well higher up. Chickweed is a weak-stemmed annual with leaves usually 5–40 mm long (up to 50 mm); white campion is a biennial or short-lived perennial from a stout taproot, with leaves usually 4–8 cm long (2 to 15 cm), so a leaf 2–5 cm long does not tell them apart. Chickweed's sepals are separate and usually 4–6 mm long, and its white petals are divided almost to the base; white campion's calyx is a tube 12–25 mm long and each petal is two-lobed. Chickweed has 3 styles and a capsule opening by 6 teeth; female white campion flowers have 5 styles and a capsule with usually 10 teeth. White campion is eaten too, cooked.
lookalikes.name: White campion

preparation.text: Raw in salads, blitzed into a pesto, or wilted briefly.

recipes.method: Chickweed and Italian parsley, roughly half and half, long stems removed; 1 small garlic clove, crushed with salt; freshly shelled walnuts (or other nuts); extra virgin olive oil; a little grated parmesan (optional); lemon juice. Fill a food processor with the chickweed and parsley leaves and chop them; they reduce down a lot. Add the garlic, then the walnuts, and pour in olive oil until it becomes a purée. Mix in a little parmesan if you want it creamier, then add lemon juice a squeeze at a time, tasting as you go; it keeps the pesto bright green and balances it. Finish with a drizzle of oil for gloss. The author keeps it for at least a week in the fridge and uses it in sandwiches, on pizza, through pasta or to lift other dishes. She notes that picked chickweed itself does not keep in the fridge, so make the pesto the day you pick it.
recipes.title: Chickweed pesto

recipes.method: Chickweed, as large and lush as you can find; freshly shelled walnuts; a few olives; halloumi; a squirt of lemon juice; a splash of avocado oil. Fry the halloumi. Add the walnuts, olives and fried halloumi to the chickweed. Dress it simply with the lemon juice and avocado oil. Eat it the day you pick the chickweed; the author finds it does not keep in the fridge. She makes the chickweed the star of the bowl rather than an extra.
recipes.title: Chickweed salad

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard. 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: Written for the author's mixed wild leaves. Of his lists, this catalogue covers dandelion and hairy bittercress (pungent), chickweed and hawthorn leaves (mild), and gorse flowers and flowering currant blossom (extras). He warns to be extra careful identifying leaves before the plants flower. Pungent leaves; mild leaves; a few extras; walnut oil; elderberry vinegar; salt and pepper; a little mustard; fermented greens; pickled buds. Mix pungent and mild leaves about 1 to 3, then scatter a few extras over the top. Dress simply with walnut oil, elderberry vinegar, salt, pepper and a little mustard; he finishes it with fermented greens and pickled buds.
recipes.title: Wild summer salad

recipes.method: Written for chickweed, with sweet chestnuts. Makes 2. Boil chestnuts in water for 10 minutes, drain them and let them cool a little, then halve them and scoop out the flesh; process it to a fine flour. Mash a heaped 125 ml (½ cup) of this chestnut flour with ½ avocado and a little salt. Spread it on 2 nori sheets, add fenugreek sprouts and a bunch of chickweed, and roll them up.
recipes.title: Chickweed and chestnut nori wraps

recipes.method: Written for chickweed, nasturtium and onion weed. Soak 500 ml (2 cups) chickpeas overnight, drain and rinse them well, and sprout them for 48 hours, rinsing twice a day, until the tails are as long as the peas; or cook them, as the author also allows. 500 ml (2 cups) sprouted chickpeas; 185 ml (¾ cup) tahini (the author grinds whole sesame seeds instead); 2–4 garlic cloves, minced; the juice of 2 large lemons and 1 orange; 125 ml (½ cup) olive oil; 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt; 5 ml (1 tsp) cumin; a big handful of chickweed, some nasturtium leaves, a small bunch of onion weed leaves and a sprig of parsley or another herb. Process the chickpeas with the citrus juice until still slightly chunky, then add everything else and process to the consistency you want.
recipes.title: Raw chickpea hummus with wild greens

recipes.method: Written for cleavers, violet leaves, chickweed, red deadnettle and bittercress. A small handful of cleavers; 4 violet leaves; a handful of chickweed; 3 or 4 stems of red deadnettle; a small handful of bittercress; a big handful of bok choy, kale or silverbeet; 1 banana, peeled; 1 apple (whole without the stalk if organic, otherwise peeled); 1 mandarin (with its peel if organic, otherwise peeled); 1 or 2 kiwifruit, peeled; 1 small or ½ large avocado; 500 ml (2 cups) water, more if the blender struggles. Wash the weeds and greens, put them in the blender, snip them up a bit with scissors and add the water. Blend on low until the greens break down, then on high until smooth. Add the fruit and avocado and blend again, low and then high, until creamy.

summary.text:
Mild, sweet and abundant in every neglected garden bed in the country.
Chickweed (Stellaria media) is an annual of the pink family, Caryophyllaceae. New Zealand plants belong to subspecies media, and it has also been recorded here as Alsine media.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands and on the Kermadec, Chatham, Antipodes, Auckland and Campbell Islands; naturalised from Europe, first recorded wild in 1832.

warnings: Always break a stem and check for milky sap before picking a mat — petty spurge is almost everywhere in New Zealand gardens, where chickweed grows too.
The leaves contain saponins, so do not eat large quantities: paralysis has been reported from eating too much.

edibleParts.text: The fruit and the leaves. The fruit is eaten raw; it is a juicy, berry-like fruit 17–20 mm long, green to yellowish, that stays closed when ripe and is full of tiny seeds in a dark, sweet, thick jelly. The leaves are eaten baked or pickled; raw, they are harshly tannic and barely edible.

habitat.text: In New Zealand it grows on coastal rocky sites, mostly steep banks and cliffs. It has also been collected on raised upper beach sand that high tides occasionally reach, and recorded on waste ground by a beach. It tolerates drought, wind, salt spray and sandy soils.

harvestEthics.text: Not a legally declared pest, but on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and it hybridises with the native ice plant. Harvest as much as you like, but do not damage the dunes while gathering, and spread no stem fragments or garden waste: even small pieces can grow into new plants.

identification.text:
Mat-forming trailing perennial herb. Stems to 6 m long, glabrous, 2-angled, subwoody at base. Leaves smooth, sharply 3-angled, linear, acute, scarcely tapered to connate base, 35–90 × 5–12 mm, 5–12× as long as wide; keel denticulate near apex. Flowers 6.5–8 cm diameter. Calyx glabrous; longest sepals 25–45 mm long. Petals spreading, purple, paler near base, 10–35 mm long. Stamens 4–10 mm long; filaments yellow or pinkish, hairy at base; anthers pale yellow. Stigmas 8–11. Seeds brown, often asymmetrically obovoid, 1–1.3 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Carpobrotus aequilaterus sensu (Haw.) N.E.Br.]
Stems occasionally root where they touch the ground.
Leaves bitter-tasting. Fruit indehiscent, fleshy, mucilaginous; locules as many as stigmas. [Genus description, from: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Very similar to South African ice plant, but easily told apart when flowering: this plant has smaller, purple flowers.
Hybrids with the native ice plant have flowers 4–5.2 cm across, with purplish petals that later turn purplish pink.

lookalikes.howToTell: Best told apart in flower. South African ice plant has pale yellow petals that turn pinkish orange or dull pink with age, on flowers 8–10 cm across; this plant's petals are purple, paler near the base, on flowers 6.5–8 cm across. South African ice plant's leaves are 70–120 × 12–17 mm, against 35–90 × 5–12 mm here, but the ranges overlap, so do not rely on leaves out of flower.
lookalikes.name: South African ice plant

lookalikes.howToTell: Native ice plant is smaller in every part. Its flowers are 2–4 cm across, with petals uniformly white to deep pink, against 6.5–8 cm and purple here. Its leaves are mostly 20–30 mm long (6–40 mm) and 4–6 mm wide (up to 9 mm), against 35–90 × 5–12 mm here. Its stems are round in section, not 2-angled, and its fruit is a capsule whose cells have lids, where this plant's fruit stays closed. Plants with purplish flowers 4–5.2 cm across may be hybrids between the two.
lookalikes.name: Native ice plant

summary.text:
Carpobrotus chilensis, the Chilean sea fig, also called purple-flowered ice plant or angled pigface, is a mat-forming succulent in the ice plant family Aizoaceae, naturalised in New Zealand since 1969.
New Zealand sources give its origin as California and Chile, or South America, and it was brought in as a garden ornamental. In New Zealand it was long called Carpobrotus aequilaterus, the name of a very different-looking Western Australian endemic.
The Flora of New Zealand (1988) recorded it at Patea in Taranaki and Pukerua Bay near Wellington, and in Canterbury and Otago. Herbarium specimens have since recorded it wild on beaches in Golden Bay. It is not a legally declared pest, but it is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. It forms natural hybrids with the native ice plant, Disphyma australe.
Animals eat the fruit and spread the seed. Its stems root where they touch the ground, and stem pieces moved in soil or dumped with garden waste grow into new plants.

identification.text:
In the most common variety, the fruit is roughly pear-shaped, somewhat flattened and with coarse wrinkles, ranging from 10–25 cm long, with thin green skin fused with green to white flesh, and a single, large, flattened stone. This seed or stone can be up to 10 cm long by 7 cm wide. Some varieties have spiny fruits. Depending on the variety, a single fruit can weigh up to 1.2 kg. Most New Zealand chokos are green, and smooth or covered in small spines. It flowers as the days shorten, so in New Zealand flowers may not appear until late summer or early autumn.
The chayote vine can be grown on the ground, but as a climbing plant, it will grow onto anything, and can easily rise as high as 12 m when support is provided. It has heart-shaped leaves, 10–25 cm wide and tendrils on the stem. The plant bears male flowers in clusters and solitary female flowers.
Told from moth plant (Araujia sericifera), whose pods look like choko fruit, by its more grape-like leaves and its tendrils: moth plant climbs by twining, its leaves are opposite and greyish-downy underneath, and its leathery pods hold kapok-like pulp and many seeds with silky tufts, not one large stone.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at how it climbs: choko holds on with tendrils on the stem; moth plant's stems twine. Look at the leaves: choko's are heart-shaped, 10–25 cm wide and more grape-like; moth plant's are 1.5–6 cm wide, ovate-oblong or oblong, in opposite pairs, dark green above and glaucous-white and downy underneath. Cut the fruit open: choko's holds a single large, flattened stone in firm green to white flesh; moth plant's thick, leathery pod holds kapok-like pulp and many dark brown seeds, 7–8 mm long, each with a silky tuft 3–5 cm long. In flower, moth plant's are white, deeply bell-shaped, about 2–2.5 cm long, sometimes streaked pinkish mauve inside, usually 2–4 together; choko's are small, white or greenish, the male ones in clusters and the female ones single. The fruits are of much the same pear shape and size (choko's 10–25 cm long, moth plant's pods up to 10, sometimes 12, cm long), and both grow around gardens and over hedges in the Auckland area and the Bay of Plenty. Moth plant is poisonous: its milky sap is poisonous in every part.
lookalikes.name: Moth plant

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: māwhai's are only about 6–10 mm long, egg-shaped, and densely covered in spines 1.6–3.6 mm long with backward-pointing barbs; choko's is a pear-shaped, pale green fruit 10–25 cm long holding a single large, flattened stone, and even the spiny kinds grown in New Zealand carry only small spines. The two have been confused when not in fruit: choko's leaves are larger and darker green, heart-shaped and 10–25 cm wide; māwhai's are grey-green, 3.5–19.5 × 4.5–20 cm, sharply 5- or 7-lobed with toothed edges and rough to the touch, and its stems carry harsh hairs. Māwhai's white male flowers, 4.5–7.8 mm across, come 8–19 along a long stalk, and its female flowers 8–11 together in a head; choko's male flowers are in clusters and its female flowers single. Both grow in the northern North Island: māwhai in coastal and lowland forest, scrub and bracken, and spreading into farmland and urban wasteland; choko near gardens and over hedges and fences. No record of māwhai as food was found, and it is At Risk – Naturally Uncommon.

preparation.text: Pick the fruit from about 5–7 cm long, before the seed has enlarged, when it is most tender, up to about 10–20 cm; smaller fruit are less sweet and suit savoury dishes, and larger, sweeter fruit can go into jams and preserves. Eat young fruit raw like cucumber. Steam, boil, bake, fry, mash or stir-fry older fruit, peeled and cut up with the central seed removed; it need not be peeled to be cooked or fried in slices. The seed is nutty when cooked and can be deep-fried. Pick the shoots down to the second leaf from the growing tip and cook them, with the young leaves, as a green vegetable, like asparagus: steam them or add them to stir-fries. Boil, bake, roast or fry the tuberous root like a potato, or candy it in syrup.

recipes.method: 1 choko, peeled with the seed removed; 1 scrubbed yacon; a quarter of a red cabbage; the juice of 1 lime; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) coconut sugar; 60 ml (¼ cup) coconut thread; 60 ml (¼ cup) raisins; 60 ml (¼ cup) mung bean sprouts; 4 sprigs of mint; 45 ml (3 tbsp) aioli (egg, aquafaba or tofu based); black pepper. Grate into a large bowl 1 choko, peeled with the seed removed (peel it whether you eat it raw or cooked; it is firm), and 1 scrubbed yacon. Add a quarter of a red cabbage, sliced as finely as you can, the juice of 1 lime, 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and 2.5 ml (½ tsp) coconut sugar, and toss; adding the lime and salt straight away takes away the choko's slightly astringent feel. Then add 60 ml (¼ cup) coconut thread, 60 ml (¼ cup) raisins, 60 ml (¼ cup) mung bean sprouts, 4 sprigs of mint, 45 ml (3 tbsp) aioli (egg, aquafaba or tofu based) and some black pepper, and toss well. Serves 4. It keeps well in the fridge.
recipes.title: Choko and yacon slaw

recipes.method: 1 kg choko (4–6 fruit); 30 ml (2 tbsp) plain salt; 750 ml (3 cups) cider vinegar; 125 ml (½ cup) raw sugar; 5 ml (1 tsp) pickling spice, or 5 ml (1 tsp) yellow mustard seed and a sprig of dill per jar, or a bay leaf and a few whole peppercorns per jar. Peel the chokos, take out the seed, cut them into quarters and then into spears about as thick as your thumb. Put them in a glass, plastic or stainless steel bowl, mix in the salt, cover and leave for an hour to dry-brine. Meanwhile heat six clean glass jars of about 400 ml in the oven at 125 °C for 30 minutes, and boil their lids in a pan of water for 10 minutes. Bring the vinegar, sugar and spices to the boil and simmer for 5–10 minutes. Drain the liquid off the chokos without rinsing them. Take the jars out with tongs and stand them on a wooden board or tea towel; put any dill or bay leaves straight into the jars. Pack the spears evenly into the jars, ladle the hot vinegar over them, and screw the boiled lids on tightly. Store in a cool, dark place and wait at least three weeks before eating. They keep for about two years.
recipes.title: Choko pickle

recipes.method: 12–18 g (2–3 tbsp) dried shrimp; 600 g choko; 22 ml (1½ tbsp) canola, vegetable or almond oil; 35 g shallots or onion, sliced; 2 cloves garlic, smashed; a few slices of ginger; 300 ml water or broth; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) sea salt (1.25 ml, ¼ tsp, if using broth); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) chicken bouillon powder (optional); sliced spring onions and toasted sesame seeds to serve. Rinse the dried shrimp and soak them in cold water for 30 minutes (or hot water for 15–20 minutes), then drain. Peel the chokos, cutting the skin off any deep ridges with a paring knife. Slice off the top, stand each one cut side down and halve it, trim any skin left on the bottom ridges, and dig out the seed. Cut each half lengthwise into two, slice 6–12 mm thick, and rinse and drain the slices. Heat the oil in a wok over medium-high heat and cook the shallots, garlic, ginger and shrimp for 1–2 minutes. Add the choko, water or broth, salt and bouillon powder and stir. Cover and cook for 7–8 minutes, until the choko is fork-tender but still a little firm. Taste the broth and add salt if needed. Serve topped with spring onions and sesame seeds. Serves 2. For a vegan version, cook a few diced shiitake mushrooms with the choko and use vegetable broth.
recipes.title: Chinese stir-fried choko

recipes.method: 500 g choko (2 medium); 22 ml (1½ tbsp) oil; 1 cm ginger, sliced; 2–3 large cloves garlic, sliced; 1 green or red chilli, chopped (optional); 2.5 ml (½ tsp) chilli powder or flakes; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) sea salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground cumin; a pinch (⅛ tsp) of turmeric (optional); 1 small tomato, deseeded and chopped (about 80 ml, ⅓ cup); 30 ml (2 tbsp) unsweetened desiccated coconut; 15 ml (1 tbsp) toasted sesame seeds or 30 ml (2 tbsp) roasted, skinned peanuts; 30 ml (2 tbsp) chopped coriander leaves. Peel the chokos over a bowl of water, rinsing them often to wash off the slippery sap, then trim both ends, halve them lengthwise, take out the seed and pith, and cut into pieces about 2 cm across. Heat the oil in a pan and fry the ginger, garlic and chilli for a minute. Add the choko and salt and stir-fry over medium-high heat for 4 minutes. Stir in the chilli powder, cumin and turmeric, add the tomato and stir-fry for another 4–5 minutes. Add about 80 ml (⅓ cup) water (very young chokos may not need it), cover and cook for about 10 minutes, adding a splash more water if the pan dries out, until tender but still a little crunchy. Taste for salt. Lightly crush the sesame seeds or peanuts in a mortar, then stir them in with the coconut and coriander. Serves 4, with rice, dal or flatbreads.
recipes.title: Spiced choko

recipes.method: 3 chokos (about 225 g each); 45 ml (3 tbsp) vegetable oil; 3 cloves garlic, finely chopped; 1 medium brown onion, finely diced (about 250 ml, 1 cup); 25 ml (1 tbsp plus 2 tsp) fish sauce; freshly ground black pepper. Peel the chokos and halve them lengthwise. With the tip of a knife or a spoon, take out the seed and the white part around it. Lay each half cut side down, cut it in half lengthwise, then slice it thinly across. Heat the oil in a 30 cm non-stick or cast-iron frying pan over medium heat until it shimmers. Cook the garlic, stirring now and then, for about 2 minutes, until it just starts to brown. Add the onion and cook for about 3 minutes, until it begins to soften. Add the choko and cook, stirring often, for about 10 minutes, until tender and cooked through. Stir in the fish sauce and season with pepper. Serves 6.
recipes.title: Sautéed choko

summary.text:
Choko (Sicyos edulis, long known as Sechium edule), also called chayote, is a climbing vine of the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae) from Central America, introduced to New Zealand.
It is grown in gardens, where it was once a common cover for backyard sheds and bare fences, and was recorded as naturalised in 1989. It is a perennial: frost kills the leaves back in late autumn and winter, but it resprouts from the crown in spring, and in the lower South Island it usually needs cover to ripen fruit. Herbarium specimens from the North Auckland, South Auckland and Nelson land districts and the Bay of Plenty include plants growing wild near gardens, some described as apparently naturalised, and it is not uncommon around Tauranga. It is not on the Department of Conservation's list of environmental weeds or in any regional pest management plan.

warnings: The sap that oozes from the fruit when it is peeled can irritate the skin: wear gloves when peeling and handling it.
Choko is a strong diuretic: eating it in large amounts has caused severe low blood potassium in a pregnant woman, which returned to normal once she stopped. Eat it in moderation.

identification.text:
Perennial herb, with slender or sometimes fairly stout caulorrhiza. Hairs soft, retrorse or antrorse, generally appressed and often short, sometimes spreading. Stems slender, prostrate or spreading, with more or less retrorse hairs; branches usually many. Basal leaves rarely persistent through growing season; petioles to 12–(19) cm long; hairs retrorse and dense. Lamina usually to 3–(4) cm diameter, reniform to orbicular or broadly ovate, lobed 3/4-⅞ way to midrib; lobes (3)–5, narrowly to broadly obovate-cuneate, obovate-elliptic, obovate-oblong, or oblong, with appressed hairs on both sides or glabrous above, rounded to acute or mucronate at apex; larger lobes usually with 2 more or less oblong or elliptic secondary lobes. Cauline leaves smaller, with fewer lobes. Peduncles (with pedicels) usually 1–3–(4) cm long, filiform, with dense, retrorse hairs; bracteoles subulate or linear-subulate; flowers 1–(2). Sepals 3–5–(6) × 1–2.5 mm, lanceolate to elliptic, broadly elliptic or more or less ovate, usually with green margin, sometimes completely purple; hairs more or less spreading, often very short and antrorse towards apex, sometimes few. Petals 4–5 × 2–2.5 mm, broadly obovate, pink. Mericarps 2–3 mm long, with more or less dense hairs; beak (6)–7–10 mm long. Seed 1.5–1.9 mm long, oblong, distinctly alveolate.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped or cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Cinquefoil geranium and Solander's geranium are separated on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in Solander's geranium, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in Solander's geranium. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of Solander's geranium overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Solander's geranium's root is recorded as food.

Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of turnip-rooted geranium overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. summary.text:
Geranium potentilloides, belongs to the family Geraniaceae, and is a small prostrate perennial herb. The species is commonly referred to as Soft Cranesbill or Cinquefoil geranium.
Geranium potentilloides is native to the south-east of Australia, New Zealand and Indonesia.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Auckland southwards, widespread and common; South Island: Nelson, Marlborough, and collected once between Akatore and Glenledi (South Otago).

edibleParts.text: Young shoots and tips before flowering.

sources: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA) — restated
habitat.text:
Hedges, garden edges, fence lines, damp waste ground; scrambles over anything nearby.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): commonest among shrubs and tall herbs around cultivated areas, in waste places, forest margins, clearings and scrub, sometimes on newly exposed surfaces, rough pastures and cliff faces.

sources: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA) — restated
identification.text: Long, weak, square stems that cling to skin and clothing with tiny hooked hairs. Leaves in whorls of five to eight narrow blades around the stem. Tiny white four-petalled flowers, then small round burrs that stick to everything.

preparation.text: Cook — the hooks make it unpleasant raw. Wilt like spinach, blend into soup, or steep the fresh plant as a tea.

recipes.method: Fresh cleavers stems and leaves, enough to loosely fill a 950 ml jar; boiling water; ice and a sprig of mint, to serve. Loosely fill the jar with the cleavers and pour boiling water over them. Put the lid on and leave to steep for 4–6 hours. Strain, keep it in the fridge, and drink it over ice with a sprig of mint.
recipes.title: Cleavers tea

recipes.method: Written for Galium aparine in the UK. Serves 6. 100 g bunch of cleavers tops; 2 tablespoons olive oil; 2 garlic cloves, finely chopped; 2 medium onions, finely chopped; 2 red capsicums, roughly chopped; 1 red chilli, finely chopped; 400 g can of plum tomatoes; 50 ml elderberry pontack or Worcestershire sauce; ½ teaspoon hot pepper sauce; 1 tablespoon toasted seaweed such as nori or dulse; 1.5 litres hot water; salt and black pepper. Rinse the cleavers and snip off the roots with scissors. Warm a little of the oil in a saucepan and sweat the garlic and onions for 5 minutes, until they start to soften. Stir in the capsicums, then hold the bunch of cleavers over the pan and snip it in with scissors in 1–2 cm lengths, so the stems can't wind round the blender later. Cook for 5 minutes more. Pour in the hot water and add all the seasonings, then simmer for 15 minutes, until the capsicums are tender. Take the pan off the heat, let it cool and adjust the seasoning. Blend the cooled soup until completely smooth, with a stick blender or in a jug blender. Reheat and serve with finely chopped chives or wild garlic on top. The author sometimes adds a little crème fraîche or crumbled feta.
recipes.title: Cleavers and red pepper soup

recipes.method: The author's greens, picked from roadsides around Whangaroa Harbour, were nasturtium, kawakawa, fennel, samphire, fat hen, wild mustard, cleavers and clover. The author warns that New Zealand roadsides are still sprayed with glyphosate, so pick with care. 1 garlic clove (or 4 peeled onion weed bulbs); 60 ml (¼ cup) macadamia nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) grated parmesan, dairy or plant-based (or 125 ml, ½ cup, macadamias and no parmesan); 750 ml (3 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml extra-virgin olive oil; salt and pepper. Makes about 350 g. Blend in a food processor to the texture you like. Good on crackers or toast, as a side, or stirred through soup, pasta or rice.
recipes.title: Wild Whangaroa pesto

recipes.method: Written for cleavers, violet leaves, chickweed, red deadnettle and bittercress. A small handful of cleavers; 4 violet leaves; a handful of chickweed; 3 or 4 stems of red deadnettle; a small handful of bittercress; a big handful of bok choy, kale or silverbeet; 1 banana, peeled; 1 apple (whole without the stalk if organic, otherwise peeled); 1 mandarin (with its peel if organic, otherwise peeled); 1 or 2 kiwifruit, peeled; 1 small or ½ large avocado; 500 ml (2 cups) water, more if the blender struggles. Wash the weeds and greens, put them in the blender, snip them up a bit with scissors and add the water. Blend on low until the greens break down, then on high until smooth. Add the fruit and avocado and blend again, low and then high, until creamy.
recipes.title: Winter health boosting smoothie

summary.text: Sticky willy. The clinging spring weed with whorls of leaves and hooked stems that sticks to your clothes — mild, and one of the first greens of the season.

warnings: Pick young and before the burrs form; older growth is rough and bitter.
The sap can cause contact dermatitis in sensitive people.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Often on or near hedges in settled areas, spreading to waste sites, roadsides, and footpaths, also gardens.
It also grows on bush and shrubland margins, along streams and on the coast, and invades tussockland, fernland, bare ground and dunes. It grows most strongly in open, sunny places.

harvestEthics.text: It is a pest plant, on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds and under sustained control across the Auckland region. It smothers native plants and stops seedlings establishing. Harvest as much as you like, and carry no tubers or seeds elsewhere.

identification.text:
Climbing or scrambling, dioecious or monoecious perennial with tuberous woody rootstock; stems to about 3 m long, glabrous, flexuous. Leaves all similar. Petioles slender, equal to or often longer than lamina. Lamina 3–8 × 2–6 cm, more or less triangular or hastate with 2 long basal lobes at 45° to petiole, otherwise entire, slightly puberulent on main veins below when young; sinus broad and rounded; apex acuminate to cuspidate. Panicle pyramidal, with small leaves in the lower axils only. Pedicels filiform, long, glabrous. Perianth 1.5–2 mm long, green; outer segments more or less ovate-oblong, becoming strongly reflexed in female flowers. Fruit valves (4)–6–9–(9.5) mm diameter, orbicular, entire, prominently reticulate, cordate, yellow, pink to crimson; tubercles 0. Nuts about 3 mm long, glossy light brown; keels almost winged. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It scrambles over hedges, shrubs and fences on stems up to about 3 m long, from brown, woody, beet-like tubers that in old plants can be more than 10 cm across. The arrowhead-shaped leaves have pointed basal lobes; the ribbed stems start green and turn red with age. Small green to pink flowers in clusters at the top of the plant become papery, three-winged, heart-shaped fruit, yellow, pink or crimson.
In New Zealand the tubers are kūmara- or beetroot-like, 5–20 cm long with yellow flesh, with long weak rhizomes running from them. The stems are short-lived, growing each year from the tubers, and zigzag as they climb; they redden with age, drought or cold. The light green, soft, slightly fleshy leaves have basal lobes pointing downwards. Flowers come at the top of the plant from November to March. The fruit is green at first, then pink to crimson, and ends straw-coloured to pale brown in large cascading clusters. No other climber here has both tubers and showy pink seed capsules.

lookalikes.howToTell: Climbing dock's stems are ribbed and it scrambles over its support rather than twining round it. Its flowers are tiny (1.5–2 mm), green to pink, in large branched clusters at the top of the plant, followed by masses of papery, heart-shaped, three-winged fruit, yellow, pink or crimson. Its leaves are 3–8 cm long with pointed basal lobes and a broad, rounded notch, and it grows from brown tubers with yellow flesh. Pink bindweed's stems are smooth and twine round other plants; its flowers are single pink trumpets, usually 5–6 cm long (3–7 cm), each with two large bracts hiding its base; its leaves are 3–14 cm long (rarely 17), the basal lobes usually rounded and the notch deep; its roots are white. Both have arrowhead-shaped leaves and both smother hedges and scrub on coastal, lowland and town land, so leaf shape alone does not separate them.

preparation.text: Strip the leaves off the stems, which can be woody. Use them raw in salads and green sauces or as a sharp garnish. Cooked, they lose some sharpness and colour and become silky and sweet-sour; in Indonesia they are baked with fish in place of tamarind.

recipes.method: Written for climbing (rambling) dock in Australia, with farmer's friend and dandelion leaves. Makes about 8 servings. 500 ml (2 cups) climbing dock leaves; 125 ml (½ cup) farmer's friend leaves; 125 ml (½ cup) dandelion leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) parsley leaves; 2 crushed garlic cloves; 2 tbsp drained capers; 125 ml (½ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; a dash of red wine vinegar; 1 tsp Dijon mustard; the juice of 1 lemon; sea salt and pepper. Put 500 ml (2 cups) climbing dock leaves, 125 ml (½ cup) farmer's friend leaves, 125 ml (½ cup) dandelion leaves, 250 ml (1 cup) parsley leaves, 2 crushed garlic cloves and 2 tbsp drained capers in a food processor and chop finely. With the motor running, add 125 ml (½ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, a dash of red wine vinegar, 1 tsp Dijon mustard and the juice of 1 lemon, and process until combined. Season with sea salt and pepper and leave it to stand for 10 minutes. Serve as a dipping sauce, condiment or marinade.

summary.text:
Rumex sagittatus, synonym Acetosa sagittata, commonly known as turkey rhubarb or rambling dock or potato vine, is a herbaceous perennial plant native to southern Africa, which has become a weed in Australia and New Zealand.
The plant is native to southern Africa, where it occurs from Malawi and Zambia south to South Africa. It has become naturalised in many parts of Australia near urban areas, from Queensland to eastern Tasmania. In New Zealand it grows mainly near the coast: in the North Island especially from Northland to the Bay of Plenty and south to Wellington, and in the South Island mainly around Tasman Bay (Nelson), with occasional plants near Blenheim and Picton.
It spreads by seed or by resprouting from the tuber. The tubers persist and can grow more than 10 cm across, especially in old plants on light soil. They may be broken up by tractors or road graders and each fragment may be able to regrow; they can also be difficult to find with removal of plants by hand.
It was brought to New Zealand as an ornamental and recorded wild by 1935. It is sometimes grown for its colourful fruit, and has been used to dye wool. It is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds and under sustained control across the Auckland region, where it smothers native plants and stops seedlings establishing.
A young plant can fruit within its first year and set thousands of seeds, which can lie dormant in the soil for at least two years. Seeds and tubers travel on the wind, in fresh and salt water, in moved soil and in dumped garden waste. It copes with wet and drought, dying back to its tubers in drought and, in cooler places, over winter, then regrowing in spring; after fire it resprouts from the tubers. Other names include arrow dock and arrowhead vine.
In the Bay of Plenty, where it is common and widespread, it is an advisory pest: the regional council does not enforce its control, which is left to landowners and occupiers.

warnings: It contains oxalic acid, which gives the leaves their sharp taste. Do not eat it in large amounts, and leave it alone if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.
It is a pest plant controlled with herbicide sprays such as metsulfuron-methyl or glyphosate. Pick only where you know it has not been sprayed.

In the Auckland region it must not be bred, sold, distributed, released or planted. It regrows from its tubers and rhizomes and spreads by seed, so carry no living pieces elsewhere: rot them in a covered barrel of water, burn them, or send them to green waste, a refuse transfer station or landfill.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Usually damp places such as river banks and beds, ditches, drains and swampy places, also pastures and waste places in high rainfall areas, sometimes just above high tide level on beaches.
New Zealand's national wetland plant list rates it FAC (facultative): it is common both in wetlands and on dry land.

identification.text:
Glabrous, short-lived, tap-rooted perennial; stems rather thin, wiry, flexuous, spreading, green to dark red, to about 1 m tall. Petioles of basal leaves often very long, particularly in subaquatic plants. Lamina of lower leaves (3)–7–20–(23) × (1)–1.5–3.5 cm, oblong or ovate-oblong, more or less membranous; margin often undulate and crisped; base broad-cuneate, rounded or cordate; apex acute or subacute. Stem leaves progressively smaller and extending about ⅔ along inflorescence branches. Inflorescence many-branched, spreading and flexuous, becoming twisted. Whorls all distant; flowers probably protandrous, bisexual, small, dense. Pedicels slender, reddish. Perianth (0.7)–1–5 mm long; outer segments ovate, obtuse, not reflexing at fruiting; inner segments greatly enlarging at fruiting. Fruiting valves 2–2.8–(3.2) mm long, ovate, reticulate, entire, rounded at apex, generally becoming dark red, each with a large tubercle occupying ?-3/4 valve width. Nut 1.5–2 mm long, dark glossy brown or reddish brown, acutely angled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Its flower whorls are all spaced well apart along spreading branches that twist as the fruit ripens, and small leaves run about two-thirds of the way up the branches. Each of the three fruit valves carries a large, smooth, oblong swelling (tubercle), all three well developed. Plants can be very reddish, especially in fruit.
It usually branches from below the middle of the stem, and its stiff branches spread wide rather than standing upright; the stems zig-zag. The stalks of the basal leaves are usually about as long as the blade. The fruiting heads turn rusty brown and stand out, and the ripe fruits snap off their slender jointed stalks when brushed.

lookalikes.howToTell: Curled dock's flower whorls are mostly packed together on erect branches, with few or no leaves among them; clustered dock's are all spaced apart along spreading branches that twist as they fruit, with small leaves about two-thirds of the way up. Curled dock's fruit valves are larger (3–4.5 mm), often with only one much larger tubercle; each of clustered dock's (2–3.2 mm) has a large tubercle. Curled dock's leaf base tapers into the stalk; clustered dock's is broadly wedge-shaped, rounded or heart-shaped. Both can have wavy, curled leaf edges.
lookalikes.name: Curled dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Broad-leaved dock's lower leaves reach 15 cm wide (rarely 20); clustered dock's are only 1–3.5 cm wide. Broad-leaved dock's flower whorls are usually packed together and its fruit valves have teeth 1–1.7 mm long on their edges and a prominent rosy tubercle; clustered dock's whorls are all spaced apart, on branches that twist as they fruit, and its valves (2–3.2 mm) are entire, each with a large tubercle.
lookalikes.name: Broad-leaved dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Fiddle dock's lower leaves are flat and pinched in the lower half above two large rounded lobes (occasionally plain and oblong); clustered dock's are oblong, often wavy and curled, and sometimes slightly pinched part way down, but usually not as sharply. Both have spaced whorls on branches that twist as they fruit, but fiddle dock's fruit valves have spines up to 2 mm long on their edges, while clustered dock's are entire.
lookalikes.name: Fiddle dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Foxglove is deadly. Its leaves are hairy (sometimes almost hairless above) and grey-felted beneath, with scalloped edges and a base that narrows into a long winged stalk, on densely hairy stems; clustered dock is hairless all over, and its lower leaves are oblong, only 1–3.5 cm wide (foxglove's 3.5–12 cm), with often wavy, curled edges and a broadly wedge-shaped, rounded or heart-shaped base. Every dock leaf stalk is wrapped at its base by a papery sheath (ochrea). If a leaf is felted or hairy underneath, leave it.
lookalikes.name: Foxglove

preparation.text: Pick the leaves young, before the flower stalk rises, when they become more bitter and astringent. Take out the central vein, boil the leaves and throw the water away: this softens the bitterness and lowers the oxalic acid. Use them as cooked greens.

recipes.method: Written for dock generally — the author thinks his leaves were most likely curled dock but is not certain; the New Zealand version below names broad-leaved and curled dock; clustered dock is very bitter, more so as it ages, so use only young leaves. Serves 4. You need 170 g young dock leaves, washed; salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to finish; 50 g (¼ cup) basmati or other long-grain rice; 1 small onion, chopped; 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped garlic; 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped fresh oregano; a pinch of ground cumin; 1 litre chicken or vegetable stock; 1 large egg, beaten; black pepper; and plenty of fresh lemon juice. Drop the dock leaves into boiling salted water for a few seconds until just wilted, cool them in cold water and squeeze them dry (about 180 ml). Toast the rice on a tray in a 175 °C oven until just golden, then simmer it, covered, with a pinch of salt and 125 ml water until tender. Chop the dock both ways so no long strands are left. In a 3-litre pot, soften the onion and garlic in the oil over medium heat for about 10 minutes, until just browning at the edges. Add the stock, dock, oregano and cumin, bring to a simmer and season, then add the rice and simmer gently for about 10 minutes. Pour the beaten egg in a spiral over the surface without stirring and let it heat through. Serve with a drizzle of olive oil, black pepper and enough lemon juice that the soup tastes lemony. For a simpler version without egg (Wild Botanica, New Zealand): soften the onion and garlic, wilt the chopped leaves (central veins removed) in the pot, add the stock, cumin, oregano and salt, simmer for 10 minutes, then stir through 60 ml (¼ cup) cooked rice and finish with lemon juice.
recipes.title: Dock soup with rice, egg and lemon

summary.text:
Rumex conglomeratus, known as clustered dock and sharp dock, is a plant of the family Polygonaceae; an older name for it is Rumex acutus. It is native to Europe, North Africa and Asia Minor and was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1867. Kew's Plants of the World Online gives a wider native range, east to Central Asia and the western Himalaya and also South Africa, and lists it as introduced in the Americas, Japan, Korea, Tasmania and Norfolk Island as well as both main islands of New Zealand. It grows throughout the North and South Islands.
It is a weed of pasture and cultivated ground, though in Australia it is less aggressive than curled dock. It spreads by seed: ripe fruits break off when people, animals or machinery brush the dry branches, and travel on the wind (the valves act as sails), in mud, and on water (the tubercles act as floats). Pieces of the crown and upper taproot cut up by cultivation can regrow. Red-veined dock (Rumex sanguineus) has been reported from New Zealand, but the Flora of New Zealand (1988) found no specimens and suggests plants so named may have been clustered dock, which can also be very reddish.

warnings: It contains oxalic acid, which gives the leaves their sharp taste. A little is fine, but large amounts can lock up calcium and other minerals in food; cooking lowers the oxalic acid. Take particular care, or leave it alone, if you are prone to rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.
Large amounts of dock leaves that are not properly cooked can cause nausea, stomach cramps, vomiting and headache.

identification.text: Cap 3–6 cm across, low-domed and usually with a small raised centre when young, later sunken in the middle and often with a tiny nipple at its centre; dry, without zones, smooth or finely scaly. Its colour is grey with a lilac tinge, ranging to pale grey-brown or brownish grey with a lead-grey cast. The edge is tightly rolled under when young and only slightly curled at maturity. Gills thin and fairly close, joined to the stem or running a little down it, pale pinkish buff. The milk is rather watery and white, and does not change colour in the air. Stem 2–5 cm long and 0.7–1.1 cm thick, even, solid, dry and smooth, the colour of the cap or paler. Flesh soft, dirty white to pale fawn, unchanging. It smells faintly of coconut, and tastes mild at first, then slightly acrid. Spore print creamy white.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Coconut milk cap's milk is white, rather watery and unchanging, its cap is greyish lilac, pale greyish brown or brownish grey with leaden tints rather than orange, and it smells of coconut - faintly, in the New Zealand description. It grows under silver birch; saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine.

identification.text:
Erect biennial. Stems hispid, hollow, grooved, green to reddish brown, 60–150–(200) cm high. Basal leaves pinnately 3-foliolate or 1-pinnate with up to 9 leaflets, petiolate; leaflets densely hispidulous below, sparsely to moderately above, ternately or pinnately lobed and serrate, c. 5–20 cm long; lobes acute or obtuse; stem leaves similar to basal, more often pinnately 3-foliolate with reduced petiole; petiole usually tinged purple toward base. Umbels 5–20 cm diameter; rays 12–30; bracts 0–7, linear, 8–15 mm long; bracteoles c. 6, linear, up to 15 mm long. Flowers numerous, white or tinged pink; outer flowers irregular and up to 10 mm diameter. Fruit glabrous, ovate-elliptic, light brown, 7–10 mm long; vittae conspicuous, 0.2–0.5 mm wide at base.
Flowers December–February.
Told from giant hogweed (H. mantegazzianum) by its shorter stems, up to 150, sometimes 200, cm high; its stems and leaf stalks, green or tinged reddish brown or purple, not blotched and spotted reddish purple; and its main umbels with fewer than 30 rays (more than 50 in giant hogweed).

lookalikes.howToTell: Giant hogweed is poisonous: its sap on the skin followed by sunlight causes burns and blisters that can scar, and sap in the eyes can cause blindness, so do not touch it. Look at the stem and leaf stalks without touching them: giant hogweed's are blotched and spotted reddish purple, especially towards the base of the stem; common hogweed's are green or tinged reddish brown or purple, and its leaf stalks are usually tinged purple at the base, so look for blotches and spots, not just a purple tinge. Count the rays of the main umbel: common hogweed's has fewer than 30; giant hogweed's has more than 50. Measure the umbels: common hogweed's are 5–20 cm across; giant hogweed's are usually 30–60 cm (sometimes only 20 cm). Common hogweed's stem is 60–150, sometimes 200, cm tall; giant hogweed's grows up to 350 cm tall and 10 cm thick, so a stem over 2 m is giant hogweed, but a shorter one may be either. Common hogweed's leaflets are about 5–20 cm long; giant hogweed's reach 50, sometimes 100, cm. Look under the umbel: common hogweed has 0–7 bracts; giant hogweed usually has about 12. Common hogweed's flowers are white or tinged pink, the outer ones up to 10 mm across; giant hogweed's are white, the outer ones up to 15 mm across. Ripe fruit: common hogweed's is 7–10 mm long with oil canals 0.2–0.5 mm wide at the base; giant hogweed's is about 10 mm long with canals 0.5–1 mm wide. Both grow in waste places and gardens, in the Wellington area, Canterbury and Otago, and 'cow parsnip' is listed as a name of both, so neither place nor name rules giant hogweed out. Neither is food.

summary.text:
Common hogweed (Heracleum sphondylium), also called cow parsnip and keck, is a biennial of the carrot family (Apiaceae) from Europe, the Mediterranean, western and northern Asia and north-west Africa, naturalised locally in New Zealand.
It was first recorded wild here in 1939. It grows on the coast north of Wellington City in the North Island, and around Christchurch, in South Canterbury and around Dunedin in the South Island.
It is a smaller relative of giant hogweed (Heracleum mantegazzianum), a poisonous Unwanted Organism, and 'cow parsnip' is also listed among giant hogweed's names, so the name alone does not tell the two apart.
DOC's weeds database does not classify it as a weed, and it is not on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.

warnings: Common hogweed is not given here as food. The food uses recorded for it come from overseas and disagree on whether it can be eaten raw, and serious reactions to eating it, including anaphylactic shock, have been reported.

Its sap contains furanocoumarins. Sap on the skin followed by sunlight can cause phytophotodermatitis: about 24–48 hours later the skin turns red and inflamed and often blisters, and dark marks can stay for several years.

Giant hogweed, which is poisonous and an Unwanted Organism, can be confused with common hogweed, grows in the same waste places and gardens, and 'cow parsnip' is one of its names too. Do not touch any large hogweed until you have checked the stems, leaf stalks and umbels as described in Lookalikes.

edibleParts.text: None.

habitat.text: In clumps on the ground, growing from buried wood or tree roots, often in lawns and other grass, parks, gardens and disturbed ground, and around stumps. In New Zealand it has been collected with karaka, English oak, grey and crack willow, apple and tree of heaven, and among grasses.

harvestEthics.text: Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.

identification.text:
It grows in tight clumps. The cap is 3–10 cm across, grey to grey-brown, egg- to bell-shaped at first and later more convex, furrowed, and splitting at the rim, which often curls up and tatters as it matures. It is mostly smooth, with at most a small patch of small, flattened scales in the centre. It melts from the edge inward into black ink.
The gills are very crowded and free of the stem or attached to it, white at first, then grey or pinkish, and black as they dissolve. The stem is 5–17 cm tall and 0.6–2 cm thick, whitish to grey, hollow, with no ring. The flesh is thin and pale grey. The spore print is black. New Zealand specimens reach about 12 cm tall and 6 cm across.
A shaggy inkcap is white and covered in large, upturned shaggy scales, has a loose ring on its stem, and grows from soil, not in clumps from wood.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are inkcaps that melt into black ink, and both come up in grass. Shaggy inkcap is white and covered in large, upturned shaggy scales, has a loose ring on its stem, and grows singly or in groups from soil. Common inkcap is grey to grey-brown, its cap furrowed and mostly smooth, with at most a few small flat scales in the centre; it has no ring, and it grows in tight clumps from buried wood or around stumps. Shaggy inkcap contains no coprine; common inkcap makes alcohol poisonous for days.

summary.text:
The common inkcap is a grey-brown inkcap that comes up in tight clumps from buried wood, often in lawns and other grass. Like the shaggy inkcap, its cap and gills melt into a black, inky liquid as it ages; the ink was once used for writing.
It contains coprine, which makes it poisonous with alcohol: drinking within about three days of eating it brings on a reaction like that of the anti-drinking drug disulfiram, hence its other name, tippler's bane. Eaten young with no alcohol it is edible, but because the reaction can follow a drink days later, this guide treats it as not for eating.
It is common across the Northern Hemisphere and has also been found in South Africa and Australia. Biota of New Zealand gives its origin here as uncertain (the New Zealand Organisms Register gives it as unknown) and notes that the name is used in a broad sense, which may take in a related species, Coprinopsis depressiceps. New Zealand herbarium collections come from Auckland to Dunedin, and it is in the New Zealand checklist of agarics (Segedin & Pennycook 2001).

warnings: It contains coprine. Drinking alcohol within about three days before or after eating it causes flushing of the face, nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, a racing or pounding heart and tingling in the limbs, starting within minutes of the drink.
If anyone has eaten it and then had alcohol, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Kelp that has come loose and washed ashore is the gentlest to collect; even then, take a little from several places, as the piles on the beach are also habitat. If you cut a living plant, use a sharp knife and leave the holdfast so it can regrow.
Attached plants may not be taken from the East Otago taiāpure; only unattached kelp cast ashore may be taken there. Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.

identification.text:
Grows to about 1 m. A single large blade, deeply divided into lobes, smooth or wrinkled, on a cylindrical, unbranched, trunk-like stipe. The holdfast is a clump of finger-like cylindrical branches (haptera). Golden brown. Reproductive tissue shows as darker patches on the lobes. The blade is rough and leathery, often with many small raised bumps, and has no midrib.
Told from wakame by the midrib: wakame has a strap-like midrib up the blade once it is larger than about 10 cm, a flattened stipe, a smooth, thin blade and, when mature, a frilly reproductive structure at the base of the stipe. Young plants are difficult to tell apart before wakame's midrib develops.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look down the middle of the blade: wakame has a strap-like midrib, continuing from the stalk, once the plant is larger than about 10 cm (it starts to show from about 5 cm); this kelp has no midrib. This kelp's stipe is cylindrical and trunk-like; wakame's is flattened and strap-like. This kelp's blade is rough and leathery, often with many small raised bumps; wakame's is smooth, thin and fragile. Mature wakame has a frilly reproductive structure (the sporophyll) at the base of the stalk, thicker and often darker brown than the blade and deeply folded, spiralling round the stalk when big; this kelp has none, and its reproductive tissue shows as darker patches on the lobes. Young plants are difficult to tell apart before wakame's midrib develops. Lobes, colour and holdfast do not separate them: both have a blade that can be deeply divided into lobes, both can be golden brown, and both have a holdfast of finger-like branches. Size does not either: this kelp grows to about 1 m, wakame to 1 m and up to 3 m. Both grow from the low intertidal into the subtidal. Wakame grows on any hard surface, including wharf piles, ropes, moorings, boat hulls and concrete, and is found in almost all of New Zealand's international ports and harbours; this kelp grows on moderately exposed or exposed coasts.

preparation.text: Take kelp that is freshly washed up, soon after high tide or a storm, and rinse off all the sand in fresh water. Use it fresh: trim off the tough stems and slice the blade into thin ribbons for pickling, or blanch for 10–30 seconds, when it turns bright green, and add it to soups or stir-fries. Or dry it: in the sun it takes 2–3 days and turns from golden brown to dark green, or use a dehydrator in cold, damp weather; then chop or grind it and add it towards the end of cooking. Dried pieces flavour stock and dashi: put them in tepid water and warm it gradually without boiling. Dried blades can be softened in water and wrapped round fish to bake. Soaking seaweed in water, with or without heat, lowers its iodine content, by up to 90%.

recipes.method: Written for common kelp (Ecklonia radiata) washed up on the south coast of New South Wales. Makes 4 × 250 ml jars. 1 kg fresh kelp; 650 ml water; 250 ml white wine vinegar; 100 g white sugar; 1 tsp black peppercorns; 1 tsp coriander seeds; 1 tsp mustard seeds. Sterilise the jars and lids: 20 minutes before you need them, heat the oven to 110 °C and line an oven tray with baking paper; boil the jars and lids in a large pot of water for 10 minutes, drain, and stand them upside down on the tray in the oven until completely dry, without touching the rims or insides. Keep them in the oven until you fill them. Rinse the kelp thoroughly in fresh water to get rid of any sand, trim off any tough stems, and slice it into thin ribbons. Bring the water, vinegar, sugar and spices to the boil in a saucepan; once the sugar has dissolved, take it off the heat. Add the kelp to the hot pickling liquid: it turns vivid green at first, then quickly dulls. Pack it firmly into the jars, top up with the pickling liquid so the kelp is completely covered, and seal. The page gives no keeping time.
recipes.title: Pickled kelp

recipes.method: Written for dried New Zealand kombu leaves (the blade of Ecklonia radiata). Serves 2. 2 large dried kelp blades, softened in water; 2 pieces of salmon; tamari or soy sauce; 1 lemon, thinly sliced; a handful of fresh herbs (dill, thyme, tarragon or fennel); salt (kelp or seaweed salt if you have it) and pepper. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Line an oven tray with baking paper and lay the 2 softened blades on it. Put a piece of salmon on each and drizzle with tamari. Cover with the lemon slices and herbs, season, and wrap each blade diagonally round its fish. Bake for about 10 minutes, until the fish is just cooked, and serve straight away. Other fish fillets can be cooked the same way.
recipes.title: Kelp-wrapped baked salmon
