identification.text:
Annual, at first stemless, later usually with 1 or more hairy stems; plant extremely variable in size, from prostrate to about 50 cm high and about 75 cm wide, not musk-scented. Leaves to about 15 cm long, pinnate, hairy, sometimes densely so, sometimes glandular; petiole longer in rosette and lower cauline leaves. Leaflets sessile, ovate, deeply and finely pinnately dissected with linear to lanceolate lobes, often densely covered in white hairs. Stipules triangular, often broad, membranous, ciliate, silvery; midrib green, forming an acute or mucronate apex. Umbels (2)–5–12-flowered; bracts broad-ovate, membranous, with green keeled midrib forming an acute to short-acuminate apex. Peduncles densely covered in glandular hairs, often longer than upper cauline leaves; pedicels more or less equal to calyx at anthesis. Sepals (2.5)–3–5 mm long at anthesis, lanceolate, hirsute or glandular, mucronate. Petals 4–6 mm long, elliptic or oblong-elliptic, usually pink or mauve-pink, rarely white; claw short, hairy. Stamens about 3 mm long; filaments widened at base, without lateral teeth, usually pinkish; anthers dark purple. Staminodes narrow-lanceolate. Fruit beak 3–3.5 cm long, with appressed hairs. Mericarps densely hirsute with hairs of differing lengths; apical pits eglandular, with a prominent shallow glabrous furrow beneath.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In open, exposed habitats, especially on poor or stony soils, the plants are usually more or less red, as well as being very small and depauperate.
Common storksbill is a herb that typically grows in rosettes pressed flat to the ground, with a deep tap root that allows it to survive through the summer on dry soils. It can develop stems up to 60 cm long that are sometimes red and sometimes green, and may be erect or prostrate, and have simple or glandular hairs which become more abundant towards the top. Plants with glandular hairs are sticky, but those with simple hairs are much less so. It has no scent. The stems bear bright pink flowers which often have dark spots on the bases. The long seed-pod, shaped like the bill of a stork, bursts open in a spiral when ripe, sending the seeds (which have long tails called awns) into the air.
Seedlings have long-stalked, violin-shaped seed leaves, rounded at the tip and notched at the base; the first true leaves are elongated and lobed.
Musky storksbill (Erodium moschatum) looks very similar. It smells of musk when bruised, is clammy with dense glandular hairs, and its leaflets are lobed into more or less ovate, toothed lobes rather than finely cut; its stipules and bracts are blunt to rounded, not acute to short-pointed. In flower, musky storksbill's fertile stamens usually have a small tooth on one or both sides of the widened base (rarely none); common storksbill's have none. Common storksbill's seed segments have glandless pits at the top; musky storksbill's pits are glandular.

lookalikes.howToTell: Young plants of both are rosettes of finely divided, fern-like leaves, and both grow in waste places and riverbeds. Common storksbill's leaves and stems are hairy, sometimes densely so; hemlock is hairless throughout, and its leaf stalks have no hairs. Crush a leaf: hemlock smells foetid; common storksbill has no scent. Hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided, with segments 5–40 mm long; common storksbill's are once divided into stalkless leaflets that are themselves deeply and finely cut, up to about 15 cm long in all. Stem colour is not a safe test: common storksbill's stems can be red, and hemlock's are usually spotted or blotched purple. Grown on, hemlock stands erect, up to 2–(3) m, with hollow stems and many white flowers about 2 mm across; common storksbill lies along the ground or rises to about 50 cm, with clusters of (2–)5–12 flowers, petals 4–6 mm long, usually pink or mauve-pink but rarely white, followed by fruits with a beak 3–3.5 cm long. Mistakes are likeliest with very young plants; if a rosette is hairless or smells foul, do not eat it. Hemlock is deadly poisonous; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: Musky storksbill looks very similar and grows in the same places, though common storksbill tends to grow on drier, less fertile sites. Crush a leaf: musky storksbill usually smells of musk, though not always strongly; common storksbill has no musky smell. Musky storksbill is densely glandular and clammy; common storksbill is usually much less clammy. Common storksbill's leaflets are deeply and finely cut into narrow, linear to lanceolate lobes, giving fern-like foliage; musky storksbill's are lobed into more or less ovate, toothed lobes. Common storksbill's stipules and bracts end in an acute to short-pointed tip; musky storksbill's are blunt to rounded. In flower, look at the fertile stamens: musky storksbill's filaments usually have a small tooth on one or both sides of the widened base (rarely none); common storksbill's have none. Petal colour and the 3–3.5 cm fruit beak do not separate them. Musky storksbill's leaves are eaten too; see its own entry.

preparation.text: Add young leaves to salads, sandwiches and soups, or cook them as a pot herb; they can be used in recipes that call for the leaves of beet, plantain, sow thistle or amaranth. The leaves are picked in early spring, before the flowers appear, and cooked as greens. Raw, the leaves are bitter, hairy and astringent; boiling makes them more palatable, so cook leaves eaten in quantity. Wash them well, as the hairy leaves trap sand and grit. The leaves can also be cooked as for spinach, added to stews as a wild vegetable, or cooked with a mix of other greens as a pie filling.

recipes.method: Serves 4. 450 g young greens picked before the plants flower — storksbill alone or with other young wild greens; about 4 litres water; 45 ml (3 tbsp) coarse salt; extra-virgin olive oil; 1 lemon, cut into wedges; flaky salt to finish. Soak the freshly picked greens in cold water for 10 minutes. Bring the water and coarse salt to the boil in a large lidded pot, add the greens, cover and bring back to the boil. Uncover and cook for about 1 minute, stirring until all are wilted, then taste one: some greens take longer than others, so cook on until they are tender and taste good to you. Drain in a colander for a minute, turning them over, then spread them in a warmed serving dish and drizzle with olive oil. Serve with the lemon wedges and flaky salt.
recipes.title: Horta (Greek boiled wild greens)

recipes.method: Written for leylek gagası, a Turkish name for storksbills; the recipe names no species. 1 bunch of young storksbill; 1 brown onion; about 50 ml rice; about 50 ml olive oil; 1 dessertspoon of salt (5–10 ml); about 300 ml hot water. Pick off any tough or yellowed parts, wash the greens several times in plenty of water until no sand is left, and leave them to drain. Chop the onion and fry it in the olive oil until it just colours. Chop the greens roughly, add them and fry for a while. Add the salt, rice and hot water, cover and cook until the rice is done. Serve warm.
recipes.title: Storksbill with rice (Turkish style)

summary.text:
Erodium cicutarium, also known as common stork's-bill, redstem filaree, redstem stork's bill or pinweed, is a herbaceous annual – or in warm climates, biennial – member of the family Geraniaceae of flowering plants. It is native to Macaronesia, temperate Eurasia and north and northeast Africa, and was introduced to North America in the eighteenth century, where it has since become naturalised, particularly in the deserts and arid grasslands of the southwestern United States. It is also naturalised elsewhere, including South America and southern Africa.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands and the Chatham Islands, very common throughout. Naturalised from Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia, first recorded in 1855. It flowers from September to May. New Zealand plants are subspecies cicutarium. It is also called storksbill, alfilaria, common crowfoot, pin clover and pin grass. It is commoner in drier places and in the South Island than musky storksbill, which favours fertile North Island pastures, though each turns up in the other’s territory. The genus name comes from the Greek erodios, 'a heron', because the style and ovaries together look like a heron.
It is a weed of turf and pasture. Its sharply pointed fruits can pierce the skin of sheep and work into the flesh, more often than those of musky storksbill. The long awn of each fruit winds and unwinds with the humidity, burying the seed in the soil.
Sheep and lambs that eat a lot of storksbill can become sensitive to sunlight (photosensitisation): it has been seen in lambs grazing herbage that was mainly storksbill in Australia and New Zealand (North Canterbury and Hawke's Bay). The agent responsible has not been identified.

warnings: Young plants are rosettes of finely divided, fern-like leaves, like those of hemlock, which is deadly. Common storksbill's leaves and stems are hairy; hemlock is hairless throughout and smells foetid when crushed. Do not pick very young plants you are unsure of; flowering and fruiting plants are much easier to name (see the lookalikes).

Sheep and lambs that graze mostly storksbill can become sensitive to sunlight (photosensitisation). The substance responsible has not been identified, and whether it affects people is not known. No source gives a safe quantity for people.

In lawns and pastures it is controlled with herbicides such as MCPA, 2,4-D, dicamba, picloram with triclopyr, and bentazone. Avoid plants on roadsides, heavily grazed ground or sprayed areas, and pick it only where you know none has been used.

identification.text:
Slender to stout scrambling or tufted annual; stem sparsely hairy. Leaves sparsely to densely hairy; tendrils branched; leaflets in (3)–4–8 pairs, often alternate, linear to elliptic to obovate, (5)–10–30–(40) mm long; stipules simple or with 1, adaxial, basal lobe, or dentate, usually with a dark spot. Inflorescence much shorter than leaves, 1–2–(4)-flowered. Peduncle much shorter than flowers, rarely more or less equal to flowers. Pedicel 1–5 mm long. Calyx somewhat gibbous at base; calyx teeth more or less equal, shorter than, equal to, or longer than the tube. Corolla usually purple, reddish purple or rose, sometimes white or pink, (8)–12–28 mm long; limb of standard longer than claw. Pod more or less glabrous or puberulent, blackish or brownish black, constricted or not between seeds, 5–12-seeded, (20)–30–60 mm long; seeds light or dark brown with dark spots; hilum ⅙-⅕ of circumference.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Flowers or seeds are needed to identify vetches. Common vetch is told from other vetches by its leaves with 4–8 pairs of leaflets, its large flowers in short clusters, and its more or less equal calyx teeth. Yellow vetch (Vicia lutea), established only on Banks Peninsula, is very similar but has a pale yellow corolla, sometimes tinged purple, and unequal calyx teeth.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers and pods. Yellow vetch's corolla is pale yellow, sometimes tinged purple, and its calyx teeth are unequal: the lower teeth about as long as the calyx tube, the upper ones much shorter. Common vetch's corolla is usually purple, reddish purple or rose, sometimes white or pink, and its calyx teeth are more or less equal. Yellow vetch's pods are moderately hairy and hold 3–6 seeds; common vetch's are more or less hairless or finely downy and hold 5–12. The leaves do not separate them: both have tendrils and several pairs of leaflets, and leaflet sizes overlap, so flowers or seeds are needed. Both grow on Banks Peninsula, the only place yellow vetch is established. Yellow vetch's only food records are for its seeds, which are not given as food here (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Yellow vetch

preparation.text: Pick only young, tender shoots and leaves, taking a little from many plants rather than stripping one, and leave plants that are dusty or growing in contaminated places. Young shoots can be eaten raw, as in pesto or salad, but only a small helping at a time; cooking them as a green vegetable is the more cautious way to try them. Cook young pods before eating them. Do not eat the seeds (see warnings).

recipes.method: 2 packed cups (500 ml) young common vetch shoots and leaves, 1 tbsp olive oil, 1 small garlic clove, finely chopped, 1 tsp lemon juice, salt and black pepper; toasted sesame seeds or grated parmesan are optional. Wash the vetch well under running water and remove tough stems. Blanch the greens in a saucepan of boiling water for 2–3 minutes and drain well. Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat, cook the garlic briefly, then add the greens and sauté for another 2–3 minutes until tender. Season with a little salt and pepper and finish with the lemon juice. Serve as a small side dish.
recipes.title: Lemon-garlic vetch greens

recipes.method: 100 g pine nuts, 2 garlic cloves, 2–3 good handfuls of very young, tender common vetch shoots, a generous splash of olive oil and 50 g grated parmesan. Pound the pine nuts, garlic, vetch shoots and oil together in a large mortar and pestle, or blend them in a food processor, and work in the parmesan. Serve on pasta, stir through risotto, spread on bruschetta or serve alongside meat.

summary.text: Common vetch, also called vetch or tare (Vicia sativa), is a scrambling or tufted annual of the pea family, Fabaceae, introduced to New Zealand from western and southern Europe to western Asia and North Africa and first recorded here in 1867. It is a very common weed throughout New Zealand: common to abundant throughout the North and South Islands, in lowland disturbed areas on Stewart Island and Codfish Island, and on the Kermadec and Chatham Islands. It varies greatly in leaf form, in the number of flowers in a cluster, and in flower and pod size; reduced, narrow-leaved plants grow in dry stony sites and more robust, broader-leaved plants in wet places, and one plant can bear several leaf forms as it develops. Some New Zealand plants fit var. sativa, a stout plant with broad leaflets and a corolla over 18 mm long, or the narrow-leaved vetch, var. angustifolia (also treated as subsp. nigra), a slender plant with narrow leaflets and a corolla under 18 mm long, but many plants are intermediate. Its seed is long-lived in the soil and is scattered when the pods burst open. It is not a listed pest plant.

warnings: The seeds contain the nerve toxins γ-glutamyl-β-cyanoalanine and β-cyanoalanine, and cyanogenic glycosides. They are toxic to animals with a simple stomach, people included, and damage the nervous system, with signs such as convulsions and leg paralysis.

Soaking does not lower the main seed toxin enough and boiling only reduces it; in the vetch varieties tested it remains too high for animals with a simple stomach. The seeds are not given here as food.
The seeds also contain vicine and convicine, the compounds that cause favism from broad beans: in people with G6PD deficiency they break down red blood cells, and favism can be fatal.

habitat.text:
Montane and subalpine sites of low fertility: indigenous and introduced scrub, tussock grassland, pasture and open forest. It also takes over shrubland, herbfields, fernland, bare and mineralised ground, screes and volcanic land, and grows above the native treeline; to about 1500 m in the North Island and 1000 m in the South Island.
Once established it tolerates drought, frost, wind, salt, damp or dry ground and poor soils, and copes with poor drainage a little. It will not establish in dense forest but tolerates partial shade. It regrows after damage and grazing unless all the foliage is removed, and trees over 2 m survive fire.

identification.text:
A resinous large shrub or small to medium tree, upright or spreading, often branched almost to the ground. The bark is reddish brown, grey on the surface, cracked into small plates. The needles come in pairs, 3.5–6.5 cm long, often twisted and generally yellowish green. The woody cones are small, 3–6 cm, usually point down or back along the branch, have a short slender prickle on each scale, and stay closed on the tree long after they ripen. Short needles in pairs and small prickly cones together set it apart from the other wild pines in New Zealand.
Branches straight or somewhat twisted. Shoots brown, hairless. Buds cylindrical or cylindrical-ovoid, purplish brown, strongly resinous, scales pressed tight. Needles 2 per bundle, (2.5–)3.5–6.5 cm × 0.8–1.5 mm, not or somewhat twisted, usually pointing forward; resin canals midway; the sheath very short after the first year. Male cones 5–15 mm long, cylindrical. Young female cones stalkless, the scales tipped with a bristle. Mature cones long-persistent, often not opening until long after maturity, almost stalkless, 3–6 × 2–3.5 cm, broadly egg-shaped, lopsided at the base; scale ends shining yellowish brown or brown before maturity, convex, with a short slender prickle that sometimes falls. Seed wing lopsided but almost oblong, about 1 cm long. Wild New Zealand trees vary a lot in needle length and twist and in cone shape, size and symmetry.

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the needles in a bundle and look at the cones. Radiata pine has needles in threes, 6–15 cm long, deep or dark green, mostly towards the ends of the branches; its cones are big, 6–13 cm, in clusters of 1–6, pointing back along the branch but not down, without a prickle on the scales; its bark is thick and deeply ridged. Contorta pine has needles in pairs, 3.5–6.5 cm, often twisted and yellowish green; its cones are 3–6 cm, usually point down or back, and have a short prickle on each scale; its bark cracks into small plates. Radiata pine's seeds are eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Monterey pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have needles in pairs. Corsican pine's needles are longer, 6–16 cm, and scarcely twisted; its cones are 4–9 cm, symmetrical, with at most a tiny prickle, and fall at or soon after ripening. Contorta pine's needles are 3.5–6.5 cm, often twisted and yellowish green; its cones are 3–6 cm, lopsided, prickly, and stay closed on the tree for years. Corsican pine's seeds, needles and young cones are eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Corsican pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have needles in pairs. Austrian pine's needles are long, up to 16 cm, dark green, stiff and scarcely twisted; its cones are 4–9 cm, symmetrical, with no spikes, and are shed each year. Contorta pine's needles are 3.5–6.5 cm, often twisted and yellowish green; its cones are 3–6 cm, lopsided, prickly, and stay closed on the tree for years. Austrian pine's seeds, needles and young cones are eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Austrian pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have needles in pairs and keep their prickly cones closed on the tree for years. Bishop pine's needles are 7–15 cm, greyish or bluish green; its cones are 6–9 cm, mostly in clusters of 4–5, with stout rigid prickles. Contorta pine's needles are short, 3.5–6.5 cm, often twisted and yellowish green; its cones are 3–6 cm, with a short slender prickle on each scale. Bishop pine's young green cones are made into syrup (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Bishop pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have short needles in pairs and small cones of the same size; look at the cones. Scots pine's needles are 2.5–7 cm, twisted and bluish or grey-green, often looking silvery; its cones are small, 3–6 cm, on a short stalk that curves back, with no prickles, and fall whole each year; high on the trunk the bark turns orange-brown and flaky. Contorta pine's cones are almost stalkless, have a short slender prickle on each scale, and stay closed on the tree for years; its needles are 3.5–6.5 cm, generally yellowish green. Scots pine's young needles, male cones, seeds and inner bark are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Scots pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are bushy pines with short needles in pairs that grow wild in the same high country; look at the cones. Dwarf mountain pine is usually a dense shrub or small tree; its cones are 2.5–5.5 cm, symmetrical, upright, almost stalkless, with no prickles; its needles are 3–7 cm, dark green, curved but not twisted. Contorta pine's needles are 3.5–6.5 cm, often twisted and yellowish green; its cones are 3–6 cm, lopsided at the base, with a short slender prickle on each scale, and stay closed on the tree for years. Dwarf mountain pine's young cones are made into syrup (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mountain pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have short needles in pairs and lopsided cones; look at the cone scales. Mountain pine usually grows as a tree; its cones are lopsided, with the lower scales on the upper side drawn out downwards into hooks, sometimes with a blunt prickle. Contorta pine's needles are 3.5–6.5 cm, often twisted and yellowish green; its cones are 3–6 cm, lopsided at the base, with a short slender prickle on each scale, and stay closed on the tree for years. Mountain pine's young cones are made into syrup (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mountain pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have short needles in pairs and cones that stay closed on the tree for years, and they grow wild together and can cross; look at the shoots and cones. Jack pine's shoots and needles are strongly twisted, the needles 1–5 cm and deep green; its cones are 2.5–5.5 cm, narrow, smooth with no prickles, point forward or out, and curve sharply towards the tapering tip. Contorta pine's shoots and needles are not or only slightly twisted, the needles 3.5–6.5 cm and generally yellowish green; its cones are broadly egg-shaped and lopsided at the base, usually point down or back, and have a short slender prickle on each scale. Jack pine's inner bark and young cones are eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Jack pine

preparation.text:
The cones often stay shut for years and may only open after strong heat, so warm closed cones until they open, then shake out the winged seeds. Take inner bark in early spring, when the male cones are shedding pollen: it tastes mild then and of turpentine later in the season. It was stripped in long ribbons and eaten fresh, boiled, cooked like spaghetti, chewed, dried, or mashed into a pulp and baked as cakes.
For syrup, pick cones while they are still green and soft enough to cut through with a knife; brown, woody or opened cones will not do. Green cones ooze sticky resin, so wear gloves. Throw out any with holes or insects. Smaller cones give a stronger flavour; large ones can be cut up so more fit in the jar.

recipes.method: Pack 225 g (about 500 ml) young green contorta pine cones and 450 g brown sugar into a 1 litre jar. Leave in a warm, sunny place for 30 days, shaking it now and then. For the first few weeks open the jar occasionally to let out gas, as the mixture may ferment. Scrape the cones and sugar slush into a pot, add 30 ml water, and bring to a brisk simmer for 5–10 minutes, just until the sugar melts (reducing it further makes it crystallise as it cools). Strain, discard the cones and bottle the hot syrup. It keeps best in the fridge once opened. Use it like maple syrup: on pancakes, fresh fruit or soft cheese, or a little in desserts and dressings.
recipes.title: Mugolio (young pine cone syrup)

recipes.method: Put 10 young green contorta pine cones in a jar and top up with 500 g brown sugar, shaking so the sugar settles round the cones. Close the jar and leave it for about 2 weeks, until all the sugar has turned to syrup. Pass it through a sieve and bottle. Add it to marinades or pour it over pancakes.
recipes.title: No-cook green pine cone syrup

Origin 'pest' 23/11/2026: NZPCN biostatus Exotic, year naturalised 1957, origin Rocky Mountains, north-west America, introduced to stabilise eroding high-country pasture; Biota of New Zealand, 'Pinus contorta Douglas ex Loudon' (https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/c1251509-926f-4118-b61a-0b39b8d4b0aa) and 'Pinus contorta Loudon' (https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/b489ce31-98a3-4d96-ba64-b91124a481e2), retrieved 23/11/2026 — biostatus Exotic, Wild, New Zealand (Webb, Sykes & Garnock-Jones 1988); vernaculars contorta pine, lodgepole pine, tamarack pine; NZTCS has no record (searched 23/11/2026). National Pest Plant Accord species, Unwanted Organism and DOC environmental weed (NZPCN, DOC Weeds database). NZ presence: iNaturalist NZ 327 research-grade wild observations (API, retrieved 23/11/2026).

Caution careRequired 23/11/2026: four independent food records for this species — Plants For A Future, 'Pinus contorta' (https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Pinus+contorta, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026 (inner bark raw or cooked, 'A famine food, it is only used when all else fails', ready 'when the male cones are producing pollen', turpentine taste as the season advances; seed raw or cooked; sap as a drink; pitch chewed as gum); University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, Forest Research and Outreach, 'Lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta)' (https://ucanr.edu/site/forest-research-and-outreach/lodgepole-pine-pinus-contorta, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026 ('In the spring, long ribbons of the sugar-rich inner bark were stripped off to eat. This inner bark could be stored or mashed to make bread'); Nature Alberta, PlantWatch, 'Lodgepole Pine' (https://plantwatch.naturealberta.ca/choose-your-plants/lodgepole-pine/index.html, restated; its references include Kershaw 2000, Edible and medicinal plants of the Rockies, and Turner 1997, Food plants of Interior First Peoples), retrieved 23/11/2026 (inner bark eaten in spring, chewed, 'cooked it like spaghetti', dried; 'The nourishing seeds were also eaten'); USDA Forest Service, Fire Effects Information System, 'Pinus contorta var. latifolia' (https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/tree/pinconl/all.html, public domain, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026 ('Native Americans boiled the inner bark of Rocky Mountain lodgepole pine for food'). careRequired, as on radiata pine: radiata pine looks alike (card) and the conifer warnings apply. Not used: PFAF's sap and gum and UC ANR's needle tea (one record each); PFAF's vanillin flavouring (an industrial by-product of pulpwood). Inner bark is given although the larch and Douglas fir entries leave it out (single source there, and Galloway Wild Foods calls removing cambium 'a serious and possibly life-threatening imposition' on the tree): here four records name it, and the tree is an Unwanted Organism that councils control — flagged for the owner.

Months [] 23/11/2026: year-round — the seeds sit in cones that stay on the tree, often closed, long after they ripen (Flora of New Zealand: 'Mature cones long-persistent, often not opening until long after maturity'; DOC Weeds database: cones 'may only open after exposure to high temperatures'). The inner bark is a spring harvest (PFAF), but no New Zealand source dates pollen shedding for this species.

PFAF check 23/11/2026: Plants For A Future, 'Pinus contorta' (https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Pinus+contorta, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026 — edible uses in the caution line; Known Hazards: none given on this page (the genus-level dermatitis line comes from its Pinus radiata page, as on monterey-pine); its British cultivation notes are not New Zealand habitat; medicinal uses not used; Other Uses (tan or green dye from the needles, roots braided into rope, pitch for waterproofing, glue and wood preservative, turpentine and rosin, wood, needle terpenes inhibiting germination) go to docs/plans/useful-plants.md.

IV (Webb, Sykes & Garnock-Jones 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY-NC-SA), 'Pinus contorta Douglas ex Loudon' (https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/59dddafc-97ac-4248-8034-9687b3a685cb), retrieved 23/11/2026 — abbreviations spelled out, restated; NZ Plant Conservation Network, 'Pinus contorta' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/pinus-contorta/, all rights reserved, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026; Weedbusters, 'Contorta pine' (https://www.weedbusters.org.nz/all-about-weeds/weed-list/contorta-pine/, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026; Department of Conservation, Weeds database 'Pinus contorta' (https://weeds.doc.govt.nz/species/pinus-contorta, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026; Department of Conservation, 'Wilding conifers' (https://www.doc.govt.nz/nature/pests-and-threats/weeds/weeds-that-pose-serious-threats/wilding-conifers/, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026; National Wilding Conifer Control Programme, 'Resources' (https://www.wildingpines.nz/resource, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026.

Contorta pine is the most targeted wilding conifer (NZPCN), so herbicide is a real risk. Not added: Massey University's Poisonous Plants of New Zealand database, 'Isocupressic acid' (https://poisonousplants.massey.ac.nz/plantToxins/isocupr.html, retrieved 23/11/2026), lists 'Lodgepole pine Pinus contorta' among plants with isocupressic acid (no amount given), a cause of abortion in cattle — a livestock line, not a human warning.

summary.text:
Contorta pine, or lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta), is an evergreen pine of the pine family (Pinaceae) from the Rocky Mountains and north-western North America. Its seeds and spring inner bark are edible.
In New Zealand: It was planted for forestry, erosion control and shelter, and especially to hold high-country pasture that was eroding from burning, heavy stocking and rabbits; it has been widely planted in montane areas, the seed often sown from the air. It was first recorded wild in 1957. It grows wild on the Volcanic Plateau, especially in and around Tongariro National Park, and in the South Island in inland Canterbury (from the Hanmer area to the Mackenzie Basin), Otago, South Westland and Southland. It is the most aggressive naturalised conifer at medium to high altitudes and has invaded large areas. Wild trees vary so much that they cannot be assigned to subspecies, and the name contorta pine has mostly replaced lodgepole pine here.
It cones from as young as three years, a 12-year-old 5 m tree sets about 15,000 viable seeds a year, and the wind carries the seed many kilometres. It forms dense, often pure stands, especially on poor soils, and takes the forest above the native treeline; its litter suppresses the plants beneath, and stands draw down ground water in summer. Wilding conifers now cover more than 1.8 million hectares of New Zealand and spread by about 5% a year, and contorta pine is rated the worst of them, with the youngest coning age and the farthest spread.
It has been an Unwanted Organism under the Biosecurity Act since 2001 and is a National Pest Plant Accord species: it cannot be bred, propagated, distributed or sold. It is on DOC's list of environmental weeds and in regional pest plans from Northland to Southland and the Chatham Islands.

method.text: Needles: simmered, not boiled, in a covered pot of water until the water has coloured, then lifted out; wet fabric is kept in the bath at a gentle heat for about an hour, longer for a stronger colour. Scoured hemp with no mordant, dyed in an aluminium pot, came out a soft mauve-clay, and one bath coloured several pieces. The needles are also listed as giving a tan or green dye. Cones: soaked in water for a day to soften, cut into pieces, boiled for up to four hours (a lower heat loses less dye) and strained through muslin; cotton dyed for an hour and left to cool in the bath came out beige to light brown, mordanted or not, and the bath was used again the next day. On cotton and silk, cone tannins give beiges with orange and pink hues.

recipes.method: A box of pine needles about 30 × 20 cm; a 20-litre aluminium pot of cool water; a piece of hemp fabric about 1 × 1.5 m. Scour the fabric in a 40 °C wash with fragrance-free powder and about 250 ml (a cup) of baking soda, no fabric softener, then soak it in water for about an hour. Put the needles in the pot of water, cover, and bring to a simmer without boiling; turn the heat down a little and keep it there until the water has the colour you want. Lift out the needles with a fine sieve (straining through muslin gives a more even colour). Add the wet fabric, push out the air bubbles with a wooden spoon so it is all under, and keep it at a gentle heat for about an hour, stirring now and then; leave it longer for a stronger colour. Wring it out, wash and rinse it with fragrance-free powder and no softener, and dry it out of direct sun. The same bath dyes several pieces in turn.

method.text: Tinder: needles left to dry for a season, or dry ones from the forest floor, catch fire easily, more so with a little pitch. Fatwood, the dense amber wood soaked with resin in the stumps and lower branches of dead pines, is shaved into thin slivers and lit with a spark or flame, and still lights when damp. Glue: resin that has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground is gathered rather than cut from the tree, melted (on a hot rock beside a fire, for example), mixed with finely ground ash or powdered charcoal and left to cool; it is reheated to use. A little water softens old pitch into a soft glue, and pine shavings or sawdust worked into it make a wood filler. Oil or strong alcohol takes pitch off your hands. Incense: needles tied into a bundle with natural twine and dried for about two weeks. Cleaner: chopped needles covered with vinegar in a glass jar, with baking paper under the lid so it does not corrode, left for two weeks and strained; the vinegar is mixed with baking soda and castile soap for cleaning.

method.text: Resin is gathered from what has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground rather than cut from the tree, at any time of year. It sticks to everything, so keep a knife and jar just for it; oil, then soap, takes it off your hands, and rubbing alcohol off clothes. Large lumps melt faster if frozen and broken up with a hammer inside a thick paper bag. Warmed with an equal amount of beeswax, mixed and left to set in its container, it makes a simple balm; melted into an oil, strained and firmed with beeswax it makes a balm for dry or cracked skin, lips and hands.

recipes.method: 60 ml (¼ cup) pine resin; 125 ml (½ cup) oil such as olive or almond; 15–30 g grated beeswax. Melt the resin in the oil in a double boiler over a low heat. Strain through a coffee filter or a strainer, return to the double boiler, add the beeswax and heat gently until it has melted. Pour into tins or jars and store somewhere cool and dark.
recipes.title: Pine resin balm

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) pine resin; 250 ml (1 cup) olive oil, or another oil safe for skin; 125–190 ml (½–¾ cup) grated beeswax; 35 drops rosemary essential oil. Put the resin and oil in a glass jar in the top of a double boiler and simmer, stirring, until the resin melts; this can take several hours. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine sieve and return it to the double boiler. For every 250 ml of resin and oil add 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) grated beeswax (more gives a firmer balm) and heat gently until it melts. Pour into jars or tins, stir 5 drops of the essential oil into each, and put the lids on straight away so the scent stays in. Leave to cool and set, and store somewhere cool and dark. Use it on dry or cracked skin, as a lip or hand balm, or overnight on the face.
recipes.title: Pine resin and olive oil balm

identification.text:
Slender to rather stout spreading shrub up to 2–(3) m tall; branches with dark red-brown bark; branchlets pubescent to glabrous. Leaves on pubescent petioles 2–3 mm long. Stipules triangular, subacute to obtuse, with scattered patches of short hairs, ciliolate. Lamina glabrous, coriaceous, oblong to broad-oblong to obovate to elliptic (several forms usually on one plant), (7)–9–15–(20) × (3)–5–8 mm, obtuse to truncate or retuse, narrowed abruptly to petiole. Midrib and many secondary veins evident. Flowers solitary on decurved peduncles. Male without calyx; corolla subcampanulate, lobes ovate, acute, about equal to tube. Female with small, obtuse teeth; corolla tubular, lobes acute, longer than tube. Drupe crimson, broad-oblong, 6–7 mm long.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]
The stipules usually carry a prominent dark denticle. Leaf blades are fresh yellowish-green to dark green, with 1–2 pits on the underside. Unlike hūpiro, the crushed leaves do not smell of rotten eggs.

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: hūpiro's leaves smell strongly of rotten eggs or dung, Coprosma colensoi's do not. Hūpiro's leaves are thin, usually 30–50 mm long (as small as 20 mm); Coprosma colensoi's are leathery and usually 9–15 mm long (up to 20 mm). Hūpiro's flowers sit singly at the tips of the branchlets and face upwards; Coprosma colensoi's hang on bent-down stalks. Hūpiro's fruit is pale to full orange without red flecks, 7–10 mm long; Coprosma colensoi's is crimson, 6–7 mm long. Stunted hūpiro has small leaves and is easily confused, and the two hybridise freely where they meet, so plants with mixed features are common. Hūpiro's fruit is eaten.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Coprosma colensoi's branching is much less rigid; Coprosma rigida's branches are stiff and spread at wide angles. Coprosma rigida's leaf tip is flat or dented and fringed with very small hairs (a hand lens helps). Coprosma colensoi's flowers hang on bent-down stalks; Coprosma rigida's sit singly at the tips of short branchlets. Coprosma colensoi's fruit is crimson, 6–7 mm long; Coprosma rigida's is whitish, orange-yellow or pale orange, about 4–6 mm long and usually clearly pinched between its two stones. Neither is known as food.
lookalikes.name: Coprosma rigida

summary.text: Coprosma colensoi is a spreading shrub of the family Rubiaceae, up to 2–(3) m tall, endemic to New Zealand. It grows on the North, South and Stewart Islands, from Mount Moehau southwards, and is assessed Not Threatened (2023). It hybridises freely with hūpiro (Coprosma foetidissima) wherever the two meet, and the hybrid swarms are so varied that the limits of the species are hard to draw. Narrow-leaved forms were once described as a separate species, Coprosma banksii. Two other older names, Coprosma myrtillifolia var. linearis and Coprosma pseudo-colensoi, are also now placed under it. New Zealand nurseries sell it as a hardy shrub for native plantings, banks and rock gardens.

warnings: No record of Coprosma colensoi as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
It grows with hūpiro, whose fruit is eaten, and hybridises freely with it, so intermediate plants are common. Check the leaves and fruit (see Lookalikes).

identification.text: Prostrate, densely matted shrub 0.1–0.2 m tall and 2–5 m across, with long-trailing, wide-angled branches. Bark of mature twigs dark silver-grey to almost black and corky, dark green underneath. Juvenile leaves mottled brown. Adult leaves oval (broadly elliptic to oblanceolate), glossy, with curved margins and a pale underside; in sun 3.5–12 × 1.5–2.5(–3.5) mm and dark green to almost orange-green, in shade up to 20 × 4.5 mm. The leaf tip ends in a small nipple-like point (a 'bull nose'). Male and female flowers grow on separate plants. Fruit plain cream to pale lemon when fresh. Seeds 3.1–4.1(–4.4) × 2.0–2.5 mm, oblong-elliptic or elliptic, pale orange-yellow to light orange-yellow.

lookalikes.howToTell: Coprosma distantia is a prostrate, trailing shrub 0.1–0.2 m tall; Coprosma obconica is upright, 2–3.5 m tall. Coprosma distantia's fresh fruit is plain cream to pale lemon; Coprosma obconica's is greenish or translucent white, streaked or blotched dark violet-purple. Coprosma distantia's seeds are larger, about 3.1–4.1 mm long, oblong-elliptic, pale orange-yellow and scarcely notched; Coprosma obconica's are about 3 mm long, pale grey or white, clog-shaped and clearly notched. In the wild Coprosma distantia grows only on serpentinite at the Surville Cliffs, North Cape; Coprosma obconica grows near Taihape and Masterton and in the South Island, and has been found on ultramafic rock only twice. Both have the same nipple-like leaf tip, so leaves alone do not separate them. Neither is known as food.

summary.text: Coprosma distantia is a rare, low, sprawling shrub of the family Rubiaceae, endemic to New Zealand. It is known only from the 120 ha of serpentinite rock at the Surville Cliffs, in the North Cape Scientific Reserve, where it is very common. It was first described as a subspecies of Coprosma obconica (C. obconica subsp. distantia). It is assessed At Risk – Naturally Uncommon (2023). Nothing seriously threatens it now, but no seedlings have yet been seen, and the whole Surville Cliffs ultramafic flora is at some risk from spreading pampas, needle bush and downy hakea, fire and browsing animals. A few specialist nurseries and botanic gardens grow it, apparently all from one female plant collected in 1979.

identification.text: Upright, heavily branched divaricating shrub 2–3.5 m tall and 0.8–1 m wide, with wide-angled branches. Bark of mature twigs brown or pale silver-grey and papery, green underneath. Adult leaves in pairs, broadly elliptic to oblanceolate, 3.5–12 × 1.5–2.5(–3.5) mm, light greyish green, glossy, sometimes mottled yellow, paler underneath, with thickened, down-curved margins and no pits on the underside; the veins are hardly visible. The blunt leaf tip ends in a small nipple-like point (a 'bull nose'). Juvenile leaves are mottled brown or green and often also grow at the base of adult plants. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants. Fruit about 5 mm across when fresh, greenish white or translucent white, variously striped or blotched dark violet-purple, broader than long and tapering to its stalk like an inverted cone. Seeds pale grey or white, clog-shaped, about 3 × 2.2 mm.

summary.text: Coprosma obconica is a rare, heavily branched shrub of the family Rubiaceae, endemic to New Zealand. Its species name means 'inverted cone'. In the North Island it grows in scattered populations near Taihape and one near Masterton; in the South Island it ranges from D'Urville Island and North-west Nelson south to Otago and Southland, and seems to be absent from Westland. It is assessed At Risk – Declining (2023), and Regionally Critical in Otago and Wellington (2025). Weeds and the loss of lowland podocarp forest are the main threats, and dolomite mining at Mt Burnett threatens one of the largest populations. Its fleshy fruit is spread by fruit-eating animals. A few specialist nurseries and botanic gardens grow it. It grows very slowly, rarely sets fruit unless male and female plants grow together, and does best in full sun or light shade on well-drained, preferably limy soil. Prostrate, trailing plants with plain cream to pale lemon fruit, once treated as a subspecies, are now the separate species Coprosma distantia. Coprosma obconica subsp. obconica is a synonym.

identification.text:
Erect shrub up to 2–(5) m tall, with stiff divaricate branches; bark reddish brown; branchlets wiry, somewhat shining. Leaves on petioles 2–3 mm long. Stipules triangular, acute, ciliolate, with terminal denticle or not. Lamina thick, coriaceous, glabrous, obovate to oblong, rounded to subtruncate at apex, cuneately narrowed to base, about 10–20 × 3–9 mm. Midrib and principal secondary veins evident, at least below. Flowers solitary, terminal on short branchlets. Male without calyx; corolla broadly campanulate, lobes broad-ovate acute, equal to tube. Female with short obtuse calyx-teeth; corolla with short tube and rather long, narrow, acute lobes. Drupe orange-yellow or white, more or less obovoid, about 4–6 mm long.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]
The twigs branch at wide angles; young twigs are fuzzy and older ones shiny orange or red. The leaves have red margins and are widest near the tip, which is often dented and fringed with very small hairs (a hand lens helps). The fruit is usually clearly pinched between its two stones.

lookalikes.howToTell: Coprosma rigida's branches are stiff and spread at wide angles; Coprosma colensoi's branching is much less rigid. Coprosma rigida's leaf tip is flat or dented and fringed with very small hairs (a hand lens helps). Coprosma rigida's flowers sit singly at the tips of short branchlets; Coprosma colensoi's hang on bent-down stalks. Coprosma rigida's fruit is whitish, orange-yellow or pale orange, about 4–6 mm long and usually clearly pinched between its two stones; Coprosma colensoi's is crimson, 6–7 mm long. Neither is known as food.
lookalikes.name: Coprosma colensoi

lookalikes.howToTell: Thick-leaved coprosma's leaves are pale to white underneath, which sets it apart from all other coprosmas, including Coprosma rigida. Coprosma rigida's leaves are obovate to oblong, about 10–20 mm long; thick-leaved coprosma's are round to oval or broadly oblong, usually 6–10 mm long, with rolled-under edges. Coprosma rigida's fruit is egg-shaped, wider towards the tip, about 4–6 mm long, orange-yellow or white; thick-leaved coprosma's is round, 5–6 mm across, yellow or white. The two occasionally cross, so plants with mixed features occur. Neither is known as food.
lookalikes.name: Thick-leaved coprosma

summary.text: Coprosma rigida is an erect shrub of the family Rubiaceae, up to 2–(5) m tall with stiff, wide-angled branches, endemic to New Zealand. Its species name means 'rigid'. It grows on the North and South Islands, from Kaitaia in the north to Dunedin and Southland. It is assessed Not Threatened (2023) nationally, but Regionally Declining in Northland (2026) and Regionally Vulnerable in Auckland (2025). Male and female flowers are on separate plants, and its fleshy fruit is spread by fruit-eating animals. It occasionally crosses with Coprosma crassifolia. Three plants Colenso collected near Dannevirke and named Coprosma aurantiaca, C. lentissima and C. turbinata are now placed under it.

warnings: No record of Coprosma rigida as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

identification.text:
A medium-sized to large pine, narrow and conical to columnar when young, with a slender crown and few side branches. The needles come in pairs, 6–16 cm long, light green, fairly flexible and not very sharp, in moderately dense clusters towards the shoot tips. The cones are 4–9 cm, egg-shaped and symmetrical, yellowish brown or brown, often hanging, and fall at or soon after ripening; the scales have at most a tiny prickle. The bark is fissured and peels in large plates, grey on the surface and cream to pale brown beneath. Austrian pine, the other wild subspecies, has denser, stiffer, sharp-pointed dark green needles on a bushier tree; the two grade into each other and young trees are very hard to tell apart.
Shoots shining brown or yellowish brown, hairless. Buds egg-shaped and tapering to a slender point, sometimes cylindrical, not or only thinly resinous; scales pressed tight, brown in the centre with a narrow to broad white, ragged margin, so the bud can look almost white. Needles 2 per bundle, (4–)6–16 cm × 1–1.5 mm, straight or curved, scarcely twisted, moderately thick; resin canals midway; thickened cells under the skin usually in 1–2 rows (3–5 in black pine); the sheath about 1.5 cm long at first, wearing away to a basal fringe. Male cones 1–1.5 cm long, broadly cylindrical. Young female cones stalkless or almost so, the scales with or without a small curved point. Mature cones stalkless, solitary or clustered, 4–9 × 2.5–3.5 cm when closed, egg-shaped to conical; scale ends keeled, with a very small, often falling, prickle. Seed wing slightly lopsided, 1–2 cm long. Wild New Zealand trees vary a lot.

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the needles in a bundle. Radiata pine has needles in threes, 6–15 cm long, deep or dark green; its cones are 6–13 cm, lopsided at the base, and stay on the tree. Corsican pine has needles in pairs, 6–16 cm, light green; its cones are 4–9 cm, symmetrical, and fall at or soon after ripening. Radiata pine's seeds are eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Monterey pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have needles in pairs. Contorta pine's needles are short, 3.5–6.5 cm, often twisted and yellowish green; its cones are 3–6 cm, lopsided at the base, with a short prickle on each scale, and stay closed on the tree for years. Corsican pine's needles are 6–16 cm and scarcely twisted; its cones are 4–9 cm, symmetrical, with at most a tiny prickle, and fall at or soon after ripening. Contorta pine's seeds and spring inner bark are eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Contorta pine

lookalikes.howToTell: The two are subspecies of one pine and grade into each other; young trees are very hard to tell apart. Feel the needles: Corsican pine's are light green, fairly flexible and not very sharp, in moderately dense clusters, on a narrow, conical to columnar tree. Austrian pine's are thick, stiff, dark green and sharp, in dense masses near the shoot tips, on a bushy, wide-spreading tree. The cones are alike. Both are eaten the same way (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Austrian pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have long needles in pairs; look at the cones. Bishop pine's cones are lopsided, 6–9 cm, with stout rigid prickles, mostly in clusters of 4–5, and stay closed on the tree for many years; its needles are greyish or bluish green, stiff and sharp. Corsican pine's cones are symmetrical, 4–9 cm, with at most a tiny prickle, and fall at or soon after ripening; its needles are light green, fairly flexible and not very sharp. Bishop pine's young green cones are made into syrup (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Bishop pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have needles in pairs and cones that fall each year. Scots pine's needles are 2.5–7 cm, twisted and bluish or grey-green, often looking silvery; its cones are small, 3–6 cm, on a short stalk that curves back, with no prickles, and fall whole each year; high on the trunk the bark turns orange-brown and flaky. Corsican pine's needles are much longer, 6–16 cm, light green, flexible and scarcely twisted; its cones are 4–9 cm, stalkless, with at most a tiny prickle. Scots pine's young needles, male cones, seeds and inner bark are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Scots pine

preparation.text: The cones fall at or soon after ripening, so gather them as they mature. Spread them on a tray somewhere warm and dry until they open (it can take about a week), then shake out the seeds and rub them between your hands to free the papery wings. The seeds are small and fiddly to collect; they need no shelling or roasting, though roasting gives a nutty flavour, and they keep in the freezer for up to two months. For tea, chop a handful of needles, pour boiling water over them, steep for 10 minutes and strain. Wear gloves when picking cones or needles: the sap is very sticky.

recipes.method: Mix 4 tablespoons (60 g) soft butter with 2 tablespoons (30 ml) ground Corsican pine seeds, 1–2 cloves garlic, crushed and finely chopped, and a little salt, pepper and herbs to taste. Refrigerate overnight to let the flavours develop. Spread on baked potatoes, cooked vegetables, crackers or toast. For croutons, toast bread, spread both sides with the butter, cut into cubes and bake at 200 °C for 10–15 minutes, turning once, until golden and crunchy.
recipes.title: Pine seed butter

recipes.method: Put 250 ml young green cones in a saucepan with 750 ml water, bring to the boil and simmer, partly covered, for about 30 minutes. Cover tightly and leave overnight. Strain, keeping the cones, and measure the liquid; add the same volume of sugar (about 200 g for each 250 ml), stir to dissolve and boil until the bubbles start to hold their shape and it thickens a little. Return a few of the cones, boil for a few more minutes, then cool and bottle. Kept tightly closed in a cool place it lasts a few months, and mellows as it stands. Use it to flavour drinks or desserts, or spoon it over pancakes.

(11/11/2011), https://forageporage.wordpress.com/2011/11/11/kid-friendly-austrian-pine-needles-to-nuts/, restated, retrieved 23/11/2026 (seeds 'tiny, tasty pine nuts', eaten unroasted or roasted, shell 'not necessary to remove'; needle tea; a pine nut butter recipe); Conservation Garden Park (Jordan Valley Water Conservancy District, Utah), 'Austrian Pine' (https://conservationgardenpark.jvwcd.gov/plants/241/austrian-pine/, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026 ('Edible: Yes'; seeds edible but small and difficult to collect; older needles steeped for tea; young female cones cooked, pickled or made into syrups or jams); Biblioteca degli Alberi Milano (BAM), 'Black pine' (https://bam.milano.it/en/schede-botaniche/pino-nero/, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026 ('The pine nuts inside are edible'); Paticheri, 'Pine Syrup Panna Cotta' (17/12/2023), https://www.paticheri.com/2023/12/17/pine-syrup-panna-cotta/, restated, retrieved 23/11/2026 (a syrup of Corsican pine buds, immature male and female cones and young conelets, strained out). Months [] 23/11/2026: no New Zealand source dates cone ripening or seed fall for this pine. The Flora says the cones fall 'at or soon after maturity'; Conservation Garden Park's 'September to November' and Paticheri's autumn harvest are northern-hemisphere seasons and are not shifted. summary.text:
Corsican pine (Pinus nigra laricio) is an evergreen pine of the pine family (Pinaceae) from Corsica, Sicily and southern Italy. It is one of two subspecies of European black pine (Pinus nigra) growing wild in New Zealand; the other is Austrian pine. Its seeds are edible, its needles make a tea, and its young cones flavour a syrup.
In New Zealand: It was first recorded wild in 1925. There are thousands of hectares of it in state forests from Northland to Southland, particularly in cooler areas such as the Rotorua–Taupō area and inland Canterbury. It grows wild in the North and South Islands, and in some inland parts of the South Island, such as the Amuri Range in north Canterbury, the Rakaia Valley and the Mackenzie Basin, it is aggressive and has invaded many hectares of scrub and grassland. Young wild trees have also been collected on the Rai Saddle, on the road from Nelson to Blenheim. It was known earlier in New Zealand as Pinus nigra var. maritima, and first recorded as Pinus laricio.
Its cones are produced very freely, and even fairly young trees set large quantities of viable seed. It is slower to mature than contorta pine but can spread very large distances. Pinus nigra is on DOC's list of environmental weeds and in regional pest plans from Northland to Southland and the Chatham Islands.

method.text: Needles: simmered, not boiled, in a covered pot of water until the water has coloured, then lifted out; wet fabric is kept in the bath at a gentle heat for about an hour, longer for a stronger colour. Scoured hemp with no mordant, dyed in an aluminium pot, came out a soft mauve-clay, and one bath coloured several pieces. The needles are also listed as giving a tan or green dye. Cones: soaked in water for a day to soften, cut into pieces, boiled for up to four hours (a lower heat loses less dye) and strained through muslin; cotton dyed for an hour and left to cool in the bath came out beige to light brown, mordanted or not, and the bath was used again the next day. On cotton and silk, cone tannins give beiges with orange and pink hues. Bark: in Corsica this pine was used to dye fishing nets, as Aleppo pine bark was in Italy.

recipes.method: A box of pine needles about 30 × 20 cm; a 20-litre aluminium pot of cool water; a piece of hemp fabric about 1 × 1.5 m. Scour the fabric in a 40 °C wash with fragrance-free powder and about 250 ml (a cup) of baking soda, no fabric softener, then soak it in water for about an hour. Put the needles in the pot of water, cover, and bring to a simmer without boiling; turn the heat down a little and keep it there until the water has the colour you want. Lift out the needles with a fine sieve (straining through muslin gives a more even colour). Add the wet fabric, push out the air bubbles with a wooden spoon so it is all under, and keep it at a gentle heat for about an hour, stirring now and then; leave it longer for a stronger colour. Wring it out, wash and rinse it with fragrance-free powder and no softener, and dry it out of direct sun. The same bath dyes several pieces in turn.

method.text: Tinder: needles left to dry for a season, or dry ones from the forest floor, catch fire easily, more so with a little pitch. Fatwood, the dense amber wood soaked with resin in the stumps and lower branches of dead pines, is shaved into thin slivers and lit with a spark or flame, and still lights when damp. Glue: resin that has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground is gathered rather than cut from the tree, melted (on a hot rock beside a fire, for example), mixed with finely ground ash or powdered charcoal and left to cool; it is reheated to use. A little water softens old pitch into a soft glue, and pine shavings or sawdust worked into it make a wood filler. Oil or strong alcohol takes pitch off your hands. Incense: needles tied into a bundle with natural twine and dried for about two weeks. Cleaner: chopped needles covered with vinegar in a glass jar, with baking paper under the lid so it does not corrode, left for two weeks and strained; the vinegar is mixed with baking soda and castile soap for cleaning.

method.text: Resin is gathered from what has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground rather than cut from the tree, at any time of year. It sticks to everything, so keep a knife and jar just for it; oil, then soap, takes it off your hands, and rubbing alcohol off clothes. recipes.method: 60 ml (¼ cup) pine resin; 125 ml (½ cup) oil such as olive or almond; 15–30 g grated beeswax. Melt the resin in the oil in a double boiler over a low heat. Strain through a coffee filter or a strainer, return to the double boiler, add the beeswax and heat gently until it has melted. Pour into tins or jars and store somewhere cool and dark.
recipes.title: Pine resin balm

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) pine resin; 250 ml (1 cup) olive oil, or another oil safe for skin; 125–190 ml (½–¾ cup) grated beeswax; 35 drops rosemary essential oil. Put the resin and oil in a glass jar in the top of a double boiler and simmer, stirring, until the resin melts; this can take several hours. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine sieve and return it to the double boiler. For every 250 ml of resin and oil add 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) grated beeswax (more gives a firmer balm) and heat gently until it melts. Pour into jars or tins, stir 5 drops of the essential oil into each, and put the lids on straight away so the scent stays in. Leave to cool and set, and store somewhere cool and dark. Use it on dry or cracked skin, as a lip or hand balm, or overnight on the face.
recipes.title: Pine resin and olive oil balm

identification.text:
Erect perennial herb up to 2 m tall. Stems stout, often deeply, longitudinally grooved, hollow; dark green, green to yellow-green, sometimes spotted maroon; finely hairy. Leaves alternately arranged, 3-pinnate, dark green, green to yellow-green, borne on stout, deeply channeled, finely pubescent to glabrescent petioles, these dark green to green often maroon-spotted adaxially and near base; lamina of basal leaves up to 0.8 × 0.8 m; lamina of cauline leaves up to 0.1 × 0.5 m; segments 15–50 mm, acute. Umbels compound, rays 6–15, bearing numerous white flowers, these 3–6 mm diameter, petals 5, apices notched. Fruits, initially green, maturing brown, lanceolate, 6 mm long, glabrous and smooth.
The tiny hairs on the stem, rachis and leaf stalks are difficult to see but can easily be detected by touch. Bracts under the umbel are few or none; the small umbels carry several bracteoles. The main stem meets the roots in a single primary taproot which can branch further below the surface. From the roots lateral rhizomes can form.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand; all parts are poisonous if eaten. Its leaves are similar to cow parsley's, both have white flowers in compound umbels, both flower in spring and both grow in waste places, so place and season do not rule hemlock out. Do not rely on height or stem spots: cow parsley in New Zealand grows up to 2 m and its stems and leaf stalks are sometimes spotted maroon, while hemlock grows up to 2–(3) m with stems usually, but not always, purple spotted or blotched. Feel the stem: hemlock is hairless throughout; cow parsley's stem is finely hairy, the hairs easier to feel than to see, though its leaf stalks can be almost hairless. Look under the umbels: hemlock has about 4–8 narrow, pointed, down-turned bracts beneath each umbel; cow parsley has few or none. Ripe fruit separates them: hemlock's are dark brown, 2.5–3 mm long, with slender, often wavy ribs; cow parsley's are lanceolate, about 6 mm long, hairless and smooth. Hemlock smells foetid when crushed. Check every one of these on every plant.
lookalikes.name: Hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: At a distance wild carrot can look like cow parsley. Look under the umbel: wild carrot has numerous bracts, each divided into narrow linear segments; cow parsley has few or none, and they are not divided. A few central flowers of a wild carrot umbel are sometimes red or purple; cow parsley's flowers are white. Wild carrot's ripe fruits are ovoid, 2.5–3 mm long and spiny; cow parsley's are lanceolate, about 6 mm long and smooth. Wild carrot's stem is bristly-hairy, more or less solid and up to 120 cm tall; cow parsley's is finely hairy, hollow and up to 2 m. Both stems are hairy, so hairiness alone does not separate them. Both carry their own cautions; see wild carrot's entry.
lookalikes.name: Wild carrot

lookalikes.howToTell: Giant hogweed is poisonous: its sap on the skin followed by sunlight causes burns and blisters that can scar, and sap in the eyes can cause blindness, so do not touch it. Look at the leaves: cow parsley's are 3-pinnate, finely divided into pointed segments 15–50 mm long; giant hogweed's basal leaves have just three broad, deeply lobed leaflets, each up to 50, sometimes 100, cm long. Look under the umbel: giant hogweed usually has about 12 linear bracts 10–15 mm long; cow parsley has few or none. Count the rays: cow parsley's umbels have about 6–15; giant hogweed's main umbel has more than 50. Ripe fruit: cow parsley's is lanceolate, about 6 mm long and smooth; giant hogweed's is flattened, ovate-elliptic and about 10 mm long, with conspicuous oil canals. Look at the stem without touching it: giant hogweed's is bristly and up to 10 cm thick; cow parsley's is finely hairy. Do not rely on height or stem spots: cow parsley grows up to 2 m and its stems and leaf stalks are sometimes spotted maroon, and giant hogweed's are blotched and spotted reddish purple. Both grow along roadsides, in ditches and in waste places in Canterbury, Otago and Southland, so place does not rule giant hogweed out. Check every one of these on every plant.
lookalikes.name: Giant hogweed

preparation.text: Eat the leaves raw in small amounts in salads, cook young leaves as a potherb, or use the leaves fresh or dried like garden chervil, as a garnish or seasoning for eggs, potatoes, beans, fish, soups and casseroles. Young stems can be peeled and eaten raw or steamed and served with butter; how thick the skin is depends on the stem's age. The flavour is sharper than garden chervil's, grassy and parsley-like, with a hint of liquorice or aniseed.

recipes.method: Makes 2 jars. Enough cow parsley stems to fill the jars; 400 ml cider vinegar; 4 tbsp runny honey; ½ tsp turmeric; ¼ tsp ground cloves; 1 tsp whole yellow mustard seeds; ¼ tsp whole celery seed. Wash the stems and cut them to fit the jars with room left to cover them in vinegar. Boil them hard for 1 minute, drain and let them cool. Sterilise the jars with boiling water. Bring the vinegar to the boil with the honey and spices, then take it off the heat. Pack the stems into the jars, pour the spiced vinegar over to cover, and seal with rubber-lined lids. Best after two months, though they can be eaten after a few days.
recipes.title: Sweet pickled cow parsley stems

recipes.method: Serves 4. 200 g peeled cow parsley stems; 5 oranges; 1 lemon; 2 tbsp brown rice syrup; 3 whole cloves; 50 g chopped dried dates; ½ tsp ground cinnamon; ½ tsp cardamom seeds (not pods). Heat a slow cooker on high. Peel the stems (young ones have thin skins, older ones thick) and chop them small. Peel four oranges and slice them into thin rounds; juice the fifth orange and the lemon. Grind the cloves and cardamom to a powder and whisk all the spices into the juice with the rice syrup. Layer half the orange slices in the cooker, scatter the stems and dates over, top with the rest of the orange, and pour the spiced juice over. Cover, turn to low and cook for 4 hours.
recipes.title: Spiced cow parsley and orange compote

recipes.method: A good handful of young cow parsley shoots; 2 garlic cloves; parmesan; walnuts; a pinch of salt; olive oil. Pound the peeled garlic with the salt in a mortar. Roughly chop the cow parsley and grind it to a paste (a food processor is easier), then add the walnuts and pound or pulse again. Stir in half the parmesan, drizzle in some oil, then add most of the rest of the cheese. Taste and keep adding cheese or oil until the flavour and texture suit you.
recipes.title: Cow parsley pesto

summary.text: Cow parsley (Anthriscus sylvestris) is a biennial or short-lived perennial herb of the carrot family (Apiaceae), native to most of Europe, south and east to North Africa and Siberia, and naturalised in New Zealand. It is also called wild chervil and keck. The Flora of New Zealand (1988) rejected it from the naturalised flora because no voucher specimen supported the earlier record; the first vouchered record was collected in Christchurch in 2002. It has been deliberately cultivated, especially in the South Island, and is now rapidly spreading, mostly from gardens; it is well established in the South Island from the Nelson region east and south to Otago, and has also been collected at Te Anau. It spreads by seed and by rhizomes from its roots. It is not on DOC's list of environmental weeds. New Zealand nurseries sell it as a frost-hardy garden perennial, including 'Ravenswing', a cultivar with deep purple-black leaves.

warnings: Hemlock, one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand, has leaves similar to cow parsley's and white flowers in compound umbels, and both grow in waste places and flower in spring. In New Zealand cow parsley grows up to 2 m and its stems are sometimes spotted maroon, so neither height nor stem spots tell them apart. Before you pick, check every character described in Lookalikes.
Cow parsley itself is suspected of being poisonous to mammals, or mildly toxic.
Cow parsley has many poisonous relatives that look like it. Eat it only when every check in Lookalikes is certain; when in doubt, leave it.

identification.text:
Low-growing shrub; creeping stems up to 1 m long, rooting at nodes, terete, glabrous; armature of small prickles restricted to young stems. Leaves reduced to a single leaflet; leaflet lamina coriaceous, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20)–25–90 × 5–22 mm, sometimes with a pair of obscure lobes near base, glabrous on both surfaces or with sparse scattered hairs on midrib, veins and margins, bronze-green on upper surface, paler on lower, sharply serrate-dentate. Inflorescence a few-flowered panicle or flowers solitary. Petals white. Drupelets red. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
R. parvus has relatively large bisexual flowers whereas the other indigenous spp. have small flowers and are dioecious.
NZPCN's newer description gives separate male and female flowers instead, and calls them smaller and usually solitary (NZPCN, restated).
The sterile hybrid R. ×barkeri is often sold as this species; it has three-leaflet leaves and does not flower (NZPCN).

lookalikes.howToTell: Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet, where blackberry's have (3–)5(–7); creeping lawyer creeps along the ground, blackberry arches and scrambles. Ripe creeping lawyer fruit is red, but blackberry is red too before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit.
lookalikes.name: Blackberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet; bush lawyer's have three or more. Young plants and flowering shoots of other brambles sometimes have single-leaflet leaves too, so judge by the leaves on mature stems.
lookalikes.name: Bush lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet; white-leaved lawyer's have three or more. Young plants and flowering shoots of other brambles sometimes have single-leaflet leaves too, so judge by the leaves on mature stems.
lookalikes.name: White-leaved lawyer

preparation.text: Eat the ripe red fruit raw or cook it.

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. Makes 6 jars of 250 ml. The recipe is somewhere between a jam and a jelly: the juice is pressed rather than dripped through a bag, so it sets cloudy. 1 litre berry juice (fresh or thawed frozen berries put through a cold-press juicer), 300 ml cold-pressed apple juice, the juice of 3 lemons, 1.3 kg white sugar, 10 whole cloves and the zest of an orange. Wash the jars and dry them, open end up, in a 120 °C oven for about 15 minutes, leaving them in the warm oven until needed; boil the lids for 5 minutes and let them air-dry. Put the berry, apple and lemon juices and the sugar in a jam pan, dissolve the sugar over low heat, then bring to the boil. Add the cloves and orange zest, skim off foam as it rises, and boil to setting point — about 30 minutes for the author, giving a soft set. Ladle the hot jelly into the hot jars and seal.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry jelly

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. 400 g berries, 500 ml white wine vinegar and 100 g white sugar. Warm the vinegar with the sugar until it has dissolved. Put the berries in a large clean jar or a non-reactive bowl, pour the warm vinegar over them and leave overnight. Strain gently through a fine sieve or muslin and pour into a sterilised bottle or jar. The author uses it to quick-pickle wafer-thin slices of raw beetroot (3 tablespoons of vinegar and ¼ teaspoon of sea salt for 2 small beetroot, soaked at least 15 minutes) served with goat's cheese.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry vinegar

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. Muddle a big handful of berries (fresh or frozen) in a cocktail shaker, add 60 ml tequila blanco, 30 ml Cointreau, 60 ml fresh lime juice and 60 ml sugar syrup, shake hard over ice and pour. Strain it if you don't want the seeds.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Lawns, golf courses. Recorded elevations range from 30 to 120 m.
In turf it forms thick mats on rooting runners, small enough to escape the mower (Massey). It also grows in gardens (NZPCN).
