identification.text:
It often flowers while its short stem is still leafy to the ground. The leaves are yellow-green to green, sometimes red-spotted, with slightly recurved margins; the tepals are narrow, recurved and three-nerved, and the stigma is shortly three-lobed. The fruit is round, about 4–5 mm across.
Plant rarely more than 2 m high, usually not very stiffly erect. Leaves 30–60–(100) × 1–2 cm, more or less narrowed above base to short petiole; midrib prominent abaxially towards base. Panicle very lax, about 60 cm long, branches slender. Flowers small, widely spaced, very shortly pedicellate, whitish or pink externally; segments 4–5 mm long. Berry bluish or blue-flecked.
[From: Flora of New Zealand Online, 'Cordyline pumilio' factsheet.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Cabbage tree grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Dwarf cabbage tree (Cordyline pumilio) is rarely more than 2 m tall and often flowers while its short stem is still leafy to the ground; its leaves are 30–60–(100) × 1–2 cm, more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base; its panicle is very open, up to about 60 cm long, with slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers that are whitish or pink outside, and its berries are bluish or flecked with blue, 4–5 mm across. In short: dwarf cabbage tree is usually no more than 1–(2) m tall with a main stem 1–2 cm across and leaves rarely over 2 cm wide, its flower cluster large for the plant but with very slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers; cabbage tree's main stem soon exceeds 2 cm across even on a young plant, and its leaves are mostly over 2 cm wide. Hybrids between the two have been described from the far north (C. × matthewsii, Carse 1926), some almost enlarged copies of dwarf cabbage tree, so an in-between plant there may be neither.
lookalikes.name: Cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Forest cabbage tree grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Dwarf cabbage tree (Cordyline pumilio) is rarely more than 2 m tall and often flowers while its short stem is still leafy to the ground; its leaves are 30–60–(100) × 1–2 cm, more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base; its panicle is very open, up to about 60 cm long, with slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers that are whitish or pink outside, and its berries are bluish or flecked with blue, 4–5 mm across. In short: dwarf cabbage tree is usually no more than 1–(2) m tall with a main stem 1–2 cm across and leaves rarely over 2 cm wide, its flower cluster large for the plant but with very slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers; forest cabbage tree's main stem soon exceeds 2 cm across even on a young plant, and its leaves are mostly over 2 cm wide. A hybrid between the two has been described (C. × gibbingsae, Carse 1929) that looks like a small, stemless forest cabbage tree, so an in-between plant may be neither.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaves and how they sit. Tūrutu grows as several leafy fans together, its leaves in two rows, each folded around the next at the base; the leaf sheath is often reddish and narrows above into a strongly keeled part where the two halves are almost completely fused, the blade is tough, glossy above and dull underneath with many fine veins, and the leaves are green to dark green with dark bands 2–4 mm wide along the edges. Its side rhizomes sometimes carry young shoots 10 cm or more from the parent. Dwarf cabbage tree's leaves are crowded in a tuft, yellow-green to green (sometimes red-spotted), more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base and the margin slightly recurved. Leaf size does not separate them: tūrutu's are (15)–25–60–(100) cm long and 1–1.5 cm (to 1.8 cm) wide, dwarf cabbage tree's 30–60–(100) cm long and 1–2 cm wide. In flower and fruit they differ more: tūrutu's flowers are greenish white and nod on thread-like stalks 1.5–4 cm long, and its berries are 6.5–17 mm long, grey-white and dull to glossy violet-blue, with spongy flesh; dwarf cabbage tree's flowers are small and widely spaced on very short stalks, whitish or pink outside, in a very open panicle up to about 60 cm long, and its berries are round, 4–5 mm across, bluish or flecked with blue. Both grow in forest and gumland scrub in the northern North Island, and both can carry berries from March to May. Two other native Dianella species, D. latissima and D. haematica, look much like tūrutu. Tūrutu's berries are reported as poisonous (see its page).

preparation.text:
“Young seedlings were carefully selected and planted out, and in the following year the root was fit for use. The plant was then dug up, stacked in small piles, and dried in the sun; while drying, the fibrous roots were burned off, and when sufficiently dry the roots were scraped and baked slowly, requiring twelve to eighteen hours to cook them. These were chewed, or pounded and washed and squeezed, to extract the saccharine matter, which was eaten with their fern root to give it a relish.”
Roots tied separately for baking in bundles of hangehange, Geniostoma rupestre.
Roots dug up and dried, sometimes eaten raw.

summary.text:
The dwarf cabbage tree, tī rauriki or tī koraha, is a narrow-leaved shrub endemic to the North Island of New Zealand.
It is usually stemless, its stems buried beneath the soil, and is more often confused with Dianella or Libertia than with other cabbage trees. It grows in the North Island from Te Paki (North Cape) to Kāwhia Harbour in the west and the Bay of Plenty in the east.

sources: Useful Temperate Plants (Ken Fern, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0), 'Malva neglecta'

Knox, C. 2013: A Forager's Treasury (owner's copy, all rights reserved, restated), pp. 89–90 'Herb mallows' (Malva sylvestris, M. neglecta, M. parviflora) — leaves raw or cooked, flowers, green seedpods ('mallow peas')
edibleParts.text: Leaves, raw or cooked; flowers; and the young green seedpods. Leaves and young shoots - raw or cooked. They can be added in quantity to salads, and make an excellent lettuce substitute, they can also be cooked as greens. The leaves are mucilaginous. Some people find this mucilaginous texture unpleasant, especially if the leaves are cooked. Immature seeds - raw or cooked. The seeds can be eaten raw or cooked and have a nutty flavour. Mature seeds can be cooked like rice or grains.

sources: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), 'Malva neglecta'

identification.text:
Dwarf mallow is a prostrate, downy plant, growing to approximately 60 cm, with a tough taproot. Its flower stalks are shorter than the leaf stalks, so the leaves partly hide the flowers.

The smooth-backed mericarps clothed in short hairs distinguish this species. It has often been recorded in New Zealand as M. rotundifolia.

Annual or short-lived perennial, procumbent to ascending herb. Stems sparsely to densely clothed in stellate hairs. Leaves sparsely to moderately clothed in mostly stellate hairs above, densely hairy below, reniform to orbicular, cordate, shallowly 5–7-palmately lobed and crenate, 1–7–(8) cm diameter; petioles (2)–4–20 cm long; stipules triangular, 3–6 mm long. Flowers in axillary clusters of 2–5; fruiting pedicels 1–8 cm long; epicalyx segments linear to narrowly ovate-oblong, shorter than calyx; calyx teeth ovate-triangular, acuminate, with stellate hairs and ciliate, not enlarged at fruiting; petals white to lilac, often with lilac to pink veins, usually at least twice as long as calyx, (7)–8–15 mm long. Mericarps 12–15 per fruit, hairy, rarely sparsely so, smooth or faintly reticulate on back; edges sharply angled but not winged.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. The two are separated by cheeseweed mallow's shorter petals, enlarged fruiting calyx and net-veined fruit segments with winged edges. Both are low herbs with round to kidney-shaped, lobed leaves of overlapping size (1–8 cm and 1–7(–8) cm across) and flowers in clusters in the leaf joints, so the leaves do not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Petal lengths overlap between 12 and 15 mm, and common mallow can have pale pink flowers, so on a pale, mid-sized flower use the fruit: hairy and smooth-backed in dwarf mallow, usually hairless and strongly net-veined in common mallow. Dwarf mallow lies flat or ascends and common mallow ascends or stands upright, so an ascending plant fits both. Leaf shape and size overlap. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. The fruit separates them: strongly net-veined on the back in French mallow, smooth or faintly veined (and hairy) in dwarf mallow. Petal lengths overlap (6–10 mm against (7–)8–15 mm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and are unchanged in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Both have palmately lobed, toothed leaves whose sizes overlap (island mallow 2–15(–20) cm across, dwarf mallow 1–7(–8) cm), so use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Both have round, palmately 5–7-lobed, round-toothed leaves, so the leaves do not separate them; use the petal length, the epicalyx and the fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Tree mallow

preparation.text: The raw leaves are hairy, so shred them or mix them with other textures. They are best boiled: the mucilage swells and gives soups, casseroles and sauces a rich, melting texture; they do not sauté or fry well except in fritters. The flowers make a garnish or go into salads, or can be cooked very briefly. Pick the little round seedpods while green and tender, take them out of their husks, and eat them raw or boiled, or add them to stir-fries, soups and casseroles. The root can stand in for egg white in meringue: bring the roots to the boil in water, simmer until the water turns quite thick, then whisk the liquid like egg whites. Getting a froth firm and stable enough is hard with any mallow but true marshmallow root, so expect it to take practice. In Spain the unripe fruits are eaten raw as a treat (Arraia-Maeztu, Álava), and in Cazorla and Santiago-Pontones (Jaén) people eat the little fruits, called panecillos.

recipes.method: Written for mallow in general; the author gives khobiza as Malva neglecta or Malva parviflora. Serves 2. ½ tbsp olive oil, 1 small onion, thinly sliced, about 500 ml roughly chopped mallow leaves, a pinch of salt and black pepper, and a squeeze of lemon. Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat and fry the onion for 2–3 minutes. Add the mallow, toss, and season with salt and pepper. Add the lemon and serve straight away. Keep leftovers in the fridge for a couple of days only.
recipes.title: Palestinian sautéed mallow (khobiza)

recipes.method: Written for mallow (Malva neglecta and other species) by herbalist Erin Smith. 2–3 large handfuls of mallow leaves, 2 tbsp (30 g) butter, 1 large or 2 small onions, finely sliced, 1 large carrot, chopped, 2 celery sticks, chopped, 1 large garlic clove, crushed, about 1 litre of good chicken or vegetable stock, 1 medium potato, 2 tbsp (30 ml) yoghurt or crème fraîche (optional), a pinch of grated nutmeg, salt and black pepper, and chopped herbs (chives, parsley, rosemary or thyme). Soften the onion, carrot, celery and garlic in the butter without browning. Add the stock (and the potato, chopped — the page lists it but does not say when it goes in), bring to the boil and simmer until the potato and carrot mash with a fork. Add the mallow leaves and simmer 5–10 minutes. Season with salt, pepper and nutmeg, purée with a hand blender, return to the pan, stir in the cream and warm through. Serve with a little yoghurt or cream and chopped herbs (chives, parsley, rosemary or thyme).
recipes.title: Blended mallow soup

recipes.method: Written for mallow generally; the post shows dwarf mallow. 250 ml (1 cup) sunflower seeds, soaked and dried; 250 ml (1 cup) pumpkin seeds or cashews, soaked; 250 ml (1 cup) chopped mallow greens; 250 ml (1 cup) mallow water; the juice of 1 lemon; 1 small garlic clove; 10 ml (2 tsp) salt. For the mallow water, steep chopped mallow leaves and stems in cold water for several hours or overnight, until the water is as thick as egg white. Process everything in a food processor or blender until smooth. Serve it with carrot or celery sticks or on crackers, and keep it in an airtight container in the fridge.
recipes.title: Mallow spread

Knox 2013 p. 90 does not say it fails, only that making meringue from any mallow's mucilage but true marshmallow root (Althaea officinalis) 'is a challenge that has frustrated many a forager', because the froth is hard to make firm and stable; that is now stated beside the method instead of being the reason to cut it (owner rule: keep sourced uses, raise a specific doubt). summary.text:
Dwarf mallow, Malva neglecta, is an annual or short-lived perennial herb of the mallow family (Malvaceae), native to Europe, south-western Asia and north-western Africa. In the United States it is called common mallow, the name used here for Malva sylvestris.
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North Island, in eastern areas of the South Island from the Marlborough Sounds to Southland, where it is common, and on the Chatham Islands. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1867.

warnings: When grown on nitrogen rich soils (and particularly when these are inorganic), the plant tends to concentrate high levels of nitrates in its leaves.
It has a high nitrate content, similar to that of arugula.

identification.text:
A small tree or a dense shrub with several stems. The bark is dark brownish grey and peels in small thin flakes, so the trunk often looks rather smooth. The needles come in pairs, short (mostly 3–7 cm), dark green, stiff and curved but not twisted, with a sharp tip, and the dense foliage tends to point forward. The cones are small, 2.5–5.5 cm, dark brown, more or less upright, symmetrical, with no prickles, almost stalkless, and do not stay long on the tree after ripening. Short dark green needles in pairs, a bushy habit and small, symmetrical, stalkless cones set it apart. Scots pine has bluish, twisted needles and its cones hang on a short stalk; mountain pine usually grows as a tree and has lopsided cones with some scales drawn out and hooked downwards.
Shoots green, becoming brown, hairless. Buds broad-cylindrical or cylindrical-egg-shaped, resinous; scales pressed tight, purplish. Needles 2 per bundle, (2–)3–7(–9) cm × 1–1.5 mm; resin canals near the edge; the sheath about 1.5 cm long, soon wearing away to a basal fringe. Male cones under 1 cm long, broad-cylindrical. Young female cones shortly stalked or almost stalkless, the scales with a prominent short point. Mature cones 2.5–5.5 × 2.5–5 cm when open, egg-shaped or conical-egg-shaped; scale ends flat or sometimes convex on the upper side, especially in slightly lopsided cones, with a very small point and no prickle. Seed wing more or less oblong, about 1 cm long.

lookalikes.howToTell: Close relatives with short needles in pairs, and trees with cones in between are common where they grow together; look at the habit and the cones. Mountain pine usually grows as a tree; its cones are lopsided, with the lower scales on the upper side drawn out downwards into hooks, sometimes with a blunt prickle. Dwarf mountain pine is usually a dense shrub or small tree; its cones are 2.5–5.5 cm, symmetrical, upright, almost stalkless, with no prickles; its needles are 3–7 cm, dark green, curved but not twisted. Mountain pine's young cones are made into syrup (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mountain pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have short needles in pairs and small cones without prickles; look at the needles and the cone stalk. Scots pine's needles are 2.5–7 cm, twisted and bluish or grey-green; its cones are 3–6 cm, symmetrical, and hang on a short stalk that curves back; high on the trunk the bark turns orange-brown and flaky. Dwarf mountain pine is usually a dense shrub or small tree; its cones are 2.5–5.5 cm, symmetrical, upright, almost stalkless, with no prickles; its needles are 3–7 cm, dark green, curved but not twisted. Scots pine's young needles, male cones, seeds and inner bark are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Scots pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are bushy pines with short needles in pairs that grow wild in the same high country; look at the cones. Contorta pine's needles are 3.5–6.5 cm, often twisted and yellowish green; its cones are 3–6 cm, lopsided at the base, with a short slender prickle on each scale, and stay closed on the tree for years. Dwarf mountain pine is usually a dense shrub or small tree; its cones are 2.5–5.5 cm, symmetrical, upright, almost stalkless, with no prickles; its needles are 3–7 cm, dark green, curved but not twisted. Contorta pine's seeds and spring inner bark are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Contorta pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small pines with short needles in pairs; look at the shoots and cones. Jack pine is a spreading open tree whose shoots and needles are strongly twisted, the needles 1–5 cm and deep green; its cones are narrow, curved sharply towards the tapering tip so they look lopsided, pale or yellowish brown, and stay closed on the tree for many years. Dwarf mountain pine is usually a dense shrub; its needles are 3–7 cm, dark green, curved but not twisted; its cones are symmetrical, egg-shaped, more or less upright, dark brown, and do not stay long on the tree after ripening. Jack pine's inner bark and young cones are eaten too (see its page).

preparation.text: Pick cones while they are still green and soft enough to cut through with a knife; brown, woody or opened cones will not do. Green cones ooze sticky resin, so wear gloves. Look the cones over and throw out any with holes or insects. Smaller cones give a stronger flavour; large ones can be cut up so more fit in the jar.

recipes.method: Pack 225 g (about 500 ml) young green dwarf mountain pine cones and 450 g brown sugar into a 1 litre jar. Leave in a warm, sunny place for 30 days, shaking it now and then. For the first few weeks open the jar occasionally to let out gas, as the mixture may ferment. Scrape the cones and sugar slush into a pot, add 30 ml water, and bring to a brisk simmer for 5–10 minutes, just until the sugar melts (reducing it further makes it crystallise as it cools). Strain, discard the cones and bottle the hot syrup. It keeps best in the fridge once opened. Use it like maple syrup: on pancakes, fresh fruit or soft cheese, or a little in desserts and dressings.
recipes.title: Mugolio (young pine cone syrup)

recipes.method: Put 10 young green dwarf mountain pine cones in a jar and top up with 500 g brown sugar, shaking so the sugar settles round the cones. Close the jar and leave it for about 2 weeks, until all the sugar has turned to syrup. Pass it through a sieve and bottle. Add it to marinades or pour it over pancakes.

Other uses, owner link round 26/11/2026: the owner pasted 13 pages and said these uses apply to most pines, to be double-checked. Owner's answers 26/11/2026: pages that name only 'pine' apply to every pine unless a species-level claim blocks it; resin glue, the resin-and-beeswax balm and pitch or fatwood tinder are in (narrowing plan decision 1's 'resin is not carried over', which still keeps turpentine and rosin out); needle incense and the needle-vinegar cleaner are craft; needle baskets only on pines whose needles reach 10 cm. For Dwarf mountain pine: needle baskets left off because its needles are short (3–7 cm), and the baskets are made from long needles; bark dye left off because Guarrera 2006 names only Aleppo pine, Corsican pine and maritime pine. Checked for a species-level block: this entry's warnings and its Known Hazards, re-read 26/11/2026 (Plants For A Future: the genus-wide dermatitis line only), hold no skin or handling claim beyond the genus-wide dermatitis line (wood, sawdust and resins of various pines can cause dermatitis in sensitive people), which is repeated as the craft and skin-care warning; the pregnancy and cattle warnings concern eating needles and stay on the food page. Months are [] for every use: needles and cones are on or under the tree all year, and resin 'can be harvested at any time of the year' (LearningHerbs). summary.text:
Dwarf mountain pine (Pinus mugo) is an evergreen pine of the pine family (Pinaceae) from the mountains of Europe, from France and Italy eastwards. Its young green cones are steeped in sugar to make a pine syrup, mugolio.
In New Zealand: It was widely planted for erosion control and afforestation, particularly in the Craigieburn Mountains, where it now covers considerable areas where there is no native beech forest. It copes with severe climates almost as well as contorta pine and often bears many cones, but the Flora (1988) found it a less aggressive spreader, growing wild mainly near planted trees in Kaweka Forest Park and inland Canterbury along the Lewis Pass Road and around Craigieburn. It has since been recorded naturalised above Lake Chalice in Marlborough and around Ohakune. It was long known here as Pinus montana.
It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds and in regional pest plans from Northland to Southland and the Chatham Islands, most of them for progressive containment; in the high country it invades alpine scree.

method.text: Needles: simmered, not boiled, in a covered pot of water until the water has coloured, then lifted out; wet fabric is kept in the bath at a gentle heat for about an hour, longer for a stronger colour. Scoured hemp with no mordant, dyed in an aluminium pot, came out a soft mauve-clay, and one bath coloured several pieces. The needles are also listed as giving a tan or green dye. Cones: soaked in water for a day to soften, cut into pieces, boiled for up to four hours (a lower heat loses less dye) and strained through muslin; cotton dyed for an hour and left to cool in the bath came out beige to light brown, mordanted or not, and the bath was used again the next day. On cotton and silk, cone tannins give beiges with orange and pink hues.

recipes.method: A box of pine needles about 30 × 20 cm; a 20-litre aluminium pot of cool water; a piece of hemp fabric about 1 × 1.5 m. Scour the fabric in a 40 °C wash with fragrance-free powder and about 250 ml (a cup) of baking soda, no fabric softener, then soak it in water for about an hour. Put the needles in the pot of water, cover, and bring to a simmer without boiling; turn the heat down a little and keep it there until the water has the colour you want. Lift out the needles with a fine sieve (straining through muslin gives a more even colour). Add the wet fabric, push out the air bubbles with a wooden spoon so it is all under, and keep it at a gentle heat for about an hour, stirring now and then; leave it longer for a stronger colour. Wring it out, wash and rinse it with fragrance-free powder and no softener, and dry it out of direct sun. The same bath dyes several pieces in turn.
recipes.title: Mauve-clay hemp dye

method.text: Tinder: needles left to dry for a season, or dry ones from the forest floor, catch fire easily, more so with a little pitch. Fatwood, the dense amber wood soaked with resin in the stumps and lower branches of dead pines, is shaved into thin slivers and lit with a spark or flame, and still lights when damp. Glue: resin that has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground is gathered rather than cut from the tree, melted (on a hot rock beside a fire, for example), mixed with finely ground ash or powdered charcoal and left to cool; it is reheated to use. A little water softens old pitch into a soft glue, and pine shavings or sawdust worked into it make a wood filler. Oil or strong alcohol takes pitch off your hands. Incense: needles tied into a bundle with natural twine and dried for about two weeks. Cleaner: chopped needles covered with vinegar in a glass jar, with baking paper under the lid so it does not corrode, left for two weeks and strained; the vinegar is mixed with baking soda and castile soap for cleaning.

method.text: Resin is gathered from what has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground rather than cut from the tree, at any time of year. It sticks to everything, so keep a knife and jar just for it; oil, then soap, takes it off your hands, and rubbing alcohol off clothes. Large lumps melt faster if frozen and broken up with a hammer inside a thick paper bag. Warmed with an equal amount of beeswax, mixed and left to set in its container, it makes a simple balm; melted into an oil, strained and firmed with beeswax it makes a balm for dry or cracked skin, lips and hands.

recipes.method: 60 ml (¼ cup) pine resin; 125 ml (½ cup) oil such as olive or almond; 15–30 g grated beeswax. Melt the resin in the oil in a double boiler over a low heat. Strain through a coffee filter or a strainer, return to the double boiler, add the beeswax and heat gently until it has melted. Pour into tins or jars and store somewhere cool and dark.
recipes.title: Pine resin balm

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) pine resin; 250 ml (1 cup) olive oil, or another oil safe for skin; 125–190 ml (½–¾ cup) grated beeswax; 35 drops rosemary essential oil. Put the resin and oil in a glass jar in the top of a double boiler and simmer, stirring, until the resin melts; this can take several hours. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine sieve and return it to the double boiler. For every 250 ml of resin and oil add 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) grated beeswax (more gives a firmer balm) and heat gently until it melts. Pour into jars or tins, stir 5 drops of the essential oil into each, and put the lids on straight away so the scent stays in. Leave to cool and set, and store somewhere cool and dark. Use it on dry or cracked skin, as a lip or hand balm, or overnight on the face.
recipes.title: Pine resin and olive oil balm

identification.text:
Shallowly taprooted, erect monoecious annual, moderately clothed in short-stalked stinging hairs, otherwise sparsely to densely hairy. Stem with lateral branches usually present, up to 60 cm high. Leaves ovate or elliptic, acute, obtuse to truncate at base, coarsely serrate, (1)–2–8–(10) cm long. Petiole about ⅔ as long as lamina. Stipules 4 per node, entire, 1–3 mm long. Racemes with numerous male and female flowers, up to 1.5–(3) cm long. Perianth segments of female flowers extremely unequal, glabrous to hairy; margins ciliate. Achene ovoid, light brown, 1.5–2 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Ongaonga (tree nettle) is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m tall; dwarf nettle is a soft, branched annual herb up to 60 cm. Ongaonga's leaves are pale green and triangular to ovate-triangular, with white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long on the leaf teeth, young stalks and leaf veins; ongaonga's stinging hairs are long-stalked and dwarf nettle's short-stalked. Ongaonga has 2 stipules at each node, dwarf nettle 4. Its sting has killed: in 1961 a young man died of paralysis and breathing problems several hours after walking through tree nettles. Young ongaonga can be confused with other native nettles, so do not touch a stinging plant unless you are sure it is not woody.
lookalikes.name: Ongaonga

lookalikes.howToTell: Stinging nettle is a perennial up to 1.5 m that spreads by rhizomes into patches and seldom branches; dwarf nettle is a branched annual up to 60 cm with a short taproot. Stinging nettle's leaves are 5–25 cm, the end tooth longer than the teeth beside it; dwarf nettle's are 2–8 cm and rounder, the end tooth about as long as its neighbours. Stinging nettle's flower clusters, up to 9 cm, are one sex, usually on separate plants; dwarf nettle's clusters, up to 3 cm, usually carry male and female flowers together. Both sting, and both are eaten young and cooked.
lookalikes.name: Stinging nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush nettle is a native perennial that spreads by rhizomes, with light green, triangular leaves 2–6 cm long (sometimes up to 12 cm), a squared-off to slightly heart-shaped base and 9–10 (sometimes 12) teeth on each side; its lowest flower clusters are all male and the upper ones all female. Dwarf nettle is an annual with a short taproot and ovate to elliptic leaves 2–8 cm long, and its flower clusters usually carry male and female flowers together. Bush nettle grows in forest, forest margins and shaded places; dwarf nettle in gardens, farms and waste ground.
lookalikes.name: Bush nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Southern nettle is a stout, bushy native up to about 1 m whose branches lie down and root before turning upright, with broadly ovate, dark green leaves 10–20 cm long, the leaf stalk often carrying a pair of small leaflets near its base; its stinging hairs are mainly on the leaf edges and the veins underneath, and are often few or none. Dwarf nettle is an annual up to 60 cm with a short taproot and leaves 2–8 cm long. Both grow on the Chatham Islands; dwarf nettle is absent from Fiordland. No record of southern nettle being eaten has been found, and it is At Risk – Declining.
lookalikes.name: Southern nettle

preparation.text: Wear stout gloves to pick, and use only the young leaves. Cooking or thoroughly drying the leaves destroys the stinging hairs; pouring boiling water over them stops the sting. Blanching in salted water for 30–60 seconds, or steaming, removes the sting; leaves to be dried need no blanching first. Tops that have started to set seed are tougher. To freeze, blanch, drain, squeeze out the water and bag.

recipes.method: Written for common stinging nettles in North America (Urtica dioica 'and similar'); Forager Chef's nettle guide counts Urtica urens among the common nettles it covers. Serves 6. About 225 g nettles; 1 cup diced celery; 2 cups diced leeks; 2 diced shallots; 1 small diced onion; 3 tbsp butter; about 1 litre chicken stock; 2 cups diced potato; 120 ml cream; salt and white pepper; crème fraîche and chopped dill or mint, to serve. Blanch about 225 g nettles in salted boiling water until just wilted, about 30 seconds, cool them in cold water, squeeze dry and finely chop a handful to finish the soup. Sweat 1 cup diced celery, 2 cups diced leeks, 2 diced shallots and 1 small diced onion in 3 tbsp butter over medium heat for 5 minutes. Add about 1 litre chicken stock and 2 cups diced potato and simmer until tender, about 15 minutes. Add the blanched nettles and blend, then stir in the chopped nettles and 120 ml cream and season with salt and white pepper. Serve with crème fraîche and chopped dill or mint.
recipes.title: Classic stinging nettle soup

recipes.method: Written for common stinging nettles in North America (Urtica dioica 'and similar'); Forager Chef's nettle guide counts Urtica urens among the common nettles it covers. Serves 2. About 225 g young nettle tops; 3 large crushed garlic cloves; 3 tbsp olive oil, plus more to serve; salt and pepper; a pinch of chilli flakes; ½ cup ricotta; lemon wedges. Wash about 225 g young nettle tops and steam them, covered, over boiling water for 2–3 minutes until tender. Meanwhile warm 3 large crushed garlic cloves in 3 tbsp olive oil over medium heat for at least 10 minutes until browned, then discard the garlic. Add the steamed nettles to the oil, season with salt, pepper and a pinch of chilli flakes, gently fold in ½ cup ricotta and warm through. Serve warm or at room temperature with olive oil and lemon wedges.
recipes.title: Steamed nettles with ricotta

recipes.method: Written for stinging nettle in Britain; the recipe does not name the species. Serves 6. 25 g butter; 150 g nettle leaves, washed; 200 g feta, crumbled; 50 g parmesan, grated; the zest and juice of a lemon; 1 egg, beaten; grated nutmeg; seasoning; 7 filo sheets; 75 g melted butter; 1 tbsp sesame seeds. Brown 25 g butter in a large frying pan, add 150 g washed, still-damp nettle leaves and cook for about 6 minutes until wilted; cool, squeeze out the liquid and chop roughly. Mix with 200 g crumbled feta, 50 g grated parmesan, the zest and juice of a lemon, two-thirds of a beaten egg, grated nutmeg and seasoning. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan). Lay 3 filo sheets end to end, overlapping by about 5 cm, brush with some of 75 g melted butter, add 3 more sheets and more butter, then a seventh sheet in the middle. Spoon the filling in a line about 2 cm wide along one long edge, tuck in the ends, roll into a long sausage and coil it into a spiral about 20 cm across in a shallow round pan or on a buttered baking tray. Brush with the rest of the egg, scatter with 1 tbsp sesame seeds and bake for 40–45 minutes until golden.
recipes.title: Nettle spanakopita

recipes.method: Written for stinging nettle in Britain; the recipe does not name the species. Serves 4. 200 g nettle leaves; 1 tbsp olive oil; a 200 ml tub of crème fraîche; 1 tsp wholegrain mustard; 140 g blue cheese, crumbled; seasoning; 4 slices of sourdough. Wilt 200 g nettle leaves in 1 tbsp hot olive oil for 1 minute, cool briefly and chop roughly. Mix with a 200 ml tub of crème fraîche, 1 tsp wholegrain mustard, half of 140 g crumbled blue cheese, and seasoning. Toast 4 slices of sourdough on both sides under the grill, spread with the nettle mix, top with the rest of the cheese and grill until golden and bubbling.
recipes.title: Nettle and blue cheese rarebit

recipes.method: Written for stinging nettles; the recipe says Urtica dioica or U. urens will do. About 450 g nettle leaves, stripped from their stems; 4 tbsp ghee, olive oil or coconut oil; 4 finely chopped garlic cloves (or 1 tsp asafoetida); a 2.5 cm piece of fresh ginger, finely chopped; 1 small jalapeño or serrano chilli, finely chopped (optional); 1 tbsp turmeric powder; 1 tsp ground coriander; 1 tsp whole cumin seed; about 450 g coarsely chopped spinach or chard; salt; 120 ml cream (or crème fraîche or coconut cream). Bring about 4 litres of water to the boil, add about 450 g nettle leaves stripped from their stems and boil for 5 minutes, then drain in a colander. In a frying pan, heat 4 tbsp ghee, olive oil or coconut oil and fry 4 finely chopped garlic cloves (or 1 tsp asafoetida), a 2.5 cm piece of finely chopped fresh ginger, 1 small finely chopped jalapeño or serrano chilli if you like, 1 tbsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp ground coriander and 1 tsp whole cumin seed. Add about 450 g coarsely chopped spinach or chard and stir to coat in the spices, then add the nettles and a few pinches of salt. Cover and cook, stirring every few minutes and adding a little water if it sticks, until the greens are soft but not mushy. Take off the heat, stir in 120 ml cream (or crème fraîche or coconut cream), adjust the salt and serve warm with dal and rice or chapati.
recipes.title: Nettle saag

recipes.method: Written for nettles: the author eats both perennial and annual (dwarf) nettle, and gives this soup from Richard Mabey's Food for Free (1972). 4 large handfuls of nettle tops, picked with gloves; 1 large onion; 50 g butter or coconut oil; 2 potatoes; 1 litre vegetable stock; 15 ml (1 tbsp) crème fraîche or yoghurt; salt, pepper and grated nutmeg. Strip the nettles from the thicker stalks and wash them. Melt the butter and cook the chopped onion gently until translucent. Add the nettles and the chopped potatoes and cook 2–3 minutes, then add the stock and simmer 20 minutes, crushing the potatoes now and then with a wooden spoon. Season, with a little grated nutmeg, and finish with a swirl of crème fraîche or yoghurt; blend it first if you want a smoother soup.
recipes.title: Nettle and potato soup

recipes.method: Written for nettles: the author eats both perennial and annual (dwarf) nettle. Put 30 g dried nettle leaves, or two handfuls of cut-up fresh leaves, in a 1-litre preserving jar, fill it with boiling water, put the lid on and leave it to steep overnight at room temperature. The author drinks 1 or 2 cups a day. For an ordinary cup of tea, steep about a teaspoon of leaves in a teapot for 5 minutes.
recipes.title: Overnight nettle infusion

summary.text:
Urtica urens, commonly known as annual nettle, dwarf nettle, small nettle, dog nettle, burning nettle, or bush nettle is a herbaceous annual flowering plant species in the nettle family Urticaceae.
The native distribution of Urtica urens includes most of Europe except the British Isles, northern Asia, north and northwest Africa.
In the British Isles, Urtica urens is an archaeophyte, an ancient introduction. It has been introduced to all other continents of the world except Antarctica.
It is reputed to sting more strongly than Urtica dioica (common nettle).
In New Zealand it is the commonest nettle, usually just called stinging nettle. First recorded wild here in 1846, it is locally common throughout both main islands — except Northland and Taranaki, Westland and Fiordland — and on the Chatham Islands.
The genus name Urtica comes from the Latin verb urere, 'to burn'. The name bush nettle is also used for this species overseas; in this guide, Bush nettle is the native Urtica sykesii, a different plant.
In New Zealand its leaves feed the caterpillars of the red admiral and yellow admiral butterflies.

warnings: Use only young leaves. Older leaves develop gritty crystals (cystoliths) that are widely held to irritate the kidneys.
Nettles in paddocks, along fence lines and under trees may be sprayed with MCPA, 2,4-D or glufosinate. Pick from ground you know.

identification.text:
Annual herb. Stems erect, softly hairy, to 1 m tall. Leaves sparsely to densely hairy. Rosette and lower stem leaves lyrate-pinnatifid or pinnatifid to almost lyrate-pinnate, 5–10–(30) × (1)–2–8–(15) cm; terminal lobe ovate to triangular to hastate; lateral lobes in 1–5 pairs, narrow-lanceolate or triangular, entire, sinuate or coarsely toothed. Upper stem leaves usually smaller with narrower, but not linear-filiform lobes, or hastate, or ovate and not lobed. Racemes often flexuous, ebracteate, glabrous or sparsely hairy, 20–40–(60) cm long. Pedicels 3–5 mm long, elongating to about 10 mm long at fruiting, sparsely hairy. Sepals usually hairy, 3–5 mm long, not horned. Petals yellow, 6–10 mm long. Anthers 1–1.5 mm long; filaments longer than sepals. Silique glabrous or hairy, spreading, linear-cylindric, (40)–60–100 × 1–1.5 mm; style 0.5–2 mm long. Seeds oblong, brown, about 1 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The stems are wiry and branch at about 45 degrees. The very long, slender pods stick out from the stem at 45–90 degrees, on short stalks almost as thick as the pod. As a seedling it is almost identical to hedge mustard; in the rosette its end lobe is longer and more pointed.

lookalikes.howToTell: As seedlings the two are almost identical. In the rosette, hedge mustard's end lobe is short and rounded; eastern rocket's is longer and more pointed. In flower, hedge mustard's petals are 3–4 mm long, against eastern rocket's 6–10 mm, and its sepals about 2 mm, against 3–5 mm. Hedge mustard's pods are short, 10–15–(20) mm, and pressed flat against the stem; eastern rocket's are (40)–60–100 × 1–1.5 mm and spread away from it.
lookalikes.name: Hedge mustard

lookalikes.howToTell: Flowers do not separate them: both have yellow petals 6–10 mm long. Field mustard's stems are hairless and its upper leaves are smooth, bluish-green, not lobed and clasp the stem; eastern rocket's stems are softly hairy and its leaves sparsely to densely hairy. Field mustard's pods are (30)–40–60 × 2–5 mm and end in a seedless beak 6–10 mm long; eastern rocket's are longer and thinner, (40)–60–100 × 1–1.5 mm, with no beak or a very short one.
lookalikes.name: Field mustard

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild radish's flowers are larger: its petals are 13–20 mm long, usually pale yellow or white and usually veined with mauve, against eastern rocket's yellow 6–10 mm. Wild radish's pods are (2)–3–8–(9) mm wide, pinched between the seeds, on stout stalks 1–2 cm long; eastern rocket's are slender, 1–1.5 mm wide and (40)–60–100 mm long, on stalks 3–5 mm long that lengthen to about 10 mm.
lookalikes.name: Wild radish

summary.text:
Eastern rocket, Sisymbrium orientale, is an annual herb of the mustard family (Brassicaceae).
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) it grows throughout the North and South Islands and on the Kermadecs, naturalised by 1932 from southern Europe, Asia Minor and North Africa. It is also called Indian hedge mustard and oriental mustard.
In Britain it arrived mainly as a contaminant of grain, was found growing wild by 1858, and has since become more frequent in some areas.
New Zealand fungus collections record it as a host of Albugo candida, Leptosphaeria maculans, Mycosphaerella brassicicola and Pleospora herbarum.

warnings: Do not gather it from heavily fertilised ground or places that catch run-off: the leaves may be full of nitrates, which are toxic in high doses.

Brassicaceae plants are known for their tendency to accumulate heavy metals, a trait that makes them valuable for the phytoremediation of contaminated soils. However, this same ability necessitates careful monitoring, as the accumulation of heavy metals can also pose potential health risks.

habitat.text:
Riverbanks, old farm shelter belts, roadsides, abandoned gardens.
A plant of the coast and lowlands, growing in scrub, along forest margins and in vegetation people have modified.
Waste places, hedgerows, roadsides, scrub, forest margins and in most other modified plant communities.

identification.text: Small tree with opposite compound leaves of five to seven toothed leaflets, corky warty bark, and large flat-topped sprays of tiny cream flowers, followed by drooping clusters of small purple-black berries.

lookalikes.howToTell: Tutu is highly poisonous, and eating its fruit has been linked with many deaths of children in New Zealand. Both have opposite leaves (tutu occasionally in whorls of three), so leaf arrangement does not separate them. Tutu's leaves are simple, (30)–50–80–(100) mm long, dark shining green above, with flat or slightly wavy margins; elder's are compound, of (3)–5–7 leaflets toothed except towards the base. Tutu's flowers hang in slender drooping strings (10)–15–20–(30) cm long, followed by fruit of succulent dark purple petals about 4 mm long around the seeds; elder's tiny white flowers are in large flat-topped clusters mostly 10–20 cm across, followed by round berries 4–8.5 mm across, usually shining black. Season does not separate them: tutu flowers October to March and fruits November to April. If you are unsure which you are looking at, harvest neither.
lookalikes.name: Tutu

lookalikes.howToTell: Rowan's leaves are alternate, with up to 8 pairs of leaflets plus one at the tip; elder's grow in opposite pairs and have (3)–5–7 leaflets. Rowan's ripe berries are deep orange to scarlet and glossy, 5–10 mm across, with the sepals left as a small dark star on the tip; elder's are usually shining black, 4–8.5 mm. Rowan usually has one erect trunk; elder often grows as many stems from the base. Raw rowan berries contain parasorbic acid, which irritates the stomach: cook, freeze or dry them before eating.
lookalikes.name: Rowan

preparation.text: Flowers into cordial, fritters or a sparkling wine. Berries MUST be cooked and strained — cooked into syrup, jelly or wine. Never eat raw berries.

recipes.method: Makes just over 1 litre. 20 elderflower heads (more if they are small or you want a stronger taste); 1 litre boiling water; 75 g citric acid; 1 kg sugar; 4 lemons. Pick heads whose flowers are white, not yellow or brown, and fully open, ideally mid-morning on a sunny day, and use them as soon as you can; left too long they start to smell sour. Pick out insects, large leaves and brown bits, but don't rinse the flowers, or the cordial loses flavour. Put the flowers in a large pot and pour the boiling water over them. Add the citric acid and sugar and stir until they dissolve. Grate in the lemon zest, cut the lemons into quarters, add them and stir. Cover the pot and leave to infuse for at least 24 hours. Strain through muslin or a fine strainer into another pot, squeezing the pulp hard to get all the flavour out. Sanitise bottles or jars by washing them in soapy water, rinsing, then filling them with boiling water for 5 minutes and emptying them. Funnel in the cordial, filling to overflowing so little air is left, and keep it in a cool, dark place; refrigerate once opened. It is strong: dilute it with still or sparkling water, or mix it into drinks or cakes.
recipes.title: Elderflower cordial

recipes.method: Written for elderflowers in Britain; the page names no species. Serves 4. 12 freshly picked large elderflower heads, each cut with a length of stalk; sunflower oil, for deep-frying; icing sugar, to dust; 1 lemon, quartered, to serve. For the batter: 80 g plain flour; 20 g cornflour; 1 tablespoon caster sugar; 225 ml chilled sparkling water; 1 egg white. Put the flour, cornflour and sugar in a large bowl, add the sparkling water and mix very briefly and lightly, just until combined. Leave it to stand for an hour. Meanwhile, shake any insects out of the flower heads without washing them, and trim each stalk to about 5 cm below the head to use as a handle. When you are ready to fry, whisk the egg white to soft peaks and fold it gently into the batter with a metal spoon. Heat the oil to 190 °C in a deep-fryer; or use a wide, deep pan no more than a third full, over high heat, until a drop of batter rises at once in a ring of bubbles. Hold a flower head upside down by its stalk, dip it into the batter and let the excess drip off. Lower it gently into the oil, where it will spread and float, and use the stalk to push it under a little so all the batter cooks. Fry one at a time until light golden and crisp, then lift out by the stalk and rest on kitchen paper for a moment. Dust with icing sugar and serve with lemon wedges to squeeze over. Eat the flowers off the stalk, not the stalk itself (see Warnings).
recipes.title: Elderflower fritters

recipes.method: Written for elderberries in England; the page names no species. 900 g Bramley (cooking) apples, washed but not peeled or cored, quartered, bruises cut out; 450 g elderberries, washed and stripped from the stalks; 900 ml water; 1 cinnamon stick and 5 cloves, tied in muslin; granulated cane sugar (450 g for every 600 ml of juice). Snip each berry cluster off the tree with scissors. At home, hold a cluster by its stalk and push the berries off with the prongs of a dinner fork. Put the fruit, the bag of spices and the water in a preserving pan, bring to the boil, then lower the heat and cook gently until the fruit is soft. Crush the fruit with the back of a wooden spoon to release the juice and keep cooking until it is a soft pulp, then take out the spices. Tip the pulp into a jelly bag or muslin tied with string and hang it over a large bowl somewhere cool overnight. Don't squeeze the bag, or the jelly will be cloudy. Next day, measure the juice and allow 450 g sugar for every 600 ml. Put the juice and sugar in a clean preserving pan over low heat and stir until the sugar dissolves, then raise the heat and boil until setting point: 105 °C on a sugar thermometer, or a teaspoon dropped on a chilled saucer wrinkles when pushed once it has cooled. Skim if needed, pour into sterilised jars and seal. To sterilise the jars, run them through the hottest dishwasher cycle, or wash them by hand and dry them in the oven at 120 °C for 20 minutes. The author serves it with autumn game.
recipes.title: Elderberry jelly

recipes.method: Written for elderberries in the UK; the page names no species. Makes about 250 ml. 250 g ripe elderberries; 250 ml apple cider vinegar; ½ star anise; 3 cloves; 2 black peppercorns; a small shaving of mace; 1 cm fresh ginger, bruised; ½ small shallot, thinly sliced; 20 g soft brown sugar, or to taste. Strip every berry off its stalks with a fork and rinse them well. Put the berries in a casserole dish with the vinegar, cover, and bake in a slow oven at 100 °C until the berries are soft. Strain the liquid into a jug, then push the rest of the juice through the sieve with a potato masher. Put the juice in a pan with the spices and shallot, cover, and simmer on a very low heat for 25 minutes. Strain again and return the liquid to the pan. Add the sugar and warm it until it dissolves, then boil hard for 2–3 minutes until it turns syrupy. Cool, bottle and store in a dark place. The author leaves it to mature for years before use.
recipes.title: Pontack (elderberry ketchup)

recipes.method: 10–16 large elderflower heads (or 1 tablespoon dried elderflowers for each fresh head); 650 g sugar; 4.5 litres of cold water; 1 lemon; 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar. Pick 10–16 large elderflower heads in full bloom, on a sunny morning if you can. Shake out the insects but don't wash them. To be careful, snip the flowers off the thick stalks. Dissolve 650 g sugar in 4.5 litres of cold water — warm a little of the water to dissolve the sugar, cool it, then mix it into the rest. In a large bucket or bowl, combine the sweetened water with the flowers, the juice and quartered skin of 1 lemon, and 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar. Cover and leave for 4 days, somewhere cool; if mould forms, scrape off the mat of flowers on top and carry on. Fine-strain into clean screw-top plastic fizzy-drink bottles, leaving a few centimetres of air at the top. Never use corked bottles, and avoid glass flip-tops: you can't feel the pressure through them, and they are far more dangerous if they burst. Leave at room temperature for 6–14 days. From day 6, squeeze the bottles every day, and as soon as the bases start to round out, ease the caps to let off some (not all) of the pressure; a forgotten bottle can explode. Once it tastes right, move it to the fridge to slow the fermentation, and keep checking the pressure. The author uses whole heads, green stalks and all, as is traditional. The source says one tablespoon of dried elderflowers replaces one good-sized fresh head. The author drinks it between 2 and 4 weeks; it is lightly alcoholic after a week and starts turning vinegary at 5–6 weeks. The source notes that the yeast comes from the flowers, so in a cool room it can take a while to get going. The author sometimes uses an infused vinegar, such as pineapple weed vinegar, for a twist.
recipes.title: Elderflower champagne

recipes.method: If a batch of elderflower champagne goes flat and vinegary, mix it with some live vinegar (with its mother). Leave it in an open container covered with cheesecloth, somewhere dark, for 2–3 months, until it reaches about 3–4% acidity. Use it for pickling.
recipes.title: Elderflower champagne vinegar

recipes.method: Ripe elderberries; apple cider vinegar (or white wine vinegar), 500 ml for every 350 g of berries; sugar, 350 g for every 260 ml of liquid. Strip the ripe berries off every stalk — freezing the heads first makes this easier — and weigh them. For every 350 g of berries add 500 ml apple cider vinegar (or white wine vinegar) in a jar or tub. Cover and leave for 5 days, stirring now and then. Strain, pressing the berries, and throw them away. Add 350 g sugar for every 260 ml of liquid, simmer for 10 minutes, and bottle. The recipe's final simmer is essential: raw elderberries are not safe to eat. The recipe works with less sugar too, if you want it less sweet.
recipes.title: Elderberry vinegar

summary.text:
Two harvests from one tree — cordial in early summer, syrup in autumn. The berries must be cooked.
Native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa, elder was first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1867. It grows wild from Auckland to Wellington, though uncommon north of the Volcanic Plateau, is very common in many parts of Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago and Southland, and reaches Stewart Island. It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.

warnings: Raw berries, leaves, bark and stems contain cyanogenic glycosides and can cause vomiting. Cooking destroys them in the fruit.
Strip the berries fully off the green stalks before cooking — the stalks are the toxic part most often left in.
Shake flower heads to evict insects; do not wash them or you rinse away the aromatic pollen.

associations.note: Bluefoot bolete grows on the ground under oak, its most-recorded host here.
Deadly. Death cap grows under oak in parks, gardens and arboreta.
Porcini has been recorded under English oak.
Poisonous. Fly agaric has been recorded under English oak.

identification.text:
A large, wide-spreading, deciduous tree, to about 30 m tall in cultivation, with very rough, dark grey, deeply fissured bark. Shoots hairless, brown or brownish green, with small raised pores. Leaf stalk usually under 2 mm long, but sometimes up to 10 mm. Leaves on adult shoots usually 4.5–18 × 3–9 cm, narrowly to broadly egg-shaped with the widest part towards the tip, hairless when mature or slightly hairy on the midrib underneath, dull above, thin, with 3–7 pairs of rounded lobes; the largest lobes at the widest part of the leaf. The leaf base has small ear-like lobes that almost or entirely hide the short leaf stalk. Male catkins 3–9 cm long. Acorns ripen in their first year, 1–3 together on a fruiting stalk 3–13 cm long. Cup usually 1.5–2 cm across, with egg-shaped, finely hairy, more or less flat-lying scales. Acorn 2–4 cm long, oblong, a quarter to a third enclosed by the cup.
Sessile oak, also grown in New Zealand and hybridising with English oak, has a longer leaf stalk, the leaf base wedge-shaped to slightly heart-shaped and not hiding the stalk, and a very short fruiting stalk often hidden by the small cluster of acorn cups.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hawthorn has sharp thorns along its branches; English oak has none. Hawthorn's leaves are smaller, 25–70 mm, deeply cut into 3–7 pointed-tipped lobes; English oak's adult leaves are usually 4.5–18 cm, with 3–7 pairs of rounded lobes and small ear-like lobes at the base hiding the very short stalk. Hawthorn has flat clusters of white five-petalled flowers and dark red haws 7–11 mm across, each with usually one stone; English oak has hanging catkins and acorns 2–4 cm long in a scaly cup. A young tree with lobed leaves and no flowers or fruit is told apart by the thorns.
lookalikes.name: Hawthorn

lookalikes.howToTell: Holm oak is evergreen, with thick, leathery, unlobed leaves 3–8 cm long, glossy above and usually grey-felted underneath, sometimes with small spiny teeth; English oak is deciduous, with thin, dull leaves cut into 3–7 pairs of rounded lobes. Holm oak's acorns are smaller, 1.5–2 cm long and egg-shaped, a third to two-thirds enclosed by the cup, on a short, felted stalk; English oak's are 2–4 cm long and oblong, a quarter to a third enclosed by the cup, on a fruiting stalk 3–13 cm long. Fallen acorns are told apart by size and shape, and by the leaves overhead.
lookalikes.name: Holm oak

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are big deciduous oaks whose acorns are eaten once leached; look at the leaves and acorns. Red oak's leaves are larger, 11–20 cm, with 3–5 pairs of pointed, bristle-tipped lobes, a wedge-shaped base and a leaf stalk up to 6 cm long, and turn deep red in autumn; its acorns take two years to ripen, are 2–2.5 cm and egg-shaped, about a quarter in a shallow cup, on a stalk 1–1.5 cm long. English oak's leaves have 3–7 pairs of rounded lobes with no bristles and small ear-like lobes at the base that almost hide the very short stalk; its acorns are 2–4 cm and oblong, on a fruiting stalk 3–13 cm long. Red oak's acorns are more bitter and need longer leaching (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Red oak

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are big deciduous oaks whose acorns are eaten once leached; look at the leaves and acorns. English oak's leaves have 3–7 pairs of blunt, rounded lobes with no bristles, and small ear-like lobes at the base that almost hide the leaf stalk, usually under 2 mm long; its acorns ripen in their first year, are 2–4 cm long and oblong, on a fruiting stalk 3–13 cm long. Pin oak's leaves (about 5–16 cm) have five or seven lobes ending in bristle-tipped teeth, with deep sinuses and tufts of hair where the veins meet beneath; its acorns take two years to ripen and are small, about 1–1.6 cm and rounded, in a thin, shallow cup. Pin oak's acorns are more bitter and need much longer leaching than English oak's (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Pin oak

preparation.text: Gather acorns once they are ripe and brown, leaving any that are badly discoloured, soft, light or holed. Spread them in a single layer in an airy place out of the sun; after a few days of drying they shell easily by hand or with a nutcracker. Shell them, then soak them in water; each time the water turns brown, pour it off and add fresh water, until it stays clear and the acorns no longer taste bitter. Hot water is quicker and suits acorns kept whole or in chunks; cold water takes a few days, changed every day, keeps the starch and suits flour. Chopping or grinding the acorns before soaking speeds it up. Shelled acorns darken in the air, so shell them straight into water if you want pale flour.

recipes.method: Ripe acorns, shelled and leached in hot water (see preparation); salt. Spread the damp, leached chunks on a baking tray, sprinkle with salt and toast on a high heat for 15–20 minutes, until the colour starts to darken. Cool before eating, or add them to a winter stew.
recipes.title: Roasted acorns

recipes.method: Ripe acorns, shelled and leached in hot water (see preparation). Lay them in an ovenproof dish and roast on a low heat for 1½–2 hours to dry them slowly, moving them around often so they don't catch. They brown as they dry: take them out when they reach a light or dark roast, as you prefer. Cool, grind and brew like coffee. It has no caffeine and tastes unlike ordinary coffee.
recipes.title: Acorn coffee

recipes.method: 100 g caster sugar; 100 g leached, roasted acorns. Melt the sugar in a saucepan over a low heat, shaking the pan gently as it melts and darkens. When it is dark brown, add the acorns and stir gently. Take off the heat, pour onto a baking tray lined with baking paper and leave to cool and harden at room temperature.
recipes.title: Acorn brittle

recipes.method: Ripe acorns. Shell them straight into a bowl of water to keep them pale. Grind, blitz or chop them small, cover with cold water in a bowl or jar and change the water every day until the bitterness has gone, usually a few days. Strain through muslin over a bowl, gather the cloth and squeeze out the water. Spread the damp meal on a baking tray and dry it in a low oven, which can take a couple of hours. Blitz to a fine powder in a blender and keep it in the fridge or freezer. Use it as you would wheat flour.
recipes.title: Acorn flour

recipes.method: 550 g leached acorns, whole or halved (see preparation); 6 tsp sea salt; 500 ml malt vinegar; 150 g sugar; ½ tsp each ground black pepper, allspice, cloves and cinnamon; 1 tbsp freshly grated ginger. Soak the acorns for 24 hours in water with the salt, drain and leave to air-dry for a few hours. Bring the vinegar, sugar, spices and ginger to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes. Pack the acorns into jars, cover with the spiced vinegar and seal. They can be eaten after two weeks but are best after three to six months.
recipes.title: Spiced pickled acorns

recipes.method: Written for leached acorn meal from any oak. 6 cups (1.5 litres) leached acorn meal (see preparation); 6 cups (1.5 litres) spelt or other bread flour; ½ tbsp salt; fresh yeast; water; sesame, poppy or sunflower seeds. Mix the acorn meal, flour and salt in a large bowl. Dissolve the yeast in ½ cup (125 ml) lukewarm water and stir it in, then knead well, adding water or flour until the dough is neither stiff nor sticky. Cover with a cloth and leave to rise overnight. Knead again and shape into two loaves; score the tops, brush with water and sprinkle with seeds. Bake at 200 °C for 45 minutes. Makes two large loaves.
recipes.title: Acorn and spelt bread

recipes.method: Written for leached acorn meal from any oak. 2 cups (500 ml) leached acorn meal (see preparation); 2 cups (500 ml) hot water; 2 cups (500 ml) maize flour; ½ tsp salt. Simmer the acorn meal, hot water and salt in a saucepan for 15 minutes, stirring now and then so it doesn't stick. Take off the heat and blend until smooth. Mix in the maize flour to a stiff dough that isn't sticky, adding a little more flour if needed, and leave to cool (it keeps overnight in the fridge). Roll into small balls and pat or press them into thin flat cakes. Toast in a hot pan with little or no oil, or bake at 200 °C for 15 minutes. Serves four.
recipes.title: Acorn and maize talos

recipes.method: Written for English and sessile oak acorns. Use leached acorn flour (see Acorn flour). 250 ml acorn flour; 250 ml plain flour; 5 ml sugar; 10 ml baking powder; 2 eggs; 60 ml melted butter, plus butter for the pan; 500 ml milk. Whisk the two flours, sugar and baking powder together. Whisk the melted butter, eggs and milk until smooth, add them to the dry mix and whisk until just combined; add more milk if it is too thick or more flour if too thin, as acorn flour varies — it should pour but not run. Heat a non-stick pan over medium heat with a small knob of butter and fry each pancake 2–3 minutes, until bubbles show on top and the underside is lightly browned, then flip and cook 1–2 minutes more. Add butter to the pan as needed. Serve hot with honey or syrup.
recipes.title: Acorn pancakes

summary.text:
English oak (Quercus robur), also called oak, common oak, pedunculate oak or truffle oak, is a large, wide-spreading deciduous tree of the beech family (Fagaceae) from Europe and western Asia, naturalised in New Zealand since 1880.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands, a sporadic escape from cultivation. It is widely planted, particularly in colder areas; mature trees usually fruit heavily and self-sown plants often come up near them. New Zealand trees vary a great deal in leaf size and lobing and in the length of the acorn stalk and the size and shape of the acorns, and some of the variation suggests hybrids with sessile oak, which is also grown here. It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.
Nurseries sell it as the classic long-lived oak of New Zealand parks and gardens, fairly slow-growing and valued for its durable heartwood timber; its leaves turn yellow in autumn (Southern Woods; Black Bridge Nurseries).

warnings: Raw acorns are bitter with tannins, which can be toxic: always leach them first.
Eating too many acorns can cause digestive upsets.

sources: Useful Temperate Plants (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0)
edibleParts.text:
Fruit - raw or cooked. Rich in vitamin C, the fruit has a very acid flavour and is mainly used in preserves, though children and some adults seem to like it raw when it is fully ripe.
Young leaves - used as a flavouring or as an acid nibble. They can be used in much the same way as sorrel (Rumex acetosa).

sources: Flora of New Zealand Series vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
habitat.text: Mainly found around old homesteads and to a limited extent in plantations and areas of reverting pasture, scrub and grassland in the vicinity of original plantings.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Glabrous, deciduous shrub to about 2 m high. Shoots angled. Spines generally 3-partite, shorter than 1.5 cm long on adult shoots. Petiole to 1 cm long; lamina 2–8 × 1–2.5 cm (often some very small leaves on flowering spurs), elliptic to obovate, membranous, dull green above, usually serrulate, sometimes entire; base attenuate; apex obtuse. Flowers in racemes to about 6 cm long at anthesis. Bracts 1–2 mm long, ovate or lanceolate-ovate. Pedicels 5–10 mm long. Perianth segments medium yellow, those of outermost whorl smaller, ovate; innermost sepals about 5 mm long, obovate; petals about 5 mm long, obovate, more or less rounded at apex. Nectaries about 1 mm long, prominent, orange. Stamens 2–3 mm long. Ovules 2. Stigma sessile. Berry 9–11 mm long, oblong, scarlet or crimson-scarlet, shining.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: European barberry is deciduous and its berries are scarlet to crimson-scarlet, shining, without bloom, oblong and 9–11 mm long; Darwin's barberry is evergreen and its berries are black or nearly so, with a whitish bloom, round and 5–7 mm across. European barberry's leaves are thin, dull green, usually finely toothed and 2–8 cm long; Darwin's barberry's are glossy dark green above, with spiny lobes, up to about 3.5 cm. European barberry's spines are mostly three-parted and under 1.5 cm long; Darwin's barberry's split into five. Spiny stems and yellowish flowers in clusters do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Darwin's barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: European barberry's berries are scarlet to crimson-scarlet, shining and without bloom, oblong, 9–11 mm long; barberry's are reddish black under a heavy whitish bloom, with dark red juice. European barberry is plainly deciduous, its leaves thin, dull green above and usually finely toothed; barberry is evergreen or partly deciduous, its leaves shining above, somewhat leathery (almost thin in shady, moist places) and often turning reddish in autumn. European barberry grows to about 2 m with spines under 1.5 cm; barberry to about 7 m with spines up to 2.3 cm. Leaf size, yellow flowers in clusters up to about 6 cm, and old homestead and plantation sites do not separate them. In New Zealand barberry has usually been called B. vulgaris, even in Allan's 1940 flora, so a name in print is no guide.

preparation.text:
The dried fruit is still often used as a condiment, it is very popular in Uzbekistan, for example, where it is used to make the national dish known as 'Plov'.
A refreshing lemon-like drink can be made from the fruit.
The dried young leaves and shoot tips make a refreshing tea.
In Europe, the berries have been traditionally used as an ingredient in making jam. The berries are high in pectin which makes the jam congeal as it cools after having been boiled. In southwestern Asia, especially Iran, the berries are used for cooking, as well as for jam-making. In Iran, barberries are commonly used as a currant in rice pilaf.
Eaten raw, European barberries are usually flavoured with something, because they can be very sour; cooking or drying mellows the sourness.
Wear gloves to pick them, as the shrubs are very thorny, and strip the berries from their stalks indoors. The seeds are large for the size of the berry: for jam, cook the berries until soft and press them through a fine sieve to hold back the seeds, stalk bits and the small black flower remains at the tip of each berry.

recipes.method: From a German herbal page about the common barberry (Berberis vulgaris). 1 kg washed berries; 500 ml water; 500 g jam-setting sugar of the 2:1 kind. Bring 1 kg washed berries to the boil with 500 ml water and simmer for about 20 minutes. Pour through a sieve and catch the juice. Mix the juice with 500 g jam-setting sugar of the 2:1 kind (Gelierzucker 2:1, sugar with added pectin for twice its weight of fruit), bring back to the boil, boil hard for about 4 minutes and pour into sterilised jars.
recipes.title: Barberry jelly

recipes.method: Written for European barberry (Berberis vulgaris) by a forager who picks it wild from hedgerows in Vermont. 450 g stemmed barberries (about 3 cups); 250 ml water; sugar, the same volume as the pulp (about 375 ml). Put 450 g stemmed barberries (about 3 cups) in a saucepan with 250 ml water and simmer gently for about 5 minutes, mashing, until the berries fall apart and release their juice. Press through a fine sieve to remove the seeds, stalk bits and black flower remains; sieve again through a finer sieve or muslin for a smoother jam; expect about 375 ml of pulp. Return it to a clean pan with the same volume of sugar (about 375 ml for 375 ml of pulp), bring to a rolling boil over high heat and boil, stirring all the time, for 2 to 3 minutes, until it starts to gel; test on a plate chilled in the freezer; it sets soft and spoonable. Ladle into two hot, sterilised 250 ml jars, leaving 6 mm headspace. Keep in the fridge or freezer, or process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes (15 minutes above about 1,800 m) and leave undisturbed for 12 to 24 hours before checking the seals. Keeps 12 to 18 months in sealed jars; once opened, refrigerate and use within 2 to 3 weeks.
recipes.title: Barberry jam

summary.text:
European barberry, Berberis vulgaris, also called common barberry, is a deciduous shrub of the barberry family (Berberidaceae), up to about 2 m tall, native to Europe.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): South Island: Canterbury, Otago, especially inland.
European barberry was introduced to New Zealand in the early period of European settlement, and seems to have been mainly planted in the South Island.
In New Zealand, where it has been naturalised since 1875, it spreads both by seed and by suckering; it sets a great deal of seed, which birds and people carry (NZPCN).

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.

associations.note: Porcini has been recorded under European beech.
Bluefoot bolete has been recorded under European beech.
Deadly. Death cap has been recorded under European beech.
Poisonous. Fly agaric has been recorded under European beech.

identification.text: A large tree, up to 40 m, with a smooth grey trunk. Leaves oval with a defined point, alternate on short stalks, lightly downy when young and becoming larger and smoother, with straight, raised, pale veins underneath. Flowers small hanging pompoms that appear with the new leaves in spring. In autumn the rough brown husks split open to show two triangular-sectioned nuts about 2 cm long. Beech often grows in stands, and the leaves of past years form a dense carpet beneath it with very little undergrowth.

summary.text: European beech (Fagus sylvatica), also called common beech, is a large deciduous tree of the beech family (Fagaceae), native to Europe from Norway south and east to Spain, Greece, western Russia and the Crimea. In New Zealand it is planted, and it is listed among the plants naturalised or casual here. It is not one of New Zealand's native beeches. Introduced fungi grow with it as root partners, among them death cap.

warnings: Do not eat the nuts in large quantities: large quantities may be toxic.
