identification.text:
Annual herb to 0.45 m tall. Stems decumbent to erect; hairs of two types: dense, bifarious, antrorse, short, eglandular; and sparse, long, uniform, eglandular or sometimes glandular. Leaf bud indistinct; leaves separating while very small, opposite-decussate, erecto-patent to spreading; lamina thin, elliptic to ovate or sub-orbicular, becoming deltoid above, 5–20 mm long, 3–12 mm wide, dull green above, pale green to pinkish beneath; midrib and secondary veins distinct; surfaces eglandular-pubescent above and beneath, at least on veins; margin pubescent, serrate-crenate to serrate-dentate; teeth in 3–6 pairs; apex obtuse to sub-acute; base truncate to sub-cordate; petiole 0–4 mm rarely to 10 mm long. Inflorescence a terminal spike or raceme, 5–40 mm long; flowers crowded, distant at fruiting, 5–60, all bisexual; bracts alternate, lowest leaf-like, becoming lanceolate-elliptic, longer than pedicels; pedicels erecto-patent, 0–2 mm long, eglandular-pubescent all around. Calyx lobes 4, sub-acute to acute, unequal (the posterior ½–¾ the anterior), 1.5–3.0 mm long, elongating to 5–6 mm at fruiting, glandular- and eglandular-hairy. Corolla 2–3 mm diameter; tube white and yellow, 1 mm long, shorter than calyx, glabrous; lobes 4, blue, rarely white or pinkish, erecto-patent, unequal, elliptic to orbicular, 1.0–1.5 mm long, rounded; nectar guides dark blue. Stamen filaments white, 0.5–1.0 mm long; anthers blue. Style glabrous, about 0.5 mm long. Capsules angustiseptate, obcordate, glandular- or eglandular-ciliate on edges, 2.5–3.0 mm long, 3–4 mm at widest point. Seeds ellipsoid, flattened, smooth, pale brown, 1–1.2 mm long.
Veronica arvensis plants can be recognised by a combination of characters: short, bifarious, mixed with long, uniform stem hairs, leaves toothed but not deeply lobed, tiny bright blue (very rarely white) sessile flowers in a terminal inflorescence, small, obcordate ciliate capsules, and flattened seeds.
Veronica verna plants have a similar growth form, with sessile, small blue flowers and flattened seeds, but can be distinguished by having only short stem hairs (glandular above), upper leaves and lower bracts lobed to at least halfway, and pubescent faces on the capsules (glandular on capsule margins).Veronica triphyllos plants have rather larger blue flowers, digitately lobed leaves, densely glandular inflorescence and calyx, much longer pedicels at fruiting, larger capsules, and cup-shaped seeds.
Veronica arvensis plants have been misidentified as Veronica polita. Veronica polita plants have rather larger flowers with longer pedicels, and even their uppermost bracts are leaf-like. Their capsule lobes are rounded, only weakly flattened, and hairy all over. Their seeds are wrinkled and cup-shaped.
Out of flower it looks much the same as bird's-eye speedwell, only smaller, with similar leaves and hairs; size is not reliable, as it can grow quite large in flower gardens. In flower, its small blue flowers and heart-shaped fruits sit at the bases of the leaves without stalks. Unlike turf speedwell, it has no creeping stems (Massey).
Its lower bracts are leaf-like, so each flower looks as if it sits alone in a leaf base (NZPCN). Turf speedwell has hairless leaves and mainly white flowers (Massey).

lookalikes.howToTell: Bird's-eye speedwell's flowers are 8–12 mm across, each alone on a long, slender stalk (5–15 mm, longer in fruit); field speedwell's are tiny, 2–3 mm across, and sit almost stalkless (stalks 0–2 mm) among small bracts at the stem tips. Bird's-eye speedwell's leaves are 6–35 mm long with 3–8 pairs of teeth; field speedwell's are 5–20 mm with 3–6 pairs. Out of flower they look much the same: both are hairy, with paired, toothed leaves of similar shape, and both grow in gardens, crops, lawns and waste ground. Size alone does not separate them, as field speedwell can grow large in gardens. Bird's-eye speedwell's young leaves and shoots are eaten, but its record as food is thin.
lookalikes.name: Bird's-eye speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Turf speedwell's leaves are almost hairless; field speedwell's are hairy on both faces, at least on the veins, and its stems carry two kinds of hairs. Turf speedwell is a perennial whose lower stems creep and root at the joints; field speedwell is an annual with no creeping stems. Turf speedwell's flowers are pale blue fading to whitish, 3–5 mm across, on stalks 1–3 mm long; field speedwell's are bright blue, 2–3 mm across, almost stalkless. Both grow low in lawns throughout New Zealand, with small paired, toothed leaves and four-lobed flowers in a spike at the stem tips, so habitat and leaf shape do not separate them. Turf speedwell's record as food is thin, so it is not given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Turf speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping speedwell's flowers are 8–10 mm across, each alone on a thread-like stalk 15–40 mm long; field speedwell's are tiny, 2–3 mm across, and sit almost stalkless (stalks 0–2 mm) among small bracts at the stem tips. Creeping speedwell is a perennial whose stems creep flat and root at the joints, forming dense mats; field speedwell is an annual with no creeping stems. Creeping speedwell sets no fruit in New Zealand; field speedwell sets small heart-shaped capsules. Both are hairy, both have small, toothed leaves of overlapping size (creeping speedwell 3–8 mm long, field speedwell 5–20 mm) and both grow low in lawns, so hairiness, leaf size and habitat do not separate them. No food use of creeping speedwell has been confirmed; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Creeping speedwell

summary.text:
Veronica arvensis, common names: wall speedwell, corn speedwell, common speedwell, rock speedwell, field speedwell, is an annual flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae. The species is a common weed in gardens, pastures, waste places, and cultivated land.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: throughout. South Island: throughout. Kermadec Islands, Chatham Islands, Stewart Island, Campbell Island/Motu Ihupuku. First recorded by Kirk in 1864.
In New Zealand it normally grows as a winter annual, germinating in autumn, flowering in spring and dying off in spring (Massey).
It is native to temperate Eurasia and North Africa, and was naturalised in New Zealand by 1864 (NZPCN). Colenso described a New Zealand plant as Veronica hirsuta in 1892; that name is now treated as the same species (Biota of New Zealand).

identification.text:
Field woundwort is an annual herb with branched, square stems up to 45 cm long, growing with a sprawling or erect habit. The stems are pale green and covered with patent, sparsely glandular hairs up to 2 mm long. Plants are easily uprooted to reveal a mass of short, white, fibrous roots at the base of the plant and sometimes along any horizontal stems close to the base. The leaves are arranged in opposite, decussate pairs, with no stipules, and petioles of up to 4 cm long; the blade is simple and oval, up to 4 cm long, with a truncate base and between 7 and 12 rounded teeth per side. They are dull, medium green on the upper surface and paler beneath, hairy on both sides.
The inflorescence consists of a terminal spike with up to 8 false whorls (actually two opposite clusters that look like a whorl) of 4 to 7 flowers, each with a short pedicel of up to 1.5 mm. The whorls are subtended by a pair of leaf-like bracts which are stalked at the base of the inflorescence, becoming sessile towards the top of the plant. There is also one tiny bracteole at the base of each cluster of flowers. The lower whorls are widely spaced, but the upper ones are more crowded towards the tip of the plant. The flowers are zygomorphic with a 5 lobed calyx tube 5 to 7 mm long, and two lipped corolla 6 to 8 mm. The upper lip is entire and the lower lip is three lobed, with the central lobe much larger. It can be white, pink or purple.
In New Zealand it tends to scramble across the ground rather than stand upright, and its flowers are lilac (Massey). In very dry, stony places such as river beds, plants are often only a few centimetres tall (Flora of New Zealand). Seedlings have stalked leaves (University of Queensland key).

lookalikes.howToTell: Field woundwort's flowers are small — 6–7 mm long, with a small upper lip that is not hooded and is shorter than the lower lip, the tube no longer than the calyx; red deadnettle's are 10–14 mm long with a hooded upper lip. Field woundwort's stem is much hairier, and its bracts are stalkless. Both are weeds of gardens, crops, waste places and river beds, and young plants are easily confused. Field woundwort poisons livestock (staggers) and is listed as poisonous in New Zealand; some people eat it, but do not.
lookalikes.name: Red deadnettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Field woundwort's flowers are small — 6–7 mm long, with a small upper lip that is not hooded and is shorter than the lower lip, the tube no longer than the calyx; henbit's are about 15 mm long with a hooded upper lip, on a long, narrow tube. Field woundwort's stem is much hairier. Henbit's leaves among the flowers are stalkless, broad and kidney-shaped, clasp the stem and look unlike its other leaves; field woundwort's are stalkless too, but oblong, oval or nearly round, like its upper leaves — so stalkless leaves alone do not separate them. Both are weeds of gardens, crops and waste places, and young plants are easily confused. Field woundwort poisons livestock (staggers) and is listed as poisonous in New Zealand; some people eat it, but do not.

lookalikes.howToTell: Bird's-eye speedwell's flowers are flat, 8–12 mm across, with four sky-blue lobes (rarely white) striped dark, each alone on a long, slender stalk; field woundwort's are two-lipped, 6–7 mm long, pink or lilac, and grow in clusters around the stem up a leafy spike. Speedwell's stem is round; field woundwort's is square. Both are hairy, sprawl across the ground, have paired, toothed leaves of much the same size, flower all year, and grow in gardens, fields, waste places, roadsides and river beds, so none of these tells them apart. Bird's-eye speedwell's young leaves and shoots are eaten, but its record as food is thin.

summary.text:
Stachys arvensis is a species of flowering plant in the mint family known by the common names field woundwort and staggerweed. It is native to Europe, Western Asia, and North Africa. It is known on other continents as an introduced species and widespread weed.
In New Zealand it is common to abundant throughout the North and South Islands, including offshore islands, and on Raoul Island in the Kermadecs (Flora of New Zealand); it was naturalised by 1867 (NZPCN). It can germinate at any time of year, mostly in spring and autumn, and many of the selective herbicides used in cereal crops do not kill it (Massey).

warnings: It poisons livestock: animals that eat too much of it develop staggers, and sheep have drowned after staggering into a creek. It is listed as poisonous in New Zealand. Some people eat it, but do not.
Red deadnettle and henbit, which are eaten, grow in the same places and look alike when young.

identification.text:
Some canes have compressed internodes in the lower part, giving them a tortoise shell-like appearance.
Fairly dense thicket-forming with rhizomes running extensively. Culm usually 3–6 m (often taller in cultivation), glaucous when young, green during the first year, yellow afterwards, erect, with white waxy ring beneath nodes when young; nodes on some shoots congested and sometimes zigzag towards base; internodes swollen and often asymmetric. Culm-sheath light mauve-brown or pinkish brown, mottled dark purplish, especially towards apex; auricles and oral bristles 0; sheath-blade narrow linear, flat, often with greenish pink marginal band. Branches spreading widely to give an open network. Leaf-sheath with long oral bristles. Auricles 0. Ligule minutely puberulent. Leaf-blade usually 5–13–(15) × 0.7–2–(2.7) cm, lanceolate, abaxially glaucescent, acuminate.
[From: Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Check the leaves: arrow bamboo's blades reach 25–30 cm long and 3.5–4 cm wide, glossy dark green above, against fishpole's usually 5–13 cm and under 3 cm wide. Arrow bamboo has one branch per node, sometimes two or three at the upper nodes, where fishpole usually has three, the middle one small or missing and the other two markedly unequal. Its canes are round, not notched, and dark green; fishpole's internodes are flattened or grooved on alternate sides above each node (usually round below the lowest branches), and its canes turn yellow after the first year, with crowded nodes and swollen, often lopsided internodes near the base of some canes. Height does not separate them (arrow bamboo 3–5 m, fishpole usually 3–6 m), and both have a white band below the nodes (on fishpole, on young canes). Arrow bamboo's young shoots are edible cooked, with a rather bitter flavour.
lookalikes.name: Arrow bamboo

lookalikes.howToTell: Black bamboo's canes are green at first and either stay green or turn black or heavily black-blotched in their second year; fishpole's turn yellow after their first. Because some naturalised black bamboo stays green, a green stand does not rule it out — look at the nodes and sheaths instead. Black bamboo's nodes are all more or less evenly spaced; some of fishpole's canes have crowded, sometimes zigzag nodes and swollen, often lopsided internodes near the base. Black bamboo's cane sheaths are uniformly purple or purple-flushed, with prominent dark auricles on the main shoots; fishpole's are light mauve-brown or pinkish brown mottled dark purple, with no auricles. Both have a white waxy ring below the nodes on young canes, and their heights overlap (black bamboo 4–7 m, fishpole usually 3–6 m), so neither helps. Both have edible young shoots, cooked.

sources: Food Standards Australia New Zealand, 'Cassava and bamboo shoots' (consumer page, page last updated 2 October 2025), https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/cassava, retrieved 19/11/2026 — restated
preparation.text: Do not eat the shoots raw. Cut a fresh shoot in half lengthwise, peel away the outer leaves and trim off any fibrous tissue at the base. Slice it thinly into strips and boil in lightly salted water for 8–10 minutes, then throw the cooking water away before using the shoots in other dishes.

recipes.method: Cut the shoots at about 8 cm above the ground, 5 cm below the soil; the canes are slender, about 15 mm, thicker in their native China. Handle the husk with care: it is many overlapping brown layers covered in fine, sharp hairs. Run a knife up the side of the shoot to slit it, then unwrap and throw away the layers until you reach the pale core; cut off the pointed tip and the fibrous base. They are said to be the sweetest of the genus, with very little bitterness, but cook them: cover with water and boil for 20 minutes, change the water and simmer until tender. If they are still bitter, boil again in fresh water for 5 minutes, and repeat until the flavour is milder.
recipes.title: Preparing fresh shoots

recipes.method: Serves 4. About 400 g of shoots (about 10, large and small), 200 ml kombu tsuyu (Japanese kelp-based soup base), 400 ml water, and sugar and chilli to taste. Peel off the brown outer sheaths but keep the white inner skin, which is edible and tastes like menma; cut off the hard tip. Cut into bite-sized rounds, keeping the skin-only parts in longer pieces as they come apart easily. The page says these shoots have no bitterness and simmers them straight in the broth; the warning on this page asks for a first boil, so boil them first as in 'Preparing fresh shoots'. Simmer in the tsuyu and water over a medium-low heat, checking now and then: the base pieces take about 15 minutes, the skins about 20.
recipes.title: Hoteichiku simmered in kombu tsuyu

recipes.method: Use about the same weight of chicken, prawns or pork as of shoots, plenty of spring onion, and tom yum paste, garlic, ginger, sugar, salt and oil to taste. Halve the shoots and put them in boiling water; peel off the hard sheaths but keep the soft inner skin at the tip. Cut the shoots and meat into bite-sized pieces. Fry the garlic and ginger in oil over a low heat until fragrant, add the meat and cook it through. Add the shoots and stir until they are coated in the oil, then stir in the tom yum paste and season with sugar and salt. Finish with the spring onion.
recipes.title: Hoteichiku tom yum stir-fry

summary.text: Phyllostachys aurea is a species of bamboo, and is of the 'running bamboo' type, belonging to the diverse Bambuseae tribe. Brought here from south-eastern China as an ornamental and naturalised since 1977, it is named on DOC's list of environmental weeds.

warnings: Fresh bamboo shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides, which can break down to release hydrogen cyanide. They must be fully cooked before eating; do not eat them raw.

habitat.text: In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): A very bad weed of cultivated and waste ground, particularly in open places with loose soil but sometimes amongst taller vegetation.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series, 'Oxalis vallicola' (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) — pale form, abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Perennial acaulous herb with thick, fleshy, glassy white, contractile root below the main bulb which is surrounded by numerous small bulbils; tunic brown; scales 3–7-nerved. Leaves 3-foliolate. Petiole (5)–10–50 cm long, glabrous or sparsely hairy; stipular wing broad, membranous, long-ciliate. Lamina of leaflets equal or nearly so, sessile, 12–50 × 18–80 mm, broadly fishtail-shaped, shallowly and broadly 2-lobed, glabrous except for more or less hairy base, finely reticulate beneath, not punctate; calli 0 or inconspicuous. Inflorescence about 10–50 cm tall, pseudoumbellate, about 5–15–(20)-flowered, glabrous or nearly so; pedicels very variable in length, more or less deflexed at first, usually glabrous. Bracts at pedicel base, about 3 mm long, lacking calli. Sepals 3–5.5 mm long, lanceolate-elliptic to elliptic, glabrous; calli 2, orange, prominent, apical. Petals about 1.2–1.5 cm long, oblong-obovate, pink, glabrous. Stamens at 2 levels; filaments of longer set about 4–5 mm long, hirsute above, glabrous and dilated below, shorter set sparingly hairy. Styles shorter than stamens, glabrous or hairy. Capsule not seen.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

Pale form: some plants have broadly heart-shaped (not fishtail-shaped) leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm, with a rather shallow notch, hairless above and hairy or hairless below, with no orange dots; flower clusters 7–26 cm long with 8–15 flowers, hairless or hairy; and petals 9–15 mm long, whitish or very pale mauve-pink. Flora of New Zealand vol. IV describes these as Oxalis vallicola and notes they are often confused with fishtail oxalis and pink shamrock; NZ Flora Online now includes them in this species.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, 'Oxalis vallicola'.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are pink-flowered sorrels with no leafy stem, their leaves all rising from the base, and several flowers in a cluster at the top of a tall stalk. Look at the base of the plant: fishtail oxalis grows from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, with a thick, fleshy, glassy white root below it; shamrock wood sorrel grows from a short, thick, fleshy rhizome, rough with old leaf-base scars, and has no true bulbils. Look at the leaflets: fishtail oxalis's are broadly fishtail-shaped, shallowly and broadly two-lobed, 12–50 mm long and 18–80 mm wide, hairless except near the base, with no orange dots or only faint ones; shamrock wood sorrel's are broadly heart-shaped with a narrow notch up to a third of their length, with flattened hairs on both faces, a tuft of hairs at the base and a band of orange dots along the edge. Fishtail oxalis's petals are about 1.2–1.5 cm long, pink and hairless; shamrock wood sorrel's are 9–16 mm long, usually rose with darker veins, with a band of flattened hairs on the outside, so length overlaps. Flower number overlaps too: fishtail oxalis about 5–15 (up to 20), shamrock wood sorrel (4)–7–35. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. The tests above that do not rest on leaflet shape or petal colour still hold for it. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Shamrock wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are pink-flowered sorrels with no leafy stem, growing from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, with a thick, fleshy, glassy white root below it, and both are weeds of cultivated and waste ground. They are alike in size and flower colour; the orange dots under the leaflets settle it. Pink shamrock's leaflets are broadly heart-shaped and rounded, 10–35 mm long and 12–48 mm wide, with a rather narrow notch, hairy beneath and finely dotted underneath with raised orange spots, especially round the edge; fishtail oxalis's are broadly fishtail-shaped, shallowly and broadly two-lobed, 12–50 mm long and 18–80 mm wide, hairless except near the base, with no orange dots or only faint ones. Pink shamrock's flower clusters carry long curly hairs; fishtail oxalis's are usually hairless or nearly so. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. Its leaflet shape and flower-cluster hairs then match pink shamrock's, but it still has no orange dots under the leaflets. Petals do not separate them safely: pink shamrock's are 1.5–2 cm long, pink to rose; fishtail oxalis's about 1.2–1.5 cm, pink. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pink shamrock

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel has leafy stems, spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and each flower stalk carries a single flower. Fishtail oxalis has no leafy stem: its leaves all rise from the base, from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, and it carries about 5–15 (up to 20) flowers in a cluster on a stalk about 10–50 cm tall. Pale-pink wood sorrel's petals are 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white; fishtail oxalis's are about 1.2–1.5 cm long, pink. Pale-pink wood sorrel's petals can be as short as 1 cm, so petal size alone does not separate them. Pale-pink wood sorrel's leaflets carry an irregular row of orange dots just inside the edge; fishtail oxalis's have none or only faint ones and are broadly fishtail-shaped. Leaflet size overlaps: pale-pink wood sorrel's are 4–16 mm long, fishtail oxalis's 12–50 mm. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. The tests above that do not rest on leaflet shape or petal colour still hold for it. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pale-pink wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Purple wood sorrel carries a single flower on each stalk, 1–11 cm long, forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base. Its leaflets are broadly obovate with a rounded tip, sometimes slightly notched, with long hairs fringing the edges, and its sepals carry a dense fringe of long white hairs and have no orange dots. Fishtail oxalis carries about 5–15 (up to 20) flowers in an umbel-like cluster on a stalk about 10–50 cm tall, its petals about 1.2–1.5 cm long, pink. Its leaflets are broadly fishtail-shaped, shallowly and broadly two-lobed, 12–50 mm long and 18–80 mm wide, and its sepals are hairless, with two prominent orange dots at the tip. What does not separate them: both have no leafy stem, with all the leaves rising from the base; both grow from bulbs that make bulbils, though purple wood sorrel's outer bulb scales are dark brown or blackish, shining and sticky and fishtail oxalis's are brown or pale fawn-brown; and fishtail oxalis's leaflets have no orange dots or only faint ones, so leaflet dots do not help. Purple wood sorrel's petals can be as short as 10 mm, so petal length points to purple wood sorrel only when the petals are longer than 16 mm. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. The tests above that do not rest on leaflet shape or petal colour still hold for it. Do not eat purple wood sorrel; see its own entry.

preparation.text: Eat the leaves and stems raw in salads, or cook them, with the bulbs, with other greens or potatoes as a leafy vegetable. The leaves are also made into chutney, soup, a cool drink or tea, and are pickled. Use it in moderation.

IV (cited above), 'If not checked it can cover recently cultivated soil with a dense mass of foliage which arises from the numerous small bulbils scattered during cultivation'; Royal Horticultural Society, 'Oxalis' weed page (all rights reserved, facts only), https://www.rhs.org.uk/weeds/oxalis, retrieved 03/11/2026 — bulbils 'can remain viable in the soil for several years'. Months (03/11/2026): leaves, stems, flowers and bulbs are eaten, so the window is the union of the flowering window, Flora of New Zealand 'FL Nov–Jun' (NZFO 'Flowering: Nov.–Jun.'), and the months with iNaturalist research-grade wild NZ records at or above a quarter of the peak month (peak April, 102 records; quarter 26: December to May qualify, June has 1, July to November 0–9): November to June. Himalayan Wild Food Plants gives the edible parts 'from beginning of spring season to pre-winter' in the Western Himalaya, which fits; not used to set months.

Origin checked 03/11/2026: NZTCS has no record (findNztcsSpeciesByCriteria 'Oxalis latifolia', 0 results); NZ Organisms Register (https://data.nzor.org.nz/names/search?query=Oxalis%20latifolia): Exotic, Present, New Zealand; NZPCN 'Oxalis latifolia' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/oxalis-latifolia/): Biostatus Exotic, year naturalised 1958; NZ Flora Online Biostatus Exotic. Not on DOC's List of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024 (Science for Conservation 340) and not in Wildland Consultants 2021 Contract Report 5396 for the PCE, Appendix 2 (text searched: only Oxalis pes-caprae), so not a pest despite Flora's 'very bad weed' (a crop and garden weed). summary.text:
Oxalis latifolia is a species of flowering plant in the woodsorrel family known by the common names garden pink-sorrel and broadleaf woodsorrel. It is native to Mexico and parts of Central and South America. However, it has propagated to other parts of the world.
It is known on most other continents as an introduced species and a noxious weed and invasive species, as it infests many types of agricultural crops.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: widespread and often abundant; South Island: northern half; Kermadec Islands: Raoul Island. Naturalised from tropical South America; Flora of New Zealand dates its naturalisation to 1958, though herbarium sheets have it overrunning a garden at Normanby, Taranaki, in 1942 and established as a garden weed in Christchurch in 1945. Herbarium sheets also record it wild in Canterbury: as a garden weed in Christchurch and Lincoln, on a Christchurch roadside and a South New Brighton dune walkway, and in grassland at Amberley. O. latifolia is somewhat less widespread than the related O. debilis, but where it occurs is generally common and often abundant. If not checked it can cover recently cultivated soil with a dense mass of foliage which arises from the numerous small bulbils scattered during cultivation. O. intermedia A. Rich. is sometimes considered to be the correct name of this species.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

It spreads by the many small bulbils around its bulb, which are scattered when the soil is dug or moved; left unchecked it can cover freshly cultivated soil with a dense mass of leaves, and the bulbils can stay alive in the soil for several years. Dig it only where you mean to clear it, and do not move soil it grows in.
It grows with pink shamrock and shamrock wood sorrel, pink-flowered sorrels that look very like it (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
Unarmed, deciduous, moderately aromatic shrub, 1–2–(3) m high; branches and shoots erect, tomentulose or glandular hairy when young. Leaves plicately folded in bud, with petioles to about 8 cm long, slightly clasping at base; lamina very broadly ovate or deltoid, (3)–4–8–(10) × (3.5)–4–9–(10) cm, often smaller on upper part of flowering stems, deeply palmately-lobed, with 3–5 broadly ovate, coarsely serrate lobes, glabrate or hairy, dull, somewhat rugose with impressed veins above, glabrate to hairy or sometimes tomentose below, sparsely to densely covered with almost colourless, inconspicuous glandular scales; base subcordate to deeply cordate. Racemes pendent, usually 15-many-flowered; flowers not fragrant. Hypanthium 4–7 mm long, cylindric, pale pink to deep red, with scattered simple eglandular or glandular hairs. Sepals 4–6.5 mm long, more or less elliptic-oblong, pale pink to deep red, glabrous or with simple or glandular hairs, reflexed at anthesis. Petals 3–5 mm long, spathulate or obovate, white ageing pink to rose. Filaments 1–2.5 mm long. Fruit 5–7 mm diam., globose, black, opaque and usually with a whitish bloom, more or less glandular; flesh with little taste.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In plain terms: a shrub 1–2 m high, sometimes 3 m, with deeply lobed, dull, somewhat wrinkled leaves that smell resinous when crushed. Drooping clusters of 15 or more flowers open in late winter and spring (August to November). Wild plants usually have pale flowers; garden cultivars have deeper rose or crimson ones. The round black berries, 5–7 mm across and usually dusted with a whitish bloom, ripen from November to March and have little taste. It differs from blackcurrant in its pink to red flowers and its small, almost colourless glandular scales (see the lookalikes).

lookalikes.howToTell: Blackcurrant has small greenish-white flowers, 5 to 15 in a cluster, with a short round green or reddish-green cup behind them; flowering currant has pink to deep red flowers, 15 to many in a cluster, with a long narrow tube. Blackcurrant's leaves have prominent yellow glandular scales underneath and a strong smell when bruised; flowering currant's scales are small and almost colourless and its leaves only moderately aromatic. Both shrubs have aromatic leaves, so smell alone does not separate them. Blackcurrant's berries are 7–10 mm, black, with no whitish bloom, very aromatic and moderately sweet; flowering currant's are 5–7 mm, usually with a bloom and little taste. Blackcurrant is edible; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Blackcurrant

preparation.text: Flowers: scatter them raw over salads and puddings, sprinkle them over savoury and sweet dishes, or infuse them into a syrup, cordial, vinegar or vodka (see the recipes). Dried, the flowers make a tea. Used alone they give a pink result. The berries are tart, have little taste and are high in tannin, seed and hair, so they need more sugar and processing than other currants. They are cooked into jam, jelly, cordial, wine, syrup, fruit leather or chutney; they can be eaten fresh, and North American peoples also stewed, dried and canned them.

recipes.method: Flowering currant flowers; equal parts sugar and water; lemon juice, citric acid or flowering currant vinegar, for a cordial. For a syrup, infuse the flowers into a syrup of equal parts sugar and water by heating gently, without boiling. Using only the flowers gives a pink syrup. Cool, and keep in sterilised jars in the fridge for a couple of weeks. Pour it over puddings or add it to gin. For a cordial, sharpen the syrup to taste with lemon juice, citric acid or the flowering currant vinegar below; this also helps it keep. Dilute to drink.
recipes.title: Flowering currant syrup and cordial

recipes.method: Flowering currant flowers; cold white wine or apple cider vinegar; flowering currant syrup or cordial, or honey, for a shrub or oxymel. Infuse the flowers straight into cold white wine or apple cider vinegar for a week, then strain. Use it in salad dressings or as a pickling liquor. Mix the vinegar with flowering currant syrup or cordial for a shrub, or with honey for an oxymel, to add fruity sourness to gin drinks.
recipes.title: Flowering currant vinegar and shrub

recipes.method: Flowering currant flowers; vodka; flowering currant cordial, syrup or shrub, to sweeten. Infuse the flowers in vodka for no more than a week, strain, and sweeten to taste with flowering currant cordial, syrup or shrub.
recipes.title: Flowering currant liqueur

recipes.method: The author's elderflower champagne with flowering currant flowers in place of the elderflowers. He gives no amount; for a subtler flower he says to use more plant material than the 10–16 elderflower heads. Flowering currant flowers; 650 g sugar; 4.5 litres of cold water; 1 lemon; 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar. Dissolve 650 g sugar in 4.5 litres of cold water — warm a little of the water to dissolve the sugar, cool it, then mix it into the rest. In a large bucket or bowl, combine the sweetened water with the flowers, the juice and quartered skin of 1 lemon, and 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar. Cover and leave for 4 days, somewhere cool; if mould forms, scrape off the mat of flowers on top and carry on. Fine-strain into clean screw-top plastic fizzy-drink bottles, leaving a few centimetres of air at the top. Never use corked bottles, and avoid glass flip-tops: you can't feel the pressure through them, and they are far more dangerous if they burst. Leave at room temperature for 6–14 days. From day 6, squeeze the bottles every day, and as soon as the bases start to round out, ease the caps to let off some (not all) of the pressure; a forgotten bottle can explode. Once it tastes right, move it to the fridge to slow the fermentation, and keep checking the pressure. The author drinks it between 2 and 4 weeks; it is lightly alcoholic after a week and starts turning vinegary at 5–6 weeks. The source notes that the yeast comes from the flowers, so in a cool room it can take a while to get going.
recipes.title: Flowering currant champagne

recipes.method: Written for the author's mixed wild leaves. Of his lists, this catalogue covers dandelion and hairy bittercress (pungent), chickweed and young hawthorn leaves (mild), and gorse flowers and flowering currant blossom (extras). He warns to be extra careful identifying leaves before the plants flower. Pungent leaves; mild leaves; a few extras; walnut oil; elderberry vinegar; salt and pepper; a little mustard; fermented greens; pickled buds. Mix pungent and mild leaves about 1 to 3, then scatter a few extras over the top. Dress simply with walnut oil, elderberry vinegar, salt, pepper and a little mustard; he finishes it with fermented greens and pickled buds.
recipes.title: Wild summer salad

recipes.method: Makes 4 ramekins. Panna cotta: 25 g flowering currant flowers (about 375 ml loosely measured); 150 ml milk; 400 ml double cream; sugar to taste (the page adds sugar but gives no amount); 2½ sheets platinum-grade gelatine; ¼ tsp vanilla bean paste. Ginger crumble: 1 heaped tbsp butter; 2 heaped tbsp plain flour; 1 heaped tbsp demerara sugar; 1 tsp ground ginger. Keep back a quarter of the flowers for decorating and soak the rest in the milk for 1–2 hours. Soak the gelatine in cold water for 5 minutes. Pour the milk and flowers into a pan with the cream, sugar and vanilla, bring to a simmer and take off the heat. Sieve into a clean pan, squeeze the gelatine and stir it in until dissolved. Pour into the ramekins and chill for at least 4 hours. To serve, heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan), rub the crumble ingredients together until crumbly and bake on a lined tray for 10 minutes until golden. Scatter the crumble and the kept flowers over the panna cottas.
recipes.title: Flowering currant panna cotta

recipes.method: 80 flowering currant flower heads; 300 g caster sugar; 300 ml water. Sterilise a 600 ml bottle or jar: wash it in hot soapy water and heat it in the oven at 100 °C for at least 30 minutes. In a pan over medium heat, stir the sugar into the water until it dissolves. Pick any insects and leaves off the flowers, add the flowers to the syrup and simmer for about 15 minutes until syrupy. Strain through a fine sieve or muslin, pour into the sterilised bottle (sterilise the funnel too), seal and refrigerate; it keeps about three months in the fridge. Dilute with cold still or sparkling water and serve with ice.
recipes.title: Flowering currant cordial

recipes.method: The blossom is a small flavouring here; the author offers rose petals or fresh rosemary instead. 250 ml stout or porter; 250 ml butter; 185 ml unsweetened cocoa powder; 500 ml sugar; 165 ml yoghurt or sour cream; 2 large eggs; 1 tbsp vanilla; 500 ml plain flour; 2½ tsp baking soda; 3 tsp flowering currant blossoms, plus more to decorate. Heat the oven to 180 °C and butter a 23 cm springform tin. Warm the stout in a pan over medium heat, add the butter and let it melt, take it off the heat and whisk in the cocoa and sugar. Beat the yoghurt or sour cream, eggs and vanilla together until even, then whisk them into the stout mixture. Whisk in the flour, blossoms and baking soda. Pour into the tin and bake for 50–60 minutes, until a skewer comes out with crumbs clinging to it. Cool in the tin on a rack. Serve with lightly sweetened whipped cream or vanilla ice cream, scattered with more blossoms if you like.
recipes.title: Chocolate stout cake with flowering currant blossom

recipes.method: Makes about 1 litre. About 1–1.25 litres (4–5 cups) flowering currant flowers; 2 tbsp lemon juice; 500 ml boiling water; agave syrup or another light-coloured liquid sweetener, to taste; 1 can coconut milk. Shake the flowers to dislodge any insects; there is no need to wash them. Put them in a jar with the lemon juice and pour over the boiling water. Leave to cool, then cover and keep in the fridge overnight. Strain, discard the flowers and sweeten the pink liquid to taste. For ice blocks, freeze the liquid as it is in moulds. For the dessert, stir or blend in the coconut milk, pour into a container with room for it to expand, and freeze for 3–4 hours; stir, then freeze until set. Let it stand a few minutes at room temperature before scooping.
recipes.title: Flowering currant frozen dessert and ice blocks

summary.text:
The flowering currant (Ribes sanguineum), also called red flowering currant, blood currant, winter currant or pink-flowering currant, is a deciduous shrub in the gooseberry family (Grossulariaceae). It is native to western North America and was naturalised in New Zealand by 1904.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) it is commonly cultivated for its early spring flowers in the colder parts of the country, and is a common and sometimes aggressive escape in the eastern South Island. The Flora records it in the Hutt Valley in the North Island and from Marlborough to Southland in the South Island, mainly in drier areas, especially the Port Hills, the Waitaki Valley and the Queenstown area. Herbarium sheets also record wild plants at Karori in Wellington (1978) and on the Pahaoa River in eastern Wairarapa (2010, probably grown from dumped garden waste). It is sometimes called Ribes glutinosum in New Zealand, but this is usually treated as a variety (var. glutinosum) of R. sanguineum; wild plants vary from those with plain hairs to those with many glandular hairs.
It is on DOC's list of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024. It forms dense stands along waterways and in shrublands, crowding out native plants. It sprouts from root crowns, especially after fire, its stems root where they touch the ground, and birds and small mammals spread its seed.

warnings: It is an environmental weed that is controlled with herbicide (cut-and-paste, basal bark and foliar sprays). Pick only where you know it has not been sprayed.

identification.text:
Large, suckering, spiny shrub up to 3–(4) m high when mature and several m diameter; stems brownish olive, smooth, shining and glabrous when young, often forming dense thickets. Leaves distributed along length of first-year, non-flowering stems, and in fascicles on short shoots on older flowering stems; petiole 6–12 mm long, green or red-tinged, glabrous; blade obovate to elliptic, finely serrate to crenate, (30)–50–80–(100) × 20–50 mm, acute and often curled at tip, attenuate to petiole at base, glabrous, more or less shining and deep green on upper surface, paler below; leaves of short shoots on flowering stems similar but smaller; stipules prominent, reniform, up to 12 × 20 mm, crenate. Flowers in fascicles of (3)–4–5, 25–35 mm diameter, more or less sessile. Sepals fused at base; lobes broadly ovate to oblong, 3–5 mm long, green, glabrous, with hyaline ciliate margins. Petals 5, more or less overlapping, suberect or spreading, broad-ovate to orbicular, 12–20 mm diameter, shortly clawed; limb white to bright pink to scarlet. Stamens shorter than petals; filaments coloured as in petals. Fruit up to 60 mm diameter, more or less broadly ovoid to subglobose but often misshapen, yellowish and often brown-speckled, indented at base and apex. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Genus Chaenomeles (Flora of New Zealand): Flowers solitary or fascicled, distributed along stems, those on older wood appearing before leaves and those on younger wood usually appearing with or after leaves. Stamens 40–60. Chaenomeles species have more or less spiny branches, usually glabrous leaves, sometimes hairy on midrib beneath, the flowers few in fascicles, mainly produced before the leaves but with scattered flowers later, erect sepals, and the fruit less than 70 mm long.
The flowers mostly open on bare branches, before the glossy leaves; garden cultivars run from white and green-tinged white through pink and coral to vermilion and scarlet. The fruit is green to yellow, about the size of a small lemon, and stays rock hard even when ripe.

lookalikes.howToTell: Quince is unarmed, or only rarely slightly spiny; flowering quince is a spiny shrub. Flowering quince leaves are finely toothed, hairless, and more or less shining deep green above; quince leaves have entire margins and are white- to grey-woolly beneath. Flowering quince flowers come in clusters of (3)–4–5, 25–35 mm across, mostly before the leaves, with erect sepals; quince flowers sit singly at the ends of short leafy shoots, 30–50 mm across, with sharply bent-back, densely woolly sepals that stay on the fruit. Flowering quince fruit is up to 60 mm across, often misshapen and brown-speckled; quince fruit is usually 80–150 mm long and more or less finely downy. Flower colour helps only at the red end: flowering quince can be white, pink or scarlet, quince white to pink. Height does not separate them (both are suckering shrubs that can form thickets, flowering quince up to 3–(4) m and quince up to 5–(8) m), and both fruits are yellowish and fragrant. Quince fruit is eaten cooked.

preparation.text: Leave the fruit on the shrub until it begins to fall, until the skin turns yellow, or until after a frost. Raw, the fruit is rock hard and sour; cooking softens it and brings out its fragrance. For jelly, quarter the fruit, just cover it with water, boil until soft and mushy, strain off the juice and boil it with sugar to setting point. Ripe fruit is tart and needs more sugar than apple. Freezing the fruit first softens it for cutting. Cut fruit browns, so drop the pieces into water with lemon juice as you chop. The fruit is high in pectin, so jams and jellies set without added pectin. Sources differ on texture: chopped small it can soften in 5–10 minutes, or keep some crunch even after long stewing. For a clear jelly, let the juice drip through cloth overnight without squeezing; a longer boil with sugar alone turns the jelly reddish. Quince recipes can be used, but the fruit is much smaller than ordinary quince, so go by weight or volume rather than by number of fruit.

recipes.method: Written for japonica (Chaenomeles, the red-flowered shrub with yellow-green apple-like fruit). Ingredients: japonica fruit (the author gathered about a kilo of windfalls), water, and sugar — jam (setting) sugar or ordinary sugar — at a kilo for every litre of juice. Keep the fruit for a few days in a bowl in a warm room. Quarter it, put it in a large pot, just cover with water and boil until soft and mushy. Strain the juice off the pulp; the author skips the jelly bag and accepts a cloudy jelly. Measure the juice and boil it with the sugar: with jam sugar, boil vigorously for one minute; with ordinary sugar, keep boiling until a teaspoonful on a cold saucer wrinkles into a set after a few seconds. The source gives no jarring instructions.
recipes.title: Japonica jelly

recipes.method: Written for Japanese quince (Chaenomeles japonica). Ingredients: 750 g Japanese quince, water to cover, 3 large stalks of tarragon plus 3 more sprigs for chopping, and caster sugar at 400 g for every 600 ml of juice; 3 jam jars and wax discs. Sterilise the jars and lids. Quarter the fruit and take out the seeds; wrap about half the seeds in muslin (for pectin) and put the bag in a pan with the fruit. Cover with water, bring to the boil and simmer until tender, 40 minutes to an hour and a half depending on how bletted the fruit was. Strain through muslin, keeping the liquid (the pulp can go into jam). Measure the liquid and weigh out the sugar. Heat the liquid, sugar, tarragon stalks and the seed bag gently, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then bring to a rolling boil without stirring until it reaches 104.5 °C, or passes the fridge test. Take off the heat, lift out the seed bag and tarragon stalks, stir in the finely chopped tarragon and leave to cool for 10–15 minutes so the herb spreads evenly. Pour into the sterilised jars to within a couple of mm of the top, lay the wax discs on wax side down and screw the lids on tightly while hot.
recipes.title: Japonica and tarragon jelly

recipes.method: Written for flowering quince (Chaenomeles speciosa), fruit about the size of a small lemon; adapted by the author from a Simply Recipes quince jam. Ingredients: 10–12 flowering quinces (about 950 ml, 4 packed cups, once minced), 830 ml (3½ cups) water, 30 ml (2 tablespoons) lemon juice, the zest of one lemon and 700 g (3½ cups) sugar. Makes about three 250 ml jars. Wash the fruit and cut it in half; remove the core, seeds and any blemished bits, rinse, and do not peel. Mince the fruit finely with a large knife or a food processor. Put two small plates in the freezer for testing the set. Bring the water to the boil in a large heavy pan, add the minced fruit, lemon juice and zest, lower the heat and simmer until the fruit is soft, about 10 minutes. Add the sugar, bring back to the boil and stir until it has all dissolved. Lower the heat to medium-high and cook uncovered, stirring now and then, until the jam turns pink and thickens, about 30–50 minutes. To test, dab a little hot jam on a cold plate, wait a few seconds and run a finger through it: if the streak stays, it is ready; if not, cook a few minutes more and test again. Mash with a potato masher for a less chunky jam. Ladle into sterilised jars, wipe the rims clean, and screw on lids sterilised in boiling water. Turn the jars upside down under a tea towel; when cool, turn them upright and press the lids. A lid that springs back has not sealed: keep that jar in the fridge.
recipes.title: Flowering quince jam

recipes.method: Written for Japanese flowering quince (Chaenomeles japonica); the author's own recipe, loosely based on a Greek quince jam. Makes 1 litre. Ingredients: 800 g whole fruit (about 600 g once cored and chopped), 400 g sugar, 1 lemon (zest and juice), 4–6 whole cloves and 1 tablespoon rosewater (optional). Put the jars in an oven at 75 °C until needed. Put half the lemon juice in a large bowl and half-fill it with cold water. Wash, quarter, core and slice the fruit thinly, dropping each handful into the lemon water as you go so it does not brown. Drain and weigh the fruit; if it is not 600 g, use sugar at 2 parts to 3 parts fruit. Put the fruit in a stainless steel pan with just enough water to nearly cover it and bring to the boil; cook 5–10 minutes until soft. Add the sugar, cloves, zest and half the remaining lemon juice, lower to medium heat and cook, stirring now and then with a wooden spoon, until the fruit breaks down and the liquid reduces to the thickness you want. Add the last of the lemon juice and the rosewater and boil 15 minutes more. Take off the heat and leave to stand 15–30 minutes, then ladle into the hot jars and seal. Lower the sealed jars into a tall pot of hot (not yet boiling) water, bring to the boil and process for 5–10 minutes, then cool on a wooden board. After 12–24 hours, check the seals: any jar that has not sealed goes in the fridge and is eaten within a week. This makes a soft jam; for a firmer set, use less water at the start or cook the fruit until about half the water has evaporated before adding the sugar.
recipes.title: Flowering quince jam with cloves and rosewater

recipes.method: Ingredients: 4 flowering quince fruits; 200 g (1 cup) sugar; 100 ml water. Cut the fruit into slices about 5 mm thick and remove the seeds. Bring the sugar and water to the boil in a saucepan and cook until the sugar has dissolved. Add the slices, cover and cook gently for about 1 hour, checking often in the last 15 minutes and adding a little more water if it gets too dry. Lift out the slices and leave them to cool.
recipes.title: Candied flowering quince slices

recipes.method: Ingredients: 450 g flowering quince fruit, seeds removed, chopped; 340 g onions, finely chopped; 225 g brown sugar; 250 ml (1 cup) cider vinegar; a handful of raisins (optional); chilli flakes or fresh chillies, finely chopped, to taste. Put everything in a saucepan, bring to the boil, then simmer gently, stirring now and then, until thick — about 2 hours on a low heat. Spoon into hot sterilised jars and seal.

summary.text:
Flowering quince (Chaenomeles speciosa), also called japonica, Japanese quince or Chinese quince, is a large, suckering, spiny shrub native to China.
Its fruit is up to 60 mm across, roughly egg-shaped to round but often misshapen, yellowish and often brown-speckled; when freely produced it is used for jellies like ordinary quince.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Japonica or Japanese quince is one of our commonest cultivated shrubs, but is not common as a fully naturalised plant. However, it is frequently a long-persistent, suckering relic in abandoned gardens. A number of cultivars, mainly distinguished by flower colour, are grown and wild plants can be expected to reflect this range of colour. Naturalised in North Auckland (Mangamuka Hill), Nelson (Little Wanganui) and Christchurch; native to China, first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1988.
In New Zealand it is also called japonica, a name also used for the related Japanese quince (Chaenomeles japonica), which is grown here but not naturalised. 'Chinese quince' is also the name of a different tree, Pseudocydonia sinensis. Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and wild, with herbarium records from North Auckland, Taranaki, Wellington, Nelson, Westland and Canterbury. The name speciosa means handsome. It is sold in New Zealand garden centres as a flowering shrub and hedge plant.

warnings: The raw fruit is very harsh, sour and acid and is not eaten raw; cook it.

No seed analysis for this species was found. The seed is likely to contain cyanogenic glycosides, which release cyanide when digested: the seeds of the related Japanese quince (Chaenomeles japonica) contain them, and eating Chaenomeles seeds without pretreatment may be hazardous. Remove the seeds, or strain them out with the pulp.

habitat.text: On the ground under trees, as a root partner: above all radiata pine and Douglas fir, and also birch, oak, beech, larch, eucalypts and other introduced trees, and native southern beech, mānuka and kānuka. It turns up in plantations older than about six years, in parks and gardens, and in native beech forest.

harvestEthics.text: Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.

identification.text:
Young ones come up as round, white to yellowish balls covered in a warty veil, and at this stage can be mistaken for a puffball. Cut one in half from top to bottom: inside is the outline of a cap over a stem, with fine gill lines, and an orange to yellow layer just under the cap skin.
The cap opens from rounded to flat, 5–25 cm across, bright red to orange-red, fading to orange or yellow-orange with age or rain; old caps can turn up at the rim and darken to a bronze sheen. It is sticky when wet and dotted with white to yellowish warts, often in rings, which rain can wash off. The cap skin peels away. The gills are white to cream, free of the stem and crowded. The stem is 8–20 cm tall and 1–2.5 cm thick, white, with a persistent white to pale yellow ring, and swells into a bulb at the base ringed with bands or patches of veil, not a cup. The flesh is white and firm. The spore print is white.
A yellow-capped form also grows under radiata pine.
Other red-capped fungi here have no white warts, and none has a skirt-like ring on the stem. The other Amanita species in New Zealand are all poisonous too.

lookalikes.howToTell: A young fly agaric can look like a small puffball from outside: a round, white to yellowish ball on the ground, covered in a warty veil. Cut it in half from top to bottom. A fly agaric button shows the outline of a cap over a stem, with fine gill lines and an orange to yellow layer just under the skin. A giant puffball is solid, even, pure white flesh with no structure inside. Fly agaric grows near trees, as a root partner; giant puffball grows mostly in pasture, and its skin is smooth to slightly lumpy, not warty.

Gadgil 2005 (on the same page and on Virtual Mycota https://virtualmycota.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/vM_Species_Details.aspx?pk=312): 'This is the classic toadstool familiar to everyone. It is one of the most common and striking agarics associated with introduced tree species in New Zealand. Unlike most introduced mycorrhizal fungi, it has been recorded in indigenous forests in association with Nothofagus and Leptospermum … A. muscaria may be locally common in Nothofagus forests in several areas in the South Island … found only in older (>6-year-old) plantations'; distribution Northland to Southland and the Chatham Islands; 'Pileus scarlet, paling to orange at the margin … sprinkled with remnants of the volva forming white warty patches which are often arranged concentrically … Gills crowded, free, white … membranaceous white to yellowish annulus … spore print white'. Ridley 1991: 'Context of pileus white, with orange to pale luteous directly under the pileipellis … basal bulb crowned with concentric bands or squarish warts'. Stevenson 1962: 'up to 25 cm. diam.' The Hidden Forest, 'Amanita muscaria' https://www.hiddenforest.co.nz/fungi/family/amanitaceae/amani02.htm (retrieved 19/11/2026): 'found commonly under pine, but also under eucalyptus, birch and native beech. When in the button stage, the universal veil is quite yellow soon fadeing to white'; 'Cap: 50-250 mm diameter … bright red to orange-red when fresh, often fading to orange, yellow-orange … Universal-veil remnants form white to yellowish warts … these may wash off in rain'; 'Gills: White to cream, free, crowded'; 'Stipe: 80-200 mm tall, 10-25 mm thick … Ring: persistent, white … Volva: Not a saccate cup; instead appears as concentric, friable rings or patches on the bulb … Flesh: White, firm … Season: Autumn … Edible: Poisonous'; amani01 is the yellow form ('Ectomycorrhizal with introduced Pinus radiata'). Its 'it can be made safe with some preparation' is not used. Wikipedia 'Amanita muscaria' (raw, retrieved 19/11/2026; CC BY-SA 4.0): buttons 'emerge from the soil looking like white eggs … Dissecting the mushroom at this stage reveals a characteristic yellowish layer of skin under the veil'; 'A. muscaria is the fungal equivalent of a weed in New Zealand'. The cut-button photo's observer: 'Orange colour seen immediately on cutting' (iNaturalist 45742614).

summary.text:
Fly agaric is the red-and-white toadstool of children's books, and one of the commonest and most striking mushrooms under introduced trees in New Zealand. It is poisonous.
It was brought in with exotic trees; Biota of New Zealand's earliest specimen is from 1920, and it is now recorded from Northland to Southland and on the Chatham Islands. Unlike most introduced root-partner fungi it has moved into native forest with southern beech, mānuka and kānuka, and it can be locally common in beech forest in parts of the South Island; it has been called the fungal equivalent of a weed here. Its name comes from an old use: pieces of the dried mushroom in a saucer of milk attract flies, which become intoxicated, fall in and drown.
Massey University's poisonous plants database records poisoning in cattle and goats as well as people, one case in a dog and a possible case in a kitten.

warnings: It is poisonous. Eating it can cause nausea and vomiting. Symptoms start within a few minutes to two or three hours of eating: watering eyes, drooling and sweating, severe stomach pain and watery diarrhoea, hallucinations, and manic behaviour or deep sleep. Severe poisoning brings delirium, convulsions and coma, and some effects can last for days. Deaths are rare.
Young fly agarics can be mistaken for puffballs. Cut every puffball in half from top to bottom before eating it: a fly agaric button shows the outline of a cap, gills and stem.
If anyone may have eaten it, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766.

Forest margins.
In New Zealand: common in coastal, lowland and lower montane forest, occasionally reaching subalpine habitats in the South Island, often in shrubland, and tolerant of a wide range of situations.

identification.text: A shrub or small tree up to 4 m tall, with one to many stems 10–15 cm across rising from ground level, sparingly branched. The leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, lanceolate (somewhat paddle-shaped), broadest about the middle and drooping from there, and narrowed above the base into a long, narrow, channelled stalk; the flat midrib is prominent for the whole length of the leaf. The panicle is 1–2 m long, often smaller, broadly pyramidal and openly branched, its lower bracts green and leaf-like. The flowers are white, sweetly perfumed and about 10 mm long. The fruit is round, 4–5 mm across, and white, bluish-white or blue.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cabbage tree grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Forest cabbage tree (Cordyline banksii) grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Cabbage tree grows to the size of a small tree with a thick trunk and many branches, and its leaf stalk is flat and ill-defined, at least three-quarters as wide as the widest part of the blade; forest cabbage tree rarely approaches tree form and, if tall, usually has several more or less equal main stems, and its leaf stalk is narrow, long (up to a quarter of the blade's length) and deeply channelled, widening rather abruptly into a much wider blade that droops at the tip, with a prominent midrib and several stronger side nerves. Both have white, scented flowers, so flower colour does not separate them. Where the two overlap at about 90–300 m on the northern tip of the Tararua Range, about half the plants cannot be put strictly in either species.
lookalikes.name: Cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf cabbage tree is rarely more than 2 m tall and often flowers while its short stem is still leafy to the ground; its leaves are 30–60–(100) × 1–2 cm, more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base; its panicle is very open, up to about 60 cm long, with slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers that are whitish or pink outside, and its berries are bluish or flecked with blue, 4–5 mm across. Forest cabbage tree (Cordyline banksii) grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Dwarf cabbage tree is usually no more than 1–(2) m tall with a main stem 1–2 cm across and leaves rarely over 2 cm wide, its flower cluster large for the plant but with very slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers; forest cabbage tree's main stem soon exceeds 2 cm across even on a young plant, and its leaves are mostly over 2 cm wide. A hybrid between the two has been described (C. × gibbingsae, Carse 1929) that looks like a small, stemless forest cabbage tree, so an in-between plant may be neither.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain cabbage tree grows to about 8 m with massive, rather sparingly branched stems; its leaves are up to 1–2 m × 10–15 cm, broadly sword-shaped, drooping only with age, glaucous underneath, narrowed above the base to a short stalk, with a broad, conspicuous midrib that is often reddish, the stronger nerves often reddish too; its panicle is tightly compact, 60–160 cm long, its crowded, rather fleshy flowers on longer stalks than in the other species, and its berries are bluish, about 6 mm across. Forest cabbage tree (Cordyline banksii) grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Mountain cabbage tree stands apart from all the others on its leaves: up to 10–15 cm wide, glaucous underneath, with a strong, often reddish midrib and main nerves, and a tightly compact flower cluster. The other species' leaves are rarely over 10 cm wide, often much less, not or scarcely glaucous underneath, and their flower clusters are lax and open. Forms intermediate between these two have been recorded.

preparation.text: Cabbage trees, this species among them, give a leaf heart: peel back the tough outer leaves of a leaf head until the paler shoot and heart show, stripping too few rather than too many at first; boil or bake it for 6 minutes or less, depending on its size, and treat it like an artichoke heart.

summary.text:
The forest cabbage tree, tī ngahere, is a shrub or small tree endemic to New Zealand.
In New Zealand it is common throughout the North Island and widespread through the northern half of the South Island, reaching about Haast in the west, with occasional unconfirmed reports from coastal Fiordland; in shrubland it grows with Cordyline pumilio and often hybridises with it.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Mostly open disturbed areas, especially poor pastures, scrub and forest margins, stony river beds, roadsides, tracksides.
On the West Coast of the South Island it grows up to about 1000 m.
On the national wetland plant list it is an obligate upland plant: almost always on dry ground, rarely in wetlands.

identification.text:
Biennial or short-lived perennial. Basal rosette giving rise to densely hairy simple stems to about 2.5 m high. Petiole long and winged; upper stem leaves with much shorter petioles. Lamina 10–25 × 3.5–12 cm, lanceolate to elliptic or ovate, hairy to glabrate above, more or less grey-tomentulose with crisped hairs beneath, crenate or crenulate; base cuneate to attenuate. Racemes to about 60 cm long, with many nodding flowers. Bracts lanceolate, shortly glandular-hairy, decreasing in size upwards, longer than pedicels; pedicels tomentulose, 5–15 mm long. Calyx 8–17 mm long, shortly glandular-hairy, deeply lobed; lobes imbricate, ovate, obtuse or acute. Corolla mostly 3.5–5 cm long; tube campanulate and inflated above constricted base, usually pinkish purple with dark purple white-ringed spots in lower part, sometimes pure white, glabrous; lobes short and rounded. Stamens included. Capsule 10–15 mm long, ovoid. Seeds oblong, alveolate, truncate. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Before it flowers it is a rosette of hairy leaves (grey-felted beneath) with scalloped edges, the base narrowing into a winged stalk. White-flowered plants are often found among the purple ones. It flowers from October to January. In its first year it grows only the rosette, which stays green through winter; the flower spike rises from it the next spring. On wild plants the flowers hang along one side of the spike; garden strains may carry them all round it, and are also sold in white and apricot.

lookalikes.howToTell: Broad-leaved dock's leaves are hairless above, with smooth, slightly wavy edges and a heart-shaped to rounded base, and each leaf stalk is wrapped at its base by a papery sheath (ochrea); foxglove's are hairy (sometimes almost hairless above), grey-felted beneath, with scalloped edges and a base that narrows into a winged stalk.
lookalikes.name: Broad-leaved dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Curled dock's leaves are smooth (finely downy only on the midrib near the base beneath), with strongly wavy, curled edges, and each leaf stalk is wrapped at its base by a papery sheath (ochrea); foxglove's are hairy (sometimes almost hairless above), grey-felted beneath, with scalloped edges. Both narrow into the stalk.
lookalikes.name: Curled dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Lesser burdock's basal leaves are broadly triangular, 25–40 cm long (15–55) and 13–30 cm wide, with a heart-shaped base and a hollow stalk; foxglove's are lance-shaped to oval, 10–25 cm long and 3.5–12 cm wide, narrowing gradually into a long, winged stalk. Both are felted beneath and have scalloped edges, so those don't separate them. Foxglove flowers from October to January in a tall spike of hanging bells; burdock flowers from January to April in thistle-like heads that become burs.
lookalikes.name: Lesser burdock

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mullein's rosette leaves are covered all over in greyish or white star-shaped hairs that stay woolly, on top as well as underneath, and are only shortly stalked; foxglove's are hairy to almost hairless on top, grey-felted underneath, and narrow into a long, winged stalk. Both have finely scalloped edges, their leaf sizes overlap, and both grow on poor pastures, stony river beds and roadsides, so none of those tells them apart. Mullein flowers in a dense, woolly spike of flat yellow flowers 1.5–2.5 cm (rarely 3 cm) across; foxglove in a spike of nodding pinkish-purple or white bells. Mullein's leaves and flowers are made into tea, strained of their irritating hairs; its seeds are not eaten.
lookalikes.name: Common mullein

lookalikes.howToTell: Clustered dock is hairless all over; its lower leaves are oblong, 1–3.5 cm wide, with often wavy, curled edges and a broadly wedge-shaped, rounded or heart-shaped base, and each leaf stalk is wrapped at its base by a papery sheath (ochrea). Foxglove's leaves are 3.5–12 cm wide, hairy (sometimes almost hairless above) and grey-felted beneath, with scalloped edges, narrowing into a long winged stalk, on densely hairy stems.
lookalikes.name: Clustered dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Fiddle dock's lower leaves have two large rounded lobes at the base and are pinched in above them like a fiddle (occasionally plain and oblong), flat, finely downy beneath only towards the base, and each leaf stalk is wrapped at its base by a papery sheath (ochrea); foxglove's are lance-shaped to oval, hairy (sometimes almost hairless above) and grey-felted beneath, with scalloped edges, narrowing into a long winged stalk.
lookalikes.name: Fiddle dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Foxglove's leaves are hairy (sometimes almost hairless) above and grey-felted beneath with crisped hairs; rough comfrey's are very scabrid, the upper side densely covered with rigid, bulbous-based hairs. The description of rough comfrey gives no underside character, and the thick leaves of comfrey and foxglove are very difficult to tell apart in spring, so the leaves alone do not separate them. The flowers do: foxglove's hang in a raceme to about 60 cm long, the corolla mostly 3.5–5 cm long, usually pinkish purple with dark white-ringed spots, sometimes pure white; rough comfrey's are in clusters (cymes), 12–17 mm long, light purple or purplish blue at first, becoming blue.
lookalikes.name: Rough comfrey

summary.text:
Foxglove is native to western Europe and Morocco and was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1867. It is a serious weed and one of the commonest naturalised plants in the wetter parts of the country, and it is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds. It was once grown in New Zealand as a source of the drug digitalin; its leaves are the source of digitoxin, still used for heart failure. It is still sold here by seed companies and nurseries as a garden flower, and it self-seeds freely. The genus name comes from the Latin digitus, finger, for the shape of the flowers, and purpurea means purple. It is now placed in the plantain family (Plantaginaceae); older New Zealand books put it in the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae).
In New Zealand it is very widespread on the North, South and Stewart Islands, but often absent from drier areas, and it is abundant on the West Coast of the South Island (Flora of New Zealand, restated).

warnings: Every part of this widespread weed and garden plant is very poisonous, to people and to some animals. The leaves, flowers and seeds contain cardiac glycosides (digitoxin and digoxin) that cause a slow pulse, nausea, vomiting and an irregular heartbeat, and can stop the heart.
Its leaves have been eaten by mistake for edible greens: in Italy a woman needed cardiac intensive care after eating a homemade pie made with five foxglove leaves sold to her as borage.
Before the flower spike appears, the rosettes can look like dock, burdock and common mullein.

identification.text:
Much-branched, usually evergreen shrub up to 2.5 m high; twigs villous, particularly when young, round and ribbed. Leaves usually sparsely to densely clothed in appressed hairs on both surfaces, sometimes subglabrous above, petiolate, 3-foliolate; leaflets shortly petiolulate, obovate, acute to obtuse and shortly mucronate, 7–20–(30) × (3)–4–10–(12) mm; terminal leaflet larger than lateral leaflets; stipules triangular to lanceolate, up to 2.5 mm long. Inflorescence a cluster, with axis shorter than 10 mm long, of 4–7 flowers, terminating short lateral branches; pedicels about 3 mm long. Calyx densely hairy, bilabiate; upper lip deeply 2-fid; lower lip shortly 3-lobed. Corolla yellow to golden yellow, 9–13 mm long; standard glabrous. Pod densely villous, oblong, 3–6-seeded, about 18–20 mm long; seeds green to black, ellipsoid or orbicular, flattened, about 2.5 mm diameter.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Teline monspessulana (L.) K.Koch]
Reduced forms of Montpellier broom with smaller leaves and fewer and smaller flowers sometimes occur in very dry situations.
It flowers from May to November. Older stems are ridged, woody and grey-brown. Ripe pods turn dark brown to black, and once they have burst open they twist into a coil.

lookalikes.howToTell: Sweet broom's flowers are in elongated racemes at the ends of the shoots, 10–30 or more on a stalk 10–130 mm long, and are 13–18 mm long; Montpellier broom's are in clusters of 4–7 at the ends of short side branches, on a stalk under 10 mm long, and are 9–13 mm long. Sweet broom can grow into a small tree up to 6 m high; Montpellier broom is a shrub up to 2.5 m. Both have leaves of three leaflets, and their hairiness overlaps, so leaves do not separate them. Plants with shorter, fewer-flowered racemes (stalk about 10–30 mm) are naturalised here; they may be the garden hybrid Cytisus × spachianus or hybrids between the two, and in hybrids the cluster stalk can reach about 4 cm, so a plant in between cannot be named from its flowers. Neither is eaten.
lookalikes.name: Sweet broom

lookalikes.howToTell: Gorse is sharply spiny: on a grown plant the leaves are reduced to spines, the main ones rigid, furrowed and 15–30 mm long. Montpellier broom has no spines, and its leaves have three leaflets all its life. Gorse's flowers are single, 13–20 mm long; Montpellier broom's are 9–13 mm long, in clusters of 4–7 at the ends of short side branches. Gorse seedlings have leaves of three hairy leaflets, so a seedling's leaves do not separate it from broom. Both grow in scrub, waste places and coastal places.
lookalikes.name: Gorse

lookalikes.howToTell: Scotch broom's twigs are green and more or less five-angled, it loses its leaves, and its flowers are single or paired in the leaf angles, 16–25 mm long, with a hairless calyx; its pods are black, 15–60 mm long, hairy only along the edges. Montpellier broom's twigs are round and ribbed, it is usually evergreen, and its flowers are 9–13 mm long in clusters of 4–7 at the ends of short side branches, with a densely hairy calyx; its pods are densely hairy all over, about 18–20 mm long. Both have leaves of three leaflets and yellow pea flowers, and grow in waste places and scrub.

summary.text:
Genista monspessulana, commonly known as French broom, Montpellier broom, or Cape broom (Australia), is a woody leguminous perennial shrub. It is native to the Mediterranean, Asia Minor and the Azores. While it may still be commonly sold in some garden stores, it is considered an invasive plant in most places where it has been introduced.
G. monspessulana and related plants are common in European shrublands.
In New Zealand: locally common throughout the North Island, and throughout the South Island except Westland; naturalised by 1872. The species has been previously known in New Zealand as Cytisus monspessulanus or C. candicans; early records of C. capensis are also referable to T. monspessulana.
Its pods burst open explosively on warm days, throwing the seed.
The plant begins seed production once it reaches a height of approximately 40 cm, and each plant can live for 10–20 years. One mature plant can produce 10,000 seeds per season. The generous seed production and the plant's ability to re-sprout after cutting or burning help it to invade new habitat vigorously when introduced.
It was brought to New Zealand as an ornamental. Other English names for it are Canary broom and soft broom.
It first flowers when about two years old. The bursting pods throw seed 1–5 m from the plant, and the seed is carried further by machinery, moving soil and water, and by ants and birds. The seeds are hard-coated and can stay alive in the soil for more than 20 years; fire and soil disturbance set off mass germination of this seed bank.
As a legume it fixes nitrogen. On gumland and other poor soils the extra nitrogen can let forest plants or further weeds crowd out the specialised orchids, ferns and herbs that grow there.
In South Africa, where it is not yet a major invader, soil under established stands held 909 to 22,727 seeds per square metre (median 1,970), and 60% of plants resprouted after being cut and their stumps treated with herbicide.
It is considered toxic to stock that graze it heavily, but no cases of poisoning have been reported in Australia.

warnings: French broom flowers, and perhaps all parts, are toxic.
French broom foliage and seeds contain a variety of quinolizidine alkaloids, especially in young leaves.
The leaves and seeds contain alkaloids which are poisonous to many large domestic animals.

It is a pest plant in New Zealand: it is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and the regional pest management plans of Auckland, Gisborne, Manawatū-Whanganui, Canterbury, Otago and the Chatham Islands name it.

edibleParts.text: The aerial parts and leaves, as a flavouring and in drinks. In Morocco the aerial parts are drunk; in Algeria they are boiled beneath couscous as it steams, to scent it; in Spain the aerial part is used to make a liqueur, and the leaves to season olives. Each use is recorded from a single area, by few people, and the main databases of useful plants list no edible use for this species.
