identification.text:
Bushy shrub to about 1 m high, often grey and with stellate tomentum, strongly aromatic. Leaves sessile, linear to narrow-oblong, sometimes revolute, mostly 2–3 cm long, pinnate with obtuse leaflets to pinnatifid or crenulate, with scattered simple hairs in the stellate tomentum. Peduncle to 30 cm long, much longer than spike; spike 3–4.5 cm long, broad-cylindric, dense. Fertile bracts 7–11 mm long, broad-ovate, apiculate, purplish; sterile apical bracts 7–10 mm long, ovate, ovate-lanceolate, to nearly elliptic, mauve-blue. Calyx 5–7 mm long, tubular, more or less tomentose outside; dorsal appendage broadly reniform to suborbicular, more or less mucronate. Corolla 8–10 mm long; tube longer than calyx by about 2 mm; limb mauve, somewhat irregular; lobes 1.5–2.5 mm long. Nutlets about 1.5 mm long, oblong, not mucilaginous when wet.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is distinguished from all other species in section Stoechas by its pinnate or toothed leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: French lavender's leaves are toothed or cut along the edges (pinnate-dentate), much less commonly only scalloped; topped lavender's leaves are entire. French lavender's flowers are mauve; topped lavender's are dark purple. French lavender's flower stalk, up to 30 cm, is much longer than its spike; topped lavender's is about as long as its spike. The sterile bracts crowning the spike are 7–10 mm long in French lavender, 1–2 cm in topped lavender. Wetted, topped lavender's nutlets turn mucilaginous; French lavender's do not. Leaves that are often grey with star-shaped hairs, a strong aromatic smell and a crown of sterile bracts on the spike do not separate them: both belong to the same section of the genus.

summary.text:
Lavandula dentata, the fringed lavender or French lavender, is a species of flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae, native to the Mediterranean, Macaronesia and north-eastern Africa (Flora of New Zealand).
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: naturalised around old house sites in 2 former settlements on Rangitoto Island. Toothed lavender is a very common cultigen in lowland areas of the North Island and northern parts of the South Island. The common name French lavender is sometimes wrongly applied to this species; it should be reserved for L. stoechas.
Other names: toothed lavender (Flora of New Zealand Online, NZPCN); fringed lavender (Wikipedia).

warnings: No toxicity study of this plant in people or other mammals was found. Its essential oil contains camphor, at 15.62% to 49.75% in Moroccan samples, and in some plants is mostly 1,8-cineole; its make-up varies widely between plants.

edibleParts.text: Leaves - raw or cooked. A very mild flavour with a mucilaginous texture, they make a very acceptable part of a mixed salad, or a good filling for a salad sandwich, though they are somewhat boring on their own. The cooked leaf has a rather slimy texture. Seed - raw. Best used before it is fully mature, the seed has a pleasant nutty taste but it is rather small and fiddly to harvest.

identification.text:
Annual or short-lived perennial, procumbent, ascending or erect herb. Stems sparsely to moderately hairy with usually simple hairs. Leaves glabrous to sparsely hairy with usually simple hairs and rarely stellate hairs above, sparsely to moderately hairy below, reniform to orbicular, obtuse to cordate at base, shallowly or moderately 5–7-palmately lobed and crenate, 1–10–(15) cm diameter; petioles 1–20–(30) cm long; stipules broadly ovate with acute apex, 2–8 mm long. Flowers in axillary clusters of (1)–2–6; fruiting pedicels 2–10–(15) mm long; epicalyx segments narrowly ovate-oblong to broadly ovate, more or less equal to calyx at flowering; calyx teeth broadly ovate-triangular, sparsely hairy with simple or stellate hairs and ciliate on teeth but lower tube more or less glabrous, slightly enlarged at fruiting; petals pale lilac or pink with darker veins and tips, about 2× length of calyx, 6–10 mm long. Mericarps 8–9–(10) per fruit, often hairy when immature but usually becoming glabrous, strongly reticulately veined on back; edges sharply angled but not winged.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
New Zealand material has petals shorter than the 10–12 mm given in European Floras, possibly indicating that plants have come from the eastern part of the species' range. M. nicaeensis is distinguished from small forms of M. sylvestris by the glabrous base of the calyx tube, from M. neglecta by the strongly reticulately veined mericarps, and from M. parviflora by the squared edges of the mericarps and longer petals.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. They are separated by the edges of the fruit segments (squared in French mallow, slightly winged in cheeseweed mallow) and French mallow's longer petals. Both have strongly net-veined fruit, so the veining does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. French mallow is separated from small forms of common mallow by the hairless base of the calyx tube (hairy in common mallow); common mallow also has slightly longer petals and longer fruiting stalks. Both have strongly net-veined fruit segments, so the veining does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. The fruit separates them: strongly net-veined on the back in French mallow, smooth or faintly veined (and hairy) in dwarf mallow. Petal lengths overlap (6–10 mm against (7–)8–15 mm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and are unchanged in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.

preparation.text: They make an excellent garnish when chopped and fried in olive-oil with onions and spices. A particularly famous preparation are the Khubeza patties. In Villarino de los Aires (Salamanca, Spain) the green, unripe fruits are eaten raw.

recipes.method: Written for mallow in general; the page names no species. The author was told by Turkish cooks that large mallow leaves are used as wrappers for dolma, and went looking for the biggest-leaved mallows they could find. Serves 8. Large mallow leaves, about 240 ml short- or medium-grain rice (not long-grain, which sets hard when cold), about 240 ml water, ½ onion, finely chopped, about 225 g fresh mushrooms, finely chopped, about 80 ml pesto, 3 tbsp (45 ml) olive oil, and salt. Prepare the leaves as you would grape leaves: boil them in salted water for a minute or two, cool them in iced water, and let them drip dry. Heat a large frying pan over high heat, add the mushrooms and shake the pan often until they give up their water. When most of it has gone, add the onion, oil and a little salt and fry until the onion starts to colour. Add the rice, toast it for a minute, then add about 240 ml water and a little salt, turn the heat to medium and cook until the water is absorbed. Take off the heat, let the rice cool, and stir in the pesto (with a little more oil if the pesto is dry). Lay a leaf smooth side down, base towards you, and put about a tablespoon of filling in a short log across the bottom, leaving at least 1 cm clear at each side. Fold the bottom up once, fold in the sides and roll up; leaves vary in size, so adjust the filling to suit. Pack the rolls seam side down and snug together in a steamer insert or on the bottom of a large pot, up to three layers deep; mallow rolls do not need weighing down. Add water to just below the rolls, cover, bring to the boil and steam gently for 40 minutes to an hour, until the rice is no longer crunchy. Serve warm or at room temperature; they keep a week in the fridge.

summary.text:
French mallow, Malva nicaeensis, is an annual or short-lived perennial herb of the mallow family (Malvaceae), native from the Mediterranean to western Asia.
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North Island and in Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury and North Otago. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1957, though Flora of New Zealand says it was present much longer and had been confused with other mallows.

identification.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Deciduous, erect shrub to about 1.5 m high, densely suckering and forming low thickets; stems many, sometimes with glandular hairs; armature of occasional, narrow, almost straight prickles and more abundant acicles. Leaves with 2-3 pairs of leaflets; petiole 20-55 mm long, usually with eglandular hairs, often with glandular hairs also, sometimes glabrate; stipules […] glabrous or with a few eglandular hairs, with numerous marginal glandular hairs. Lamina of leaflets (15)-25-60 × (10)-15-35 mm, broadly elliptic, glabrous and usually deep green and slightly shining above, hairy on lower part of midrib and veins beneath, otherwise glabrous, somewhat rugose; margins 1-2-serrate, with glandular hairs; base rounded or slightly subcordate; apex rounded or obtuse to acute. Flowers 1-3, double, 50-90 mm diameter, fragrant; pedicels usually with numerous glandular hairs and some acicles, occasionally glabrate. Sepals ovate, acute to long-acuminate, tomentose inside, with few to numerous small glandular hairs outside; outer sepals pinnatifid to pinnatisect with linear lobes. Petals about 20-30 mm long, broadly obovate, rose, crimson or purplish rose. Styles free, slightly exserted, hairy. Fruit not seen.
The double or semi-double flowers are 5–7 cm across, and fruit is not formed or only sparingly. Glandular hairs on the young shoots, flower stalks and calyx are never so dense that they look mossy.
The apothecary rose ('Officinalis') has spreading thorny stems to about 1 m. Its leathery, oval to elliptic leaflets are smooth and dull green above and hairier beneath. The strongly scented, semi-double, rose-pink to light red flowers are borne singly or two to four together.

preparation.text: Scatter the petals over salads as a garnish, make them into jam, crystallise them or preserve them in syrup, or dry them to flavour tea, drinks and cakes. Rose water is made by cold-infusing the petals. Pick freshly opened flowers early in the morning and pluck the petals, removing leaves, insects and debris. For drying, pick on a dry day before the flowers are fully open, remove the stamens and dry the petals quickly so they keep their colour and scent; store them in a tin and use within four months. The white base of each petal is slightly bitter and is traditionally trimmed off. Petals contain no pectin, so jam needs added pectin. Rose water can also be made by simmering the petals until their colour fades. Sugared petals keep in the freezer.

recipes.method: Written for apothecary roses (Rosa gallica) and 'Charles de Mills'. Ingredients: 4 cups (1 litre) rose petals, cleaned and pressed down into the cup; 4 cups (1 litre) sugar; 2 cups (500 ml) cold water; juice of 2 lemons; 1 envelope liquid pectin; 2 tablespoons (30 ml) rose water, optional. Put the petals in a large bowl, mix in the sugar by hand, cover tightly and leave in a cool spot for 4 hours so the petals sweat. Tip into a large saucepan, add the water and stir until the sugar dissolves, then add the lemon juice. Heat over medium heat until it boils (about 10 minutes), stirring so it does not scorch, and boil for 1 minute. Add the liquid pectin, return to a rapid boil for 2 minutes and test the set; take off the heat when it gels and stir in the rose water if using. Skim off foam, ladle into clean half-pint (about 250 ml) jars leaving about 6 mm (1/4 inch) headspace, seal, and process in a water-bath canner for 10 minutes plus the altitude adjustment. The source gives the yield as 5 half-pint jars in the text but says 7 jars in the method. For jelly, strain through cheesecloth before adding the pectin.
recipes.title: Rose petal jam

recipes.method: Written with apothecary rose petals. Ingredients: 1 pasteurised egg white beaten with a little water (or simple syrup, or prepared meringue powder); granulated sugar; fragrant, unsprayed rose petals, rinsed and patted dry; a small watercolour brush. Cut off and discard the white base of each petal, which is bitter. Paint both sides of each petal with the egg wash, sprinkle both sides with sugar, and leave on baking or wax paper to dry overnight. Petals done with syrup hold their shape less well than with egg wash. Use as decorations on cakes, puddings, sweets, biscuits and pastries; store in the freezer if not using straight away.
recipes.title: Sugared rose petals

recipes.method: Written with apothecary rose petals. Ingredients: fragrant, unsprayed rose petals, rinsed and patted dry; sugar; a clean jar with a seal. Cut off and discard the white base of each petal. Sprinkle sugar over the bottom of the jar, then a layer of petals, and keep layering sugar and petals until the jar is full. Store in a cool, dark cupboard for several weeks; remove the petals before use if you like. Use to flavour or top pastries, biscuits and sweets, stir into tea or lemonade, or sprinkle over scones and shortbread.
recipes.title: Rose sugar

recipes.method: Written for unsprayed garden roses generally (damask roses suggested), not for this species. Ingredients: 1/2 cup (125 ml) fresh rose petals; 1–1 1/2 cups (250–375 ml) water. Pick the roses early in the morning. Put the petals in a saucepan, pour the water over, cover and bring to the boil, then simmer until the colour fades from the petals. Leave covered to cool completely, strain through cheesecloth or a fine strainer into a dark bottle, and keep in the fridge for up to several weeks. Use in cakes and biscuits or add to herbal tea.

summary.text:
Rosa gallica, the Gallic rose, French rose, or rose of Provins, is a species of flowering plant in the rose family, native to southern and central Europe eastwards to Turkey and the Caucasus.
R. gallica was one of the principal shrub roses cultivated by the early European settlers and soon became popular with Maori people also. Its suckering habit meant that it was easy to propagate. Several cultivars were grown; all those that have persisted and have been collected wild have fragrant, rather stiffly erect, flattened and double flowers and rarely form hips, even in cultivation. By far the commonest cultivars now wild are 'Charles de Mills', with crimson petals when first expanded, and 'Anais Segales' with purple-crimson petals from early anthesis. 'Officinalis' and 'Antonia d'Ormois' have also been recorded wild.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: North Auckland, Auckland; South Island: Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago. It is almost certainly more widely distributed than indicated above.
Rosa gallica was one of the first species of rose to be cultivated in central Europe.
It was naturalised in New Zealand by 1966. Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and wild, with herbarium records from Canterbury and North Auckland. It is one of the parents of the cabbage rose and the moss rose.
Its cultivar 'Officinalis' is the apothecary rose, also called the Red Rose of Lancaster and Old Red Damask; it was International Herb of the Year in 2012 and is sold by New Zealand rose nurseries.

warnings: Use petals only from roses that have not been sprayed. Florist roses, and roses sprayed with pesticides or fungicides, are not safe to eat.
If hips are found, the layer of hairs around the seeds just beneath the flesh irritates the mouth and digestive tract; remove it before eating.
Rose thorns can cause an infection in some people if they scratch the skin or break off in it.

identification.text:
A stout-stemmed climber that sprawls over the ground or climbs trees, with long aerial roots hanging from the stems. The leaves are large, leathery, glossy and dark green, 25–90 cm long and 25–75 cm wide, deeply split from the edge and pierced with holes between the edge and the midrib; young plants have smaller, whole leaves without holes. The tiny flowers are crowded on a thick cream spike (spadix), hooded by a white bract (spathe) up to 30 cm long.
The fruit is the spike swollen into a green cob up to about 25 cm long and 3–5 cm across, covered in hexagonal scales. It takes more than a year to ripen: the lowest scales turn yellow and lift first, the scales then fall away from the base upwards to show soft cream flesh, and the fruit gives off a strong sweet smell of banana and pineapple.

preparation.text: Pick the fruit when its lowest scales start to yellow and lift and it begins to smell sweet, then stand it upright in a jar or wrap it in a paper bag at room temperature. It ripens from the base up over several days: each day, brush off the scales that come away easily, cut the exposed flesh from the hard core and eat it, and leave the rest to ripen. Brush away the black fibres between the segments; a little citrus juice helps. Try a fingernail-sized piece first and wait ten minutes: if your mouth stings or burns, that part is not ripe yet.

recipes.method: 450 g ripe fruit flesh, cut from the core; 100 g sugar; 2 tbsp lemon juice; a pinch of salt. Makes about 500 ml. Chill a few metal spoons in the freezer. Cut the flesh into large chunks, leaving out any badly bruised pieces. Put the fruit, sugar, lemon juice and salt in a heavy 2–3 litre pan over medium heat and mash roughly. Bring to the boil and keep boiling, stirring often, for about 20 minutes, until thick; skim off any black seeds that rise. To test, drip a little onto a chilled spoon and run a finger through it: if the track stays, it is ready. Spoon into two clean 250 ml jars, cool, seal and keep in the fridge for up to three weeks. No pectin is needed.

summary.text:
A large climber of the arum family from the tropical forests of southern Mexico to Panama, grown in New Zealand as a garden and house plant and also called monstera, Swiss-cheese plant or cheese plant. It has escaped mainly from dumped garden waste and spreads by pieces of stem, including stems carried downstream by floods; seed is occasionally set, and small plants near some colonies may be seedlings. It is often found as a long-lived relic where a garden once stood.
Wild plants are recorded mostly from Northland and Auckland, including Great Barrier and Little Barrier Islands (the first wild collection, 1978), and from New Plymouth; a Whanganui plant from garden waste did not persist. Cold keeps it to mild, frost-free places. It is not regarded as a serious weed, but in Auckland's Mount Eden rock forest dense patches stop native seedlings from coming up and it climbs into the trees.

warnings: Eat only fully ripe fruit, where the scales have come away by themselves. Unripe fruit and every other part of the plant hold needle-like calcium oxalate crystals that cause immediate burning pain and swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue and throat. Get urgent medical help if the lips or tongue swell, or if breathing or swallowing becomes hard.
Even ripe fruit can cause a quick, itchy, swollen rash (hives) in some people, and some find irritating crystals left in the ripe pulp.
The sap of the leaves and stems can irritate the skin.

identification.text:
Gynodioecious, deciduous shrub or small tree, more or less erect and bushy or lianoid; trunk to about 20 cm thick when of tree form; bark more or less peeling. Branchlets hairy when young. Petioles slender, often filiform, 0.5–5.5 cm long, more or less hairy, particularly on upper side. Lamina (2)–3–8–(10) × (1)–2–4 cm, usually ovate to broad-ovate or ovate-oblong, less commonly suborbicular, elliptic or lanceolate-ovate, green above, glaucous or silvery beneath, often suffused with red or purple; midrib and sometimes main lateral veins hairy beneath; base usually broad-cuneate, truncate or rounded, occasionally subcordate; apex rounded to obtuse and mucronate, or acute to acuminate. Flowers solitary or few in clusters, on young shoots or more or less cauliflorous, usually pendulous; pedicels 7–15 mm long, filiform. Floral tube 8–20 mm long, more or less purple. Sepals 6–14 mm long, narrow-triangular, green or purplish, eventually more or less reflexed. Petals 1–5 mm long, dark purple, elliptic. Stamens of ☿ flowers well-exserted; filaments 6–10 mm long, more or less purple. Style 1.7–3.5 cm long, much longer than stamens; stigma capitate. Berry about 10 mm long, ellipsoid-oblong, dark purple or almost black.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
A shrub, much-branched from the base; branchlets slender, sometimes scandent; leaves ovate to orbicular, usually less than 5 cm long. Plants are intermediate in size and habit between tree fuchsia and scrambling fuchsia.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the trunk and branching: tree fuchsia is a tree with a distinct trunk, to about 12 m high with a trunk to 60 cm thick, and keeps its trunked form even when it is much reduced in exposed places; Fuchsia ×colensoi is a shrub much-branched from the base, with slender branchlets that sometimes climb, or a small tree with a trunk to about 20 cm thick. Look at the leaves: tree fuchsia's are usually lance-shaped to narrowly egg-shaped or oblong, usually more than 5 cm long, with a pointed to drawn-out tip; Fuchsia ×colensoi's are usually egg-shaped to broadly egg-shaped or oblong-egg-shaped, less often almost round, usually less than 5 cm long, with a rounded to blunt tip ending in a short point, or a pointed to drawn-out one. Leaf size and shape overlap (tree fuchsia 2–14 cm long, sometimes 1.5 cm; Fuchsia ×colensoi 3–8 cm, sometimes 2 cm or 10 cm, and both can have oblong-egg-shaped leaves), and tree fuchsia has smaller leaves in exposed places, so leaves alone do not separate them. Flowers and berries do not separate them: the floral tube (tree fuchsia 7–20 mm, Fuchsia ×colensoi 8–20 mm), the sepals (5–16 mm against 6–14 mm) and the berries (both about 10 mm long, ellipsoid-oblong, dark purple to almost black) overlap. Fuchsia ×colensoi is intermediate in size and habit between tree fuchsia and scrambling fuchsia, probably their hybrid though this is not confirmed, and in many areas grows with both. Tree fuchsia's ripe berries are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Tree fuchsia

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the main stems: scrambling fuchsia is a liane whose stout main stems, to about 5 m long and 5 cm thick, sprawl when they lack support; Fuchsia ×colensoi is usually a shrub or small tree whose branches may be slender and scrambling but not its main stems, though some plants are lianoid. Without support, both can form a somewhat similar ball-like shrub of interlacing branchlets. Look at the leaves: scrambling fuchsia's are broadly egg-shaped to almost round, usually 25–30 mm long, with a slightly heart-shaped to squared-off base; Fuchsia ×colensoi's are usually egg-shaped to broadly egg-shaped or oblong-egg-shaped, less often almost round, usually 3–8 cm long, with the base usually broadly wedge-shaped, squared-off or rounded, occasionally slightly heart-shaped. Leaf size overlaps (scrambling fuchsia 25–30 mm, sometimes 10 mm; Fuchsia ×colensoi 3–8 cm, sometimes 2 cm or 10 cm), so a plant with small, round leaves may be either. Flowers and berries do not separate them: the floral tube (scrambling fuchsia 7–15 mm, Fuchsia ×colensoi 8–20 mm), the sepals (6–10 mm against 6–14 mm) and the dark purple berries (5–10 mm against about 10 mm) overlap. Fuchsia ×colensoi is intermediate in size and habit between scrambling fuchsia and tree fuchsia, probably their hybrid though this is not confirmed, and in many areas grows with both. No food record written for scrambling fuchsia was found (see its page).

summary.text:
Fuchsia ×colensoi is an endemic New Zealand fuchsia, probably the hybrid of tree fuchsia (Fuchsia excorticata) and scrambling fuchsia (Fuchsia perscandens).
The hybrid nature of F. × colensoi has not been confirmed, but plants are intermediate in size and habit between the putative parents, F. excorticata and F. perscandens. In many areas it occurs with both putative parents, but is also sometimes found where one or both are absent. It is often commoner than F. perscandens but seldom commoner than F. excorticata.
Field evidence makes it almost certain that a number of forms attributed to F. colensoi are the progeny of the cross F. excorticata × perscandens.
It grows on the North Island, locally from the Waikato southwards, throughout much of the South Island, where it is common in many areas, and on Stewart Island. It has also been collected wild in Northland, in a small streamside swamp at Pipiwai.

warnings: Its food record is thin: a plant database and an overseas nursery record the berries as eaten, and no New Zealand record written for this fuchsia was found. That they are harmless also rests on a general record for all New Zealand's native fuchsias.
It often grows with tree fuchsia and scrambling fuchsia and is intermediate between them, so check the trunk, stems and leaves (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
Erect, monoecious annual, sparingly branched, farinose at least when young, sometimes brownish purple or reddish purple. Stems to 2.5 m high, much less in impoverished soil, stout, angular. Leaves below inflorescence (excluding those at base of plant) with petioles to 5 cm long; lamina 5–30 × 3–20 cm, triangular-hastate, ovate, or sagittate-ovate, narrower in inflorescence, irregularly dentate, sinuate, to almost entire; base deeply or shallowly cordate to truncate; apex rounded to acute. Inflorescence terminal, narrow-paniculate, to 40 cm long; branches slender. male flowers: perianth about 0.5 mm long, green with hyaline margin. female flowers: dimorphic, most with 2 bracteoles and perianth 0, otherwise with 5-lobed perianth and bracteoles 0. Bracteoles free, orbicular or suborbicular, very shortly stalked, entire, without appendages or tubercles, strongly accrescent, 6–12–(15) mm diameter at fruiting. Fruit circular to broad-elliptic, flattened, dimorphic: in perianth flowers 1.5–2.5 mm diameter and horizontal, in bracteolate flowers 2.5–4.3 mm diameter and vertical; pericarp removed fairly easily. Testa shining black, almost smooth.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The reddish purple form grows wild alongside the commoner green one, especially in Central Otago.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the habit and the fruit. Garden orache is erect, usually over 75 cm tall, with a stout, rigid, angled main stem; its lower leaves are 5–30 cm long on stalks up to 5 cm, triangular-arrow-shaped or ovate, with a heart-shaped to squared-off base. Common orache is prostrate or spreading, sometimes with an erect main stem but otherwise lax, with ribbed, more or less slender stems and leaves 2–7 cm long, mostly narrowly lance-shaped to elliptic with a wedge-shaped base. In fruit, most of garden orache's female flowers sit between two free, round, untoothed bracteoles with no bumps or appendages, 6–15 mm across; common orache's bracteoles are triangular, joined in their lower part and usually 2.5–8.5 mm long.
lookalikes.name: Common orache

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the habit and the fruit. Garden orache is erect, usually over 75 cm tall, with a stout, rigid, angled main stem; its lower leaves are 5–30 cm long on stalks up to 5 cm. Spear-leaved orache is prostrate or spreading to nearly erect, with more or less slender stems; its lower leaves are 1–9 cm long on slender stalks 1–2.5 cm long, mostly triangular-arrow-shaped and toothed above the basal lobes. In fruit, most of garden orache's female flowers sit between two free, round, untoothed bracteoles with no bumps or appendages, 6–15 mm across; spear-leaved orache's are triangular-arrow-shaped to ovate, usually toothed and generally with appendages, up to 9 mm long. Large-fruited spear-leaved orache can have bigger bracteoles without appendages, so check the habit and leaves too.
lookalikes.name: Spear-leaved orache

preparation.text: Leaves picked before the plant is about 15 cm tall make a mild, tender salad leaf; older leaves are better steamed, stir-fried, added to soups or cooked like spinach, and large ones can be wrapped around a filling. Pinch out the growing tips again and again and eat them as spinach. The taste is salty and spinach-like, and the red forms taste the same as the green but turn a dish pink. Cook it with sorrel to soften sorrel's sourness. Keep the leaves in a bag in the fridge and use them within a few days. Grind the seed into a meal for soups, or mix it with flour for bread; it is small and fiddly to harvest.

recipes.method: Written for red garden orache. Serves 4. 3 bunches of garden orache, red or green; 1 carrot; 1 onion; 100 g rice; 10 black peppercorns; 1–2 eggs; 250–500 ml (1–2 cups) borș (the Romanian fermented wheat-bran liquid), or lemon juice, vinegar or sauerkraut juice to taste instead; salt; a small bunch of fresh lovage; 3 litres water; sour cream, to serve. Finely chop the onion, grate the carrot and cut the orache leaves into thin strips. Put the water and peppercorns in a large pot with the onion, carrot and orache, bring to the boil and simmer for 20 minutes. Add the rice and simmer for 10 minutes more, until it is tender. Heat the borș in a small pan until it just boils, then stir it into the soup a little at a time, tasting, until it is as sour as you like. Whisk the egg and pour it slowly into the boiling soup, stirring all the time, so it sets in ribbons. Season well with salt, turn off the heat and stir in the chopped lovage. Serve hot, with sour cream on the side.
recipes.title: Romanian orache soup (ciorbă de lobodă)

recipes.method: Washed garden orache leaves, on their own or with green lettuce; 1 garlic clove, roughly chopped; a pinch of salt; a scant 5 ml (1 tsp) Dijon mustard; 10 ml (2 tsp) plum jam, or any other jam; 60 ml (4 tbsp) rice wine vinegar; 120 ml (½ cup) extra-virgin olive oil. Blend the garlic, salt, mustard, jam, vinegar and oil until smooth. Dress the leaves with it and add other chopped vegetables if you like.
recipes.title: Garden orache salad with plum jam dressing

recipes.method: About 2 cups of garden orache leaves, washed and roughly chopped; 1 onion, chopped, or garlic instead; 15–30 ml (1–2 tbsp) olive oil; salt and pepper; 2 cups hot cooked pasta, preferably a twisted shape; optional: toasted pine nuts or walnuts, crumbled blue cheese or grated parmesan. Fry the onion in the oil over a moderately high heat until soft. If you are using garlic, add it now, with the orache, salt and pepper, so it does not burn. Cook until the leaves wilt, about 2 minutes. Toss with the hot pasta and any of the extras, and serve.
recipes.title: Pasta with garden orache

recipes.method: 2 tablespoons oil; 1 cup (250 ml) chopped onion; 2–3 cups (500–750 ml) chopped red garden orache; 1 cup (250 ml) rice; 2 garlic cloves, crushed; 2 cups (500 ml) chicken stock or water; 1 teaspoon salt. Fry the onion in the oil until translucent. Add the orache and cook it down, stirring. Add the rice and garlic, with a little more oil if needed to coat the grains, and cook until the rice looks chalky. Add the stock and salt, bring to a simmer, cover and cook about 25 minutes; test, and give it 5 minutes more if needed. Serve as a side dish.
recipes.title: Red orache rice

recipes.method: Serves 4. The large raw leaves stand in for rice-paper wrappers. Quick carrot pickle: 2 tablespoons rice vinegar; 1½ teaspoons sugar; ¼ teaspoon fine salt; 1 medium-large carrot. Sauce: 1 tablespoon peanut butter; 3 tablespoons Thai sweet chilli sauce; about 1 tablespoon rice vinegar; about ¼ teaspoon fine salt. Rolls: 2 bunches bean-thread noodles; 8 large garden orache leaves; a handful of mint leaves; ½ cup (125 ml) cooked, peeled small prawns. Stir the vinegar, sugar and salt together in a wide bowl, cut the carrot into thin sticks and toss them in it. Mix the peanut butter with the chilli sauce, thin with rice vinegar and season with salt. Boil the noodles briefly until tender, drain and rinse in cold water. Cut the thick lower 2–3 cm of midrib out of each orache leaf. Lay each leaf upside down, top it with noodles, carrot, mint and prawns, roll from base to tip and set seam-side down. Serve with the sauce.
recipes.title: Garden orache salad rolls

recipes.method: Translated from Russian (лебеда садовая, garden orache). 100 g garden orache leaves; 2 eggs, hard-boiled; 100 g cooked beetroot; mayonnaise and mustard to taste. Chop the leaves finely, grate the beetroot coarsely and chop the eggs finely. Mix them, dress with mustard and mayonnaise to taste and serve on lettuce leaves.
recipes.title: Garden orache and beetroot salad

recipes.method: Translated from Russian (лебеда садовая, garden orache). 50–70 g plain vermicelli; 700 g garden orache leaves; 100 g butter; 150 g flour; 2 eggs; ham or bacon; grated cheese; salt and pepper; sunflower oil for the dish. Boil the vermicelli and rinse it in cold water in a colander. Boil the orache leaves in salted water for 7–10 minutes, rinse under cold running water and drain well. Melt the butter in a hot pan and fry the flour until golden, then add the vermicelli and orache and stir for 5 minutes. Beat in the eggs, add the ham or bacon, salt and pepper and mix. Spread in an oiled baking dish, top with grated cheese and bake at 150–160 °C until the cheese is golden.
recipes.title: Garden orache, vermicelli and cheese bake

summary.text:
Atriplex hortensis, known as garden orache, red orache or simply orache (also spelled orach), mountain spinach, French spinach, or arrach, is a species of plant in the amaranth family used as a leaf vegetable that was common before spinach; it is still grown as a warm-weather alternative to spinach. It is native to eastern Europe and western and central Asia.
In New Zealand it has been recorded wild since 1958, in Hawke's Bay and Wellington and in Canterbury and Central Otago, mostly near gardens. Herbarium specimens come mainly from Canterbury, with one from Marlborough. It was presumably brought here to eat but is not commonly grown; the reddish purple cultivar 'Rubra' is sometimes grown and has gone wild with the commoner green form. An early New Zealand record of patience dock (Rumex patientia), a European pot herb unknown here, was probably this plant.
New Zealand heritage seed companies sell green and red forms as a leaf vegetable, and the ruby-and-gold cultivar 'Ruby Gold' is sold for flower gardens for its seed heads, which dry well.
hortensis comes from the Latin hortus 'garden' and means growing in gardens.

warnings: Plants grown on fertilised ground can concentrate harmful amounts of nitrate in their leaves.
The seed contains saponins: cook it thoroughly, changing the water once, and do not eat it in large quantities.
The seeds and fruits are purgative and can cause vomiting.
In herbal medicine the leaves are classed as diuretic, emetic and purgative.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous perennial. Stems ascending to erect, sparsely hairy, 10–30 cm long. Leaves (2)–4–8 cm long, with short hairs, with 3–7 crenations each side. Basal leaves ovate, petiolate; stipules pinnatifid. Stem leaves becoming narrow-elliptic, cuneately narrowed to short petiole; stipules pinnatifid, 1/2–3/4 leaf length, with leaflike terminal lobe, and 3–7 linear lateral lobes. Peduncles erect, in axils of upper leaves, glabrous; bracts small, dentate. Flowers 2.5–4 cm diameter. Sepals narrowly-triangular, acute, 10–20 mm long; appendages 4–8 mm long. Petals usually violet, orange, yellow or cream, longer than the sepals, the lowest and lateral bearded; spur 3–6 mm long, equal to or slightly longer than the sepal appendages. Style geniculate at base, 1.5–2 mm long; stigma globose. Capsule ellipsoid, glabrous, 7–12 mm long. Seeds obovoid, pale brown, 2 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In plain terms (restated from the Flora's description and genus key): a short-lived perennial with creeping underground stems, ascending stems up to 30 cm, toothed leaves and deeply divided leaf-like stipules. Its flowers are much larger than those of the wild violets, 2.5–4 cm across, in violet, orange, yellow or cream, often with a dark blotch. Smaller flowers, up to 2.5 cm across, on an annual with no underground stems point to wild pansy.

summary.text: Garden pansy (Viola × wittrockiana), the Flora's 'pansy', is a cultivated hybrid in the violet family (Violaceae) bred partly from heartsease (Viola tricolor); NZPCN dates its naturalisation in New Zealand to 1940. The Flora recorded it only near Tauranga and in Canterbury, most likely persisting from dumped garden waste but establishing from seed in places; iNaturalist research-grade records now run from Auckland to Rakiura and the Chatham Islands. It has also been called Viola tricolor var. hortensis in New Zealand, and Biota of New Zealand lists heartsease, ladies' delight and stepmother's flower among its names. Biota treats New Zealand records of Viola tricolor as recorded in error, most likely garden pansy, and the national plant checklist no longer lists V. tricolor. New Zealand nurseries sell it as an edible flower for pots and borders. It is an exotic species.

identification.text:
Erect, glabrous, aromatic biennial. Stems more or less solid, striate, up to 1 m high. Basal leaves 2–(3)-ternate or pinnate, petiolate; ultimate segments ovate-cuneate, lobed and crenate, crispate in cultivars, c. 10–30 mm long, sessile or petiolulate; stem leaves reduced toward the apex with narrow-oblanceolate, often entire or lobed, but not serrate, segments. Umbels 2–10 cm diameter; rays 7–20; bracts 1–4, entire or 3-lobed; bracteoles 5–12, linear to spathulate, entire or rarely 2–3-lobed. Flowers numerous, greenish yellow, c. 2 mm diameter. Fruit broadly ovoid, 2.5–3 mm long, grey-brown with lighter ribs.
The forms cultivated as a herb are selections of the same species, usually with crispate leaves. Cultivation escapes quickly revert to the wild form.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand; all parts are poisonous if eaten. Look at the flowers: parsley's are greenish yellow, hemlock's white, both about 2 mm across. Look at the stem: parsley's is more or less solid and up to 1 m high; hemlock's is hollow, up to 2–(3) m, and usually spotted or blotched purple, sometimes only tinged purplish or pink, particularly toward the base — the marks may be absent or hard to see on very young plants, so an unmarked stem does not rule hemlock out. Crushed hemlock has a foetid, unpleasant smell; parsley is aromatic. Leaf shape, the bracts under the umbels and the fruit size overlap and do not separate them. Both grow in waste places and forest margins, so place does not rule hemlock out.

preparation.text: Use the leaves as a garnish or flavouring in salads and cooked dishes, fresh or added towards the end of cooking; for most palates the flavour is too strong to eat in quantity, though parsley is the main ingredient of tabbouleh. The stems can go in with the leaves for a stronger flavour. Parsley is part of a bouquet garni and of fines herbes, and it can be blended into herb butter. Picking the leaves regularly encourages fresh growth. The leaves are hard to dry, though dried parsley keeps for up to a year; they freeze easily, chopped in a freezer bag or in ice-cube trays with water. They make a tea, fresh or dried. The stems can be dried and ground to colour food. The roots can go into soups, sauces and roasts. The seeds are strong: use half a teaspoon or less in a tea.

recipes.method: Written for chickweed, nasturtium and onion weed. Soak 500 ml (2 cups) chickpeas overnight, drain and rinse them well, and sprout them for 48 hours, rinsing twice a day, until the tails are as long as the peas; or cook them, as the author also allows. 500 ml (2 cups) sprouted chickpeas; 185 ml (¾ cup) tahini (the author grinds whole sesame seeds instead); 2–4 garlic cloves, minced; the juice of 2 large lemons and 1 orange; 125 ml (½ cup) olive oil; 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt; 5 ml (1 tsp) cumin; a big handful of chickweed, some nasturtium leaves, a small bunch of onion weed leaves and a sprig of parsley or another herb. Process the chickpeas with the citrus juice until still slightly chunky, then add everything else and process to the consistency you want.
recipes.title: Raw chickpea hummus with wild greens

recipes.method: The author's weeds were chickweed, nasturtium, dandelion, pūhā, ox-eye daisy and plantain, with parsley and garden herbs (the page does not say which plantain). She also adds a handful of New Zealand spinach; it is At Risk and its page says to blanch it first, so it is left out here. 5 rosemary sprigs about 12 cm long; a handful of parsley; a big handful of chickweed; 4 large nasturtium leaves; a handful of thyme sprigs 5 cm long; a few dandelion leaves; a small pūhā plant; 10 ox-eye daisy leaves; 8 plantain leaves; 5 sage leaves; 6 garlic cloves; 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt; about 30 ml (⅛ cup) cider vinegar; 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) olive oil, starting with the smaller amount; 5 ml (1 tsp) honey, or to taste; the juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml (½ cup) walnuts. Strip the leaves from the thyme and rosemary and wash any leaves that need it. Blend everything in a high-speed blender or food processor until smooth, pushing it down with the tamper. Keep it in the fridge or freezer.
recipes.title: Wild weed pesto

recipes.method: 185 ml (¾ cup) softened butter; 80 ml (⅓ cup) packed, cut celery leaves; 80 ml (⅓ cup) chopped fresh parsley; 80 ml (⅓ cup) spring onions with their tops; 15 ml (1 tbsp) each fresh sage, thyme and marjoram; 1 ml (¼ tsp) freshly ground black pepper. Blend or process everything together until well mixed. It keeps for a week in the fridge.
recipes.title: Herb butter

recipes.method: Makes about 185 ml (¾ cup). 60 ml (¼ cup) parsley; 45 ml (3 tbsp) red wine vinegar; 4 garlic cloves, minced (about 2½ tbsp); 30 ml (2 tbsp) oregano leaves; 10 ml (2 tsp) crushed red pepper (chilli flakes); salt and black pepper; 125 ml (½ cup) extra virgin olive oil. Process the parsley, vinegar, garlic, oregano and chilli until smooth, and season. Tip it into a bowl, pour the oil over and leave it at least 20 minutes. It can go in the fridge overnight; bring it back to room temperature to serve. It goes with grilled steak, fish and chicken, steamed vegetables and roast meat.
recipes.title: Chimichurri

recipes.method: Makes about 250 ml. 250 ml (1 cup) fresh parsley (any kind; the author prefers curly); 250 ml (1 cup) water; 250 ml (1 cup) sugar. Bring everything to the boil in a saucepan, turn off the heat and stir until the sugar has dissolved. Leave it to steep for 30 minutes, strain out the leaves and pour it into a clean container. It keeps two to three weeks in the fridge, or freeze it. Use it in tea, smoothies and cocktails; the author mixes it with cucumber juice and lime juice over ice.
recipes.title: Parsley syrup

recipes.method: Serves 6. 1.5 litres (6 cups, loosely packed) flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped by hand; 125 ml (½ cup) fine bulgur wheat; 250 ml (1 cup) fresh mint leaves, finely chopped; 450 g ripe tomatoes, seeded and finely diced; 2 cucumbers, seeded and finely diced; 1 small red onion, minced; the juice of 4 lemons; 125 ml (½ cup) extra virgin olive oil; sea salt, black pepper and allspice. Soak the bulgur in the juice of two lemons, without water, for 20 minutes. Wash the parsley whole, dry it completely, then chop it fine with a very sharp knife; a food processor bruises it into a sludge. Salt the tomato and let it drain for 10 minutes. Mix everything with the rest of the lemon juice, the oil, salt, pepper and a pinch of allspice, and rest it for 15 minutes so the bulgur finishes softening. Serve with cos lettuce leaves as scoops.
recipes.title: Tabbouleh

recipes.method: Serves 4. 500 ml (2 cups) flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped and completely dry; 1.1 kg skin-on salmon fillet, portioned; 250 ml (1 cup) panko breadcrumbs; 6 garlic cloves, grated; 2 lemons, zest and juice; 80 ml (⅓ cup) extra virgin olive oil; 30 ml (2 tbsp) Dijon mustard; salt and black pepper. Mix the parsley, panko, garlic, lemon zest, oil, salt and pepper until the mixture clumps when squeezed; wet parsley would steam the crust soft. Pat the salmon dry, season it and brush the top thinly with the mustard. Press the parsley mixture on in a thick, even layer. Roast at 220 °C for 12–14 minutes, until the crust is set and just golden at the edges. Rest it for 3 minutes and finish with lemon juice.
recipes.title: Parsley-crusted salmon

recipes.method: Serves 6. 375 ml (1½ cups) chopped flat-leaf parsley, plus leaves to finish; 1.4 kg baby potatoes, halved; 8 garlic cloves, finely minced; 125 ml (½ cup) olive oil or duck fat; 85 g butter; 125 ml (½ cup) grated parmesan (optional); flaky salt and black pepper. Parboil the potatoes in well-salted water for 8 minutes, drain them and shake them hard in the colander to rough up the edges. Toss them in hot oil on a preheated oven tray and roast at 220 °C for 35 minutes, turning once, until deep gold. Warm the butter with the garlic without letting it sizzle. Tip the potatoes into a bowl, pour the garlic butter over and toss them with the chopped parsley while everything is still very hot; parsley added before roasting turns to bitter black flecks. Finish with salt, pepper, the cheese if using and a last handful of parsley leaves.
recipes.title: Roast potatoes with garlic and parsley

recipes.method: Serves 4. 250 ml (1 cup) finely chopped flat-leaf parsley, plus leaves to finish; 900 g chicken breasts, butterflied and pounded thin; 170 g cold unsalted butter, cubed; 3 lemons, juiced, plus slices; 80 ml (⅓ cup) capers, rinsed; 250 ml (1 cup) dry white wine; 250 ml (1 cup) flour for dredging; olive oil; salt and black pepper. Pound the chicken to an even 6 mm, season it and dredge it lightly in seasoned flour. Sear it in olive oil with a little butter over medium-high heat, 3 minutes a side, until golden, and keep it warm. Deglaze the pan with the wine, scraping, and reduce it by half; add the lemon juice and capers. Off the heat, whisk in the cold butter a cube at a time until the sauce is glossy and thick. Stir in the parsley, chopped at the last moment with a very sharp knife, return the chicken briefly to coat it, and serve with lemon slices and whole parsley leaves.
recipes.title: Chicken piccata with parsley

recipes.method: Serves 4. 375 ml (1½ cups) finely chopped flat-leaf parsley; 900 g large prawns, shell on or peeled; 225 g softened unsalted butter; 10 garlic cloves, minced; 2 lemons, zest and juice; 125 ml (½ cup) dry white wine; a pinch of chilli flakes; salt; grilled sourdough to serve. Mash the butter with two-thirds of the parsley, the garlic, lemon zest, chilli and salt. Pat the prawns dry and sear them in a little oil in a hot, wide pan, 60–90 seconds a side, taking them out just short of done. Lower the heat, deglaze with the wine and reduce it by half. Off the heat, whisk in the parsley butter until the sauce comes together, then return the prawns to warm through. Finish with the lemon juice and the rest of the parsley, and serve with the bread.
recipes.title: Garlic butter prawns with parsley

summary.text: Garden parsley, also called wild parsley (Petroselinum crispum), is an aromatic biennial herb of the carrot family (Apiaceae), probably from south-eastern Europe or western Asia, first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1867. In the North Island it grows in scattered places in Northland and the Bay of Plenty and in Auckland City, and is locally common in Wellington Province, and a 1991 herbarium specimen records it as a very local weed of damp pastures in the Awaroa Valley near Kāwhia; in the South Island it grows in coastal Marlborough, North Canterbury, Christchurch and Banks Peninsula, North Otago and Dunedin, and was collected once from Cobden near Greymouth; it also grows at Halfmoon Bay on Stewart Island. The forms grown as a herb are selections of the same species, usually with curled leaves, and plants that escape from gardens quickly revert to the flat-leaved wild form. It is not a pest plant.

warnings: Hemlock, one of New Zealand's most poisonous plants, is a close relative with similar umbels of tiny flowers, and it grows in the same waste places and forest margins. Before you pick, check the flowers and the stem as described in Lookalikes.

Parsley sap on the skin followed by sunlight can cause phytophotodermatitis: 24–48 hours later the skin turns red and inflamed and often blisters, and dark marks can stay for several years. Vegetable pickers get it on their hands and fingers; gloves prevent it.

Do not use parsley essential oil or concentrated parsley preparations in pregnancy: parsley has a long history of use as an abortifacient, and its apiol and myristicin are reported to cause this. The concern is with concentrated parsley, not the amounts eaten in ordinary food.

Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.
An Unwanted Organism and National Pest Plant Accord species: it must not be sold, propagated, bred or spread anywhere in New Zealand. If you think you have found it, report it to your regional council, which can advise on control.
In the Auckland region you also must not plant it. Auckland Council asks you not to try to control it yourself: report it to pestfree@aucklandcouncil.govt.nz.

identification.text:
Erect biennial. Stems hispid, hollow, grooved, reddish purple blotched and spotted, particularly toward base, up to 350 cm high and 10 cm diameter. Basal leaves moderately hispidulous below, sparsely above, pinnately 3-foliolate, petiolate; leaflets ovate to ovate-lanceolate, deeply ternately or pinnately lobed and irregularly double serrate, up to 50–(100) cm long; lobes usually acute to acuminate; stem leaves similar to basal, with petiole often reduced to sheathing part only; petioles reddish purple blotched and spotted. Umbels (20)–30–60 cm diameter; rays (20)–50–70–(100), the primary umbels more than 50-rayed; bracts usually c. 12, linear, 10–15 mm long; bracteoles 8–12, linear, up to 15 mm long. Flowers numerous, white; outer flowers irregular and up to 15 mm diameter. Fruit glabrous, ovate-elliptic, light brown, c. 10 mm long; vittae conspicuous, 0.5–1 mm wide at base.
Giant hogweed is easily distinguished in the field by its size and flattened seeds with conspicuous oil canals, and further from cow parsnip (H. sphondylium) by the spotted and blotched stems and petioles.
In its first year the big leaves form a rosette at the base; from December to February of its second year it sends up a tall, leafy flowering stalk. The stems carry sturdy bristles that hold the toxic sap.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers: wild parsnip's are yellow, 1–2 mm across; giant hogweed's are white, the outer ones up to 15 mm across. Before either flowers, go by the leaves: wild parsnip's are usually once-pinnate, with about 5–10 pairs of lobed, coarsely toothed leaflets up to 15 cm long; giant hogweed's basal leaves have three deeply lobed leaflets, each up to 50, sometimes 100, cm long. Look at the umbels: wild parsnip's are 3–19 cm across with 7–30 rays and 0–2 bracts 2–4 mm long beneath; giant hogweed's are usually 30–60 cm across (sometimes only 20 cm), its main umbel has more than 50 rays, and it usually has about 12 bracts 10–15 mm long. Giant hogweed's bristly stem, up to 350 cm tall and 10 cm thick, and its leaf stalks are blotched and spotted reddish purple; wild parsnip's stem is finely hairy, grooved and up to 150, sometimes 200, cm tall. Ripe fruit: giant hogweed's is about 10 mm long with conspicuous oil canals 0.5–1 mm wide at the base; wild parsnip's is 4–6 mm long with slender canals. Both grow in wet waste places and along ditches and stream banks, and 'wild parsnip' is also one of giant hogweed's names, so neither place nor name rules giant hogweed out. Wild parsnip's root is eaten, but its sap also burns skin in sunlight (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Wild parsnip

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaves: cow parsley's are 3-pinnate, finely divided into pointed segments 15–50 mm long; giant hogweed's basal leaves have just three broad, deeply lobed leaflets, each up to 50, sometimes 100, cm long. Look under the umbel: giant hogweed usually has about 12 linear bracts 10–15 mm long; cow parsley has few or none. Count the rays: cow parsley's umbels have about 6–15; giant hogweed's main umbel has more than 50. Ripe fruit: cow parsley's is lanceolate, about 6 mm long and smooth; giant hogweed's is flattened, ovate-elliptic and about 10 mm long, with conspicuous oil canals. Look at the stem without touching it: giant hogweed's is bristly and up to 10 cm thick; cow parsley's is finely hairy. Do not rely on height or stem spots: cow parsley grows up to 2 m and its stems and leaf stalks are sometimes spotted maroon, and giant hogweed's are blotched and spotted reddish purple. Both grow along roadsides, in ditches and in waste places, so place does not rule giant hogweed out. Cow parsley's leaves are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Cow parsley

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stem and leaf stalks without touching them: giant hogweed's are blotched and spotted reddish purple, especially towards the base of the stem; common hogweed's are green or tinged reddish brown or purple, and its leaf stalks are usually tinged purple at the base, so look for blotches and spots, not just a purple tinge. Count the rays of the main umbel: common hogweed's has fewer than 30; giant hogweed's has more than 50. Measure the umbels: common hogweed's are 5–20 cm across; giant hogweed's are usually 30–60 cm (sometimes only 20 cm). Common hogweed's stem is 60–150, sometimes 200, cm tall; giant hogweed's grows up to 350 cm tall and 10 cm thick, so a stem over 2 m is giant hogweed, but a shorter one may be either. Common hogweed's leaflets are about 5–20 cm long; giant hogweed's reach 50, sometimes 100, cm. Look under the umbel: common hogweed has 0–7 bracts; giant hogweed usually has about 12. Common hogweed's flowers are white or tinged pink, the outer ones up to 10 mm across; giant hogweed's are white, the outer ones up to 15 mm across. Ripe fruit: common hogweed's is 7–10 mm long with oil canals 0.2–0.5 mm wide at the base; giant hogweed's is about 10 mm long with canals 0.5–1 mm wide. Both grow in waste places and gardens, in the Wellington area, Canterbury and Otago, and 'cow parsnip' is listed as a name of both, so neither place nor name rules giant hogweed out. Neither is food: common hogweed's sap also burns skin in sunlight (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Common hogweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand; all parts are poisonous if eaten. Both are tall plants with hollow stems spotted or blotched purple and white flowers in compound umbels, both flower in December and January, and both grow in waste places and damp ground, so stem spots, season and place do not separate them. Look at the leaves: hemlock's are 2–4-pinnate and fern-like, finely divided into segments 5–40 mm long; giant hogweed's basal leaves have three broad, deeply lobed leaflets, each up to 50, sometimes 100, cm long. Measure the umbels: hemlock's are 1–8 cm across with 4–16 rays; giant hogweed's are usually 30–60 cm across (sometimes only 20 cm), and its main umbel has more than 50 rays. Hemlock's flowers are about 2 mm across; giant hogweed's outer flowers reach 15 mm. Hemlock's stem is hairless and up to 2, rarely 3, m tall; giant hogweed's is bristly, up to 350 cm tall and 10 cm thick — look at it without touching it. Ripe fruit: hemlock's is dark brown and 2.5–3 mm long; giant hogweed's is flattened, light brown and about 10 mm long, with conspicuous oil canals. Neither is food.
lookalikes.name: Hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have white flowers in compound umbels and both grow in waste places. Wild carrot is much smaller: its stem is bristly-hairy, more or less solid and up to 120 cm tall; giant hogweed's is hollow, up to 350 cm tall and 10 cm thick, and blotched and spotted reddish purple — look at it without touching it. Wild carrot's leaves are 2–3-pinnate, divided into segments about 15–40 mm long; giant hogweed's basal leaves have three broad, deeply lobed leaflets, each up to 50, sometimes 100, cm long. Wild carrot's umbels are 2–12 cm across and usually curl concave as they fruit, with numerous bracts divided into narrow linear segments beneath; giant hogweed's are usually 30–60 cm across (sometimes only 20 cm), with about 12 undivided linear bracts. A few central flowers of a wild carrot umbel are sometimes red or purple; giant hogweed's are all white. Ripe fruit: wild carrot's is ovoid, 2.5–3 mm long and spiny; giant hogweed's is flattened, smooth and about 10 mm long, with conspicuous oil canals. Wild carrot carries its own cautions, including hemlock; see its entry.
lookalikes.name: Wild carrot

summary.text:
Giant hogweed (Heracleum mantegazzianum), also called cartwheel flower, wild rhubarb and giant carrot, is a huge, poisonous biennial of the carrot family (Apiaceae) from south-west Asia, naturalised locally in New Zealand.
Probably brought in as an ornamental, it was first recorded wild here in 1968. It grows near Dannevirke, Napier and Wellington City in the North Island and at scattered places in Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago and Southland, mainly in the eastern South Island; in Otago it has been recorded on the coast from Oamaru to the Catlins and in Central Otago. Weedbusters and the Otago Regional Council also list 'wild parsnip' among its names: the plant this app calls wild parsnip is a different species, Pastinaca sativa.
One plant produces up to 50,000 viable seeds, which are carried mostly by water but also by wind and gravity, and can stay dormant in the soil for at least 5 years; people spread it by moving contaminated soil and by planting it. It forms dense colonies that crowd out native plants and grasses, and when it dies down in winter it leaves stream banks bare and open to erosion.
It is an Unwanted Organism and a National Pest Plant Accord species, so it cannot be sold, propagated or distributed anywhere in New Zealand, and it is an Organism of Interest in the Otago Regional Pest Management Plan 2019–2029; Auckland Council also bars planting it in the Auckland region. DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds leaves it out, counting it among the unwanted organisms whose impact is on human health.

warnings: Do not eat or touch any part of giant hogweed. It is poisonous, and it can cause permanent damage if touched or eaten.

Its sap on the skin makes the skin react to sunlight: it burns, swells and blisters, and can leave pigmentation and long-lasting scars, and affected skin may stay sensitive to sunlight for years. Even dust from weed-eating it irritates the skin. Sap in the eyes can cause temporary or permanent blindness.

If you must work near it, wear gloves and eye protection and cover your arms and legs, and do not use a mower or line trimmer on it. Clothing and tools that touch it stay hazardous until cleaned. Wash any skin that touches it straight away, keep it out of the sun and seek medical advice; the National Poisons Centre is on 0800 764 766.

Wild parsnip and cow parsley, which are eaten, can be confused with giant hogweed, and 'wild parsnip' is also one of giant hogweed's own names. Check the leaves, umbels and bracts as described in Lookalikes before touching or picking any large umbellifer.

harvestEthics.text: It is an Unwanted Organism and a National Pest Plant Accord species: anywhere in New Zealand it must not be sold, given away, moved between locations, grown, bred or propagated. In the Waikato it is illegal for anyone but the regional council to remove or disturb it — don't pick it there; report it on 0800 800 401. In Canterbury it is in Environment Canterbury's eradication programme: don't try to control it yourself, and report every sighting to the council. In Tasman and Nelson the regional pest plan's knotweed rule (Asiatic, giant and hybrids) is for eradication, and occupiers must report any sighting to Tasman District Council within five days. Elsewhere, check your regional council's rules first, and carry no living piece anywhere new.

identification.text:
Giant rhizomatous herb forming large thickets; stems glabrous, green, 2–4 m high, about 2 cm diameter, woody at base. Petiole 2–6 cm long, often reddish, channelled above, with 3 pits at base on dorsal side except in some inflorescence leaves. Lamina 10–30–(40) × 5–22–(30) cm, broad- to oblong-ovate, glaucescent below, entire to somewhat undulate, usually glabrous when mature, or sometimes puberulent towards base of veins on upper side, with more than 14 pairs of lateral veins; base shallow- to deep-cordate; sinus wide; apex acute to cuspidate. Ochreae to 6 cm long, glabrous, soon deciduous. Panicle branches solitary or fascicled, at least the lower branches shorter than or equal to the petioles, erect to spreading, densely puberulent. Bracts small, more or less puberulent, acuminate or long-cuspidate. Pedicels 0.5–3 mm long, glabrous, jointed in lower half. Perianth 1–2 mm long at anthesis (excluding basal decurrent wing), white or greenish white; segments broad- or oblong-obovate, keeled. Filaments to about 1.5 mm long. Stigmas fimbriate. Fruit valves prominently winged. Nut not seen. Flowers November–April.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4]
It does not produce mature fruit or seed in New Zealand. Like Japanese knotweed it is deciduous, dying back to the root base in winter.
Told from Japanese knotweed (Reynoutria japonica), with which it is sometimes confused, by its green stems 2–4 m tall, usually 3 pits on the back of the petiole base, and leaves with more than 14 pairs of lateral veins and a usually deeply cordate base. Japanese knotweed has (0.5–)1–2(–2.5) m, more or less glaucous to reddish stems, a single pit at the petiole base, and leaves with fewer than 14 pairs of lateral veins and a truncate or subcordate base.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at a grown leaf: Japanese knotweed's blade is 8–23 cm long with fewer than 14 pairs of side veins, and its base is usually straight across, sometimes shallowly heart-shaped (especially on non-flowering shoots); giant knotweed's is 10–30 (sometimes 40) cm long with more than 14 pairs of side veins, and its base is usually deeply heart-shaped, rarely only shallowly so. Look at the back of the leaf-stalk base: Japanese knotweed has a single pit, giant knotweed usually 3 (some leaves in the flower heads lack them). Japanese knotweed's stems are usually 1–2 m tall (0.5–2.5 m), more or less bluish-grey to reddish; giant knotweed's are 2–4 m tall and green, sometimes reddish-brown. Japanese knotweed's flower-head branches are longer than the leaf stalks; at least the lower branches of giant knotweed's are no longer than them. These tests are on grown leaves and stems. Both grow on roadsides near houses, so place does not separate them, and their hybrid, Bohemian knotweed, is also recorded in New Zealand. Japanese knotweed's young shoots are eaten (see its page), and both are Unwanted Organisms under the same rules.
lookalikes.name: Japanese knotweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at grown mid-stem leaves. Bohemian knotweed's base varies from almost straight to moderately heart-shaped, often on the same plant, and its blade is 5–30 cm long; giant knotweed's base is usually deeply heart-shaped, rarely only shallowly so, and its blade is 10–30 (sometimes 40) cm long. Bohemian knotweed's stems are 2–5 m tall, mottled reddish brown and darker at the nodes; giant knotweed's are 2–4 m tall and green, sometimes reddish-brown. Height, leaf size and stem colour overlap, so these are hints rather than proof: in Canterbury Bohemian knotweed is commonly misidentified as giant knotweed. No food use is given for Bohemian knotweed (see its page), and both are Unwanted Organisms under the same rules.
