summary.text:
The tall, purple-blotched umbellifer that kills people who think they have found fennel, parsley or wild carrot. Every part is poisonous if eaten.
Hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand, and probably the commonest of all the naturalised members of the carrot family (Apiaceae) here. Edible plants that can be confused with it include cultivated and wild carrot, parsnip, fennel and parsley, with potentially fatal results; in New Zealand pasture it is probably most likely to be confused with wild carrot.
Native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, it was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1872. It is very common throughout the North and South Islands, though only occasional on the West Coast of the South Island, and is also recorded at Halfmoon Bay on Stewart Island and on the Chatham Islands.
Most livestock recognise it as poisonous and leave it alone; poisoning is most likely when animals are pushed hard to eat it or after it has been sprayed, which seems to attract them. In the Auckland region it is a pest plant under the Regional Pest Management Plan, set for sustained control. The name maculatum is Latin for 'blotched'.

warnings: Every part — leaf, stem, root, seed — is poisonous if eaten. The poison paralyses the breathing muscles and can kill.
Wear gloves if you pull it, and do not eat with unwashed hands after handling it. Children have died after using the hollow stems as blowpipes, and dead stems stay poisonous for up to three years.
If you suspect any contact with food, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766 immediately.

edibleParts.text: The young leaves and shoots can be eaten raw or cooked, as can the stems and flowers. Henbit dead-nettle has a slightly sweet and peppery flavour, similar to celery. Young leaves are added to salads or used as a potherb. The leaves, stems and flowers can also be made into a tea.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Waste places such as roadsides, railway yards and building sites, also on arable land.
Throughout New Zealand it springs up in parks, pastures, wasteland and home gardens.
In New Zealand it is a common weed of cropping land, especially in the South Island.
It grows into slightly drier places than red deadnettle, which takes a little more shade.

identification.text:
Annual herb with hairy or nearly glabrous, more or less erect stems to about 30 cm, but often shorter than 5 cm high in dry situations. Petioles long and slender. Lamina 5–20 × 5–20 mm, ovate or oblong-ovate, crenate, sometimes more deeply cut, sparsely to moderately clothed in usually more or less appressed hairs; base broad-cuneate, truncate to cordate. Bracts to about 2.5 × 2 cm, very broadly ovate, hairy; base cordate, amplexicaul. Calyx 5–7 mm long, with more or less silky tomentum; teeth linear-subulate, about equal to tube. Corolla about 15 mm long, pinkish purple; tube erect, narrow, long-exserted, glabrous inside; upper lip 3–5 mm long, tomentose outside, with 3 purple blotches inside; lateral lobes of lower lip 0 (sometimes flowers cleistogamous and corolla remaining closed and included in calyx). Nutlets 1.8–2.2 mm long, patterned white, sharply angled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is often found alongside Lamium purpureum (red dead-nettle), for which it is easily mistaken, because the two species bear not only similar leaves, but also similar bright pink to purple flowers. They can, however, be distinguished from one another by the form of the leaves on their respective flowering stems; those of red dead-nettle are petiolate, while those of henbit dead-nettle are sessile.
Some N.Z. populations are almost or completely cleistogamous whilst in other places the flowers are chasmogamous and conspicuous.
In the field: the stem is square and often purplish, and the leaves are aromatic when rubbed. The lower leaves have long stalks and the lower leaf pairs are set wide apart; the upper leaves are stalkless, and a pair can look almost joined into one leaf wrapped round the stem. The leaves have a few deep, rounded teeth and a crinkled surface. The flowers, often with darker spots, come from the top of the stem and usually stand above the highest leaves. After flowering the calyx teeth close up. The lower stems can root at the joints.
Seedlings: the seed leaves are round with a flat tip and a notched base, on stalks.

lookalikes.howToTell: Henbit's bracts — the leaves under the upper flower clusters — are stalkless, broadly ovate and clasp the stem, unlike its lower leaves; red deadnettle's bracts are like its leaves and short-stalked. Henbit's flower tube is long, narrow and hairless inside; red deadnettle's has a conspicuous ring of hairs inside near the base. Henbit's flowers usually stand above its top leaves, which are held upright; red deadnettle's flowers sit under the top few pairs of leaves, which droop and give the stem tip a pagoda-like look. Henbit's leaves have fewer, deeper and blunter teeth. Both grow in the same waste places and crops, and both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Red deadnettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Henbit's bracts — the leaves under the upper flower clusters — are stalkless, broadly ovate and clasp the stem; cut-leaved deadnettle's bracts are like its deeply toothed leaves, with short stalks. Henbit's flower is about 15 mm with a long, narrow tube; cut-leaved deadnettle's is 11–15 mm. Both grow on waste ground and in gardens.
lookalikes.name: Cut-leaved deadnettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Field woundwort's flowers are small — 6–7 mm long, with a small upper lip that is not hooded and is shorter than the lower lip, the tube no longer than the calyx; henbit's are about 15 mm long with a hooded upper lip, on a long, narrow tube. Field woundwort's stem is much hairier. Henbit's leaves among the flowers are stalkless, broad and kidney-shaped, clasp the stem and look unlike its other leaves; field woundwort's are stalkless too, but oblong, oval or nearly round, like its upper leaves — so stalkless leaves alone do not separate them. Both are weeds of gardens, crops and waste places, and young plants are easily confused. Field woundwort poisons livestock (staggers); it is listed as poisonous in New Zealand; some people eat it, but do not.
lookalikes.name: Field woundwort

lookalikes.howToTell: Ground-ivy is a creeping perennial whose stems root at the joints; every leaf, even among the flowers, is on its own slender stalk, and its flowers are blue or blue-violet. Henbit is an annual whose leaves among the flowers have no stalk and clasp the stem; its flowers are pinkish purple, on a long, narrow, upright tube. Both grow on disturbed ground around buildings, and both are eaten. Ground-ivy is local in the southern North Island and the South Island.
lookalikes.name: Ground-ivy

preparation.text: Pick it young and tender: older plants are not harmful but get tough and woody. The hairy leaves put some people off eating them raw. Its flavour has a musty edge, which goes well with mushrooms. To freeze, blanch it as you would kale.

recipes.method: Written for henbit in the United States. About 1 litre (4 cups) of henbit shoots; 45 ml (3 tbsp) butter; 5 ml (1 tsp) curry powder; 2 whole cloves; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground cinnamon; 30 ml (2 tbsp) flour; 185 ml (¾ cup) sour cream. Chop the henbit shoots, cover with water and boil for 10 minutes. In another pan melt the butter with the curry powder, cloves and cinnamon, cook for a minute, stir in the flour and cook a minute more. Whisk in 125 ml (½ cup) of the henbit's cooking water until smooth, then add the drained henbit and the sour cream and cook on low for 15 minutes.
recipes.title: Spicy henbit

recipes.method: Written for henbit. Serves 4. Noodles: about 225 g henbit leaves; 1 garlic clove; 2 eggs; 15 ml (1 tbsp) olive oil; 250 ml (1 cup) plain flour, plus 125 ml (½ cup) for dusting; 185 ml (¾ cup) semolina. Sauce: 250 ml (1 cup) chopped mushrooms; 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter; salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) flour; 250 ml (1 cup) mushroom or other stock; a little thyme; 125 ml (½ cup) light cream; 60 ml (¼ cup) grated parmesan, plus more to serve. Wilt the henbit leaves in 60 ml (¼ cup) water over medium heat, about 5 minutes; drain, cool under cold water and squeeze dry. Purée with the garlic, eggs and olive oil. Mix the 250 ml flour (keep the dusting flour aside) with the semolina, make a well, work in the purée and knead for 10 minutes into a dough that no longer sticks. Rest it under a damp cloth for 30 minutes, roll each quarter thin, roll up loosely and cut into noodles 6–12 mm wide. For the sauce, cook the mushrooms in the butter with salt until their liquid has evaporated, stir in the flour for 2 minutes, then add the stock a splash at a time with the thyme until thick; finish with the cream. Boil the noodles in salted water for 3 minutes, drain, toss with the sauce and the parmesan, and serve with more cheese.
recipes.title: Henbit noodles with mushroom sauce

recipes.method: Written for henbit in Tennessee. Serves about 6. 4 garlic cloves, chopped; 1 onion, chopped; 30 ml (2 tbsp) olive oil; 1.5 litres (6 cups) chicken or vegetable stock; a 440 g can of cannellini beans, drained and rinsed; 250 ml (1 cup) small pasta; 375 ml (1½ cups) chopped henbit; parmesan to serve, if you like. Fry the garlic and onion in the olive oil until translucent, about 10 minutes. Add the stock and bring to the boil, then add the beans and pasta and boil until the pasta is tender, 8–10 minutes. Add the henbit and cook a few minutes until wilted. Season with salt and pepper and serve with parmesan.
recipes.title: Cannellini bean and henbit soup

summary.text:
Lamium amplexicaule, commonly known as henbit dead-nettle, is a species of Lamium native to most of Europe, Asia and northern Africa.
Henbit dead-nettle is native to most of Europe, Asia and North Africa, and has since been spread around the world by human activity.
It is widely naturalised in eastern North and South America, New Zealand, South Africa and Tasmania.
Its status in Great Britain and Ireland is disputed; some sources give it as native, while others cite it as an archaeophyte.
It propagates freely by seed, where it becomes a key part of a meadow ecosystem; sometimes entire fields will be reddish-purple with its flowers before spring ploughing.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1880 and is widespread and common in the North and South Islands.
Besides its open flowers it makes small ones that never open and pollinate themselves, often in the cooler part of the year when few pollinators are about.
It is also called fairy horns: a plucked flower can be blown like a little horn.

warnings: Henbit is listed as poisonous in New Zealand. The poisonings on record are of grazing animals: sheep, and probably cattle and horses, develop staggers — staggering after exercise, stiff hind legs, rapid shallow breathing, shivering and trembling — mostly after grazing cereal stubble holding mature plants.
It is a weed of cropping land, where it is sprayed with herbicides. Pick from ground you know has not been sprayed.

Field woundwort (staggerweed), which poisons livestock, grows in the same places and looks alike when young. Check for henbit's long flower tube and the broad leaves clasping the stem under the flowers; field woundwort's leaves there are stalkless too, but oblong to oval like its upper leaves.

Modified habitats, including railway yards, gardens, roadsides, forest margins, remnant forest stands and scrub.
Herb Robert usually grows in partial or complete shade, but on occasions plants are seen in open sites.

identification.text:
Annual or biennial hairy taprooted herb, with a characteristic scent. Stems decumbent to spreading, to about 50 cm long, lax, often red where exposed to strong light, sometimes with base thickened; internodes short and leaves rosette-like. Petioles long and slender on lower leaves, often reddish, glabrous or hairy. Lamina palmate, to about 9 × 10 cm, broad- or triangular-ovate, usually becoming red with age; lobes 3–5, at least the terminal petiolulate, pinnately divided to varying degrees, more or less appressed-hairy; ultimate segments usually mucronulate. Inflorescence very diffuse; flowers paired; peduncles usually longer than pedicels; peduncles and pedicels with long- and short-stalked glands. Sepals (at anthesis) 6.5–8 mm long including apical awn, ovate, prominently 3-nerved, with hairs as on pedicels. Petals (7.5)–10–11.5 mm long, obovate-oblanceolate, pink or rose except for white margin of claw; limb equal to claw; apex rounded. Filaments pinkish; anthers orange. Mericarps 2.5–3 mm long, glabrous or hairy, with 4–6 transverse ridges. Seed smooth. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Small herb Robert is an annual or biennial, hairy, taprooted herb with a characteristic scent; its stems are sprawling to nearly upright and reach about 30 cm; its leaves are 1.5–5–(7) × 2–6–(8) cm, cut very deeply into 5 lobes; its flowers are paired, with pink to rose petals 6–9 mm long; its anthers are yellow; its fruit segments are 2.5–3 mm long, with many close cross-ridges on their upper two-thirds. Herb robert is an annual or biennial, hairy, taprooted herb with a characteristic scent; its stems reach about 50 cm; its leaves reach about 9 × 10 cm, with 3–5 lobes; its flowers are paired, with pink or rose petals (7.5)–10–11.5 mm long; its anthers are orange; its fruit segments (mericarps) are 2.5–3 mm long, with 4–6 cross-ridges. They are separated on the petals, usually 10–11.5 mm in herb robert and 6–9 mm in small herb Robert, and the anthers, orange in herb robert and yellow in small herb Robert. The two have sometimes been confused; small petals, yellow pollen and more, closer ridges on the fruit segments together are the signs of small herb Robert, which is also generally more upright, with smaller leaves. No single sign settles it: herb robert's petals can be as short as 7.5 mm, inside small herb Robert's range, and both species have yellow pollen, so anther colour alone can be hard to read. Both are scented, both have paired pink flowers and deeply divided leaves that turn red, and their fruit segments are the same length. No source read records small herb Robert as food.

preparation.text: The fresh leaves are put in a mug of hot water as a tea, or the leaves and flowers dried for tea in winter.

recipes.method: 30 g herb robert; 30 g basil leaves; 1 garlic clove, crushed; olive oil; 40 g Parmesan or Pecorino, finely grated; the juice of half a lemon; salt and black pepper. Blend 30 g herb robert, 30 g basil leaves and 1 crushed garlic clove with enough olive oil to make a loose purée. Stir in 40 g finely grated Parmesan or Pecorino and the juice of half a lemon, then season with salt and black pepper to taste. Keeps well frozen in ice-cube trays.
recipes.title: Herb robert and basil pesto

recipes.method: Written for plantain, herb Robert, nasturtium seeds, oxtongue or rosemary, singly or together (the page does not say which plantain). Chop the plant material and pack it loosely in a jar. Fill the jar with apple cider vinegar to cover the plants completely, let it sit a little, and poke out any air bubbles under the leaves with a chopstick. Cap it, with a piece of plastic under a metal lid so the vinegar doesn't eat the metal, label it and leave it in a cool place for 2–6 weeks, then strain the vinegar into a bottle. Use it in salad dressings, soups and pestos, or sweetened with honey by the spoonful.
recipes.title: Herbal vinegar

recipes.method: The author's greens were the leaves of Indian, alpine (woodland) and garden strawberries, red deadnettle, wall lettuce, herb Robert and nasturtium. A handful of mixed strawberry leaves, stems removed (they are tough); a handful of beetroot leaves and stems; several stems of red deadnettle with their flowers; 5 wall lettuce leaves; 5 herb Robert leaves; red nasturtium flowers and several leaves; a few celery and small kale leaves, optional. Blend the leaves and flowers with 500–750 ml (2–3 cups) water, then add 1 punnet of strawberries, 1 red apple, 2 kiwifruit and 2 bananas and blend again.
recipes.title: Wild and tame strawberry smoothie

summary.text:
Geranium robertianum, commonly known as herb-robert or, in North America, as Robert's geranium, is a species of cranesbill that is widespread throughout the northern hemisphere and introduced to some countries in the southern.
The main areas of distribution of herb-robert are throughout Europe northwards to the Baltic and eastwards as far as Russia. It also occurs in north Africa and it is considered also to be native in north America, although in some western states it is regarded as a weed.
The IUCN has not assessed the threat status of this species, but in some countries it is classified as Least Concern.
It grows at altitudes from sea level to 700 m at Great Dun Fell in England and up to 2,400 m in Kashmir.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island; South Island: widely naturalised but commonest in the North Island. It has been recorded as naturalised since 1878 (NZPCN).

warnings: In Cantabria, Spain, it is regarded as poisonous and handled with care, though the records name no case of poisoning and no toxic compound.
Its safety has not been established in pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand it is a plant of coastal and lowland habitats and favours damper places. It grows in wet forest and forest margins, light gaps in forests (such as windfall gaps), shrublands, streamsides and riverbeds, damp gullies, roadsides, exotic plantations, farm hedges and wasteland. It prefers sunny sites but tolerates moderate to deep shade, frost, damp and most soils.
Herbarium specimens record it on roadsides and road banks, at the margins of native and beech forest and in forest clearings, on river and stream banks, in scrub with gorse and bracken, and under pine plantations; one was collected in 2026 beside a track in a wet ditch with kiokio and rangiora at Upper Hutt.

identification.text:
Shrub to 2–(3) m high; stems hollow, glabrous, green, glaucous at first. Petiole 0.5–2–(5) cm long, purplish, with hairy groove on upper side. Lamina 4–14–(24) × 1.5–8–(12) cm, ovate or broad-ovate, mostly entire, sometimes 5–9-lobed (rarely divided almost to midrib) with rounded sinuses, becoming glabrous except for midrib and bases of main veins; base rounded to cordate; apex long-acuminate. Inflorescence 3–8 cm long at flowering. Bracts mostly 1–3 cm long, sessile, broad-ovate, aristate-acuminate, more or less glandular-hairy, usually deep reddish purple. Calyx small, hidden by bracts; lobes very unequal. Corolla about 1.5 cm long, funnelform, white; lobes rounded at apex, much shorter than tube, with glandular-hairy margins. Stamens shortly exserted. Style longer than stamens. Berry 7–10 mm diameter, subglobose, dark brownish purple, glandular-hairy. Seed 1.1–1.5 mm long, obovoid-ellipsoid, shining brown, minutely white-dotted. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Unlike Japanese honeysuckle, it is a shrub, not a climbing vine.

preparation.text: Eaten raw when fully ripe, with a flavour of toffee or burnt sugar; the berries can also be used like any soft fruit, in jams, jellies and sauces. They are extremely soft and burst when picked, so they are best eaten straight from the bush or frozen until there are enough for a recipe. The berries ripen a few at a time down each spike, so gathering enough for a recipe takes several visits. They can also be dried until still soft and blended to a paste as a filling. The berries are ripe when they burst easily as you pick them.

recipes.method: Makes about 20. Pastry: 142 g fine rice flour; 84 g vegetable margarine; 28 g finely ground almonds; 28 g light muscovado sugar; 14 g cornflour; ½ tsp baking powder; ¾ tsp xanthan gum; a pinch of salt; 1 dessertspoon rapeseed oil; 1 tbsp water; ½ tsp vanilla extract. Filling: 266 g dried but still soft Himalayan honeysuckle berries. Pulse the dry pastry ingredients briefly in a food processor, add the rest and pulse for about 10 seconds; wrap and chill for an hour. Blend the berries to a paste. Roll the pastry out on floured baking paper into a rectangle 3–4 mm thick. Shape the filling into a thin sausage on another sheet, flip it onto the pastry leaving a border, roll the pastry over to enclose it and seal the edges. Chill for 30 minutes, turn onto a greased tray, cut into 2.5 cm pieces spaced apart and bake in a preheated oven at 180 °C for 10–15 minutes, until barely golden. Cool on a rack.
recipes.title: Himalayan honeysuckle berry rolls

recipes.method: Makes one 23 cm pie. Pastry: 250 g plain flour; 1 tbsp sugar; ¼ tsp salt; 125 g cold butter, cubed; 3–4 tbsp iced water. Filling: 500 g fully ripe Himalayan honeysuckle berries; 100 g sugar, or to taste; 2 tbsp cornflour; 1 tbsp lemon juice; ½ tsp ground cinnamon (optional). To finish (optional): 1 egg, beaten, and 1 tbsp sugar. Mix the flour, sugar and salt, rub in the butter until the mixture looks like coarse crumbs, then add the iced water a tablespoon at a time until the dough just comes together. Shape into a disc, wrap and chill for 30 minutes. Cook the berries, sugar, cornflour, lemon juice and cinnamon in a pan over medium heat, stirring, for 5–7 minutes until thick, then cool. Roll out half the dough to line a 23 cm pie dish and pour in the cooled filling. Roll out the rest for a lid, seal the edges and cut a few slits; brush with egg and sprinkle with sugar if you like. Bake in an oven preheated to 190 °C for 40–45 minutes, until the crust is golden and the filling bubbles. Cool for at least an hour before slicing; good with vanilla ice cream, custard or yoghurt.

summary.text:
Himalayan honeysuckle (Leycesteria formosa), also called pheasant berry, is a deciduous or semi-evergreen, many-stemmed shrub of the honeysuckle family, Caprifoliaceae, from the temperate Himalaya.
In New Zealand it was introduced as an ornamental and has been naturalised since 1878. It is an environmental weed, named in the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds in New Zealand, and regional pest plans list it for sustained control in Northland and Auckland and progressive containment on the West Coast, and as an organism of interest in Canterbury. In Auckland it must not be bred, distributed, released, sold or planted, and it is also a pest under the Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area Notice. Birds, water and possibly mammals spread the seed, as do dumped garden waste and moved soil, and new plants quickly form dense thickets. It colonises light wells, slips and other gaps and quickly replaces native pioneer species.
Herbarium specimens show it growing wild in both main islands, from the Waitākere Ranges near Auckland to the Catlins.

warnings: The fruit may be poisonous. In New Zealand a steer had a cerebral infarction (a stroke) that was associated with eating the plant. Eat only fully ripe berries: there is no record of the leaves, stems or unripe berries being eaten as food.
Eating too many berries, raw, cooked or dried, can cause loose stools, and the berries have no long tradition of use: try a few first and increase slowly.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Lowland to high montane grassland and open habitats, such as cliffs, river banks, lakesides, sometimes in swampy ground.
From the coast to alpine country it is a sparse part of grassland and other open places such as cliffs, river banks, lake sides and grey scrub, and occasionally grows in swampy ground (NZPCN, restated).
It is found sparsely in grassy fields and open land generally. It inhabits an elevation range from coastal to alpine, within a range of sea level to 1,400 metres.

identification.text:
Mentha cunninghamii shares a mint odour with other species within the Mentha (mint) genus, but in appearance is very distinct from many other mints.
Gynodioecious perennial; stems more or less creeping, very slender, branched, puberulent, especially on angles. Leaves sessile or with short hairy petioles to 4 mm long. Lamina 2–15 × 2–15 mm, broad-ovate to suborbicular, not rugose, entire or shallowly crenate, dotted with glands and usually glabrous except for nerves on lower surface; base broad-cuneate or truncate; apex rounded. Flowers axillary, in clusters of 1–2–(3); pedicels prominent, puberulent. Calyx 3–4 mm long, narrow-campanulate, densely hairy and with glandular dots; teeth triangular, ciliate, much shorter than tube, acute. Corolla about 6 mm long, white, glabrous; tube not exserted; lobes subequal; uppermost lobe more or less 2-fid. Stamens more or less exserted. Nutlets 1–1.3 mm long, more or less broad-ellipsoid, slightly angled, smooth.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It looks quite unlike any of the naturalised mints in New Zealand; in a sward of native turf it is often first noticed by its mint smell (NZPCN, restated).
It forms loose patches up to 300 mm across, with purple to purple-red stems, bright green to yellow-green leaves and fragrant flowers (NZPCN fact sheet, restated).

summary.text:
Mentha cunninghamii, known commonly as New Zealand mint or Māori mint, is a species within the Mentha (mint) genus, endemic to New Zealand.
Mentha cunninghamii is endemic to the four islands of North Island, South Island, Chatham Island and Stewart Island in New Zealand.
Flowering November to April (Flora of New Zealand vol. IV); the New Zealand Plant Conservation Network gives October to April.
As of 2018, New Zealand's Department of Conservation's New Zealand Threat Classification System (NZTCS) assesses Mentha cunninghamii's conservation status as "At Risk: Declining." The system uses the Declining status to indicate populations that currently possess large populations, but are experiencing declines that could eventually lead to a listing as "Threatened."
Its biostatus is endemic, and the 2023 assessment of New Zealand vascular plants (de Lange et al. 2024) keeps it At Risk – Declining, as in 2017 and 2012 (NZTCS, restated).
It is threatened by habitat degradation from livestock, irrigation and drainage, and by weed competition (NZPCN, restated).
Māori used the leaves for scent, including as one ingredient of a scent compound made with taramea gum, and used the plant to induce sweating (Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga, restated).
It has been suggested that it may actually be more closely related to members of the Micromeria genus.

warnings: Hioi is At Risk – Declining. One book records the leaves and flowers as eaten, but no second record of food use was found, so it is not given as food here. Māori use is recorded for the scented leaves and as a medicine to induce sweating, not as food.

identification.text:
A large evergreen tree, to about 25 m tall in cultivation, with rough, fissured bark. Shoots and buds covered in grey felt. Leaf stalks 5–15 mm long, grey-felted. Leaves 3–8 × 1.5–3.5 cm, usually oval-oblong or lance-shaped, less often broadly elliptic, thick and leathery, untoothed or sometimes with small spiny teeth (the leaves of young and vigorous shoots are often spiny-toothed), deep shining green and hairless above, usually grey or whitish felted underneath; the base broadly wedge-shaped or rounded. Male catkins 1.5–2.5 cm long, clustered. Acorns ripen in their first year, 1–3 together on a short, felted stalk. Cup 1.3–2 cm across, with flat-lying, egg-shaped, finely felted scales. Acorns mostly 1.5–2 cm long, egg-shaped, a third to two-thirds enclosed by the cup. Acorns are green when young and ripen to dark red-brown before they fall.
Cork oak, an evergreen oak planted in some North Island places, has soft, thick, pale, corky bark; holm oak's bark is hard and grey.

lookalikes.howToTell: English oak is deciduous, with thin, dull leaves cut into 3–7 pairs of rounded lobes; holm oak is evergreen, with thick, leathery, unlobed leaves, glossy above and usually grey-felted underneath. English oak's acorns are larger, 2–4 cm long and oblong, a quarter to a third enclosed by the cup, on a fruiting stalk 3–13 cm long; holm oak's are 1.5–2 cm long and egg-shaped, a third to two-thirds enclosed by the cup, on a short, felted stalk. Fallen acorns are told apart by size and shape, and by the leaves overhead.

preparation.text: Acorns picked from the tree keep better than fallen ones; don't store them for months, as stored acorns spoil and go mouldy. A few days of drying makes them easier to shell, and an upturned mortar and pestle cracks them well. Taste an acorn first. Bitter acorns need their tannins leached out: soak them, whole or ground, in plenty of water that you change often until the bitterness has gone, which can take days or weeks for whole acorns but much less for ground ones. Once the leached acorns are dried, their papery, bitter skin rubs off. Leached acorns can be dried and ground into flour to thicken stews or mix into bread, and roasted acorns ground as a coffee substitute.

recipes.method: Thick acorn pancakes, savoury or sweet. Makes 4–6. For the flour: gather ripe brown acorns with no mould or holes, take off the cups and throw out damaged ones. Shell them with a knife as you would chestnuts and rinse the kernels. Cover with cold water and bring to the boil; when the water turns brown (5–10 minutes) pour it off and replace it with fresh, and repeat until the water stays clear or only lightly coloured (2–5 changes, depending on how bitter they are). Or soak the kernels in running water, or water changed very often, for hours or days until the bitterness has gone. Dry them in a low oven or in the open air and grind to flour in a blender or mill. Galettes: 150 g acorn flour; 50 g wheat flour (or another flour, to hold them together); 1 egg; a pinch of salt; 200–300 ml water or milk; 15 ml olive oil; herbs (thyme, rosemary) or spices (paprika, cumin) if you like. Mix the flours and salt, make a well, break in the egg and start mixing, then whisk in the water or milk gradually to a batter a little thicker than for crêpes. Rest it about 15 minutes. Heat a non-stick pan over medium heat with a little of the oil, ladle in some batter and spread it into a thick disc, and cook 2–3 minutes a side until golden. Serve hot with salad, grilled vegetables or cheese, or sweet with honey, maple syrup or jam (for a sweet batch use a pinch of sugar instead of salt, and add cinnamon or vanilla). They keep 1–2 days in the fridge wrapped in a clean cloth.
recipes.title: Acorn galettes

recipes.method: Chef Jorge Asenjo's bread with acorn flour (leached and ground as in the acorn galettes recipe). 100 g sourdough starter; 200 g water; 100 g acorn flour; 233 g wheat flour; 7 g salt. Mix the starter with the water, add both flours and mix evenly, then add the salt last so it does not touch the starter directly. Knead four times, once every 40 minutes, to build the gluten. Leave to ferment in the fridge for at least 12 hours. Bake covered at 240 °C with a dish of water on the oven floor for steam, then uncover, lower the oven to 170 °C and bake about 30 minutes more.

summary.text:
Holm oak (Quercus ilex), also called holly oak or evergreen oak, is a large evergreen tree of the beech family (Fagaceae) from the Mediterranean region, naturalised in New Zealand since 1983.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Auckland City area, Rangitoto Island; South Island: Quail Island (Banks Peninsula). It is commonly planted, especially in parks, domains and large estates, and is the only evergreen oak commonly grown here. Planted trees vary a great deal; the leaves on young and vigorous shoots can look like holly, but on the adult branches of the form usually grown in New Zealand they are nearly always untoothed.
Trees usually bear a heavy crop of acorns every four to six years, with lighter crops in between.

warnings: Eating too many acorns can cause digestive upsets.

edibleParts.text: Root, raw or cooked, before the plant flowers; once it flowers the root usually turns tough. Flowers, raw, in salads. Leaves, raw or cooked, picked before the flowers appear; they turn bitter after that. Leaves and flowers can be bitter, though the leaves can also taste of cabbage and mustard. The seed and green seed pods are not listed here: see Warnings.

identification.text:
Biennial, roots often swollen. Stems erect, leafy, hairy, branching above, to 1 m tall. Leaves cordate, acute, dark green, hairy, bluntly or coarsely dentate; lower leaves petiolate, opposite, 5–10–(20) × 3–5–(15) cm; upper leaves subsessile, alternate, 3–5–(8) × 1.5–3–(4) cm. Racemes to 30 cm long. Sepals hairy, 7–9 × 1.5–2.5 mm. Petals purple, rarely white, 15–22 × 6–8 mm. Silicle elliptic (lanceolate when immature), 2.5–4 × 2–3 cm, obtuse at both ends; carpophore 8–15 mm long; style 5–8 mm long. Seeds dark brown, 5–8 mm diameter 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
When a silique is ripe and dry, a valve on each of its sides readily falls off, and its seeds fall off a central membrane which has a silvery sheen; the membrane can persist on a plant throughout a winter depending on the weather.

lookalikes.howToTell: Honesty has heart-shaped, dark green, hairy leaves with blunt or coarse teeth, on a biennial plant, and its fruit is a broad, flat, elliptic disc 2.5–4 × 2–3 cm. Stock has narrow, lance-shaped leaves that are entire to shallowly lobed, densely felted and grey-green, tufted at the tips of stout woody stems that carry conspicuous leaf-base scars, and its pod is long and narrow, 50–120 × 3–5 mm. Flower colour and size do not separate them: honesty petals are purple (rarely white), 15–22 mm, and stock petals are pink to purple, 18–25 mm. Stock flowers are eaten as a vegetable or used as a garnish.

summary.text:
Honesty, Lunaria annua, is a biennial herb of the mustard family (Brassicaceae), its roots often swollen.
In New Zealand it is recorded from Auckland, Palmerston North, Horowhenua and Wellington in the North Island; Canterbury (Christchurch, Banks Peninsula, Ashburton) and Dunedin in the South Island; and Stewart Island. It is native to south-eastern Europe and was first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1940.
New Zealand plants belong to subsp. annua. White-flowered cultivars are sometimes referred to as var. albiflora, but do not merit varietal rank.
Lunaria annua L. (Brassicaceae) is an ornamental plant newly identified in Europe as a promising industrial oilseed crop for its valuable very-long-chain monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs), especially erucic acid (EA) and nervonic acid (NA).

warnings: Do not eat the seed or the seed pods. The seeds accumulate toxic lunarine and lunaridin alkaloids. Several foraging sources list the seed as a mustard substitute and the green pods as a horseradish-hot vegetable, but none of them mention the alkaloids, and no source gives a safe amount.

Before it flowers, honesty is easy to confuse with several other species, and the leaves and roots are best taken at that stage. Make sure of the plant from its heart-shaped, toothed, hairy leaves, and leave it if in doubt.

identification.text:
Spreading deciduous tree, to about 10 m high and sometimes much taller, usually armed with stout spines on the trunk and branches; the spines are simple or branched, 2–10 cm long and sometimes up to 18 cm. Leaves alternate, 15–20 cm long, either once divided (pinnate) with 5–15 pairs of leaflets or, more often, twice divided (bipinnate) with 2–7 pairs of side branches each carrying 12–30 leaflets; leaflets elliptic to egg-shaped, mostly 10–35 mm long and 5–12 mm wide, sparsely toothed; leaf stalk 3–5 cm long, it and the leaf axis more or less hairy. Flowers small and inconspicuous, greenish or creamy-yellow, petals 4–6 mm long, in golden-hairy spikes 5–10 cm long in the leaf joints, in spring after the new leaves have formed. Pod flat, slightly curved, 15–40 cm long and 3–4 cm wide, dark brown or reddish-brown when ripe, not splitting open, with 15–25 dark brown, egg-shaped seeds about 10 mm long set in pulpy tissue.
Thornless forms are widely planted as street and garden trees, and some cultivars set few or no pods.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers, the pods and the leaves. Black locust's flowers are white, 15–23 mm long, many to a cluster; honey locust's are small, greenish or creamy-yellow, with petals 4–6 mm long, in golden-hairy spikes 5–10 cm long. Black locust's pods are 35–80 mm long with 2–8 seeds; honey locust's are 15–40 cm long and 3–4 cm wide, dark brown when ripe, with 15–25 seeds set in pulp. Black locust's leaves are once divided, with 4–10 pairs of leaflets; honey locust's are more often twice divided, though some are once divided with 5–15 pairs. Black locust's spines are up to about 1 cm long, scattered on the twigs; honey locust's are 2–10 cm long or more, often branched, on the trunk and branches. Both are planted in forms without spines and in golden-leaved forms, so missing spines or leaf colour do not tell them apart. Black locust's seeds, bark and leaves are poisonous; only its flowers are eaten (see its page).

preparation.text: The pulp of ripe pods is eaten raw; the brown outer skin of the pod is not eaten. Ripe pods soaked in water, or their juice mixed with water and sugar, make a sweet drink. The pulp in older pods turns bitter. Mature seeds are hard: soak them overnight or boil them until tender, remove the hulls, and cook them, for example in a stew. Raw or cooked young seeds, cooked young pods and roasted seeds as a coffee substitute have each been recorded in one source only, so they are not given here.

recipes.method: 4 tbsp (60 ml) oil or fat, 1 tbsp honey locust seeds, 1 small onion, 2 small tomatoes, a handful of dried, seasoned meat such as fish or fowl, and a pinch of salt and pepper or other seasoning. Take the seeds out of ripe pods, clean them, soak or boil them until tender, rinse and remove the hulls. Chop the onion and tomatoes and mix them. Warm the oil in a pan for 2 minutes, add the onion and tomato, stir and cover for 2 minutes. Add the seasoning and the prepared seeds, stir and cover for 5 minutes, then add the meat, stir and cover for 5 minutes more.

summary.text: Honey locust, a deciduous tree of the pea family (Fabaceae) from eastern North America, planted in New Zealand as a street, shade and ornamental tree. It is exotic here and casual, only sometimes found wild: it reproduces by seed, its long-lived seed is held for years in pods that stay on the tree and is spread by wind, gravity and people, and seedlings and suckers come up near planted trees. On farms it is grown for stock shade and its pods as fodder. Most garden and street trees are thornless forms, and some cultivars bear few or no pods; the thornless weeping cultivar 'Emerald Kascade' was introduced by a New Zealand nursery in 1992. In Australia it forms dense thorny thickets along rivers and in pasture and is a declared weed; in New Zealand it is not on DOC's 2024 environmental weed list.

warnings: The typical form carries long, rigid spines on the trunk and branches, simple or branched, 2–10 cm and up to 18 cm long. They can cause serious injuries, and they stay dangerous on dead wood. Thornless forms are common in planting.

Eat only the pod pulp and the cooked seeds, not the pod skin, which is high in tannins. The plant contains potentially toxic compounds: the twigs and leaves contain alkaloids, one of which, gleditschine, causes stupor and loss of reflexes.

Black locust, a pea-family tree with divided leaves also planted in New Zealand streets and parks, has poisonous seeds, bark and leaves, and only its flowers are eaten. Make sure of the tree before eating any pod or seed (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
It grows in dense clusters on wood, the stem bases swollen and joined together. The cap is 3–8 cm across, olive-buff to olive-brown, with a sprinkling of very small dull brown scales at the centre. It is convex at first with a strongly down-rolled edge, then flat or shallowly dished; when fresh it is moist and clearly lined (striate) at the edge, and it dries matt. The flesh is creamy white.
The gills run a little way down the stem, or are notched just before it, and are moderately crowded with many short ones between; they are creamy white, turning dull fawn. The stem is 4–7 cm long and 4–8 mm thick, tough and solid, often tapering to the base; it is fawn above a thin ring that soon disappears, and brown to dark purplish brown below. The spore print is white.
In infected wood, look for white sheets or fans of mycelium under the bark and black bootlace-like strands.
The lemon honeycap (A. limonea), endemic to the North Island and northern South Island, is larger and brighter: its cap is 8–13 cm across, lemon yellow, thickly scattered at the centre with dark brown tufted scales, and its stem has a substantial cottony ring. Its spore print is also white. Its edibility is uncertain: it has been eaten without ill effect, but it is also recorded as bitter and inedible.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both grow on rotting wood, including southern beech, and both can have a ring on the stem, so place and ring do not separate them. Wood nipple fungus belongs to the group of the deadly Galerina marginata and probably carries the same toxins. It is much smaller and more slender: its cap is 1–2.5 cm across, often with a prominent pointed bump in the centre, on a stem 2–4 mm thick, and it grows singly or in loose groups, rarely in tight clumps. A honey mushroom's cap is 3–8 cm across on a tough stem 4–8 mm thick, in dense clusters with the stem bases joined together. Look at the gills: rusty orange to cinnamon in the Galerina, creamy white to dull fawn in the honey mushroom. A spore print settles it: cinnamon-brown for Galerina, white for the honey mushroom.
lookalikes.name: Wood nipple fungus

preparation.text:
Never eat it raw or undercooked. Cut the mushrooms high on the stem, or trim off the tough lower stems. Rinse them well, or soak them briefly: the lower caps in a cluster catch grit, bark and spores from the ones above. Then parboil them: cover with cold salted water, bring to the boil, skim off the foam and simmer for 15–20 minutes, then pour the water away. After that, fry, stew or pickle them, or add them to sauces and soups; the caps stay firm and chewy even after long simmering. Keep small button caps whole for pickling, and chop large open ones for frying.
To keep them, freeze them after boiling, or pickle them. Dried ones stay tough when soaked again.

recipes.method: Written for honey mushrooms (Armillaria) in general. Serves 4. 1 kg fresh honey mushrooms; 1 litre water; 4 tbsp (60 ml) white vinegar, 9% acidity; 2 tbsp sugar; 1½ tbsp non-iodised salt; 4 garlic cloves; 8–10 black peppercorns; 3 bay leaves; 3–4 whole cloves. Sort and clean the mushrooms, cut off the tough lower stems and wash them in several changes of cold water. Put them in a large pot, cover with cold water and bring to the boil, skimming off the foam. Simmer for 15–20 minutes, then drain and rinse them in a colander. For the marinade, bring the litre of water to the boil, add the salt, sugar, peppercorns, bay leaves and cloves and simmer for 3–5 minutes. Add the parboiled mushrooms and cook over medium heat for another 15 minutes. Slice the garlic thinly, add it with the vinegar and simmer 2–3 minutes more, then turn off the heat. Ladle the hot mushrooms and marinade into sterilised jars, keeping the mushrooms covered by the liquid, seal with sterilised lids, cool to room temperature and refrigerate. They are ready in about 24 hours and better after a few days. To serve, drain them and toss with a little olive or sunflower oil and chopped spring onion or red onion.
recipes.title: Marinated honey mushrooms

recipes.method: Written for honey mushrooms (Armillaria) in general. Serves 2. 500 g honey mushrooms; 1 large onion (about 120 g); 3 tbsp vegetable oil; 20 g butter; 1 garlic clove; salt and black pepper; fresh parsley. Clean the mushrooms, put them in a pot of salted water, bring to the boil and simmer for 15 minutes. Drain well and pat them as dry as you can with paper towels. Cut the onion into half-rings and mince the garlic. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat, add the mushrooms and fry for 10–12 minutes, stirring now and then, until their moisture has gone and they start to brown. Add the onion, lower the heat to medium and cook 8–10 minutes more, until soft and caramelised. In the last 2 minutes add the butter, garlic, salt and pepper and toss to coat. Sprinkle with chopped parsley. Good with fried or boiled new potatoes.
recipes.title: Sautéed honey mushrooms with onion

recipes.method: Written for honey mushrooms (Armillaria) in general. Serves 4. 600 g honey mushrooms; 250 g sour cream, at least 20% fat, at room temperature; 2 medium onions; 40 g butter; 1 tbsp plain flour; 50 ml water or mushroom stock; salt and pepper; a small bunch of fresh dill. Clean the mushrooms, boil them in salted water for 15–20 minutes and drain well; chop large ones and leave small ones whole. Finely dice the onions. Melt the butter in a deep frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions until translucent, 5–7 minutes. Add the mushrooms and sauté for about 10 minutes, until lightly golden. Sprinkle over the flour and stir for 1–2 minutes. Lower the heat, add the sour cream and the water or stock and stir until smooth, adding a little more water if it is too thick. Season, cover and simmer gently for 5–7 minutes without letting it boil hard, or the sour cream may split. Stir in the chopped dill, turn off the heat and leave 5 minutes before serving, with buckwheat, mashed potato or egg noodles.
recipes.title: Honey mushrooms in sour cream

recipes.method: Written for honey mushrooms (Armillaria) in general. Serves 4. 400 g honey mushrooms; 1.5 litres water; 3 medium potatoes; 1 medium carrot; 1 medium onion; 2 tbsp vegetable oil; 1 bay leaf; 4–5 black peppercorns; salt; fresh dill or parsley. Wash the mushrooms well and trim the stems. Put them in a large pot with the cold water, bring to the boil, skim off the foam, add a pinch of salt and simmer over medium-low heat for 20 minutes. Meanwhile peel the potatoes and cut them into medium cubes; add them to the pot and cook 10–15 minutes until tender. Finely dice the onion and coarsely grate the carrot. Fry the onion in the oil until soft, add the carrot and cook 5 minutes more until golden, then add them to the soup with the bay leaf and peppercorns. Check the salt and simmer gently for 5 minutes. Turn off the heat, take out the bay leaf, cover and leave 10–15 minutes. Serve hot, with sour cream and dark rye bread.
recipes.title: Honey mushroom soup

recipes.method: Written for honey mushrooms (Armillaria) in general. Serves 4. 300 g linguine or spaghetti; 400 g honey mushrooms; 3 garlic cloves; 4 tbsp extra virgin olive oil; 60 ml dry white wine; 20 g butter; 50 g grated Parmesan; a handful of chopped fresh parsley; salt and red pepper flakes. Clean the mushrooms, parboil them in salted water for 15 minutes, drain well and pat dry. Cook the pasta in plenty of well-salted boiling water until al dente, keeping 125 ml of the cooking water before draining. Slice the garlic thinly. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat, add the garlic and a pinch of pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, without letting the garlic brown. Turn the heat to medium-high, add the mushrooms and sauté for 7–8 minutes, until crisp and golden at the edges. Pour in the wine, scrape up the browned bits and let it reduce by half, about 2 minutes. Stir in the butter, add the drained pasta and toss well, adding a splash of the pasta water if it seems dry. Stir in the parsley and half the Parmesan, season with salt and serve with the rest of the cheese.
recipes.title: Honey mushroom pasta

recipes.method: Written for North American honey mushrooms. Serves 6. Stew: 900 g venison, pork or beef shoulder, in chunks; salt and pepper; 60 ml (4 tbsp) bacon fat or lard; 30 ml (2 tbsp) sweet paprika; 15 ml (1 tbsp) smoked paprika; 60 ml (¼ cup) tomato paste; 225 g onion, diced; 225 g floury potato, peeled and diced; 170 g celeriac or parsley root, diced (or more potato); 225 g mild long peppers or 2 large red or yellow capsicums, diced; 170 g carrot, diced; 60 ml (¼ cup) dry red wine; 170 g fresh young honey mushrooms, small ones whole and large ones quartered; 2 large garlic cloves; 1.5 litres meat stock or water; 5 ml (1 tsp) chopped fresh thyme; 2 bay leaves. To finish: 225 g sour cream; 30 ml (2 tbsp) cream; ground caraway; sliced spring onions. Pat the meat dry, season and brown it in the fat. Add the onion, the other vegetables, the tomato paste and both paprikas and stir for a few minutes. In a separate pan, dry-sauté the mushrooms until golden and cooked through, at least 15 minutes. Add the garlic, wine, mushrooms, stock, thyme and bay leaves to the stew, bring to the boil, then cover and simmer gently for about 45 minutes, until the meat is tender. Mix the sour cream with the cream and a little caraway, and serve the goulash topped with it and the spring onions.
recipes.title: Honey mushroom goulash

summary.text:
Armillaria novae-zelandiae is a native honey fungus (family Physalacriaceae) of dead and living trees.
In te reo Māori it is harore, and in English the olive honeycap. It is one of four Armillaria species in New Zealand, alongside the lemon honeycap (A. limonea), A. hinnulea and A. aotearoa, and is not endemic: it also grows overseas. It is common here, with 1,858 research-grade iNaturalist records.
It is a white-rot fungus of wood and a root-rot pathogen of living trees. It spreads underground by black, bootlace-like strands (rhizomorphs) from buried wood and old stump roots, and by wind-borne spores. When native forest was cleared and planted in Pinus radiata, it survived in the old stumps and killed young pines around them, and from the 1970s to the 1990s it caused heavy losses in pine plantations and kiwifruit orchards. The cap sometimes glows in the dark.
In Mātauranga Māori, harore appearing in autumn forests foretells the future, a good fishing season or a famine depending on the region's tradition. It is a traditional Māori food, still collected by Tūhoe in Te Urewera. Because the mushrooms vanish soon after they come up, the whakataukī 'he harore rangitahi', a one-day mushroom, describes something fleeting, or a person who helps with work only briefly.

warnings: Never eat honey mushrooms raw or undercooked; raw, they cause severe stomach upset. Even well cooked, they disagree with some people, causing allergic reactions, fever-like symptoms, diarrhoea or other stomach and gut upsets. These reactions are recorded for the northern honey fungus (Armillaria mellea) and its relatives; no account of reactions to the New Zealand species was found.

Other mushrooms that grow in clusters on stumps and logs in New Zealand have brown spore prints. The spectacular rustgill (Gymnopilus junonius), common here, is inedible: it is bitter and contains neurotoxins. It is bright yellow-orange, ageing orange-brown or reddish brown, with yellow flesh, a frail ring dusted with rusty orange spores, and a rusty brown spore print. Scalycaps (Pholiota) have coarser scales that stand out and are firmly attached, and a brown spore print. A honey mushroom's spore print is white: check it before eating any.

identification.text:
Glabrous, short-lived perennial; taproot often thick; stems rather slender, branched, spreading to erect, to about 100 cm long. Petiole shorter than lamina, especially in uppermost leaves. Lamina of basal and cauline leaves (2.5)–6–22 × (0.5)–1–5 cm, linear, lanceolate-oblong, or oblong, generally with 2 rounded lobes at base, sometimes not lobed, sometimes oblique; margin not or somewhat undulate; base truncate to cordate, rarely cuneate; apex acute to long-acuminate. Inflorescence usually with leaves in the lower axils; flowers in distant whorls of 3–12, bisexual, strongly protandrous, extending downwards for ⅔ or more of stem. Pedicels prominently jointed, elongating and deflexed at fruiting. Perianth segments 1.5–2.5 mm long; outer segments lanceolate to ovate, acuminate or aristate, often tinged red, more or less spreading at fruiting; inner segments more or less broad-ovate, toothed, enlarging at fruiting. Fruiting valves about 2 × 2 mm (excluding terminal hooked spine), very broadly ovate, strongly reticulate, with about 5, red, hooked spines 2 mm long on each side; tubercles 0. Nut 2–2.5 mm long, deep glossy brown, acutely angled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The fruit valves carry red hooked spines that lock the fruiting branches together, making them look tangled, and catch on fur, hair and clothing.

lookalikes.howToTell: New Zealand dock never has hooked fruit: its valves have 1–4 straight teeth on each edge (an older Flora described them as minutely hooked), while hooked dock's carry about five red hooked spines, 2 mm long, on each side. New Zealand dock's fruiting stems zig-zag strongly into a tangled mass; hooked dock's only look tangled because the hooked fruit lock together. New Zealand dock's leaves are usually brown, narrow (up to 3 cm wide) and often wavy or curled; hooked dock's are up to 5 cm wide, usually with two rounded lobes at the base. New Zealand dock grows in bogs, wet flushes and by lakes and streams, mostly from the central North Island south; hooked dock on dry cliff tops, roadsides and stony ground, mostly in the north and in Marlborough and Nelson.

summary.text: Hooked dock, also called swamp dock, is native to south-eastern Australia and was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1948. Its hooked fruit hitch rides on passing animals, and it seems to have spread quickly in the 20th century. It has been confused with, and recorded as, the native New Zealand dock, which never has hooked fruit. In New Zealand it grows in the north of the North Island, especially on offshore islands, south to the Bay of Plenty, and in Marlborough and Nelson; it is occasional in Canterbury and Otago, and very common on Raoul Island.

warnings: It contains oxalic acid, which gives the leaves their sharp taste. A little is fine, but large amounts can lock up calcium and other minerals in food; cooking lowers the oxalic acid. Take particular care, or leave it alone, if you are prone to rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.
Large amounts of dock leaves that are not properly cooked can cause nausea, stomach cramps, vomiting and headache.

identification.text:
Annual; stems moderately to densely clothed in appressed hairs, erect or ascending, not rooting at nodes. Leaves glabrous to moderately hairy on petioles and undersurface of leaflets; petioles about 3–12 mm long; leaflets obovate, obtuse or emarginate, occasionally mucronate, cuneate at base, finely serrate, about 4–15 mm long; lateral veins thin and straight to leaflet margin; petiolules distinctly unequal in most leaves; lateral petiolules less than 1 mm long; terminal petiolule up to 3 mm long; stipules ovate, acute. Inflorescences axillary, racemose, cylindric, pedunculate, much longer than leaves; flowers 20–40; pedicels about 0.5–1 mm long; bracts subtending flowers reduced to glandular hairs. Calyx glabrous or somewhat hairy about teeth, 5-veined, not inflated at fruiting; throat open, glabrous; calyx teeth unequal, erect at fruiting; 3 lower teeth longer, lanceolate, shorter than corolla, much longer than tube; 2 upper teeth triangular, shorter than tube; sinuses obtuse. Corolla yellow, persistent, 3.5–5 mm long. Pod glabrous, straight, more or less equal to or longer than calyx, about 2 mm long, usually 1-seeded; seeds about 1 mm diameter.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is told from the other naturalised yellow-flowered clovers by the unequal leaflet stalks and the many-flowered heads. Its flower heads dry pale brown and look like small hop heads.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small sprawling or upright plants of dry waste places and grassland, with three small toothed leaflets, the middle one on a longer stalk than the other two, and heads of tiny yellow pea-type florets on stalks well above the leaves, so the leaves and the head shape alone do not separate them. Look at the florets: hop trefoil's are 3.5–5 mm long, 20–40 to a head, and stay on the head as it ages, hiding the small straight pods; black medick's are 2–3 mm long and fall off, leaving bare kidney-shaped pods coiled in about one full turn, net-veined and black when ripe, 2–3 mm across. Look at the leaflet tips: black medick's end in a distinct short point; hop trefoil's are rounded or notched and only occasionally have a short point. Sizes overlap — hop trefoil's leaflets are about 4–15 mm, black medick's about 4–20 mm. Neither has a confirmed food use here; see each page.
lookalikes.name: Black medick

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small annual clovers of dry, open ground, with three small, finely toothed leaflets, the middle one on a longer stalk than the other two on most leaves, and heads of tiny yellow pea-type florets on stalks well above the leaves. In both, the florets stay on the head as it ages and hide small straight pods, so the old heads do not separate them. Count the florets in a head: hop trefoil has 20–40, in a cylindrical head; suckling clover has 5–20, rarely up to 25, in a smaller round to cylindrical head. Floret length overlaps — hop trefoil's are 3.5–5 mm, suckling clover's 2.5–4 mm — and so do the leaflets (hop trefoil about 4–15 mm, suckling clover about 3–12 mm, both usually rounded or notched at the tip). A plant with only a few small heads of under 20 florets is not safely told apart by eye. Neither has a confirmed food use here; see each page.

summary.text:
Hop trefoil (Trifolium campestre) is a small, yellow-flowered annual clover of the pea family (Fabaceae), native from Europe to western Asia and North Africa and naturalised in New Zealand since 1867.
In the North Island it is recorded from Northland, Auckland City, Waikato, the Bay of Plenty to East Cape and Wellington Province; in the South Island from Nelson City, lowland and inland Marlborough, Canterbury and Otago; it is also on the Kermadec and Chatham Islands. Herbarium specimens also record it growing wild in Hawke's Bay (roadside gravel near Tarawera, 2025), Taranaki (Hāwera rail yard, 2004; Waverley, 2007) and Southland (Te Anau, 1980).
It was earlier known in New Zealand as Trifolium procumbens.

warnings: Do not eat it. No food use of this species is confirmed here.

Its small yellow flower heads and three leaflets look like black medick's and suckling clover's, and it is confused with both. Count the florets and check the leaflet tips and the old heads (see Lookalikes).

edibleParts.text: Young shoots and young leaves, cooked; young leaves are also eaten in salads. Only the tender tip of a shoot is used: below it the bine becomes tough and fibrous. The dried female cones (the hops) are used as a flavouring and preservative in beer, and a tea is made from the leaves and cones. The fleshy rhizomes are sometimes eaten. The cones also flavour syrups, sweets, relishes and baking.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Waste places, riverbanks, deserted gardens, often scrambling over scrub or trees at forest margins.
It grows in gardens, crops, waste places, riverbanks and lax grassland, usually next to cultivated or dumped plants, and invades disturbed forest, shrubland and margins, and fernland. It tolerates damp to dry, warm to cold, salt and damage (Weedbusters).

identification.text:
Dioecious or monoecious climber, with extensive roots. Stems striate, up to 10 m long and clothed in rough deflexed hairs. Leaves broadly ovate, not lobed or deeply 3–5-lobed; lobes acute to acuminate, serrate, more or less glabrous to sparsely hairy above, more or less glabrous to moderately hairy with yellow glandular hairs below. Petiole usually more or less equal to leaf blade. Stipules 2 per node and 2-fid or 4 per node and entire. Bracts of female flowers triangular, hairy, green, elongating and becoming yellowish at fruiting to form a cylindric-ovoid infructescence (the hop) with yellow glandular hairs especially at base of bracts. Calyx of male flowers ovate-triangular, green, hairy. Achene ovate-ellipsoid, covered by glandular calyx. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The female cones have a distinctive smell (Weedbusters).

preparation.text: Pick shoots shortly after they come up and before the leaves unfurl; the first 20 cm or less of a young shoot is tender. Shoots about 10 cm long can be blanched and eaten like asparagus. Later in the season only the growing tips stay tender, and they can be picked until the cones form. Rinse and cook lightly and quickly: steam or blanch and serve with butter and salt, boil in salted, acidulated water or cook in butter in a covered pan until tender, or fry. They go well with eggs (frittata, omelette) and in risotto. Shoots keep for about a week in a bag with a damp cloth, and can be frozen after light cooking or pickled. Pick cones when they are springy and papery with visible yellow lupulin, dry rather than damp, slightly sticky and fragrant; plants in more sun ripen sooner; orange, rancid-smelling cones are spoiled. Dry them at no more than 60 degrees and store airtight and out of the light. Hop tea is bitter.

recipes.method: Serves 2–4. Ingredients: about 55 g (2 oz) fresh hop shoots, tender parts only; about 55 g (2 oz) bacon (optional); 4 large eggs; 60 ml (¼ cup) cream or half-and-half; 2 tablespoons chopped chives or a mix of fresh herbs such as parsley, dill and coriander; salt and pepper; chive flowers to garnish (optional). Heat the oven to 150 °C (300 °F). Beat the eggs with the herbs, a pinch of salt and pepper and the cream, and set aside. In a 25 cm (10 inch) cast-iron or similar pan, cook the bacon to render its fat. Add the hop shoots, cover and cook on medium heat just to wilt them; season with a little salt. Add the egg mix and cook, stirring and swirling the pan to spread the egg. Put the pan in the oven for a minute or two to dry the top, and serve as soon as the egg sets, garnished with chive flowers if using.
recipes.title: Hop shoot frittata

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1 bunch wild hop shoots; about 225 g (½ pound) Carnaroli rice; 2–3 strawberries; 2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil; 4 tablespoons Parmesan; a small knob of butter; salt; 125 ml (½ cup) dry white wine; 1.5 litres (6 cups) boiling water or vegetable stock. Wash and chop the hop shoots and fry them very slowly in the olive oil for about 2 minutes. Add the rice, turn up the heat and stir for about 2 minutes until slightly translucent, then add the wine and let the alcohol evaporate. Add a first ladle of hot water and a good pinch of salt, lower to a simmer, and keep adding ladlefuls, stirring and letting each be absorbed before the next, for about 15 minutes. The source uses no onion or stock so the hops are not overpowered. When the rice is soft but still has a slight bite, take it off the heat, stir in the strawberries in pieces, the butter and the Parmesan, cover and rest for 3 minutes until creamy. Serve straight away, garnished with hop tips and strawberry.
recipes.title: Risotto with hop shoots and strawberries

recipes.method: Makes 2. Ingredients: 2 buckwheat crêpes; 1 bunch wild hop shoots; 1 carrot; 1 small onion; pink peppercorns in brine (about a dozen, crushed); 2 eggs; stracchino or another soft fresh cheese; butter; salt. The source gives no amount for the cheese. Soften the chopped onion and carrot with a pinch of salt and a little water for a couple of minutes, then cover and cook another 5 minutes. Rinse and chop the hop shoots and add them to the pan with the crushed pink peppercorns; cook a few minutes more. Meanwhile fry the eggs in a knob of butter so they are ready with the vegetables. Spread cheese on each crêpe, spoon the vegetables over, top with a fried egg and fold the edges towards the centre, leaving the yolk uncovered. If needed, warm for no more than a minute in a hot oven so the yolk stays runny.
recipes.title: Crespelle with hop shoots

recipes.method: Ingredients: 200 g (1 cup) sugar, or honey; 250 ml (1 cup) water; enough hop cones, picked green and closed, to sit under the syrup. Make as much syrup as you need to cover the hops. Warm the sugar and water until the sugar dissolves, without letting it boil, which changes the syrup's texture. Add the hops and leave them to infuse for at least 30 minutes; the source takes it off the heat after about 15 minutes and lets it finish infusing cold. Strain and keep in the fridge. For a thinner syrup use 1 part sugar to 2 parts water. Use it in soft drinks or tea, or with rum and a ginger syrup made the same way for a bitter cocktail.
recipes.title: Hop syrup

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1–2 dried or fresh hop cones; 500 ml (2 cups) boiling water; honey to taste (optional). Put the cones in a teapot, pour over the boiling water and infuse for 5 minutes. Sweeten if you like, strain, and drink warm or let it cool and bottle it. Hop tea is bitter, and hops make you drowsy.
recipes.title: Hop tea

recipes.method: Ingredients: 500 ml (2 cups) milk of your choice; 1–2 dried or fresh hop cones; 1 teaspoon ground turmeric; ½ teaspoon ground cinnamon; ¼ teaspoon ground ginger; 1 cardamom pod; 1 teaspoon vanilla; 1–2 tablespoons honey. Heat the milk with everything else in a small pan and simmer for 10 minutes. Strain into cups. The source drinks it at bedtime; hops make you drowsy.
recipes.title: Golden hop milk

recipes.method: Makes 20 or more. Ingredients: 125 ml (½ cup) beer (the source uses an IPA); 6 dried hop cones (the source uses the Centennial variety); 200 g (1 cup) sugar; 125 ml (½ cup) light corn syrup; a little butter; lollipop sticks. You need a sugar thermometer. Butter the backs of one or two baking trays well. Heat the beer to a light simmer, break the hop cones apart into it and take it off the heat; leave to steep for up to 10 minutes, tasting as you go, since hops vary a lot in strength. Strain and measure out 80 ml (⅓ cup) of the beer. In a heavy saucepan mix the sugar, corn syrup and measured beer, bring to the boil over medium-high heat and stir often until it reaches 150 °C; watch it closely from about 138 °C, as the temperature climbs fast and it can burn. Take it off the heat and stir constantly for about a minute as it cools and thickens. Working quickly, drop 1–3 teaspoons at a time onto the buttered trays, lay a stick flat into each with its tip near the centre and twirl it so the candy coats it. Cool completely, lift off and wrap.
recipes.title: Hop beer lollipops

recipes.method: Makes about 1.4 litres (3 US pints). Ingredients: 900 g (2 lb) pickling cucumbers, cleaned; 1 small onion, peeled; 1 small red capsicum; 500 ml (2 cups) vinegar; 1 large handful dried hop 'leaves' (the author's word for the broken-up cone petals) or 2 handfuls fresh; 60 ml (¼ cup) pickling salt; 3 garlic cloves, crushed or minced; 1 teaspoon mustard seed; ½ teaspoon celery seed; ½ teaspoon crushed chilli or 1–2 fresh jalapeños; ¼ teaspoon dill seed; ¼ teaspoon turmeric. You need sterilised jars, new lids and a large pot for processing. Cut the cucumbers, onion and capsicum into 2–3 cm pieces and chop finely in a food processor. Fill the large pot with at least 15 cm of water and bring it to the boil. In another heavy pot bring the vinegar to the boil, add the hops, mash them about and simmer for 5–10 minutes, tasting often. When it is as bitter as you want, lift out all the hops with a slotted spoon, add the vegetables and everything else and bring back to the boil. Ladle the boiling relish into the jars, leaving about 6 mm headspace, wipe the rims, put on the lids and process in the boiling water for 15 minutes. Lift out and leave to cool overnight. Check the seals next morning: any lid that pops when pressed has not sealed, so keep that jar in the fridge and use it within a few weeks. Chill well before eating.
recipes.title: Hoppy dill pickle relish

recipes.method: Serves 14; start the hop extract a week ahead. Hop extract (from the same author's 'Homemade Hop Extracts', https://celebrationgeneration.com/homemade-hop-extracts/): put 250 ml (1 cup) fresh hops, gently rinsed, or 180 ml (¾ cup) dried hop 'leaves' (cone petals) in a clean jar, pour over 500 ml (2 cups) good vodka, close tightly and shake. Keep it in a cool dark place, shaking a couple of times a day, for about a week, then taste: it should be a strong flavouring like vanilla extract, not something to drink. Strain through a fine sieve and then a coffee filter and bottle. Crust: 375 ml (1½ cups) graham cracker crumbs; 50 g (¼ cup) sugar; 5 tablespoons melted butter. Filling: 900 g (2 lb) cream cheese at room temperature; 300 g (1½ cups) sugar; 250 ml (1 cup) sour cream; 250 ml (1 cup) cream; 6 large eggs; juice of 1 lemon; 1 tablespoon hop extract. Topping: 250 ml (1 cup) citrus marmalade; juice and zest of 1 lemon; 1 teaspoon hop extract; a pinch of salt. Mix the crumbs, sugar and butter until moistened, press firmly over the base and partway up the sides of a 23 cm (9 inch) springform tin, and chill for at least 1 hour. Heat the oven to 220 °C. Beat the cream cheese and sugar just until smooth, add the sour cream, cream, eggs, lemon juice and extract and beat on low just until smooth. Pour into the crust and chill 10 minutes. Bake 15 minutes, then turn the oven down to 160 °C and bake 50 minutes more. Turn the oven off and leave the cake inside to cool for 2 hours without opening the door, then chill for at least 3 hours. For the topping, whisk everything together in a small pan over medium heat just until smooth and liquid, pour over the cold cake and chill at least 10 minutes before slicing.
recipes.title: Hopped cheesecake with citrus glaze

summary.text:
Humulus lupulus, the common hop or hops, is a species of flowering plant in the hemp family, Cannabaceae.
The plant is native to Europe, western Asia and North America.
It is a perennial, herbaceous climbing plant which sends up new shoots in early spring and dies back to a cold-hardy rhizome in autumn.
It grows best in the latitude range of 38°–51° in full sun with moderate amounts of rainfall.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Waikato, Bay of Plenty, Lake Waikaremoana, Taupo, Wellington Province; South Island: common in Nelson, North Westland, Central and South Canterbury, also recorded from Blenheim, Otago Peninsula, and Riverton (Southland). Native of Europe, West and Central Asia; first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1872. Both cultivated and wild plants in New Zealand fall within H. lupulus var. lupulus. This variety is cultivated for the glandular female infructescence which is used in brewing; plants escaped from cultivation are now well-established, persistent weeds in some areas.
It was introduced to New Zealand for agriculture (New Zealand Plant Conservation Network), and New Zealand's commercial hop varieties are grown in the Nelson region (Kiwiherb).
It grows and matures fast and takes root where its stems touch the ground, and it forms a dense canopy that stops native plants establishing (Weedbusters).
The name hop is thought to come from the Anglo-Saxon hoppan, to climb, and lupulus from the Latin lupus, wolf. Pliny wrote of hops as a garden plant whose new shoots were harvested for eating (Herb Federation of New Zealand).

warnings: Handling hops causes dermatitis in sensitive people, long known among hop pickers; about 1 in 30 people who handle the plant are affected. Hairs dislodged from the plant can irritate the eyes. The bines and cones carry scratchy hooked hairs, so wear gloves when picking a lot.

Hop cones are sedative: the hairs on them contain lupulin, a sedative and hypnotic substance. Hop preparations may impair the ability to drive or use machines, and are best not taken in large quantities within a couple of weeks of a procedure using anaesthetic. Do not combine hops with alcohol, check with a health professional before taking them with sedatives or sleep medicine, and avoid them if you have depression.

Safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and medicinal use of hop cones at these times, or when trying to conceive, is not recommended; use in children under 12 is not recommended for lack of data. Hops contain xanthohumol, which gut bacteria convert to a phytoestrogen (8-prenylnaringenin) that may bind to oestrogen receptors; people with hormone-sensitive conditions such as breast cancer or endometriosis should avoid hops.

Hops are toxic to dogs: signs are panting, high body temperature, seizures and death. Of five dogs (4 of them Greyhounds) that ate spent hops, 4 died despite treatment. Keep hops, including spent hops from brewing, away from dogs.

When picking shoots, other climbers can grow tangled through the hops, including field bindweed, which is common in New Zealand in the same waste places. None has the light green cones, so the risk is with the shoots: check every shoot has hop leaves (in opposite pairs, 3 to 5 lobes, toothed margins, rough to touch) and no tendrils. Field bindweed leaves are arrow- or spear-shaped and untoothed, apart from often a pair of teeth near the base.
It is controlled as an environmental weed with herbicide (metsulfuron or triclopyr sprays, or glyphosate or metsulfuron gel on cut stems). Pick only where you know it has not been sprayed.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Take a few leaves per shrub. DOC permission is needed to collect plants on public conservation land. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In the Auckland region (Regionally Critical), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it. In Northland (Regionally Naturally Uncommon), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text: Small shrub with leathery oval leaves blotched red, pale blue-green underneath. Chewing a fragment produces a strong chilli-like burn; lowland horopito, with unblotched glossy leaves, is only somewhat pungent.

lookalikes.howToTell: Lowland horopito's leaves are dark green and glossy above with no red blotches; horopito's are dull green and blotched with red, at least in exposed places. Lowland horopito's leaves are usually larger, 6–10 × 3–6 cm against 2–6 (rarely 8) × 1–3 cm, and pale to glaucous underneath but not white, where horopito's are glaucous to white and often pink-flushed. Lowland horopito's ripe fruit is usually bright red, rarely dark; horopito's is dark red to black. Horopito's leaves are very pungent to taste, lowland horopito's only somewhat pungent. Hybrids between the two are frequent where they meet, so some plants fit neither description.
lookalikes.name: Lowland horopito

lookalikes.howToTell: Feel the leaf: horopito's is leathery, mountain alseuosmia's thin. Mountain alseuosmia's leaves are glossy, widest towards the tip and narrowed wedge-like to the base, with a tiny point at the tip and the edge entire or with a few minute teeth, on rather stout stalks up to 10 mm long; horopito's are dull, elliptic to broadly elliptic with a wavy edge, on slender stalks 5–10 mm long. Both can show red: mountain alseuosmia's leaves are often red-edged and sometimes flecked red, horopito's blotched red in exposed places, and their leaf sizes overlap. Mountain alseuosmia is a shrub up to about 50 cm tall, unbranched or with one or two branches; horopito grows to 2 m, sometimes 3.5 m, but a small plant could be either. In flower, mountain alseuosmia's flowers are tubular, about 8–10 mm long, with five fringed lobes, white to yellowish or reddish and sweet-scented; horopito's have 5–6 separate greenish-yellow petals 4–5 mm long. Mountain alseuosmia's berries are oval, about 9–12 × 5–6 mm, bright shining red; horopito's are round, dark red to black, 3–6 mm across. Mountain alseuosmia grows in montane forest, in the North Island from Te Moehau and Mt Pirongia south, and in the South Island mainly in the west, from North-West Nelson to near Okarito; horopito grows on the North, South and Stewart Islands, east of the main divide too. No record of mountain alseuosmia as food was found (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mountain alseuosmia

lookalikes.howToTell: Northland horopito is known only from Mt Manaia and Bream Head at Whangārei Heads and from Logues Bush near Wellsford, so elsewhere it is not Northland horopito. Horopito's leaves are dull green and blotched with red, at least in exposed places, with the midvein inconspicuous above; Northland horopito's are glossy, without blemishes or blotches, with a conspicuous pale cream to yellow-green midvein above and a red midvein beneath. Both have white leaf undersides; horopito's are often pink-flushed, and Northland horopito's leaf buds and young leaves are usually hairy. Northland horopito's leaves are usually larger, 3.5–11 × 1.8–4.5 cm against 2–6 (rarely 8) × 1–3 cm, though the sizes overlap. Northland horopito is an upright shrub or small tree up to 7 m tall; horopito is a shrub up to 2 m, sometimes 3.5 m. Northland horopito's ripe fruit is black, egg-shaped to oblong, 6.4–9.8 mm long; horopito's is round, dark red to black, 3–6 mm across. Northland horopito is Threatened – Nationally Critical, and no record of it as food was found (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Northland horopito
