preparation.text: Dry and grind as a pepper substitute, or use the leaves fresh, whole or torn into large pieces, and lift them out before serving — they are thick and leathery and do not soften much when cooked. Very potent — start with far less than you think.

recipes.method: Written for wild horopito; the page names no species. 1 cup (250 ml) coarse pink sea salt; the zest of 1 lemon; the zest of 1 orange; 5 fresh horopito leaves; 2 tablespoons (30 ml) dried oregano; 1 tablespoon (15 ml) dried garlic granules. Spread the horopito leaves and the lemon and orange zest in a shallow dish and leave them on a warm windowsill for about a week, until completely dry; or dry them on a small baking tray in the oven at 80 °C for 2 hours. Put everything in a food processor and pulse to a coarse salt flecked with herbs, or pound it in a mortar and pestle. Store it in an airtight jar and sprinkle it over roast vegetables, meat or fish. The author calls it a horopito-infused citrus salt.
recipes.title: Horopito spice rub

recipes.method: Written for fresh horopito leaves in New Zealand. 190 ml water; 60 ml vinegar; 125 ml sugar; 1 teaspoon salt; a good handful of fresh horopito leaves; 3–6 garlic cloves, to taste; ¼ red capsicum; ⅓ medium carrot; 1 tablespoon cornflour; 10–15 cm piece of fresh ginger. Bring the water, vinegar, sugar and salt to a simmer in a saucepan. Add the horopito leaves, tearing them a little so they give up their heat and flavour, and simmer for 5–10 minutes. Meanwhile, finely chop or mince the garlic, deseed the capsicum and chop it as finely as you can, and finely grate the carrot. Strain out the horopito. Add the garlic, capsicum and carrot to the liquid and simmer for another 5–10 minutes. Mix the cornflour with a little more water, stir it into the hot liquid and simmer for about a minute, until it turns translucent. Take the pan off the heat. Grate the ginger, squeeze the juice out of the gratings by hand into the pan and stir it in. Pour the hot sauce into hot sterilised jars and seal. It keeps sealed in a cool, dark place for up to 6 months; refrigerate it to be sure. The author uses it as you would sweet chilli sauce.
recipes.title: Sweet horopito sauce

recipes.method: Written for dried horopito in New Zealand. Serves 4. For the granita: 125 ml golden caster sugar; 1½ teaspoons dried horopito; 100 ml cold water; 500 g strawberries, hulled and halved. For the vanilla cream: 250 g crème fraîche; 250 ml cream; 3–4 tablespoons golden icing sugar, sifted; 3 teaspoons vanilla extract or paste; edible flowers to serve (optional). Put the sugar, horopito and water in a saucepan and bring to the boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Turn off the heat and leave to infuse for at least 10 minutes, then strain through a fine sieve. Blend the strawberries with the horopito syrup until smooth, pour into a shallow tray and freeze. After 30 minutes, scrape the ice crystals from the edges into the middle with a fork. Freeze for another 30 minutes and scrape again, and repeat twice more, about 2 hours in all, then keep it frozen until you serve. Whip the crème fraîche, cream, icing sugar and vanilla to soft peaks. Spoon or pipe the cream into glasses, top with the granita and any flowers, and serve straight away.
recipes.title: Strawberry and horopito granita with vanilla cream

recipes.method: Written for dried horopito in New Zealand. Makes 10 large buns. 25 g butter; 300 ml milk; 75 ml water; 30 g honey; 375 g plain flour; 75 g wholemeal flour; 1 teaspoon dried horopito; 10 g sea salt; 10 g active dried yeast. Warm the butter, milk, water and honey in a small saucepan over low heat for about a minute, stirring now and then, just enough to take the chill off the milk and melt the butter — don't let it simmer. Put both flours, the horopito, salt and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer, pour in the warm milk mixture, stir, and leave it alone for 2 minutes until bubbly and spongy. Knead with the dough hook on medium speed for 5 minutes. Meanwhile heat the oven to 100 °C (85 °C fan) for 5 minutes, then turn it off. Cover the bowl with a damp tea towel and leave it in the warm oven to rise for 1 hour. Grease two baking trays. Turn the dough out, cut it into 85–90 g pieces, shape them into buns and space them well apart on the trays. Cover with damp tea towels, warm the oven again for 5 minutes at the same setting, turn it off and put the buns in for a second rise of about 30 minutes, or 10–15 minutes more if they have not doubled. Take them out, heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan) and bake for 10–12 minutes until golden, turning the trays halfway. Rest for 10 minutes before eating. Ovens vary, so check the dough as you go.
recipes.title: Horopito buns

recipes.method: Written for dried horopito in New Zealand. Serves 6–10. 500 g beef mince; 45 ml (3 tablespoons) vegetable oil; 2 onions, sliced; 8 garlic cloves, sliced; a thumb of fresh ginger, sliced; 1–2 teaspoons chilli flakes, to taste; 1 tablespoon coriander seeds; 2 teaspoons dried horopito; 2 teaspoons dried oregano; 250 g button mushrooms, sliced; 1–2 carrots, sliced about 1 cm thick; 2 teaspoons turmeric; 400 g can chopped tomatoes; 400 ml can coconut milk; 125 ml soy sauce; 400 g can baked beans. Fry the onions, garlic, ginger, chilli and coriander seeds in 2 tablespoons of the oil in a saucepan over medium-high heat until golden, then tip them into a bowl. Add the last tablespoon of oil, then the mince and horopito, and cook until the meat breaks up and browns. Add the oregano, mushrooms and carrot. Return the onion mixture, stir in the turmeric, then add the tomatoes, coconut milk, soy sauce and enough water to cover everything by 2 cm. Bring to the boil, then keep at a gentle boil for 30 minutes, stirring several times and keeping the meat covered with liquid. Stir in the baked beans, cook 15 minutes more, and season with salt or more soy. A little horopito goes a long way.
recipes.title: Mince, horopito and baked bean stew

recipes.method: Written for horopito leaves picked in New Zealand bush and dried; the author picks the darker red leaves for a stronger pepper flavour. Serves 4. 1 tablespoon butter or oil; 1 large onion, chopped; 500 g lamb shoulder, in 2 cm dice; 2 tablespoons flour (brown rice flour for gluten-free); 1 tablespoon smoked paprika; 2 teaspoons dried oregano; ½ teaspoon salt; ¼ teaspoon cayenne; 1 litre stock or water; 2 tablespoons tomato paste; 4 horopito leaves (or 2 bay leaves); 2 carrots and 2 potatoes, in 2 cm cubes; chopped parsley, cooked pasta and sour cream to serve. Soften the onion gently in the butter or oil in a large casserole over low heat, about 5 minutes. Toss the lamb with the flour, paprika, oregano, salt and cayenne, add it to the onion, turn up the heat and brown lightly. Add the stock or water, tomato paste and horopito leaves, cover, bring to a gentle simmer and cook on low for 1 hour. Add the carrots and potatoes and simmer 40–50 minutes more until tender. Season with more cayenne and salt, scatter with parsley and serve with pasta, sour cream and wilted winter greens. In a slow cooker: after browning, cook everything but the vegetables on low for 5–6 hours, adding them for the last hour.
recipes.title: Lamb and horopito goulash

recipes.method: Written for dried horopito in New Zealand. Serves 6–8. 2 tablespoons butter; 200 ml milk; 300 ml cream; 1 bay leaf; salt and pepper; 1.5 kg red-skinned kūmara; 2 pinches of horopito (or chopped fresh thyme); 50 g Parmesan. Heat the oven to 200 °C and butter an ovenproof dish about 30 × 20 × 6 cm. Bring the milk, cream and bay leaf to the boil, simmer a few minutes, take off the heat and season. Slice the kūmara thinly and layer it neatly in the dish. Pour over the hot cream, sprinkle with the horopito and shake the dish to spread the liquid. Scatter with Parmesan, cover with foil and bake for about 50 minutes, until a skewer goes easily into the kūmara.
recipes.title: Kūmara gratin with horopito

recipes.method: Written for dried horopito in New Zealand. 250 ml (1 cup) packed fresh basil leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) packed fresh spinach leaves; 125 ml (½ cup) freshly grated Parmesan; 125 ml (½ cup) extra virgin olive oil; 80 ml (⅓ cup) pine nuts or peanuts; 3 teaspoons minced garlic; ¼ teaspoon salt, plus more to taste; ⅛ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, plus more to taste; 1 teaspoon dried horopito (or about 30 ml fresh). Pound the basil, spinach and nuts in a mortar and pestle (or pulse in a food processor) until they start to break down. Add the garlic, horopito and Parmesan and grind a little more. Drizzle in the oil slowly until it looks like pesto, then season with salt and pepper to taste. Serve with fresh bread or stirred through pasta, and keep it in an airtight container in the fridge.
recipes.title: Horopito and basil pesto

summary.text:
Fiercely hot native leaf — a genuine NZ spice.
In New Zealand it grows on the North, South and Stewart Islands, from latitude 36° 30′ south.

warnings: The heat is genuine and builds gradually, so you may not feel it at first, and milk does not cool it. Do not chew a whole leaf to test it.
Horopito can numb some of your taste buds for a while, so what you eat or drink afterwards tastes odd; the more you have, the stronger the effect.

identification.text:
A large tree with big compound leaves of five to seven leaflets spread like fingers from one stalk. Upright cones of white flowers in spring. The nuts sit one or two to a thick green husk covered in short spikes, and are large, glossy and rounded with one pale patch. Sweet chestnut husks are densely bristly like a hedgehog and hold two or three flattened nuts with a pointed tuft.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Tree 10–15–(about 25) m tall. Twigs stout, glabrous with prominent leaf scars and large reddish brown, very viscid buds. Leaflets 5–7, sessile; central leaflets mostly 15–35 × 6–14 cm (basal leaflets smaller), obovate […], irregularly crenate-serrate. Panicles to about 30 cm high, broad-cylindric. […] Petals 1–1.7 cm long including narrow claw; limb more or less broad-oblong, white with yellow to red spot near base, very undulate and recurved. […] Capsule to 6 cm diameter, subglobose, echinate. Seeds 1–2, 3–5 cm diameter, usually more or less subglobose, often somewhat asymmetric, dark shining brown with prominent, elongated, white hilum.
A fertile hybrid, A. × carnea, is commonly cultivated in New Zealand, but spontaneous trees have not been reported. It has scarcely viscid buds, deep pink flowers and the capsules have few prickles.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaves first. Sweet chestnut's are single, long (about 15–32 cm), oblong and boldly toothed; horse chestnut's are hand-shaped, with five to seven leaflets spreading from one stalk. Horse chestnut's leaflets are toothed too, so teeth alone do not separate them. Both cases are spiny; sweet chestnut's is covered in many long, fine spines, horse chestnut's in short, more widely spaced spikes. Sweet chestnut's case usually holds two or more nuts with a tufted tip; horse chestnut's usually holds one round, glossy, dark brown conker with a large pale scar, sometimes two. Some grafted sweet chestnut varieties bear a single large nut, so nut count alone does not decide it. Sweet chestnut is edible.
lookalikes.name: Sweet chestnut

lookalikes.howToTell: Black walnut is edible. Look at the leaves: horse chestnut's have five to seven leaflets spreading like fingers from one point; black walnut's are long, with 15–23 leaflets set in pairs along a central stalk. Then the fruit: horse chestnut's case is up to 6 cm and covered in short spines, and holds one or two smooth, glossy, dark brown seeds with a large pale scar; black walnut's husk is round, 3–4 cm across, smooth and brownish-green, around one nut with a very hard, sharply ridged shell.
lookalikes.name: Black walnut

summary.text:
Conkers. The park tree whose shiny brown nuts look like sweet chestnuts and are poisonous.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): South Island: Canterbury, occasional, but nowhere fully naturalised. Horse chestnut is very commonly cultivated in both North and South Islands, especially in cooler areas.

warnings: Contains aesculin. Eating horse chestnuts causes stomach pain, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea; children who ate them have become weak, drowsy and unsteady, with muscle twitching and paralysis, and in adults 1–4 seeds have caused massive vomiting, facial swelling, low blood pressure and collapse. Keep children from eating the seeds from fallen cases.
Never roast a nut you found under a tree with hand-shaped leaves.

habitat.text: Grass on rich soil: pasture and paddocks, lawns, parks and other urban grassland, and forest margins, singly or in groups, and often in rings. In New Zealand it has been collected among browntop and Chewings fescue, on bare soil under stone-fruit trees, and once each under pine and oak. A Waikato forager finds it in paddocks that have not been cropped and resown for some years. Elsewhere it is known from well-manured fields, beside stables and bridle paths, on roadside verges and along wood edges and hedgerows.

identification.text:
A large, stout, white mushroom with a thick ring and a strong smell of aniseed or almond. The cap is usually 8–20 cm across, sometimes to 25 cm (Canterbury collections were 4–12 cm); egg-shaped or hemispherical when young, it opens convex and then almost flat. It is smooth and silky to finely fibrous, white to cream, and turns yellowish with age and where it is bruised or handled, most at the edge; old caps may crack or grow pale brownish scales. The edge is rolled under when young and often keeps scraps of veil.
The gills are free of the stem and crowded. They are pale when young — whitish, pale grey or pale pink — and stay pale for a long time, then turn grey-brown and finally dark chocolate brown. The spore print is dark brown.
The stem is 5–15 cm long and 1.5–3 cm thick, cylindrical, sometimes with a slight bulb at the base, white, turning yellowish below the ring with age and where bruised. The ring is the best feature: large, thick, double and persistent, and in a closed cap its underside is a circle of thick, cogwheel-like patches around the stem. There is no sac (volva) at the stem base.
The flesh is white and firm and changes little when cut. It yellows slowly where bruised, but the cut stem base never turns bright chrome yellow straight away. The smell — aniseed, almond or marzipan, from benzaldehyde — is the key test: smell every one.
Similar Agaricus in New Zealand: Agaricus crocodilinus has been confused with it. A native forest mushroom, an undescribed Agaricus of deep leaf litter in Auckland podocarp–broadleaf forest (the Hidden Forest's 'forest arvensis'), looks like it but has a simple, single ring with no cogwheel underneath, no almond smell and no strong yellowing; its edibility is unknown.

lookalikes.howToTell: Death cap's gills are white, turning cream, sometimes with a faint pink tinge, as it ages, but never the chocolate brown of a mature horse mushroom. Its swollen stem base sits in a white, sack-like volva that may be buried, so dig up the whole base of every mushroom. Young horse mushroom gills also stay pale for a long time, so pale gills alone do not separate them: check for a volva, look under the ring for horse mushroom's thick cogwheel patches, and smell it — horse mushroom smells strongly of aniseed or almond, while young death caps have almost no smell. A spore print confirms it: horse mushroom dark chocolate brown, death cap white. Cap colour and the ring do not separate them: death caps are usually yellow-green, olive or bronze, but an all-white form occurs, and both have a ring. Death cap grows with trees, especially oak; horse mushroom is a grassland mushroom, but it also grows at forest margins and has been collected under oak and pine in New Zealand, so grass near trees is no guarantee. Half a mature cap is reportedly a lethal dose for an adult.
lookalikes.name: Death cap

lookalikes.howToTell: Field mushroom is smaller, its gills are pink when young, its ring is thin and simple and often disappears, and its cut flesh blushes reddish. It smells pleasant but not of aniseed, and does not turn yellow. Horse mushroom is bigger and stouter, with a thick double ring that has cogwheel-like patches underneath, it yellows slowly where bruised, and it smells of aniseed or almond.
lookalikes.name: Field mushroom

lookalikes.howToTell: From a distance the two look very alike: both are big and pale with a large ring. Skirt webcap grows in soil under mānuka, kānuka or beech; its gills start whitish or pale buff and turn rusty brown, not pink then chocolate; rusty spores stain its ring and stem; young ones are wrapped in a thick web-like veil; and it has no smell. Its edibility is unknown and close relatives contain lethal toxins. Horse mushroom grows in grass, sometimes at forest margins, with pink-to-chocolate gills, a dark chocolate spore print, a thick double ring with cogwheel-like patches underneath, and a smell of aniseed or almond.
lookalikes.name: Skirt webcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Macro mushroom is another big, white grassland Agaricus with a large ring that is cogwheel-like underneath, a brown spore print and a smell of almond, and Biota of New Zealand says the two are confused. Both are eaten. Macro mushroom's gills start whitish to tan, with no pink stage; horse mushroom's start pale pink to white, then turn grey and brown. Macro mushroom's stem is stouter, with girdles of small white scales below the ring, and old ones smell of ammonia. In New Zealand mycologists separate them by spore size under a microscope.
lookalikes.name: Macro mushroom

preparation.text:
Brush off any dirt; they soak up water, so if you rinse them, pat them dry and leave them in the fridge for a few hours before cooking. Twist or cut the stem out of the cap and chop it into the dish.
The flavour is rich, with a sweet note of aniseed, and the texture firm and meaty, though older ones can be a little tough. Use them in any recipe that calls for large flat or portobello mushrooms: stuffed and baked whole, in risotto, omelettes, soups and sauces. To fry, slice them and cook in a little oil or butter over medium heat for 5–7 minutes, stirring now and then, until they give up their juice and turn golden; season.
Mature caps picked after rain can release so much water that they stew rather than fry. Pour the liquid off, keep it for stock or reduce it, add a little more fat and carry on.

recipes.method: Serves 2 as a starter. 2 large horse mushrooms; 2 shallots, finely diced; a little butter; a handful of sweet cicely leaves; 2 tbsp cream cheese; a little olive oil; 2 slices of sourdough; any other mushrooms you found; a few wild herbs and flowers. Carefully twist the stems out of 2 large horse mushrooms — still domed, with pale gills and firm caps — without damaging the caps, and chop the stems finely. Fry them gently with 2 finely diced shallots in a little butter for 4 minutes. Finely shred a handful of sweet cicely leaves, keeping a few fronds to garnish, and mix with the stems, shallots and 2 tbsp cream cheese; season. Stuff the caps, set them on a baking tray, season, drizzle with a little olive oil and bake in a medium oven for 10 minutes. Meanwhile toast 2 slices of sourdough and sauté any other mushrooms you found. Put a cap on each toast (on a slice of a big mushroom, if you have one) and dress with the smaller mushrooms and a few wild herbs and flowers. The author says tarragon works instead of the sweet cicely.
recipes.title: Horse mushrooms stuffed with sweet cicely

recipes.method: Written for horse mushrooms in the Waikato; vary the amounts to taste and to how many mushrooms you have. Horse mushrooms; olive oil; 5 garlic cloves; 1 small red chilli, seeds removed; 1 onion; parsley; 2 big tomatoes; salt and black pepper; 1 tsp honey; Parmesan. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Cut the stems off as close to the caps as you can and chop them to add to the topping. Finely chop the garlic and chilli and fry them gently in a little olive oil; add the onion, finely chopped, and fry together. Add the tomatoes, finely chopped, season, and add the parsley. Stir in the honey and cook for about 10 minutes, until reduced. Turn the caps in a dish of olive oil, spooning it over them, then lay them on a baking tray and bake for about 5 minutes. Take them out, spoon the tomato mixture generously over them and top with grated Parmesan. Grill for 6–7 minutes, watching closely, and serve at once. Bacon or other ingredients can go into the topping.
recipes.title: Grilled spicy horse mushrooms with tomato

recipes.method: Use large horse mushrooms that are still rounded, not yet flattening out. 2 large horse mushrooms; ½ red onion, chopped; 1 tbsp butter; 1 tbsp Stilton; 1 tbsp breadcrumbs; olive oil; flaky salt and black pepper; a small bunch of herbs, such as parsley, coriander, dill, chives and thyme. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Clean the mushrooms, take out the stems and chop them. Set the caps gill side up on a baking tray, put half the butter in each, season, and add a sprig of thyme to each (just the leaves if the stalks are woody). Bake for 10 minutes. Meanwhile fry the onion in a little olive oil for a minute, add the chopped stems and cook until soft, and chop the herbs. Spoon the onion and stem mixture into the baked caps and scatter over half the herbs. Crumble the Stilton on top, sprinkle with the breadcrumbs, drizzle with olive oil and bake for about 5 minutes more, until the cheese is melted and bubbling. Serve scattered with the rest of the herbs.
recipes.title: Stuffed and baked horse mushrooms with Stilton

recipes.method: 450 g horse mushrooms, cleaned and sliced; 225 g linguine or fettuccine; 2 tbsp olive oil; 4 garlic cloves, minced; 1 small onion, finely chopped; 240 ml double cream; 120 g grated Parmesan, plus extra to serve; 2 tbsp chopped parsley, plus extra to serve; salt and pepper. Cook the pasta until al dente and drain. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat and fry the garlic and onion until the onion is translucent. Add the mushrooms and cook for about 5 minutes, until they give up their juice and start to brown. Pour in the cream, bring to a simmer and cook for about 5 minutes, until slightly thickened. Stir in the Parmesan and cook for 2 minutes more, until the sauce is smooth. Toss the pasta through the sauce, season, add the parsley and toss again. Serve hot with more Parmesan and parsley.
recipes.title: Creamy horse mushroom pasta

recipes.method: Serves 4 as a first course. About 700 ml (3 US cups) shredded green cabbage, lightly salted; about 240 ml (1 US cup) sliced horse mushroom; 1 tbsp umeboshi (Japanese pickled plums, about 5), stoned; 2 tbsp vegetable oil; 2 tsp dark sesame oil; ½ tsp sugar; salt. Heat both oils in a large frying pan over medium heat, add the mushroom and sauté for 1 minute. Add the cabbage and stir until just wilted, then stir in the sugar and plums and cook for 1 minute more. Serve hot or at room temperature. Without umeboshi, use a dash of sour vinegar and 1 tbsp minced rhubarb. The author likes to add about 80 ml (⅓ US cup) of fresh or rehydrated hijiki seaweed.
recipes.title: Cabbage and horse mushroom with pickled plums

recipes.method: Serves 1, from Ralph Jackson, Lincolnshire. 1 large horse mushroom; 2 thin slices of cooked or smoked ham; 1 spring onion, roughly chopped; 1 tomato, sliced; 1 celery stick, thinly sliced; a knob of butter; cress; black pepper. Take out the stem and put the butter in its place. Lay the ham on the cap, then the spring onion, tomato and celery. Microwave for 2 minutes, less if the mushroom is smaller than a dinner plate's width. Garnish with cress and black pepper.
recipes.title: Ralph's horse mushroom feast

recipes.method: Written for cultivated white flat mushrooms, which large horse mushroom caps can replace. Serves 4. Mushrooms: 6 flat mushrooms; 60 ml (¼ cup) olive oil; juice of ½ lemon; 2 tbsp harissa paste. Flatbreads: 250 ml (1 cup) thick Greek yoghurt; 1 cup self-raising flour. Yoghurt dip: 125 ml (½ cup) thick Greek yoghurt; juice of ½ lemon; a handful of soft herbs, such as mint, coriander, flat-leaf parsley or dill, finely chopped. Stir the dip ingredients together and chill. Mix the oil, harissa and lemon juice, toss the mushrooms in it and leave to marinate for at least 30 minutes. Mix the yoghurt and flour into a smooth dough, adding flour if it is sticky, divide it into 4 and roll each out on a well-floured surface. Cook the flatbreads on a barbecue or in a dry frying pan over medium-high heat for 2–4 minutes a side, until charred in spots and golden, and keep them warm in a tea towel. Cook the mushrooms on a hot barbecue or in a frying pan for 4–5 minutes a side, until golden and cooked through. Spread the flatbreads with the yoghurt dip and top with the mushrooms, whole or sliced, and more herbs. Without harissa, mix tomato paste, olive oil, garlic, salt, cumin, chilli flakes and coriander seed; shop-bought wraps can replace the flatbreads.
recipes.title: Harissa mushrooms with yoghurt in flatbread

recipes.method: Written for cultivated small portobello mushrooms, which sliced horse mushrooms can replace. Serves 2. Pastry: 225 g flour, sifted; ½ tsp salt; 150 g cold butter, cubed; 60 ml ice water. Filling: 40 g butter; 1 onion, finely chopped; 2 garlic cloves, finely chopped; 120 g goat's cheese, crumbled; 200 g ricotta; 2 tbsp finely chopped thyme; 125 ml (½ cup) finely chopped basil, plus extra to serve; grated rind of 1 lemon; 2 eggs, lightly beaten; salt and pepper; 250 g mushrooms, thickly sliced; a drizzle of olive oil. Pulse the flour, salt and butter in a food processor to fine crumbs, add the ice water and pulse until it just comes together. Knead gently into a dough, wrap and chill for at least 30 minutes. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Roll the pastry out 3 mm thick on a floured surface, cut a 30 cm round, put it on a lined tray and chill for 15 minutes more. Meanwhile, sauté the onion and garlic in half the butter until tender, 2–3 minutes, and set aside. Melt the rest of the butter and sauté the mushrooms for 2–3 minutes, until soft; drain off the juice. Mix the onion and garlic with 80 g of the goat's cheese, the ricotta, thyme, basil, lemon rind and half the egg; season. Spread it over the pastry, leaving a 3 cm border, lay the mushrooms on top, drizzle with oil and fold the edges in. Brush the pastry edge with the rest of the egg and bake for 20–25 minutes, until crisp and golden. Serve warm with the rest of the goat's cheese and more basil.
recipes.title: Mushroom, thyme and goat’s cheese galette

Retrieved 14/09/2026; re-read 29/10/2026 at revision 1380236869 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agaricus_arvensis). From 29/10/2026 only the summary's first sentence is verbatim; the identification and habitat text is restated and combined with the sources below, and Wikipedia's British season (now May–October, was July–November), nettles (citation needed) and North American cypress and spruce associations were dropped from habitat.

Its wood sorrel, bush vetch and ground elder garnish not repeated (not catalogue plants). Origin 'introduced' stands.

Owner's links, 29/10/2026 (all retrieved 29/10/2026): The Hidden Forest 'Agaricus arvensis' https://www.hiddenforest.co.nz/fungi/family/agaricaceae/agari10.htm — cap 80–200 mm, white to cream, yellowing at the margin, brownish scales with age; gills free, crowded, pink young, dark chocolate-brown; stipe 80–150 × 15–30 mm, sometimes slightly bulbous, bruising yellowish; ring large, double, thick, persistent, cog-wheel-like scales below; flesh slowly yellowing in the stipe base and cap margin when cut; odour strong almond/anise, 'a key character'; pasturelands, urban greenspaces, forest margins; widespread and common; autumn; introduced, long established; edible; spore print dark brown; A. crocodilinus 'claimed to be often mistaken for A. arvensis' (identification, habitat, summary). The Hidden Forest 'Agaricus species' (Forest Arvensis) https://www.hiddenforest.co.nz/fungi/family/agaricaceae/agari01.htm — endemic, Auckland, lowland podocarp–broadleaf forest, deep leaf litter; simple ring, no cog-wheel; no almond odour; no strong yellowing; edibility 'Dont know' (identification). Biota of New Zealand https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/1cb17cbc-36b9-11d5-9548-00d0592d548c — Exotic, Present; 1st record Berkeley 1855; 'Confused with A. crocodilanus'; vernacular Horse Mushroom; hosts Agrostis capillaris, Festuca rubra subsp. commutata, Pinus and Quercus (1 PDD record each); collections Mid Canterbury 16, Auckland 6, Otago Lakes 2, Central Otago 1, Northland 1; Massee 1899 description (pileus 10–25 cm, stained pale yellow when bruised, flesh yellowish when cut, ring double, Northern Island, in pastures often in rings, 'Edible; preferred by many to the mushroom') and Mitchell & Walter 1999 Canterbury description (pileus 40–120 mm, white becoming yellow, yellowing intensified by bruising; lamellae free, crowded, pale grey when young, finally brown; stipe 50–150 × 15–30 mm, base round, amber yellow below the annulus with age; annulus cog-wheel-like; flesh white, little effect on cutting, yellowing on bruising; odour of anise; lawns or pasture, also bare soil under stone fruit trees) (identification, habitat, summary). Landcare Research Fungal Guide image PK 7007 https://fungalguide.landcareresearch.co.nz/WebForms/ViewLargerImage.aspx?isGenus=false&PK=7007 — cap up to 20 cm or more, introduced, always on grass in parks, cap 'sometimes stains slightly yellowish with age, but the flesh inside the stalk never stains yellow', edible and good (identification, habitat).

Owner's links, continued: Mycologic NZ 'Wild Edible Mushrooms of New Zealand' https://www.mycologic.nz/post/wild-edible-mushrooms-of-new-zealand — names horse mushroom among NZ edible field mushrooms; over fifty Agaricus species in NZ; yellow stainers (section Xanthodermatei) chemical smell, yellow staining, stem cut in half (yellow-stainer card: 'one of its yellow-staining relatives'). Its genus-wide rule that any yellow staining means don't eat is not used here, because horse mushroom itself yellows; the card gives the speed, place and smell of the staining instead. Number 8 Network, 'Mushrooms galore!' (Annette Taylor, pictures and 'mushroom wrangler' David Riddell, Gordonton, Waikato, 19/04/2017) https://www.number8network.co.nz/2017/04/19/lashings-of-delicious-mushroom/ — 'the biggest of the local mushroom varieties', 15 cm or more; 'deliciously rich flavour with a hint of aniseed'; mushrooms from mid-May one year, early April the next; harvested once fully open; rinse, pat dry, fridge several hours; look in areas not cropped and regrassed in recent years (summary, habitat, preparation, recipe). Galloway Wild Foods 'Horse Mushrooms – Edibility, Identification, Distribution' https://gallowaywildfoods.com/july-horse-mushrooms/ — yellow stainer 'virtually identical'; 'If the base of the stipe turns chrome yellow when bruised, don't eat it'; death caps in the same hedgerows and field edges; young pink-gilled caps sweetly fragrant aniseed, light, crisp and succulent; older specimens meatier, good for soups; named for horse-manured fields; wood edges, hedgerows, rings; cadmium and copper on roadside verges (edible parts, preparation, habitat, warning 1, cards). Its raw sliced young-cap salad is still not used (see the 25/10/2026 recipe line).

Owner's links, continued: ANGAIR newsletter, Neil Tucker, 'Do you know the difference? Mushroom look-alikes' (June 2016, PDF) — Australian; A. xanthodermus stains yellow when cap or stipe are scratched or rubbed, toxicity varies among people; Amanitas have white gills. Not used: its 'can have a chemical smell' for horse mushroom, which every other source contradicts (aniseed or almond; a chemical smell points to the yellow stainers). Mushroom Exam, 'Field Mushroom look-alikes' (09/10/2023, read via r.jina.ai; the site refuses plain requests) — larger than 15 cm, aniseed or almond odour. Not used: its 'gills initially white before turning pink'; the NZ descriptions give pale grey or pink, and the identification text says whitish, pale grey or pale pink. FungiOz, 'Cortinarius australiensis, a poisonous horse mushroom look-alike' https://www.fungioz.com/blog/how-to-tell-the-difference-between-the-edible-horse-mushroom-and-the-poisonous-cortinarius-australiensis-mushroom — from a distance the two look very similar; the look-alike's thick cortina mimics an Agaricus ring; its gills pale mustard then rust brown; rust-coloured spore stain on the stem; horse mushroom gills cream to pink to dark brown, cogwheel ring, horse mushroom 'can be a little tough' (warning 2, preparation). A reader's comment questions whether that species is actually poisonous; so warning 2 follows Wikipedia 'Austrocortinarius australiensis' revision 1349884782 (CC BY-SA 4.0): edibility unknown, 'should be avoided, as some of its close relatives contain lethal toxins'; whitish cap, ring remnants stained dark brown by spores, gills pale straw then rusty brown, no discernible odour, bulbous stipe; in New Zealand grows with Leptospermum (Grgurinovic 1997). iNaturalist NZ, taxon 1433823, place 6803: 67 research-grade wild observations (retrieved 29/10/2026).

Owner's links, continued: Mushroom Appreciation, 'Meadow Mushroom' https://www.mushroom-appreciation.com/meadow-mushroom.html — horse mushroom strong anise scent, lightly bruises yellow when handled; yellow stainer turns bright yellow immediately when cut or bruised, smells of iodine, phenol stronger when cooked; younger pink-gilled Agaricus best eating (field-mushroom card, edible parts). Its North American destroying angels, A. californicus and A. fissuratus are not New Zealand species and were not used. Urban Mushrooms (Penelope Zeller) 'Horse Mushroom' https://urbanmushrooms.com/index.php?id=18 — cap 7–20 cm, bruising yellow, odour almond or anise; stalk bruising yellowish 'but flesh at base is not yellow'; ring with cogwheel patches; field mushroom pink gills young and smaller; yellow foot Agaricus smells bad, yellow flesh at stem base (identification, cards, recipe). Not used: its gills 'gray/white becoming blackish brown (never pink)' — the NZ and other descriptions include pink young gills. Its general 'Cooking with Mushrooms of Lawns and Gardens' page https://urbanmushrooms.com/index.php?id=11 — be certain lawns and parks are chemical free, mushrooms soak up metals and chemicals (warning 1). The Wild Foodie, 'Horse Mushrooms and how to cook them' (12/07/2018, updated 09/09/2023) https://www.wildfoodie.co.uk/post/stuffed-and-baked-horse-mushrooms — brush, don't wash; slice and fry 5–7 minutes (preparation, two recipes). Not used: its 'mild, pleasant odour', which every other source contradicts (aniseed or almond), its nutrition claims, and the cow parsley in its wild-herb option, which is easily confused with poison hemlock.

Owner's links, continued: Gigaflop, 'Agaricus Recipes', Wild Mushroom Cookery https://www.gigaflop.co.uk/mushcook/agaricus.shtml (live page refuses requests; read from the Internet Archive capture of 02/09/2015) — mature specimens picked after rain release so much water they boil rather than fry, 'especially true of the Horse Mushroom'; pour off and keep the liquid, add more fat (preparation); 'Ralph's Horse Mushroom Feast' from Ralph Jackson, Lincolnshire (recipe; the page's ingredient line labels the mushroom 'Agaricus augustus', the prince, under a horse-mushroom title — kept as written for a horse mushroom). Not used: its cream of mushroom soup, whose 450 g of butter to 500 g mushrooms looks like a typo; its devilled and Monte Carlo mushrooms, written for button mushrooms. First Nature 'Wild mushroom recipes' https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/~recipes.php — 'Chicken Campestris', written for field mushrooms (recipe). Not used: its wild mushroom soup, where '100g (about 1 lb)' gives two quantities that do not agree. Meadow Mushrooms NZ recipes https://www.meadowmushrooms.co.nz/recipes (Rachelle Joilin, 22/09/2026) — two recipes for large cultivated mushrooms; not added: near duplicates of the stuffed-cap and fried-mushroom recipes already here ('Ricotta & Herb Stuffed Portabellos', 'Basic stuffed mushrooms'), the bao buns (deep-fried small mushrooms), and dishes where mushrooms are one ingredient among many.

Also read (29/10/2026): Pat O'Reilly, First Nature 'Agaricus arvensis — Horse Mushroom' https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/agaricus-arvensis.php — 'In New Zealand this species is commonly known as the Snowball Mushroom'; name from horse manure or perhaps size; cap 8–20 cm, exceptionally over 30 cm, yellowing with age and where bruised; double cog-wheel ring; stem base 'does not rapidly turn bright yellow', unlike the yellow stainer; aniseed smell; manured meadows, bridle paths; copper and cadmium, 'an occasional treat'; use in any recipe calling for large (portobello) mushrooms, risotto, omelettes, soups, sauces; check gills pink or brown, not white (summary, identification, habitat, warning 1, preparation, death-cap card). First Nature 'Agaricus xanthodermus — Yellow Stainer' — stem flesh 'quickly turns from white to chrome yellow, most markedly at the stem base'; cap rim chrome yellow when scratched, most marked when young and fresh; 'a few of the edible Agaricus species do bruise slightly yellow, and so it is important to check all characteristics, including odour'; looks very like horse mushroom; ink, phenol or iodine, strongest at the cut stem base, intensified on cooking; bulbous base; large white pendulous ring (yellow-stainer cards). First Nature 'Amanita phalloides — Deathcap' — gills pure white turning cream, sometimes with a slight pinkish tinge; sack-like volva; all-white form; buttons virtually odourless; hardwoods, especially oak; half a mature cap reportedly lethal. Virtual Mycota 'Amanita phalloides' (pk 321, Ridley 1991; Massee 1899) — lamellae white, spore print white, volva often buried, large white ring (death-cap cards). Wikipedia 'Agaricus arvensis' revision 1380236869 — gills 'remain white for a long time'; confusion with deadly Amanita; A. campestris smaller, no aniseed, smaller ring, no cogwheel; heavy metals in contaminated ground (death-cap and field-mushroom cards, warning 1). Field mushroom: Virtual Mycota 'Agaricus campestris var. campestris' (Mitchell & Walter 1999) flesh 'quickly reddening upon cutting or bruising', as cited on the field-mushroom card; Galloway Wild Foods: 'simple fragile rings, and faintly blushing flesh'.

summary.text:
Agaricus arvensis, the horse mushroom, is a large, robust Agaricus sought after for eating.
It is introduced in New Zealand and long established: it was first recorded here by Berkeley in 1855, and in 1899 Massee knew it from the North Island, growing in pasture. A Waikato forager calls it the biggest of the local mushrooms, and First Nature says it is often called the snowball mushroom in New Zealand. The Hidden Forest calls it widespread and common, but most herbarium collections and 11 of its 15 research-grade New Zealand iNaturalist records are from Canterbury. The name is usually put down to its liking for fields manured by horses, though some say it refers to its size.

warnings: Like other Agaricus, horse mushrooms take up heavy metals, notably cadmium and copper, from contaminated ground. Don't pick them from busy roadsides or from lawns and parks that may be sprayed or fertilised, and treat them as an occasional treat rather than a staple.

Yellow-staining Agaricus, the group around the yellow stainer (A. xanthodermus) and a notable group of poisonous Agaricus, are common in New Zealand as unnamed species, and look like a white field mushroom. Cut through the very base of the stem and scratch the cap edge: if it turns bright chrome yellow almost at once, or smells of ink, phenol or iodine, throw it out. A horse mushroom yellows only slowly and faintly, its cut stem base does not flash bright yellow, and it smells of aniseed or almond.

identification.text:
This is the commonest and most variable of the three species of Lecanopteris in New Zealand. It can be distinguished by its thick rhizomes (>4 mm diameter) with appressed blackish-brown scales, its very variable fronds, coriaceous and bright glossy green laminae, conspicuous veins and hydathodes on the upper lamina surface, and broad lamina lobes.
Epiphytic and terrestrial; creeping or climbing ferns. Rhizomes long-creeping, 3–11 mm diameter, scaly. Rhizome scales clathrate, ovate, 3–7 mm long, 1–2 mm wide, mostly appressed but with the tips sometimes squarrose, blackish-brown, entire. Fronds 45–750 mm long. Stipes 10–350 mm long, pale to chocolate brown, glabrous or with very scattered scales. Laminae very varied, from undivided or variously lobed to deeply 1-pinnatifid; undivided laminae (fertile) narrowly elliptic, 35–220 mm long, 6–30 mm wide, or (sterile) longer and broader, up to 260 mm long and 70 mm wide; lobed or pinnatifid laminae (fertile) ovate to elliptic or broadly ovate to broadly elliptic, 50–425 mm long, 35–350 mm wide, or (sterile) up to 420 mm long and 300 mm wide; lamina alate for 5–40 mm below the lowest lobe, bright glossy green, coriaceous, glabrous or with scattered scales on the costae, especially on young fronds. Lamina lobes (fertile) in 1–15 pairs, 25–185 mm long, 4–30 mm wide, or (sterile) less numerous and wider, in up to 10 pairs and up to 60 mm wide; straight, acute to acuminate, margins entire or wavy, widest about the middle. Veins reticulate, forming 2–3 series of areoles between costa and margin; hydathodes conspicuous on adaxial surface of lamina. Sori round or rarely elliptic, 2.5–5 mm wide, impressed into lamina forming low bulges on adaxial surface, in 1 row either side of costa, medial or closer to the margin; paraphyses absent; exindusiate.
Occasional aberrant forms are found, either crested at the apices or with 2-pinnatifid laminae.

summary.text:
Hound's tongue fern (kōwaowao, pāraharaha) creeps over the ground, rocks and logs or climbs tree trunks, with glossy, leathery fronds that range from undivided to deeply lobed and round sori on the underside. Its current name is Lecanopteris pustulata; it was long known as Microsorum pustulatum, and only the subspecies pustulata grows in New Zealand.
It is abundant throughout the North Island and common in coastal and lowland regions of the South Island, from sea level to over 1050 m, but largely absent from inland high country and much of Otago; it also grows on the Kermadec, Three Kings, Chatham, Solander, Stewart, Antipodes and Auckland Islands, and in eastern Australia and on Norfolk Island. Not Threatened (2023).
It is easily grown from rooted pieces of rhizome, in a hanging basket or large pot or trained over rocks and logs, and once established is drought tolerant and needs little attention.

warnings: Only about seven of New Zealand's roughly 200 ferns are edible. Eat only young fronds you are sure are hound's tongue fern.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to 3–(6) m tall, usually open-branched. Branches rather brittle, bark dark brown; branchlets glabrous. Leaves foetid when bruised, on slender narrowly winged petioles about 8–15 mm long. Stipules truncate, but produced into a usually conspicuous long denticle (subsidiary denticles may be present); ciliolate, with tufts of unequal hairs at tips. Lamina membranous to subcoriaceous, obovate to oblong to broadly ovate (several forms may be on one plant), obtuse, more or less apiculate to mucronulate, (20)–30–50 × (10)–14–20 mm. Reticulations of veins evident, at least below. Flowers solitary, terminal on branchlets. Male without calyx; corolla about 10 mm long, subcampanulate, lobes 5–7, acute, about equal to tube; stamens usually 5–7. Female with minute calyx-teeth; corolla tubular, slightly flaring, lobes 4–5, short, subacute. Drupe pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]
The leaves lie in a single plane on the branchlet and have domatia, small pits on the underside. Plants are male or female. Crushed leaves smell strongly of dung.

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; Hūpiro's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Those figures fit the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa; the North Island's wild subsp. minor has thinner, papery leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) on stalks about 10–18 mm long, and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long. Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Māmāngi's young twigs are hairy; Hūpiro's are hairless. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Mingimingi's young twigs are more or less hairy; Hūpiro's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Swamp coprosma's young twigs are hairy; Hūpiro's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Swamp coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Sand coprosma's young twigs are hairy; Hūpiro's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Sand coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: hūpiro's leaves smell strongly of rotten eggs or dung, Coprosma colensoi's do not. Coprosma colensoi's leaves are leathery and usually 9–15 mm long (up to 20 mm); hūpiro's are thin, usually 30–50 mm long (as small as 20 mm). Coprosma colensoi's flowers hang on bent-down stalks; hūpiro's sit singly at the tips of the branchlets and face upwards. Coprosma colensoi's fruit is crimson, 6–7 mm long; hūpiro's is pale to full orange without red flecks, 7–10 mm long. Stunted hūpiro has small leaves and is easily confused, and the two hybridise freely where they meet, so plants with mixed features are common. No record of Coprosma colensoi's fruit as food was found.
lookalikes.name: Coprosma colensoi

summary.text: Hūpiro, Coprosma foetidissima, also called stinkwood, is a shrub or tree of the family Rubiaceae, endemic to New Zealand. It grows on the North, South, Stewart and Auckland Islands, from Moehau in the North Island southwards.

edibleParts.text: The ripe fruit, raw, dried, or blended with other fruit into fruit leather. It looks like a strawberry but is usually described as dry and insipid, with very little flavour, likened to watermelon bitten close to the rind; its appeal is its colour and crunchy texture. The leaves, cooked as a potherb, raw in salads or dried for tea; young leaves are mild, faintly of cucumber. The flowers, as a garnish.

identification.text:
Herb with short stock, somewhat flaccid, up to 10–(15) cm high at flowering; runners greenish, slender, pilose, up to about 50 cm long and rooting at nodes and tips to form new rosettes. Basal leaves several in rosette; petiole 30–80–(160) mm long, densely pilose; leaflets obovate to narrowly ovate, subacute, obtuse to cuneate at base, bright green above, paler below, usually sparsely to moderately pilose on both surfaces especially along veins, sometimes with only scattered hairs on upper, with margins crenate to obscurely lobed; terminal leaflet 15–55 × 12–30 mm; lateral leaflets equal to terminal or slightly smaller; petiolules 1–5 mm long, pilose. Scape often only slightly exceeding leaves, pilose. Epicalyx segments broadly obovate, pilose, deflexed at fruiting, with 3–5 purple-tipped teeth. Sepals ovate-triangular, about 6–10 mm long, acuminate, purple-tipped, pilose. Petals narrowly obovate, 4–8 mm long, more or less equal to epicalyx segments and sepals, shallowly emarginate to rounded, spreading, bright yellow. Achenes uniformly scattered over and projecting from receptacle; receptacle red, swollen, up to 12 mm long, often slightly constricted near base.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Woodland strawberry has white petals, where Indian strawberry's are bright yellow. Its epicalyx segments (the leafy bracts just beneath the sepals) are narrow and more or less entire; in Indian strawberry they are broadly obovate with 3–5 purple-tipped teeth, about as long as the petals and sepals, and bent back under the fruit. Woodland strawberry leaflets are coarsely serrate in the upper half to two-thirds; Indian strawberry leaflets are crenate to obscurely lobed. Woodland strawberry fruit is usually red, occasionally white, juicy, sweet and fragrant; Indian strawberry fruit is red, dryish and semi-fleshy, with very little flavour. Woodland strawberry can carry 1 to several flowers on a stalk, so a single flower does not separate them, but Indian strawberry flowers are solitary. What does not separate them: both form rosettes with runners rooting at the nodes and tips, both have three-part leaves of overlapping size, petals up to 8 mm long and sepals of overlapping length, both have achenes scattered over and projecting from a swollen red receptacle of similar size, both grow on roadsides, wasteland and forest margins or clearings, both are recorded from Nelson, Canterbury and Dunedin, and both fruit from November to April. Woodland strawberry fruit is edible raw, cooked or as preserves, and its young leaves are also eaten.

preparation.text: Pick the fruit when fully red and firm and use it soon, as it bruises easily. Eat the berries raw, or scatter them over salads, fruit platters, cakes or yoghurt. They can be mixed with other berries to stretch a jam or jelly, and on their own make a mild jelly or juice. To keep them, air-dry or dehydrate the berries, or blend them with more flavourful fruit and dry into fruit leather. Pick young leaves for salads; older leaves are better cooked or dried for tea, and the leaves are usually used sparingly. Leaves can be folded through omelettes, wilted in butter or stirred into soups at the end of cooking.

recipes.method: Ingredients for 6 ice pops: about 250 ml (1 cup) Indian strawberries, 375–500 ml (1½–2 cups) vanilla Greek yoghurt and 2 tablespoons honey. In a food processor, blend three-quarters of the berries with a few spoonfuls of the yoghurt until smooth. Add the rest of the berries and pulse a couple of times to chop them roughly. Tip into a bowl and stir in the honey and enough yoghurt to fill the ice-pop moulds (the author's hold 500 ml in all). Fill the moulds and freeze. The berries taste faint, so use plenty; the vanilla and honey carry their flavour.

summary.text:
Indian strawberry, Potentilla indica, also called mock strawberry, is a creeping herb of the rose family (Rosaceae), native to India and eastern Asia, that spreads by runners rooting into new rosettes. Its leaves have three leaflets and its red fruit looks like a strawberry, but its flowers are bright yellow, where true strawberry's are white. The 1988 Flora of New Zealand calls it Duchesnea indica.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: frequent, especially in hill country from Kaitaia (N. Auckland) south to near New Plymouth and Bay of Plenty, Wellington (Bunnythorpe, Hutt Valley, Wellington City); S.: Nelson (Motueka, Nelson City), Canterbury Plains, Dunedin. First recorded wild in New Zealand in 1935.
Grown in gardens for ground cover and as an ornamental, this species occasionally escapes into the wild. It flowers and fruits for much of the year and locally can become a very persistent pasture pest.
Also known in New Zealand as wild strawberry. Herbarium specimens come from the North Auckland, South Auckland, Taranaki, Wellington, Nelson, Canterbury and Otago land districts, including one collected in 2021 at Bastia Hill, Whanganui.

warnings: The berries are sometimes described as poisonous. A US poison-centre review of mostly small ingestions by young children found that mock strawberries produce no toxicity and that allergic reactions are rare; one child developed hives that resolved after antihistamine.
Use the leaves sparingly; 50 raw leaves may be too many. This advice rests on a single foraging source and names no compound or case of harm.
It is a lawn and garden weed that is controlled with broad-spectrum weedkillers. Pick only from unsprayed ground away from roadsides.

identification.text:
Woody shrub up to 2–(4) m high, much-branched from base. Stems clothed in very fine stellate hairs when young, becoming more or less glabrous when older. Leaves densely clothed in fine stellate hairs, triangular to suborbicular, cordate to obtuse at base, (3)–5–7-palmately lobed to about 1/2 radius, coarsely crenate, 2–15–(20) cm diameter; petioles 3–15 cm long; stipules triangular, 3–5 mm long, deciduous. Flowers in axillary clusters of 1–4–(5); fruiting pedicels 20–50 mm long; epicalyx segments ovate-triangular, united for lower ⅓, usually about 1/2 as long as calyx, unchanged at fruiting; calyx long-tubular; calyx teeth much shorter than tube, triangular, acuminate, densely clothed in stellate hairs, somewhat recurved at fruiting; petals magenta with darker veins, 30–40 mm long. Mericarps 7–9 per fruit, glabrous or sparsely to moderately hairy, smooth on back, but a single low longitudinal rib usually present; edges sharply angled or slightly rounded.
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Lavatera assurgentiflora Kellogg]
The species is distinguished by the long-tubular calyx.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Both have palmately lobed, toothed leaves whose sizes overlap (island mallow 2–15(–20) cm across, cheeseweed mallow 1–8 cm), so use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Island mallow's petals (30–40 mm) and common mallow's (12–30 mm) only meet at 30 mm, and both are pink to purple with darker veins or markings, so the flower colour does not separate them; check the calyx, long and tube-shaped in island mallow, and the fruit, smooth with one low rib against strongly net-veined. Leaf size overlaps. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Both have palmately lobed, toothed leaves whose sizes overlap (island mallow 2–15(–20) cm across, dwarf mallow 1–7(–8) cm), so use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. They differ in the epicalyx (longer than the calyx and enlarged in fruit in tree mallow, shorter and barely changed in island mallow), the fruit segments, the calyx (shallowly bell-shaped in tree mallow, long and tube-shaped in island mallow) and the petals (15–20 mm against 30–40 mm). Both are tall, both grow at coastal sites, and both have lobed leaves up to 20 cm across and pink to purple flowers with darker veins, so the leaves and flower colour do not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.

summary.text:
Island mallow, Malva assurgentiflora (formerly Lavatera assurgentiflora), is a shrub of the mallow family (Malvaceae), native to the islands off the coast of southern California. New Zealand floras call it Californian mallow.
In New Zealand it is locally established on the east coast of the South Island from Marlborough to Otago. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1940.

habitat.text:
Established in older gardens, about hedgerows and farm shelter trees, in old farm orchards, and in grassland near homesteads and on sites of former domestic gardens, especially in damp places; in the South Island also in waste places and untended land.
It also invades heavily disturbed shrubland and forest, herbfields, damp ground, roadsides, stream margins, pasture and regenerating former pasture, and persists under regenerating canopies.

harvestEthics.text:
Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.
It is a pest plant, on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds and under sustained control across the Auckland region, where it must not be bred, distributed, released, sold or planted. It forms dense ground cover that shades out small native plants and stops native seedlings establishing. Tuber fragments grow into new plants, so if you dig it out, dispose of the seeds and tubers: rot small amounts in a covered barrel of water, or send them to green waste or landfill.

identification.text:
Erect tuberous perennials, 25–60 cm high, leaves appearing in late autumn and through winter; flowering in spring, the leafless scape with scarlet berries conspicuous in late summer. Tuber about 4 cm diameter, producing small tubers. Leaves large; laminae hastate, to 30 cm long, dark green with lighter yellow-green midrib and main veins; petioles 20–40 cm long, lower half membranous, sheathing, purple-tinged. Spathe more or less translucent, pale whitish-green, purple-tinged near base especially on inside, about 30 × 15 cm; scape shorter than petiole, greenish to reddish. Spadix about ⅓ of spathe; basal female zone about 2 cm long, a few sterile flowers above them; upper male zone about 0.8 cm long, with narrow band of sterile flowers below terminal, stipitate, yellow sterile appendage. Berries 1 cm diameter, bright red.
[From: Healy and Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]
The dark green leaves with silvery or light green midrib and main veins are distinct, as also are the greenish-white spathes. Juvenile leaves are lanceolate, adult leaves large and hastate.
The glossy leaves are present from autumn to spring, and the orange or red berries ripen on the flower stalk after the leaves die back. Arum lily (Zantedeschia aethiopica), stink lily and calla lilies lack its cream-coloured midrib and main veins.

lookalikes.howToTell: Common sorrel's leaf blades are 3.5–12 cm long and 1–3 cm wide, narrowly oblong to lance-shaped with two downward-pointing lobes at the base, and the upper leaves on its flowering stem partly clasp the stem; adult Italian arum leaves are up to 30 cm long, dark green with a paler, yellow-green to cream midrib and main veins, on stalks 20–40 cm long, and its flower stalk is leafless. Young Italian arum leaves are narrow and lance-shaped, and both plants have a sheath at the base of the leaf stalk, so leaf shape and sheath do not separate them. Common sorrel has a somewhat woody rootstock; Italian arum grows from a tuber about 4 cm across with small tubers attached. In flower, common sorrel sends up a stem to about 1 m, reddish towards the base, with a branched, reddish spike of small flowers; Italian arum has a pale greenish-white hood (spathe) about 30 cm long around a yellow spike, followed by bright red berries 1 cm across.

summary.text:
Italian arum (Arum italicum), also called Italian lily, lords and ladies and Jack in the pulpit, is a poisonous tuberous perennial of the arum family (Araceae) from Eurasia, naturalised in New Zealand.
Brought in as an ornamental, it was first collected wild in 1945, well established in a low-lying paddock at Kopu near Thames. It is scattered and well established in the North Island, especially in damp places; in the South Island it is rare to occasional, at Little Wanganui and Nelson City, Okaramio in Marlborough, and Christchurch. It forms persistent colonies or clumps, each main tuber producing up to 30 small tubers, and spreads by seed, probably carried by birds, including domestic poultry, and by water; tuber fragments also grow into new plants. It is long-lived, drought-resistant once established, tolerates most soils and recovers from heavy damage. It is poisonous and avoided by stock. Plants of the arum family are the second largest group causing hospital admissions for plant poisoning in New Zealand.
It is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds and under sustained control in the Auckland region.

warnings: Every part of Italian arum is very poisonous, including the orange to red berries. Swallowed, plants of the arum family cause severe irritation of the mouth and throat, and no member of the family can be eaten raw.
Its sap is an irritant and has a burning effect on animal tissue.

The leaves of its close relative lords-and-ladies (Arum maculatum), which Italian arum is almost identical to, are mistaken for edible sorrel. Check the veins, leaf size and root as described in Lookalikes before picking any arrow-shaped leaf.
If anyone eats any part of it, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766; if they have serious symptoms, dial 111.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Cultivation escape, on shady banks, walls, amongst rocks, mostly in the vicinity of buildings.
The original habitat for Cymbalaria muralis was narrow niches in rock faces and cliffs. It is considered very characteristic of the vegetation that grows on walls.
Common on cliffs and walls around Wellington and throughout New Zealand; it does well in full sun as well as shade (Garnock-Jones). Also on paths (Kiwicare).

identification.text:
Glabrous herb; stems often purplish. Petioles slender, to 4 cm long. Lamina 1–2.7 × 1–3.5 cm, 5-lobed, often with 2 subsidiary lobes on basal pair, more or less reniform, more or less purplish on lower surface; base cordate; lobes usually mucronate. Pedicels slender, 1–3 cm long at anthesis. Calyx 2–3 mm long; lobes lanceolate, extending nearly to base. Corolla 10–12 mm long from obtuse apex of spur to rounded apices of lower lobes, pale mauve with yellow or whitish pouch and dark lines on the upper lip. Capsule slightly longer than calyx. Seeds 0.7–0.9 mm diameter, broad-ovoid or subglobose, with prominent sinuate ridges. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The trailing stems root at the nodes and can reach about 80 cm (Kiwicare; Julia's Edible Weeds). Leaves grown in shade are bigger and slightly fleshy (Garnock-Jones). The mouth of the flower is closed by two yellow knobs, with a long nectar spur behind; once a flower is pollinated its stalk lengthens and curves down below the leaves, holding the fruit close to the ground or pushing it into a crevice (Garnock-Jones; Wikipedia).

preparation.text: Mix a few leaves into a salad with other greens. They taste pungent and acrid, like cress, and can be rather bitter and unpleasant; the taste has also been likened to raw garden peas, or called bitter with a sharp numbing feel. Scatter the flowers over the top. Because the leaves stay green all year, they are a winter green.

summary.text:
Cymbalaria muralis, commonly called ivy-leaved toadflax, is a low, spreading, trailing plant with small purple flowers, native to rocky habitats in southern Europe.
It is often cultivated in New Zealand as a pot or rock garden plant. The species has been recorded previously in New Zealand as Linaria cymbalaria.
Other names: coliseum ivy, Kenilworth ivy, mother of thousands, Oxford ivy and wandering sailor (Wikipedia). It probably came to New Zealand as a garden plant and was first reported naturalised here in 1904 (Garnock-Jones, citing Flora of New Zealand vol. IV; NZPCN).

warnings: Some caution is advised: the plant might be slightly toxic. This rests on a single British reference on poisonous plants, which deals mainly with livestock.
Its record as food is thin: salad use in southern Europe, and once as a vegetable in one Pyrenean valley. It is seldom listed in wild-food manuals.
Weedkillers are sold for spraying it on paths, driveways, walls and garden beds, including long-lasting ones that stop it coming back for an extended period. Pick from ground you know.

habitat.text: Occasional escape from cultivation, regenerating in the vicinity of planted trees, particularly in modified forest, as well as in and around plantations. Wild seedlings and saplings have been collected on a limestone cliff above tawa–rimu forest, on a track edge under a eucalypt plantation and at the edge of shrubland. Planted trees do best on deep, well-drained soils below about 600 m with good, evenly spread rainfall; they do not like dry conditions or waterlogged ground.

identification.text:
Medium to large tree. Trunk ridged or somewhat buttressed towards base. Bark reddish brown, peeling in long strips. Crown dense. Juvenile leaves 0.8–1.8–(2.2) cm long, subulate, often red in winter. Adult leaves (from coning branches) 5–15 mm long (excluding adnate, decurrent base), subulate with broad base, directed forwards, shining green; apex acute. Male strobili densely clustered at apices of small shoots, 2.5–5 mm long. Female cones 1–1.7 cm diameter when open. Bract scale apex pungent. Ovuliferous scales with about 6 spiny processes 2–3 mm long. Seed 4–5 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The persistently juvenile cultivar 'Elegans' is the commonest form in gardens and can produce cones, but no spontaneous plants of this form have been reported.

summary.text:
Japanese cedar is the only species of Cryptomeria, a genus in the cypress family (Cupressaceae); the name comes from the Greek kryptos, 'hidden', and meros, 'a part'. It is native to Japan.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1957, in the North Island in North Auckland (Omahuta, Trounson Park) and the Wairarapa (Kiriwhakapapa), and in the South Island in Marlborough (near Kahutara River) and Westland (Mahinapua). Japanese cedar is abundant in cultivation throughout New Zealand, especially in gardens, parks and domains, but also sometimes as a plantation tree. Herbarium specimens collected since record it wild in the Taumatatotara Range near Waitomo (1989), in Lismore Forest near Whanganui (1994) and at Masons Bay on Stewart Island (2009). In New Zealand it is mostly grown for shelter, and farm foresters have planted many small blocks for its timber.

warnings: Its pollen is a major cause of hay fever: around 30% of people in Japan are allergic to it.

identification.text:
Deciduous, spreading to erect tree, 4–12–(15) m high when mature, not armed; trunk tall. Lf petiole (14)–20–32–(40) mm long, glabrous or occasionally with sparse hairs; blade usually thin, usually broadly ovate to broadly elliptic, occasionally oblong or narrowly obovate, (70)–80–130–(155) × (40)–45–60–(65) mm, acuminate to long-acuminate at apex, usually rounded to subcordate or occasionally cuneate at base, glabrous above and below, with lower surface slightly paler, serrate with teeth aristate and often gland-tipped; stipules long-triangular, early deciduous. Inflorescence a corymbose cluster of (2)–3–4–(6) flowers, on short lateral shoots, sometimes clustered near branchlet tips, up to 45–(80) mm long, more or less pendent; flowers not fragrant; pedicels (10)–14–(35) mm long, glabrous, subtended by serrate bracts. Hypanthium narrowly campanulate; sepals 4–7–(8) mm long, lanceolate or subulate, acuminate, glabrous, greenish to magenta, erect to spreading or occasionally reflexed. Petals 5 or many, more or less spreading at anthesis, broadly obovate to orbicular, (12)–14–18–(20) × 9–14 mm, undulate and notched, white or pink-flushed to rose. Stamens shorter than petals; filaments whitish or flushed pale pink. Fruit shorter than 15 mm diameter, globose, glabrous, black-purple, bitter; stone smooth. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Taiwan cherry's flowers are deep pink to rose-magenta and more or less bell-shaped, the lower part of each petal staying semi-erect while the upper part eventually spreads, with magenta to dark deep red sepals; Japanese cherry's petals are white or pink-flushed to rose and more or less spread open, and its sepals are greenish to magenta. The bell-shaped flower is what sets Taiwan cherry apart. Fruit: Taiwan cherry's is glossy scarlet and egg-shaped to ellipsoid, up to 12 × 10 mm; Japanese cherry's is round, black-purple and bitter, under 15 mm across — but Japanese cherry fruit can also be red, so a red fruit does not settle it. Leaf teeth: Japanese cherry's end in a bristle and are often gland-tipped; Taiwan cherry's are pointed. Flowering overlaps: Taiwan cherry July to September, Japanese cherry August to October. Leaf size, leaf-stalk length and flower-stalk length overlap, and neither has spines.
