preparation.text: Owing to their bitter taste, the raw sakuranbo is unpalatable and rarely eaten; instead, the seed inside is removed and the fleshy part preserved.

recipes.method: About 50 g cherry blossoms (around 5 very loosely packed cups); 2 tsp flaky or fine sea salt, plus 5 g (1 tsp) more if needed; 240 ml rice vinegar; 2 tsp umezu (Japanese plum vinegar), if you have it. Pick from an unsprayed tree, choosing flowers that are just starting to open. Soak them gently in clean water, stirring lightly with your hands, then lay them out to dry or give them a quick, gentle spin in a salad spinner. Layer the flowers in a small jar, sprinkling each layer with salt, and refrigerate for 3 days. Cover with the vinegar and refrigerate for another 3 days. To keep them as a pickle, simply leave the flowers in the vinegar in the fridge; they keep 6 months or more but fade. To dry them, drain off and keep the vinegar, then spread the flowers on a tray lined with a soft cloth in a warm, dry place out of direct sun, checking once a day — about three days on average — or dry them in a dehydrator at about 35 °C for 6–8 hours. Keep the heat low, or they turn brown. Toss flowers left a little moist with a further 5 g (1 tsp) sea salt. Use the pink sakura vinegar, which is salty, like a seasoned vinegar, for example in sushi rice. They keep, dried, at room temperature, out of direct sun, for about a year; the vinegar keeps in the fridge for 6 months or more. Makes about 1 cup of flowers and 240 ml of vinegar.
recipes.title: Preserved cherry blossoms (sakura no shiozuke) and sakura vinegar

recipes.method: A handful of clean, fresh cherry blossoms with the stalks removed; water; and white sugar. Put the blossoms in a dish, pour over enough water just off the boil to cover them, cover the dish and leave to infuse for 24 hours. Strain the liquid through a fine sieve, muslin or a paper filter into a small pan and add the same quantity of sugar — 500 g sugar to 500 ml of liquid. Heat gently until the sugar dissolves, bring to the boil and simmer for 3 to 5 minutes. Funnel into a sterilised bottle and seal. Once opened, keep it in the fridge and use within 2 months. Use it as you would a subtle orgeat or maraschino, in drinks.
recipes.title: Cherry blossom syrup

recipes.method: About 2 cups of fresh cherry blossoms and about 475 ml raw apple cider vinegar. Pick flower buds and open blooms from a tree you know has not been sprayed or contaminated, leaving the leaves behind — the author advises against harvesting leaves with the flowers. Fill a glass jar about two-thirds full of flowers and top up with the vinegar. If the jar has a metal lid, put a piece of parchment or wax paper between jar and lid so the vinegar does not eat the metal. Leave to infuse for at least 2–4 weeks; pink blossoms turn it a golden fuchsia. Strain, and use it in salad dressings, marinades, soda water or cocktails.
recipes.title: Cherry blossom vinegar

recipes.method: For one drink: 75 ml sake; 15 ml dry gin; 15 ml of the cherry blossom vodka; 1 tsp cherry blossom syrup; a salted cherry blossom (or a small pinch of salt). Infused vodka: a handful of clean fresh cherry blossoms; vodka. First infuse the cherry blossoms in vodka for a couple of days, then fine-strain. Stir with ice, strain, and garnish with a fresh or salted cherry blossom.
recipes.title: Sakura martini

recipes.method: Put cherry blossoms in a jar, cover them with good mirin and leave for four days, then strain out the flowers and keep the mirin in the fridge. The author drizzles it over mild, crunchy salads and spoons it over silken tofu as a dessert.
recipes.title: Cherry blossom mirin

recipes.method: 1 Japanese or 5 Persian cucumbers, 1 tbsp (15 ml) sesame seeds toasted in a pan, 3 tbsp (45 ml) cherry blossom mirin (above), 2 tsp (10 ml) rice vinegar, ¼ tsp sea salt, and cherry blossoms to scatter. Crush the cucumbers lightly with the back of a knife or a rolling pin, break them into chunks and put them in a bowl. Roughly crush the sesame seeds in a mortar. Whisk the mirin, vinegar and salt together in a small bowl, add them to the cucumber with the sesame seeds and toss well. Turn onto a serving dish, scatter over the blossoms and serve at once. If you like, leave the salad to macerate in the mirin mixture for an hour to develop its flavour, but add the sesame seeds and blossoms just before serving.
recipes.title: Cucumber and cherry blossom salad

recipes.method: For the syrup: 100 g fresh, clean, dry cherry blossoms; 1 litre hot water; 2/3 cup (about 165 ml) white sugar; 1/4 tsp (about 1 ml) sea salt; 1/2 tsp (about 2.5 ml) citric acid. Pick only a few blossoms from each branch of a tree in full flower. Put everything in a medium saucepan over a medium heat and stir gently for about 5 minutes until the sugar dissolves. Take it off the heat and leave it to cool and steep for a couple of hours, then strain through a fine sieve into a sterilised bottle; it keeps in the fridge for up to 2 weeks. The citric acid deepens the pink and the salt lifts the flavour. To serve, put a shot of gin, 1/4 cup (60 ml) of the syrup and ice cubes in a glass, top with soda water and stir. Use the syrup sparingly.
recipes.title: Cherry blossom gin fizz

summary.text:
Japanese cherry, Prunus serrulata, also called Japanese hill cherry and Japanese flowering cherry, is a deciduous tree 4–12(–15) m tall of the rose family (Rosaceae), native to China and Japan.
Wild plants in New Zealand are the Japanese hill cherry (P. serrulata var. spontanea), with single flowers of five broad, pale pink petals; most garden Japanese cherries, the Sato Zakura, are double-flowered cultivars. It was first recorded naturalised in 1982 and is well established at Taheke in Northland, with records around the Waitematā Harbour and in Wellington City. Its seed is probably spread by birds, and it is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. Herbarium sheets also record self-sown seedlings at Hāwera in south Taranaki: more than 100 in Naumai Park in 2001, and flowering self-sown plants in a gully plantation in the town in 2012.

warnings: The plant (especially the seed and young shoots) contains cyanogenic glycosides, especially amygdalin and prunasin. When ingested, these compounds break down in the digestive tract to release cyanide.

Eat the blossoms only in small amounts, particularly raw: cherry flowers, leaves, twigs and bark contain cyanogenic compounds that release cyanide when chewed or crushed. Leave the leaves behind when picking flowers.

habitat.text: In New Zealand it is a plant of coastal and lowland communities on moderately fertile sites, growing more vigorously in deeper valley soils. It grows in scrub, forest margins, shrublands, disturbed or secondary forest, modified lowland forest, coastal areas, wetland margins, inshore islands, roadsides, farm hedges, shelterbelts, plantation forest, wasteland, rough pasture, river systems, fernland, canopy gaps, clearings and backyards. It grows best on calcareous and moist forest soils and rarely establishes on excessively drained, drought-prone sandy or stony soils. It tolerates moderate shade, frost, salt, damage, wet or dry ground and most soils, though frost limits its growth by killing the shoots, and many inland areas of the South Island are probably too dry for it.

harvestEthics.text: Listed on the National Pest Plant Accord: it must not be sold or distributed anywhere in New Zealand, and in the Auckland region it must not be bred, released or planted either. Harvest as many flowers as you like. Its long stems root where they lie and dumped stems and soil start new plants, so never dump cuttings or garden waste from it.

identification.text:
Vigorous climber, evergreen, or semi-evergreen in cold districts. Stems mostly purplish and hirsute when young. Leaves dimorphic: those produced in colder weather in early spring sinuate to deeply lobed; summer leaves and those on reproductive shoots entire. Petiole to 1.3 cm long, densely hirsute. Lamina of entire leaves 2.5–12 × 1.5–6 cm, ovate-oblong, ovate or ovate-elliptic, usually deep more or less shining green or sometimes yellowish green above, lighter green below, sometimes mottled yellow, densely hairy to glabrous on veins beneath; midrib above glabrous or hairy; base rounded, truncate or subcordate; apex obtuse to acute; leaves subtending flowers similar but smaller, all free. Flowers in axillary pairs, fragrant; peduncles 0.5–2.5 cm long, densely hirsute. Bracteoles more or less oblong-obovate, much shorter than ovaries. Calyx lobes very small, more or less narrow-triangular, fringed with long hairs. Corolla 2–4.5–(5) cm long, usually white, becoming yellow after anthesis, often flushed pink on reverse, glandular-hairy outside; tube 1–3 cm long, cylindric; limb 2-lipped; single linear lobe of lower lip recurving; upper lip 4-toothed. Stamens and style shorter than to equal to corolla limb. Ovaries separate. Berry (4)–5–7 mm diameter, broad- ovate to suborbicular, glossy black. Seed about 2 mm diameter 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The long, tough, wiry stems twine clockwise and turn woody and hollow as they mature, and the leaves are in opposite pairs.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are fragrant climbers whose white flowers can be flushed pink and whose fruit is a glossy black berry of much the same size, and the flower tubes overlap in length, so fruit and tube size do not separate them. Japanese honeysuckle's leaves are simple and entire, though leaves produced in colder weather in early spring are wavy-edged to deeply lobed; pink jasmine's leaves are pinnate, with (5)–7 stalked leaflets. Japanese honeysuckle's flowers come in pairs in the leaf axils, are two-lipped, turn yellow after opening and are glandular-hairy outside; pink jasmine carries many flowers together in panicles, each a narrow tube opening to flat, elliptic lobes, usually pink in bud. Pink jasmine's flowers are used only to scent tea.
lookalikes.name: Pink jasmine

preparation.text: Suck the nectar from the flower. The flowers can be eaten raw or cooked, or steeped in hot water for tea or to make a syrup or jelly, or soaked overnight in cold water to make a sorbet. Pick fully opened flowers, white or yellow, and a few unopened buds if you like; leave shrivelled brown ones. They wilt quickly in the heat, so use them soon after picking. Pinching off the small green tip at the base of each flower may improve the flavour. Use only the flowers: separate them from the stems and discard any leaves and berries.

recipes.method: Makes about 250 ml. 250 ml fresh Japanese honeysuckle flowers (or 125 ml dried); 310 ml water; about 200 g sugar. Shake the flowers gently to remove dirt and insects, separate them from the stems and discard any leaves and berries. Put the flowers in a heatproof glass or ceramic container, pour the boiling water over them, cover and leave at room temperature for 12–24 hours. Strain through a fine sieve and measure the liquid (about 250 ml). Heat it with an equal volume of sugar over medium-low heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then simmer for one more minute. Cool and keep in the fridge for up to 2 weeks. Add a splash to lemonade, soda water, sparkling wine or hot tea, or drizzle over fresh berries.
recipes.title: Honeysuckle syrup

recipes.method: Makes about 4 jars of 250 ml. Infusion: 625 ml fresh Japanese honeysuckle flowers with the green tips pinched off; 750 ml water. Jelly: 625 ml of the infusion; 2 tbsp lemon juice; 500 g sugar; one 50 g packet of powdered pectin for low- or no-sugar jams; ½ tsp butter (optional, to stop foaming). Put the flowers in a heatproof container, pour the simmering water over them, stir and cover loosely. Steep for 12–24 hours, moving it to the fridge after the first 2 hours. Strain, squeezing the flowers, to get about 625 ml of golden infusion (it freezes for up to 3 months). Put the infusion in a large pot and stir in the lemon juice. Take 50 g of the sugar, mix the pectin into it, stir this into the pot and bring to a rolling boil over high heat, stirring constantly. Add the rest of the sugar all at once, return to a full rolling boil and boil for exactly one minute, still stirring, adding the butter if it foams. Take off the heat and quickly pour into hot sterilised jars, leaving 5 mm headspace, wipe the rims and seal. Process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes, or leave unprocessed jars to set for 12–24 hours and keep them in the fridge for about 3 weeks.
recipes.title: Honeysuckle jelly

recipes.method: Serves 10–12. 1 litre fresh Japanese honeysuckle flowers, gently but tightly packed, leaves and stems removed; 1.33 litres cold water; 330 ml water for the syrup; 400 g sugar; a few drops of lemon juice; a pinch of cinnamon. Put the flowers in a sealable bag, cover completely with the cold water, seal so all the petals stay under water and leave overnight. Boil the 330 ml water with the sugar at a low rolling boil for 3–5 minutes, until the sugar dissolves and the syrup thickens; add the lemon juice and cool completely. Strain the flower water, gently pressing the flowers. Combine it with the syrup, add the barest pinch of cinnamon and chill. Churn in an ice-cream maker following its instructions, then firm in the freezer for 2–4 hours. Keeps for up to two weeks.
recipes.title: Honeysuckle sorbet

recipes.method: Honeysuckle tea: 125 ml simmering water; 60 ml fresh Japanese honeysuckle flowers, packed (about 30 flowers); 1½ tbsp honey. Orangeade: 3–6 oranges and 1 lemon, squeezed to make 375 ml juice. Pour the water over the flowers, steep for 10 minutes, strain and stir in the honey until it dissolves. Strain the juice. Mix 125 ml of the juice with 60 ml of the tea over a little ice and taste; add more juice if it is too sweet or more tea if it is too sharp, then mix the rest in the same ratio. Serve over crushed ice with orange slices. Keeps in the fridge for 1–2 days.
recipes.title: Honeysuckle orangeade

recipes.method: Serves 6. Infusion: 250 ml whole milk; 250 ml cream; 625 ml fresh Japanese honeysuckle flowers, not rinsed. Base: 60 ml cream; 60 ml whole milk; 100 g sugar; ½ tsp vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract; a pinch of salt. Grated lemon zest to serve (optional). Stir the milk, cream and flowers together in a glass jar, cover and refrigerate for 18–24 hours. Strain, squeezing the flowers firmly, then strain again through a fine sieve. Heat the base cream, milk, sugar, vanilla and salt in a small pan over medium heat for about 10 minutes, whisking often, until the sugar and salt dissolve. Cool to lukewarm, stir in the strained honeysuckle cream and chill until cold. Churn in an ice-cream maker (about 20–30 minutes) and serve plain or with lemon zest; store covered in the freezer.
recipes.title: Honeysuckle ice cream

recipes.method: Makes about 1.25 litres. 85 g (about 750 ml) fresh Japanese honeysuckle flowers, not washed; 1.25 litres water; 400 g sugar. Put everything in a large clean jar and stir until the sugar dissolves. Cover the mouth with muslin held on with string or a rubber band and stir every day. After several days, once it is fermenting strongly (lots of bubbles, flowers rising out of the jar), push the flowers down and keep stirring daily. Give it one more day, then strain through a fine sieve and again through a double layer of muslin. Pour into clean bottles, close and keep them in the fridge: it goes on fermenting, and a bottle left out somewhere warm can explode. Keep the strained flowers for the honeysuckle vinegar.
recipes.title: Fizzy honeysuckle cordial

recipes.method: Makes about 560 ml. 250 ml packed strained flowers left from the fizzy honeysuckle cordial, or fresh Japanese honeysuckle flowers; 560 ml white wine vinegar. Put the flowers in a clean jar and cover them with the vinegar. Leave to steep for 2 weeks, then strain through a fine sieve and again through muslin, and bottle. Unopened it keeps indefinitely; once opened, keep it in the fridge. Use it in salad dressings (it suits savoury salads with fruit), splash it into the pan when searing fish, toss it with roast root vegetables, or dilute it with chilled soda water for a drink.
recipes.title: Quick honeysuckle vinegar

recipes.method: Makes one loaf. Syrup: 250 ml fresh Japanese honeysuckle flowers; 200 g sugar; 250 ml water. Cake: 190 g plain flour; 1 tsp baking powder; ¼ tsp baking soda; 1 tsp coarse salt; 2 tbsp plus 80 ml of the syrup; 80 ml plain yoghurt; 2 tbsp grated lemon zest; 100 g white sugar; 100 g light brown sugar; 125 ml light olive oil (not extra virgin); 2 eggs, lightly beaten. For the syrup, remove leaves, stems and any dark yellow or shrivelled flowers (they can be bitter) and rinse the flowers lightly in cold water. Simmer the sugar and water until the sugar dissolves, add the flowers, take off the heat and steep for 1–2 hours; strain into a jar and keep in the fridge. For the cake, heat the oven to 175 °C and butter and flour a 23 × 13 cm loaf tin. Whisk the flour, baking powder, baking soda and salt together. Mix 2 tbsp of the syrup with the yoghurt. In a larger bowl rub the lemon zest into both sugars with your fingers, whisk in the oil until smooth, then the eggs. Fold in the flour and yoghurt mixtures without over-mixing, pour into the tin and tap it on the bench to release bubbles. Bake for 45 minutes to 1 hour, until a skewer comes out clean. Cool in the tin for 10 minutes, poke holes all over with a skewer and pour 80 ml of the syrup over it; leave to cool completely as it soaks in.
recipes.title: Honeysuckle lemon yoghurt cake

recipes.method: Makes about 500 ml. 250 ml fresh, unsprayed Japanese honeysuckle flowers; 500 ml honey. Put the honey and flowers in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water (or the top of a double boiler) and warm on low for 20–30 minutes. Turn off the heat, strain out the flowers and store the honey in a glass jar. Stir a teaspoon into black or herbal tea.
recipes.title: Honeysuckle honey

summary.text:
Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica) is a climbing honeysuckle, of the family Caprifoliaceae, from East Asia.
In New Zealand it was introduced as a garden ornamental, including for hedges, and has been naturalised since 1926; it can grow up to 15 m in a year in favourable conditions. It is widespread across the North Island and in the northern South Island. It is listed on the National Pest Plant Accord, an agreement to prevent the sale and distribution of pest plants, and is named in the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds in New Zealand. In Auckland you must not breed, distribute, release, sell or plant it (the sale and distribution bans apply across New Zealand under the Accord), and Auckland Council controls it in buffer areas of parks; in the Bay of Plenty it is an advisory species, so control is up to the landowner or occupier. It climbs over and smothers most plants from the ground to the medium canopy, and can cause canopy collapse, after which grasses or ground vines invade. It gives support to faster-growing weedy vines such as morning glory and moth plant, forms dense mats, and harbours mice. Birds, and possibly possums, spread the seed, and roading machinery and dumped vegetation, soil and fill spread the plant. It seldom sets seed, but stumps resprout and the long stems layer.
Two biological control agents, the Honshu white admiral butterfly (Limenitis glorifica) and the honeysuckle stem beetle (Oberea shirahatai), have been approved for release against it, in 2013 and 2015 respectively. The butterfly's larvae eat the leaves and the beetle's larvae bore into the stems; the butterfly has established on the Coromandel Peninsula and in the northern Bay of Plenty.

warnings: Eat only the flowers. The leaves and the shining black berries can be poisonous in large amounts, and eating a lot of the berries can upset the stomach.

Not every honeysuckle has edible flowers, and many have toxic berries. Woodbine (Lonicera periclymenum) and Lonicera × americana also grow wild in New Zealand, so use only flowers you have identified as Japanese honeysuckle: paired, two-lipped flowers on a climber with simple leaves, white turning yellow.

harvestEthics.text: It is an Unwanted Organism and a National Pest Plant Accord species: anywhere in New Zealand it must not be sold, given away, moved between locations, grown, bred or propagated. In the Waikato it is illegal for anyone but the regional council to remove or disturb it — don't pick it there; report it on 0800 800 401. Auckland Council manages every known site and asks you to report it (pestfree@aucklandcouncil.govt.nz) rather than control it. In Tasman and Nelson the regional pest plan's knotweed rule (Asiatic, giant and hybrids) is for eradication, and occupiers must report any sighting to Tasman District Council within five days. In Otago there are no rules for landowners — it is an organism of interest whose sites are recorded for possible future control — and Otago Regional Council asks you to report it (orc.govt.nz/reportpests). Elsewhere, check your regional council's rules first, report any you find on public land to your local council, and carry no living piece anywhere new.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous herb forming large clumps; stems usually 1–2(–2.5) m tall, about 1.5 cm diameter at the woody base, more or less zigzagging, glabrous, more or less glaucous to reddish. Petiole 1–5.5 cm long, more or less dark crimson, channelled above, with a single pit at base on dorsal side. Lamina 8–23 × 5–17 cm (inflorescence leaves often smaller and more elongated), broad-ovate, somewhat glaucescent below, with fewer than 14 pairs of lateral veins, often minutely puberulent on veins near base above, otherwise glabrous, more or less undulate; base usually truncate, sometimes shallowly subcordate especially on vegetative shoots; apex cuspidate. Ochreae to about 3 cm long, deciduous, glabrous. Panicles with branches clustered, to 6 cm long, longer than the petioles, erect or suberect, densely puberulent. Bracts small, glabrous or puberulent, cuspidate or cuspidate-acuminate. Pedicels longer than the bracts, glabrous, jointed in lower half. Perianth 1.5–2.5 mm long at anthesis (excluding decurrent base), white; segments obovate to oblong-obovate, keeled. Filaments to 2 mm long. Stigmas fimbriate. Valves of fruit 7–11 mm long (including broad wing); apex notched. Nut 2.5–3 mm long, obtusely angled, glossy brown. Flowers December–March.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4]
The red-purple young shoots appear early in spring. The plant is deciduous: the stems die back to the root base in winter, and old canes can take up to three years to break down.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at a grown leaf: giant knotweed's blade is 10–30 (sometimes 40) cm long with more than 14 pairs of side veins, and its base is usually deeply heart-shaped, rarely only shallowly so; Japanese knotweed's is 8–23 cm long with fewer than 14 pairs of side veins, and its base is usually straight across, sometimes shallowly heart-shaped (especially on non-flowering shoots). Look at the back of the leaf-stalk base: giant knotweed usually has 3 pits (some leaves in the flower heads lack them), Japanese knotweed a single pit. Giant knotweed's stems are 2–4 m tall and green, sometimes reddish-brown; Japanese knotweed's are usually 1–2 m tall (0.5–2.5 m), more or less bluish-grey to reddish. At least the lower flower-head branches of giant knotweed are no longer than the leaf stalks; Japanese knotweed's are longer. These tests are on grown leaves and stems. Both grow on roadsides near houses, so place does not separate them, and their hybrid, Bohemian knotweed, is also recorded in New Zealand. Giant knotweed's young shoots are eaten too (see its page), and both are Unwanted Organisms under the same rules.
lookalikes.name: Giant knotweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at grown mid-stem leaves. Bohemian knotweed's blade is 5–30 cm long, its base anything from almost straight to moderately heart-shaped, often several shapes on one plant, and its tip usually tapers gradually; Japanese knotweed's is 8–23 cm long, its base usually straight across (sometimes shallowly heart-shaped, especially on non-flowering shoots), and its tip abruptly pointed. Under a strong hand lens, the veins on the underside of Bohemian knotweed's leaf carry small, stout hairs; Japanese knotweed's are hairless, at most with tiny blunt knobs. Bohemian knotweed's stems are 2–5 m tall; Japanese knotweed's are usually 1–2 m (0.5–2.5 m). Leaf size and height overlap, so the mix of leaf bases and the vein hairs are the better tests, and the two are often mistaken for each other. No food use is given for Bohemian knotweed (see its page), and both are Unwanted Organisms under the same rules.

sources: Plants For A Future, 'Reynoutria japonica' (https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Reynoutria+japonica, retrieved 11/11/2026) — one source with Useful Temperate Plants — acid flavour, rhubarb substitute in pies, fruit soups, jams

Mark Williams, Galloway Wild Foods, 'Japanese knotweed – Identification, distribution, edibility' (18/02/2012, https://gallowaywildfoods.com/japanese-knotweed-identification-distribution-edibility/, retrieved 11/11/2026) — taste between gooseberry and rhubarb; purée, fool; peeling; cook or burn all trimmings
preparation.text: The shoots have an acid flavour, somewhere between rhubarb and gooseberry, and suit pies, fruit soups, jams, purées and fools. Peel the fibrous outer layer from larger shoots, or cook the whole shoot and pass it through a sieve; the younger the shoot, the less there is to peel. Cook or burn every trimming you bring home.

recipes.method: Juice whole raw young stems. Drink the green juice in smoothies, or pass it through a fine cloth for a clear purple juice — the author uses it as a gin mixer. Don't compost the pulp, as the author does — cook or burn it, or bag it for the transfer station (see Warnings).
recipes.title: Knotweed juice

recipes.method: Young knotweed shoots; a little sugar and water; Greek yoghurt, to serve. Avoid patches that may have been sprayed; the author watches a patch for at least a year before eating from it. Pick young shoots under 50 cm long. Chop the whole shoot without peeling it — the author doesn't peel them — stew it with a little sugar and water until soft, and pass it through a fine sieve. Serve with Greek yoghurt, or make a fool. Cook or burn every trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings). It is high in oxalic acid: eat it sparingly if you have a kidney complaint or have been told to avoid spinach or rhubarb.
recipes.title: Knotweed purée

recipes.method: Chopped young knotweed shoots; chopped sweet cicely seeds, leaves and stems; vodka. Fill a jar a third full with chopped young knotweed shoots, then to halfway with chopped sweet cicely seeds, leaves and stems, and top up with vodka. Leave for at least 2 months, shaking daily for the first 2 weeks, then strain. Sweeten to taste after steeping rather than before. Cook or burn every trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).
recipes.title: Knotweed and sweet cicely vodka

recipes.method: 280 g young knotweed shoots, thick ones under 30 cm tall, peeled and the tips discarded; 550 ml water; 24 g salt (a 3% brine); 4–5 sprigs fresh dill; 1–2 garlic cloves; 5 ml (1 tsp) black peppercorns; 1–2 small hot chillies; a couple of strips of lemon zest; 5 ml (1 tsp) dried Sichuan peppercorns. Cut the shoots into 8–10 cm lengths, toss them with the seasonings and pack them into a 1-litre jar. Dissolve the salt in the water and pour it over. Put the lid on and leave the jar at room temperature, opening it now and then to let the gas out. The pickles start to sour in a few days; after that keep them in the fridge or the cupboard. Brining keeps the stems crisp and stops them turning slimy. Unpeeled thin shoots ferment too, but are not as good. Slice them to eat with fish, in fish cakes, or with ramen. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).
recipes.title: Fermented knotweed pickles

recipes.method: 1 large roasted, peeled red capsicum (about 115 g), chopped; 85 g fermented knotweed (see Fermented knotweed pickles), cut into 1 cm rings and then quartered; 2 large spring onions (about 30 g), white and tender green parts, thinly sliced; 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil or sunflower oil; 30 ml (2 tbsp) chopped coriander, mint or basil; a little grated lemon zest; 10 ml (2 tsp) lemon juice; a pinch of chilli flakes. Mix everything in a bowl and adjust the salt, acid and heat to taste. Keep it covered in the fridge for a week or two; the flavour improves as it sits. Warm it gently before serving — spoon it over cooked fish, toss it with roast potatoes, or serve it with grilled pork or chicken. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).
recipes.title: Fermented knotweed relish

recipes.method: 450 g tender young knotweed shoots, leaves removed, peeled if you can; 150 g (¾ cup) sugar; 250 ml (1 cup) water; 2 green apples, peeled and cored (about 210 g); 30 ml (2 tbsp) glucose or corn syrup; 30 ml (2 tbsp) cornflour (optional, slows crystals forming); a pinch of salt; lime juice to taste. Roughly chop the knotweed and apples, or pulse them in a food processor. Put them in a large pan with the sugar, water, syrup, cornflour and salt and cook over medium-high heat until the apple is soft, about 10 minutes, then keep cooking until the mixture is thick. Blend until very smooth; sieve it if your shoots were older. Cool to room temperature, add lime juice to taste — don't skip it — and churn in an ice-cream maker for 30–45 minutes, until it is as thick as sour cream. Freeze in a lidded container for at least 2–3 hours. Makes about 750 ml. Add more or less apple to taste. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).
recipes.title: Knotweed sorbet

recipes.method: 1.4 kg young knotweed shoots; 1.4 kg cooking apples such as Granny Smith; 30 ml (2 tbsp) torn mint leaves (optional). Peel the apples and knotweed, chop both into 2–3 cm pieces and cook in a deep pan over medium heat, stirring now and then, until soft and the knotweed has given up its juice, about 20 minutes; reduce it a little longer if it looks watery. Blend with the mint until as smooth as you can get it. Spread about 3 mm thick on non-stick or silicone sheets and dry slowly in a dehydrator or an oven on its lowest setting until completely dry but still pliable. Store airtight. Pears can stand in for the apples; with knotweed alone, sweeten it or the leather will be brittle. Snack for 6–8. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).
recipes.title: Knotweed and apple leather

recipes.method: 10 knotweed tops; 200 g raw flatfish or cod roe; 400 ml neutral oil such as grapeseed; 10 ml (2 tsp) mustard; salt, pepper and lemon juice. For the mayonnaise, whisk the roe in a bowl until its structure breaks down. Add a little oil and whisk hard until the two bind completely, then keep adding oil a little at a time — too much at once and it curdles — until it is firm enough to stay put when the bowl is tipped. Season with salt, pepper, lemon juice and the mustard and keep it cool. Rinse the knotweed, cut it into pieces about 20 cm long and grill for a couple of minutes. Serve with the mayonnaise on the side. No grill: use a dry frying pan on full heat — you lose the smoky flavour, but it works. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).
recipes.title: Grilled knotweed with roe mayonnaise

recipes.method: For the juice: 1 litre (4 cups) water; 2 litres (8 cups) chopped knotweed stalks, leaves removed — stalks about 20–30 cm tall have more flesh and less string than taller ones. For the jelly: 800 ml (3¼ cups) knotweed juice; 60 ml (¼ cup) lemon juice; one 50 g packet powdered pectin; 800 g (4 cups) sugar. Bring the water and chopped stalks to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes. Cool, then hang the stewed knotweed in a jelly bag or muslin and let it drip for an hour or two, until you have 800 ml of juice. Put the juice, lemon juice and pectin in a large pan and bring to a rolling boil. Add all the sugar at once, bring back to a rolling boil and boil for 1 minute, stirring constantly. Take off the heat, ladle into hot sterilised jars, seal, and process in a boiling-water bath for 10 minutes. Makes about six 250 ml jars of surprisingly pink jelly; serve it over yoghurt or on bread. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).
recipes.title: Pink knotweed jelly

recipes.method: Serves 2: 2 knotweed stalks, sliced across into rings; 100 g dried rice noodles; 15 ml (1 tbsp) soy sauce; 15 ml (1 tbsp) kimchi; 1 small shallot, diced; 2 mushrooms (oyster or button), diced; 50 g edamame beans; spring onions and a few more raw knotweed rings to garnish. Cover the noodles with 500–700 ml boiling water and leave for 5 minutes. Fry the mushrooms and shallot in a little oil for 3 minutes, add the noodles with their soaking liquid, then the rest of the ingredients, and heat for a couple of minutes until warm. Top with raw knotweed rings and sliced spring onion. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).
recipes.title: Knotweed rice-noodle bowl

Please report to Auckland Council'. Waikato Regional Council, 'Japanese/Asiatic and giant knotweed' (https://www.waikatoregion.govt.nz/services/biosecurity/plant-and-animal-pests/japanese-knotweed-and-giant-knotweed/, read via r.jina.ai): 'Eradication'; 'it is illegal for anyone else to remove or disturb it'; 'do not cut, treat or try to remove it. Call 0800 800 401'; 'vegetatively from even small fragments of stem or root'; 'spread by soil movement, in garden waste'. Weedbusters, 'Asiatic knotweed' (https://www.weedbusters.org.nz/all-about-weeds/weed-list/asiatic-knotweed/): 'Check with your local regional council first'; 'Ensure all parts of the plant are securely bagged so that no plant material can escape before disposal at refuse transfer station'; glyphosate, metsulfuron and picloram gels, glyphosate/metsulfuron/picloram-triclopyr sprays. Otago Regional Council, 'Japanese knotweed' (https://www.orc.govt.nz/environment/biosecurity-and-pests/plant-pests/japanese-knotweed-r): 'only classified as an organism of interest'; 'Dig out small patches and dispose at landfill or burn'; gels with 'glyphosate, metsulfuron-methyl or triclopyr'. Galloway Wild Foods knotweed post (as above): 'Cooking or burning of all you bring home'; 'poisoned ones may continue to grow new shoots after years of treatment'. Origin 'introduced' → 'pest' under the 20/10 pest rule (NPPA; Auckland progressive containment; Waikato eradication). Recipe disposal lines changed to match (no 'or a bin' — Weedbusters sends bagged pieces to the transfer station).

Pinks fill round 11/11/2026: months set to September–November (was January–February and June–December). The eaten part is the young shoot under 50 cm (Galloway). In New Zealand the red-purple shoots 'appear early in spring' (Auckland Council), the plant is deciduous with stems dying back to the root base in winter (Waikato Regional Council), so June–August have no shoots, and it flowers December–March (Flora vol. IV), by which time the stems are mature. iNaturalist NZ research-grade, wild observations by month (82 total, retrieved 11/11/2026): Jan 9, Feb 7, Mar 9, Apr 14, May 2, Jun 2, Jul 2, Aug 0, Sep 5, Oct 9, Nov 15, Dec 8 — not used to set months (records of plants, not shoots).

A strong hand-lens is required.' Tests: this entry's Flora of New Zealand vol. IV description (stems (0.5–)1–2(–2.5) m; lamina 8–23 cm; base usually truncate, sometimes shallowly subcordate especially on vegetative shoots; apex cuspidate; veins glabrous below), with the BC key (Wilson 2007: Japanese underside veins with 'blunt knobs (scabers)', Bohemian 'small, stout hairs', Bohemian leaves 5–30 cm with base ± straight to moderately curved) and the Montana Field Guide (Japanese tip 'abrupt', Bohemian 'usually not abrupt'); Bohemian knotweed's 2–5 m from Environment Canterbury, 'Knotweed' (https://www.ecan.govt.nz/pest-search/knotweed, retrieved 11/11/2026); several leaf shapes on one plant from the Invasive Species Centre. Ranges overlap (Bohemian knotweed wild near Greymouth and at Tokaanu, and at Tapawera on iNaturalist). Risk 'edible': the Bohemian knotweed entry is careRequired on two food records. summary.text:
Japanese knotweed or Asiatic knotweed (Reynoutria japonica, synonyms Fallopia japonica and Polygonum cuspidatum) is a rhizomatous perennial herb in the dock family Polygonaceae, native to eastern Asia and introduced to New Zealand as an ornamental.
It was first recorded naturalised here in 1935 and has been found from Auckland to Dunedin; the Flora of New Zealand records it in the North Island and, in the South Island, in Marlborough and Canterbury, locally common in south-east Nelson and locally abundant in Westland, and herbarium sheets record it wild in Otago, in the bed of the Water of Leith in Dunedin. It spreads from seed, from rhizomes and from even small fragments of stem or root moved in soil, floodwater, garden waste and on machinery, and forms dense, long-lived thickets that exclude other species and prevent native seedlings establishing.
It is an Unwanted Organism under the Biosecurity Act 1993, a National Pest Plant Accord species and on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. Regional pest plans list it for exclusion in Northland, eradication in Waikato, Manawatū-Whanganui, Tasman-Nelson and Canterbury, progressive containment in Auckland, Bay of Plenty and the West Coast, and as an organism of interest in Otago and Southland.

warnings: Even small fragments of stem or root grow into new plants. Never put any of it in compost or garden waste. Cook or burn everything you bring home; bag any other pieces securely so nothing escapes, and take them to a refuse transfer station or landfill.

It is controlled with herbicide gels and sprays (glyphosate, metsulfuron-methyl, triclopyr, picloram), and a sprayed patch can keep sending up shoots. Pick only where you know it has not been treated.

It is high in oxalic acid. Eat it sparingly if you have a kidney complaint or have been advised to avoid spinach or rhubarb; people prone to rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity should take special care. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid.

identification.text:
Arborescent shrub to about 3 m high; stems few and with terminal crown of leaves. Leaves to about 40 cm long, sessile, composed of 5–9 pairs of sessile (except the terminal) leaflets, the basal pair smaller and stipule-like, the terminal leaflet largest. Leaflets of main pairs 4–7.5 × 2–3.5 cm, ovate, rigidly coriaceous, with 2–5 spiny teeth on margins; apex spiny. Racemes lax and spreading, to about 20 cm long; basal scales to 1.5 cm long, broadly ovate, membranous, dark brown. Bracts ovate, slightly shorter than pedicels at anthesis. Perianth segments to 9 mm long, ovate, imbricate except for short outermost whorl. Stamens included, shorter than inner perianth segments; filaments entire. Style very short. Berry 8–10 mm long, more or less broadly obovoid, blue-black and pruinose.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Mahonia japonica (Thunb.) DC.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Japanese mahonia's leaves are stalkless, and their lowest pair of leaflets is small and stipule-like; Oregon grape's leaves have no such pair and usually sit on a dark red stalk up to 4 cm long. Japanese mahonia has few stems to about 3 m, each crowned with leaves; Oregon grape is many-stemmed and suckering, usually about 1 m. Japanese mahonia's flower clusters are lax, spreading and up to about 20 cm; Oregon grape's reach 6–7 cm. Japanese mahonia's berries are broadly egg-shaped, 8–10 mm long; Oregon grape's round, about 10 mm across. Leaflet counts overlap (5–9 pairs against 3–7), and blue-black bloomed berries do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Oregon grape

lookalikes.howToTell: Japanese mahonia's flower clusters are lax and spreading; leatherleaf mahonia's stand upright, 7–26 cm long. Japanese mahonia's main leaflets are 4–7.5 cm long and 2–3.5 cm wide; leatherleaf mahonia's leaflets are wider, 2–6 cm, so only a wide leaflet tells. Japanese mahonia's berries are 8–10 mm long; leatherleaf mahonia's up to 15 mm. Leaflet counts (5–9 pairs against 4–10), a small lowest pair, spiny teeth and blue-black bloomed berries do not separate them. The two have long been confused: leatherleaf mahonia has been listed as a form of B. japonica ('Bealei'), so a garden label does not settle it. The two have hybridised in gardens and many seedlings are hybrids, so intermediate plants are fairly common. Some plants grown as leatherleaf mahonia in the United States have loose, spreading to hanging flower clusters and narrow leaflets, so on a planted or escaped shrub neither trait settles it.
lookalikes.name: Leatherleaf mahonia

lookalikes.howToTell: Japanese mahonia's leaves carry 5–9 pairs of ovate leaflets with 2–5 spiny teeth; mountain grape's carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped ones. Japanese mahonia's flower clusters are lax and spreading; mountain grape's dense and upright. Blue-black berries with a bloom do not separate them, and neither test settles the garden hybrid B. × hortensis ('Charity', 'Winter Sun'), whose parents are these two species.

preparation.text: Eat raw, added to muesli or porridge, or cooked.

recipes.method: Written for the berries of Japanese and leatherleaf mahonia. Base: 375 ml flour, 440 ml rolled oats, 125 ml chopped walnuts, 250 ml packed dark brown or coconut sugar, 1 tsp baking powder, ½ tsp fine salt, 1 tsp vanilla and 250 ml melted butter. Topping: 625 ml mahonia berries, 250 ml sugar, 2 tsp grated orange or lemon zest and two lavender buds. Heat the oven to 180°C and line a 20–23 cm square tin with baking paper, leaving it overhanging the sides. Stir the dry ingredients together, then work in the melted butter until crumbly. Press three-quarters of it firmly into the tin and bake for 10 minutes. Cook the berries with the sugar, zest and lavender over low heat for 15 minutes, until they pop open; cool for 5 minutes and take out the lavender. Pour over the base, scatter the rest of the crumble on top and bake for 30–40 minutes, until golden. Cool completely in the tin, lift out by the paper and cut into 12 large bars or 24 squares.

summary.text:
Japanese mahonia, Berberis japonica, is a shrub of the barberry family (Berberidaceae) up to about 3 m tall, its few stems ending in a crown of leaves. It was recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1983.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): South Island: known from 2 sites only, Botanical Hill (Nelson), just north of Clarence Bridge (coastal Marlborough).
M. japonica is fairly common in old gardens throughout New Zealand and persists for a long time without cultivation. Wild plants are presumably the result of dispersal of the fruit by birds.
Berberis bealei, native to mainland China and also widely cultivated, is usually treated as a separate species, but in the past has been listed as a cultivar of Berberis japonica. Its most obvious differences from B. japonica are in shorter, upright flowering racemes and wider leaflets.
Where it grows wild is not settled. Kew's Plants of the World Online gives Taiwan; the NZPCN says the origin is uncertain, probably southern China or northern Taiwan; Bean (Trees and Shrubs Online) doubts the Taiwan record, which rests on treating the Taiwanese M. tikushiensis as the same species; and Useful Temperate Plants suggests it may be known only in cultivation.

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.

habitat.text: Escapes from cultivation around settlements, old homesteads and plantations. Wild along river and stream banks, often in extensive colonies, and in swamps; disturbed forest and shrubland, especially beside watercourses downstream of plantations; also roadsides, scrub, grassland, pasture and drainage channels, river terraces, and coastal sand and estuary edges. It copes with hot or cold, wet or dry sites and some shade.

harvestEthics.text: An Unwanted Organism and National Pest Plant Accord species: it must not be bred, distributed, released or sold anywhere in New Zealand, and in the Auckland region it must not be planted. Its nuts float and start new colonies downstream, so harvest as much as you like but never drop, dump or plant nuts, especially near water. In Canterbury, Environment Canterbury asks you not to control it yourself but to report any you find.

identification.text: A wide-spreading tree to about 15 m high. Shoots with sticky glandular hairs; leaf scars not prominent. Buds brown and finely felted. Leaves to about 60 cm long, the stalk and central axis up to about 40 cm long and densely covered in glandular hairs. Leaflets 9–17, without stalks or nearly so, becoming hairless or nearly so above, densely hairy on the veins beneath, finely toothed though the teeth are often sparse; the lowest pair often smaller, the end leaflet mostly about the same size as the side ones; end leaflet 6–18 × 3–8 cm, oblong or oblong-oval. Male catkins to about 15 cm long; female flower spikes of 9–22 flowers, with purplish glandular hairs and prominent pink stigmas 6–7 mm long, flowering in October and November. Fruits 10–22 in long strings, upright at first and hanging when mature; each 2.5–4 cm long, broadly egg-shaped, beaked, sticky, felted and rusty brown. Shell rough and thick; its seams are thick and raised and split only with difficulty; the beak is often sharply pointed.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both edible; this is about which you have. Count and feel the leaflets: Japanese walnut has 9–17, finely toothed though the teeth are often sparse, the end leaflet about the size of the side ones; walnut has 5–9 with smooth (untoothed) edges, the end leaflet the largest and the lowest pair much smaller. Seedling walnuts can have toothed leaflets, so check an adult tree. Japanese walnut's fruits hang 10–22 together in long strings; walnut's sit in clusters of 1–3 close on the twig. Japanese walnut's fruit is 2.5–4 cm, egg-shaped, beaked, sticky and rusty-hairy; walnut's is 3.5–5 cm, nearly round, smooth and green with gland dots, not beaked. Japanese walnut's thick shell has raised seams that split with difficulty and an often sharp tip; walnut's splits easily in half along its seams when ripe.
lookalikes.name: Walnut

lookalikes.howToTell: Rhus tree's sap causes a severe skin rash, so tell them apart before you touch. Japanese walnut's leaves are bigger, to about 60 cm long, the stalk and central axis densely covered in sticky glandular hairs; rhus tree's are 20–40 cm long and hairless, often pink along the stalk and veins. Japanese walnut's leaflets are finely toothed, though the teeth are often sparse, and hairy on the veins underneath; adult rhus tree's are glossy and untoothed, but its seedlings' are strongly toothed. The leaflet counts overlap (Japanese walnut 9–17; rhus tree 4–6, rarely 7, pairs and usually one at the end), so don't count. The fruit settles it: Japanese walnut's are 2.5–4 cm long, sticky, rusty-hairy and beaked, 10–22 together in long strings, each holding a hard nut; rhus tree's are smooth, pale shiny brown berries 7–10 mm across. Japanese walnut grows to about 15 m, rhus tree to 8 m.
lookalikes.name: Rhus tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree of heaven is not food. Look at the base of a leaflet: tree of heaven's has 1–3 coarse teeth or small lobes, each tipped with a gland, and is otherwise smooth-edged; Japanese walnut's leaflets are finely toothed along the edge, though the teeth are often sparse, with no gland pads. Tree of heaven usually has more leaflets, 11–25 against Japanese walnut's 9–17, though the ranges overlap. Japanese walnut's leaf stalk and central axis are densely covered in sticky glandular hairs; tree of heaven's are hairless or finely hairy, and its crushed leaves smell strongly, like peanuts or cashews. Tree of heaven's seeds sit in flat, twisted, papery wings 3–5 cm long; Japanese walnut's fruits are 2.5–4 cm, sticky, rusty-hairy and beaked, in long strings, each holding a hard nut. Tree of heaven grows to about 25 m, Japanese walnut to about 15 m.
lookalikes.name: Tree of heaven

lookalikes.howToTell: Both edible; this is about which you have. Look at the fruit: Japanese walnut's hang 10–22 together in long strings and are egg-shaped, beaked, sticky and rusty-hairy; black walnut's are round, 3–4 cm across, one to a few together (the female flowers are only 2–5 per cluster), with a brownish-green husk. In spring, Japanese walnut's female flower spikes carry 9–22 flowers; black walnut's sit 2–5 together. Check the tip of a leaf: Japanese walnut has an end leaflet about the size of the side ones; black walnut usually has no end leaflet, or a small one, with the largest leaflets in the middle. Japanese walnut has 9–17 leaflets, black walnut usually 15–23. The counts overlap, so let the fruit decide.
lookalikes.name: Black walnut

preparation.text: Gather the nuts after they fall. The shell is thick and its seams split only with difficulty, so crack it with a hammer or nutcracker. Good kernels soaked overnight, drained, dried and roasted in a very low oven become crisp. Kernels from wild trees vary from plump and good to bitter and shrivelled; discard the bad ones. The oily kernels go rancid quickly, so keep the nuts in their shells until you use them, and in the fridge, or in the freezer for several months. For pickling, pick green fruits in summer, before the inner shell forms: a darning needle pushed through from the end opposite the stalk should go in easily.

recipes.method: Written for walnuts (Juglans regia) by New Zealand growers; green Japanese walnuts can be pickled the same way, before the inner shell forms. 1 kg fresh green walnuts; 250 g salt; 2 litres boiling water, in two lots; 1 litre malt vinegar; 400 g brown sugar; 1 tsp salt; 1 tsp pickling spice; 1 tsp black peppercorns; ½ tsp whole cloves. Push a sturdy needle through each nut and throw out any that will not pierce easily. Wear gloves, as the juice stains skin and is very hard to remove. Prick the nuts all over with a fork and put them in a large bowl. Dissolve half the salt in 1 litre of boiling water, pour it over to cover and leave in a cool place for a week. Drain, cover with a second brine made the same way and leave another week. Drain and spread the nuts in one layer on a tray, and set them outside in a sunny spot for 3–4 days, bringing them in at night, until black and dry. Bring the vinegar, sugar, teaspoon of salt and spices to the boil and simmer about 5 minutes to dissolve the sugar, then cool and strain out the spices. Bring the liquid back to the boil, pack the nuts into clean jars and pour it over so every nut is covered. Cover and keep somewhere dark for at least a month before eating. Use vinegar-proof lids, or put a layer of cling film between lid and liquid, as vinegar corrodes metal lids and taints the nuts.
recipes.title: Pickled green walnuts

recipes.method: Written for walnuts; Japanese walnut kernels can be used the same way. Serves 6. 300 g green beans; 150 ml kombu dashi, plus a little more; a splash each of soy sauce and mirin; 80 g shelled walnuts; 1 heaped tbsp white (sweet) miso; 2 tsp mirin. Season the 150 ml of dashi with the soy sauce and mirin in a wide dish. Boil the beans in plenty of water until tender but still firm, about 5 minutes after the water comes back to the boil, then drain and put them straight into the seasoned dashi instead of cold water. Dry-roast the walnuts in a pan over medium heat and grind them to a paste in a mortar (a Japanese suribachi if you have one). Mix in the miso and 2 tsp mirin and thin with a little dashi to a sauce. Cut the beans to length and toss them in the sauce, or serve the sauce alongside. The sauce keeps in the fridge; leave out the dashi until you use it.
recipes.title: Green beans in walnut miso sauce

recipes.method: Written for walnuts; Japanese walnut kernels can be used the same way. Makes 2–4 servings. 2 tbsp sugar; 2 tbsp miso (white, red or half of each); 1 tbsp mirin, sake or water; about 110 g lightly roasted walnuts; toasted sesame seeds and chilli, optional. Break the walnuts into small pieces, or chop finely if you like. Heat the sugar, miso and mirin in a small saucepan over low heat, stirring all the time, bring to the boil and cook 1 minute. Stir in the walnuts, and sesame seeds or chilli if using. Eat as a snack with drinks or with freshly cooked rice; chopped finely, it makes a sauce for grilled tofu or chicken.
recipes.title: Sweet miso walnuts

recipes.method: Written for black walnuts (Juglans nigra); Japanese walnut kernels can be used the same way. Makes about 250 ml. 2 cups (500 ml) tightly packed basil leaves; ⅓ cup (80 ml) walnut kernels; 1 garlic clove; ½ cup (125 ml) sunflower or extra virgin olive oil; ¼ tsp ground black pepper; ½ cup (125 ml) grated parmesan or grana padano. Toast the walnuts at 180 °C for about 15 minutes until fragrant but not dark, rub them in a tea towel to remove the bitter skins and cool completely. Pick the basil leaves off their stems, blanch in boiling salted water until just wilted, cool in iced water, drain and chop roughly. Blend the basil, cheese, nuts, garlic and pepper to a rough purée, then drizzle in the oil until smooth. Press cling film onto the surface and keep in the fridge, or freeze.
recipes.title: Walnut and basil pesto

recipes.method: Written for black walnuts (Juglans nigra); Japanese walnut kernels can be used the same way. Makes about 750 ml. 2 cups (500 ml) untoasted walnut kernels, skins gently rubbed off; ½ cup (about 100 g) white sugar; ¼ tsp flaky salt, plus more to taste. Read through first and have a tray lined with a non-stick mat ready. In a heavy saucepan (not thin aluminium), heat the nuts and sugar over medium-high heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon; the sugar clumps at first, then after about 5 minutes starts to melt and colour. Keep stirring until it has fully melted to a dark amber and the nuts smell toasted but not burnt, then take it off the heat at once. Tip onto the tray, spread in an even layer and sprinkle with salt while hot, without stirring it in. Cool completely, break into bite-sized pieces and store airtight in a cool, dark place for a few weeks. For a spicy version, add ¼ tsp cayenne pepper just before taking the pan off the heat.
recipes.title: Salted candied walnuts

recipes.method: Written for walnuts (Juglans regia) by New Zealand growers; Japanese walnut kernels can be used the same way. 2 tbsp butter; 2 tbsp olive oil; 300 g walnut kernels; 3 tbsp finely chopped fresh rosemary; 1 tsp ground paprika; 2 tsp salt. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Melt the butter and oil in a large roasting dish, add the nuts and toss to coat. Spread them in one layer and sprinkle with the rosemary, paprika and salt. Bake 20–25 minutes, shaking often, until browned; watch closely at the end, as they scorch easily. Tip onto paper towels to cool.
recipes.title: Rosemary and paprika roasted walnuts

recipes.method: Written for black walnuts (Juglans nigra); Japanese walnut kernels can be used the same way. 4 white fish fillets; 1 cup (250 ml) finely chopped walnut kernels; flour for coating, seasoned with salt and pepper (rice flour for gluten-free); seasoning of your choice; 1 egg, beaten; olive oil; lemon. Set out the nuts and the seasoned flour on separate plates. Season the fish, dip it in the flour, then the egg, then press it into the nuts. Heat a teaspoon of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat and fry the fish until browned on each side, about 3 minutes, watching that the nuts don't burn. Squeeze lemon juice over and serve at once.
recipes.title: Walnut-crusted fish

recipes.method: Serves 10. A firm, tofu-like set walnut sweet from Esashi in Iwate, made for the vegetarian meals of Obon and memorial services and eaten as mock sashimi or with tea; the page says to use oni-gurumi (Japanese walnut). 100 g shelled walnuts; 100 g kuzu (kudzu) starch; 100 g sugar; a pinch of salt; 900 ml water (1 litre in winter). Dipping sauce: 100 g miso; 15 ml sugar; 15–30 ml ginger juice (squeezed from grated ginger); 15 ml sake; water as needed. Grind the walnuts in a mortar until no grains are left, add the water and keep grinding, then push through a fine sieve; return what stays in the sieve to the mortar and repeat until none is left. Put the walnut liquid, kuzu and sugar in a wide, shallow pan and stir until the kuzu dissolves, then set it over the heat. Stir without stopping on medium heat for about 10 minutes, scraping the whole base with a flat spatula; when it thickens and turns glossy, lower the heat and keep working it slowly for a few minutes more (timing depends on the heat). Add the salt a few minutes before taking it off the heat — only if you will eat it as a sweet, not as mock sashimi. Pour into a container rinsed with water and cool at room temperature; long chilling spoils the texture, so put it in the fridge only about 30 minutes before eating. For sashimi, cut into slices and serve on shredded daikon with the sauce: grind the miso smooth, mix in the sugar, ginger juice and sake, and thin with water to a sauce. The walnut, kuzu and sugar are equal weights; use less sugar if you like.
recipes.title: Walnut tofu (kurumi dōfu)

recipes.method: Takako Yokoyama's all-purpose walnut paste, for sweet or savoury dishes; written for oni-gurumi (Japanese walnut) or kashi-gurumi. To crack oni-gurumi, wash the nuts in their shells, dry them well, then dry-roast them in a heavy uncoated frying pan on low heat for 30–40 minutes, stirring now and then, until scorched and split along the seam. Cool, set each on a flat stone or board on a cloth, push a flat screwdriver into the split and tap the handle with a hammer to open it, then pick out the kernels. Paste: 80 g shelled walnuts; 50 ml unsweetened soy milk; 30 ml sugar; 1.25 ml salt. Dry-roast the kernels in the same pan on low heat for 5–10 minutes until crisp, rub off any skin that comes away, and grind coarsely in a mortar. Blend with the soy milk, sugar and salt to a paste with a stick blender or food processor. Keep in a clean container in the fridge for 3 days.
recipes.title: Walnut and soy milk paste

summary.text:
Japanese walnut (Juglans ailantifolia), also known as heartnut, is a wide-spreading deciduous tree of the walnut family (Juglandaceae) from Japan and Sakhalin, introduced as an ornamental and naturalised in New Zealand since 1983.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Northland (north side of the Hokianga), Auckland, Bay of Plenty, Waikato, Waitomo State Forest, Raglan, near Rotorua (Te Mu) and Levin. It is planted in many parts of the country, especially the Bay of Plenty, Waikato and Auckland, and seedlings sometimes come up in large numbers near parent trees. Some planted trees are close to the thin-shelled heartnut variety, which has not been found wild. Wild herbarium specimens also come from further south: a podocarp forest margin in Waitaka Scenic Reserve between Piopio and Ohura, a river terrace where the Ōngarue meets the Whanganui at Taumarunui, an estuary edge at the Turakina River mouth (Koitiata), and seedlings under a tree beside Ramaroa Stream on Whareroa Farm Reserve.
Its nuts float and are carried long distances downstream in floods, and it suckers after felling, so it forms extensive colonies along rivers and streams. Long-lived, with many long-lived seeds, it grows into tall stands that stop other trees coming up, and it can block waterways. It is an Unwanted Organism and a National Pest Plant Accord species, and on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.

warnings: Walnuts are tree nuts, one of the commonest causes of food allergy in New Zealand, and can cause life-threatening allergic reactions in some people.
Rhus tree, whose sap causes a severe rash, and tree of heaven, which is not food, have similar long leaves of many leaflets. See Lookalikes.

identification.text:
Trailing herb. Stem prostrate, terete, glabrous. Leaves terete or weakly 3-angled, obtuse and mucronate at apex, clavate, tapering to shortly connate base, (5)–20–30–(50) × (4)–5–6–(10) mm; margins papillate. Flowers 2–4 cm diameter. Calyx glabrous; sepal keels smooth. Petals purple with white base, in 2 rows, 10–30 mm long. Stamens 5–7 mm long; filaments hairy at base; anthers whitish yellow. Capsule 5–12 mm diameter, valves with widely divergent expanding keels; placental tubercle 2-lobed. Seeds pale brown to brown, weakly rugose or smooth, about 1 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The white bases of the petals turn purple when dry.

lookalikes.howToTell: Native ice plant's leaves are 3-angled and sharp-pointed, often with a small point, where this plant's are club-shaped, round or only weakly 3-angled in section, and blunt with a small point. Its petals are uniformly white to deep pink, in 3–5 rows, against purple with a white base, in 2 rows, here. Native ice plant grows on coasts throughout New Zealand, mostly on cliffs, rock stacks and boulder or cobble beaches and more rarely in saltmarsh, so the two can meet in South Island saltmarshes.

recipes.method: Serves 1. Fish: 180 g snapper fillet; 1 tablespoon vegetable oil; 30 g butter; 3 lemon myrtle leaves. Buttermilk sauce: 1 shallot, finely sliced; 20 g ginger, in fine matchsticks; 200 ml vegetable stock; 1 nori sheet; 100 ml buttermilk; ¼ teaspoon xanthan gum; salt and white pepper. Leek: ½ leek; 20 g butter; vegetable stock to cover; salt and white pepper. Lemon myrtle oil (makes 500 ml): 500 ml grapeseed or other neutral oil; 10 g dried lemon myrtle leaves; 100 g spinach. To serve: a handful of jellybean ice plant leaves. For the sauce, cook the shallot and ginger gently in a pot until soft, add the stock and nori and simmer gently for 30 minutes, strain, and stir the liquid into the buttermilk; thicken with the xanthan gum using a stick blender and season. For the leek, cut it into 7 cm lengths and halve them lengthways, lay them flat in a small pan with the butter, cover with stock and simmer gently for 10–15 minutes until just tender, then lift out. For the oil, warm the lemon myrtle leaves in the oil over a low heat for 10 minutes without letting it get hot enough to scorch them, add the spinach and blend with a stick blender, then strain through an oil filter and remove any water from the spinach. For the fish, heat the oil in a pan until lightly smoking, put in the fish and turn the heat to low; cook for about 4 minutes on one side, until about 70% of the flesh has turned white, add the butter and lemon myrtle leaves and cook 1 minute more, then turn the fish, baste for 1 minute and rest it for 2 minutes. To serve, put the leek in the middle of a bowl, warm the sauce gently without boiling and pour about 125 ml (½ cup) into the bowl, and set the fish on the leek. Dress the ice plant leaves in 1 tablespoon of the lemon myrtle oil and pile them on the fish, then drizzle another tablespoon of oil over the sauce.

summary.text:
Disphyma clavellatum, the jellybean ice plant or jellybeans, is a trailing succulent herb in the ice plant family Aizoaceae, native to Australia and New Zealand. Australian botanists treat it as a subspecies of round-leaved pigface, Disphyma crassifolium subsp. clavellatum.
In New Zealand it is presumed to be a natural arrival from Australia within roughly the last 50 years, and it is classed as a Non-resident Native – Coloniser, secure overseas. It was first collected here in 1984. The Flora of New Zealand (1988) recorded it at the New River Estuary near Invercargill, and NZPCN lists it from Waimea Inlet and Riverton Estuary; iNaturalist records also come from Sandy Point near Invercargill, the Otago coast at Aramoana, Karitāne and Waikouaiti, and around Nelson and Tasman.
It is easily grown from rooted pieces, division of whole plants or fresh seed, but it is not a usual nursery plant, and it should not be planted in estuaries beyond its known New Zealand sites, where it could compete with local saltmarsh plants; native ice plant is the usual garden choice.

habitat.text: Lowland forest, often dominant in swamp forest. It grows throughout New Zealand on moist, fertile soils, and is the dominant tree of swampy lowland areas. It was formerly dominant on frequently flooded or poorly drained alluvial soils, and occasionally extends into lower montane forest. A light-loving pioneer, it establishes fairly easily on moist sites and regenerates among mānuka and gorse, overtopping them within two or three decades; small groups of young trees are sometimes seen on farmland. Planted, it does best in moist to wet sites.

identification.text:
Kahikatea is a stout conifer 50–65 m tall, New Zealand's tallest native tree, with male and female cones on separate trees. The trunk is 1–2 m across, often fluted and buttressed at the base, and bare of branches for about three-quarters of its length. Young adult trees have a distinctive narrow, columnar form, with branches starting a third to half of the way up the trunk. The bark is grey to dark grey and falls in thick, wavy flakes; the wood is white and has no smell. Near the base the roots are typically buttressed and grooved, and trees growing in clusters develop interlocking root islands that may help stop single trees falling in high winds. It lives about 600 years and reaches maturity after 250–450 years. The branchlets are slender and drooping.
Seedlings carry juvenile foliage until they are 1–2 m tall, and juvenile, semi-adult and adult foliage often grow together on the same tree. Juvenile leaves are narrow, slightly sickle-shaped and sharply pointed, 3–7 × 0.5–1 mm, spreading in two rows, and red, wine-red or dark green to green; those of young adults are up to 4 mm, dark green or red. Adult leaves are only 1–2 mm long, keeled and scale-like, pressed tightly overlapping against the stem, and brown-green or blue-grey with a waxy bloom.

As a conifer, kahikatea has no flowers. Male cones grow at the branch tips, oblong and about 10 mm long, with pale yellow pollen. Each seed sits alone at a branchlet tip on a fleshy, oblong, flattened, warty receptacle 2.5–6.5 mm long, yellow to orange-red. The seed is broadly egg-shaped to round, 4–6 mm across, purple-black and thickly covered in a waxy bloom. A male tree glows faint orange when its cones are mature, and a female tree turns red when its receptacles are ripe.

For most of the year the tree carries no cones or fruit, and in forest it is usually too tall for its foliage to be seen, so bark and tree form are the main field characters; it sheds foliage and branchlets fairly constantly, so fallen foliage can confirm it. The bark of young trees is not distinctive, but that of a mature tree is unlikely to be confused with any native conifer except miro, which usually has no buttresses and very different foliage. The columnar form of young adults, the buttressed and fluted trunk base, the scale leaves and the round seeds at the branchlet tips separate kahikatea from all other native conifers.

lookalikes.howToTell: The bark of a mature kahikatea is easily mistaken for miro's: both are grey to grey-brown and fall in thick flakes, so bark alone does not separate them. Look at the base: kahikatea's trunk is often fluted and buttressed; miro usually has no buttresses. Look at the foliage: adult kahikatea leaves are tiny scales 1–2 mm long pressed tightly against the stem (juvenile leaves 3–7 mm); miro's are flat, dark green leaves 1.5–2.5 cm long and 2–3 mm wide, spreading in two rows. Look at the fruit: kahikatea's is a round, purple-black seed 4–6 mm across on a fleshy, yellow to orange-red receptacle 2.5–6.5 mm long; miro's is a plum-like fruit up to 20 mm long, with no separate fleshy receptacle. Miro's fruit is eaten too (see its page).

summary.text:
Dacrycarpus dacrydioides, commonly known as kahikatea (from Māori) and white pine, is a large coniferous tree in the family Podocarpaceae, endemic to New Zealand.
Kahikatea is endemic to the North, South, and Stewart Islands of New Zealand, and is the only member of the genus Dacrycarpus found in the country.
It was once the dominant tree of a distinct swamp forest type that is now all but extinct in the North Island; the best examples remain on the West Coast of the South Island. Its white, odourless timber was used extensively for butter boxes in the late 1800s and early 1900s, which all but eliminated kahikatea swamp forest from the North Island and northern South Island. It is assessed Not Threatened, but very few intact kahikatea-dominated forests remain in the North Island. Riccarton Bush in Christchurch is a surviving remnant.
It is commonly sold by nurseries and is a popular garden tree; a form with distinctly blue-grey foliage is sometimes offered.
Its pollen has three air sacs, a shape distinctive in the New Zealand flora, so it is easily identified. Kahikatea has a diploid chromosome count of 20. Several different glycosides have been isolated from the leaves; the tricetin 3',5'-di-O-/β-glucopyranoside and 3'-0-β-xylopyranoside have been found only in kahikatea. The receptacles and seeds have been found to contain anthocyanins, rare in gymnosperms, which it was suggested in one 1988 paper make the fruit as a whole more attractive to prospective animal dispersers.

warnings: Only the fleshy receptacle is recorded as eaten. No record of the seed being eaten was found, so whether it is safe is not known.

identification.text:
Hairless, unarmed, soft-wooded shrub to about 3 m tall; stems angular, green or purplish. Leaves stalked, 7–35 cm long, either undivided or deeply cut (with 1–4 pairs of lobes reaching to about 10 mm from the midrib) on the same plant; undivided leaves 2–7(–10) cm wide, the lobes of cut leaves usually 0.5–3 cm wide, lance-shaped. Flowers in clusters of 2–12 on long slender stalks; the stalks of the fruit hang down. Flower 2.5–3.5 cm across (up to 4 cm), usually mauve and paler towards the edges, occasionally white (white, lavender or dark blue, usually fading to white after the flower opens), with very broad, pointed lobes. Berry 1.5–2.5 cm long, broadly egg-shaped or ellipsoid, orange (it may be yellow as it matures), hanging; the stone cells are generally not conspicuous and are smaller than the seeds. Seeds less than 2 mm across.
Sterile material of this plant and of poroporo (Solanum laciniatum) cannot be told apart to species.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flower. Kangaroo apple's is 2.5–3.5 cm across (up to 4 cm), its lobes pointed at the tip and its flower cut more clearly into five distinct petals; poroporo's is usually 4–5 cm across (about 5 cm), its lobes very broad and shallow, with notched tips and a frilled, ruffled edge. Flower colour does not separate them: kangaroo apple's is usually mauve (white, lavender or dark blue are also recorded), poroporo's violet or white. Without flowers the two cannot be reliably told apart, since sterile material of either cannot be determined to species. Fruit length overlaps (kangaroo apple's berry is 1.5–2.5 cm long, poroporo's 23–30 mm). The fruit of kangaroo apple is orange, often with a persistent green cross at its base, with stone cells generally not conspicuous and smaller than the seeds, which are under 2 mm; poroporo's is yellow or pale orange, without a persistent green cross, with conspicuous stone cells as large as or larger than its seeds, which are 2.2–2.5 mm. Leaf size and cutting overlap too (kangaroo apple's leaves are 7–35 cm long, poroporo's 10–40 cm). The two are treated as one for practical purposes: both have poisonous green or yellow berries and leaves, and fruit that is eaten only when fully ripe and orange. Poroporo is the common one; kangaroo apple is much less common and is Threatened (see its harvest note).

summary.text:
The other poroporo: a native nightshade shrub whose fully ripe orange fruit can be eaten but whose green parts are poisonous, and which is Threatened.
Solanum aviculare (Solanaceae) is native to New Zealand: the Kermadec Islands, the North Island, the South Island (south to about Banks Peninsula and Westland) and the Chatham Islands. It is also found in eastern Australia and New Guinea, and is also called kangaroo apple. It is often confused with the much more widespread and common poroporo, Solanum laciniatum, and both are called poroporo. In its typical form (variety aviculare) it is becoming less common in the northern North Island, and the Department of Conservation's 2023 assessment lists it as Threatened – Nationally Endangered; the broader-leaved variety latifolium, which grows on the Three Kings Islands and parts of the outer Hauraki Gulf and Coromandel Peninsula, is listed as At Risk – Naturally Uncommon.

warnings: Unripe green fruit contains toxic glycoalkaloids and is extremely toxic; it stays poisonous until fully ripe.
All green parts of the plant are poisonous. The leaves, flowers and unripe fruit will at the very least burn the mouth: regard them as poisonous and avoid them.

Yellow berries are poisonous as well as green ones; only ripe orange berries lose much of their toxicity. Symptoms are often delayed up to 6–12 hours and may include fever, sweating, nausea and abdominal pain.
Even very ripe fruit, cooked with a little sugar, can irritate the roof of the mouth.

habitat.text: Forest understorey and sheltered, shady places, from the coast up to montane and cloud forest. Where rainfall is high it can make up much of the shrubland and regenerating forest, and it is often common along the edges of logging tracks and roads.
