identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to about 6 m tall; trunk slender (not always developed); branches and branchlets rather stout, glabrous. Leaves on petioles about 2–5 cm long. Stipules tapering from rather broad base to 2 conspicuous denticles, glabrous. Lamina membranous to subcoriaceous, subglossy green above, paler below, broadly elliptic to obovate; apex subacute, sometimes apiculate; rather gradually narrowed to petiole; (10)–15–20 × (5)–7–10 cm.; margins sometimes waved, sometimes more or less crenulate. Reticulations close, conspicuous or evident on both surfaces. Flowers in clusters on trichotomously branched peduncles up to about 6 cm long. male with 4–5-toothed cupular calyx; corolla narrow-funnelform, lobes usually 5, acute, shorter than tube; stamens usually 5. female usually with small stipulate bracts at axils of branches; calyx-teeth usually 5, small, acute; corolla tubular, lobes 5, narrow-triangular, acute, more or less equal to tube. Drupe reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1 as Coprosma australis (A.Rich.) Robinson]

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Leaf thickness separates them: shining karamū's are thick, kanono's rather thin. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; Kanono's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Those figures fit the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa; the North Island's wild subsp. minor has thinner, papery leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) on stalks about 10–18 mm long, and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Māmāngi's young twigs are hairy; Kanono's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Mingimingi's young twigs are more or less hairy; Kanono's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Swamp coprosma's young twigs are hairy; Kanono's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Sand coprosma's young twigs are hairy; Kanono's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

summary.text: Kanono, Coprosma grandifolia, also called manono, raurēkau and large-leaved coprosma, is a shrub or tree of the family Rubiaceae, endemic to New Zealand. It grows in the North and South Islands, in the South Island reaching Lake Ianthe in the west and the Marlborough Sounds in the east.

habitat.text: Coastal to lowland shrubland, regenerating forest and forest margins, also montane forest and ultramafic shrubland, and very occasionally subalpine shrubland. It tolerates winter cold, drought and a wide range of soils. In gardens it copes with coastal sites, wind, wet ground and long dry spells.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Some kānuka are still ranked separately by the New Zealand Threat Classification System. Kunzea sinclairii and K. toelkenii are Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable: do not harvest them unless it is a life-or-death situation and you absolutely must. K. amathicola, K. linearis, K. salterae, K. tenuicaulis and K. triregensis are At Risk: if you harvest them, take only a little, and never in a way that kills them or stops them from reproducing and spreading.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text: Shrub of diverse habit, or tree up to 15 m tall or more; trunk up to 60 cm or more in diameter; bark brown, thin, shedding in long flakes. Branchlets sparsely to rather densely clad in appressed hairs when young. Leaves in fascicles of 3–5 or solitary, ± 4–12 × 1–2 mm, linear to narrow-lanceolate, acute, not pungent, glabrous or sparsely silky-hairy when young; margins sometimes ciliolate. Flowers 3–5–(7) mm in diameter, axillary, on slender pedicels up to c. 5 mm long, in 2–5-flowered cymes to solitary. Receptacle narrow-turbinate; sepals ovate, acute, persistent; petals suborbicular, ± 2 mm in diameter, shortly clawed. Capsules about equalling to slightly exceeding receptacle-rim, 2–4 mm in diameter.

lookalikes.howToTell: Feel the leaves: mānuka's are rigid and end in a sharp, prickly point; kānuka's are not sharp-pointed and are soft to grasp. Mānuka's flowers are usually borne singly in the leaf axils; kānuka's are usually in small clusters. Mānuka's sepals soon fall, and its woody capsule stands clearly above the rim of the flower cup and stays on the plant for a long time; kānuka's sepals persist, and its capsule is about level with, or only slightly above, the rim. Both have white, occasionally pink, flowers, and bark is not a reliable test: both shed it in long strips or flakes. Mānuka's leaves are brewed as a tea (see its page).

summary.text:
Kunzea ericoides, commonly known as kānuka or white tea-tree, is a tree or shrub in the myrtle family, Myrtaceae and is endemic to New Zealand.
Kānuka is abundant throughout most of New Zealand, including many northern islands. It ranges from small, many-stemmed trees about 4 m tall to trees over 30 m tall. A fairly long-lived successional tree, it is one of the few native trees that regenerates widely after fire, and it tends to form pure stands through which other trees later regenerate. Forest clearance since human settlement has greatly widened the disturbed ground it colonises, and it is probably more widespread and abundant now than it has ever been. Once treated largely as a farm weed or cut for firewood, it is now valued for honey and essential oil, and it is a key plant in restoration and erosion-control planting, especially on steep land. New Zealand nurseries sell it for coastal planting, revegetation, shelter and screening.
It was first named Leptospermum ericoides and was moved to Kunzea in 1983. Flora of New Zealand treats all New Zealand kānuka as this one species, Kunzea ericoides in a broad sense, following a 2023 genetic study that recognised a single species; the ten species named in 2014, such as Kunzea robusta, are treated as its synonyms. The New Zealand Plant Conservation Network and the New Zealand Threat Classification System still list those species separately.

warnings: A strong brew of the leaves can make you vomit.
If you drink it regularly over a long time, keep it away from meals: its tannins may reduce how well minerals are absorbed.
Kānuka essential oil is strong. Don't take it internally except under the supervision of a qualified medical herbalist, and it should not be used by pregnant or breastfeeding women.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corynocarpus_laevigatus Names the toxin class and describes the processing this entry tells the reader not to attempt. The seeds 'contain highly toxic glucosides of 3-nitropropionic acid, such as karakin'; initial symptoms are diarrhoea, nausea and restlessness, developing into more severe gastrointestinal and neurological problems. The traditional process: seeds dropped each autumn were collected into open-weave kete, washed in water to remove the outer pulp, then baked and sun-dried, which removed the toxicity. It was one of the most grown pre-European Māori food crops, alongside kūmara and aruhe — the bracken rhizome, which has its own entry here — and in Māori tradition the tree came from Hawaiki. The flesh tastes sickly sweet, of apricots or dates, and the fruit is a valuable food for kererū and the Chatham Islands pigeon.

summary.text: Listed so you can recognise it and leave it alone. The kernel is severely poisonous without traditional processing.

warnings: The kernel is poisonous unless it has been through the traditional cooking and steeping. Do not attempt it yourself: the raw kernel can cause convulsions and paralysis.
The kernel contains karakin. Poisoning can cause seizures and paralysis; symptoms include nausea and vomiting, and muscle spasms may begin several weeks later.
The orange flesh is not the hazard — the kernel inside is, and separating them reliably is not a beginner's task.
Fallen karaka fruit is a recognised poisoning risk for children and dogs. Learn the tree so you can steer them away from it.

habitat.text: Coastal, lowland and lower montane shrubland, and open places within forest, from sea level to about 1,200 m. Hardy: it copes with infertile, poorly drained and exposed ground, in full sun or shade, wind and frost. Also grows in city green spaces.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to 6 m tall; branches and branchlets spreading, stout, glabrous. Leaves opposite on rather stout petioles about 10–20 mm long. Stipules connate towards base, obtuse, glabrous, crowned by 1–2 prominent sharp denticles. Lamina coriaceous, dullish dark green above, paler below, glabrous; elliptic to elliptic-oblong to broad-ovate, acute or obtuse, more or less mucronate, gradually narrowed to petiole, about 7–12 × 3–4–(5) cm.; reticulated veins usually conspicuous on both surfaces. male in axillary many-flowered glomerules on short peduncles, glomerules again divided into dense clusters. Calyx-teeth minute; corolla subcampanulate, lobes triangular, acute, shorter than tube. female in compound clusters on trichotomously branched axillary peduncles 10–15 mm long. Calyx minute, truncate, sometimes with 1–2 teeth; corolla about 5 mm long, narrow-funnelform, lobes acute or obtuse, oblong-triangular, shorter than tube. Drupe dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrow-ovoid, 8–9 × 4–5 mm.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Leaf shape and stipule separate them: shining karamū's leaves are widest above the middle and its stipules acute; karamū's are elliptic to ovate with tapering, long-pointed (acuminate) stipules. Shining karamū's leaf is glossy, karamū's rather dull. Shining karamū's roots and inner bark are yellow, karamū's dull brown, and shining karamū lacks karamū's foul smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; Karamū's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Leaf width and fruit length separate them: karamū's leaves about 35–42 mm wide with fruit 8–9 mm long; large-seeded coprosma's about 40–80 mm wide with fruit 10–25 mm long. Widths meet at about 40 mm, so take both tests together. Those tests fit only the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa: the North Island's wild subsp. minor has leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long, so neither test separates it from karamū. Karamū's leaf margin is minutely toothed; subsp. minor's is not. Those tests fit only the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa: the North Island's wild subsp. minor has leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long, so neither test separates it from karamū. Karamū's leaf margin is minutely toothed; subsp. minor's is not. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Māmāngi's young twigs are hairy; Karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Mingimingi's young twigs are more or less hairy; Karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Swamp coprosma's young twigs are hairy; Karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Swamp coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Sand coprosma's young twigs are hairy; Karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Sand coprosma

summary.text: Karamū, Coprosma robusta, also called glossy karamū, is a shrub or tree up to 6 m tall of the family Rubiaceae, endemic to New Zealand. It grows in the North Island and in the South Island south to Banks Peninsula; naturalised populations occur in Otago and Southland, typically around planting sites, and in a small area of Chatham Island between Waitangi and Owenga.

habitat.text:
On rocks near the high-tide mark on exposed coasts, held by a holdfast; it dries out on the rock between tides.
In New Zealand (Nelson 2013): found in the upper to mid intertidal zone on open coasts; uncommon in sheltered areas.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Karengo is a taonga species with deep customary significance, and specific beds are managed by hapū. Check for rāhui before harvesting, cut rather than tear so the holdfast survives, and take only what you will use. Some areas are subject to customary management under the Fisheries Act — ask locally.
In the Kaikōura Marine Area karengo may be gathered by hand only, within a daily limit, and the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998 protects it from commercial harvesting within Ngāi Tahu's traditional seaweed-gathering grounds.
Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.

identification.text:
Thin sheets, only one cell thick, that look like small torn sheets of purplish cellophane on the rock.
In New Zealand (Nelson 2013): Blades circular to folded rosettes, strongly attached centrally by rhizoidal holdfast. Blades (1.5) 4–12 (42) cm in diameter. Colour purple to grey, bleaching to khaki-green on upper edges. It is the only species of Pyropia present on mainland shores with a marked rosette-like growth form.

preparation.text: Wash it well in fresh water to get rid of sand and stones. Softer fronds can be used fresh, or pan-fried in butter with little seasoning; tougher ones are better dried and used as a seasoning. Spread it out to air-dry; dried karengo can then be roasted until crisp, or fried gently in a little oil, and crumbled over food.

recipes.method: Fresh karengo; 15 ml (1 tbsp) sunflower, olive or coconut oil, or more as needed; salt; lime juice, tamari, paprika or cumin, if you like. Wash the karengo well to get rid of sand and stones. Dry it, either spread out in the air for a few days or patted with a tea towel. Toss it with just enough oil to coat it lightly. Spread it over a baking tray and roast at 150 °C until crisp, turning it often so it toasts evenly; it shrinks a lot, so you may want two trays going. Watch it closely, as it burns quickly. Season with a sprinkle of salt, and with lime juice, tamari, paprika or cumin if you like. Eat straight away, on their own or with a dip. The author finds they go chewy again if kept, so grinds leftovers into sea salt or seals them in a glass jar.
recipes.title: Crisped karengo

recipes.method: Dried karengo; a little olive oil; flaky sea salt, the same amount as the crushed karengo. Fry the dried karengo gently in the olive oil. Crush it and mix it with an equal amount of flaky sea salt. Keep it in an airtight container.
recipes.title: Karengo salt

recipes.method: Fresh karengo; olive oil; 1 garlic clove, crushed; the juice of 1 orange. Wash the karengo, picking over the fronds to remove sand and any small animals. Pinch off and discard the holdfast, where the frond gripped the rock. Tear the fronds into palm-sized pieces, or shred them more finely with a knife. Spread them in a shallow ovenproof dish, drizzle with olive oil, scatter over the garlic, pour over the orange juice and toss together. Bake at 180 °C for about 20 minutes, longer for thicker kinds, until the lower layers are soft and the top is slightly crisp.
recipes.title: Baked karengo with garlic and orange

recipes.method: Written for laver (Porphyra), the European relative of karengo; the author's are purple, tough and winter laver. Laver; fresh water; a little apple cider vinegar. Rinse the laver thoroughly of sand and silt. Put it in a pan with fresh water — just a little if it is fresh or already soaked, as it gives off plenty more, but more if it is dried. Cover and keep it at a bare simmer for about 3 hours, adding water so it never boils dry; a little apple cider vinegar shortens the cooking and helps it keep. When very soft, drain and squeeze it, keeping the liquid: reduced further, it is a rich stock to freeze in ice-cube trays for soups, sauces and glazes. Spread the paste left behind — the laverbread — on toast, fry it into patties (with or without oats), or use it in stews, soups, tarts and pâtés. Freeze what you won't use soon in small tubs, as it doesn't keep well.
recipes.title: Laverbread

recipes.method: Written for laver (Porphyra), the European relative of karengo; the author's are purple, tough and winter laver. Cooked, drained laverbread; pinhead oatmeal; soy sauce, miso, sea lettuce or chopped fried mushrooms; a squeeze of lemon juice; fat for shallow-frying — bacon fat is best. Blitz cooked, drained laverbread (see the laverbread recipe), then stir in pinhead oatmeal — between half and an equal volume of oatmeal to laver — until thick enough to shape. Season to taste with soy sauce, miso, dried sea lettuce or chopped fried mushrooms, and add a squeeze of lemon juice for acidity. Leave for at least an hour, better overnight, so the oatmeal swells. Shape into patties with wet hands and shallow-fry in hot (not smoking) fat — bacon fat is best — pressing them flat with a spatula until the oatmeal bronzes into a crust. They keep well frozen once cooled, and reheat in the oven.
recipes.title: Laverbread patties

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyropia Supports the 'native nori' description and explains the double genus name on this entry. Pyropia is a genus of red algae of intertidal zones and shallow water worldwide, and several of its species are what nori is made from — a two-billion-dollar industry centred on China, Korea and Japan — with nori carrying substantial vitamin B12. Many species now in Pyropia sat in Porphyra until recently, and New Zealand material drove some of that: 2013 research on New Zealand plants moved Pyropia plicata out of Porphyra. Both names are therefore in circulation for the same seaweeds, which is why this entry lists both.

summary.text:
Karengo is New Zealand's native nori. Bladed karengo is highly prized by Māori and has special status as a taonga species. It was traditionally dried in the sun, packed in baskets, and sometimes taken inland as a gift.
In New Zealand (Nelson 2013): North Island, South Island and Chatham Islands; not found on the Three Kings Islands, Stewart Island or the subantarctic islands. For many years it was incorrectly known as Porphyra columbina.

warnings: Harvest only from clean water — never near stormwater drains or sewage or industrial outfalls, in harbours, or where there is heavy boat traffic.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Kawakawa is a significant rongoā (medicinal) plant. Tikanga around its harvest matters: take only what you need, never strip a plant, and seek guidance from mana whenua. Do not harvest on DOC land without a permit.

identification.text: Heart-shaped glossy leaves, often riddled with holes from the kawakawa looper caterpillar. Jointed, swollen stem nodes. Distinctive peppery-medicinal smell when crushed. Small upright green flower spikes.

preparation.text: Traditionally, leaves with holes eaten by caterpillars were considered the best to use. Dry and steep as a tea, or use fresh leaves to wrap food. Use as a flavouring, not a bulk green.

recipes.method: Serves 4. 10 kawakawa leaves; 1 lemon; 60 ml (4 tbsp) honey; 1.25 litres (5 cups) cold water. Wash the leaves. Slice 6 of them and keep the other 4 whole for serving. Chop the sliced leaves and boil them in the water for 5 minutes. Let it cool a little, then pour it into a plunger. Add the lemon juice and honey, stir, and leave for 2 minutes. Serve in cups with a slice of lemon and a whole leaf, or let it cool and serve over ice as a summer drink. The author takes only the large leaves, leaving the young ones and those about to shoot.
recipes.title: Kawakawa tea

recipes.method: 125 ml (½ cup) caster sugar; 4 fresh kawakawa leaves, finely chopped. Mix the sugar and chopped kawakawa together in a small bowl. Make it a few days ahead if you can and keep it in a sealed jar, so the kawakawa flavours the sugar. The author rolls freshly fried mini kūmara doughnuts in it.
recipes.title: Kawakawa sugar

recipes.method: 8 kawakawa leaves; 15 ml (1 tbsp) salt flakes. Lay the leaves on a perforated baking tray and dry them in the oven at 60 °C for 5 hours. Crumble them by hand and rub them through a sieve, or grind them in a spice grinder. Mix the dried kawakawa into the salt. The recipe serves it with green-lipped mussel fritters.
recipes.title: Kawakawa salt

recipes.method: Kawakawa leaves; 500 ml (2 cups) sunflower or canola oil; a pinch of bread to test the oil. Wash the leaves — holed ones look prettiest — and dry them very thoroughly. Heat the oil in a deep pot over medium heat until a pinch of bread sizzles as soon as it goes in. Fry the leaves 2 or 3 at a time, holding a light pot lid or splatter screen over the pot as they go in, because they spit. They puff up and turn translucent within seconds and stop spitting almost at once; lift them out gently and drain on paper towels. The author serves them on grilled salmon, one crisp on each fillet with extras on the side.
recipes.title: Kawakawa crisps

recipes.method: The author's greens, picked from roadsides around Whangaroa Harbour, were nasturtium, kawakawa, fennel, samphire, fat hen, wild mustard, cleavers and clover. The author warns that New Zealand roadsides are still sprayed with glyphosate, so pick with care. 1 garlic clove (or 4 peeled onion weed bulbs); 60 ml (¼ cup) macadamia nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) grated parmesan, dairy or plant-based (or 125 ml, ½ cup, macadamias and no parmesan); 750 ml (3 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml extra-virgin olive oil; salt and pepper. Makes about 350 g. Blend in a food processor to the texture you like. Good on crackers or toast, as a side, or stirred through soup, pasta or rice.
recipes.title: Wild Whangaroa pesto

summary.text:
New Zealand's native pepper tree — a rongoā plant first and a flavouring second.
In New Zealand it is common from Te Paki south to about Ōkārito, North Canterbury and Banks Peninsula, and also grows on the Chatham Islands.

warnings: Kawakawa essential oil contains myristicin, a deliriant when consumed in high concentrations. Because of potential toxicity, be careful how much you drink as tea.

habitat.text:
On the Kermadec Islands it is the dominant canopy tree of Raoul Island, from the coastline to the highest peaks, and the main tree of both dry and wet forest.
It occurs from almost sea level to 516 m above sea level, ranging from the coastline to the highest altitudes of the islands. M. kermadecensis is commonly associated with Alsophila kermadecensis and Rhopalostylis baueri in the forests.
On the New Zealand mainland it is widely planted, especially in the North Island, and is sold in most garden centres. It sometimes comes up wild from planted trees: a herbarium specimen was collected from crevices in a boulder sea wall at New Plymouth.
In gardens it tolerates coastal exposure and prefers free-draining soil and sun. It is frost-tender, so young plants need shelter.

harvestEthics.text:
There is no reason to pick this plant. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text:
Tree up to 20 m tall in the wild (in cultivation to 10 m tall), with large canopies, often multi-trunked from base. Branches spreading, and often bearing aerial roots. Bark firm, grey to grey-brown. Branchlets very hairy, becoming hairless with age. Sometimes branches spreading and rooting where touching the ground.
Leaves arranged in opposite pairs, each pair being at right angles to the pair below, leathery, sub-orbicular, broadly ovate to elliptic-oblong, (20–)25–50 mm long, 10–20(–30) mm wide, upper surface dark green, paler below (mainly due to thick layer of grey-white hairs), leaf surface flat, not puckered, upper surface at first hairy, becoming hairless with age, lower surface mostly velvety, midrib raised, oil glands not readily visible on either surface; margins entire, but slightly rolled downwards (revolute), tips rounded or notched, leaf stalks ± 7–9 mm long, hairy.
Flowers in rounded terminal clusters, cluster-branchlets often 3-flowered, or flowers solitary on cluster axis. Flowers ± 6–8 mm in diam., mature flower stalks absent to ± 2 mm long, ± 1.5 mm wide, petals 5, crimson; sepals 5, tips free, persistent, stalks and base of flowers and outer surface of sepals all with long, copious hairs; stamens crimson (rarely pink), filaments 10–23 mm long, much longer than petals. Main flowering period: throughout the year.
Fruit dry, densely hairy, ± 5–8 mm wide, capsule dome raised above the calyx tube, calyx tube as wide as fruit, seeds released through open valves.
Of the New Zealand species M. kermadecensis is most similar to M. excelsa in that both have velvety lower leaf surfaces, but differs in that the former possesses smaller leaves and relative to its length, wider leaves (up to 50 mm long and up to 30 mm wide, as opposed to up to 120 mm long and up to 60 mm wide), and shorter stamens (filaments 10–23 mm long as opposed to 30–40 mm long).

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stamens, the long threads of the flower: pōhutukawa's are 30–40 mm long, Kermadec pōhutukawa's 10–23 mm, and its flowers are smaller (about 6–8 mm across against 8–12 mm). Pōhutukawa's leaves are larger, 25–100 mm long (sometimes to 120 mm) and 30–50 mm wide (sometimes 15 mm or up to 60 mm), elliptic to egg-shaped-oblong, with tips pointed rather abruptly or rounded but never notched; Kermadec pōhutukawa's are 25–50 mm long (sometimes 20 mm) and 10–20 mm wide (to 30 mm), almost round, broadly egg-shaped to elliptic-oblong, with rounded or notched tips. Leaves 25–50 mm long occur on both, and pōhutukawa on the Three Kings Islands has smaller leaves close to Kermadec pōhutukawa's, so go by the stamens. Kermadec pōhutukawa often has some flowers through the year but rarely flowers en masse; pōhutukawa flowers mainly in late spring and early summer, though from August to March at the extremes. On the mainland Kermadec pōhutukawa is a planted tree, mostly a slow-growing large shrub or compact tree, to 10 m in cultivation and rarely if ever a big tree; pōhutukawa grows to about 20 m. Both have leaves velvety with grey-white hairs beneath, crimson flowers and densely hairy capsules. Kermadec pōhutukawa is often sold mislabelled as pōhutukawa, and the two hybridise in cultivation. Pōhutukawa's flower nectar and stamens are used (see its page).

summary.text:
Metrosideros kermadecensis, commonly known as the Kermadec pōhutukawa, is a species of tree in the family Myrtaceae. It is endemic to the Kermadec Islands of New Zealand.
Endemic to the northern Kermadec Island group. However, widely cultivated in New Zealand (North Island especially), also in Australia and Norfolk Island. Widely planted in mainland New Zealand from, seemingly, a single clone. The clone is slow growing and forms large shrubs, or compact trees with time. Hybridises in cultivation with M. excelsa.
It is sold in most New Zealand garden centres, often mislabelled as pōhutukawa (Metrosideros excelsa). In 2017, it was reported that myrtle rust, an invasive species of fungus, was discovered growing on M. kermadecensis. It is assessed At Risk – Naturally Uncommon (2023), as an island endemic found at one location.
A variegated form, M. kermadecensis 'Variegata', is sold by New Zealand nurseries, sometimes under the name Metrosideros excelsa 'Variegata'.

warnings: No record of Kermadec pōhutukawa as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

It is often sold as pōhutukawa, and the two hybridise in cultivation, so a planted tree labelled pōhutukawa may be this species or a hybrid. Check the stamens and leaves before using the flowers (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
Woody but brittle perennial climber attached by roots to trunks of forest trees or in large masses on ground. Stems about 4 cm diameter, branched, marked with scars of old leaves. Leaves more or less tufted towards ends of stems, spirally arranged, to about 150 × 2–2.5 cm.; sheathing bases pale; tips long-attenuate, triangular in T.S.; margins, and midrib abaxially, minutely and distantly spinulose. Spadices simple and solitary in axils of several more or less foliaceous bracts at stem apex; bracts thick and succulent towards base, white to purplish. Peduncle 1–4 cm long, glabrous, whitish; spadix at flowering about 7 × 1.5 cm., cylindrical or slightly flattened, the axis quite hidden by tightly packed flowers. male of several stamens each with a long filament, ovate anther and cop. more or less confluent pollen surrounding a small rudimentary ovary; limits of individual flowers not easily determined. female with 6–12 purplish staminodes at base of flattened, vertically elongated ovary about 2–4 × 1 mm. × 2 mm tall, the long sides grooved between the staminodes; stigmas about 6–12, sessile, arranged around a long groove; locule narrow, placentae forming ridges projecting into it. Infructescence to about 15 × 3 cm on stiff woody peduncle. Individual frs (phalanges) about 8 × 2 × 10 mm., compressed laterally, thin-walled proximally, broadest about ⅓ from base and almost woody towards top. Seed about 1 mm long, narrow, on long, slender funicle.
[From: Moore and Edgar (1970) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 2.]
In plain terms: a climber with dense cane-like stems that root freely, forming tangles on the ground or climbing tree trunks. The long leaves are dark green with yellow flecks or stripes, strongly pleated and finely scabrid on the margins and midrib, and tufted at the stem ends. At the stem tips, 1–8 pale cream to yellow spadices sit among thick, succulent white to purplish bracts; the fruit is a brownish, rough-skinned cluster up to 15 cm long when ripe (NZPCN).

summary.text: Kiekie (Freycinetia banksii) is a densely branched, brittle, woody climber endemic to New Zealand, in the screwpalm family Pandanaceae and the only member of it that is native here. It grows in the North and South Islands, in the South Island reaching about the Clarence River in the east and Fiordland in the west, and is more common in the wetter parts of the South Island. It was once treated as a subspecies of Freycinetia baueriana of Norfolk Island, but the two differ in growth habit, leaf width, leaf margin, pleating and bract colour and are kept as separate species. Over much of its range rats eat the flowers and fruits and breed it poorly; possums also eat them but help disperse the seeds. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants: the male plant's bracts are the fleshier, sweeter tāwhara, and only female plants bear the fruit. Freycinetia is one of the few New Zealand plants whose flowers are said to suit pollination by bats. Kiekie is easy from fresh seed or rooted pieces, but slow to establish, and is grown as a garden climber. The leaves were widely used by Māori for plaiting and weaving, and the sweet flower bracts (tāwhara) and fruit (ureure) were a prized food, two crops a year.

warnings: Eat the fruit only when fully ripe, and take off the rough, very bitter outer skin first.
The leaf margins and midrib are finely spiny; take care when pulling stems or leaves.

habitat.text: Blechnum novae-zelandiae is a widespread terrestrial fern found in kauri, podocarp, broadleaved and beech forest, under mānuka and kānuka, in scrub and clearings, on forest margins, in Pinus radiata forest, under Salix species, in Carex swamp, in tussock, and in rough pasture. It grows on forest margins, on roadside banks and cuttings, on cliffs and rock faces, on slips, on stream and river banks, in gullies, on tracksides and overhanging banks, on pākihi soils, in ditches, along swampy creeks, on lake margins, and in wetlands, swamps, bogs and dune hollows.

identification.text:
Rhizomes short-creeping, up to 100 m long (in herbarium material), bearing scales. Rhizome scales narrowly ovate, 5–21 mm long, 1–2 mm wide, chestnut-brown, concolorous or occasionally slightly bicolorous with paler margins. Fronds strongly dimorphic; fertile and sterile fronds with similar habit, arching upwards or outwards; sterile fronds 185–2780 mm; fertile fronds on same plant equalling or shorter than the sterile, 210–2250 mm long. Sterile fronds. Stipes 35–1150 mm long, sometimes black-brown at extreme base but mostly yellow-brown, bearing narrowly ovate chestnut-brown concolorous scales and bicolorous scales with a conspicuous dark spot around the point of attachment. Rachises yellow-brown, grooved adaxially, scaly. Laminae 150–2125 mm long, 65–740 mm wide, 1-pinnate, elliptic to obovate, with an undivided apical segment, bright green, similar colour on both surfaces, red-tinged when young, coriaceous; scales on abaxial pinna costae with a dark spot around the point of attachment, but becoming concolorous towards the pinna apices and on the distal pinnae. Pinnae in 7–53 pairs, closely spaced, narrowly oblong, straight or slightly falcate, markedly reduced to small, rounded lobes at the lamina base; the longest pinnae above the middle, 32–400 mm long, 9–30 mm wide, apices acuminate, margins shallowly crenate, bases auricled, short-stalked; the basal pinnae opposite. Veins free. Fertile fronds. Stipes 100–900 mm long. Laminae 135–1350 mm long, 65–280 mm wide. Pinnae in 8–45 pairs, linear, straight or curled basiscopically, 48–320 mm long, 2–6 mm wide; short, sterile, proximal flanges present on the middle pinnae; 2–9 pairs of pinnae at the base of the lamina replaced by short, rounded, sterile lobes. Sori and indusia in one row either side of costa, continuous along most of the length of the pinna except for the proximal sterile flanges.
Note: Measurements given above are from herbarium specimens. Larger fronds are known to occur in the wild. CHR 199087, from Moumoukai, South Auckland, comprises parts of a frond said to measure 3000 mm long.

summary.text:
Kiokio (palm-leaf fern) is one of the most widespread, abundant and easily recognised ferns in New Zealand, with long, once-divided fronds that are red-tinged when young and separate, narrower fertile fronds. It is Blechnum novae-zelandiae in the Flora of New Zealand and Parablechnum novae-zelandiae in the New Zealand Threat Classification System.
It is endemic: it grows on Raoul Island in the Kermadecs, on the Three Kings Islands, through lowland and montane areas of the North Island and of the South Island from the Marlborough Sounds to Southland, and on Stewart Island and the Chatham Islands, from near sea level to 1150 m, but not in the drier parts of south Canterbury and Otago. The fronds were used to wrap food in the hāngī. It is easily grown from fresh spores or whole plants, needs room to spread and can become aggressive in a small garden, and it is a common urban 'weedy' fern in some parts of the country. Not Threatened (2023).

warnings: Only about seven of New Zealand's roughly 200 ferns are edible. Eat only young fronds you are sure are kiokio.

identification.text:
Vigorous, dioecious, high-climbing vine, glabrous except for slightly hairy young stems. Leaves simple; petioles (0.8)–1–2 cm long, eglandular; stipules minute or 0; lamina (4)–5–12–(14) × (1.8)–2–4–(5.5) cm, lanceolate to narrow-ovate or elliptic, coriaceous, dark glossy green above, entire, acute to acuminate. Flowers (1)–3–4 in cymes, fragrant. Pedicels 5–15 mm long. Bracts more or less subulate, caducous. Hypanthium 0. Perianth 4-merous; segments 5–6 mm long, more or less oblong, yellowish green; corona threads 2.5–3.5 mm long. male flowers with 4 stamens; filaments 5–6 mm long forming a short androphore bearing an abortive ovary. female flowers with short staminodes. Ovary glabrous; styles (2)–3, about 2 mm long. Fruit (2)–2.5–3 cm diameter, subglobose or broad-ellipsoid, orange; pulp reddish, sparse. Seeds 3–7 mm long, flattened, wrinkled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia's leaves are undivided and leathery and its flowers under 2 cm across, while banana passionfruit (P. tripartita)'s leaves are 3-lobed. Kōhia is dioecious: only female plants bear fruit, and only after pollen reaches them from a male plant, so a vine without fruit can still be kōhia; use the leaves. Both are edible.

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube about 6–8 cm long (published figures run from up to 6 cm to 8 cm), with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and published lengths run from up to 9 cm to 14 cm. Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia's leaves are undivided and leathery and its flowers under 2 cm across, while banana passionfruit (P. tarminiana)'s leaves are 3-lobed. Kōhia is dioecious: only female plants bear fruit, and only after pollen reaches them from a male plant, so a vine without fruit can still be kōhia; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia's leaves are undivided and leathery and its flowers under 2 cm across, while black passionfruit's leaves are 3-lobed. A young black passionfruit's leaves are undivided too, so on a young plant go by texture: kōhia's are leathery, black passionfruit's thin. Kōhia is dioecious: only female plants bear fruit, and only after pollen reaches them from a male plant, so a vine without fruit can still be kōhia; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Black passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Pink-flowered passionfruit has downy young shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, grey- or white-felted underneath and dark shining green above; its stipules are pinnate, with dark thread-like segments almost to the base of a very narrow central strip; its flowers have a floral tube (4)–4.5–5 cm long, pink petals and violet-blue corona threads; its fruit is 4–7 cm across, round or slightly flattened, yellow and finely downy. Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia's leaves are undivided and leathery and its flowers under 2 cm across, while pink-flowered passionfruit's leaves are 3-lobed. Kōhia is dioecious: only female plants bear fruit, and only after pollen reaches them from a male plant, so a vine without fruit can still be kōhia; use the leaves. Both are edible.

summary.text:
Kōhia, Passiflora tetrandra, also called New Zealand passionflower and New Zealand passionfruit, is a high-climbing vine of the passionflower family (Passifloraceae), endemic to New Zealand and the only passionflower native here.
It grows in the North and South Islands, at the margins of lowland forest, from near North Cape to about latitude 44° (Allan 1961), which reaches Banks Peninsula.

identification.text:
Biennial, sometimes short-lived perennial. Stems branched above, (20)–40–60–(90) cm tall. Rosette leaves deeply lyrate-pinnatifid, sparsely hairy, especially on petiole and margins, or glabrous, (3)–7–25 × (1)–2–6 cm; terminal lobe ovate to oblong; lateral lobes in (4)–5–8 or more pairs, the distal pair usually wider than the terminal lobe; margins entire, sinuate, toothed or lobed. Upper stem leaves deeply pinnatifid with deflexed lobes at base; terminal lobe narrow-oblong or cuneiform, usually 3-lobed or 3-fid; lateral lobes in (1)–2 pairs, linear. Racemes to 30 cm tall; pedicels erecto-patent at fruiting, about 5 mm long. Sepals glabrous, 3–4 × 0.8–1.5 mm. Petals 6–8 × 2–3 mm. Silique erecto-patent, (30)–40–70 × 1.5–2.5 mm; style 1–1.5 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In plain terms: seeds usually germinate in autumn and form a rosette that stays green through winter. Its leaves are hairless or sparsely hairy, deeply divided into rounded lobes, and smell of mustard when crushed. The next season it sends up upright stems, branched above, with clusters of bright yellow four-petalled flowers, then long, thin pods angled upwards. In New Zealand it flowers and fruits mainly from October to December, sometimes from August and as late as May.

lookalikes.howToTell: Bog yellow cress has much smaller flowers: its yellow petals are only about as long as the sepals (1.5–2.5 mm), against 6–8 mm in land cress. Its pods are short and plump, 2–7 mm long, with the seeds in two rows; land cress's are long and narrow, 30–70 mm, with the seeds in one row. Both have yellow flowers and deeply lobed leaves with lobes at the base, and both can grow by rivers and streams, so colour, leaves and place do not separate them. Bog yellow cress's young leaves and stems are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Bog yellow cress

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping yellowcress has smaller flowers, with yellow petals 3–5 mm long against 6–8 mm in land cress. Its pods, when they form, are 10–15 mm long with the seeds in two rows; land cress's are 30–70 mm with the seeds in one row. Creeping yellowcress often sets no pods at all, and it spreads into patches by creeping underground parts, where land cress grows from a stout taproot. Both have yellow flowers and deeply lobed leaves, and both grow on riverbeds and cultivated or waste ground, so colour, leaves and place do not separate them. Creeping yellowcress has no reliable food record.
lookalikes.name: Creeping yellowcress

lookalikes.howToTell: Watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, and grows in streams, ditches and drains; land cress has yellow flowers on upright stems from a stout taproot, and grows on river banks, roadsides and waste land. Land cress's pods are 30–70 mm long; watercress's are 8–18 mm. Both have lobed leaves and a hot, cress-like taste, so taste does not separate them. Watercress is edible; cook it if it comes from water below grazing land.
lookalikes.name: Watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Some farmers wrongly call twin cress 'land cress', but the plants are easy to tell apart. Twin cress lies along the ground, smells foetid when crushed, has tiny white petals shorter than the sepals (or none) and tiny paired pods about 1.5 mm long. Land cress is an erect biennial (20–)40–60(–90) cm tall with yellow petals 6–8 mm long and long thin pods (30–)40–70 mm long. Twin cress leaves are eaten raw or cooked for their hot, cress-like taste; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Twin cress

lookalikes.howToTell: Narrow-fruited watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, and grows in streams, ditches and drains; land cress has yellow flowers on upright stems from a stout taproot, and grows on river banks, roadsides and waste land. Narrow-fruited watercress's pods are (10–)15–25(–30) mm long; land cress's are (30–)40–70 mm. Both have lobed leaves, so the leaves alone do not separate them. Narrow-fruited watercress is edible; cook it if it comes from water below grazing land.
lookalikes.name: Narrow-fruited watercress

preparation.text: Use the young leaves raw in salads and sandwiches, or cook them like spinach or in soups. The taste is strongly peppery, hotter than watercress, so raw it is usually mixed with milder leaves; the leaves are hotter in summer. As a potherb the leaves are parboiled, rinsed, then cooked until tender with fat and salt. The young flowering shoots are the hottest part; wilting them over very low heat for a short time softens their bite and bitterness. The leaves grow hotter and more bitter as the season goes on, and old leaves from a rosette that has overwintered can be fibrous and strong: pick the tender new leaves, and add stronger ones to milder cooked greens. Sautéing or steaming mellows them. Cook the young flowering stem like broccoli raab while it is still tender; once it toughens, use the yellow flowers to garnish salads and other dishes. Sprout the seeds for salads.

recipes.method: Serves 4. Ingredients: 1 medium onion, chopped; 340 g potatoes, peeled and chopped; 55 g butter; 100 g land cress; 850 ml vegetable or chicken stock; 280 ml milk; 100 ml double cream; salt and pepper. Sweat the onion and potato gently in the butter in a covered pan for 5 minutes. Add the land cress and cook 5 minutes more, then add the stock and simmer for about 20 minutes, until the potatoes are cooked. Add the milk and cream and blend, but only briefly: over-blending makes the potato gluey. Season to taste and serve with a few small leaves and a swirl of cream. The source advises against using watercress instead.
recipes.title: Land cress and potato soup

recipes.method: Written for creasy greens, the Appalachian name for land cress. Ingredients: about 225 g of chopped land cress leaves; half to 1 yellow onion, diced; 2–3 tablespoons (30–45 ml) of oil or fat (the author's grandmother used bacon fat); 2 tablespoons (30 ml) of pepper vinegar; salt. Rinse the leaves. Heat the fat in a frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion until caramelised. Add the leaves and sauté for a few minutes, until they darken and soften. Add a few splashes of pepper vinegar, cook 1 minute more, take off the heat and salt to taste.
recipes.title: Greasy creasies

recipes.method: Written for mixed wild greens; wintercress (land cress), wild turnip (field mustard) and purple dead nettle (red deadnettle) are the author's choices. Serves 5. Ingredients: half an onion; 4 cloves garlic; 4 cups (about 1 litre) washed, coarsely chopped wild greens; 2 cups (about 500 ml) raw, coarsely chopped chickweed tops; 120 ml extra virgin olive oil; 60 ml tahini; 125 ml freshly toasted whole pecans; 85 g feta; salt. (The source's list also names a further half cup, about 125 ml, of chickweed.) Sauté the onion and half the garlic in some of the olive oil until the onion begins to turn translucent. Add the greens and sauté until tender, then take off the heat and let cool. Put the chickweed, pecans, the rest of the oil, the tahini, the feta and the remaining garlic in a blender or food processor. Add the cooled greens a little at a time, blending between additions, until the pesto is coarsely ground; don't overload the blender. Add more oil for a creamier pesto, and salt to taste. For a milder pesto use more chickweed and fewer mustard greens. Serve as a dip, spread on flatbread or pizza, or toss through pasta or vegetables.
recipes.title: Wild greens, pecan and feta pesto

recipes.method: Written for creasy greens, naming both land cress and its relative Barbarea vulgaris. Ingredients: about 1.4 kg land cress, with stems; 4 litres water; 250 ml vinegar; 2 Tabasco peppers; 8 cloves garlic (the source says only '8 garlic'); 30 ml black pepper; 1 onion, quartered; 2 chunks smoked fatback. Strip the leaves from the stems and keep the stems. Wash the leaves in two changes of water, then put them in a pot with everything else. Bring quickly to the boil, then simmer slowly for two to four hours. Lift out the greens, strain the liquid and serve the greens. For the pot likker, put the stems into the strained liquid and cook a few hours more, adding more fatback and vinegar if you like. Take out the stems, cool the liquid and skim the fat from the top; use it as a base for soups and stews or drink it as a broth.
recipes.title: Creasy greens and pot likker

summary.text:
Land cress, Barbarea verna, is a biennial, sometimes short-lived perennial, herb of the mustard family (Brassicaceae).
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) it is recorded from Northland, Auckland, Waikato, Rotorua, Taranaki, Wairarapa and Wellington, and from Nelson, Canterbury and Otago, naturalised by 1869 from southern, western and central Europe. It has also been called Barbarea praecox in New Zealand. Miller first named it Erysimum vernum in 1768; Ascherson moved it to Barbarea in 1860. Other New Zealand names are American cress and upland cress, and the NZ Plant Conservation Network lists it as winter cress. The genus is named after St Barbara, to whom wintercress was dedicated.
Te Papa holds a Wellington specimen, collector and date unknown, identified by Phil Garnock-Jones in 1979 (SP062053). Manaaki Whenua's herbarium has about 37 databased New Zealand records: Canterbury 8, Wellington 8, Nelson 5, Otago 2, one each from North Auckland and Westland, and 12 not placed in a region.

warnings: It can grow tangled with creeping buttercup, which is toxic: make sure every leaf you pick is land cress.

Avoid places that may have been sprayed or polluted, and pick at least 9 m from roads. Fields that look abandoned may still be sprayed, and some weedkillers take about a week to kill a plant, so sprayed greens can still look healthy.

habitat.text: On the ground in towns and gardens: in bark and wood-chip mulch on landscaped beds, in gardens and planters, on bare soil in suburban yards, and in potting mix in nursery pots. Pine bark mulch is a common setting. The same spot often fruits year after year.

identification.text: Fruit body 6–20 cm tall. The cap is 3–15 cm tall and 2–9 cm wide, conical to broadly conical or occasionally egg-shaped, and covered in pits and ridges: 12–20 main vertical ridges joined by many horizontal cross-ridges, giving a laddered look. The ridges are pale to dark grey when young, becoming dark greyish brown to nearly black with age; they start bluntly rounded and later become sharp or worn. The pits are vertically elongated, grey to dark grey when young and greyish brown, greyish olive or brownish yellow when mature. The cap meets the stem in a small groove about 2–5 mm deep and wide. Stem 3–10 cm tall and 2–6 cm wide, often a little thicker at the base, whitish to pale brownish and bruising ochre to brown with age, smooth or finely mealy, becoming ridged and grooved lengthwise as it matures. The cap is hollow, with whitish flesh 1–3 mm thick; in the stem the flesh is sometimes arranged in chambers or layers. Spore print cream.

preparation.text: Always cook morels thoroughly; never eat them raw. Halve large ones lengthwise and swish them in cool water to wash grit out of the pits, then pat them dry. They release a lot of water as they start cooking — let it cook off.

recipes.method: Written for morels in general (Morchella), of which landscaping black morel is one; cook them thoroughly. Serves 4. 450 g fresh morels; 30 g (2 tbsp) unsalted butter; 1 shallot, finely chopped; salt and pepper; 5 ml (1 tsp) fresh thyme leaves; 15 ml (1 tbsp) lemon juice; a splash of dry sherry or Madeira; 250 ml (1 cup) cream; vol-au-vent cases or toasted brioche to serve. Clean and trim the morels, halving large ones. Melt the butter in a large frying pan over medium heat and soften the shallot until just translucent. Add the morels, turn them in the butter and season. Sauté for about 7 minutes, then stir in the thyme and lemon juice and raise the heat. When the lemon juice has evaporated, add the sherry and cook until it has evaporated too. Lower the heat to medium, stir in the cream and cook until thickened. Check the seasoning and spoon over the pastry cases or brioche. Serve at once.
recipes.title: Morels in cream

recipes.method: Written for morels in general (Morchella), of which landscaping black morel is one; cook them thoroughly. 340–450 g fresh morels; 250 g (2 cups) flour; 15 ml (1 tbsp) salt; 10 ml (2 tsp) ground black pepper; 5 ml (1 tsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) onion powder; 2 eggs; 125 ml (½ cup) milk; lard, butter or vegetable oil for frying. Halve large morels lengthwise and leave small ones whole; swish them in a bowl of cool water to loosen grit, lift out and pat dry. Mix the flour and seasonings in one bowl and whisk the eggs and milk in another. Pour fat into a large frying pan to about 1 cm deep and heat it to 165–175 °C. Dust the morels in the seasoned flour, dip them in the egg wash and then in the flour again, shake off the excess and fry in a single layer without crowding, at least 3–4 minutes a side so they are fully cooked, adjusting the heat so they don't burn. Drain on paper towels, keeping finished batches warm in a low oven, and serve with lemon wedges.
recipes.title: Fried morels

recipes.method: Written for morels in general (Morchella), of which landscaping black morel is one; cook them thoroughly. Serves 4. About 1 litre beef, chicken or vegetable stock; 500–750 ml (2–3 cups) water; 30 g (2 tbsp) butter; 125 ml (½ cup) minced shallot, leek or onion; 2 garlic cloves, minced; 400 g (2 cups) risotto rice; 225 g fresh morels, chopped (or 30 g dried); salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) chopped chives or parsley; 125 ml (½ cup) grated pecorino or parmesan. Bring the stock and 500 ml of the water to a gentle simmer. In another pot heat the butter over medium-high heat and soften the shallot for 3–4 minutes. Add the garlic, morels and rice and cook for 2–3 minutes, stirring often. When the liquid from the morels has evaporated, add 125 ml of hot stock and stir well, with a little salt; keep stirring, adding another 125 ml as each lot is absorbed, until the rice is cooked through but still firm. Stir in the cheese with a little more stock, add the herbs and serve at once. With dried morels: pour 500 ml boiling water over them, cover and steep 30 minutes, squeeze them out over the bowl, chop them, strain the soaking water through a paper towel and use it in place of the 500 ml of water.
recipes.title: Morel risotto

recipes.method: Written for morels in general (Morchella), of which landscaping black morel is one; cook them thoroughly. 450 g morels, sliced lengthwise; 45 g (3 tbsp) butter; 2 spring onions, chopped; 125 ml (½ cup) dry white wine; salt. Melt the butter in a frying pan, add the morels and spring onions and cook until the morels are lightly browned. Lift the morels and as much of the onion as is easy onto a plate with a slotted spoon, leaving the butter in the pan. Add the wine and salt and boil, watching closely, until it reduces to a syrup. Return the morels and onions, toss together briefly and take off the heat. Serve over chicken, beef, vegetables, rice or pasta.
recipes.title: Morels in white wine

recipes.method: Written for morels in general (Morchella), of which landscaping black morel is one; cook them thoroughly. Serves 4. 750 ml (3 cups) morels, sliced lengthwise; 4 salmon fillets (about 225 g each); 45 g (3 tbsp) butter; 3 garlic cloves, minced; 250 ml (1 cup) dry white wine; 30 ml (2 tbsp) lemon juice; salt and pepper. Melt the butter in a large frying pan over medium heat and cook the garlic for 1 minute. Add the morels and cook until they begin to brown, then pour in the wine and cook, stirring often, until it has almost evaporated; tip the morels into a bowl. Lay the fillets skin side down in a grill pan, sprinkle with the lemon juice (and a little butter if liked) and grill without turning until cooked through, checking after 6 minutes. Season and spoon the morels over each fillet.
recipes.title: Salmon with morels

recipes.method: Written for morels in general (Morchella), of which landscaping black morel is one; cook them thoroughly. Serves 4. 750 ml (3 cups) morels, sliced lengthwise; 4 boneless, skinless chicken breasts, flattened if you like; 60 g (4 tbsp) butter; 125 ml (½ cup) chicken stock; 125 ml (½ cup) cream; 30 ml (2 tbsp) lemon juice; 60 g (½ cup) flour; 3 shallots, chopped; 3 garlic cloves, minced; salt and pepper. Heat the oven to 150 °C. Melt half the butter in a large frying pan over medium heat, dust the chicken in the flour and brown it on both sides, 8–10 minutes. Move it to a baking dish and bake until heated through. Meanwhile melt the rest of the butter in the pan and cook the morels, shallots and garlic for 3 minutes, stirring often. Add the stock and reduce by half, then add the cream, lemon juice, salt and pepper and cook down to a sauce. Spoon the sauce over the chicken.
recipes.title: Chicken with morels and cream

recipes.method: Written for morels in general (Morchella), of which landscaping black morel is one; cook them thoroughly. 225 g morels, sliced lengthwise; 60 ml (¼ cup) milk; 45 g (3 tbsp) butter; 3 spring onions, chopped; 6 eggs. Melt the butter in a large frying pan and cook the morels and spring onions until the morels start to brown. Meanwhile beat the eggs with the milk. Pour the eggs into the pan and scramble until cooked as you like them. Serve on toast.
recipes.title: Scrambled eggs with morels

recipes.method: Written for morels in general (Morchella), of which landscaping black morel is one; cook them thoroughly. 225 g fresh morels, sliced lengthwise; 30 g (2 tbsp) butter; 2 bunches asparagus, cut into 2.5 cm pieces; 1 shallot, chopped; 2 garlic cloves, minced. Melt the butter in a frying pan over medium heat and add the shallot, garlic, morels and asparagus. Cook until the morels are browned and the asparagus is tender, usually 8–10 minutes.
recipes.title: Asparagus and morels

recipes.method: Written for morels in general (Morchella), of which landscaping black morel is one; cook them thoroughly. Serves 4. 300 g fresh morels; 100 g white bread; 4 large onions; 125 ml (½ cup) sherry; 60 g (4 tbsp) butter; 100 g hard cheese such as gruyère or parmesan, grated; 30 ml (2 tbsp) sugar; 1–1.5 litres chicken stock; a pinch each of ground nutmeg and cloves; salt. Rinse the morels well, chop them coarsely and simmer them for 5 minutes in a pot with 250 ml (1 cup) water, the cloves and salt. Cook the onions in the butter for 15 minutes, add the sugar and cook 10 minutes more until caramelised. Pour in the sherry and cook until the alcohol has evaporated, then add the stock and simmer gently for 30 minutes. Add the morels with their liquid, season with nutmeg and salt, bring to the boil and take off the heat. Toast the bread, top it with the cheese and a few of the morels and bake at 180 °C for 5 minutes. Ladle the soup into bowls and serve with the croutons.
recipes.title: Onion and morel soup with cheese croutons

recipes.method: Written for morels in general (Morchella), of which landscaping black morel is one; cook them thoroughly. Serves 2. 2 veal loin steaks; 15 ml (1 tbsp) clarified butter (ghee); salt, pepper and ground paprika. Sauce: 20 g dried morels; 1 shallot, finely chopped; 100 ml dry white wine; 100 ml beef stock; 180 ml cream; 15 ml (1 tbsp) lemon juice; 5 ml (1 tsp) cornflour. Soak the morels in warm water until soft, then strain, keeping 100 ml of the soaking liquid. Bring the steaks to room temperature and heat the oven to 60 °C. Sear the steaks in the clarified butter for 1–2 minutes a side, season and keep them warm in the oven. In the same pan soften the shallot with the morels, add the wine and simmer briefly, then add the stock and the soaking liquid and reduce by half. Stir in the cream, thicken with the cornflour mixed with a little cold water and season with the lemon juice, salt, pepper and paprika. Pour over the steaks.
recipes.title: Steak with dried-morel cream sauce

Saprobic (or possibly mycorrhizal) on soil. Spring fruiting, these fungi often appear at the same site year after year. Four species have been reported from New Zealand; however they have not been investigated for the region taxonomically. Edible and choice, but can be confused with the macroscopically similar Gyromitra, which is highly poisonous. Gyromtira occurs in New Zealand in native forests and in pine plantations, whereas Morchella has been found only in urban areas.' Jerry Cooper (Manaaki Whenua mycologist), comment on Geoff Ridley's 'The "Morel" of the Story' (https://sporesmouldsandfungi.wordpress.com/2021/06/01/the-morel-of-the-story/, 01/06/2021): 'Here is a link to a record of Morchella importuna. It occurs most years in the re-cycled milk cartons that "Trees For Canterbury" use in their nursery in Christchurch' and 'M. importuna is a look-alike and one of the most common "weedy" Morchella species that has spread around the planet.' MycoLogic (NZ spawn seller; https://www.mycologic.nz/outdoor-patches): 'Black Morels (Morchella importuna) … are occasionally found by a lucky few in mulched garden landscaping, with the most common denominator being a coniferous mulch, usually pine bark chips'; 'In New Zealand, this is usually anywhere from early September through to November'. Food records written for this species: Wikipedia ('It is considered a choice edible mushroom'; 'sought after as a choice edible mushroom. Raw morels are poisonous and should always be cooked') and MycoLogic (sells it as a culinary morel, 'Morels are one of the most coveted of culinary mushrooms in the world'); the Fungal Guide's 'Edible and choice' covers every New Zealand morel. summary.text: An introduced black morel that fruits in spring in landscaped places — bark and wood-chip mulch, gardens and nursery pots. Its pitted, ladder-ridged cap darkens to nearly black with age. In New Zealand it has been found only in places people have made; herbarium specimens come from suburban Rotorua and a Christchurch nursery. Spawn is sold in New Zealand for starting a garden patch in conifer mulch over loamy soil; the seller says the far north may not get enough winter chill for it to fruit.

warnings: Never eat morels raw or undercooked: they have caused vomiting, diarrhoea and stomach pain, and dizziness, balance problems and disorientation.

Poisonous false morels (Gyromitra) grow in New Zealand, in native forest and pine plantations. Their caps are lobed and contorted, sometimes saddle-shaped, without the morel's orderly network of ridges and pits. False morels are not safe to eat, cooked or raw.
Some people react badly even to edible mushrooms, so eat only a small amount the first time you try one.

habitat.text: Grassland, scrub and open forest. Montane and subalpine, on sites of low fertility, including tussockland; it grows in harsh conditions where there has been no grazing, oversowing or topdressing. It does not tolerate frost at the spring flush, dense shade or poor drainage, tolerates partial shade and is slightly intolerant of drought; it regrows after damage if some green foliage remains, and fire kills plants under 2 m. Planted, it needs light and well-drained soils, prefers natural shelter and slopes that shed cold air, and grows productively up to 900 m.
