identification.text:
Small or medium-sized tree (large in cultivation), pyramidal when young, irregular in shape later. Branchlets more or less drooping. Bark grey, pinkish below, fissured and forming small plates. Long shoots yellow, glabrous, appearing ribbed because of elongated, pad-like persistent leaf bases. Short shoots stout, about 5 mm long, grey. Leaves on short shoots in fascicles of 40–65, 1.5–4 cm × about 0.5 mm at 1/2 way along leaf, grass-green, very soft; midrib raised on either side. Male and female strobili or cones surrounded by thin, brown bud scales with dense marginal tuft of curly brown hairs. Female cones about 1 cm long at anthesis; bract scales prominent, crimson, with subulate, green apical point. Mature cone 1.5–3.5 × 1.7–2.5 cm when open, broadly ovoid-oblong; ovuliferous scales 40–50, broad-ovate or suborbicular, not prominently recurved, vertically striated with outer margin rounded; bract scales usually concealed at maturity, sometimes a small part of subulate tip exposed. Seed with large, broad, asymmetric wing.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The leaves are needle-like, light green, 2–4 centimetres long which turn bright yellow before they fall in the autumn, leaving the pale yellow-buff shoots bare until the next spring.
Male cones are yellow and hang from the lower sides of the branchlets; female cones are crimson red and upright, maturing to brown.
Japanese larch is best distinguished from L. decidua by the greenish conelets and the recurved margins of the mature ovuliferous scales which give an almost rosetted appearance to the cone. Japanese larch also has less dense, more regular needle clusters.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are deciduous conifers with soft needles in tufts on short woody shoots, and they are planted in the same places and cross, so some trees are hybrids that look in between; look at the cones and the needle clusters. European larch's young female cones are crimson, with prominent crimson bract scales; its ripe cones are 1.5–3.5 cm, with scales that are not prominently recurved; its needles are 1.5–4 cm and grass-green, with 40–65 in a dense, irregular cluster. Japanese larch's young female cones are greenish and the scale margins of its ripe cones curve outwards, giving an almost rosetted look; its needles are 2–5 cm and light green, in clusters that are less dense and more regular. Japanese larch's young needles are eaten the same way (see its page).

preparation.text: Steep the young needles in hot water for tea, or make a cordial (see the recipe). Use them on the day you pick them, as their aroma fades quickly.

recipes.method: Written for European larch. The author makes it by his nettle cordial method, with young larch needles in place of the nettle. Equal parts water and white sugar (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar); at least a cupful (about 250 ml) of young larch needles, pressed down; a little citric acid or lemon juice, or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar. Pick the young needles in spring, while they are bright, almost luminous green and taste sharp, like sorrel. Make a syrup of equal parts water and white sugar (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar), heating gently and stirring until the sugar dissolves. Add at least a cupful (about 250 ml) of needles, pressed down, or more. Keep it on the heat until steaming hot, but don't let it boil. Strain out the needles. Stir in a little citric acid or lemon juice, or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar, until it tastes slightly sharp. It keeps for several weeks in the fridge.

summary.text:
European larch (Larix decidua) is a rather open-branching deciduous conifer in the pine family (Pinaceae), native to Europe and western Asia and widely planted in New Zealand.
The seeds are an important food for some birds, notably siskin, redpoll, and citril finch, while the buds and immature cones are eaten by capercaillie.
Larch needles (including L. decidua and L. sibirica) are the only known food for caterpillars of the case-bearer moth Coleophora sibiricella; its cone scales are used as food by the caterpillars of the tortrix moth Cydia illutana.
Larch canker is a major disease in Europe but is not present in New Zealand.
In New Zealand it is naturalised in the South Island in inland high country areas, especially the Amuri Range (North Canterbury) and Mackenzie County (South Canterbury); it was first recorded wild in 1919. Larch or European larch is mainly grown as a forest and plantation tree in colder parts of New Zealand, especially in the Rotorua area and the high country of the South Island. In the Mackenzie Basin it has become so extensively naturalised and aggressive that control measures have become necessary. It was introduced as an ornamental, is grown in parks and gardens, and has been planted on a small scale for timber, as farm shelter and to control erosion in the high country, where it tends to spread unless grazed. It is listed as an environmental weed, and regional pest management plans put it under progressive containment in Waikato, Bay of Plenty, Hawke's Bay, Wellington, Tasman-Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago and Southland, site-led control in Gisborne, and list it as an organism of interest on the Chatham Islands. The seed is spread by the wind, with 130,000–170,000 seeds per kilogram of cones, and stays viable for 3–5 years in dry storage; trees live more than 80 years. Hybrid larch, the cross between European and Japanese larch, is sterile and does not spread as wildings.

warnings: Larch bark taken by mouth, or larch oil spread over large areas of skin, may cause kidney damage. Allergies such as hives, rashes and contact dermatitis are possible.
Take extra care in pregnancy: many sources recommend against eating or drinking any conifer while pregnant.
Try only a little the first time: allergic reactions to conifers are not common, but are more likely than with most foods.
Do not pick from trees that may have been sprayed: wilding conifers are controlled with herbicide.

associations.note: Always found with larch, here mostly European larch in plantations.
Also recorded with Japanese larch.
Also recorded with Norway spruce overseas.

identification.text: Cap 5–15 cm across, sticky and smooth, golden brown to yellow ochre, often paler towards the edge and streaked or blotched with lemon or golden yellow. Underneath there are yellow pores, not gills, running a little down the stem. Stem 5–10 cm long, yellow to yellow-ochre, with a conspicuous ring and no dark dots. Flesh lemon to creamy yellow, changing little or not at all when cut; taste mild.

lookalikes.howToTell: Slippery jack grows under pines; larch bolete grows only under larch. Both have a slimy cap, yellow pores and a ring. Slippery jack's cap is dull reddish or chocolate brown, and its stem has small dark dots above a large sheathing ring that is purplish underneath. Larch bolete's cap is golden brown, often streaked lemon or golden yellow, and its stem has no dark dots.

preparation.text: Peel off the slimy cap skin and remove the pore layer, then cook thoroughly. It holds a lot of water; slicing, drying and rehydrating improves it.

recipes.method: Serves 2. 400 g fresh larch boletes, caps peeled; 1 red onion or 4 shallots; 4 carrots; 300 g buckwheat; butter or olive oil; salt and pepper; parsley. Boil the buckwheat. Peel and coarsely grate the carrots and fry them briefly in olive oil, then add the cooked buckwheat and fry lightly until golden. Meanwhile slice the mushrooms finely. Chop the onion and soften it in butter or olive oil, add the mushrooms and cook them together for 15–20 minutes. Season with salt and pepper and serve over the buckwheat with parsley scattered on top.
recipes.title: Fried larch boletes with carrot buckwheat

recipes.method: Written for slippery jack (Suillus luteus), a close relative; prepare larch boletes as above, peeling the caps and removing the pores. Serves 4. 300 g mushrooms, peeled and cut into bite-sized pieces; 1.5 litres water; 3 medium potatoes; 1 medium carrot; 1 medium onion; 30 g butter; 1 tbsp vegetable oil; 1 bay leaf; salt and black pepper; a small bunch of dill. Bring the mushrooms and water to the boil, skim off the foam and simmer gently for 20 minutes. Add the peeled, diced potatoes and cook 15 minutes more. Meanwhile soften the chopped onion in the butter and oil, then add the grated carrot and cook until golden. Stir the onion and carrot into the soup with the bay leaf, salt and pepper and simmer 5–7 minutes. Take off the heat, remove the bay leaf, stir in the chopped dill and leave covered for 10 minutes before serving. For a creamier soup, stir in 125 ml cream in the last 2 minutes.
recipes.title: Larch bolete soup with potato and dill

recipes.method: Written for slippery jack (Suillus luteus), a close relative; prepare larch boletes as above, peeling the caps and removing the pores. Serves 2. 400 g mushrooms; 500 g floury potatoes; 1 large onion; 4 tbsp vegetable oil; 20 g butter; 2 garlic cloves; salt and pepper. Pat the peeled mushrooms dry and cut them into thick wedges; cut the potatoes into chips, slice the onion thinly and chop the garlic. Cook the mushrooms in a dry pan over medium-high heat until the water they release has gone, 8–10 minutes, then add 2 tbsp oil, the butter and the onion and fry until both are well browned; season. In a second pan fry the potatoes in the remaining oil, leaving them alone for the first 5 minutes, until golden and tender, 15–20 minutes in all. Salt the potatoes, add the mushrooms, onion and garlic and toss for 2 minutes. Serve hot.
recipes.title: Larch boletes with fried potatoes

recipes.method: Written for slippery jack (Suillus luteus), a close relative; prepare larch boletes as above, peeling the caps and removing the pores. Serves 4. 300 g tagliatelle or fettuccine; 350 g mushrooms, sliced; 150 ml cream; 50 ml dry white wine; 3 garlic cloves; 40 g butter; 1 tbsp olive oil; a small handful of parsley; 50 g grated parmesan; salt and black pepper. Parboil the sliced mushrooms in salted water for 10 minutes and drain well. Cook the pasta until al dente, keeping 125 ml of its water. Warm the crushed garlic in the butter and oil for a minute, then lift it out. Fry the mushrooms in the garlic butter for 5–7 minutes until starting to brown, add the wine and let it bubble almost away, then lower the heat, add the cream and simmer 3–4 minutes; season. Toss the pasta through the sauce, loosening it with pasta water if needed. Off the heat stir in the chopped parsley and half the parmesan, and serve with the rest on top.
recipes.title: Tagliatelle with larch boletes and cream

recipes.method: Written for slippery jack (Suillus luteus), a close relative; prepare larch boletes as above, peeling the caps and removing the pores. 450 g mushrooms, sliced; 250 ml chicken, vegetable or beef stock; 250 ml white wine; 2 tbsp butter, divided; 4 large shallots and 4 large garlic cloves, finely chopped; 2 tbsp chopped parsley; 3 tbsp flour; salt and black pepper. Soften the shallots and garlic in 1 tbsp butter in a large heavy pan for 2–3 minutes. Add the mushrooms and a pinch of salt and cook 6–8 minutes until they give up their liquid (in batches if the pan is small). Add the rest of the butter and, once melted, stir in the flour to a paste. Whisk in the wine slowly and cook over medium-low heat, whisking, until as thick as gravy, adding stock or water if it gets too thick. Stir in the parsley until wilted, season and serve over wild rice.
recipes.title: Larch boletes in white wine over rice

summary.text: An introduced slippery jack that grows only under larch. Its sticky golden-brown cap is often streaked with yellow.

warnings: Slippery jacks upset some people's stomachs. Peeling the cap and removing the pores is thought to lower the risk.
Some people react badly even to edible mushrooms, so eat only a small amount the first time you try one.

habitat.text: Mostly coastal forest and scrub, including on offshore islands, from sea level to about 560 m; also gullies and above streams.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to 5–(10) m. tall; branches and branchlets stout, glabrous. Leaves on stout petioles about 12–25 mm long. Stipules connate into broad membranous sheath tipped by long sharp denticle. Lamina subcoriaceous, broad- to elliptic-ovate, obtuse or subacute to mucronulate, about 9–13 × 4–8 cm. Midrib prominent, secondary veins and reticulations evident. male in compound glomerules on axillary peduncles 10–15 mm long; calyx-teeth minute; corolla about 9 mm long, subcampanulate, lobes ovate-triangular, acute, shorter than tube. female 2–5 together, on simple or branched peduncles 20–70 mm long; calyx-teeth acute; corolla tubular, widening above, lobes acute, shorter than tube. Drupe orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Leaf width and fruit length separate them: karamū's leaves about 35–42 mm wide with fruit 8–9 mm long; large-seeded coprosma's about 40–80 mm wide with fruit 10–25 mm long. Widths meet at about 40 mm, so take both tests together. Those tests fit only the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa: the North Island's wild subsp. minor has leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long, so neither test separates it from karamū. Karamū's leaf margin is minutely toothed; subsp. minor's is not. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; large-seeded coprosma's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Māmāngi's young twigs are hairy; large-seeded coprosma's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Mingimingi's young twigs are more or less hairy; large-seeded coprosma's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Swamp coprosma's young twigs are hairy; large-seeded coprosma's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. summary.text: Large-seeded coprosma, Coprosma macrocarpa, is a shrub or tree of the family Rubiaceae, endemic to New Zealand. Subspecies macrocarpa is confined to the Three Kings Islands and has naturalised around Auckland and Wellington; subspecies minor grows in the North Island and nearby offshore islands from North Cape south to Kawhia Harbour and Hicks Bay.

identification.text:
Large, narrow-pyramidal tree; branches usually present to near ground and more or less drooping towards the apex. Bark thick, fibrous, reddish brown, fissured. Branchlets in horizontal sprays, green or, less commonly more or less glaucous (mostly glaucous in cultivation), aromatic when bruised. Sapling quickly passing into adult condition. Scale leaves appressed; facial pairs on lateral shoot systems (excluding 1–3 year terminal brown shoots) mostly 1–2 mm long, broad-ovate, subacute, with gland on back elongated and appearing as a translucent dot in transmitted light; lateral pairs similar but mostly 1.5–2.5 mm long, with whitish stomatal lines on lower side more or less evident when fresh. male strobili 2–5 mm long; pollen sacs deep pink to crimson. female cones blue when young, brownish with bluish bloom and 6–9 mm diameter when mature; scales 8; umbo a small ridge. Seeds 2–4 on each scale, with conspicuous resin tubercles; wing narrower than or equal to to seed.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The combination of acute scale leaves with translucent glands, obviously larger lateral than facial leaves, and bright crimson male cones, distinguishes C. lawsoniana from C. obtusa and C. pisifera, which are cultivated abundantly in New Zealand, in the adult stage.
It can reach 50 m. Cypresses (Cupressus) look similar but do not have its flattened branchlet sprays; Thuja has flattened sprays too, but its cones of both sexes are quite different. Of the several Chamaecyparis species grown in New Zealand, Lawson's cypress is the one with brightly coloured male cones.

summary.text:
Lawson's cypress, also called Port Orford cedar, is a conifer in the cypress family (Cupressaceae), brought to New Zealand as an ornamental.
The species is native to southwestern Oregon and northwestern California, and grows from sea level up to 1,500 metres in the valleys of the Klamath Mountains, often along streams. It fares best at the north end of its range.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1940. Lawson's cypress is a very common cultivated garden, park, domain and windbreak tree. There are a number of cultivars grown in New Zealand, mainly differing in habit and foliage colour, but spontaneous plants usually have green foliage and the typical narrow-pyramidal habit.
It spreads by seed: a female cone holds up to 32 seeds, and a mature tree may carry as many as 10,000 cones. It was on the Department of Conservation's 2008 consolidated list of environmental weeds but is not on the 2024 list.
North Island; South Island: scattered localities throughout, especially cooler areas with a moderate to high rainfall.

warnings: Lawson's cypress has been queried as a cause of abortion in cattle, like macrocarpa, but there is little hard evidence for it.
Cypresses are more likely than needled conifers to cause allergic reactions, including skin rashes.

habitat.text:
Lawns and other open turf, typically dry and poor but also wet or rich ground, and urban areas; also disturbed or regenerating native vegetation, often on track edges, rarely in dense forest. Coast to subalpine (to 1100 m), mostly lowland.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Open rocky slopes, rock crevices, stony ground, old screes, short turf, poor or open pastures and tussockland, open scrub, cliff faces, river beds, beaches, waste places, lawns, plantations, cultivated ground, common to abundant, sea level to c. 1500 m.

identification.text:
Perennial; primary root slender to stout, occasionally to about 10 mm thick. Stems glabrous to densely hairy (hairs usually antrorse, occasionally dense and patent), more or less filiform, creeping, prostrate or nearly so, rooting at nodes, much-branched and often mat-forming. Leaves 3-foliolate. Petiole 5–40 mm long, with patent or antrorse hairs, these sparse to dense; stipules adnate, truncate or rounded at apex. Petiolules very short. Lamina of leaflets equal, 1–9 × 1.5–12 mm, obcordate, sometimes broadly so, with width greater than length, with narrow to broad sinus and rounded lobes, glabrous or hairy above, glabrate or with appressed hairs beneath, ciliate or eciliate, often purplish below; calli 0. Flowers solitary, rarely paired; peduncle glabrate to densely clothed in antrorse hairs, generally geniculate at apex; pedicel (4)–8–25 mm long. Bracts 1–3 mm long, more or less linear-subulate, hairy, situated at base or at middle of pedicels; calli 0. Sepals 2.3–3.5–(4) mm long, oblong-lanceolate, oblong, or ovate-elliptic, glabrate or with antrorse hairs; calli 0. Petals 4.5–9–(13) mm long, more or less oblong-obovate, yellow, often pink-flushed outside, glabrous. Stamens at 2 levels, glabrous or nearly so; filaments united at base, those of longer whorl about 1.5 mm long. Styles shorter than or longer than longer stamens, densely hairy. Capsule (3)–7–10–(13) mm long excluding styles, broadly cylindric, cylindric-ovoid or conic, glabrous to densely hairy; hairs short, patent or retrorse, sometimes glandular. Seed 1–1.3–(1.5) mm long, broad-ellipsoid; transverse ridges 7–13, subacute, sometimes white-topped; grooves deep. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Least yellow sorrel creeps: its stems are more or less thread-like, prostrate or nearly so, root at the nodes and often form mats. Bermuda buttercup appears stemless, with its leaves all rising from the base on stalks 6–22 cm long, and grows from a bulb with underground runners that bear many small bulbils. Measure a leaflet and a petal, remembering the ranges almost meet: least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long and its petals 4.5–9 mm (up to 13 mm); Bermuda buttercup's leaflets are 10–32 mm long and its golden petals 2–2.8 cm (from 1.5 cm). Least yellow sorrel's flowers are solitary, rarely paired, and it sets a capsule 7–10 mm long (3–13 mm at the extremes); Bermuda buttercup usually carries 3–18 flowers (occasionally 1) hanging on a stalk 15–45 cm long (from 7 cm), and no capsule has been seen on it in New Zealand. Yellow flowers, notched leaflets and purple in the leaf do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Bermuda buttercup

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping wood sorrel looks like a larger least yellow sorrel, with much the same leaves, creeping stems and yellow flowers, so size and flower count are the tests, and size changes with growing conditions. Creeping wood sorrel's leaflets are 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm) and up to 23 mm wide, and its leaves are normally about 20 mm across; least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long and its leaves typically under 10 mm across. Count the flowers on a stalk: creeping wood sorrel carries 1 to 5, usually at least two; least yellow sorrel's are solitary, rarely paired. Creeping wood sorrel's capsule is mostly 10–18 mm long, least yellow sorrel's mostly 7–10 mm, though the ranges meet. Creeping wood sorrel is more often in garden beds and nurseries, least yellow sorrel in lawns. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. White clover's leaflets are 5–25 mm long, least yellow sorrel's 1–9 mm long. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves or stems: both creep and root at the nodes, both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually stalkless on the leaves beneath it, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Red clover's hairy stems stand erect or lie along the ground at the base and do not root at the nodes; least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats. Red clover's leaflets are 15–40 mm long, least yellow sorrel's 1–9 mm long. Out of flower, leaflet size is a guide, as the published ranges do not meet. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Alsike clover's hairless stems stand erect or rise from the base and do not root at the nodes; least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats. Alsike clover's leaflets are 10–35 mm long, least yellow sorrel's 1–9 mm long. Out of flower, leaflet size is a guide, as the published ranges do not meet. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have small yellow flowers and three small leaflets that are often notched at the tip, and both grow in lawns. Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long. Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Suckling clover's stems lie along the ground or rise a little and do not root at the nodes; least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats. On most suckling clover leaves the middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the side ones (under 1 mm); least yellow sorrel's three leaflets are equal, on very short stalks. Leaflet size does not separate them: suckling clover's are about 3–12 mm long, least yellow sorrel's 1–9 mm. Season does not either: suckling clover is an annual that flowers from October to June, and least yellow sorrel flowers in every month. Suckling clover has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Suckling clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Small, starved plants of Oxalis rubens can be hard to tell from least yellow sorrel. Least yellow sorrel's stems are thread-like, creep flat, root at the nodes and often form mats; Oxalis rubens's sprawl or stand nearly erect, up to about 50 cm, and do not root at the nodes, or only slightly. Least yellow sorrel's flowers are usually smaller, petals 4.5–9 mm (up to 13 mm) against Oxalis rubens's 6–14 mm, and solitary, rarely paired, against 1–3 (up to 4) on a stalk. Least yellow sorrel's capsules are mostly 7–10 mm long (3–13 mm at the extremes), broadly cylindric, cylindric-ovoid or conic; Oxalis rubens's are 10–23 mm and cylindric. What does not separate them: leaflet size overlaps (least yellow sorrel 1–9 mm long, Oxalis rubens 3–13 mm), both can have a stout root (least yellow sorrel's occasionally to about 10 mm thick), and both grow on beaches and in open coastal turf. Oxalis rubens has no record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Oxalis rubens

preparation.text: Add the leaves to salads, cook them as a pot herb with milder greens, or use them to give a sour taste to other food. The flowers can be eaten raw in salads. The leaves are very small and fiddly to pick.

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) lemon juice and 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) maple syrup or honey. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the sorrel and stir for 1–2 minutes, until it wilts. Put it in a blender or food processor with the lemon juice and the syrup or honey and blend until well combined. Serve it straight away, or refrigerate it and warm it before use; the author finds it even better the next day. The author serves it on fish, or as a dipping sauce for grilled prawns.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel sauce

recipes.method: About 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, stems or flowers, or a mix, about 250 ml (1 cup) water, and maple syrup or another sweetener to taste. The amounts are rough: use as much sorrel as you like and enough water to cover it. Blend the sorrel and water until well combined, strain through a fine sieve and sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel 'lemonade'

recipes.method: Equal parts wood sorrel, sugar, and water; the author usually uses 250 ml (1 cup) of each. Put everything in a saucepan and bring it to a simmer, stirring. Simmer for 15–30 minutes, strain through muslin (cheesecloth) and pour into sterilised bottles. The author uses it in tea, topped up with soda water, over ice cream or fresh strawberries, or in vinaigrettes and marinades.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel syrup

recipes.method: The recipe uses one part leaves to three parts water. Fresh wood sorrel leaves; boiling water; sweetener to taste (optional). Put the leaves in a container, pour the boiling water over them and leave to steep for 5–15 minutes. Strain out the leaves and sweeten to taste if you like. Drink it hot, or pour it over ice for an iced tea.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel tea

recipes.method: 2 cloves garlic, minced; olive oil for cooking; 2 spring onions, chopped; 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock; 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish; 3 medium mint leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk; salt and pepper. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks. Heat a little olive oil in a small saucepan and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the spring onions. Cover with the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, then add the sorrel for about 30 seconds. Take it off the heat, add the mint and blend smooth with a stick blender (or an ordinary blender). Stir in the coconut milk and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until well chilled, a couple of hours, and serve garnished with the sorrel flowers.
recipes.title: Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

recipes.method: About 450 g (1 lb) Italian or breakfast sausage; 1 medium spaghetti squash; several cups of wood sorrel, washed and drained, stems removed (the recipe gives no closer amount); olive oil; 1 red onion, halved and sliced; 1 egg; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk or any milk; 1 garlic clove, minced; 15 ml (1 tbsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) tarragon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) black pepper; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground sage. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Halve the squash, spoon out the seeds and stringy threads, set the halves cut side up on a baking tray, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and bake for 20–25 minutes, until the flesh gives a little when pressed. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts. Take the squash out of the oven and scrape out the flesh with a fork (careful, it will be hot). Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.
recipes.title: Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel

recipes.method: Two handfuls of wood sorrel, chopped; potato and kūmara, boiled first and sliced; cream. Layer the sorrel with the sliced potato and kūmara in a baking dish, pour cream over the top and bake at 180 °C until it starts to brown.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel, kūmara and potato gratin

recipes.method: Chop a big handful of wood sorrel leaves, stalks and flowers and mix them through a potato salad dressed with a cream dressing.
recipes.title: Potato salad with wood sorrel

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: The author's greens were puha, sow thistle, nasturtium, onion weed, wild fennel, oxalis, wild mustard and wild celery; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 1 diced onion; 1 potato, scrubbed and diced; 2 sliced garlic cloves; 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 1.3 litres water; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked pepper; extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil, to serve; edible weed flowers. Serves 4. Cut the vegetables and greens to similar sizes. Fry the onion in the oil for a minute, then add the potato and garlic (the method also adds fennel bulb and celery stalks, which the ingredient list leaves out) and fry for another minute. Add the water, cover, bring to the boil and simmer until the potato is soft. Add the greens with the salt and yeast and cook for 3 minutes, until just tender — added at the end, they keep their colour. Blend until smooth (push it through a sieve if your blender isn't powerful), season with the pepper and more salt if needed, and serve drizzled with extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil and scattered with edible weed flowers.
recipes.title: Wild greens soup

Recipes copied 16/10/2026 from creeping-wood-sorrel (owner: "yeah copy the recepies to the sorrels", after "the recipies are interchangeble betwwen sorrel species"). None is written for Oxalis exilis: seven are written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally, and the gratin and potato salad for Oxalis incarnata. This page records no edible parts of its own; the recipes rest on the owner's word that wood sorrel recipes are interchangeable. Provenance as recorded on creeping-wood-sorrel: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (cups at 250 ml, 1 tbsp = 15 ml, 1 tsp = 5 ml; every page all rights reserved; retrieved 15/10/2026; supplied by the owner). None is written for this species: each is written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally. The sauce, 'lemonade' and syrup from Kate MacQuarrie, 'Wood Sorrel Recipes', PEI Untamed, 09/07/2023 (https://www.pei-untamed.com/post/wood-sorrel-recipes) — written for 'the Wood Sorrels' of Prince Edward Island, no species named; 'grilled shrimp' given as prawns; the lemonade's 'leaves, stems, and/or flowers' and its note that the author does not measure are kept. 'Wood sorrel cooler' is Sunny Savage's 'Oxalis Cooler' as given in Green Deane, 'Oxalis: How To Drown Your Sorrels', Eat The Weeds (dated 16/01/2018 on the page, with reader comments from 2012; https://www.eattheweeds.com/oxalis-how-to-drown-your-sorrels/; the owner's second link, https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/oxalis-deppei/, is a tag page showing the same article) — written for Oxalis generally, the article naming the Florida species including O. corniculata; 1 US quart is about 946 ml; the recipe does not strain the drink and neither does this. 'Wood sorrel tea' from Jesse, 'Wood Sorrel: Identification, Uses, and Precautions', Feral Foraging, 11/07/2024 (https://feralforaging.com/wood-sorrel/) — written mainly for O. stricta and O. violacea; the page gives the ratio only as '1:3' after 'Gather wood sorrel leaves' and 'Pour over boiling water', without saying by volume or by weight, so 'one part leaves to three parts water' is this guide's reading. 'Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup' from Valerie Zemba, 'Chilled Lemony Wood Sorrel Soup', Very Vegan Val, 03/07/2019 (https://veryveganval.com/chilled-lemony-wood-sorrel-soup/) — written for 'Oxalis stricta and others'; scallions given as spring onions, vegetable broth as stock; the rinsing and stripping step is from the page's prose above the recipe card. 'Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel' from Chosen Weeds Farm, 'Cooking With Wood Sorrel', 15/03/2017 (https://thechosenweeds.com/cooking-with-wood-sorrel/) — written for the purple-leaf wood sorrel that grows in the author's south-east Texas garden; 400 °F given as 200 °C, 1 lb as about 450 g; 'Several cups' of sorrel kept because the page gives no closer amount; the page says only 'Combine mixture with the egg' after forking out the squash, and the method keeps that wording rather than saying where the squash goes. Not used from the recipe pages (15/10/2026): the casserole page's 'If you are short on time you can skip the oven step', because skipping the final bake would leave the stirred-in egg uncooked; Feral Foraging's statements that all species of wood sorrel are edible and can be used in similar ways (genus-level claims), its estimate that about 30 g a day, several times a week, is safe and its view that oxalate warnings are overblown (it contradicts every other page read here and is not a trusted source for a safety amount), and its cold-infusion and dried-leaf variants; Green Deane's statements that cooking reportedly renders oxalic acid harmless, particularly with calcium, that eating a lot raw can leach calcium from the bones, and that the juice curdles milk for cheese, and that all parts including the root bulb are edible (said of the Florida species as a group); the casserole page's medicinal and vitamin claims; the reader comment on Eat The Weeds suggesting more sorrel for a sharper cooler. Two of the owner's links have no recipe: Rachel Lambert, 'Wild Food: Wood Sorrel family', Wild Walks Southwest, 07/05/2021 (https://wildwalks-southwest.co.uk/wild-food-wood-sorrel-family/), and Diego Bonetto, 'How to identify and eat wood Sorrel', 10/08/2021 (https://www.diegobonetto.com/blog/wood-sorrel-id-forage-edible-weed) — both name O. corniculata among the species they describe. Lambert says all of them have a lemony, tart flavour and uses them in salads, in soups and as an edible decoration; Bonetto says the stalks, flowers and leaves are eaten raw or cooked, in salads and as a garnish; recorded here for edibleParts and preparation, which were empty on creeping-wood-sorrel when this was written (15/10/2026). Gratin and potato salad, as recorded on pale-pink-wood-sorrel: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (all rights reserved; retrieved 16/10/2026; supplied by the owner): Johanna Knox, 'Wood sorrel (Oxalis incarnata)', Wild Picnic, 16/07/2009, https://wildpicnic.blogspot.com/2009/07/wood-sorrel-oxalis-acetosella.html — the gratin and the potato salad. The post was first written as O. acetosella; a commenter (AJB, 26/11/2009) identified the plant pictured as 'the South African Ox. incarnata', which the author accepted, and the title now names O. incarnata. The blog covers Wellington and the Wairarapa; the post does not say where the plant grew. Not used as recipes: adding it to apple, peach or pear pie and a jelly (suggestions, not made by the author); its use to curdle milk for cheese (the author had not got it to work).

summary.text:
Oxalis exilis, the least yellow sorrel or shady woodsorrel, is a small herbaceous plant found in Australia and New Zealand.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North, South and Stewart Islands; Kermadec Islands. Also indigenous to Australia and probably Norfolk Island. O. exilis is by far the commonest species of section Corniculatae in New Zealand and is almost certainly indigenous.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

edibleParts.text:
Fruit - raw or cooked. A pleasant acid flavour, it is nice when added to muesli or porridge. Unfortunately, there is relatively little flesh and a lot of seeds.
Berberis bealei has berries that are used in pies, jellies, jams, beverages and confections. The yellow flowers are eaten or used to make a lemonade-like drink.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand: native and exotic forest, forest margins and shrubland, most likely near gardens or historic sites (Environment Canterbury, for the four mahonias growing wild here); recorded growing wild in the Christchurch Botanic Gardens.
In the south-eastern United States, where it is naturalised: open woodlands and shrublands, 100–500 m (Flora of North America).
In its native range: Forests, forest margins, weedy slopes, streamsides, roadsides and thickets; at elevations from 500 - 2,000 metres.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Berberis bealei' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Berberis bealei is a multi-stemmed, evergreen shrub or small tree with irregular, strong upright stems that have limited branching. It grows up to 8 metres tall, is upright, and is scarcely branching. The leaves are up to 50 centimetres long, with 4–10 pairs of leaflets, plus a much larger terminal leaflet. The sessile leaflets have spines and the terminal leaflets are larger than others.
The flowers are borne in an erect raceme up to 30 cm long. The berries are blue or dark purple coloured egg-shaped berries, up to 15 millimetres long, that turn bluish black with a greyish bloom. Fruits hang in grapelike clusters and are glaucous, covered with a white waxy coating. The erect stems are stiff and unbranched.

lookalikes.howToTell: Leatherleaf mahonia's leaves are up to about 50 cm long with 4–10 pairs of leaflets and a much larger terminal one; Oregon grape's are up to about 25 cm with 3–7 pairs. Leatherleaf mahonia's flower clusters stand upright, 7–26 cm long; Oregon grape's reach 6–7 cm. Its berries are egg-shaped and up to 15 mm long; Oregon grape's round, about 10 mm across. Leatherleaf mahonia has stiff upright stems and can reach 8 m; Oregon grape is a low, many-stemmed, suckering shrub, usually about 1 m. Leaflet counts overlap at 4–7 pairs, and dark bloomed berries and spiny leaflets do not separate them. Leatherleaf mahonia's berries are also described as globose, so shape alone does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Oregon grape

lookalikes.howToTell: Leatherleaf mahonia's flower clusters stand upright, 7–26 cm long; Japanese mahonia's are lax and spreading. Leatherleaf mahonia's leaflets are wider, 2–6 cm, against Japanese mahonia's 2–3.5 cm, so only a wide leaflet tells. Leatherleaf mahonia's berries reach 15 mm long; Japanese mahonia's are 8–10 mm. Leaflet counts (4–10 pairs against 5–9), a small lowest pair, spiny teeth and blue-black bloomed berries do not separate them, and leatherleaf mahonia has been listed as a form of B. japonica ('Bealei'). The two have hybridised in gardens and many plants raised from seed are hybrids, so intermediate plants seem to be fairly common in gardens. Plants grown under the name leatherleaf mahonia in the United States are also described with loose, spreading to hanging flower clusters and narrow leaflets, so on a planted or escaped shrub neither trait settles it.
lookalikes.name: Japanese mahonia

lookalikes.howToTell: Leatherleaf mahonia's leaves carry 4–10 pairs of broad leaflets, roundish to ovate and 2–6 cm wide; mountain grape's carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped ones, 1–2.5 cm wide. Leatherleaf mahonia's berries are up to 15 mm long; mountain grape's up to 8 mm. Upright flower clusters, a tall habit and dark blue bloomed berries do not separate them, and the garden hybrid 'Arthur Menzies' has both as parents.

preparation.text: The berries can be eaten raw but the seed to pulp ratio is large so most of these berries are boiled and strained.

recipes.method: Written for the berries of Japanese and leatherleaf mahonia. Base: 375 ml flour, 440 ml rolled oats, 125 ml chopped walnuts, 250 ml packed dark brown or coconut sugar, 1 tsp baking powder, ½ tsp fine salt, 1 tsp vanilla and 250 ml melted butter. Topping: 625 ml mahonia berries, 250 ml sugar, 2 tsp grated orange or lemon zest and two lavender buds. Heat the oven to 180°C and line a 20–23 cm tin with baking paper, leaving it overhanging the sides. Stir the dry ingredients together, then work in the melted butter until crumbly. Press three-quarters of it firmly into the tin and bake for 10 minutes. Cook the berries with the sugar, zest and lavender over low heat for 15 minutes, until they pop open; cool for 5 minutes and take out the lavender. Pour over the base, scatter the rest of the crumble on top and bake for 30–40 minutes, until golden. Cool completely in the tin, lift out by the paper and cut into 12 large bars or 24 squares.

summary.text:
Leatherleaf mahonia, Berberis bealei, is an evergreen shrub of the barberry family (Berberidaceae), native to mainland China. It has been treated as the same species as Berberis japonica, but the two differ consistently in certain floral and leaf characters.
In New Zealand: Flora of New Zealand Online and NZPCN list it as exotic, as Berberis bealei with the synonym Mahonia bealei; neither describes it.
Biota of New Zealand records it as a casual exotic (growing wild but not naturalised), after Heenan, de Lange et al. (2004). In the south-eastern United States it has escaped gardens and naturalised, and North Carolina lists it as invasive; it spreads by seed and by suckers, which can form a colony, and birds eat the fruit.

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.
The berries contain berberine, which can upset the stomach, especially in children. Eating the poisonous parts (bark, leaves, roots and sap) can cause stomach upset, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous, lemon-scented herb with branched puberulent stems ascending to about 60 cm. Leaves and bracts petiolate. Lamina 2–8.5 × 1–7 cm, elliptic to broad-ovate, hairy, sometimes only sparsely hairy above, prominently crenate-serrate; base more or less truncate in larger lower leaves, cuneate in upper smaller leaves and bracts. Verticels generally 3–10-flowered. Calyx about 8 mm long; nerves prominent, with long, white, pilose hairs; upper teeth broad-triangular, aristate; lower narrow-triangular, aristate. Corolla 12–15 mm long, white (sometimes tinged pink); lobes hairy outside. Nutlets 1.7–2 mm long, almost black.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Crushed leaves smell strongly of lemon. The mints share its square stems but smell of mint.
Large bushy plants lacking the characteristic lemon scent were found in the Kauaeranga Valley, Thames district. They are not foetid, although the mint-like scent is quite different to the ordinary lemon balm.

lookalikes.howToTell: Lemon balm and spearmint both have square stems and opposite leaves, and both are aromatic. Spearmint's flowers are in narrow spikes at the stem tips, the central spike 4–12 cm long. Its calyx is 1.5–2.2(–3.5) mm long, and its mauve or pinkish corolla is 3–5 mm long with a four-lobed, scarcely two-lipped limb. Lemon balm's flowers are in whorls of generally 3–10 among stalked, leaf-like bracts. Its calyx is about 8 mm long, with prominent nerves, long white hairs and unequal teeth, and its corolla is 12–15 mm long, clearly two-lipped, with a curved tube. Spearmint's leaves are stalkless or very shortly stalked; lemon balm's leaves are stalked. Crushed lemon balm leaves usually smell strongly of lemon, and spearmint has a strong spearmint smell. But lemon balm plants without the lemon scent, smelling of mint, have been found in New Zealand, so smell is a clue, not a test. The flower tests are the surest. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Wild spearmint

preparation.text: Use the leaves mainly as a flavouring: in salads and cooked foods, fish dishes, pesto and ice cream. A lemon-flavoured tea is made from the fresh or dried leaves. The flavour is delicate and fades fast, and does not stand up to strong flavours: add the leaves at the last minute, even to cooked dishes. Use them in place of mint; in green, fruit, cucumber, potato and chicken salads; chopped into soups and stews; or stirred into scone and muffin dough with a pinch of lemon zest. To scatter over food, tear the leaves by hand: chopped, they soon taste of grass clippings. The fresh leaves bruise and brown easily, and tender leaves turn black when cooked, so for a jam infuse them in the sugar instead. They go well in black or green tea, and can be frozen in ice cubes for summer drinks; cover tea while it brews to keep in the aromatic oils. The leaves are best freshly picked, but dry well if dried gently, as heat and light take their aroma: spread stems and leaves in a single layer with good airflow, out of the light, at about 25 °C for the first day and no more than 35 °C after that, and strip the leaves once they are crisp. Plants cut back hard after flowering put up a fresh flush of leaves.

recipes.method: Tender lemon balm leaves; equal parts sugar and water; lemon juice, citric acid or the lemon balm vinegar below. Use the tender leaves. For a syrup, infuse them into a syrup of equal parts sugar and water by heating gently, without boiling. Cool, and keep in sterilised jars in the fridge for a couple of weeks. Pour it over puddings or use it in cocktails. For a cordial, sharpen the syrup to taste with lemon juice, citric acid or the lemon balm vinegar below; it keeps better and gains a pleasing sharpness. Dilute to drink, or use it for a gimlet.
recipes.title: Lemon balm syrup and cordial

recipes.method: Tender lemon balm leaves; cold apple cider vinegar; lemon balm syrup or cordial, or honey. Use the tender leaves. Infuse them straight into cold apple cider vinegar for a week, then strain. Use it in salad dressings or as a pickling liquor. Mix the vinegar with lemon balm syrup or cordial for a shrub, or with honey for an oxymel, to give cocktails a gentle acidity.
recipes.title: Lemon balm vinegar and shrub

recipes.method: Tender lemon balm leaves; vodka; lemon balm cordial, syrup or shrub. Use the tender leaves. Infuse them in vodka for no more than 3 days, strain, and sweeten to taste with lemon balm cordial, syrup or shrub.
recipes.title: Lemon balm liqueur

recipes.method: The author's elderflower champagne with lemon balm leaves in place of the elderflowers, or added to them. He gives no amount for the leaves. 650 g sugar; 4.5 litres of cold water; lemon balm leaves, or elderflowers and lemon balm leaves; the juice and quartered skin of 1 lemon; 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar. Dissolve 650 g sugar in 4.5 litres of cold water — warm a little of the water to dissolve the sugar, cool it, then mix it into the rest. In a large bucket or bowl, combine the sweetened water with the flowers or leaves, the juice and quartered skin of 1 lemon, and 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar. Cover and leave for 4 days, somewhere cool; if mould forms, scrape off the mat of flowers on top and carry on. Fine-strain into clean screw-top plastic fizzy-drink bottles, leaving a few centimetres of air at the top. Never use corked bottles, and avoid glass flip-tops: you can't feel the pressure through them, and they are far more dangerous if they burst. Leave at room temperature for 6–14 days. From day 6, check the bottles regularly by squeezing them, and as soon as the bases start to round out, ease the caps to let off some (not all) of the pressure — a forgotten bottle can explode. Once it tastes right, move it to the fridge to slow the fermentation, and keep checking the pressure. The author drinks it between 2 and 4 weeks: it is lightly alcoholic after a week and starts turning vinegary at 5–6 weeks. The recipe's yeast comes from the flowers, so in a cool room it can take a while to get going.
recipes.title: Lemon balm champagne

recipes.method: Lemon balm leaves; wood sorrel (oxalis) leaves; a little sugar; crab-apple verjuice; cracked ice; gin; soda. Muddle lemon balm and wood sorrel (oxalis) leaves with a little sugar and crab-apple verjuice. Add cracked ice, then gin and soda to taste.
recipes.title: Wild mojinto

recipes.method: Lemon balm; 70 ml gin; 35 ml elderflower limoncello; 35 ml dry vermouth; 15 ml pineapple weed shrub (pineapple weed vinegar mixed with syrup); a splash of lemon balm champagne; lemon balm and elderflowers, to garnish. Muddle lemon balm in a glass with 70 ml gin, 35 ml elderflower limoncello, 35 ml dry vermouth and 15 ml pineapple weed shrub (pineapple weed vinegar mixed with syrup). Top up with a splash of lemon balm champagne, to taste. Garnish with lemon balm and elderflowers placed so that you smell them as you drink.
recipes.title: The Elderbalm

recipes.method: 1 egg white; a little water; lemon balm leaves; sugar. Beat the egg white with a very little water. Dip each leaf in it, then in sugar, and lay the leaves on a baking tray lined with baking paper. Dry them in the oven at about 95 °C until they look dry but not browned: check after 20 minutes, then every 5–10 minutes. Use them to garnish ice cream or tarts.
recipes.title: Candied lemon balm leaves

recipes.method: Serves 2. Pickled shallot: 1 large shallot; 1 tbsp honey; 30 ml vinegar; 60 ml water; ½ tsp salt; ¼ tsp pepper. Salad: 1 large telegraph (English) cucumber; virgin sunflower oil or extra virgin olive oil; salt and pepper; 5–6 lemon balm leaves, to taste. Bring the honey, vinegar, water, salt and pepper to the boil, then turn off the heat. Peel and trim the shallot, slice it into 3 mm rings and pour the hot liquid over them; chill. Halve the cucumber lengthways, scrape out the seeds with a spoon and slice it 6 mm thick. Arrange the slices on a chilled plate, season with salt, pepper and oil, scatter over the pickled shallot, then tear the lemon balm into roughly 1 cm pieces over the top and serve at once. An ordinary cucumber works too, peeled and seeded. A variation: salt the sliced cucumber, drain off the water it gives, and dress it with a little yoghurt.
recipes.title: Cucumber salad with lemon balm and pickled shallot

recipes.method: Makes 5–6 jars of about 250 ml. 900 g raspberries; 1.1 litres (4½ cups) white sugar; 1 bunch lemon balm, flowers removed; the juice of 1 lemon (listed in the recipe, though its steps do not say when to add it). A day ahead (12–14 hours), rub the lemon balm leaves and stalks into the sugar until it is fragrant, cover, and leave it to sit: tender leaves turn black when cooked, so the herb flavours the sugar instead. Pick out the stalks and any loose leaves. Sterilise the jars, lids and any equipment, and get a water bath ready. Heat the raspberries gently in a large non-reactive pan, pressing them against the pan, for about 10 minutes, until very soft and juicy. Push 250 ml of the fruit through a fine sieve to take out some of the seeds, and return it to the pan. Add the sugar and stir over low heat until it dissolves, then boil rapidly for 10–15 minutes, until the jam passes the wrinkle test or reaches 104 °C. Take it off the heat for at least 3 minutes, fill the sterilised jars, and process them in the water bath for 10 minutes.
recipes.title: Raspberry and lemon balm jam

recipes.method: After a recipe in Janet Ross's Leaves from our Tuscan Kitchen (1899). 60 ml olive oil, divided; 1 garlic clove; a handful of lemon balm leaves, torn or roughly chopped; 500 g drained, cooked cannellini beans; 1 tbsp white wine vinegar; salt and plenty of pepper; 80 g finely grated Parmesan; 1 egg, beaten; 250 ml dried breadcrumbs; 2 tbsp butter. Warm half the oil with the garlic and lemon balm in a wide frying pan over low to medium heat for 5 minutes to infuse. When the garlic is golden, add the beans and stir them through the herbs, then add the vinegar, salt and pepper and cook gently for 5–10 minutes, until some of the liquid has cooked off. Off the heat, mash the beans, mix in the Parmesan and chill until completely cold and firm. Roll tablespoons of the mixture into walnut-sized balls, then into little cylinders, and coat each in egg and then breadcrumbs. Heat the rest of the oil with the butter over medium heat and pan-fry the croquettes in batches until golden; if loose crumbs burn in the pan, wipe it out and start again with fresh oil and butter. Serve hot or warm.
recipes.title: Cannellini bean croquettes with lemon balm

summary.text:
Lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) is a perennial herbaceous plant in the mint family.
Melissa officinalis is native to south-central Europe, the Mediterranean Basin, Central Asia and Iran, but is now naturalized in the Americas and elsewhere around the world.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands: scattered localities throughout. Naturalised from Eurasia, first recorded in 1904. Lemon balm has been widely cultivated in New Zealand since the early period of European settlement. The strongly lemon-scented leaves are used for flavouring and once were used medicinally.
Other names include melissa and sweet balm, and it is sometimes called bee balm too.
It is not to be confused with bee balm (genus Monarda).

warnings: Taken as a medicine to aid sleep, lemon balm leaf may in theory cause drowsiness and impair your ability to drive or use machines, and the risk may increase with alcohol, other sedatives or large doses.
Its safety in pregnancy and breast-feeding has not been established, so medicinal use then is not recommended. Medicinal use in children under 12 is not recommended either, for lack of data.

In laboratory and animal studies, water extracts of the leaf may inhibit thyroid-stimulating hormone; whether this matters in people is not known. As a precaution, avoid large amounts if you have an underactive thyroid or take thyroid hormone medicine.

identification.text:
Polygamodioecious tree with spreading branches, up to 12 m tall, trunk up to 6 dm diameter, bark pale. Leaves alternate, often approximate, 5–10–(15) × 2.5–4 cm, on rather slender petioles 1–2 cm long. Lamina subcoriaceous, glossy, scented, elliptic to elliptic-oblong, acute to subacute, narrowed to petiole; margins usually undulate, midrib pale. Flowers fragrant, in terminal compound umbels, subcorymbosely arranged. Peduncles and pedicels with scattered hairs; peduncles 1–2 cm long, pedicels about 5 mm long. Sepals ovate to narrow-ovate, pale, membranous, about 2 mm long; petals narrow-oblong, yellowish, 5–7 mm long. Capsules glabrous, finely granulate, ovoid to elliptic in outline, 5–6 mm long; valves 2 or sometimes 3; seeds immersed in viscid pulp, remaining more or less covered by papery endocarp at dehiscence.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]
Leaf buds are sticky and resinous, and the crushed leaves smell strongly of ivy or resin. Told from all other native and introduced pittosporums in New Zealand by its yellow-green, mottled leaves with wavy margins and its pale yellow to yellow flowers in compound umbels.

summary.text: Lemonwood or tarata (Pittosporum eugenioides) is an evergreen tree of the pittosporum family (Pittosporaceae), endemic to New Zealand. It is common in the North and South Islands. Its crushed leaves have a strong scent, described as of ivy or resin, or of lemon. The very fragrant pale yellow to yellow flowers open from October to December, and the fruit, a small capsule with black sticky seeds, is present from October to January. It is commonly cultivated, often as a variegated form. It grows easily from fresh seed and can also be grown from semi-hardwood cuttings. It is assessed Not Threatened (2023). Pittosporum means 'pitch seed', and eugenioides 'like Eugenia', from its resemblance to that unrelated myrtle genus.

warnings: Only the resin is recorded as chewed. No record covers eating the leaves, flowers or seeds of lemonwood.
Some Pittosporum species contain saponins, and poisonous properties are recorded throughout the genus.

identification.text:
Plants openly branched, 1–1.5 m tall. Stems grooved, with sparse to dense cobwebby eglandular and subsessile glandular hairs, rarely glabrous or farinose. Basal leaves deltoid to broadly deltoid, green and sparsely hairy above, whitish and densely felted beneath, (15)–25–40–(55) × (10)–13–30–(35) cm; base cordate; apex subacute to obtuse; margin crenate to bluntly dentate with apiculate vein endings; petioles hollow. Upper leaves similar to basal, becoming smaller. Inflorescence racemose; peduncles 0–1–(3) cm long. Capitula (12)–15–20 × (14)–20–30 mm. Involucral bracts straw yellow, greenish or purplish, glabrous or with sparse to dense cobwebby hairs; margins with short, stiff, tapered, forwardly directed denticles, at least on the innermost bracts. Florets equal to or longer than involucral bracts; corolla reddish purple. Achenes 5–7 mm long; pappus 1.5–3.5 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In its first year it is only a rosette of large leaves over a long, deep taproot; the flowering stem rises in the second year or later, and the plant dies once it has flowered and set seed. The pale undersides of the leaves have fuzzy, raised, light-coloured veins. The flower heads look like small thistles: reddish-purple centres in a spiky green ball of bracts. As the heads dry the bracts harden into hooks, and the burs cling to clothes, fur and wool. It flowers from January to April and fruits from February to May.
Greater burdock (A. lappa) has larger, longer-stalked flower heads and solid stalks to its lower leaves; lesser burdock's are hollow. In New Zealand greater burdock is known only around Morrinsville and at scattered sites in Canterbury and Otago. Coltsfoot looks like a burdock rosette, but its leaves are broadly heart-shaped with the veins spreading from the base like fingers, not triangular. Winter heliotrope has large kidney-shaped basal leaves and flower heads like burdock's that never form burs.

lookalikes.howToTell: Broad-leaved dock's leaves are oblong ovals, often finely downy beneath, especially on the veins, with smooth, slightly wavy edges and a papery sheath (ochrea) round the base of each stalk; lesser burdock's basal leaves are broadly triangular, 25–40 cm long (up to 55), whitish and densely felted beneath, with scalloped to bluntly toothed edges and hollow stalks. Dock leaves are glossy; burdock's are matt.
lookalikes.name: Broad-leaved dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Foxglove is deadly. Its rosette leaves are lance-shaped to oval, 10–25 cm long and 3.5–12 cm wide, and narrow gradually into a long, winged stalk; lesser burdock's basal leaves are broadly triangular, 25–40 cm long (15–55) and 13–30 cm wide, with a heart-shaped base and a hollow stalk. Both are felted grey or white beneath and have scalloped edges, so neither of those tells them apart. In flower there is no confusion: foxglove flowers from October to January in a tall spike of hanging bells, burdock from January to April in thistle-like heads that turn into burs. If a leaf narrows into a winged stalk, leave it.
lookalikes.name: Foxglove

preparation.text:
Dig roots from first-year rosettes, before any flowering stem appears; once it rises, much of the root's food value is gone and it turns woody. The taproot runs deep and is hard to get out whole: dig a deep hole beside the plant and lever the root sideways into it, or settle for the top part. Plants in soft, rich soil give thicker roots than those in stony ground. Wash and peel the roots and cut away the tough top few centimetres; on large roots, cut off the outer layer and use the core, as the outside stays woody even when cooked. Cut root darkens fast, so drop the pieces into water with a little vinegar or lemon as you go, but don't leave them there overnight or they curl. Small roots and the thin tips are good raw. Cut the rest into thin matchsticks to stir-fry or simmer, or slice and boil or roast them like carrot or parsnip. Washed roots keep for up to a couple of months in a closed container in the fridge.
Cut flowering stems while they are young and slice easily with a knife, before the flower heads form; later they cook up stringy and fibrous. Strip off the leaves, peel off the thick outer skin with a knife and then the stringy fibres beneath with a vegetable peeler, and keep the peeled stems in lemon water. Simmer them in stock until tender, 30–45 minutes, then brown them in butter or add them to soups; raw, they can be shaved very thin and crisped in iced water. Unpeeled stems keep for weeks in the fridge.
Cut leaf stalks before the flowering stem rises. Scrub off the bitter coating, slice them thinly and boil until very tender.

recipes.method: Written for greater and lesser burdock. Thin strips of burdock root; oil; sea salt; cornflour and sesame seeds, for a sesame version. Clean the roots, peeling large ones a little, and slice them into thin strips. Line a plate or two with kitchen paper. Heat oil in a frying pan over a medium-high heat; it is ready when a test piece floats up and the oil bubbles. Fry the strips for a few minutes, until crisp and lightly browned, lift them onto the paper with a slotted spoon and sprinkle with sea salt. For a sesame version, dip the raw strips in cornflour before frying, and toss the hot chips in sesame seeds mixed with a little salt; serve straight away.
recipes.title: Burdock root chips

recipes.method: Written for burdock root generally — the author treats lesser and greater burdock roots as interchangeable in recipes. 225 g burdock root (1 large); 225 g carrot (1 large); 1 tbsp maple syrup or sugar; 1 tbsp mirin or apple cider vinegar; 2 tbsp soy sauce; 1 tsp fish sauce (optional); 310 ml (1¼ cups) water; 2 tbsp toasted sesame oil; ½ tsp finely grated ginger (optional); 2 tsp toasted sesame seeds and 2 tsp sliced Chinese chives (both optional), to garnish. Wash the burdock well, trim the ends and cut it into 15 cm lengths. Peel each length, cut it on the diagonal into 5 mm-thick ovals, stack a few and cut into 5 mm matchsticks, dropping them into cold water as you go. Cut the carrot the same way and keep it separate. In a 25 cm pan or wok, bring the burdock and 250 ml of the water to the boil, cover and cook 5 minutes, then pour off the water. Add the carrot, maple syrup, mirin or vinegar, fish sauce, soy sauce, ginger, half the sesame oil and the remaining 60 ml water, and stir-fry over a high heat until the pan is nearly dry. Off the heat, stir in the rest of the sesame oil and the chives. Garnish with the sesame seeds; serve warm, cool or at room temperature.
recipes.title: Kinpira gobo

recipes.method: Written for burdock root generally — the author treats lesser and greater burdock roots as interchangeable in recipes. 225 g cleaned, peeled burdock root; 225 g mild fresh mushrooms; 2 tbsp soy sauce; 2 tbsp apple cider or rice wine vinegar; a good pinch of chilli flakes (optional); 2 tbsp ghee, lard or cooking oil; a small handful of sliced fresh herbs such as coriander, mint or basil; 30 g sliced spring onions or green garlic; salt. Cut the burdock on the diagonal into 5 mm rounds, stack them and cut into 5 mm matchsticks; slice the mushrooms 5 mm thick. Boil the burdock in water for 5 minutes and drain well. Heat the fat in a wide pan and cook the burdock and mushrooms until the mushrooms are cooked. Add the soy sauce, chilli and vinegar and cook down, tossing. Season with salt and chilli, toss in the spring onions and herbs, fry a minute more and serve hot. To serve it cold as a salad, use oil (sesame oil is good) instead of ghee or lard.
recipes.title: Braised burdock and mushrooms

recipes.method: Written for burdock root generally — the author treats lesser and greater burdock roots as interchangeable in recipes. Lemon juice, for the peeling water; 170 g burdock root; 500 ml (2 cups) cream; 900 g floury potatoes; 2 tbsp unsalted butter, plus a knob to serve; salt and white pepper; some sliced chives, to serve. Peel the roots into water sharpened with lemon juice, then slice them thinly. Heat the oven to 120 °C. Bring the burdock and cream to a simmer in a small non-reactive pot, season lightly, then cover and bake until the burdock is tender, 30–45 minutes. Blend until smooth, adding a little water if needed, and pass through a sieve; the purée can be made a day or two ahead, or frozen (blend it again after thawing). Peel the potatoes and boil them in lightly salted water until tender, about 15 minutes. Rice them, stir in the burdock cream and the butter, and season. Serve with a knob of butter and some sliced chives.
recipes.title: Burdock mashed potatoes

recipes.method: Written for burdock root generally — the author treats lesser and greater burdock roots as interchangeable in recipes. 225 g burdock root; 60 ml (¼ cup) water; 190 ml (¾ cup) rice or apple cider vinegar; 1 tsp salt or 1 tbsp soy sauce; 4 tbsp sugar. Optional spices: a few slices of fresh ginger, 2 tsp turmeric (or 1 tbsp carrot or beetroot powder, for colour), 1 tsp Sichuan peppercorns, 2 dried hot chillies, 1 large garlic clove, 1 tsp yellow mustard seed, 2 makrut lime leaves, 5 allspice berries and a small handful of dill. Peel the burdock and cut it into 7.5 cm lengths. Bring everything else to the boil, then cool, and take out the dill. Spoon the spices into the bottom of the jar or jars, pack in the burdock, and pour in the liquid, leaving 1 cm headspace; put the lids on. Lower the jars into a large pot of boiling water that covers them by 5 cm, cover, and once it is back at the boil, process for 10 minutes. Lift out, label, date and store in the pantry.
recipes.title: Yamagobo (pickled burdock root)

recipes.method: Written for burdock root generally — the author treats lesser and greater burdock roots as interchangeable in recipes. 900 g pork spare ribs in 2–3-bone pieces; 250 ml (1 cup) carrots, quartered and sliced 5 mm; 250 ml (1 cup) each diced onion, leek (white and tender green) and fennel; 500 ml (2 cups) puréed canned whole tomatoes; 2 litres chicken stock; 750 ml (3 cups) peeled burdock root sliced into 5 mm rounds; 225 g shiitake caps sliced 5 mm; 2 tbsp minced fresh ginger; 60 ml (¼ cup) oil; salt; a bouquet garni (5 allspice berries, 5 cloves, 2 star anise, 2 fresh bay leaves and a halved bulb of garlic); cooked millet to taste (or quinoa, wild rice, sorghum or lentils); hot chilli oil, or sesame oil and chopped chilli, to serve; fresh coriander. Sweat the leek, onion and ginger in the oil, add everything else and simmer gently for about 2 hours, until the meat comes off the bones. Season with salt and cool quickly, then pick the meat off the ribs, chop it and return it to the soup. Just before serving, add cooked millet to taste (or quinoa, wild rice, sorghum or lentils). Serve with hot chilli oil, or sesame oil and chopped chilli, and fresh coriander. The author says to treat the amounts as a rough guide.
recipes.title: Pork rib and burdock soup

recipes.method: Written for the flower stalks of greater and lesser burdock. 450 g peeled burdock flower stalks (see Preparation); 1 small carrot; 1 celery stick; 1 small onion; about 1 litre (4 cups) vegetable stock, enough to cover; a sprig of fresh thyme; 1 bay leaf; fresh herbs; salt; 125 ml (½ cup) white wine if you like; butter, for browning (optional). Cut the vegetables into 7.5 cm pieces. Put everything in a pan, bring to a simmer, season the liquid lightly with salt, and cook gently until the burdock is just tender, 30–45 minutes. Let the stalks cool in the liquid, then strain out and discard the aromatic vegetables, keeping the burdock and the liquid (it can cook another batch, or be the broth for a vegetable stew). Keep the cooked stalks in a sealed container in the fridge. To serve, cut them into 1 cm pieces and reheat them in their liquid, or brown them in butter. To serve with roast meat, use red wine for half the stock; it stains them purple.
recipes.title: Burdock flower stalks à la barigoule

recipes.method: Written for the flower stalks of greater and lesser burdock. 225 g peeled carrot and 225 g peeled burdock flower stalk, each roll-cut into pieces about 2 cm (slice on the diagonal, turn the piece half a turn, slice again); lemon water; 1 small garlic clove; a good pinch of sugar; 2 tbsp butter; salt and black pepper; and, optionally, a small handful of greens such as parsley, and chives, mint or basil to finish. Keep the peeled stalks in the lemon water. Bring a small pot of lightly salted water to the boil. Blanch the carrots about 30 seconds, until just al dente, and cool them in cold water; blanch the stalks 60 seconds (less for very young ones) and cool them too. Drain both. Crush the garlic and warm it in the butter for a minute or two, without letting it burn. Add the vegetables and cook until tender, seasoning with the sugar, salt and pepper. Toss in the greens and herbs and serve hot.
recipes.title: Burdock flower stalks with carrots

recipes.method: Written for the flower stalks of greater and lesser burdock. 4 thick sections of flower stalk about 15 cm long, skinned and peeled; 1 litre (4 cups) vegetable stock; ¼ lemon; salt; a little oil or fat; sesame oil, sliced hot chilli and sesame seeds, to finish. Shave the stalks as thin as you can into long noodles with a vegetable peeler or a mandoline. Simmer gently in the stock with the lemon, seasoned lightly with salt, until just tender, 15–20 minutes, and drain. Warm a little oil or fat in a pan and cook the noodles over a medium-low heat until very lightly browned; they turn grey as they cook, which is normal. Finish them with sesame oil, sliced hot chilli and sesame seeds, as the author did. Makes two small servings.
recipes.title: Burdock flower stalk noodles

recipes.method: Written for the flower stalks of greater and lesser burdock. 115 g each of carrot, onion and celery; 225 g peeled burdock flower stalks; 1–2 bay leaves; 3 tbsp flavourless oil; about 1 litre (4 cups) really good stock, enough to cover; optionally 115 g diced mushrooms or 250 ml (1 cup) chopped cooked meat; salt; a dash of lemon juice; fresh herbs such as chives or parsley; olive oil or another flavoured oil, to serve. Dice the vegetables, and cut the burdock into slightly larger pieces, keeping it in lemon water until needed. Sweat the vegetables (and the mushrooms, if using) in the oil, then add the stock, burdock and bay leaves and simmer until tender, about 20 minutes. Add the meat, if using, and warm it through. Season with salt, add the lemon juice and herbs, and serve with a drizzle of olive oil or another flavoured oil.
recipes.title: Burdock flower stalk soup
