summary.text:
Arctium minus, commonly known as lesser burdock, little burdock, louse-bur, common burdock, button-bur, cuckoo-button, or wild rhubarb, is a biennial plant native to Europe.
The plant is native to Europe, but has become introduced elsewhere such as Australia, North and South America, and other places.
In New Zealand it is also called burdock or common burdock; its older scientific name is Lappa minor. It comes from Europe and western Asia, arrived by accident, and was first recorded growing wild here in 1894. It is occasional throughout the North and South Islands except Westland. Each plant makes many seeds, carried by wind and water and on animals and people. The specific name minus is Latin for smaller.
DOC lists it among New Zealand's environmental weeds (2024). In Auckland it is under sustained control across the region and is a pest in the Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area: it must not be bred, distributed, released, sold or planted there. Gisborne's regional pest plan has it under progressive containment, and Canterbury and Otago list it as an organism of interest. The burs tangle in sheep's wool and can injure livestock.
Its relative greater burdock (A. lappa) is grown in Japan as a root vegetable, gobo. Lesser burdock has been gathered from the wild for food, and for fibre to make paper.

warnings: The tiny hairs on the seeds are irritating and toxic if breathed in: take care with ripe burs, and don't collect the seed in any quantity. Handling the plant can also cause contact dermatitis.

Burdock is a pest plant under control throughout the Auckland region and in pest plant strategies elsewhere, and may be sprayed with herbicide, so pick it only where you know no herbicide has been used.

habitat.text: Pasture, meadows, lawns and rough grassland on rich, acidic soil, most often where sheep or cattle have been grazing. It does not typically grow directly on the dung. It grows singly or in groups. In New Zealand it grows in high-altitude grasslands.

identification.text:
Cap 5–25 mm across and about as tall, sharply conical to bell-shaped, and usually tipped with a small distinct nipple. Colour shifts with moisture: ochre to pale brown or dark chestnut brown when damp, with the gill lines showing through the margin, fading to pale buff as it dries. A damp cap is tacky, with a gelatinous skin that peels away if you bend the margin back.
Gills are narrow and moderately crowded, pale brown at first, darkening to purple-brown with paler edges. The stipe is 4.5–14 cm long but only 1–3.5 mm thick, slender, often wavy, and has no ring. Spore print is dark purple-brown.
Any part handled or bruised stains bluish.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both grow in grass, so habitat does not separate them. Cap shape is the first check but not a certain one. A liberty cap is sharply conical to bell-shaped, often tipped with a small nipple, and keeps that shape as it ages. A mower's mushroom is conical or bell-shaped when young but opens out to broadly convex and lacks the liberty cap's point. A liberty cap stains bluish where it is handled or bruised, and its stem is sometimes blue towards the base. The mower's mushroom's flesh does not change colour when cut. Bend back a piece of a damp liberty cap and a thin gelatinous skin peels away (not once the cap has dried out); the mower's mushroom is not described as having this skin. Mower's mushroom gills are broad and often go mottled as the spores ripen. A liberty cap's gills are narrow and moderately crowded, darkening to dark grey or purple-brown. Both can have paler gill edges, so the edges do not separate them. The spore print will not decide it either: liberty cap very dark purple-brown, mower's mushroom dark brown, sometimes purplish to nearly black.

The legal claims on this page, checked against the Act rather than a summary of it. Schedule 1 (Class A controlled drugs) lists Psilocine, Psilotsin and Psilocybine by name and formula. Section 7(1)(a) makes it an offence to procure, possess, consume, smoke or otherwise use a controlled drug, and section 7(2)(a) sets the penalty at 'imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months or to a fine not exceeding $1,000 or to both where a Class A controlled drug was the controlled drug' — which is what this entry's warning says. Note that section 7(2) applies 'without prejudice to any liability under section 6', the dealing provision, which carries life imprisonment for a Class A drug: the same handful of mushrooms can be charged either way depending on quantity and circumstance. Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, read on legislation.govt.nz 06/10/2026. https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1975/0116/latest/DLM436100.html

The fungus itself is a prohibited plant, which is a second offence this page did not mention. Section 2 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 defines 'prohibited plant' to include 'any fungus of the genera Conocybe, Panaeolus, or Psilocybe from which a controlled drug can be produced or which contains a controlled drug' — so cultivating it is an offence under section 9, separately from possessing it under section 7. This page previously carried no lookalike card at all, although its identification text names the characters an identification turns on. The card introduces no fact that was not already on one of the two pages: the nipple, the peelable gelatinous skin and the blue-green bruising come from this entry’s identification, and the convex nippleless cap, the absence of a peelable skin, the mottled gills and the absence of blueing come from mowers-mushroom.identification. It also records that the spore print does not separate them, because that entry gives a deep brown print with a purplish cast against the dark purple-brown given here. Written by the assistant on the owner’s instruction; flagged here so it is greppable and reversible.

A note on the risk level of that card. It is set to unpalatable, not toxic, because that is what the mower’s mushroom entry itself says — its only warning is that the mushroom is unpalatable. No claim about psilocybin in Panaeolus foenisecii is made on either page, in either direction, because nothing cited on either page settles it. Note separately that section 2 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, quoted above, names Panaeolus alongside Psilocybe, but it reaches only a fungus of that genus ‘from which a controlled drug can be produced or which contains a controlled drug’, so the Act does not itself decide the question for this species and neither does this guide.

(1) Both cards stated the liberty cap's nipple flatly, where liberty-cap.identification says 'almost always tipped with a small distinct nipple' — the hedge is restored on both, because a nippleless liberty cap is precisely the specimen a hardened card fails to warn about, and it is the first character a reader checks. (2) 'darken evenly' was removed: it is not a claim either page makes about the liberty cap, whose gills are recorded as darkening to purple-brown with paler edges; it had been carried across from the mower's mushroom page, which contrasts its own mottled gills with 'an even colour'. Both cards now give each species' gills as its own page gives them. (3) 'sometimes' was restored to the mower's mushroom's purplish spore-print cast. (4) 'their seasons overlap through autumn' was replaced by the actual overlap of the two months arrays, April to June, which runs past autumn. No new fact was introduced by this correction and nothing was deleted from either page.

summary.text:
A small, sharply conical grassland mushroom with a nipple-tipped cap that bruises blue. It contains psilocybin, which makes it a Class A controlled drug in New Zealand.
Like other Psilocybe species it feeds on decaying organic matter; it is thought to live on decaying root remains.
Biota of New Zealand gives its origin in New Zealand as uncertain and lists collections from Auckland, Nelson, North and Mid Canterbury, the Mackenzie and Dunedin.

warnings: Magic mushrooms, and the psilocybine and psilocine in them, are Class A controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. Picking or carrying one is possession of a Class A drug.

Maximum penalties are six months' imprisonment and/or a $1,000 fine for possession, and life imprisonment for supplying or manufacturing. This entry is here so you can recognise the species, not so you can collect it.

associations.note: Poisonous. Fly agaric has been recorded once under lilly pilly.

habitat.text:
Occasional in the vicinity of planted trees, mainly in scrub or on waste ground.
It can establish in existing forest under low light. In the Auckland region it grows in forest, plantations, roadsides and gardens. Herbarium collections record self-sown seedlings in regenerating forest, a swamp-forest remnant and a shaded stream gorge, some far from any parent tree, and among garden shrubs.

harvestEthics.text:
An Unwanted Organism and National Pest Plant Accord species: it must not be bred, distributed, released or sold anywhere in New Zealand. Birds carry its seed into native forest, which it can invade. Harvest as much as you like, and do not spread the seed: put it in green waste or landfill.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text:
Tree (6–15 m high in cultivation). Leaves very aromatic when crushed; petiole usually c. 5 mm long. Lamina 4–12–(15) × 2–5–(8) cm, ovate or elliptic-ovate, coriaceous, glossy above, dotted with glands below; veins parallel and prominent below; base cuneate or narrow-cuneate; apex obtusely cuspidate or acuminate. Flowers shortly pedicellate. Hypanthium (including pseudopedicel) 3–5 mm long; calyx lobes 4, deciduous. Petals 4, c. 2 mm long, forming a small calyptrum, whitish. Stamens to c. 3 mm long, whitish. Fruit subglobose to broad-oblong or obovoid, often slightly flattened, usually 1–1.7–(3) cm diameter, pinkish mauve or white, with apical cavity. Seed large.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Acmena smithii (Poir.) Merr. & L.M.Perry.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Brush cherry's fruit is crimson to crimson-purple, oblong to obovoid and glossy, with its calyx lobes (2–4 mm long) still on the tip; lilly pilly's fruit is pinkish mauve or white, nearly round to broadly oblong or obovoid and often slightly flattened, with a hollow at the tip, and its calyx lobes fall off. Brush cherry's flowers are showier, with petals about 4 mm across and stamens to about 13 mm long; lilly pilly's petals are about 2 mm long and its stamens to about 3 mm. Lilly pilly's leaves are broader for their length (ovate or elliptic-ovate, usually 2–5 cm wide); brush cherry's are often narrowly elliptic, mostly 1–3.5 cm wide, on branchlets that more or less hang down. In New Zealand lilly pilly flowers from October to January, brush cherry from January to July. Look at the young branchlets: only brush cherry has a small pocket just above where each pair of leaves joins the stem; lilly pilly has none. Angles alone do not separate them, as both can be four-angled or shortly four-winged. Otherwise the two are very similar, with glossy, aromatic leaves, parallel veins and reddish new leaves. Brush cherry's fruit is eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Brush cherry

lookalikes.howToTell: Magenta lilly pilly's flowers are showier, with free, spreading petals 4–5 mm long and stamens 6–15 mm long; lilly pilly's petals are about 2 mm long, joined into a small cap, and its stamens reach about 3 mm. Magenta lilly pilly's fruit is round to egg-shaped, with somewhat swollen calyx lobes at the tip; lilly pilly's is nearly round to broadly oblong or obovoid and often slightly flattened, with a hollow at the tip where the calyx lobes have fallen. Lilly pilly's leaves are broader for their length: ovate or elliptic-ovate and usually 2–5 cm wide, against magenta lilly pilly's lanceolate to obovate leaves 1.5–3 cm wide that taper to the base. Fruit colour does not separate them: magenta lilly pilly's is usually magenta but can be white, pink or purple, and lilly pilly's is pinkish mauve or white. Cut a fruit open: magenta lilly pilly's single large seed usually shows lines of division marking its many embryos, which sets it apart from the other Syzygium species in New Zealand. Magenta lilly pilly's fruit is eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Magenta lilly pilly

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: tree privet's berries are bluish or purplish black with a powdery bloom, no more than 6 mm long, in dense clusters, each with a ribbed seed about 5 mm long; lilly pilly's fruit is pinkish mauve or white, usually 1–1.7 cm across (up to 3 cm), with a hollow at the tip and one large seed. Lilly pilly's new leaves are reddish, unlike tree privet's. Tree privet's flowers are small and tubular, with a white tube about 1.5 mm long, four reflexed lobes 2–2.5 mm long and only two stamens; lilly pilly's four tiny petals, about 2 mm long, are joined into a small cap that falls, and it has numerous stamens. Lilly pilly's leaves are very aromatic when crushed and dotted with glands underneath, on stalks usually about 5 mm long; tree privet's are not described as aromatic or gland-dotted, and their stalks are mostly 1–2 cm long. Lilly pilly's twigs are often four-angled or shortly four-winged; tree privet's shoots are more or less round, with prominent lumpy warts. Both are evergreen trees with glossy, opposite leaves of overlapping size (lilly pilly usually 4–12 cm long, tree privet 5–13 cm), and both grow in scrub and on waste ground, so leaf shape and place do not separate them. Tree privet's berries are poisonous.
lookalikes.name: Tree privet

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: swamp maire's is deep crimson and glossy, 10–15 mm across, with its very short, broad calyx lobes still on the tip; lilly pilly's is pinkish mauve or white, usually 1–1.7 cm across (up to 3 cm), with a hollow at the tip where the calyx lobes have fallen. Swamp maire's white stamens are long, 5–12 mm (up to 15 mm), so its flowers look brushy; lilly pilly's stamens reach only about 3 mm. Swamp maire's leaves are mostly 2.5–6 cm long and 1–2.5 cm wide, with wavy edges; lilly pilly's are usually larger, 4–12 cm long (up to 15 cm) and 2–5 cm wide, so small lilly pilly leaves overlap swamp maire's in size. Otherwise the leaves look much alike, thin, shiny, elliptic and in opposite pairs on both, so go by the fruit and flowers. With a hand lens, swamp maire's anther sacs are usually parallel; lilly pilly's anther lobes spread apart. Both have small white or whitish petals, about 2–3 mm, joined into a cap that falls, and lilly pilly sometimes grows with swamp maire in urban forest remnants, so place does not separate them. Swamp maire's fruit is edible, but it is a threatened native tree: do not pick it unless your life depends on it (see its page).

preparation.text: Eaten fresh, or made into jams, jellies or drinks. Each fruit holds one large seed.

recipes.method: 2 litres (8 cups) lilly pilly fruit; about 625 ml (2½ cups) sugar; 3 lemons. Wash the fruit well, throwing out any underripe fruit, stems and leaves. Put it in a pot and add just enough water to cover it, holding the floating fruit down with a plate or lid while you measure. Bring to the boil and boil for an hour; the fruit will fade to a pale mauve. Pour the fruit and liquid into a bowl lined with a large cheesecloth, tie the cloth into a bag and hang it over the bowl for several hours or overnight to drip. Squeeze it only lightly, or the juice turns cloudy. Measure the juice and, for each cup (250 ml), add 1 cup of sugar and the juice of 1 lemon. Heat slowly, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then boil, skimming off the foam. Stay with it: after about 15–20 minutes the bubbles turn thick and syrupy and pop slowly. Lower the heat so it doesn't scorch, and test by putting a teaspoonful on a plate in the freezer for 5 minutes: if it wrinkles when pushed, it is ready; if not, boil a few minutes more and test again. No pectin is needed. Pour into hot, sterilised jars and seal at once with the lids. Makes about 2 × 375 ml jars.

summary.text:
An evergreen tree of the myrtle family from eastern Australia. In New Zealand it is commonly grown as an ornamental tree and windbreak in warmer parts, and has been naturalised since 1982 in the Bay of Islands, the Whangārei area and Auckland. Self-sown seedlings have also been collected near Te Puke in the Bay of Plenty and in Whanganui. Its New Zealand name is monkey apple; lilly pilly is the Australian name, sometimes used here.
It is an Unwanted Organism and a National Pest Plant Accord species, and is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. Birds, kererū among them, carry its seed into native forest, where it can establish in shade, outcompete native trees and become a dominant canopy tree. Its sale and propagation are banned nationwide, but trees and hedges planted before the ban are still common in gardens. It is very susceptible to myrtle rust.

warnings: Tree privet, a weed tree with poisonous purple-black berries, can look similar. Lilly pilly's berries are white to pink and its new leaves are reddish; tree privet's new leaves lack that red colour.

identification.text:
Stout annual herb up to 80–(100) cm high. Stems glabrous, usually simple or sometimes somewhat branched at base. Stem leaves always alternate, glabrous, lanceolate to linear, usually obovate or oblong at base of stem, acuminate, 3-nerved, entire, (5)–10–40 mm long; leaves subtending inflorescence-branches single, similar to stem leaves but usually somewhat smaller. Inflorescence of few to numerous flowers in a diffuse compound dichasium or corymb; sepals elliptic to suborbicular, acuminate, (5)–6–10 mm long, shorter than capsule, with glabrous entire margins; petals white or pale to dark blue, 2–3× as long as sepals, (10)–12–18–(20) mm long; styles united for about ⅓ length. Capsule glabrous, subglobose, indehiscent or subdehiscent, (6)–8–10–(12) mm diameter; seeds elliptic and narrowed to base, shiny light to dark brown, 4–5 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In plain terms (restated from the Flora's description and genus key): an upright, hairless annual up to about 80 cm (rarely 1 m), usually with one stem and narrow, three-veined leaves 1–4 cm long. The flowers are white or pale to dark blue, with petals 1–2 cm long, and are followed by round capsules 6–12 mm across that stay closed or barely split, holding shiny brown seeds 4–5 mm long. Pale flax (L. bienne), which is common throughout New Zealand, looks much the same but is smaller in every part: petals 7–11 mm, sepals 4–6 mm, capsules 5–7 mm that split open, and seeds 2.5–3.5 mm; it can live for more than a year and its inner sepals are often fringed. Linseed flowers from October to April.

preparation.text: Gather the seed heads once the capsules have turned yellow and are just starting to split, dry them, and thresh out the seed. Use it whole or ground in bread, baking and cereals, or sprout it for salads; in baking, ground seed can stand in for about a quarter of the flour. Whisked with about three times its volume of cold water and left for 10 minutes, ground seed thickens into a gel that replaces egg in baking (about 1 tbsp ground seed and 2½ tbsp water for each egg). Toasting the seed lightly, 10–12 minutes at 180°C until slightly darker, bursts the husks so that it releases a sticky gum when wet. Whole seed is hard to digest and can cause wind. Whole seed keeps well, but ground seed left open to the air at room temperature can go rancid in as little as a week, so grind it as you need it or keep it sealed in the fridge or freezer.

recipes.method: Makes about 32. 60 ml (¼ cup) linseed; 125 ml (½ cup) water; 125 ml (½ cup) wholemeal flour; 125 ml (½ cup) wholegrain oats; ½ tsp baking powder; ½ tsp salt; 75 g cold butter, cubed; 2 tbsp honey. Soak the linseed in the water overnight. Heat the oven to 160°C. Whizz the flour, oats, baking powder, salt and butter in a food processor to fine crumbs, then add the soaked linseed and the honey and pulse until the mixture comes together. Roll it out evenly between two sheets of baking paper about 40 × 30 cm until it covers the paper, lift it onto a baking tray, peel off the top sheet and use it to line a second tray. Score into crackers about 8 × 3 cm. Bake for 10 minutes, then cut the crackers apart and move half to the second tray, spacing them out, with any browned edges towards the middle. Bake for another 30–35 minutes, swapping the trays halfway; from 30 minutes take out any that are browning too fast. Cool on a rack.
recipes.title: Oat, linseed and honey crackers

recipes.method: Makes one 20 cm loaf. 1¼ tsp dried yeast (or 4 tsp Surebake); 250 ml (1 cup) warm water or milk; 1 tsp sugar; 250 ml (1 cup) wholemeal flour; 375 ml (1½ cups) high grade flour; 1 tsp salt; 50 g butter; 2 tbsp treacle or golden syrup; 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) linseed, plus about 60 ml (¼ cup) more for the top. Stir the yeast into the warm water and sugar and leave 15 minutes until frothy, then stir in the treacle. Rub the butter into the flours and salt (or whizz them in a food processor), add the yeast mixture and work to a very soft, moist dough, adding a little water if needed, then mix in the linseed; by hand, knead for 10 minutes until smooth. Put the dough into a well-greased 20 cm loaf tin, scatter linseed over the top, cover with greased plastic wrap and leave in a warm place for about 1 hour, until it has doubled and reached the top of the tin. Bake at 200°C for 30–35 minutes, until the loaf sounds hollow when tapped underneath. Turn out at once to cool on a rack.
recipes.title: One-rise linseed loaf

recipes.method: Makes 16. 250 g medjool dates; 2 tsp ground cinnamon; 325 ml cold water; 75 g goji berries; 75 g pumpkin seeds; 150 g brown linseed; 50 g cocoa nibs; 25 g chia seeds; 25 g cornflakes; 100 g rolled oats (not instant). Heat the oven to 180°C (160°C fan) and line the base and sides of a 20 cm square tin with baking paper. Pit the dates, tear them into a small saucepan with the cinnamon and the water, bring to the boil and let them bubble for 5 minutes, then take off the heat and mash with a fork to a rough purée. Put all the other ingredients into a large bowl, add the date purée and mix until everything is evenly combined. Press firmly into the tin and bake for 30 minutes, until firm and set, golden on top and darker at the edges. Cool in the tin before cutting into bars. With ordinary dried dates, use 350 g pitted dates and 400 ml water and simmer for about 10 minutes, until soft enough to mash.
recipes.title: Date, linseed and seed breakfast bars

recipes.method: Makes one loaf. 25–50 g golden linseed; 475 ml warm water; 1 sachet (about 2½ tsp) instant dried yeast; 100 ml plain yoghurt; 450 g cornflour; 1 tsp salt; 1 tsp caster sugar; 50 g psyllium husk powder; 50 ml olive oil, plus extra for brushing. Heat the oven to 180°C and toast the linseed on a tray for 10–12 minutes, until slightly darker. Mix the water and yeast, then stir in the yoghurt and the seed. In a large bowl toss together the cornflour, salt, sugar and psyllium, pour in the yeast mixture and the oil and mix to a smooth, thin batter. Over about 5 minutes it thickens into a sticky dough; knead it for 10 seconds on the bench, return it to the bowl, cover and leave for 30 minutes. Line a tray with baking paper, shape the dough into a fat log the length of the tray, brush with oil, cover and leave to rise for 30 minutes. Heat the oven to 240°C, slash the top with a sharp knife, dust with a little cornflour and bake for about 40 minutes, until deep golden brown. Cool on a rack before slicing.
recipes.title: Gluten-free toasted linseed loaf

recipes.method: Makes one small loaf, 12 slices. 260 g finely ground golden linseed (weighed after sifting); 220 ml warm water; 2 tsp (8 g) baking powder; ½ tsp salt. Heat the oven to 175°C (no fan) and line a baking tray with baking paper. Grind the linseed to a fine flour in a blender or coffee grinder, stopping before it clumps (ground too long it turns to seed butter), sift it, regrind and sift whatever stays in the sieve, then weigh out 260 g. Whisk the linseed flour, baking powder and salt in a large bowl, add the water and stir for about 30 seconds, until it turns sticky and holds together in one lump; if it stays crumbly, add up to 20 ml more water, 10 ml at a time. Rest the dough for 10 minutes. With wet hands, shape it on the tray into a loaf no taller than about 6 cm, handling it as little as possible, and cut three diagonal slashes about 1 cm deep across the top. Bake for 75 minutes, until the crust is crunchy and golden brown, and cool completely on a rack before slicing. Each slice holds about 22 g of linseed (see the warning on daily amounts). Keeps up to 2 weeks sealed in the fridge, or sliced and frozen for up to 6 months; toast straight from the fridge or freezer.
recipes.title: Four-ingredient linseed bread

recipes.method: 900 g chicken tenderloins (or boneless, skinless chicken breast cut into strips); 250 ml (1 cup) ground linseed; ½ tsp salt. Heat the oven to 220°C and line a baking tray with baking paper. Mix the linseed and salt, then dip the chicken pieces in it until evenly coated. Lay them on the tray and bake for 15–18 minutes (smaller nuggets 8–10 minutes), until the chicken is cooked through to 74°C in the centre. For a change, replace half the linseed with grated parmesan, or add 1–2 tsp curry powder to the coating.
recipes.title: Linseed-crumbed chicken tenders

summary.text: Linseed, also called flax, common flax or linen flax (Linum usitatissimum), is an annual in the flax family (Linaceae), grown for its oily seed and for linen fibre. It is known only in cultivation and is not native anywhere; the Flora notes it may come from pale flax (L. bienne), from which it differs only in its generally larger size and its capsules that barely split. In New Zealand it is a casual escape, recorded since 1870, at Palmerston North and Levin in the North Island and at Nelson City, Seddon, lowland Canterbury and Otago, and Invercargill in the South Island. New Zealand seed suppliers also sell it as a quick, easy garden annual for its blue flowers. It is unrelated to the harakeke (Phormium) that New Zealanders also call flax. It is an exotic species and is not listed as a pest (see the origin check in the sources).

warnings: Linseed contains cyanogenic glycosides, which release cyanide. A joint FSANZ and MPI survey found no recorded human poisonings and no acute risk from eating it, but worked out that an adult goes over the safe one-day limit above about 32–33 g of seed.
Eat only the seed: the rest of the plant carries the same cyanide-releasing compounds, and the New Zealand Flora lists the plant as poisonous.

identification.text:
A medium-sized to large, open pine. The bark is lightly to moderately fissured, grey on the surface and pinkish beneath, with broad ridges. The needles come in threes, mostly in tufts at the ends of the shoots, 13–21 cm long (from 9 cm), slender, semi-rigid and bright green. The cones are 7–12 cm, stalkless, egg-shaped to oblong, brown and symmetrical, each scale with a recurved spine 3–5 mm long; they open, and then fall whole. Needles in threes with prickly, symmetrical cones that open and fall whole set it apart: ponderosa pine's cones leave their basal scales on the branch and are generally larger, and slash pine's cones are short-stalked.
Shoots greenish or yellowish, hairless. Buds broadly cylindrical, not or scarcely resinous; the scales reddish brown, free and often spreading, prominently fringed. Needles 1–1.3 mm wide; resin canals in the middle; sheaths usually 0.5–1 cm long on mature needles. Male cones 1.5–2 cm long, narrowly cylindrical. Young female cones stalkless or nearly so, the scales sharply pointed. Mature cones more or less hanging, 5–8 cm wide when open; the scale ends more or less flat except for a crosswise keel. Seed wing oblong, about 2 cm long. Saplings cannot readily be told from slash pine.

lookalikes.howToTell: Saplings cannot readily be told apart; look at older trees and cones. Slash pine nearly always has some needles in pairs among the threes, 16–26 cm, rigid, glossy and grass-green; its cones are 12–15 cm on an obvious short stalk, and its bark is reddish brown in thin flaky plates. Loblolly pine has needles in threes, 13–21 cm, slender, semi-rigid and bright green; its cones are 7–12 cm, stalkless, with a recurved spine on each scale, and fall whole after opening; its bark is grey on the surface and pinkish beneath. Slash pine's young green cones are used for syrup (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Slash pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have long needles in threes and symmetrical, prickly cones that open and fall; look at what the cone leaves behind. Ponderosa pine has needles in threes, 10–23 cm, stout, rigid and dull green; its stalkless cones open and fall but leave a ring of basal scales on the branch, and the tree is more open. Loblolly pine has needles in threes, 13–21 cm, slender, semi-rigid and bright green; its cones are 7–12 cm, stalkless, with a recurved spine on each scale, and fall whole after opening; its bark is grey on the surface and pinkish beneath. Ponderosa pine's seeds and inner bark are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Ponderosa pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have needles in threes; look at the cones. Radiata pine has needles in threes, 6–15 cm, deep or dark green; its cones are lopsided, 6–13 cm, and stay on the tree for years. Loblolly pine has needles in threes, 13–21 cm, slender, semi-rigid and bright green; its cones are 7–12 cm, stalkless, with a recurved spine on each scale, and fall whole after opening; its bark is grey on the surface and pinkish beneath. Radiata pine's seeds and young male cones are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Monterey pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have long, slender needles in threes and grow wild in Rotoehu Forest; look at the needles and the cones. Mexican weeping pine has very slender, flexible, grass-green needles in threes, 13–28 cm, hanging down below the branches, and shining brown buds standing upright, often at right angles to the shoot; its cones, 6–9 cm, curved and lopsided, point backwards in clusters and stay closed on the tree for years. Loblolly pine has needles in threes, 13–21 cm, slender, semi-rigid and bright green; its cones are 7–12 cm, stalkless, with a recurved spine on each scale, and fall whole after opening; its bark is grey on the surface and pinkish beneath. Mexican weeping pine's young green cones are used for syrup (see its page).

preparation.text:
Cut away the outer bark to reach the white inner bark (cambium) over the wood. Peel it into thin sheets, the thinner the better, and cook them until brown and crisp all over.
For syrup, pick cones while they are still green and soft enough to cut through with a knife; brown, woody or opened cones will not do. Green cones ooze sticky resin, so wear gloves. Throw out any with holes or insects. Smaller cones give a stronger flavour; large ones can be cut up so more fit in the jar.
For tea, finely chop fresh green needles and steep about 30 ml of them in 300 ml of hot but not boiling water for up to ten minutes.

recipes.method: Pack 225 g (about 500 ml) young green loblolly pine cones and 450 g brown sugar into a 1 litre jar. Leave in a warm, sunny place for 30 days, shaking it now and then. For the first few weeks open the jar occasionally to let out gas, as the mixture may ferment. Scrape the cones and sugar slush into a pot, add 30 ml water, and bring to a brisk simmer for 5–10 minutes, just until the sugar melts (reducing it further makes it crystallise as it cools). Strain, discard the cones and bottle the hot syrup. It keeps best in the fridge once opened. Use it like maple syrup: on pancakes, fresh fruit or soft cheese, or a little in desserts and dressings.
recipes.title: Mugolio (young pine cone syrup)

recipes.method: Put 10 young green loblolly pine cones in a jar and top up with 500 g brown sugar, shaking so the sugar settles round the cones. Close the jar and leave it for about 2 weeks, until all the sugar has turned to syrup. Pass it through a sieve and bottle. Add it to marinades or pour it over pancakes.
recipes.title: No-cook green pine cone syrup

summary.text:
Loblolly pine (Pinus taeda) is an evergreen pine of the pine family (Pinaceae) from the south-eastern United States. Its inner bark was eaten in spring by some Native American peoples, and is an emergency food rather than a good one.
In New Zealand: It was introduced for forestry and first recorded wild in 1957. It is grown on a small scale for timber in the warmer parts of the North Island, and sometimes regenerates freely from planted trees, especially in Waitangi State Forest in Northland; it has also been found wild on the Coromandel Peninsula and on a road cutting in Rotoehu Forest in the Bay of Plenty. Its seed is spread by the wind.
It is in the Northland and Greater Wellington regional pest plans.

method.text: Needles: simmered, not boiled, in a covered pot of water until the water has coloured, then lifted out; wet fabric is kept in the bath at a gentle heat for about an hour, longer for a stronger colour. Scoured hemp with no mordant, dyed in an aluminium pot, came out a soft mauve-clay, and one bath coloured several pieces. The needles are also listed as giving a tan or green dye. Cones: soaked in water for a day to soften, cut into pieces, boiled for up to four hours (a lower heat loses less dye) and strained through muslin; cotton dyed for an hour and left to cool in the bath came out beige to light brown, mordanted or not, and the bath was used again the next day. On cotton and silk, cone tannins give beiges with orange and pink hues.

recipes.method: A box of pine needles about 30 × 20 cm; a 20-litre aluminium pot of cool water; a piece of hemp fabric about 1 × 1.5 m. Scour the fabric in a 40 °C wash with fragrance-free powder and about 250 ml (a cup) of baking soda, no fabric softener, then soak it in water for about an hour. Put the needles in the pot of water, cover, and bring to a simmer without boiling; turn the heat down a little and keep it there until the water has the colour you want. Lift out the needles with a fine sieve (straining through muslin gives a more even colour). Add the wet fabric, push out the air bubbles with a wooden spoon so it is all under, and keep it at a gentle heat for about an hour, stirring now and then; leave it longer for a stronger colour. Wring it out, wash and rinse it with fragrance-free powder and no softener, and dry it out of direct sun. The same bath dyes several pieces in turn.

method.text: Tinder: needles left to dry for a season, or dry ones from the forest floor, catch fire easily, more so with a little pitch. Fatwood, the dense amber wood soaked with resin in the stumps and lower branches of dead pines, is shaved into thin slivers and lit with a spark or flame, and still lights when damp. Glue: resin that has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground is gathered rather than cut from the tree, melted (on a hot rock beside a fire, for example), mixed with finely ground ash or powdered charcoal and left to cool; it is reheated to use. A little water softens old pitch into a soft glue, and pine shavings or sawdust worked into it make a wood filler. Oil or strong alcohol takes pitch off your hands. Incense: needles tied into a bundle with natural twine and dried for about two weeks. Cleaner: chopped needles covered with vinegar in a glass jar, with baking paper under the lid so it does not corrode, left for two weeks and strained; the vinegar is mixed with baking soda and castile soap for cleaning.

method.text: Resin is gathered from what has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground rather than cut from the tree, at any time of year. It sticks to everything, so keep a knife and jar just for it; oil, then soap, takes it off your hands, and rubbing alcohol off clothes. Large lumps melt faster if frozen and broken up with a hammer inside a thick paper bag. Warmed with an equal amount of beeswax, mixed and left to set in its container, it makes a simple balm; melted into an oil, strained and firmed with beeswax it makes a balm for dry or cracked skin, lips and hands.

recipes.method: 60 ml (¼ cup) pine resin; 125 ml (½ cup) oil such as olive or almond; 15–30 g grated beeswax. Melt the resin in the oil in a double boiler over a low heat. Strain through a coffee filter or a strainer, return to the double boiler, add the beeswax and heat gently until it has melted. Pour into tins or jars and store somewhere cool and dark.
recipes.title: Pine resin balm

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) pine resin; 250 ml (1 cup) olive oil, or another oil safe for skin; 125–190 ml (½–¾ cup) grated beeswax; 35 drops rosemary essential oil. Put the resin and oil in a glass jar in the top of a double boiler and simmer, stirring, until the resin melts; this can take several hours. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine sieve and return it to the double boiler. For every 250 ml of resin and oil add 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) grated beeswax (more gives a firmer balm) and heat gently until it melts. Pour into jars or tins, stir 5 drops of the essential oil into each, and put the lids on straight away so the scent stays in. Leave to cool and set, and store somewhere cool and dark. Use it on dry or cracked skin, as a lip or hand balm, or overnight on the face.
recipes.title: Pine resin and olive oil balm

Try only a little the first time: allergic reactions to conifers are not common, but are more likely than with most foods.
Do not pick from trees that may have been sprayed. Wilding conifers are controlled with herbicide.

edibleParts.text: Ripe fruit, eaten raw or cooked: sweet and juicy, tasting like a cross between apricot and plum with a citrus tang. It is good fresh, in fruit salads, stewed for breakfast, in pies, puddings and baking, as jam or cordial, and in savoury sauces, pickles and chutneys. Leaves, brewed as a tea (biwa-cha, a traditional Japanese herbal tea of dried loquat leaves). The seeds are not eaten (see Warnings).

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Hillsides, scrub, plantations, wasteland near sites of cultivation.
It grows in forest, shrublands, coastal slopes, roadsides, wastelands, plantations and gardens (Auckland Council), and invades disturbed forest and shrubland and inshore islands, mainly in the northern North Island. It tolerates wet to dry conditions, hot to moderately cool temperatures, most soils and moderate shade (Weedbusters).

identification.text:
Tree up to 8 m high when mature;  trunk well developed;  primary stems erect;  secondary stems spreading;  young stems stout, white-tomentose; older stems with prominent leaf scars, becoming greyish brown and transversely calloused.  Leaves near branch tips;  petiole  about 15 mm long, stout;  blade oblanceolate to narrowly elliptic, 150–350–(400) × 75–100–(130) mm, acute, tapering to cuneate or slightly auriculate base, very coriaceous, more or less rugose, dark green and glossy above, thinly grey- or brown-tomentose below (very young leaves completely brown-tomentose), serrate at least in upper 1/2 (sometimes obscurely);  stipules long-triangular, more or less attenuate, pilose.  Inflorescence of many flowers;  pedicels 5–8 mm long, brownish tomentose.  Sepals fused for most of length;  lobes 2–4 mm long, brown-tomentose.  Petals white or ivory, oblong,  about 7–8 × 3–4 mm, shallowly emarginate.  Fruit pyriform to broadly ellipsoid-oblong or subglobose, up to 50 × 35 mm;  skin yellow, more or less tomentose;  flesh sweet. 
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The seeds are large and brown (Weedbusters). The flowers, borne from late autumn into winter, are strongly scented, with a vanilla-almond fragrance (NZ Tree Crops Association).

preparation.text: Pick when golden and ripe: yellow-orange with no green left and soft to the touch; before that it is too tart. Cut the clusters off with snips rather than pulling single fruit, which tears the skin; picking in bunches with the stalks on helps. The fruit spoils fast once picked, so use it within a day or two and keep it in the fridge, as it browns quickly. Remove the large seeds and the membrane around them (for jam the membrane can be left in); the seeds stain fingers and nails black, so wear gloves for a big batch. The skin peels off easily but is thin enough to leave on for jam and chutney. Eat fresh, stew with a little sugar, or use in pies, sauces, chutney and jam; slightly underripe fruit has enough pectin to set a jelly. To freeze, halve and seed the fruit, blanch it to stop it browning, cool, freeze in a single layer on a tray, then bag it. For leaf tea, scrape the furry hairs off the underside of the leaves first, as they can irritate the throat.

recipes.method: 2.5 kg loquats; 1.25 kg white sugar; juice of half a lemon; 1/8 tsp ground cinnamon (optional); jam setting sugar (optional). For smaller batches keep the ratio of 2 parts fruit to 1 part sugar by weight. Wash the loquats, cut off the flower end and halve them; scoop out and discard the stones and the papery sack around them. Cut each half into quarters, weigh, and put in a large pan with half that weight of sugar; leave for about an hour for the juices to run. Add the lemon juice and cinnamon if using. Stir over a medium heat until the sugar dissolves, bring to the boil, then simmer for about 60 minutes until it is a golden slurry. Let it cool, blend with a stick blender to the texture you like, then bring back to the boil until thick, adding a tablespoon or two of jam setting mix if it is still too runny. Pour into sterilised jars and seal. Makes about 2.5 litres.
recipes.title: Loquat jam

recipes.method: Filling: 1 kg loquats with the seeds removed; 7 tbsp sugar; 1 tbsp flour; 1/4 tsp almond essence; 1 tsp cinnamon; 2 tsp lemon juice. Topping: 1 cup (250 ml) flour; 1 tsp baking powder; 1/4 tsp baking soda; 1/2 tsp salt; 1/2 cup (125 ml) sugar; 3/4 cup (185 ml) milk; 3 tbsp butter; 3 tbsp brown sugar to finish. Mix the filling ingredients and leave for half an hour (the source does not name the dish; use a baking dish). Pulse the topping ingredients in a food processor until combined, spoon over the filling and sprinkle with the brown sugar. Bake at 180 °C for 20–30 minutes. Serve hot with whipped cream, yoghurt or ice cream.
recipes.title: Loquat cobbler

recipes.method: 680 g loquats, washed, seeded and cut small; 450 g onion, chopped; 225 g apples, grated; 450 g sugar; 2 tsp mustard; 2 tsp sea salt; 1 tsp curry powder; 1 tbsp mustard seeds, crushed; 1 tbsp molasses; 2 tbsp fresh ginger, peeled and cut into thin strips; 500 ml apple cider vinegar; 500 ml water; 60 ml raisins or currants. Put everything in a large pot and bring to the boil, then cook gently, stirring often so it does not stick, for about 1–1½ hours until soft and well coloured. Pour into hot sterilised jars, leaving about 1 cm headroom, seal, and process the jars for 10 minutes in a boiling-water bath; refrigerate and use any that do not seal. The sealed jars keep in a cool dark place for 9 months.
recipes.title: Loquat chutney

recipes.method: 900 g loquats (about 600 g once stoned); 1 cup (250 ml) soft brown sugar; 3 cups (750 ml) malt vinegar; 1 onion, chopped; 2 cloves garlic; 1/2 tsp salt; 1/2 tsp black pepper; 1/4 tsp cayenne pepper; 6 whole cloves (or 1/2 tsp ground cloves). Wash, halve and stone the loquats. Put them in a large saucepan with everything else, bring to a low boil, then simmer for about an hour, stirring now and then, until the liquid has reduced and the fruit has collapsed. Cool slightly, blend until smooth (take care, hot sauce burns), pour into sterilised jars and seal. Makes about 1 litre; good with chicken.
recipes.title: Loquat barbecue sauce

recipes.method: Topping: 2 tbsp unsalted butter, melted; 3/4 cup (150 g) brown sugar; about 25 medium loquats, halved and seeded. Cake: 1 3/4 cups (220 g) plain flour; 1 1/2 tsp baking powder; 1/2 tsp baking soda; 1/2 tsp salt; 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon; 110 g unsalted butter; 3/4 cup (150 g) sugar; 2 tsp vanilla extract; 2 large eggs at room temperature; 3/4 cup (180 ml) milk. Heat the oven to 190 °C. Mix the melted butter with the brown sugar. Lay the loquats cut side down in a greased cake pan and pour the butter-sugar over them. Sift the flour, baking powder, soda, salt and cinnamon together. Cream the butter and sugar for 4–5 minutes until smooth, beat in the eggs and vanilla, mix in the dry ingredients, then the milk, without overmixing. Pour the batter over the loquats and bake for about 40 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean. Cool for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a plate before the caramel sets; serve warm or at room temperature. Serves 8.
recipes.title: Loquat upside-down cake

recipes.method: 3 cups (750 ml) loquats, washed and seeded; 1 tsp fenugreek seeds; 2 tsp mustard seeds; 1 tsp red chilli powder, or to taste; 1 tsp salt, or to taste. Tempering: 2 tsp oil; 1/2 tsp mustard seeds; 2 pinches asafoetida. Dry the washed loquats well, halve, seed and cut into long wedges (peeling is optional). Toast the fenugreek seeds in a dry pan for 45 seconds to a minute until light brown, then pop the 2 tsp mustard seeds in the same pan; grind both to a fine powder. Heat the oil, pop the 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, add the asafoetida and take off the heat. Mix the loquats with the chilli powder, salt, ground spices and the tempering and leave for an hour. Mix again, adjust the salt and chilli, and leave another 30 minutes before serving with rice and dal or yoghurt rice. Keeps in the fridge for up to a week.
recipes.title: Instant loquat pickle

recipes.method: 4 medium loquat leaves (or about 1 tbsp crushed dried leaves per cup); 3 cups (750 ml) water; sweetener, optional. Pick fresh, medium-sized green leaves, rinse and dry them. Scrape the furry hairs off the underside with a small knife (they can irritate the throat), cut out the thick middle vein, and slice or tear the leaves into small pieces. Put them in a pot with the water, bring to the boil, then simmer gently for 10 minutes. Turn off the heat, cover and steep for another 10 minutes. Strain and drink hot, or over ice; the longer it simmers, the darker and stronger it gets. For dried leaves, air-dry or oven-dry young leaves, crush and store in a jar.
recipes.title: Loquat leaf tea

recipes.method: A guide rather than a strict recipe: scale it to your dish. Base: crushed Weet-Bix and pitted dates, bound with a little fruit juice. Filling: cottage cheese, Greek yoghurt and thick loquat purée, sweetened to taste. Blitz the base ingredients in a food processor, bind with juice and press into a greased flan dish. Blend the filling ingredients and pour over the base. Refrigerate until firm and serve with extra fruit and yoghurt.
recipes.title: Loquat cheesecake (no-bake)

summary.text:
Loquat (Eriobotrya japonica; Chinese 枇杷, pípá) is an evergreen tree up to 8 m high, with large, leathery leaves clustered near the branch tips and edible yellow fruit.
E. japonica is widely grown in warm temperate countries for its attractive appearance and edible fruit and is very common north of the Volcanic Plateau in New Zealand. On a hillside behind Paihia (Bay of Islands), a large wild population occurs with fruits ranging from pyriform to subglobose.
Also called Chinese medlar and Japanese medlar. It is native to the hills of south-central China and has been cultivated in Japan for more than 1000 years; the genus name comes from the Greek for 'wool' and 'cluster', and the Chinese name pipa likens the fruit to the lute of that name. Early New Zealand cookery writers such as Aunt Daisy give recipes for it, so it is not a recent arrival (NZ Tree Crops Association).
Birds, especially kererū, spread the seed, as do people and dumped garden waste; gardens, wastelands and exotic plantations are common seed sources. It forms tall stands that replace native low-canopy and mid-tier species (Weedbusters) and can invade intact native forest canopy (Auckland Council). It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.
In Auckland it is a sustained-control pest across the whole region and a pest under the Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area Notice. Since 1 September 2022 it may not be bred, distributed, released, sold or planted there (an existing plant may be moved within the same property), and a loquat planted in breach of these rules must be destroyed if an authorised person directs it (Auckland Council).
The NZ Plant Conservation Network and DOC's 2024 weed list use the name Rhaphiolepis bibas; Biota of New Zealand keeps Eriobotrya japonica as the current name.

warnings: The seeds contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide: raw seeds hold 2–5% amygdalin, so a single seed of about 2 g can carry 2.4–5.9 mg of cyanide. They are hard and bitter and unsuitable to eat; remove them. Do not take powdered loquat seed, home-made or bought, unless analysis has confirmed it safe: products on sale have tested high enough in cyanide that a teaspoon could exceed the safe acute dose.
The leaves also contain cyanogenic glycosides, though much less than the seeds; drinking a leaf infusion carries a low risk of cyanide poisoning. Amygdalin has also been recorded in the fruit peel.
Eat only ripe fruit: a 5-year-old child who ate 4 unripe loquats became drowsy and dazed and was back to normal after about 2 hours (a single reported case).
It is controlled as an environmental weed with herbicide (metsulfuron sprays, metsulfuron gel on cut stumps, or basal bark spray). Pick only where you know it has not been sprayed.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In the Auckland region (Regionally Critical), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it. In Northland (Regionally Naturally Uncommon), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text:
Erect shrub or tree up to 8 m tall, bark dark. Leaves on slender petioles ± 2 cm long; lamina elliptic-oblong to elliptic-obovate to ovate-oblong, 6–10 × 3–6 cm, obtuse to subacute, rather coriaceous, dark green and glossy above, glaucous below, somewhat pungent to taste; midrib and veins evident below. Flowers ± 1 cm diameter, in axillary fascicles of 3–5–(10) on pedicels 5 mm to 1 cm long or more; calyx subentire to shallowly lobed; petals 5–6, greenish yellow, narrow-oblong to narrow-obovate, 5–6 mm long; stamens 6–15; carpels 3–6; fruits red (rarely dark), 5–6 mm diameter, mesocarp slightly fleshy; seeds 3 to 6, black, angled.
Leaf undersides are pale to glaucous but not white, leaf edges are wavy, and the ripe fruit is orange to red. Told from horopito by its leaves, which are not blotched and are glossy above, and by its fruit, usually bright red.

lookalikes.howToTell: Horopito's leaves are dull green and blotched with red, at least in exposed places; lowland horopito's are dark green and glossy above with no red blotches. Horopito's leaves are usually smaller, 2–6 (rarely 8) × 1–3 cm against 6–10 × 3–6 cm, and glaucous to white underneath and often pink-flushed, where lowland horopito's are pale to glaucous but not white. Horopito's ripe fruit is dark red to black; lowland horopito's is usually bright red, rarely dark. Horopito's leaves are very pungent to taste, lowland horopito's only somewhat pungent. Hybrids between the two are frequent where they meet, so some plants fit neither description.
lookalikes.name: Horopito

lookalikes.howToTell: Feel the leaf: lowland horopito's is rather leathery, mountain alseuosmia's thin. Both have glossy leaves, but mountain alseuosmia's are often red-edged and sometimes flecked red, while lowland horopito's have no blemishes or blotches. Mountain alseuosmia's leaves are widest towards the tip and narrowed wedge-like to the base, with a tiny point at the tip, 2–2.5 cm wide (sometimes 3.5 cm), on rather stout stalks up to 10 mm long; lowland horopito's are elliptic-oblong to elliptic-obovate or ovate-oblong, 3–6 cm wide, with a wavy edge, on slender stalks about 2 cm long. Leaf lengths overlap: usually 7 cm (2.5–10 cm) against 6–10 cm. Mountain alseuosmia is a shrub up to about 50 cm tall, unbranched or with one or two branches; lowland horopito grows to 7–8 m, but small lowland horopito plants closely resemble mountain alseuosmia. In flower, mountain alseuosmia's flowers are tubular, about 8–10 mm long, with five fringed lobes, white to yellowish or reddish and sweet-scented; lowland horopito's are about 1 cm across, with 5–6 separate greenish-yellow petals 5–6 mm long, often several together in the leaf joints. Both have red berries: mountain alseuosmia's are oval, about 9–12 × 5–6 mm; lowland horopito's are round, 5–6 mm across. Mountain alseuosmia does not grow north of Te Moehau and Mt Pirongia. No record of mountain alseuosmia as food was found (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mountain alseuosmia

lookalikes.howToTell: Northland horopito is known only from Mt Manaia and Bream Head at Whangārei Heads and from Logues Bush near Wellsford, and until 2003 its plants were taken for lowland horopito or for hybrids between lowland horopito and horopito. Both are upright shrubs or small trees, to 7–8 m, with glossy leaves without blotches and a conspicuous pale midvein above. Turn a leaf over: Northland horopito's underside is white with a red midvein; lowland horopito's is pale to glaucous but not white, with a pale midvein. Northland horopito's leaf stalks are 4–11 mm long, red-brown to maroon; lowland horopito's are slender, about 2 cm long. Northland horopito's leaf buds and young leaves are usually hairy on the edges, undersides and stalks; lowland horopito is hairless. Leaf sizes overlap: 3.5–11 × 1.8–4.5 cm against 6–10 × 3–6 cm. Northland horopito's flowers are single or in twos or threes, with cream petals; lowland horopito's are greenish yellow, often several together. Northland horopito's ripe fruit is black, 6.4–9.8 mm long; lowland horopito's is red to orange-red, rarely dark, 5–6 mm across. Northland horopito is Threatened – Nationally Critical, and no record of it as food was found (see its page).

summary.text:
Lowland horopito (Pseudowintera axillaris), also called lowland pepper tree, is a pungent-leaved shrub or small tree of the Winteraceae, endemic to New Zealand.
It grows on the North and South Islands from latitude 35° south, extending to 42° in the South Island west of the main divide; it is scarce north of Auckland and reaches to near Westport. The Winteraceae is one of the most primitive families of flowering plants. Lowland horopito hybridises frequently with horopito (P. colorata) where the two meet, and browsing animals find it unpalatable. Te Arawa call the fruit matou. It is grown from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in March–April, and its seeds are spread by birds. It is ranked Not Threatened (2023).

warnings: The heat builds gradually, so you may not feel it at first, and milk does not cool it. Nibble lightly on a leaf before you use more. A leaf infusion can leave a burning feeling in the throat and chest.

Horopito can numb some of your taste buds for a while, so what you eat or drink afterwards tastes odd; the more you have, the stronger the effect. A brew of lowland horopito leaves strongly dulls the taste of sweet, and possibly bitter, things, but not of salt or sour.

habitat.text: Asplenium lyallii is a terrestrial fern found frequently on limestone, marble, or calcareous mudstone or sandstone, but also on greywacke, and on andesite and basalt in the western Waikato. It grows under open broadleaved, beech and kānuka forest, amongst the roots of Corynocarpus laevigatus, with Phormium on coastal cliffs, in coastal scrub, among coastal rocks, and on sand. At higher altitudes it occurs on mossy boulders under forest, on river banks, or in the open on rocky ground, on banks, on cliffs, in rock crevices, under overhangs and around caves.

identification.text:
An extremely variable spleenwort of limestone and other base-rich rock. Sheltered lowland plants have large, twice-divided, dark glossy fronds; exposed high-altitude plants have small once-divided fronds, dull grey-green on both sides. The lower pinnae are usually at least lobed or divided on the side towards the frond tip, and the terminal segment is short and lobed.
Terrestrial or rupestral ferns. Rhizomes erect or short-creeping, bearing scales. Rhizome scales narrowly ovate, 8–25 mm long, 1–4.5 mm wide, brown, clathrate. Fronds 12–900 or rarely up to 1160 mm long. Stipes 4–400 mm long, pale brown abaxially and proximally, green adaxially and distally, bearing abundant narrowly ovate scales with filiform apices. Rachises green or sometimes brown abaxially, bearing abundant scales. Laminae 1–2-pinnate, narrowly ovate or ovate or elliptic, narrowed to a short pinnatifid or rarely undivided terminal segment with serrate margins similar to or more deeply incised than the primary pinnae; laminae 8–550 or rarely to 770 mm long, 5–230 mm wide, dark shiny green on adaxial surface and paler on abaxial surface or dull grey-green on both surfaces, herbaceous or coriaceous, bearing scales abaxially and sometimes adaxially, lacking hairs. Primary pinnae in 1–18 pairs below an undivided or pinnatifid apical segment, not overlapping; proximal pinnae ovate or narrowly ovate, those at mid-lamina narrowly ovate or narrowly oblong; the longest pinnae at or below the middle, 2–155 mm long, 1.5–60 mm wide; pinna apices obtuse or acute or acuminate, margins serrate, bases stalked; proximal pinnae bearing 1–6 pairs of secondary pinnae in the proximal half, or partially lobed or divided acroscopically, or occasionally not divided or lobed (on smallest fronds). Secondary pinnae ovate to elliptic, the longest 7–45 mm long, 4–16 or rarely up to 25 mm wide; apices obtuse, margins entire or serrate, bases stalked. Sori away from margins; indusia 3–14 mm long or rarely only 1 mm long in very small plants, straight; free margins of indusia entire. Mean spore size 40–54 μm long, 27–35 μm wide; perispores prominently winged and ridged.
Small 1-pinnate fronds can be confused with Asplenium lepidotum or small fronds of Asplenium oblongifolium and Asplenium obtusatum, but Asplenium lyallii has larger spores than the other species. The stipe scales of Asplenium oblongifolium are also narrower, with longer filiform apices, and scales are absent from the adaxial pinna surfaces. Plants of Asplenium obtusatum have generally thicker fronds and are strictly coastal in habitat.

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining spleenwort narrows to a long undivided terminal segment like its pinnae, its pinnae are not lobed or divided, its stalk scales are narrow with long thread-like tips, and its upper pinna surfaces have no scales; Lyall's spleenwort has a short lobed terminal segment and usually lobed or divided lower pinnae. Small once-divided fronds can be told apart for certain only by spore size under a microscope. The young shoots of shining spleenwort are a recorded Māori food.
lookalikes.name: Shining spleenwort

lookalikes.howToTell: Small plants are the hardest to tell apart, as Asplenium lepidotum has abundant scales on the upper surface of its pinnae like some once-divided Lyall's spleenwort. Look at the frond tip: Lyall's spleenwort's terminal segment is lobed, or cut deeper than the outer edges of the pinnae; Asplenium lepidotum's is undivided or has one lobe near its base, cut no deeper than the pinnae. Asplenium lepidotum is never twice-divided, and its undivided fronds reach 125 mm, against only 12 mm in Lyall's spleenwort. Spore size (40–54 μm long in Lyall's spleenwort, 37–42 μm in Asplenium lepidotum) needs a microscope. Asplenium lepidotum grows only in the north-west of the South Island; the two grow together at Tākaka Hill and near Īnangahua. No record of Asplenium lepidotum as food was found.
lookalikes.name: Asplenium lepidotum

lookalikes.howToTell: Shore spleenwort generally has thicker, fleshier fronds, dull green on both surfaces, and a less divided terminal segment; Lyall's spleenwort's terminal segment is short and lobed, cut as deep as or deeper than the pinnae. Shore spleenwort grows only on the coast, never beyond the reach of salt spray, so a plant growing inland is not shore spleenwort; Lyall's spleenwort grows both inland and on coastal cliffs and rocks. Lyall's spleenwort's spores are generally larger (40–54 μm long against 40–43 μm), but the sizes overlap and need a microscope. Both grow on the coasts around Cook Strait, in the south of the South Island, and on Stewart Island and the Chatham Islands. No record of shore spleenwort as food was found.
lookalikes.name: Shore spleenwort

summary.text:
Lyall's spleenwort is an endemic fern, named after David Lyall, surgeon and naturalist on HMS Erebus and Terror and later the Acheron. It favours limestone, marble and other base-rich rock and is often found at cave entrances. Its minute spores are dispersed by wind. It hybridises with several other spleenworts, including shore spleenwort, Asplenium appendiculatum, Asplenium chathamense, hanging spleenwort and Asplenium gracillimum. Allan's 1961 Flora calls it Asplenium anomodum.
In the North Island it grows on the west coast from Mt Karioi to south Taranaki and in the east from the Gisborne and Hawke's Bay ranges to Wellington; in the South Island it is mostly in the east, from north-west Nelson through Marlborough, Canterbury, coastal Otago and Southland into Fiordland and south Westland, and on Stewart Island and the Chatham Islands, from sea level to 1400 m. Not Threatened (2023).
In gardens it is slow-growing but makes an attractive pot plant or a plant for a shaded rock wall.

warnings: No record of Lyall's spleenwort as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

Small once-divided fronds can be confused with shining spleenwort, whose young shoots are eaten, and the two grow in the same parts of the North Island and the north of the South Island. Check the terminal segment and the stalk scales before picking any spleenwort (see the lookalikes).

edibleParts.text: The cap and stem, cooked.

habitat.text: Grassland: pasture, lawns and grassy verges, singly or in rings. In New Zealand it has been found in sheep-grazed coastal grassland and among salt-tolerant plants near the shore.

identification.text:
A big white mushroom. The cap is 5–12 cm across when young and can reach 20 cm or more, whitish, sometimes flushed pale yellow or brown, and often cracks into warty scales like crocodile skin. It can turn slowly yellowish where bruised, especially near the edge.
The gills are free of the stem, whitish to tan when young and dark brown when mature, with no pink stage. The stem is 6–20 cm long and 2–4 cm thick, with a large white skirt-like ring that is cogwheel-like underneath, and girdles of small white scales below it. The flesh is white and firm; cut, the stem may flush pink to cinnamon. Young ones smell faintly of almond or aniseed, old ones of ammonia. The spore print is brown.
Its spores are larger than the horse mushroom's (about 9–11 µm long), which is how New Zealand mycologists tell the two apart.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are big, white grassland Agaricus with a large ring that is cogwheel-like underneath, a brown spore print and a smell of almond, and both are eaten. Horse mushroom gills start pale pink to white, then turn grey and brown; macro mushroom gills start whitish to tan, with no pink stage. Macro mushroom's stem is stouter, with girdles of small white scales below the ring; horse mushroom's stem is smooth and its cap smoother. Old macro mushrooms smell of ammonia. None of these is reliable in New Zealand: mycologists here tell the two apart by spore size under a microscope, the macro mushroom's spores being larger.

preparation.text: Always cook it. Pick young ones: old, ammonia-smelling ones are poor eating. Check for maggots: even young ones are often full of them. It can also be dried. Use it like a large cultivated (portobello) mushroom, in risotto, omelettes, soups and sauces.

summary.text:
Agaricus crocodilinus, the macro mushroom, is a large white Agaricus of grassland, named for its cap, which can crack into warty scales like crocodile skin. It was first recorded in New Zealand in 2006, and Biota of New Zealand says it is confused with the horse mushroom.
It is rarely recorded here: iNaturalist has three research-grade New Zealand records, from coastal grassland in Hawke's Bay and Otago and from Southland, and a few unconfirmed ones from Otago, Canterbury and Nelson. Biota gives its origin as uncertain and the NZ Organisms Register as unknown; Virtual Mycota lists it as exotic, under the name Agaricus urinascens. Overseas the macro mushroom is eaten and well regarded; New Zealand's registers treat the European A. urinascens and A. macrosporus as the same species.

warnings: It can accumulate cadmium, a toxic metal, even in areas that are not polluted. Eat it in moderation, and don't pick it from roadsides, industrial sites or polluted ground.

Yellow-staining Agaricus, the group around the yellow stainer (A. xanthodermus) and a notable group of poisonous Agaricus, are common in New Zealand as unnamed species, and look like a white field mushroom. Cut through the very base of the stem and scratch the cap edge: if it turns bright chrome yellow almost at once, or smells of ink, phenol or iodine, throw it out. A macro mushroom's cut stem flushes pinkish to cinnamon and smells of almond, or of ammonia when old; a slow yellowing of the cap does not rule out either.

harvestEthics.text: Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text: A dense, bushy, upright tree to 15 m tall, with a trunk up to 35 cm across and brown bark that is flaky to hard, rough and fissured. Young stems have smooth internodes above and below the nodes. The leaves are opposite, lanceolate to oval and widest above the middle, 30–100 mm long and 15–30 mm wide, with a tapered, sharp-pointed tip and a wedge-shaped base, on stalks 2–10 mm long. They are hairless, glossy green above and paler below, with numerous side veins, a vein inside the leaf margin that is usually visible, and small, rather scattered oil glands. New growth is coppery. The flowers come in clusters at or near the ends of young branches, mainly from summer to early autumn: the funnel-shaped calyx is green at first and turns red, the round white petals are 4–5 mm long, free and spreading, and the numerous white stamens are 6–15 mm long, longer than the petals. The fruit is berry-like, round to egg-shaped, 15–25 mm wide and magenta, occasionally white, pink or purple. It holds a single large seed, which usually shows lines of division marking its many embryos; this sets its fruit apart from the other Syzygium species in New Zealand.

lookalikes.howToTell: Lilly pilly's flowers are smaller: its petals are about 2 mm long, joined into a small cap, and its stamens reach about 3 mm; magenta lilly pilly has free, spreading petals 4–5 mm long and stamens 6–15 mm long. Lilly pilly's fruit is nearly round to broadly oblong or obovoid and often slightly flattened, with a hollow at the tip where the calyx lobes have fallen; magenta lilly pilly's is round to egg-shaped, with somewhat swollen calyx lobes at the tip. Lilly pilly's leaves are broader for their length: ovate or elliptic-ovate and usually 2–5 cm wide, against magenta lilly pilly's lanceolate to obovate leaves 1.5–3 cm wide that taper to the base. Fruit colour does not separate them: lilly pilly's is pinkish mauve or white, and magenta lilly pilly's is usually magenta but can be white, pink or purple. Cut a fruit open: magenta lilly pilly's single large seed usually shows lines of division marking its many embryos, which sets it apart from the other Syzygium species in New Zealand. Lilly pilly's fruit is eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Lilly pilly

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the strong young shoots: brush cherry's are more or less four-winged, the wings running down from each leaf stalk and joining just above the next pair of leaves in a small pocket or hump; magenta lilly pilly's shoots are at most angled, with smooth internodes and no pocket. This works even on young plants. Cut a fruit open: magenta lilly pilly's seed usually shows lines of division marking its several embryos; brush cherry's seed has a single embryo. Magenta lilly pilly's fruit is round to egg-shaped and usually magenta, but can be white, pink or purple; brush cherry's is oblong to obovoid and crimson to crimson-purple, so colour alone is not reliable. Leaf size and the white flowers overlap. Magenta lilly pilly is sometimes sold in New Zealand under brush cherry's scientific name, so a garden label does not settle it. Brush cherry is much less often planted than magenta lilly pilly, and its wild seedlings are uncommon. Brush cherry's fruit is eaten too (see its page).

preparation.text: Eaten fresh, or cooked into jams; it also makes a cordial and a cold fruit drink. Each fruit holds a single large seed.

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) magenta lilly pilly fruit; 2 tablespoons sugar; 750 ml (3 cups) boiling water; ice (optional). Wash the fruit, put it in a bowl and sprinkle over the sugar. Pour over the boiling water and leave to stand until almost cold. Mash with a potato masher to crush out the juice, then pour the fruit and juice through a sieve into a jug to remove the stones and pulp. Chill in the fridge, or add a few ice blocks, to serve. Serves 2.
recipes.title: Lilly pilly summer drink

recipes.method: 1 kg magenta lilly pilly fruit; 750 ml (3 cups) water; juice of 2 lemons; 750 ml (3 cups) sugar; 3 teaspoons citric acid. Put the washed fruit in a large saucepan with the water and bring to the boil, then cover and simmer for 20 minutes until cooked. Let cool. Line a sieve with a jelly bag or flannelette and set it over a large clean saucepan; tip in the cooked fruit and its juice and pour in the lemon juice. Gather the bag around the fruit and squeeze and twist it until all the juice is forced out, then discard the remains. Bring the liquid to a rapid boil, stir in the sugar and citric acid, and when they have completely dissolved, pour through a funnel into hot, clean bottles and seal. To drink, put 1–2 tablespoons in a glass and dilute with tap or soda water. Refrigerate after opening. Makes about two 750 ml bottles.
recipes.title: Lilly pilly cordial

recipes.method: 550 g magenta lilly pilly fruit, weighed after the stones are removed; 385 g white sugar; 1–2 lemons; 2 apples. The evening before, juice the lemons and soak their pips overnight in a little water to draw out pectin. Wash the fruit and take the stone out of each one (a cherry pitter helps). Weigh the pitted fruit and add sugar at 70% of its weight (700 g sugar per 1 kg fruit); stir and leave to stand until juicy. Slice the apples thinly into a small pot, cover with about 1 cm of water and simmer until the water has halved and turned light golden, then strain off this liquid and add it to the fruit. Put the fruit mixture in a heavy-based pot with the lemon juice and the soaking water from the pips (without the pips). Bring to the boil, then simmer: after about 12–15 minutes the fruit turns translucent and the jam thickens. Test a drop on a chilled plate; if it is still runny, simmer a little longer and test again. Ladle into hot, sterilised jars and seal while hot. Makes about 2 × 350 ml jars.
recipes.title: Magenta lilly pilly jam

summary.text: A tree of the myrtle family from coastal rainforest in New South Wales, where it is uncommon in the wild and listed as threatened, but it is widely cultivated. In New Zealand it is planted in parks and gardens or for shelter, and self-sows freely; it grows in lowland areas of the North Island and is uncommon in the South Island. Biota of New Zealand lists it as a casual exotic, not fully naturalised. It is often sold in New Zealand under the name S. australe (brush cherry), a name once misapplied to this species, and the two are commonly confused. It is not on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.

habitat.text: Coastal to lower montane forest, mostly near the coast and in the lowlands. Often part of the subcanopy in coastal kauri forest or mixed pōhutukawa and hardwood forest, and occasionally the dominant canopy tree.

identification.text: Tree up to about 10 m tall; trunk 20–40 cm in diameter; branches rather close-set; branchlets slender, pubescent. Leaves on petioles winged in the upper half, (8)–12–(20) mm long; lamina rather thin, hairless, ovate to broad-elliptic to oblong, sometimes almost round, the apex rounded or notched, about 50–60 × 35–40 mm; leaves of young plants smaller, about 15–25 × 10–17 mm. Drupe white, broad-oblong, about 7 mm long. Adult leaves are somewhat glossy, dark green or yellow-green above and often mottled with maroon or purple, and pale wine-red underneath. The thin, mottled leaves have a small pit where the veins join. Young plants have small spoon-shaped leaves like those of Coprosma spathulata; run a finger along a young branchlet: in māmāngi it feels smooth, while in C. spathulata it is finely wrinkled and feels like a cat's tongue.

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Kanono's young twigs are hairless; Māmāngi's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Karamū's young twigs are hairless; Māmāngi's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Shining karamū's young twigs are hairless; Māmāngi's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Both can have a rounded or notched leaf tip, so the tip does not separate them; taupata's leaf is very glossy, māmāngi's only somewhat glossy. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Those figures fit the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa; the North Island's wild subsp. minor has thinner, papery leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) on stalks about 10–18 mm long, and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma's young twigs are hairless; Māmāngi's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Hūpiro's young twigs are hairless; Māmāngi's are hairy. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long.
