identification.text:
Perennial stoloniferous herb. Stems trailing, glabrous, up to 1 m long. Leaves glabrous, all similar but becoming smaller near inflorescence, pinnate, petiolate, 2–10–(25) × 1–5 cm; basal auricles very small; leaflets rounded, ovate; margins entire or sinuate. Pedicels glabrous, slender, erecto-patent, spreading to deflexed at fruiting, (8)–12–20–(30) mm long. Sepals 2.5–3.5 × 1 mm. Petals white, (4)–5–6 × 1.5–2.5 mm. Silique glabrous, narrow-oblong to linear, curved, (10)–15–25–(30) × about 1.5 mm; valves with distinct midrib at least below; style about 1 mm long. Seeds in about 1 row per locule, brown, about 1 mm long, reticulate with 100–150 polygonal depressions per face. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Rorippa microphylla (Rchb.) Hylander]
A bright green, sturdy herb that creeps or stands upright, with small white flowers from spring through summer. The leaves smell peppery when crushed, and turn brown or purple in autumn and winter. It is very like watercress, and the surest difference is in the seeds: see Lookalikes.

lookalikes.howToTell: The two are very alike and the leaves do not separate them. The surest test is the ripe seeds: narrow-fruited watercress has them in a single row in each half of the pod, each seed with 100–150 small pits per face; watercress has them in two distinct rows, with 20–50 coarse pits. Narrow-fruited watercress also tends to have larger flowers (petals 5–6 mm long against 4–6 mm), longer flower stalks (12–20 mm against 10–15 mm) and narrower pods (about 1.5 mm wide against 2–2.5 mm). Its leaves turn brown or purple in autumn and winter. Both grow in the same streams and drains. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Water celery's leaflets are toothed, in 2–8 pairs; narrow-fruited watercress's are rounded, with smooth or wavy edges, and smell peppery when crushed. In flower, water celery has small compound umbels of tiny white flowers on short stalks opposite the leaves, with 4–8 small bracteoles under each small umbel; narrow-fruited watercress has white flowers in spikes, followed by narrow curved pods. Both grow in streams and drains. Water celery is edible, but it is an umbellifer, and deadly hemlock — another umbellifer — also grows on damp ground in New Zealand, so be certain of the identification.
lookalikes.name: Water celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Bog yellow cress has yellow petals only about as long as the sepals (1.5–2.5 mm), usually stands upright from a taproot, and its leaves are deeply lobed with toothed edges. Narrow-fruited watercress has white petals, about twice as long as the sepals, and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, with rounded leaflets with smooth or wavy edges. Bog yellow cress's pods are short and plump, 2–7 mm long; narrow-fruited watercress's are slender, 10–30 mm. Both grow in wet places, so place does not separate them. Bog yellow cress's young leaves and stems are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Bog yellow cress

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping yellowcress has yellow flowers on upright stems and spreads by creeping underground parts; its upper leaves are cut into narrow, toothed or untoothed lobes. Narrow-fruited watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, with rounded leaflets with smooth or wavy edges. Both grow in wet ground and both have petals about twice as long as the sepals, so place and petal length do not separate them. Creeping yellowcress has no reliable food record.
lookalikes.name: Creeping yellowcress

lookalikes.howToTell: Land cress has yellow flowers on upright stems from a stout taproot, and grows on river banks, roadsides and waste land; narrow-fruited watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, and grows in streams, ditches and drains. Land cress's pods are (30–)40–70 mm long; narrow-fruited watercress's are (10–)15–25(–30) mm. Both have lobed leaves, so the leaves alone do not separate them. Land cress's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Land cress

preparation.text: Raw only if it comes from water with no sheep or cattle grazing above it; otherwise cook it, which kills liver fluke. The plant is very sensitive to pollution, so pick only from clean water. For mustard, grind the seeds and mix with cold water: the heat develops over 10–15 minutes. Hot water, vinegar or salt stops that reaction and gives a mild but bitter mustard.

recipes.method: Serves 4. 500 g meaty pork ribs; 1 bunch watercress, washed thoroughly; 6 dried Chinese dates, red or black; a 2 cm piece of ginger, sliced lengthwise and smashed; 2 tsp salt; 1 tsp sugar. Cover the ribs with water by about 5 cm in a large pot and bring to a rolling boil, then drain in a colander to get rid of fat and scum and return the ribs to the pot. Trim the watercress, separate the leaves from the stems and chop the stems small. Add about 2 litres of water, the watercress stems, dates and ginger and bring to the boil over high heat. Cover and simmer gently over medium heat for 45 minutes to an hour, until the ribs are tender. Add the leaves and simmer about 10 minutes more, until they turn dark green. Stir in the salt and sugar and serve straight away.
recipes.title: Pork rib and watercress soup

recipes.method: Written for wild watercress (Nasturtium officinale) by an American chef. Serves 4. 450 g (1 lb) fresh watercress; salt; soft salted butter or extra virgin olive oil; lemon wedges or vinegar, to serve. Wash the watercress, picking out insects and debris, and dry it well, ideally in a salad spinner. Put a thin film of water in a large pot, fill the pot with the watercress and cover it. Set it over medium-high heat for a few minutes until the pot is very hot, then lift the lid and stir. Cover again for a minute or two, stir, and repeat until the watercress has wilted. Keep cooking and tasting, adding a splash of water if it dries out, until it is tender: young shoots are quick, older leaves can take 15 minutes or more. Turn off the heat and pour off what little water is left. Toss with a drizzle of olive oil and salt, taste, and serve with lemon or a dash of vinegar, or butter at the table. The author also steams it in a steamer basket over 5–8 cm of boiling water, covered on low heat, until tender, but prefers the pot method for watercress.
recipes.title: Steamed watercress

recipes.method: Fills a 30 cm tart tin. Pastry: 125 g very cold butter; 250 g sieved plain flour; 50 g finely grated parmesan; 1 tsp icing sugar; salt; plenty of black pepper; just enough water. Filling: 500 g watercress leaves, with some white flowers kept for garnish; 20 g butter; the juice of 1 orange; 3 large eggs plus 2 extra yolks; 300 ml double cream; 200 g grated parmesan; salt and pepper; 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts. Heat the oven to 180 °C. For the pastry, grate 125 g very cold butter into 250 g sieved plain flour, 50 g finely grated parmesan, 1 tsp icing sugar, salt and plenty of black pepper. Rub together lightly, keeping it cool, then add just enough water to form a rough ball (less water, less shrinking). Chill for 30 minutes, roll out and line the tin, patching where needed. Prick the base, chill for 20 minutes, then blind-bake with baking paper and beans for 15 minutes; remove them and bake on until lightly toasted. For the filling, strip 500 g watercress leaves from the fibrous stalks (some stalk is fine — just a coarser tart), keeping some white flowers for garnish. Melt 20 g butter in a large heavy pan over a medium heat, add the watercress and the juice of 1 orange, and sweat gently for 10 minutes, stirring often. Blitz it with its juices, then beat it hard with 3 large eggs and 2 extra yolks, 300 ml double cream, all but a handful of 200 g grated parmesan, and plenty of salt and pepper — the more air, the more it rises. Pour into the case, sprinkle with the reserved parmesan and 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts, and bake for 20–25 minutes, until bronzed and only slightly wobbly in the middle. Cool a little and scatter the watercress flowers on top.
recipes.title: Watercress and parmesan tart

summary.text:
Narrow-fruited watercress, Nasturtium microphyllum, is a perennial aquatic herb of the mustard family (Brassicaceae) with trailing stems up to 1 m long.
In New Zealand it is called one-rowed watercress; its seeds sit in a single row in each half of the pod. It is an exotic from Europe, brought in as a culinary herb and recorded naturalised in 1954. It is common throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands, and commonest in the South Island. It spreads by seed and by pieces of stem that break off and root. It grows with watercress in New Zealand's cold springs, where a 1976 study looked at the two together. The name microphyllum means 'small leaf'.

warnings: Liver fluke risk: plants in water draining from land where sheep or cattle graze can carry Fasciola hepatica. Cooking kills it; eating raw does not.

identification.text:
Scrambling perennial; stems glabrous, angled, broadly winged. Leaves glabrous; tendril branched in upper leaves, sometimes simple in lower leaves; leaflets in 1 pair, usually lanceolate to linear, rarely narrowly elliptic, narrowly acute to acuminate, 50–130 mm long; veins parallel; stipules lanceolate to linear, with 1 narrow basal lobe, less than 1/2 as wide as stem (about 1–3 mm wide), (5)–10–20 mm long. Inflorescence longer than leaves, (2)–5–8-flowered; pedicels 4–10 mm long. Calyx glabrous, slightly or not gibbous at base; calyx teeth unequal, narrowly triangular, shorter than tube. Corolla purple-pink, 13–17 mm long. Pod glabrous, brown, 8–15-seeded, 40–70 mm long; seeds reticulate-rugose.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Broad-leaved sweet pea (Lathyrus latifolius), much more commonly naturalised, is very similar; it has larger flowers, (15)–20–30 mm long, usually elliptic leaflets, and broad stipules, (3)–5–15 mm wide, at least half as wide as the stem.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stipules, the leafy flaps where each leaf joins the stem: narrow-leaved everlasting pea's are lance-shaped to linear, about 1–3 mm wide and less than half as wide as the stem; broad-leaved sweet pea's are broader, (3)–5–15 mm wide, usually about as wide as the stem or wider and at least half as wide. Narrow-leaved everlasting pea's flowers are smaller, 13–17 mm long, (2)–5–8 to a stalk; broad-leaved sweet pea's are (15)–20–30 mm long, (4)–8–14 to a stalk. Narrow-leaved everlasting pea's leaflets are usually lance-shaped to linear, rarely narrowly elliptic, 50–130 mm long; broad-leaved sweet pea's are narrowly to broadly elliptic, 30–100 mm long (to 120 mm), but its shoots late in the flowering season may have narrow, almost linear leaves and as few as 2 flowers, so go by the stipules. Narrow-leaved everlasting pea's calyx teeth are all shorter than the calyx tube; broad-leaved sweet pea's lower teeth are as long as the tube or longer. Narrow-leaved everlasting pea's pods are 40–70 mm long, broad-leaved sweet pea's 60–110 mm. Both are scrambling perennials with broadly winged stems, one pair of leaflets and branched tendrils, and broad-leaved sweet pea also grows in South Canterbury and Otago, where narrow-leaved everlasting pea is established. Neither is eaten.

summary.text: Narrow-leaved everlasting pea, also called flat pea (Lathyrus sylvestris), is a scrambling perennial of the pea family, Fabaceae, native to Europe, north-west Africa, Asia Minor and the Caucasus, and first recorded in New Zealand in 1958. It is established only locally, in South Canterbury and North and Central Otago, and is rarely recorded. It is very similar to the much more commonly naturalised broad-leaved sweet pea (Lathyrus latifolius), from which it differs in its smaller flowers and narrower leaflets and stipules. It is also grown in gardens as an ornamental, and has been grown in a West Auckland garden.

warnings: Narrow-leaved everlasting pea is not given here as food. No record of it as food was found, and its seeds are recorded as toxic.
Its seeds contain a nerve-active amino acid, diaminobutyric acid, in very high concentration, and the same toxin is found in its leaves.

All parts of the plant, but especially the seed, contain a toxic amino acid, made at about the time the seed starts to develop. Eaten in quantity it can cause lathyrism, a very serious disease of the nervous system: paralysis of the muscles below the knees and back pain, followed by weakness and stiffness of the legs and growing loss of coordination.
It is poisonous to livestock: sheep fed hay cut when the plant was bearing seed developed a potentially fatal nervous illness, with seizures, muscle trembling and twisting of the neck.

habitat.text:
Lawns, paths, paddocks, roadsides and any compacted ground. Everywhere.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Generally open modified places, particularly poor pastures, also a pioneer of river beds, landslips, coastal sands and talus, and cliff faces, common on many small offshore islands and often in remote coastal areas where very few other naturalised species occur.
It copes with drought better than greater plantain.
On New Zealand's national wetland plant list it is rated facultative upland: it sometimes grows in wetlands but usually on dry ground.

identification.text:
A flat rosette of narrow, lance-shaped leaves with three to seven prominent parallel veins running their length; tear a leaf across and the veins pull out like strings. The flower is a short brown head on a tall leafless stalk, ringed with pale stamens. Greater plantain (Plantago major) has wider, oval leaves and a longer flower spike and is used the same way.
The flower stalk is 12–70 cm tall and strongly ribbed, and the dense head is up to about 6 cm long, with the brown fruits clustered near its tip. A tuft of silky white hairs, often purplish, sits at the base of each leaf stalk. New Zealand plants have either white or yellow anthers; both are common. It flowers from July to April. It has a persistent taproot. Each small capsule holds one or two seeds, 2–3 mm long and medium to dark brown.

lookalikes.howToTell: Buck's-horn plantain's leaves usually have one to four pairs of narrow lobes or teeth, like antlers, a single main vein, and are 1–5 mm wide (up to 10); narrow-leaved plantain's are entire or only slightly toothed, 5–48 mm wide, with 3–7 veins running their length. Buck's-horn's flower stalk is not ribbed and is 3–45 cm long; narrow-leaved plantain's is strongly ribbed and 12–70 cm long. Both are hairy rosettes that flower from July to April, so neither tells them apart.
lookalikes.name: Buck's-horn plantain

lookalikes.howToTell: Greater plantain's leaves are broad ovals, up to 16 cm wide, on a distinct stalk; narrow-leaved plantain's are long and narrow, 0.5–4.8 cm wide, tapering into a short, ill-defined stalk with a tuft of silky white hairs at the base. Greater plantain's flower stalk is not ribbed, and its fruits run far down a spike up to 30 cm long; narrow-leaved plantain's stalk is strongly ribbed, with a short, dense head, to about 6 cm, and the brown fruits clustered near the tip. Small greater plantains can have narrower leaves, so check the flower stalk too. Both have veins running the length of the leaf and both flower from July to April, so neither of those tells them apart.
lookalikes.name: Greater plantain

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp plantain's flower stalk is round, not ribbed, and densely hairy near the top, and its narrow spike is usually more than 10 cm long when mature; narrow-leaved plantain's stalk is strongly ribbed and its head is short and dense, to about 6 cm. Swamp plantain's petals curl up into a small, pointed, upright cone and its stamens are usually hidden; narrow-leaved plantain's stamens stick out around the head. Swamp plantain grows in swamps, bogs, lake and river edges and wet grassland, and flowers only from November to January. Leaf widths overlap — up to 8 cm in swamp plantain, 0.5–4.8 cm in narrow-leaved plantain — and both have parallel veins, so leaves alone do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Swamp plantain

preparation.text:
Young leaves shredded finely into salads, or cooked — older ones are stringy and best in soup or as a tea.
Pull the stringy ribs out of the leaves; the very youngest leaves are least fibrous. The unopened flower heads can be eaten raw, and taste of raw button mushrooms. Cook the seeds, or grind them into flour. The green seeds rub off the heads easily; if they don't come away, the heads are still in flower.

recipes.method: Serves 3. 6 handfuls young ribwort plantain leaves, torn; 3 aubergines, cut into 4 mm slices; 1 onion, sliced; 4 garlic cloves, sliced; 1 avocado, halved and sliced; 400 g Greek strained yoghurt; 400 g passata; rapeseed oil; grated cheddar; cracked black pepper. Boil the plantain leaves for 3 minutes, drain, squeeze out the water, chop them finely and set aside. Blanch the aubergine slices in salted water, drain and set aside. Fry the onion and garlic in a little oil until soft, stir in the plantain for 30 seconds, then add the passata and cook down to a thick sauce; season with black pepper. Lay half the aubergine in an ovenproof dish and cover it with the avocado slices. Pour on half the sauce and spread the yoghurt over it. Add the rest of the aubergine, then the rest of the sauce, and scatter cheese on top. Bake at 160 °C for about 30 minutes, until done. The author gives the oven only as '160 degree'; it is read here as °C.
recipes.title: Aubergine and avocado bake with ribwort plantain

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard (the page does not say which plantain). 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Use it as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: The author's greens were dock, onion weed, nasturtium, plantain, baby wild mustard, dandelion, sow thistle and a violet leaf (the page does not say which plantain). 2 crushed garlic cloves; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 500 ml (2 cups) firmly packed wild greens, sliced very thinly; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper; 125 ml (½ cup) roughly chopped pistachios, walnuts, almonds or brazil nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp hearts, pumpkin or sunflower seeds; and 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, hemp seed oil or a mix. Makes about 750 ml (3 cups). To slice the greens, sort them into similar shapes, bunch and twist a few leaves together and slice as thinly as you can — this suits the tougher, stringier ones such as plantain, mustard and dock. Toss everything together. Serve as a side or salad, in a wrap or sandwich, or with pasta, risotto, eggs, or sausages and mash. It keeps at least 4 days in a sealed jar in the fridge.
recipes.title: Weedolata (wild-greens gremolata)

recipes.method: Made with narrow-leaved plantain seeds; the author suggests greater plantain's longer heads if you find them. Makes about 28. 135 g pumpkin seeds, 20 g linseeds, 20 g (about 125 ml) green plantain seeds, 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt or seaweed salt, 100 g plain flour, 100 g wholemeal or spelt flour, 7 g nettle powder (optional), 50 ml vegetable oil, 200 ml just-boiled water. Rub the green seeds off the heads. Mix 135 g pumpkin seeds, 20 g linseeds, 20 g (about 125 ml) green plantain seeds, 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt or seaweed salt, 100 g plain flour and 100 g wholemeal or spelt flour, plus 7 g nettle powder if you like. Stir in 50 ml vegetable oil and 200 ml just-boiled water; it will look like stiff, soggy porridge. Heat the oven to 140 °C (120 °C fan). Roll the dough out between two sheets of baking paper to the thickness of one seed, cut it into rectangles about 5 × 2 cm, and lift them onto two baking trays. Bake for an hour or a little more, until light brown and crisp. Cool, and keep in an airtight container.
recipes.title: Plantain seed crackers

recipes.method: Written for plantain seed heads, greater or narrow-leaved; the author's own plant is narrow-leaved plantain. The brown seed heads of plantain, with or without their stalks; butter or olive oil; thyme; salt. Pick the brown seed heads, with or without their stalks. Heat enough butter or olive oil to coat a cast-iron pan over medium-high heat, add the heads and toss them for 2 minutes. Add thyme and a sprinkle of salt and cook 1–2 minutes more, stirring now and then, until the heads are toasted and the seeds just begin to fall off; add more fat if they look dry. Serve straight away; the stalks make handles, but are too tough to eat.
recipes.title: Plantain seed heads with butter and thyme

recipes.method: Written for plantain seeds, greater or narrow-leaved. 1 handful of plantain seeds; 3 handfuls of pumpkin seeds; 3 handfuls of sesame seeds; a generous splash of tamari or soy sauce. Mix 1 handful of plantain seeds with 3 handfuls of pumpkin seeds and 3 of sesame seeds. Toast them lightly in a non-stick frying pan, then add a generous splash of tamari or soy sauce, toss to coat, and let any excess cook off. Tip into bowls and eat as a snack.
recipes.title: Spiced plantain seed mix

recipes.method: Written for plantain, herb Robert, nasturtium seeds, oxtongue or rosemary, singly or together (the page does not say which plantain). Chop the plant material and pack it loosely in a jar. Fill the jar with apple cider vinegar to cover the plants completely, let it sit a little, and poke out any air bubbles under the leaves with a chopstick. Cap it, with a piece of plastic under a metal lid so the vinegar doesn't eat the metal, label it and leave it in a cool place for 2–6 weeks, then strain the vinegar into a bottle. Use it in salad dressings, soups and pestos, or sweetened with honey by the spoonful.
recipes.title: Herbal vinegar

recipes.method: The author's weeds were chickweed, nasturtium, dandelion, pūhā, ox-eye daisy and plantain, with parsley and garden herbs (the page does not say which plantain). She also adds a handful of New Zealand spinach; it is At Risk and its page says to blanch it first, so it is left out here. 5 rosemary sprigs about 12 cm long; a handful of parsley; a big handful of chickweed; 4 large nasturtium leaves; a handful of thyme sprigs 5 cm long; a few dandelion leaves; a small pūhā plant; 10 ox-eye daisy leaves; 8 plantain leaves; 5 sage leaves; 6 garlic cloves; 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt; about 30 ml (⅛ cup) cider vinegar; 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) olive oil, starting with the smaller amount; 5 ml (1 tsp) honey, or to taste; the juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml (½ cup) walnuts. Strip the leaves from the thyme and rosemary and wash any leaves that need it. Blend everything in a high-speed blender or food processor until smooth, pushing it down with the tamper. Keep it in the fridge or freezer.
recipes.title: Wild weed pesto

recipes.method: Written for plantain and dandelion, with celery leaves and parsley (the page does not say which plantain). A small handful of celery leaves; 4 branches of parsley (go easy: it can take over); 4 leaves each of plantain, dandelion and kale. Blend the greens in 750 ml–1 litre (3–4 cups) water, then add 1 banana, 250 ml (1 cup) frozen blueberries, 1 kiwifruit and ½ avocado and blend again.
recipes.title: Thick and creamy green smoothie

IV (Webb et al. 1988, via Flora of New Zealand Online): Plantago coronopus 'Lamina (10)–30–120–(200) × 1–5–(10) mm', '1–(2)-pinnatisect, rarely entire, with 1–4 pairs of linear, acute to subulate lobes or teeth', 'main vein usually 1', 'Scapes 3–45 cm long, not ribbed'; Plantago lanceolata 'Lamina 2–20 × 0.5–4.8 cm', '3–7-veined', 'entire or slightly toothed', 'Scape 12–70 cm long', 'strongly ribbed'. Leaf widths meet at 5–10 mm, so width is given with its range, not as a test on its own. Flowering 'Jul.–Apr.' for both (Flora Online), hairs and rosettes in both — ruled out. Ranges overlap: buck's-horn on coasts, lake margins and waste places (NZPCN), narrow-leaved plantain on lawns, roadsides and disturbed ground throughout. No card to greater plantain (P. major): its broad oval leaves give no plausible confusion and no source names one. Both cards risk 'edible'.

Vein count corrected 26/10/2026 (owner: 'find the truth'), 'three to five' → 'three to seven': Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988, via Flora of New Zealand Online https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Plantago-lanceolata.html) describes New Zealand plants as '3–7-veined'; Minnesota Wildflowers (https://www.minnesotawildflowers.info/flower/english-plantain) agrees, '3, 5 or 7 prominent veins'. The commoner '3–5' (Wikipedia 'Plantago lanceolata' after Blamey's Wild Flowers of Britain and Ireland; Illinois Wildflowers) and NSW Flora's '5-veined' all fall inside the Flora of New Zealand range, so they undercount rather than contradict it.

summary.text:
Ribwort. The lawn weed with the stringy, parallel-veined leaves — a tough but reliable green, and a traditional folk remedy, crushed fresh, for insect bites and stings.
It is also called English plantain, lamb's tongue, rib-grass and ripple grass. It came from Eurasia and was first recorded growing wild in New Zealand in 1855, and is now common to abundant throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands, and grows on the Kermadec, Chatham and Campbell Islands. Farmers sow improved cultivars, such as Agritonic, in pasture mixes: stock eat it, it carries more copper and zinc than ryegrass or clover, and it helps reduce nitrate leaching from grazing animals. It is pollinated mostly by the wind, and only now and then by bees. 100 g of fresh leaves give about 22 kcal, with 2.1 g of protein and 3.7 g of fibre.

warnings: Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed. Pick from ground you know.
Plants beside busy roads can hold high levels of lead and cadmium. Pick away from traffic.

identification.text:
Unmistakable round shield-shaped leaves with the stem joining at the centre, and bright orange, yellow or red spurred trumpet flowers. Sprawling, often smothering.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Glabrous aromatic annual or short-lived perennial with long trailing or scrambling, succulent stems, sometimes climbing to 2 m high. Leaves simple, peltate. Petioles to about 30 cm long, usually not coiling. Lamina to about 18–(21) cm diameter, suborbicular, often slightly asymmetric, entire but often sinuate, glaucescent beneath. Flowers usually solitary, sometimes in clusters of 2–3 […]; spur 2.5–3.3 cm long, more or less curved, tapering, usually pale orange. Corolla moderately irregular, (2)–3–4 × (1.7)–2.2–3.3 cm, usually yellow or orange to scarlet, sometimes semi-double with 7–8 petals […]. Fruits dry […], remaining green until abscission.
No species is easily confused with it in New Zealand (NZPCN).

preparation.text: Leaves and flowers raw in salads. Green seed pods brined and pickled as 'poor man's capers'. If the flowers taste too strong, use only the petals: the centre carries most of the flavour. Turn the leaves over to check for aphids and caterpillar eggs, and shake the flowers to dislodge insects. Leaves and flowers keep their pepperiness when dried, and keep about a year in a jar. Pick from plants you know have not been sprayed. Flower buds can be pickled like the green seeds. For winter shoots, sow saved seed thickly in a tray indoors or on heat and cut the shoots at 6–8 cm for salads and stir-fries.

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) nasturtium seed pods, picked young and light green; 60 ml (¼ cup) salt; 500 ml (2 cups) water; 250 ml (1 cup) apple cider vinegar; 15–30 ml (1–2 tbsp) sugar; 1 bay leaf. Split the pods into single seeds and rinse off any dirt. Dissolve the salt in the water in a jar and add the seeds; the brine tames their strong mustardy bite. Keep them under the brine — a plastic bag pushed down into the jar works — and leave at room temperature for a couple of days. Lift them out, soak them in cold water for an hour, and drain. Warm the vinegar and sugar in a small pan until the sugar dissolves and the vinegar just simmers. Pack the seeds into hot sterilised jars, pour the hot vinegar over, add the bay leaf and seal. Use them wherever you would use capers. The author keeps them in the fridge and says they last indefinitely there.
recipes.title: Pickled nasturtium seed pods

recipes.method: 3 cups (about 750 ml) nasturtium leaves, well rinsed; a bowl of iced water; 60 ml (¼ cup) olive oil; 1 medium shallot, finely diced; the juice of 1 lemon. Bring a pot of water to the boil, drop in the leaves, turn off the heat and let them wilt for about 30 seconds. Scoop them straight into the iced water, leave them 2 minutes, then spread them on a clean tea towel to dry. Blend the leaves with the olive oil in a food processor until smooth and bright green. Strain through a colander lined with paper towel, letting the oil drip through. Stir in the shallot and a squeeze of lemon juice just before serving. Keep it in a clean jar in the fridge and use within 3 days. The author drizzles it over fish or prawns, swirls it through pumpkin or potato soup, or stirs it into mayonnaise or yoghurt.
recipes.title: Nasturtium leaf oil

recipes.method: Written for nasturtium and nipplewort together. 6 large field mushrooms; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil plus another 60 ml for frying; the leaves of 1 rosemary stalk, chopped; salt and pepper; 600 g nasturtium and nipplewort leaves, roughly chopped; 250 ml water; 1 onion (the method uses one, though the ingredient list leaves it out); 4 crushed garlic cloves; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 250 ml (1 cup) roughly chopped walnuts; 240 g cream cheese, plant-based or dairy; 1 slice of bread, broken into small pieces. Serves 4. Toss the mushrooms with the first 60 ml of oil, the rosemary, 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper and leave them to marinate. Cook the greens in a lidded pot with the water and 5 ml (1 tsp) salt on high heat for 5 minutes, turning them, until wilted; cool them under cold running water, squeeze out the water and chop again. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Fry the mushrooms in the second 60 ml of oil, open side down, for 4 minutes, then 4 minutes on the other side, until golden, and set them open side up in a baking dish. In the same pan soften the onion for 5 minutes, add the garlic, greens, lemon zest and juice and cook a minute, then stir in the walnuts, cream cheese, bread, 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper off the heat. Pack the filling into the mushrooms, drizzle with olive oil and bake for 20 minutes until golden. Good on soft polenta or mashed kūmara and potato.
recipes.title: Nasturtium and nipplewort stuffed mushrooms

recipes.method: 400 g dried pasta and 5 ml (1 tsp) salt for the water. Sauce: 1 litre (4 cups) nasturtium flowers, 375 ml (1½ cups) ricotta or soaked cashews, 30 ml (2 tbsp) parmesan or nutritional yeast, 2 garlic cloves, 1 chilli (optional), 1 tomato, 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, the zest and juice of 2 lemons, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) salt, 5 ml (1 tsp) black pepper and 80 ml (⅓ cup) water from the pasta pot. To finish: 1 bunch asparagus, ends snapped off; 4 roughly chopped tomatoes; 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil; salt and pepper; 80 ml (⅓ cup) grated parmesan or hemp parmesan; 80 ml (⅓ cup) finely chopped parsley; a few more nasturtium flowers and leaves. Serves 4. Boil the pasta in the salted water for about 8 minutes, until just cooked, adding the asparagus for the last 2 minutes. Meanwhile blend the sauce ingredients until smooth. Drain the pasta, take out the asparagus and cool it briefly under cold water, then return the hot pasta to the pot and stir in the sauce. Season the tomatoes with salt, pepper and the second measure of oil. Top the pasta with the asparagus, tomatoes, parsley, parmesan and a few more nasturtium flowers and leaves.
recipes.title: Nasturtium flower pasta

recipes.method: 4 medium oranges; 1 litre (4 cups) sugar, plus 2 Tbsp; 2 Tbsp pectin; 25 nasturtium flowers. Peel 2 of the oranges and cut them into small cubes. Finely cut the other 2 with their peel on, and put all the orange in a pan. Gently wash the flowers and tear the petals into the pan. Mix the pectin with the 2 Tbsp of sugar and add it. Cook over medium heat, stirring now and then, until it boils. Add the rest of the sugar and boil for 10 minutes. Skim off the foam and pour into jars. The author does not say to sterilise or seal the jars, or how long the jam keeps.
recipes.title: Nasturtium petal and orange jam

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) nasturtium flowers, closely packed; 1 garlic clove; 1 chilli; 500 ml apple cider vinegar. Wash the flowers and put them in a sterilised jar. Peel and slice the garlic and add it, then the chilli, slit in half. Fill the jar with the vinegar, put on the lid and shake well. Keep it in a cool, dark place for a week, then strain through a sieve lined with kitchen paper into small sterilised bottles. Use it as you would chilli sauce or Tabasco.
recipes.title: Nasturtium flower hot sauce

recipes.method: 12 nasturtium flowers; 125 ml (½ cup) cream cheese; 1 Tbsp finely chopped herbs, two kinds, such as dill and chives; salt and pepper. Dip the flowers in cool water and leave them a moment to clear out dirt and insects, then shake them gently. If you are not filling them straight away, keep them between paper towels in a container in the fridge. Mix the herbs into the cream cheese and season. Take the stamens out of the middle of each flower, especially for anyone with allergies or hay fever. Spoon about a teaspoon of the mixture into each flower and serve. The author says to know where your flowers came from, so you can be sure they have not been sprayed with pesticide.
recipes.title: Cream cheese stuffed nasturtium flowers

recipes.method: Serves 1, with rim salt for 6–8 glasses. 60 ml tequila; 15 ml orange liqueur; petals from 3–4 nasturtium flowers; ice; 60 ml orange juice; 15 ml lime juice; 15 ml agave nectar; 60 ml (¼ US cup) flaky sea salt; 1 Tbsp granulated sugar; petals from 6–8 more nasturtium flowers. For the rim, pulse the salt, sugar and the petals from the 6–8 flowers in a small food processor until the petals are finely chopped, and spread it on a small plate. Wet the rim of the glass with a little lime or orange juice, press it into the salt-sugar, and add ice. Muddle the tequila, orange liqueur and the petals from the 3–4 flowers in a cocktail shaker. Add ice, the orange juice, lime juice and agave, and shake hard. Strain into the glass, garnish with a nasturtium flower if you like, and serve straight away.
recipes.title: Nasturtium margarita

recipes.method: Nasturtium leaves, flowers or both, as many as you like; any salt, sea, rock or table, the same weight as the dried nasturtium powder; a clean, dry jar with a lid. Turn the leaves over to check for caterpillar eggs and aphids, and shake the flowers to dislodge insects. Dry them in a dehydrator following its instructions, or in an oven on a low setting with the door open. Grind them to a powder in a blender, food processor or mortar. It need not be fine. Mix in an equal weight of salt, crushing lumpy salt finer first. Store it in a labelled jar in a cool, dark place. It keeps about a year. Good in marinades, sauces and salad dressings, and on chips. Made with leaves only it is green, and flowers add yellow and red flecks.
recipes.title: Spicy nasturtium salt

recipes.method: Nasturtium flowers, enough to fill a jar loosely; cider vinegar, or another light vinegar such as white wine or white balsamic, to fill the jar; a light weight to hold the flowers under, such as folded greaseproof paper. Shake each flower to dislodge aphids and fill the jar loosely. Fill the jar with vinegar, weigh the flowers down and put on the lid. Glass or stone preserving weights are too heavy for these flowers. Leave it in a cool, dark place for 2–4 weeks: the longer it infuses, the stronger it tastes. Strain through a muslin-lined sieve into a clean, labelled jar. The vinegar turns rose pink. Use it in salad dressings, sauces and dips.

summary.text:
Garden escapee with peppery leaves, edible flowers, and seed pods that pickle into passable capers.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: warmer lowland parts, especially in coastal areas; South Island: mainly northern coastal areas but occurring south to Southland; Stewart Island: Halfmoon Bay; Kermadec Islands: Raoul Island, occasional. Native to the northern Andes, it was first recorded naturalised here in 1883. The species is very commonly cultivated and there are many cultivars differing in flower colour, extent of petal doubling and habit; many such forms have not yet been found wild.

warnings: Strongly peppery, and it can irritate the lining of the stomach and gut; it is not advised for infants or small children, or for people with stomach ulcers or kidney disease.

identification.text:
Perennial rosette herb. Leaves all basal, linear to oblong or linear- oblanceolate, simple, usually dentate, sometimes runcinate-pinnatifid, glabrous or with sparse multicellular hairs, especially above, (3)–5–15–(30) × (0.7)–1–1.5–(4.5) cm; terminal lobe narrowly deltoid to oblong, obtuse, truncate at base; lateral lobes triangular, deflexed or recurved, entire or toothed on distal margin; petiole and proximal part of midrib hollow. Scape stout, hollow, usually sparsely cobwebby above, sometimes glabrous, (2)–5–20–(30) cm tall. Capitula 1.5–3–(4) cm diameter. Involucral bracts glabrous; outer bracts lanceolate to ovate, more or less attenuate, green or reddish, erect at flowering, suberect to patent at fruiting, with scarious margins; inner bracts narrowly triangular to linear, acute, green, erect, with scarious margins. Florets usually golden yellow, rarely paler. Achene body usually orange-brown to dull greenish brown, rarely cream, ribbed, clavate-fusiform, 2.5–4 mm long; ribs each with (3)–5–7 teeth on distal ⅓-⅔, the distal teeth slightly longer than the proximal; cone tapering or narrowly cylindric, (0.5)–1–2 mm long, concolorous with the body. Beak usually pale, sometimes dark, slender, 4.5–8 mm long. Pappus white, 4–7 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Check the bracts under the flower head. The native dandelion's outer bracts are erect at flowering and usually have pale papery margins; the introduced dandelion's are strongly bent back at flowering and fruiting and have no papery margins. The seed differs too: (3)–5–7 teeth on each rib over the top third to two-thirds of the native dandelion's achene, against 3–(5) teeth on the top third in the introduced dandelion. Both have a hollow, leafless flower stem with a single head, hollow leaf stalks, and hairless or sparsely hairy leaves, so none of those separates them; nor does leaf shape, since some native dandelions have deeply lobed leaves. The introduced dandelion's heads are usually the larger, 3–5 cm across against 1.5–3 cm (sometimes 4 cm). The introduced dandelion's leaves, flowers and roots are eaten (see its page).

summary.text:
Biota of New Zealand and the New Zealand Plant Conservation Network name it Taraxacum zealandicum and treat it as endemic; Flora of New Zealand calls it Taraxacum magellanicum, a species also native to South America. Biota of New Zealand notes that 'The taxonomic status of T. zealandicum needs to be thoroughly investigated' (Heenan 2004).
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Tongariro National Park, Kaweka Range, Kaimanawa Range, Ruahine Range, Tararua Range; S.: throughout; St.: N.W. coast; Ch., Ant., A., C.
It is now scarce over much of its former range. Its 2023 national assessment is At Risk – Declining; it was assessed Not Threatened from 2004 to 2017 (NZPCN, restated).
Flora of New Zealand describes three forms: over most of its range, plants of damp montane to alpine grassland and herbfield whose leaves are not often deeply lobed; in lowland South Canterbury and the Chatham Islands, plants with deeply lobed leaves, in lowland grassland, river terraces, forest remnants and damp coastal sites; and on Stewart Island, plants of coastal sand dunes with usually simple, toothed leaves (sometimes deeply lobed), very pale seeds and pale yellow florets (restated).

habitat.text:
In New Zealand it is abundant on coastal banks, rocks and cliffs.
It grows mostly on cliff faces, rock stacks and boulder or cobble beaches, and only rarely inland. On the Kermadec Islands it grows on rock stacks, cliff faces, banks, and cobble and boulder beaches, and near bird nesting grounds.
Planted, it needs full sun and free-draining soil, is not fussy about fertility or moisture and tolerates long dry spells, though young plants can be frost-sensitive.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. On the Kermadec Islands the plants are subspecies stricticaule, which is at risk: if you harvest it there, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text:
Trailing herb. Stem terete, glabrous. Leaves 3-angled, acute, often mucronate, tapering to connate base, (6)–20–30–(40) × 4–6–(9) mm; margins usually smooth, rarely papillate. Flowers 2–4 cm diameter. Petals uniformly white to deep pink, in 3–5 rows, 1–3 cm long. Stamens 4–6 mm long; inner filaments hairy at base. Stigmas (5)–6–8–(10). Capsule valves with parallel or more or less divergent expanding keels; placental tubercle rounded or 0. Seeds brown, obovoid, rugose, about 1 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Chilean sea fig is larger in every part. Its flowers are 6.5–8 cm across, with purple petals paler near the base, against 2–4 cm and uniformly white to deep pink here. Its leaves are 35–90 × 5–12 mm, against mostly 20–30 mm long (6–40 mm) and 4–6 mm wide (up to 9 mm) here. Its stems are 2-angled and woody at the base, not round in section, and its fruit stays closed, where this plant's fruit is a capsule whose cells have lids. Plants with purplish flowers 4–5.2 cm across may be hybrids between the two.
lookalikes.name: Chilean sea fig

lookalikes.howToTell: Jellybean ice plant's leaves are club-shaped, round or only weakly 3-angled in section, and blunt with a small point at the tip, where this plant's are 3-angled and sharp-pointed. Its petals are purple with a white base and sit in 2 rows, against 3–5 rows of petals uniformly white to deep pink here. In New Zealand it is known only from a few South Island saltmarshes and estuaries, often in places flooded at high tide; this plant grows mostly on cliffs, rock stacks and boulder or cobble beaches, and more rarely in saltmarsh.
lookalikes.name: Jellybean ice plant

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stem: native ice plant's is round and smooth; Chatham Island ice plant's is flattened, 2-angled and rough with tiny pimples (papillae). Native ice plant's leaf edges are usually smooth but rarely pimply, where Chatham Island ice plant's are pimply, so go by the stem; on the Kermadec Islands native ice plant (subspecies stricticaule) has pimply leaf edges but still a round, smooth stem. Native ice plant's leaves are mostly longer, 20–30 mm (6–40 mm) against mostly 10–15 mm (4–30 mm), but the ranges overlap. Native ice plant's seeds are brown and wrinkled; Chatham Island ice plant's are yellowish brown to brown and distinctly pimply; both are about 1 mm long. Both are trailing succulents with 3-angled, pointed leaves and flowers 2–4 cm across with 3–5 rows of petals, white to deep pink here and white to purple on Chatham Island ice plant, so flower colour does not separate them. Both grow on the coasts of the Chatham Islands, and Chatham Island ice plant grows nowhere else, so any ice plant picked there needs the stem check. Chatham Island ice plant was once counted as part of native ice plant. No record of Chatham Island ice plant as food was found (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Chatham Island ice plant

summary.text:
Disphyma australe, horokaka or New Zealand ice plant, is a trailing succulent herb in the ice plant family Aizoaceae, endemic to New Zealand.
Subspecies australe grows on coasts throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands and on the Three Kings and Chatham Islands. Subspecies stricticaule grows only on the Kermadec Islands, where it is widespread and common. In the 2023 national assessment subspecies australe is Not Threatened, and subspecies stricticaule is At Risk – Naturally Uncommon, as an island endemic.
It forms natural hybrids with both naturalised ice plants, South African ice plant and Chilean sea fig. The hybrid with South African ice plant, ×Carpophyma mutabilis, has mostly sterile pollen and forms no fruit. The Chatham Island ice plant, Disphyma papillatum, was once counted as part of this species.
Its fleshy capsules are spread by animals that eat them, and possibly by wind and water. It is grown in gardens as a fast-growing groundcover over rocks and the edges of retaining walls, and in coastal plantings to help hold sand. It is easily raised from rooted pieces and fresh seed.

habitat.text:
On rocks or stones between the tides, on both sheltered and exposed shores — most often on rock platforms and in rock pools, where it gets plenty of light and enough seawater not to dry out.
In New Zealand it is common at mid-tide level, often in dense mats.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Keep off the mats as much as you can: trampling damages them, and heavy trampling can almost wipe them out.
Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.

identification.text: Branched chains of hollow beads joined to one another by thin constrictions, attached to the rock by a small disc. Plants are up to 30 cm long, sometimes 50 cm. Yellow-green to grey-brown. Bead size varies with the habitat and how exposed the shore is. The fertile structures are scattered over the beads and show clearly as small bumps.

preparation.text:
Eat the beads raw while fresh, or slice the tender tips into salads or over cream cheese on crackers. Heated, the beads turn bright green, which makes them a garnish. They also pickle well in a sweet vinegar brine; rinse them well in fresh water first to remove sand and small animals.
It spoils quickly once picked, so eat or process it the same day; kept in seawater in the fridge it lasts a little longer.

recipes.method: Makes four 250 ml jars (or two 500 ml jars). 1 kg Neptune's necklace; 500 ml (2 cups) white wine vinegar; 250 ml (1 cup) fine caster sugar; 500 ml (2 cups) water; 1 slice fresh ginger; 5 ml (1 tsp) coriander seeds; 5 ml (1 tsp) wild peppercorn berries; 5 ml (1 tsp) mustard seeds. Sterilise the jars: wash them well in soapy water, put them in a cold oven and heat it to 110 °C, then leave them for 10 minutes once it gets there, or until completely dry. Rinse the Neptune's necklace thoroughly in fresh water to remove any sand or tiny stowaways. Put the ginger and spices in the jars, then pack in the seaweed. Warm the vinegar, sugar and water in a saucepan over low heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then bring to the boil and take off the heat. Fill the jars with the hot liquid so it covers the seaweed completely and sits 1–2 cm below the rim; let them stand a few minutes and top up if needed. The seaweed turns brighter green. To make sure the jars are well sealed, turn them upside down for a few minutes while still warm. Sealed jars keep up to a year in a cool, dry place away from sunlight; once opened, up to 4 weeks in the fridge. Use as any other pickle — with cheese, roast vegetables, or a roast sesame dressing.

summary.text:
Neptune's necklace (Hormosira banksii), also called bubbleweed, is a native brown seaweed made of branched chains of hollow, olive-brown beads, common on rocky shores between the tides.
In New Zealand it grows around the North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands. It is also native to Australia, including Lord Howe and Norfolk Islands.
It forms a canopy over the rock that shelters many small shore animals; where the canopy is removed, almost all the species living with it are lost.
It is assessed as Not Threatened in New Zealand, with low confidence because the data are poor.
The name sea grapes is also used for it, and for Caulerpa (sea grapes in this catalogue).

warnings: Neptune's necklace is a brown seaweed, and brown seaweed can contain very high levels of iodine. High levels of iodine can cause thyroid problems, so eating it more than every once in a while may be unsafe, especially when pregnant or breastfeeding.
Harvest only from clean water — never near stormwater drains, in harbours, or where there is heavy boat traffic, and not straight after a storm, when stormwater carries city debris into the sea.
Neptune's necklace takes up metals from the seawater around it.
Cut from higher up the plant — never pull it off the rock by its base.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Lowland to montane grassland, open places, especially bogs, wet flushes, lake and streamsides.
It prefers damp, boggy ground that can be flooded for months at a time.
On the national wetland plant list it is a facultative wetland plant: usually found in wetlands, occasionally on drier ground.

identification.text:
Glabrous, much-branched, divaricately spreading herb with stout tap-root; branches and branchlets together up to about 50 cm long, rather slender. Lower leaves with slender petioles from longer than to much shorter than lamina. Lamina (1)–3–15–(17) × (0.2)–0.4–2.5–(3) cm, linear to narrow-oblong or elliptic, usually brown, rarely green; margins more or less undulate and often crisped or even crenulate; base cuneate to truncate or cordate, sometimes widened; apex obtuse or subacute. Upper leaves smaller, linear to ovate-oblong, gradually decreasing to 2 cm long or less. Inflorescence of numerous, rather distant whorls of 6–12, bisexual, protandrous flowers; leaves subtending whorls gradually reduced towards inflorescence apex; pedicels rather slender, glabrous, often short. Perianth segments 1.5–3 mm long; outer segments lanceolate or narrow-ovate, apiculate, more or less spreading at fruiting; inner segments ovate to almost rhombic, acuminate. Fruit valves strongly reticulate, with (1)–2–3–(4) straight teeth on each margin; tubercles usually 0, sometimes 1, narrow and towards base. Nut (1.5)–1.8–2.3 mm long, pale brown, lustrous, sharply angled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Its leaves are bronze-green; the young rosette leaves reach about 15 cm, and the leaves up the zig-zag flowering stems shrink to under 5 cm as the stems spread to about half a metre. Hooked dock looks similar, but New Zealand dock never has hooked fruit.
It flowers from November to April. The tiny flowers are greenish-yellow to brown, with cream anthers.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hooked dock's fruit valves carry about five red hooked spines, 2 mm long, on each side, which catch on clothing; New Zealand dock never has hooked fruit — its valves have 1–4 straight teeth on each edge (an older Flora described them as minutely hooked). Hooked dock's leaves are up to 5 cm wide, usually with two rounded lobes at the base; New Zealand dock's are usually brown, narrow (up to 3 cm wide) and often wavy or curled. Hooked dock grows on dry cliff tops, roadsides and stony ground, mostly in the north and in Marlborough and Nelson; New Zealand dock in bogs, wet flushes and by lakes and streams.
lookalikes.name: Hooked dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Curled dock stands upright, with stems to about 1 m and erect branches whose flower whorls are mostly packed together; New Zealand dock is low and spreads sideways, its slender zig-zag branches together about 50 cm long, with many small whorls (6–12 flowers each) spaced well apart. Curled dock's lower leaves are larger, 6–30 × 1.5–6.5 cm, and taper into the stalk; New Zealand dock's are 3–15 × 0.4–2.5 cm, usually brown and only rarely green. Both have wavy, curled leaf edges, so the edges don't separate them. In fruit, curled dock's valves are 3–4.5 mm with smooth or finely scalloped edges and 1–3 deep red swellings (tubercles); New Zealand dock's have 1–4 straight teeth on each edge and usually no tubercle. Curled dock's nut is dark brown; New Zealand dock's pale brown.
lookalikes.name: Curled dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Broad-leaved dock's lower leaves are big ovals up to 35 × 15 cm (rarely 50 × 20) with a heart-shaped to rounded base, on erect stems 30–100 cm tall with flower whorls usually packed together; New Zealand dock's are narrow, 3–15 × 0.4–2.5 cm, usually brown and only rarely green, on low, sideways-spreading zig-zag branches with small whorls spaced well apart. Both have teeth on the fruit valves, but broad-leaved dock's valves (3.5–5 mm) carry one prominent rosy swelling (tubercle) 2–2.5 mm long; New Zealand dock's usually have none.
lookalikes.name: Broad-leaved dock

summary.text: New Zealand dock is endemic and very closely related to the Australian Rumex dumosus. Its species name, flexuosus, means winding; older names for it are Rumex brownianus and Rumex cunninghamii. It has been confused with the naturalised hooked dock, and old records based on that confusion (including one from the Kermadecs) gave it a misleading range. Old museum records place it on Kawau Island, in Northland and near Auckland, but there are no recent ones, and it is now regionally extinct in Auckland; an engineer's record of it in the Waitākere Ranges was never confirmed by a museum specimen or any other record. Because it is mistaken for the introduced docks, it is both crowded out by them and pulled out as a weed. Its national status is Not Threatened (2023). Māori names: runa (explained in 1899 as 'water or juice from the dock plant'), rungarunga. It grows from the mountains of the central North Island southwards, down to sea level in parts of the South Island and on Stewart Island, and on Campbell Island; it is mostly uncommon in the north.

warnings: Like other docks, it can be harmful if too much is eaten at one time. Eat only a little.

identification.text:
Cap 5.5–13 cm across, convex when young and flattening or sinking in the centre with age, dry and finely powdered to velvety under a lens; dark brown to almost black, sometimes with salmon patches, and without concentric zones. Gills light orange to salmon with dark brown edges, thick, moderately crowded, up to 9 mm deep, attached to slightly running down the stem. Stem 4.5–8 cm long and 1.3–2.8 cm thick, more or less even, coloured like the cap. The milk is viscid, white, unchanging in the air, and dries pale cream. The flesh is granular and white at first, then runs through pink, salmon and orange-red to wine red where it is cut or broken. Gills taste mild and the flesh turns slowly faintly acrid; no distinctive smell. Spore print ochraceous. Solitary or in groups under beech.

Lactarius novae-zelandiae McNabb, described from New Zealand, is a similar large and dark brown to brownish black species from this subgenus. The species differs by the lamellae that are moderately crowded and have dark brown edges, a character that was not observed in L. megaplinthogalus. The latex in this New Zealand species is unchanging and not staining the lamellae pinkish to blackish. The context does change to pink, salmon, and orange-red to finally vinaceous on exposure to air. The pseudocystidia are sparse and scattered. The spores are larger (9–12 × 8.2–10.5 µm).

The macroscopic appearance of this taxon is striking, and the fact that there was a 44-year gap between the initial records (1968–1971) and subsequent records (2015–2018) suggests it is uncommon.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. This one's milk is white, does not change, and dries pale cream. Its flesh does change, slowly, from white through pink, salmon and orange-red to wine red where cut - so judge the milk, not the cut flesh. Its cap is dark brown to almost black and unzoned, often with dull salmon patches near the centre, where saffron milk cap's is pale orange to salmon. It grows under beech; saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine.

The endemic it is most easily confused with, and that confusion has no page here. McNabb's own note separates this species from Lactarius sepiaceus, another New Zealand endemic under beech: both are dark greyish brown to brownish black, dry and finely bloomed, azonate and wrinkled, with white unchanging latex and dark brown gill edges. The differences are that L. sepiaceus has pale creamy-white to cream gills rather than light orange to salmon ones, flesh that stays white apart from very faint salmon tints rather than running through pink and orange-red to wine red, a white spore print rather than an ochraceous one, and prominently apiculate reticulate spores. L. sepiaceus has no iNaturalist NZ records and so no entry in this catalogue. summary.text:
This striking milkcap is endemic of New Zealand, where it is apparently ectomycorrhizal with Fuscospora truncata, growing in relatively mature forests.

There has been extensive surveying of the Russulaceae by Ross McNabb in the 1960/70s and by Jerry Cooper and Pat Leonard from 2005 onwards, and there are three known and extant sub-populations of this species. The single original locality from which the species was described (Karamea) has been lost due to the conversion of forest habitat to pasture.

Since 2017, two additional locations in Nelson and Buller have been identified and confirmed from sequence data. These locations significantly change the value of the area of occupancy (AOO of known sites), making the 2017 IUCN assessment of Endangered no longer appropriate. The distribution of records suggests some degree of regional restriction, but as an associate of beech, the potential distribution of this species remains considerable, and there is no reason to suspect population decline. For that reason, the panel re-assessed this species as Naturally Uncommon.

habitat.text:
Wet coastal cliffs and talus, rarely on sand or salt meadow.
On the coast, usually on cliff faces in or around damp seepages, often with the blue-green alga Nostoc and the fern Blechnum blechnoides, and mostly on base-rich rock such as basalt, calcareous mudstone, siltstone, limestone or apatite-rich greywacke. On some offshore islands it extends up into coastal scrub and coastal herbfield, and it occasionally grows on stabilised sand dunes.

harvestEthics.text: This species is at risk. If you harvest it, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In Northland (Regionally Critical), the Auckland region (Regionally Endangered), Otago (Regionally Endangered) and the Wellington region (Regionally Vulnerable), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it.

identification.text:
Biennial to perennial. Roots tap and fibrous; taproot swollen above. Stem erect, simple or branching above, finely grooved or ribbed, glabrous, (5)–15–60–(100) cm tall. Leaves thick, glaucous, dull, glabrous, lanceolate to narrowly oblong to linear-oblanceolate, (3)–8–20–(55) × (1)–3–6–(15) cm; margins dentate. Rosette and lower stem leaves tapering to base, pinnatifid to less than 1/2 way to midrib; lobes broadly triangular, spreading or slightly deflexed. Upper leaves not lobed, narrowly triangular to linear or narrowly oblanceolate, with more or less rounded amplexicaul auricles at base. Inflorescence cymose to umbellate; capitula few to many. Involucre 10–15 mm long, turbinate to cylindric; bracts imbricate, recurved at fruiting, glabrous or sometimes the outer with a row of median broad-based trichomes, occasionally densely white-tomentose at base. Receptacle glabrous. Florets 1½× length of involucre; corolla tube slightly longer than ligule; ligules spreading, yellow. Achenes elliptic, brown, strongly flattened, (3)–3.5–4 × 1.3–1.8 mm, 3-ribbed on each face, winged; spaces between ribs smooth; wings and ribs smooth. Pappus fine, white, about equal to involucre.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In the field: very large, thick, dull blue-grey leaves that are not spiny set it apart from the introduced sow thistles. All parts bleed white latex when broken, and the stem is hollow. The rosette spreads 30–40 cm, with broader, more lettuce-like leaves than the introduced sow thistles, and the flowering stem stands up to about 1 m.

lookalikes.howToTell: New Zealand sow thistle's leaves are thick, dull and blue-grey, with toothed margins that are not spiny; common pūhā's (Sonchus oleraceus) are soft, edged with small spine-tipped teeth, and range from mid or dark green to blue-grey, so leaf colour alone does not separate them. New Zealand sow thistle's upper leaves are not lobed and clasp the stem with more or less rounded lobes; common pūhā's upper leaves are usually lobed and clasp the stem with pointed lobes. New Zealand sow thistle lives two years or more from a taproot swollen at the top; common pūhā is an annual. In seed, New Zealand sow thistle's achenes are winged and smooth between the ribs; common pūhā's are not winged and are finely wrinkled crosswise. Common pūhā is edible: its leaves are widely eaten as greens.
lookalikes.name: Pūhā / Sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: New Zealand sow thistle's leaves are thick, dull and blue-grey, with toothed margins that are not spiny; prickly sow thistle's (Sonchus asper) are firm, more or less shiny and usually green (rarely blue-grey), with prickly-spined teeth. Both have upper leaves that clasp the stem with rounded lobes, and both have winged achenes, smooth between the ribs, so neither the leaf base nor the seed separates them. New Zealand sow thistle's taproot is swollen at the top; prickly sow thistle's taproot is not described as swollen. Prickly sow thistle is edible: it is recorded as a popular Māori food (pūhā tiotio).
lookalikes.name: Prickly sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: Perennial sow thistle spreads by creeping roots; New Zealand sow thistle (Sonchus kirkii) grows from a taproot swollen at the top. New Zealand sow thistle's leaves are thick, dull and blue-grey; perennial sow thistle's are firm, dark green and paler beneath. Perennial sow thistle's involucre is 15–18 mm long and its bracts carry tangled short white hairs and long yellow glandular bristles (an Australian description allows hairless bracts too); New Zealand sow thistle's is 10–15 mm, its bracts hairless, sometimes with a row of broad-based hairs on the outer ones or densely white-woolly at the base. Both clasp the stem with rounded lobes, so the leaf base does not separate them. In seed, perennial sow thistle's achenes have 5 ribs on each face, are not winged and are closely wrinkled; New Zealand sow thistle's have 3 ribs, are winged, and are smooth between the ribs. Perennial sow thistle is edible: its young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Perennial sow thistle

preparation.text: Eat raw or cooked. The leaves are tougher and more bitter than common pūhā's (Sonchus oleraceus). Squeezing them under running water washes out some of the bitter juice, and blanching them for a minute in salted boiling water calms the bitterness.

summary.text:
Sonchus kirkii, also known as New Zealand sow thistle, or shore puha is a herb in the Asteraceae family.
Endemic to New Zealand: the Three Kings, North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands. Its conservation status is At Risk – Declining (2023). The introduced prickly sow thistle and common pūhā grow faster and can take over the places it prefers. It probably once grew in a wider range of habitats and has retreated to coastal cliffs where weeds compete less. It is declining over most of its range, especially in the North Island; on the south Wellington coast it was very common until the mid-1980s and has since gone from many sites, through weeds and rock quarrying but also from apparently stable native habitats, for reasons not yet known. Auckland and Otago both rate it Regionally Endangered (2025).
It is thought to be the pūhā Māori ate before European settlement; common pūhā, from Europe, was naturalised by 1832 and has taken its place as the everyday pūhā.
It grows easily from fresh seed and is short-lived, best treated as an annual.

habitat.text:
Frequent but rather local on coastal sands, dunes and stony beaches.
In New Zealand: the coastal strand — beaches among driftwood and seaweed, sand dunes, boulder and cobble beaches, cliff faces and rock ledges. It also turns up in landfills and as a casual weed in towns, and some coastal plants may have started from garden waste.

harvestEthics.text: This species is at risk. If you harvest it, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In the Auckland region (Regionally Endangered), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it.

identification.text:
Herb with decumbent branching stems, softly woody towards base. Leaves on petioles up to 2 cm long; lamina ovate-rhomboid to triangular, obtuse to subacute, entire to slightly sinuate or shallowly lobed, more or less densely papillose. Flowers solitary or occasionally paired, occasionally unisexual, sessile or nearly so, about 7 mm in diameter; perianth yellowish. Calyx tube broad-turbinate, lobes broad-triangular, obtuse. Stamens 10–20. Ovary 3–8-celled, styles 3–8. Fruit 8–10 mm long, subturbinate, angled; seeds 4–10; horns 2–4, hardened.
The plant cultivated as New Zealand spinach has much larger leaves than the wild plant.

lookalikes.howToTell: Beach spinach is most reliably told apart when fruiting: its fruit is a round, succulent berry 5–8 mm long, pink to dark red, with no horns and 1–3 seeds, where this plant's is typically top-shaped and angled, 8–10(–15) mm long, with 2–4 hardened horns and 4–10 seeds. Out of fruit, look at the flower stalks: beach spinach's flowers sit on slender stalks, 5–30 mm long, against the stalkless or nearly stalkless flowers here. Do not go by leaf shape, the papillae on the thick leaves or the yellow flowers; the two share all of these.

summary.text:
Tetragonia tetragonioides, commonly called New Zealand spinach, warrigal greens or by its Māori name of Kōkihi, is a flowering plant in the fig-marigold family (Aizoaceae). It is often cultivated as a leafy vegetable.
It is a widespread species, native to eastern Asia, Australia, and New Zealand. It has been introduced and is an invasive species in many parts of Africa, Europe, North America, and South America.
In New Zealand it is indigenous to the Kermadec, Three Kings, North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands, where it grows on the coastal strand. Its 2023 national assessment is At Risk – Naturally Uncommon.

warnings: The leaves are high in oxalates, higher than spinach, and boiling leaches much of the soluble oxalate into the water. Blanch the leaves in boiling water for one to two minutes, discard the water and refresh them in cold water before cooking. People with a history of kidney stones should eat it only in moderation.

identification.text:
Annual herb. Stems erect, branched above, finely ribbed, with fine crisped eglandular hairs especially below, 15–100–(150) cm tall. Leaves glabrous or sparsely to densely hairy; margins ciliate. Rosette and lower stem leaves petiolate, lyrate-pinnatifid; terminal lobe large, broadly ovate to deltoid to orbicular, bluntly dentate, (1.5)–3–8 × (1.5)–3–8 cm; lateral lobes in (0)–1–3 pairs, the distal pair equal to or less than width of terminal lobe, the proximal pairs successively smaller, all dentate. Upper leaves undivided, becoming sessile, linear-lanceolate to ovate, sharply dentate to serrate, smaller than lower leaves. Capitula in diffuse corymbose panicles; peduncles longer than 2× length of involucre. Involucre 5–8 mm long; bracts glabrous except for ciliate apex, strongly veined or keeled, erecto-patent; outer bracts 1–1.5 mm long. Florets few, about 1.5× length of involucre; corolla yellow; tube shorter than ligule. Achenes fusiform, glabrous, pale, about 20-ribbed, 3–5 mm long; pappus 0. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The small pale-yellow flower heads open only in sunlight and close in the afternoon.

lookalikes.howToTell: Wall lettuce is hairless all over; nipplewort's stems carry fine crinkled hairs, especially low down, and its leaf margins are fringed with hairs, though the leaf surfaces range from hairless to densely hairy. Count the florets: wall lettuce's heads have usually 5, nipplewort's 8 to 15. Wall lettuce's leaf end-lobe is large, triangular or kidney-shaped and itself three-lobed, coarsely toothed with prominent water pores (hydathodes) at the tooth tips; nipplewort's is broadly ovate to triangular to round, bluntly toothed and not three-lobed. Under the head, nipplewort's bracts are strongly veined or keeled; wall lettuce's inner bracts are linear, strictly erect and often purplish, with 2–4 very short outer ones. In seed, wall lettuce's achenes are dark brown to black, shortly beaked and topped with a white pappus; nipplewort's are pale, without beak or pappus. Both have milky sap, lyre-shaped lower leaves with a large end lobe, small yellow heads in a loose branched spray, and grow at forest margins and roadsides. Wall lettuce's leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they can taste extremely bitter (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Wall lettuce

lookalikes.howToTell: Break a stem or leaf: nipplewort's sap is milky, mountain fireweed's is watery. Nipplewort's florets are all strap-shaped and yellow; mountain fireweed has no strap-shaped florets, only a yellow disc 2–3 mm across of tiny tubular ones. In seed, nipplewort's achenes are hairless, pale and have no pappus; mountain fireweed's are sparsely papillate and topped with fine white pappus hairs about 6 mm long. Both can have lyre-shaped, lobed leaves and yellow heads in a loose spray and grow at forest margins and in disturbed places, though mountain fireweed grows mostly from 600 to 1500 m. Mountain fireweed is a native plant with no food record, and its genus, Senecio, is known for liver-damaging pyrrolizidine alkaloids (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mountain fireweed
