edibleParts.text: Young leaves and shoots, flower buds, flower heads and the root. The leaves are eaten raw or cooked; the young shoots are finely chopped into salads and, being pungent, are best used sparingly or mixed with other salad plants. The leaves taste aromatic and slightly lemony, and the plant can be bitter, so the youngest plants are best. Young shoots and buds can also be lightly steamed. Unopened flower buds are marinated or pickled in vinegar and used like capers. Flower heads are eaten raw in salads or used as a garnish; the yellow disc is mild and almost crunchy. The root is eaten raw — a use that rests on a single source.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Waste places, especially roadsides, grasslands, riverbeds, and forest margins.
In New Zealand it is most common in waste places, especially along roadsides, and also grows in dairy pasture (Massey University, restated), often in poorer or wetter dairy pastures (Stuff, restated).
It is a typical grassland perennial wildflower, growing in a variety of plant communities including meadows and fields, under scrub and open-canopy forests, and in disturbed areas. It grows in temperate regions where average annual rainfall exceeds 750 mm, and often where soils are heavy and damp. It is often a weed of degraded pastures and roadsides.

identification.text:
Scarcely scented, perennial herb. Stems erect, up to about 1 m tall, usually sparsely to densely villous below and glabrous above, rarely hairy or glabrous above and below, striate, simple or branched at base or sometimes above, rooting toward base. Basal and lower cauline leaves long-petiolate, elliptic, obovate or spathulate, obtuse at apex, cuneate, coarsely 1–2-serrate, crenate, or shallowly 1–(2)-pinnatifid, usually glabrous, sometimes sparsely hairy on petiole and midrib, very rarely moderately hairy, up to 12–(18) × 2–(4) cm; cauline leaves similar to basal but above becoming smaller, apetiolate, narrow-oblong, amplexicaul, with few distant teeth or sometimes entire, and often auriculate at base. Involucral bracts 3–8 mm long, glabrous; margins and apex brown, membranous; inner bracts with extended, broad, apical flap. Capitula solitary or few in corymbs, (25)–30–60–(65) mm diameter; ray florets (9)–18–33; ligules white; disc florets numerous, yellow. Achenes about 2.5 mm long, dark brown with pale ribs; achenes of disc florets mostly more or less terete, with 10 more or less equal ribs, and corona 0; achenes of ray florets similar to those of disc florets, but sometimes flattened with lateral ribs somewhat extended, 3 ribs on outer surface and 5 ribs on inner surface, rarely achene 3-angled, sometimes with irregular corona about 0.3 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It varies somewhat in hairiness, and in the number, size, and shape of the ligules. Much of this variation can be seen within a single population, and all forms are easily distinguished from L. maximum.
Leucanthemum maximum, the other naturalised Leucanthemum in New Zealand, has narrow-elliptic, evenly toothed basal and lower stem leaves, stems hairless or with a few scattered hairs, and heads (50)–70–120 mm across (Flora of New Zealand key, restated).
It grows as a rosette at first, then as taller clumps with upright, leafy flower stems (Massey University, restated).
While it is small it can be confused with the common lawn daisy, with stinking mayweed (stinking chamomile) and with scentless chamomile (Stuff, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Lawn daisy's flower stalk is leafless, 3–15 cm long (up to 25 cm), and rises from a flat rosette with a single head 15–25 mm across. Ox-eye daisy's flowering stems are leafy and erect, up to about 1 m tall, with one or a few heads usually 30–60 mm across (25–65 mm at the extremes), so the two meet only at about 25 mm. Ox-eye's upper stem leaves are stalkless, narrow and clasp the stem, often with ear-like lobes at the base; its basal leaves are long-stalked, coarsely toothed, scalloped or shallowly lobed, and up to 12 cm long (rarely 18 cm). Lawn daisy's leaves are spoon-shaped to oblong, usually 20–60 mm long (10–80 mm at the extremes), with 2–6 pairs of shallow teeth and one main vein. Lawn daisy's rays are often tinged pink to reddish purple underneath or at the tip; ox-eye's are white. What does not separate them: white rays around a yellow disc, and young rosettes — both have spoon-shaped, scalloped basal leaves, though ox-eye's rosettes grow into taller clumps while lawn daisy's stay small and flat. Common lawn daisy is eaten too — its young leaves, flower buds and petals (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Common lawn daisy

lookalikes.howToTell: Leaves separate them best: stinking mayweed's are cut three times into narrow, almost thread-like segments with a somewhat feathery look, while ox-eye daisy's basal leaves are long-stalked and coarsely toothed, scalloped or at most shallowly lobed, and its upper stem leaves are narrow, stalkless and clasping, with a few distant teeth or none. Stinking mayweed is a strongly foetid annual; ox-eye daisy is a scarcely scented perennial whose stems root towards the base. Stinking mayweed's receptacle carries narrow, pointed scales among the inner florets; ox-eye daisy's has none. What does not separate them: head size overlaps (stinking mayweed about 15–30 mm across, up to 35 mm; ox-eye usually 30–60 mm, 25–65 mm at the extremes), so heads of 25–35 mm need the leaf, smell or scale tests; ray number overlaps (8–21 against 9–33); both have white rays around a yellow disc, and both grow on roadsides, waste places and pasture. Stinking mayweed is not a food plant: its juice is acrid, touching or eating it can cause allergies in some people, the foliage may irritate skin, and there are reports of toxicity.
lookalikes.name: Stinking mayweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Roman chamomile is a low, creeping, sweetly aromatic perennial whose hairy stems lie along the ground or rise to about 20 cm; ox-eye daisy's flowering stems stand erect, up to about 1 m. Roman chamomile's leaves are cut three times into narrow segments with a feathery look, 15–50 mm long; ox-eye's are coarsely toothed, scalloped or shallowly lobed, the basal ones up to 12 cm long (rarely 18 cm). Roman chamomile's receptacle carries small, blunt scales among the florets; ox-eye's has none. Heads: Roman chamomile's are about 8–20 mm across (up to 30 mm), ox-eye's usually 30–60 mm (25–65 mm at the extremes), so they meet only between 25 and 30 mm. What does not separate them: white rays around a yellow disc, and place — both grow on roadsides, waste places and pasture. Roman chamomile's fresh or dried flowers are used for herb tea and its young sprigs as a seasoning (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Roman chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: Leaves separate them best: ox-eye daisy's basal leaves are long-stalked and coarsely toothed, scalloped or at most shallowly lobed, and its upper stem leaves are narrow, stalkless and clasp the stem; scentless chamomile's are cut about three times into thread-like segments with a feathery look. Cut a head in half: ox-eye's receptacle is flat or slightly domed, scentless chamomile's conical. Ox-eye daisy is a perennial that roots at the base of its stems and spreads by short rhizomes; scentless chamomile is an annual or biennial. What does not separate them: smell — both are almost scentless; head size — ox-eye usually 30–60 mm across (25–65 mm at the extremes), scentless chamomile about 30–50 mm; white rays around a yellow disc; and place — roadsides, waste places and pasture. There is no record of scentless chamomile being eaten.
lookalikes.name: Scentless chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: Leaves separate them best: ox-eye daisy's basal leaves are long-stalked, elliptic, obovate or spoon-shaped, coarsely toothed (sometimes doubly), scalloped or shallowly lobed, and up to 12 cm long (rarely 18 cm); Shasta daisy's are narrow-elliptic, evenly toothed with single teeth, and up to about 30 cm long. Heads: ox-eye's are usually 30–60 mm across (25–65 mm at the extremes), Shasta daisy's usually 70–120 mm (50 mm at the smallest), so they meet only between 50 and 65 mm. Ox-eye's stems are usually hairy below, rarely hairless; Shasta daisy's are hairless or have a few scattered hairs. What does not separate them: both are scarcely scented perennials up to about 1 m tall, with white rays around a yellow disc, narrow, stalkless upper leaves that clasp the stem, and no scales on the receptacle, and both grow on roadsides, waste places and pasture. Shasta daisy is a garden escape, occasional in the wild; it has no reliable record as food, is listed as mildly toxic if eaten, and can irritate the skin (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Shasta daisy

preparation.text: Pick the youngest plants. Chop the leaves into salads, sandwiches, omelettes, raita or tabbouleh, or cook them in soups, stews and sauces; steam young shoots and buds lightly. For capers, pack unopened buds into jars and cover them with strained, spiced vinegar; they can be eaten after a day but are best left a month. Use only fresh flower heads, not wilted or browning ones, and check them for insects.

recipes.method: Makes two 0.25 litre jars. 500 ml brown rice wine vinegar; 1 teaspoon sea salt; 1 teaspoon red peppercorns; 1 teaspoon mace; 2 garlic cloves, chopped; enough oxeye daisy flower buds to fill two 0.25 litre screw-top jars. Put the vinegar in a small saucepan with everything except the buds, bring it to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes. Take it off the heat and leave it for at least an hour, until warm or cold. Meanwhile pack the buds into the jars as tightly as you can. Strain the vinegar through a sieve to remove the spices, pour it into the jars to the top and cap them. They can be eaten after 24 hours but are best left to mature for a month.
recipes.title: Oxeye daisy capers

recipes.method: Serves 2; to go with curry and other spicy food. 20 g oxeye daisy leaves; 150 ml coconut milk; 150 g natural yoghurt; the juice of half a lime. Roughly chop the leaves, put them in a bowl with the yoghurt, coconut milk and lime juice, mix thoroughly and leave at room temperature for 10 minutes before serving.
recipes.title: Oxeye daisy raita

recipes.method: Serves 2; quinoa replaces the usual bulgur wheat. ½ cup (125 ml) cooked quinoa, cold; a handful of chopped parsley; a handful of chopped oxeye daisy leaves; ¼ cup (about 60 ml) chopped fresh mint; 4 medium tomatoes, chopped; ¼ cup (about 60 ml) light olive oil; the juice of 1 lemon; ½ teaspoon sea salt; 1 garlic clove, finely chopped. Put the cold quinoa in a bowl, add the parsley, oxeye daisy leaves, mint and garlic, mix well and leave for 30 minutes or until you are ready to serve. Just before serving add the tomatoes, oil, lemon juice and salt, mix well, leave for 15 minutes and serve.
recipes.title: Oxeye daisy tabbouleh

recipes.method: Serves 2 as a light lunch. A handful of young oxeye daisy greens, chopped; 2 garlic cloves, crushed; 14 cherry tomatoes, quartered; 1 teaspoon red wine vinegar; olive oil; salt and pepper; rustic bread. The page gives no amount of oil and does not say when the daisy greens go in; its title and serving step call it a 'tomato and oxeye daisy mix'. Put the ripe, room-temperature tomatoes in a bowl with the garlic and vinegar, mix, season with salt and pepper and leave for 15 minutes. Slice and lightly toast the bread, drizzle it generously with olive oil, top with the tomato and oxeye daisy mix and serve at once.
recipes.title: Oxeye daisy bruschetta

recipes.method: Serves 2 as a main, inspired by Vietnamese street food. 800 g firm tofu; 1 tablespoon lemon juice or vinegar; 3 garlic cloves, crushed; 300 g fresh tomatoes, diced; 100 g oxeye daisy greens, chopped; 2 tablespoons 'gia vi' seasoning (grind 2 teaspoons sugar, 1 teaspoon sea salt, 1 teaspoon ground black pepper and 1 teaspoon dried onion pieces to a powder); 2 lemongrass stalks; 4 tablespoons tamari; 1 tablespoon sesame oil; ½ teaspoon chipotle chilli flakes; 100 ml water; oil for frying. Bring 500 ml water to the boil, add the cubed tofu and the lemon juice and simmer for 10 minutes; drain and pat dry. Heat the oven to 200 °C (fan 180 °C). Bake the tofu cubes on baking paper for 20 minutes. Gently fry the garlic in 2 tablespoons of oil for about 30 seconds, stirring so it does not burn, then add the tomatoes and the baked tofu and stir well. Stir in 2 tablespoons of the gia vi and ¼ teaspoon of the chilli flakes (the ingredient list gives ½ teaspoon). Bruise the lemongrass until it splinters and add it with the chopped daisy greens. Pour in the 100 ml water and simmer for about 15 minutes until the sauce thickens. Off the heat, stir in the sesame oil and serve on millet or rice. The ingredient list includes tamari but the steps never say when to add it.
recipes.title: Oxeye daisy greens and baked tofu

recipes.method: The author's weeds were chickweed, nasturtium, dandelion, pūhā, ox-eye daisy and plantain, with parsley and garden herbs (the page does not say which plantain). She also adds a handful of New Zealand spinach; it is At Risk and its page says to blanch it first, so it is left out here. 5 rosemary sprigs about 12 cm long; a handful of parsley; a big handful of chickweed; 4 large nasturtium leaves; a handful of thyme sprigs 5 cm long; a few dandelion leaves; a small pūhā plant; 10 ox-eye daisy leaves; 8 plantain leaves; 5 sage leaves; 6 garlic cloves; 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt; about 30 ml (⅛ cup) cider vinegar; 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) olive oil, starting with the smaller amount; 5 ml (1 tsp) honey, or to taste; the juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml (½ cup) walnuts. Strip the leaves from the thyme and rosemary and wash any leaves that need it. Blend everything in a high-speed blender or food processor until smooth, pushing it down with the tamper. Keep it in the fridge or freezer.
recipes.title: Wild weed pesto

recipes.method: The author says the amounts are approximate and untested. 3 cups (750 ml) oxeye daisy greens; ½ packet of phyllo pastry; ¼ cup (60 ml) butter, melted; 85 g mascarpone (more if you want it creamier); ¼ cup (60 ml) honey; a few sprigs of thyme; a pinch of sea salt. Heat the oven to 175 °C. Cut the phyllo into rectangles of about 25 × 20 cm and brush the bottom and top layers with melted butter. Saute the greens lightly in a little butter, then chop them finely or whizz them in a food processor. Mix with the mascarpone, 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the honey, the salt and 1 tsp thyme leaves, spread thinly over the phyllo and roll up. Brush all over with melted butter or olive oil, dust with thyme leaves and bake for 15–20 minutes until golden and browning.
recipes.title: Oxeye daisy phyllo rolls with mascarpone and honey

summary.text:
Leucanthemum vulgare, commonly known as the ox-eye daisy, oxeye daisy, dog daisy, marguerite (French: Marguerite commune, "common marguerite") and other common names, is a widespread flowering plant native to Europe and the temperate regions of Asia, and an introduced plant to North America, Australia and New Zealand.
The species is native to Europe, and to Turkey and Georgia in Western Asia.
The species is widely naturalised in many parts of the world, including North America, and is considered to be an invasive species in more than forty countries.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands: throughout, lowland to montane; Stewart Island: Halfmoon Bay area; Campbell Island. Native range temperate Eurasia; naturalised in New Zealand by 1867.
The oxeye daisy is a common and conspicuous roadside weed. The species has been previously known in New Zealand as Chrysanthemum leucanthemum.
In New Zealand it can be troublesome in dairy pasture because cows tend not to eat it, but never where sheep graze, as they eat it readily; it is not susceptible to the selective herbicides normally used in pasture, and its short rhizomes make it hard to control (Massey University, restated).
Sheep, goats and horses eat it, but cows and pigs dislike its bitter taste, so beef and dairy farmers can lose a good deal of pasture where it takes hold (Stuff, restated).
The Department of Conservation lists it among New Zealand's environmental weeds (2024), as a fully naturalised plant with more than minor impacts in natural ecosystems.

warnings: Eat it sparingly: the leaves are pungent and can be bitter, very large amounts can cause sickness, and eating many of the yellow flower centres may cause indigestion.

Ox-eye daisy contains sesquiterpene lactones, strong inducers of allergic contact dermatitis, sometimes with sensitivity to sunlight; allergy to daisies usually shows as contact dermatitis, and people sensitised to other daisy-family plants (Asteraceae) may cross-react.

In New Zealand dairy pasture it is controlled with herbicides — 2,4-D, clopyralid, aminopyralid, metsulfuron, thifensulfuron-methyl, flumetsulam or triclopyr/picloram, often as spot treatments, or glyphosate in a weed wiper — so pasture plants may have been sprayed.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Lowland habitats, especially open coastal sites in grass, among rocks, sand, in waste places and disturbed roadside communities.
Mostly coastal, sometimes inland on limestone bluffs, and especially common on sand dunes and the sandy soils around them. It usually grows up through other plants and is easily missed except when in flower.

identification.text:
Perennial with primary root stout, occasionally to 5 mm wide. Stems decumbent to more or less erect, to about 50 cm tall, slender, weak, branched, not or slightly rooting at the nodes, glabrate to densely covered in more or less antrorse, and often crisped hairs. Leaves 3-foliolate. Petiole usually 1–10 cm long, glabrate or covered with long patent to antrorse hairs; stipules generally less than 1.5 mm long, completely adnate, sometimes reduced and merely simulating a dilated petiole base, usually ciliate. Petiolules very short. Lamina of leaflets equal, 3–13 × 4–18 mm, obcordate or broadly obcordate, with divergent lobes, and sinus generally more than 1/2 lamina length, glabrous above, with hairs below mainly confined to midrib, more or less ciliate; calli 0. Flowers 1–3–(4); peduncle 1.5–7 cm and pedicels 0.3–2 cm long, longer at fruiting, both with more or less antrorse, slightly curling hairs. Bracts 1–2.5 mm long, linear-subulate, densely hairy, situated at base of pedicels; calli 0. Sepals 3–5 mm long, oblong-lanceolate, oblong-elliptic to oblong-ovate, with antrorse, appressed hairs; calli 0. Petals 6–14 mm long, oblong-obovate to almost obdeltate, yellow, glabrous. Stamens at 2 levels, glabrous; filaments united towards base. Styles shorter than to longer than longer stamens, densely hairy. Capsule 10–23 mm long excluding styles, cylindric, densely hairy; hairs short, retrorse or sometimes almost patent, sometimes glandular. Seeds 1.2–1.7 mm long, oblong-ellipsoid; transverse ridges 8–10, obtuse; grooves deep.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Usually told from creeping wood sorrel by its sprawling to erect stems that do not root at the nodes, its thick taproot, its small stipules and its more or less spreading leaflet lobes.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have yellow petals, three notched leaflets and long, cylindric, hairy capsules, and the sizes overlap: Oxalis rubens's leaflets are 3–13 mm long, creeping wood sorrel's (2.5)–5–18 mm; petals 6–14 mm against 4.5–10–(13) mm; capsules 10–23 mm against (6)–10–18–(20) mm; 1–3 (up to 4) flowers on a stalk against 1–5. Look at how it grows: Oxalis rubens's stems sprawl or stand nearly erect, up to about 50 cm, and do not root at the nodes, or only slightly; creeping wood sorrel's lie along the ground or rise a little, up to about 40 cm, and often root at the nodes. Look at the base of each leaf stalk: Oxalis rubens's stipules are tiny, generally under 1.5 mm long and fused all along the stalk, sometimes looking like no more than a widened stalk base; creeping wood sorrel's are usually 2–3 mm long and broad, with a free, square-cut tip. Oxalis rubens's two leaflet lobes usually spread apart. Oxalis rubens has a stout taproot, up to 5 mm wide, where creeping wood sorrel's main root is slender; but the purple-leaved form of creeping wood sorrel also has a thicker taproot, so judge the stems and stipules first. Oxalis rubens grows mostly in open lowland coastal places (grass, rocks, sand dunes), creeping wood sorrel mostly in and around settlements, gardens and cultivated ground; both turn up in waste places and on roadsides. Creeping wood sorrel is eaten; Oxalis rubens has no record as food.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Small, starved plants of Oxalis rubens can be hard to tell from least yellow sorrel. Least yellow sorrel's stems are thread-like, creep flat, root at the nodes and often form mats; Oxalis rubens's sprawl or stand nearly erect, up to about 50 cm, and do not root at the nodes, or only slightly. Least yellow sorrel's flowers are usually smaller, petals 4.5–9 mm (up to 13 mm) against Oxalis rubens's 6–14 mm, and solitary, rarely paired, against 1–3 (up to 4) on a stalk. Least yellow sorrel's capsules are mostly 7–10 mm long (3–13 mm at the extremes), broadly cylindric, cylindric-ovoid or conic; Oxalis rubens's are 10–23 mm and cylindric. What does not separate them: leaflet size overlaps (least yellow sorrel 1–9 mm long, Oxalis rubens 3–13 mm), both can have a stout root (least yellow sorrel's occasionally to about 10 mm thick), and both grow on beaches and in open coastal turf. Least yellow sorrel is eaten; Oxalis rubens has no record as food.

summary.text:
Oxalis rubens is a native, yellow-flowered wood sorrel: a perennial herb without bulbils, with a stout taproot. It is also indigenous to Australia, and probably Lord Howe and Norfolk Islands.
In New Zealand it is widespread on the North, South and Chatham Islands and the Kermadec Islands. An ill-defined, quite variable species, it was mostly treated by Allan (1961) as O. stricta; in New Zealand it has been confused with O. stricta, which is not in New Zealand, and with O. perennans, an uncommon weed.

warnings: Do not eat it. No record of Oxalis rubens as food was found.
Creeping wood sorrel and least yellow sorrel, which are eaten, look very like it and grow in some of the same places. See Lookalikes.

habitat.text:
Usually waste and arable land, also open disturbed, particularly moist habitats. [From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4]
New Zealand herbarium specimens also record it on the shore of Lake Rotorua, at Lake Wairarapa, on waste land at Lake Bryndwr in Christchurch, in a potato patch, and on the site of an old railway workshop in Christchurch.
Wetland status (NZPCN, from the national wetland plant list, Clarkson et al. 2021): facultative — commonly occurs both in wetlands and in non-wetlands.

identification.text:
Annual; stems more or less erect, to 1 m tall, glabrous, green or reddish, often with red spots below the more or less swollen nodes; taproot moderately stout. Leaves on main stem similar to those on branches; petioles to 3 cm long. Lamina (2)–3–15–(20) × (0.5)–1–4.5–(7) cm, lanceolate to narrow-ovate, glandular-punctate and glabrate to whitish tomentose below (sometimes hairy only on midrib), often with dark blotch on upper side, entire, ciliate; base more or less attenuate; apex obtuse or subacute. Ochreae to 1 cm long, initially green or pinkish, truncate; apex glabrous or ciliolate. Inflorescence to 4 cm long, erect, dense and cylindric, usually simple and uninterrupted, mostly terminal; pedicels short, obscured by ochrea-like bracts; peduncles sparsely to densely covered with subsessile yellow or cream glands. Perianth about 2 mm long, sparsely to moderately glandular, somewhat accrescent, usually white, sometimes pink; veins prominent, forked and recurved (anchor-shaped); segments more or less elliptic, imbricate. Nut 2.5–3 mm long, usually more or less biconvex, occasionally trigonous with rounded edges, dark brown, shining. Flowers November–April.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Polygonum lapathifolium, via the Flora of New Zealand Online factsheet.]
It is variable in New Zealand, especially in the size and hairiness of its leaves and stems. Some plants resemble two forms that are sometimes treated as separate species overseas, but intermediates occur, so New Zealand plants are treated as one broad species. Its seedling leaves are linear-lanceolate.
Probable hybrids with willow weed, apparently fairly widespread now, are robust plants with scattered forward-pointing stem hairs, leaves to 20 × 5 cm, leaf sheaths fringed with hairs to 3 mm long and closely bristly, glandular flower stalks, and deep red flowers, sometimes glandular, with anchor-shaped veins.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stalk just below the flower spike: pale willow weed's is sparsely to densely dotted with tiny yellow or cream glands; willow weed's has none, or at most a few small dark ones. With a hand lens, look at the veins of the tiny flower segments: pale willow weed's are prominent, forked and curved back like an anchor; willow weed's are straight or gently curved. Pale willow weed's flowers are also sparsely to moderately glandular; willow weed's have none. Look at the sheath where the leaf meets the stem: willow weed's is up to about 1.5 cm long and fringed with hairs; pale willow weed's is up to 1 cm long, with its tip hairless or with only tiny hairs. Flower colour tends to differ but overlaps: pale willow weed's are usually white, sometimes pink; willow weed's usually pale to deep pink, occasionally white. Leaf blotches do not separate them: both often have a dark blotch on the upper side, and willow weed's is not always present. A leaf that is whitish-felted underneath, has a stalk longer than 2 cm, or is wider than 4 cm is not willow weed's, but pale willow weed's leaves can also be nearly hairless below, short-stalked and narrow, so such leaves do not tell them apart. Pale willow weed's leaf tips are blunt or only slightly pointed; willow weed's are pointed to drawn out. Seedlings: pale willow weed's first leaves are narrow and lance-shaped; willow weed's more or less elliptic. Both have erect, dense, cylindric flower spikes up to about 4 cm long, so the spike shape does not separate them. Ripe nuts overlap: pale willow weed's 2.5–3 mm long, dark brown and shining; willow weed's 2–2.5 mm, brownish black and shining. Plants that are hard to place may be hybrids: probable hybrids, apparently fairly widespread, have pale willow weed's glandular flower stalks and anchor-shaped veins but a sheath fringed with hairs up to 3 mm long, deep red flowers and leaves up to 5 cm wide. Both grow on waste and arable land in the North and South Islands, so place does not separate them; willow weed is much the commoner. Both are recorded as possibly poisonous in New Zealand. Willow weed's leaves are eaten raw or cooked (see its page).

Lookalike card pale willow weed <-> willow weed: confusion named by Flora vol. IV ('often mistaken for P. persicaria') and Massey ('looks very similar to willow weed'). Tests from the Flora vol. IV descriptions of both — pale willow weed (Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb, Sykes & Garnock-Jones 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY-NC-SA), 'Polygonum lapathifolium L.' (https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/d55610b2-28e4-4d2b-b4de-2e765cfa755b, retrieved 11/11/2026): peduncles 'sparsely to densely covered with subsessile yellow or cream glands'; perianth 'c. 2 mm long, sparsely to moderately glandular … usually white, sometimes pink; veins prominent, forked and recurved (anchor-shaped)'; ochreae 'to 1 cm long, initially green or pinkish, truncate; apex glabrous or ciliolate'; lamina '(2)-3-15-(20) × (0.5)-1-4.5-(7) cm … glandular-punctate and glabrate to whitish tomentose below (sometimes hairy only on midrib), often with dark blotch on upper side'; 'petioles to 3 cm long'; 'apex obtuse or subacute'; 'Infl. to 4 cm long, erect, dense and cylindric'; nut '2.5-3 mm long … dark brown, shining'; seedling leaves 'linear-lanceolate'; the putative hybrid) and willow weed (Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (1988), Flora of New Zealand Series (CC BY-NC-SA), 'Polygonum persicaria L.' (https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/b9be6afd-89f9-4e77-aa7f-68fdbb79a2b9, retrieved 11/11/2026): 'peduncles eglandular'; perianth 'eglandular, usually pale to deep pink, occasionally white'; 'veins straight or gently curved'; ochreae 'to c. 1.5 cm long, fringed, often hairy'; lamina '(1.2)-4-15 × 1.2-4 cm … apex acute to acuminate', 'usually with a central dark blotch above' and 'The dark lf blotch is not always present'; 'petiole 2-12-(20) mm long'; spike 'to 4-(5) × 0.7-1.5 cm'; nuts '2-2.5 mm long … brownish black, shining'; seedling leaves '± elliptic'); the genus key (Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (1988), Flora of New Zealand Series (CC BY-NC-SA), 'Polygonum L.' (genus description and key, https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/4eb89843-2b12-405d-8562-0002dfe90fde, retrieved 11/11/2026)) couplet 12 ('Ochreae apex glabrous or ciliolate; peduncles with yellow or cream shortly stalked or sessile glands; perianth veins prominently forked (anchor-shaped)' versus 'Ochreae prominently long-ciliate; peduncles eglandular or with a few small dark glands; perianth veins ± simple'), whose second lead gives the 'few small dark glands' hedge. Massey's tests checked against the Flora: 'the ochrea doesn't have the fringe' agrees (apex glabrous or ciliolate) and is used; 'seed head is a paler pink' is kept only as a tendency (the Flora's colours overlap); 'often there is no blotch on the leaf' is not used — the Flora gives pale willow weed's leaves 'often with dark blotch'. Ranges and habitats overlap (pale willow weed N. and S., waste and arable land; willow weed throughout, gardens, arable land, waste places). Risk edible (willow weed is careRequired); reverse card risk edible (pale willow weed is careRequired). Owner link round on tūtunawai 11/11/2026 (lookalike draft, owner 11/11/2026).

summary.text:
Pale willow weed (Persicaria lapathifolia, synonym Polygonum lapathifolium) is an annual herb in the dock family Polygonaceae, native to the temperate Northern Hemisphere and naturalised in New Zealand.
It was first recorded wild here in 1904 and is generally much less common than willow weed. In the North Island it grows at scattered localities at least as far north as the Bay of Plenty; in the South Island it is locally common in North Canterbury and on Banks Peninsula, with scattered localities south to Southland. Probable hybrids with willow weed are apparently fairly widespread. It is not listed as an environmental weed or a regional pest plant.
Its young leaves are eaten cooked, and in Poland the whole shoots were once eaten as a famine food.

warnings: Pale willow weed is recorded as possibly poisonous in New Zealand.
It is often mistaken for willow weed, and probable hybrids between the two grow here. Check the flower stalks, flowers and leaf sheaths before picking (see the lookalikes).

edibleParts.text: Leaves, flowers and stems.

sources: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA)
habitat.text:
Bush, gardens, roadsides, disturbed sites, also along the seaside. Tolerates shade well.
In New Zealand: waste places and gardens, especially in shady disturbed sites, on banks, beneath hedges, windbreaks, and forest margins.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Perennial, almost glabrous herb with thick fleshy contractile root; main bulb about 2 cm long, subterranean; tunic brown, with scale nerves inconspicuous; secondary aerial bulbs or bulbils small, common in branch axils. Stems spreading to sub-erect, glabrous, with many flexuous, slender branches. Leaves 3-foliolate, glabrous. Petiole 2–7–(12) cm long; stipules forming a narrow to broad wing. Lamina of leaflets subequal, subsessile, 4–16 × 5–22 mm, mostly broadly obcordate, with more or less divergent lobes, finely reticulate beneath, with a submarginal irregular row of orange calli; base more or less narrow-cuneate, often slightly hairy. Flowers solitary; peduncles 2.5–12 cm long, filiform. Bracts about 1/2 way along pedicel, 2–2.8 mm long, linear-subulate; calli prominent. Sepals 4.5–5.5 mm long, ovate-oblong, often slightly hairy; calli 2, apical, prominent, orange. Petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes becoming almost white, glabrous; limb broad-obovate. Stamens in 2 whorls; filaments hairy, dilated towards base, shorter than 4 mm long. Styles much longer than longer whorl of stamens, hairy except near apex. Capsule not seen. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Its stems creep along the ground and root at the nodes. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: white clover's leaflets are c. 5–25 mm long, can be notched at the tip and often carry light or dark markings, so leaflet size, shape and markings overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually without a stalk, sitting among the top leaves, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Its leaf stalks and leaflet undersides are usually moderately hairy, and its leaflets, c. 15–40 mm long, usually carry a crescent-shaped mark towards the base. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless. Red clover's leaflets are mostly larger, but the ranges meet at 15–16 mm, so use size only as a guide. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Its stems are erect or ascending and do not root at the nodes, and its leaflets are c. 10–35 mm long. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Leaflet size overlaps between 10 and 16 mm, so it does not separate them. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Shamrock wood sorrel: a hairy, clump-forming plant with all its leaves in basal rosettes on stalks (3)–7–30 cm long, and no leafy stem. Its flowers come (4)–7–35 together in a branched cluster on a stalk up to c. 35 cm tall; petals 9–16 mm long, usually rose with darker veins, rarely white. Its leaflets are usually 8–35 mm long, up to 55 mm. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless. Its petals can be as short as 10 mm, so petal size alone does not separate them, and both can be pale or white. Several flowers on one stalk point to shamrock wood sorrel, but a single flower does not rule it out: its clusters can hold anything from 1 to at least 30 flowers. Look for a leafy, branched stem, which only pale-pink wood sorrel has. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Shamrock wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Pink shamrock has no leafy stem: its leaves all rise from the base, from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, and it carries 3–7 or 10–18 flowers in a cluster on a stalk up to 35 cm long. Pale-pink wood sorrel has leafy stems, spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and each flower stalk carries a single flower. Pink shamrock's leaflets are hairy beneath and its flower clusters carry long curly hairs; pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless. Petals do not separate them: pink shamrock's are 1.5–2 cm long, pink to rose; pale-pink wood sorrel's 1.7–2.2 cm, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Leaflet size overlaps (pink shamrock 10–35 mm long, pale-pink wood sorrel 4–16 mm), and both have orange dots near the leaflet edge. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pink shamrock

lookalikes.howToTell: Fishtail oxalis has no leafy stem: its leaves all rise from the base, from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, and it carries about 5–15 (up to 20) flowers in a cluster on a stalk about 10–50 cm tall. Pale-pink wood sorrel has leafy stems, spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and each flower stalk carries a single flower. Fishtail oxalis's petals are about 1.2–1.5 cm long, pink; pale-pink wood sorrel's are 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white, but can be as short as 10 mm, so petal size alone does not separate them. Fishtail oxalis's leaflets are broadly fishtail-shaped, with no orange dots or only faint ones; pale-pink wood sorrel's carry an irregular row of orange dots just inside the edge. Leaflet size overlaps: fishtail oxalis's are 12–50 mm long, pale-pink wood sorrel's 4–16 mm. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. The tests above that do not rest on leaflet shape or petal colour still hold for it. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Fishtail oxalis

lookalikes.howToTell: Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long; its stems are sparsely to densely hairy, lie along the ground or rise a little, and do not root at the nodes. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and it is almost hairless. Out of flower, do not rely on leaflet size: suckling clover's are about 3–12 mm long, pale-pink wood sorrel's 4–16 mm. On most suckling clover leaves the middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the side ones. Suckling clover has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Suckling clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Purple wood sorrel has no stem above ground: its leaves all rise from the base. Its leaf stalks and the undersides of its leaflets are hairy, the leaflet edges fringed with long hairs, and its leaflets are 10–35 mm long (up to 45 mm), broadly obovate with a rounded tip, sometimes slightly notched; the dots and streaks on them turn black when dry. Each flower stalk, 1–11 cm long, carries a single flower forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base; its sepals carry a dense fringe of long white hairs and have no orange dots at the tip. Pale-pink wood sorrel has leafy stems, spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils; it is the only oxalis in New Zealand with bulbils above ground. It is almost hairless. Its leaflets are 4–16 mm long, mostly broadly heart-shaped, with an irregular row of orange dots just inside the edge, and each sepal has two prominent orange dots at its tip (in some plants they look light brown). Each flower stalk, 2.5–12 cm long, carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. What does not separate them: both carry a single flower on each stalk, and the stalk lengths overlap. Petal length overlaps too, as either plant's petals can be as short as 10 mm, so only petals longer than 2.2 cm point to purple wood sorrel. Leaflet length overlaps between 10 and 16 mm. Look for a leafy, branched stem and orange dots on the sepal tips, which only pale-pink wood sorrel has. Do not eat purple wood sorrel; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Purple wood sorrel

preparation.text: Eat the young leaves fresh and in small amounts: in salads, finely chopped as a garnish or in green pestos. Toss the leaves and flowers through a green salad, or use the flowers as a garnish; pick the flowers by day, when they are open.

recipes.method: Two handfuls of wood sorrel, chopped; potato and kūmara, boiled first and sliced; cream. Layer the sorrel with the sliced potato and kūmara in a baking dish, pour cream over the top and bake at 180 °C until it starts to brown.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel, kūmara and potato gratin

recipes.method: Chop a big handful of wood sorrel leaves, stalks and flowers and mix them through a potato salad dressed with a cream dressing.
recipes.title: Potato salad with wood sorrel

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) lemon juice and 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) maple syrup or honey. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the sorrel and stir for 1–2 minutes, until it wilts. Put it in a blender or food processor with the lemon juice and the syrup or honey and blend until well combined. Serve it straight away, or refrigerate it and warm it before use; the author finds it even better the next day. The author serves it on fish, or as a dipping sauce for grilled prawns.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel sauce

recipes.method: About 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, stems or flowers, or a mix, about 250 ml (1 cup) water, and maple syrup or another sweetener to taste. The amounts are rough: use as much sorrel as you like and enough water to cover it. Blend the sorrel and water until well combined, strain through a fine sieve and sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel 'lemonade'

recipes.method: Equal parts wood sorrel, sugar, and water; the author usually uses 250 ml (1 cup) of each. Put everything in a saucepan and bring it to a simmer, stirring. Simmer for 15–30 minutes, strain through muslin (cheesecloth) and pour into sterilised bottles. The author uses it in tea, topped up with soda water, over ice cream or fresh strawberries, or in vinaigrettes and marinades.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel syrup

recipes.method: The recipe uses one part leaves to three parts water. Fresh wood sorrel leaves; boiling water; sweetener to taste (optional). Put the leaves in a container, pour the boiling water over them and leave to steep for 5–15 minutes. Strain out the leaves and sweeten to taste if you like. Drink it hot, or pour it over ice for an iced tea.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel tea

recipes.method: 2 cloves garlic, minced; olive oil for cooking; 2 spring onions, chopped; 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock; 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish; 3 medium mint leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk; salt and pepper. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks. Heat a little olive oil in a small saucepan and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the spring onions. Cover with the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, then add the sorrel for about 30 seconds. Take it off the heat, add the mint and blend smooth with a stick blender (or an ordinary blender). Stir in the coconut milk and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until well chilled, a couple of hours, and serve garnished with the sorrel flowers.
recipes.title: Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

recipes.method: About 450 g (1 lb) Italian or breakfast sausage; 1 medium spaghetti squash; several cups of wood sorrel, washed and drained, stems removed (the recipe gives no closer amount); olive oil; 1 red onion, halved and sliced; 1 egg; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk or any milk; 1 garlic clove, minced; 15 ml (1 tbsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) tarragon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) black pepper; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground sage. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Halve the squash, spoon out the seeds and stringy threads, set the halves cut side up on a baking tray, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and bake for 20–25 minutes, until the flesh gives a little when pressed. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts. Take the squash out of the oven and scrape out the flesh with a fork (careful, it will be hot). Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.
recipes.title: Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: The author's greens were puha, sow thistle, nasturtium, onion weed, wild fennel, oxalis, wild mustard and wild celery; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 1 diced onion; 1 potato, scrubbed and diced; 2 sliced garlic cloves; 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 1.3 litres water; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked pepper; extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil, to serve; edible weed flowers. Serves 4. Cut the vegetables and greens to similar sizes. Fry the onion in the oil for a minute, then add the potato and garlic (the method also adds fennel bulb and celery stalks, which the ingredient list leaves out) and fry for another minute. Add the water, cover, bring to the boil and simmer until the potato is soft. Add the greens with the salt and yeast and cook for 3 minutes, until just tender — added at the end, they keep their colour. Blend until smooth (push it through a sieve if your blender isn't powerful), season with the pepper and more salt if needed, and serve drizzled with extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil and scattered with edible weed flowers.
recipes.title: Wild greens soup

Origin 'introduced' stands. Kept introduced, not pest: none of NZPCN's DOC-weed, Pest Plant Accord or unwanted-organism listings appear on its page, and no regional pest management plan naming it was found (web search 15/10/2026).

Habitat as first written: Plants of South Eastern New South Wales (Lucid), 'Oxalis incarnata', Where found, author Betty Wood, CC BY 4.0, https://apps.lucidcentral.org/plants_se_nsw/text/entities/oxalis_incarnata.htm, retrieved 16/10/2026 — first two sentences verbatim; its Australian distribution ('Coast and Blue Mountains. Occasionally elsewhere.') omitted. This is an Australian habitat statement, not a New Zealand one. Habitat tags forest (bushland), urban (gardens) and disturbed (roadsides, disturbed sites). New Zealand fact, not quoted (all rights reserved): Johanna Knox, Wild Picnic blog (cited below) — grows around borders and against rises and mounds. The owner has since replaced that text with their own ('Bush, gardens, road site, disturbed sites also along the sea side. Tolerates shade well.', in the editor, by 16/10/2026), so the field's source is now this guide; spelling regularised 16/10/2026 ('road site' → 'roadsides', 'sea side' → 'seaside'). 'Along the seaside' is the owner's; no source read for this entry says it. Lucid says 'Tolerates deep shade'. The tag grassland is not supported by either text.

Summary sentences two and three: Wikipedia, 'Oxalis incarnata' (revision 1306452215; CC BY-SA 4.0), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxalis_incarnata, retrieved 16/10/2026, verbatim. Flora of New Zealand Online and Biota of New Zealand (https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/b7628927-693d-4389-8488-03820477ba6f, retrieved 16/10/2026) give the New Zealand vernacular names 'Lilac oxalis' and 'Pale oxalis', and Biota of New Zealand Biostatus Exotic, Wild; Flora of New Zealand gives 'Flowering: Jan.–Dec.'.

Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (all rights reserved; retrieved 16/10/2026; supplied by the owner): Johanna Knox, 'Wood sorrel (Oxalis incarnata)', Wild Picnic, 16/07/2009, https://wildpicnic.blogspot.com/2009/07/wood-sorrel-oxalis-acetosella.html — the gratin and the potato salad. The post was first written as O. acetosella; a commenter (AJB, 26/11/2009) identified the plant pictured as 'the South African Ox. incarnata', which the author accepted, and the title now names O. incarnata. The blog covers Wellington and the Wairarapa; the post does not say where the plant grew. Not used as recipes: adding it to apple, peach or pear pie and a jelly (suggestions, not made by the author); its use to curdle milk for cheese (the author had not got it to work).

Edibility sources (16/10/2026; warnings added 16/10/2026, preparation filled 03/11/2026 from the two sources below; edible parts since written by the owner, 'Leafs, flowers and stems.', spelling regularised 16/10/2026) — no openly licensed source found that records this species as edible (Useful Temperate Plants has no record; Plants For A Future returned no entry; Wikipedia and Flora of New Zealand say nothing of use). The only species-specific source is Johanna Knox's Wild Picnic post above (all rights reserved, so not quoted), which records: raw leaves and stalks have a bright, sour taste and suit sweet and savoury dishes; leaves and flowers in a green salad, flowers as a garnish; it goes with root vegetables, fish, chicken and cream; used in place of lemon. Its caution: high oxalic acid levels, so not too much, and avoid it if you have gout, kidney trouble or rheumatoid arthritis and are avoiding high-oxalic-acid foods. Knox's A Forager's Treasury and Langlands' Foraging New Zealand (both owned, cited above) are the book routes. Not copied from creeping-wood-sorrel, whose text is about Oxalis corniculata. Web search 16/10/2026 (owner: "do a web search and find what you can") found no openly licensed text either; details in the next line.

Web search for edibility and safety, 16/10/2026, pages saved and read in full. Species-specific, all rights reserved, facts only: (1) Heartland Folk, 'Pale Wood Sorrel ~ Oxalis incarnata', Wild Food Wednesday issue 10 (Substack, 2026, Central Highlands of Victoria, Australia), https://heartlandfolk.substack.com/p/pale-wood-sorrel-oxalis-incarnata — all aerial parts edible, leaves and flowers; young leaves sour, eaten fresh in salads, chopped as a garnish or in green pestos in small amounts; best used fresh in small amounts because of its oxalic acid; pick young tender leaves, flowers by day when open; harvest only from unsprayed sites away from roadsides; clovers named as close lookalikes; the plant goes dormant in heat and drought. Its leaflet size (1.5–3 cm long) is larger than Flora of New Zealand's 4–16 mm and is not used. (2) PictureThis, 'Pale pink-sorrel (Oxalis incarnata)' (plant-identification app wiki, author not named), https://www.picturethisai.com/wiki/Oxalis_incarnata.html — leaves edible but not in large amounts because of oxalic acid; not used further, no named author. (3) EdiblePlantDB, 'Oxalidaceae' family page, https://edibleplantdb.org/families/Oxalidaceae — lists O. incarnata with edible parts leaves and stems; an aggregated list with no author or primary source given. Genus-level, not used for this species: Wild Food UK, 'Pink-Sorrel' (Oxalis articulata page), https://www.wildfooduk.com/wild-plants/pink-sorrel/ — names pale pink-sorrel among pink-flowered Oxalis it calls 'all too similar and unnecessary to distinguish as all green leaved Oxalis are edible'. Conflict, recorded: Calflora, 'Oxalis incarnata' (https://www.calflora.org/app/taxon?crn=6012), Toxicity: 'Possible skin irritation from touching any part of this plant. Do not eat any part of this plant.' — Calflora shows the same two sentences on every Oxalis checked (O. albicans, O. corniculata, O. hirta, O. latifolia, O. oregana); its field notes say the toxicity value follows the California Poison Control System, whose 'Oxalates' class covers plants whose sap contains oxalate crystals. It is a genus-wide flag, not a finding about this species, but it is the only source found that says not to eat it. Seasonal, for the owner's months decision: Pacific Bulb Society wiki, 'South African Oxalis Five' (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US; Copyright Pacific Bulb Society, www.pacificbulbsociety.org), https://www.pacificbulbsociety.org/pbswiki/index.php/SouthAfricanOxalisFive — 'It can stay evergreen with moisture'; Massey (below) 'more active in winter'; Knox (above) cooking with it in July and pairing it with "two other herbs that you can forage for at the moment". Not found: any traditional South African food use of this species, or any source on eating its bulbs.

The seven recipes from 'Wood sorrel sauce' onward were copied 16/10/2026 from creeping-wood-sorrel (owner, 16/10/2026: "the recipies are interchangeble betwwen sorrel species"); none is written for this species. Their provenance, as recorded there: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (cups at 250 ml, 1 tbsp = 15 ml, 1 tsp = 5 ml; every page all rights reserved; retrieved 15/10/2026; supplied by the owner). None is written for this species: each is written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally. The sauce, 'lemonade' and syrup from Kate MacQuarrie, 'Wood Sorrel Recipes', PEI Untamed, 09/07/2023 (https://www.pei-untamed.com/post/wood-sorrel-recipes) — written for 'the Wood Sorrels' of Prince Edward Island, no species named; 'grilled shrimp' given as prawns; the lemonade's 'leaves, stems, and/or flowers' and its note that the author does not measure are kept. 'Wood sorrel cooler' is Sunny Savage's 'Oxalis Cooler' as given in Green Deane, 'Oxalis: How To Drown Your Sorrels', Eat The Weeds (dated 16/01/2018 on the page, with reader comments from 2012; https://www.eattheweeds.com/oxalis-how-to-drown-your-sorrels/; the owner's second link, https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/oxalis-deppei/, is a tag page showing the same article) — written for Oxalis generally, the article naming the Florida species including O. corniculata; 1 US quart is about 946 ml; the recipe does not strain the drink and neither does this. 'Wood sorrel tea' from Jesse, 'Wood Sorrel: Identification, Uses, and Precautions', Feral Foraging, 11/07/2024 (https://feralforaging.com/wood-sorrel/) — written mainly for O. stricta and O. violacea; the page gives the ratio only as '1:3' after 'Gather wood sorrel leaves' and 'Pour over boiling water', without saying by volume or by weight, so 'one part leaves to three parts water' is this guide's reading. 'Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup' from Valerie Zemba, 'Chilled Lemony Wood Sorrel Soup', Very Vegan Val, 03/07/2019 (https://veryveganval.com/chilled-lemony-wood-sorrel-soup/) — written for 'Oxalis stricta and others'; scallions given as spring onions, vegetable broth as stock; the rinsing and stripping step is from the page's prose above the recipe card. 'Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel' from Chosen Weeds Farm, 'Cooking With Wood Sorrel', 15/03/2017 (https://thechosenweeds.com/cooking-with-wood-sorrel/) — written for the purple-leaf wood sorrel that grows in the author's south-east Texas garden; 400 °F given as 200 °C, 1 lb as about 450 g; 'Several cups' of sorrel kept because the page gives no closer amount; the page says only 'Combine mixture with the egg' after forking out the squash, and the method keeps that wording rather than saying where the squash goes. Not used from the recipe pages (15/10/2026): the casserole page's 'If you are short on time you can skip the oven step', because skipping the final bake would leave the stirred-in egg uncooked; Feral Foraging's statements that all species of wood sorrel are edible and can be used in similar ways (genus-level claims), its estimate that about 30 g a day, several times a week, is safe and its view that oxalate warnings are overblown (it contradicts every other page read here and is not a trusted source for a safety amount), and its cold-infusion and dried-leaf variants; Green Deane's statements that cooking reportedly renders oxalic acid harmless, particularly with calcium, that eating a lot raw can leach calcium from the bones, and that the juice curdles milk for cheese, and that all parts including the root bulb are edible (said of the Florida species as a group); the casserole page's medicinal and vitamin claims; the reader comment on Eat The Weeds suggesting more sorrel for a sharper cooler. Two of the owner's links have no recipe: Rachel Lambert, 'Wild Food: Wood Sorrel family', Wild Walks Southwest, 07/05/2021 (https://wildwalks-southwest.co.uk/wild-food-wood-sorrel-family/), and Diego Bonetto, 'How to identify and eat wood Sorrel', 10/08/2021 (https://www.diegobonetto.com/blog/wood-sorrel-id-forage-edible-weed) — both name O. corniculata among the species they describe. Lambert says all of them have a lemony, tart flavour and uses them in salads, in soups and as an edible decoration; Bonetto says the stalks, flowers and leaves are eaten raw or cooked, in salads and as a garnish; recorded here for edibleParts and preparation, which were empty on creeping-wood-sorrel when this was written (15/10/2026).

summary.text:
Oxalis incarnata is a species of flowering plant in the woodsorrel family known by the common names pale pink-sorrel and crimson woodsorrel. It is native to southern Africa, but it can be found on other continents where it is an introduced species, often the descendant of garden escapees. It is grown and kept as an ornamental plant.
In New Zealand: North Island: especially common in coastal towns and cities; South Island: from Marlborough to Southland, but never more than locally common south of Marlborough, occasional on the West Coast; Stewart Island: Halfmoon Bay. Naturalised from South Africa, first recorded in 1944.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

identification.text:
Prostrate to low-growing shrub up to about 15 cm tall or more, forming extensive dense patches; branches decumbent to ascending; branchlets close-set, minutely puberulous when young, densely clad in erect imbricate leaves. Lamina sessile or subsessile, coriaceous, glabrous, usually brownish green above, paler below, finely nerved, about 4–9 × 1–2 mm., obovate-oblong; margins scarious to cartilaginous, finely ciliolate; abruptly narrowed to pungent tip about 2 mm long. Inflorescence of axillary solitary sessile flowers; bracts minute, apiculate. Flowers small; calyx-lobes acute. Corolla-tube cylindric. longer than twice length calyx; lobes short, acute, densely hairy on upper surfaces. Fruit orange to yellow, broad-oblong in outline, 8–9 mm long.
[From:  Allan  (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1 as Cyathodes fraseri (A.Cunn.) Allan]

summary.text: Pātōtara (Styphelia nesophila), also called dwarf mingimingi, is a low, prickly heath of New Zealand and south-eastern Australia. New Zealand books long knew it as Cyathodes fraseri or Leucopogon fraseri. Its strongly scented white flowers appear from September to January, often on the plant at the same time as the fruit. The berries were once a favourite sweet treat of Māori and Pākehā children, and the scraped root and the flowers went into traditional Māori scents. Other recorded Māori names include tōpara papa, tōtara pārae and tōtara tahuna. The name pātōtara has also been recorded for prickly mingimingi and for the parsley fern. In gardens it is easily grown from fresh seed.

warnings: Every leaf ends in a fine, sharp point about 2 mm long, so the mats are prickly to kneel on or reach into.

identification.text: A mass 4–20 cm across of dense branches that keep dividing into smaller ones, each ending in many tooth- or icicle-like spines. There is no cap and no gills. On larger fruit bodies the spines hang neatly downwards; on young ones they may point in all directions. Cream-white to light pink when young; with age it may take on pink tints and turns brown from the tips. Watery orange-brown droplets are sometimes held among the branches. The spore print is white.

preparation.text: Cook it before eating. Slice it and pan-fry in butter or oil until golden; it also goes into pasta, risotto and chowder. Young, white fruit bodies are best — older ones with yellowing spines can turn slightly bitter.

recipes.method: 400 g pekepeke-kiore; 30–45 ml (2–3 tbsp) butter or olive oil; 2 garlic cloves, minced; salt and pepper. Cut the fungus into 3 mm slices. Heat the butter or oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat, then lay the slices in a single layer. Cook for 2–4 minutes until they start to brown, turn them and brown the other side, adding the garlic for the last 1–2 minutes. Season with salt and pepper and serve straight away.

summary.text: A white, much-branched fungus whose branches end in hanging, icicle-like spines, growing on dead wood in native forest. Its Māori name is pekepeke-kiore, and it is also called fungus icicles. New Zealand records were long filed under Hericium coralloides and H. clathroides. Growers in New Zealand sell it as 'NZ lion's mane', but it is a different species from lion's mane (Hericium erinaceus).

warnings: Some people react badly even to edible mushrooms, so eat only a small amount the first time you try one.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Common to abundant in wet pastures, by rivers and lakesides, also in drier places, including bare lava and backs of sandy beaches.
It is mainly a weed of moist pastures and lawns. It tolerates some summer dryness but takes over only where rain is reliable for much of the year or the soil is poorly drained.

identification.text:
Perennial with prostrate creeping and ascending stems to about 30 cm long, hairy when aerial, glabrous when submerged. Leaves petiolate, sometimes shortly so; lamina of vegetative shoots usually 0.6–2 × 0.4–1 cm, ovate, elliptic to suborbicular, not rugose, entire or sparingly and shallowly toothed, usually glabrous when submerged, hairy and densely dotted with glands when aerial; base attenuate to rounded; apex rounded to acute. Leaves subtending the axillary verticels similar, but often smaller, hairy. Verticels axillary, spaced, with densely packed, shortly pedicellate flowers. Calyx about 3 mm long, campanulate, purple, hairy and dotted with glands outside, with prominent white hairy tuft in throat; teeth more or less forming 2 lips, acuminate, ciliate, shorter than the tube at anthesis. Corolla 4–6 mm long, mauve, hairy outside, well exserted. Stamens usually exserted at anthesis. Nutlets 0.5–0.6 mm long, bluntly angled, oblong.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The strong mint smell of the crushed foliage is the best way to recognise it. In flower, its purplish-blue flowers cluster around the bases of the leaves. The stems creep and root along the ground, with only the ends of flowering stems turning upright, and it forms dense mats in pasture and lawns. Out of flower it looks very like turf speedwell, which grows in the same places but has no mint smell.

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: pennyroyal smells strongly of mint; self-heal has no minty smell. Self-heal's flowers are usually violet, 10–15 mm long, in a dense head at the stem tip among broad bracts fringed with white hairs; pennyroyal's are mauve to purplish-blue, 4–6 mm long, packed in spaced rings in the joints of the leaves along the stem. Self-heal's leaves are larger, 1.7–6 cm long, puckered and coarsely hairy; pennyroyal's are usually 0.6–2 cm long, not puckered and dotted with glands. Both creep, root along the stems and form mats in damp lawns and pasture. Self-heal's leaves and flowers are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Self-heal

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: turf speedwell has no mint smell, pennyroyal smells strongly of mint. In flower, turf speedwell's flowers are pale blue fading to whitish, flat with four lobes, 3–5 mm across, up a spike at the stem tips; pennyroyal's mauve flowers, 4–6 mm long, crowd in rings around the stem at the leaf bases. Out of flower they look very alike: both creep and root along the ground, have small paired leaves of much the same shape and size, and grow in damp lawns and pasture. Turf speedwell's record as food is thin, so it is not given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Turf speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Smell does not separate them: crushed pennyroyal leaves have a very strong fragrance like spearmint. Look at where the flowers are: pennyroyal's are densely packed in spaced rings in the leaf joints along the stem, with a cluster of leaves at the shoot tip; spearmint's are in narrow spikes at the stem tips, the central spike 4–12 cm long. Pennyroyal's stems creep along the ground and ascend, to about 30 cm long; spearmint's ascend to about 80 cm. Pennyroyal's leaves are stalked, sometimes shortly, usually 0.6–2 cm long and not wrinkled; spearmint's are stalkless or very shortly stalked, 2.5–9 cm long, flat or wrinkled. Both have mauve flowers of similar size (pennyroyal's corolla 4–6 mm long, spearmint's 3–5 mm) and a purple or purplish calyx, so flower colour does not separate them, and both grow in damp grassy places. Wild spearmint's leaves are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Wild spearmint

lookalikes.howToTell: Smell does not separate them: crushed pennyroyal leaves have a very strong fragrance like spearmint. Apple mint is often spearmint-scented too. Look at where the flowers are: pennyroyal's are densely packed in spaced rings in the leaf joints along the stem, with a cluster of leaves at the shoot tip; apple mint's are in several narrow, densely hairy spikes at the stem tips, the central spike to about 8 cm long. Pennyroyal's stems creep along the ground and ascend, to about 30 cm long; apple mint's are erect, to about 70 cm tall. Pennyroyal's leaves are stalked, sometimes shortly, not wrinkled, usually 0.6–2 × 0.4–1 cm; apple mint's are stalkless or nearly so, broad, wrinkled, 1.5–4.5 × 0.8–3 cm, often grey-woolly beneath, with a heart-shaped or nearly heart-shaped base that often clasps the stem, so the smallest apple mint leaves overlap pennyroyal's in size. Pennyroyal's calyx is purple and its corolla mauve, 4–6 mm long; apple mint's calyx is more or less green and its corolla pale pink or whitish, 3–3.5 mm long. Both grow in pasture. Apple mint's leaves are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Apple mint

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: peppermint smells of peppermint, or of lemon in the bergamot-mint form; crushed pennyroyal leaves have a very strong fragrance like spearmint. Look at where the flowers are: peppermint's are in a rounded head or an oblong spike at the stem tips, often with a few separate whorls below; pennyroyal's are densely packed in spaced rings in the leaf joints along the stem, with a cluster of leaves at the shoot tip. Pennyroyal's stems creep along the ground and ascend, to about 30 cm long, and its leaves are usually 0.6–2 cm long; peppermint's leaves are 1–6 × 1–3.5 cm, so the smallest overlap. Both have a purple calyx and mauve flowers of similar size (peppermint's corolla 5–6 mm long, pennyroyal's 4–6 mm), so flower colour does not separate them, and both grow in wet places. Peppermint's leaves are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Peppermint

summary.text:
Mentha pulegium, commonly (European) pennyroyal, or pennyrile, also called mosquito plant and pudding grass, is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae, native to Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. Pennyroyal is a traditional folk remedy, emmenagogue, abortifacient, and culinary herb, but is toxic to the liver and has caused some deaths.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North, South and Stewart Islands. Naturalised from Europe, North Africa and Macaronesia, first recorded in 1883. Flowering November to May. Pennyroyal is so abundant in some pastures that they appear completely purple from a distance when it is flowering. It is disliked by some farmers because the strong aroma can taint milk.
Livestock avoid it, so it can take over damp pasture, and some people grow it in lawns for the smell when mowing.

warnings: Do not eat pennyroyal or make tea from it. It contains pulegone, which damages the liver. As little as 10 ml of the oil has caused moderate to severe liver damage, larger amounts have killed, and a baby given home-brewed mint tea from plants containing pennyroyal oil died of liver failure. It has a history as a flavouring and a tea, but safe amounts are not known.
It can cause miscarriage. Never use it in pregnancy.
Its crushed leaves smell strongly of mint. In damp lawns and pasture it grows among self-heal, so check every plant before picking (see the lookalikes).

edibleParts.text:
Leaves, raw or cooked, with a strong peppermint flavour, used as a flavouring in salads and cooked foods. Fresh or dried leaves make a herb tea, alone or with other herbs, and peppermint flavours ice cream, sweets and preserves. The leaves go well with new potatoes and strawberries and can be used sparingly in green and fruit salads.
The lemon-scented form, bergamot mint, has a very pungent flavour that is too aromatic for most tastes.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Streams, rivers, drains and lakes, particularly in still or slow-flowing water. Plants of peppermint are often submerged or partly so and may form dense stands. Bergamot mint grows around rivers, streams, drains and lakes, particularly in still or slow-moving water, and is often submerged or partly so.
Wetland status (NZPCN, from the national wetland plant list, Clarkson et al. 2021), for both varieties: facultative wetland — usually a wetland plant, occasionally found on dry ground.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous perennial; stems glabrous or sparsely hairy, to 60 cm or more tall, often submerged; aerial stems erect, often purple. Leaves very variable, petiolate; lamina 1–6 × 1–3.5 cm, lanceolate-elliptic, elliptic, oblong-ovate, ovate, or suborbicular, aerial leaves somewhat rugose, serrate, hairy or glabrous; base cuneate to rounded; apex sharply acute. Inflorescence of a terminal, more or less rounded head and 1–3 distinct verticels of shortly pedicellate flowers below, or an oblong spike, sometimes with 1–4 distinct verticels below, often glabrous except for calyx teeth. Calyx 3–4 mm long, tubular, purple, dotted with oil glands; teeth equal, ciliate, narrow-acuminate, much shorter than tube at anthesis. Corolla 5–6 mm long, mauve or lilac, glabrous; tube exserted. Stamens small, included. Nutlets not formed. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Leaves usually distinctly petiolate, sometimes subsessile on shoots in water, peppermint- or lemon-scented.
Var. piperita (peppermint): Leaves on flowering shoots elliptic-lanceolate or narrow-elliptic, sometimes elliptic, smelling of peppermint when bruised; inflorescence oblong or broad-oblong, nearly always longer than wide, rarely interrupted.
Var. citrata (bergamot mint): Leaves on flowering shoots broad-ovate or sometimes broadly oblong-ovate, lemon-scented when bruised; inflorescence subglobose or at least head-like, sometimes interrupted with lowest verticels discrete. Bergamot mint is more like M. aquatica than var. piperita, but lacks the hairy pedicels and calyx of this parent, as well as the exserted stamens.

lookalikes.howToTell: No single character separates every plant, so use several together. Peppermint's leaves usually have a distinct stalk, though shoots growing in water can have nearly stalkless leaves; spearmint's are stalkless or very shortly stalked. Crush a leaf: peppermint smells of peppermint, or of lemon in the bergamot-mint form; spearmint is not peppermint- or lemon-scented and often smells of spearmint. Peppermint's calyx is 3–4 mm long and its mauve or lilac corolla 5–6 mm long; spearmint's calyx is 1.5–2.2(–3.5) mm long and its mauve or pinkish corolla 3–5 mm long, so the largest spearmint flowers overlap. Peppermint's flowers are in a rounded head or an oblong spike, often with a few separate whorls below; spearmint's are in narrow spikes, the central one 4–12 cm long. Both have a purple calyx, both often have purplish or red-tinged stems, and their leaf sizes overlap (peppermint 1–6 × 1–3.5 cm, spearmint 2.5–9 × 0.7–2 cm), so these do not separate them. Peppermint is a hybrid of spearmint and water mint, and both hybridise freely with other mints, so in-between plants occur. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Wild spearmint

lookalikes.howToTell: No single character separates every plant, so use several together. Apple mint's calyx is more or less green and 1.5–2.5 mm long, and its corolla pale pink or whitish, 3–3.5 mm long; peppermint's calyx is purple and 3–4 mm long, and its corolla mauve or lilac, 5–6 mm long. Apple mint is densely hairy, its leaves often grey-woolly at least beneath; peppermint's stems are hairless or sparsely hairy and its leaves hairy or hairless. Apple mint's leaves are stalkless or nearly so, with a heart-shaped or nearly heart-shaped base that often clasps the stem; peppermint's usually have a distinct stalk (nearly stalkless on some shoots in water) and a tapered to rounded base. Crush a leaf: peppermint smells of peppermint, or of lemon in the bergamot-mint form; apple mint is not peppermint- or lemon-scented and has a fruity, minty flavour. Their leaf sizes overlap (apple mint 1.5–4.5 × 0.8–3 cm, peppermint 1–6 × 1–3.5 cm), so size does not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Apple mint

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: peppermint smells of peppermint, or of lemon in the bergamot-mint form; crushed pennyroyal leaves have a very strong fragrance like spearmint. Look at where the flowers are: peppermint's are in a rounded head or an oblong spike at the stem tips, often with a few separate whorls below; pennyroyal's are densely packed in spaced rings in the leaf joints along the stem, with a cluster of leaves at the shoot tip. Pennyroyal's stems creep along the ground and ascend, to about 30 cm long, and its leaves are usually 0.6–2 cm long; peppermint's leaves are 1–6 × 1–3.5 cm, so the smallest overlap. Both have a purple calyx and mauve flowers of similar size (peppermint's corolla 5–6 mm long, pennyroyal's 4–6 mm), so flower colour does not separate them, and both grow in wet places. Pennyroyal is poisonous to the liver; do not eat it.
