summary.text:
Raspberry (Rubus idaeus), also called red raspberry, is a red-fruited bramble from the northern temperate regions and East Asia; many variants of it are grown in gardens.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1870. Flora of New Zealand (1988) lists it in the North Island at Hunua, Wellington City and the Hutt Valley, and in the South Island scattered through Canterbury's plains and foothills, Banks Peninsula and Mt Cook, at Gabriels Gully, Beaumont and Skippers in Otago, and in Southland's Eglinton Valley.

warnings: Safety of raspberry-leaf tea in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and its use at those times is not recommended.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Never pull seaweed off by its base: trim it with scissors and leave enough on the rock for it to regrow.
Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.

identification.text: A moderately sized red seaweed made of wiry, tubular strands: a reddish-brown, spaghetti-like plant that often grows from a small holdfast on a shell or a piece of wood buried in sand. A second species, Agarophyton transtasmanicum, also grows in New Zealand estuaries, sometimes in the same places, and looks the same: the two differ only in the cells inside the strands and are told apart under a microscope or by DNA.

summary.text:
Red straw weed (Agarophyton chilense, formerly Gracilaria chilensis) is a native red seaweed found along the North and South Islands, Stewart Island and the Chatham Islands. The same species, called pelillo, grows in Chile.
Until 2020 it was not told apart from Agarophyton transtasmanicum, a look-alike from Australia and New Zealand, so older New Zealand records under its name may include that species.
It is one of New Zealand's agar seaweeds, but little has been taken here: about 3 tonnes between 2006 and 2018. Its growth is seasonal, with the most in summer.
It is assessed as Not Threatened and is secure in other parts of its range.

warnings: Harvest only from clean water — never near stormwater drains or sewage or industrial outfalls, in harbours, or where there is heavy boat traffic.

Other Gracilaria seaweeds have caused rare fatal food poisonings overseas: one death in Japan in 1993 after a meal with ogonori (Gracilaria verrucosa), and eight deaths in the Philippines in 2002–2003, where Gracilaria edulis was one of two seaweeds behind the poisonings.

identification.text:
Erect, ± hairy annual herb to c. 80 cm high, but plants often only a few cm high in impoverished conditions. Stem angular, ± hairy when young, red, especially towards base. Petiole to c. 7 cm long, often reddish, usually hairy. Lamina extremely variable according to habitat, 2–11 × 1–7 cm (smaller in inflorescence and very depauperate plants), ovate or rhombic-ovate, usually glabrate beneath and becoming glabrous above; base narrow-cuneate to attenuate; apex obtuse, sometimes mucronate. Panicles green, with elongated main spike to c. 25 cm long at fruiting, with shorter spikes in axils of uppermost leaves, the leaves sometimes very reduced. Longer bracteoles 4–8 mm long, ovate, with long subulate green tip; shorter bracteoles similar. Flowers 4–5-merous; tepals very unequal, especially in female flowers; female flowers with 1–2 longer and 3 shorter tepals, the longer 2.5–3–(4) mm, ± oblong, keeled, gradually tapering to the sharply acute or short-acuminate apex. Fruit subglobose, circumscissile, usually with prominent neck, not exceeding tepals except for the 3 persistent stigmas. Seed 1–1.5 mm diameter, lenticular, dark brown or black.
Told from Amaranthus retroflexus, also called redroot, best by the tip of the female flowers' tepals: sharply acute or short-acuminate in this plant, more or less truncate to rounded and cuspidate in A. retroflexus. In A. retroflexus the short side branches of the flower spike are densely arranged up the main spike; in this plant they are usually all towards its base, though this is not of much use for stunted plants in very poor soil.
In the field the flower head is greenish-brown and feels prickly from the sharp tips of the floral parts, and the first true leaf of seedlings has a notch at its tip.

lookalikes.howToTell: The best character is the tip of the female flowers' tepals: redroot's taper gradually to a sharply acute or short-acuminate tip; redroot amaranth's are more or less truncate to rounded and cuspidate, ending in an abrupt small point. In redroot amaranth the short side branches of the flower spike are densely arranged up the main spike; in redroot they are usually all towards its base, though this is not of much use for stunted plants in very poor soil. Both have stems red towards the base and both are called redroot, so the red colour does not tell them apart. Redroot amaranth is eaten too, with the same nitrate caution; it is the one the Flora records as poisonous to stock.
lookalikes.name: Redroot amaranth

lookalikes.howToTell: Prostrate amaranth's stems lie on or along the ground, often forming large mats, where redroot stands upright. Its flower spikes are not prickly: the bracteoles are only 1–2 mm long, against redroot's 4–8 mm with a long, fine green tip. Its fruit is 1.5–2 times as long as the tepals and does not split open; redroot's does not exceed the tepals and splits around the middle like a lid. Prostrate amaranth is eaten too.
lookalikes.name: Prostrate amaranth

lookalikes.howToTell: Purple amaranth is hairless and spreading, with stems lying along the ground, where redroot stands upright. At least most of purple amaranth's leaves have a notched tip with a small point in the notch; redroot's leaf tips are blunt, sometimes with a small point, though its first seedling leaf is notched. Purple amaranth's flower spikes are not prickly: its bracteoles are under 1 mm long and it has 3 tepals 1–2 mm long, against redroot's 4–8 mm bracteoles and 4–5 tepals, the longer 2.5–4 mm. Purple amaranth is eaten too.
lookalikes.name: Purple amaranth

summary.text:
Redroot is an upright summer annual weed of the amaranth family (Amaranthaceae), native to the south-western United States and northern Mexico and introduced to New Zealand. It is also called Powell's amaranth, and sometimes pigweed or Prince of Wales feather.
It was first recorded wild here in 1940 and is locally common to abundant throughout the North and South Islands. It has long been naturalised but has been confused with other species: the common name redroot is also applied to the closely related Amaranthus retroflexus, and plants of A. powellii have often been named A. hybridus, which is rare in New Zealand. It causes nitrate poisoning in stock but is also known as a potherb. It prefers warmer conditions than many summer annuals, dies off with the frosts of late autumn, and is most troublesome in the North Island.

warnings: It causes nitrate poisoning in stock. Amaranths, as a genus, concentrate nitrates in their leaves when grown on nitrogen-rich soil, especially where chemical fertilisers are used, so do not eat plants from fertilised ground.

Redroot amaranth (Amaranthus retroflexus), also called redroot, is often confused with this plant. It is eaten the same way, with the same nitrate caution, and has killed cattle in New Zealand; tell them apart by the tips of the female flowers' tepals (see the lookalikes).

identification.text: Hairy, erect, annual herb to c. 1 m high, but very variable in size; stems reddish towards base, densely hairy above. Petioles c. 5 cm long. Lamina 2–10 × 1–4.5 cm, ovate-lanceolate, becoming glabrous above; veins persistently hairy below; margin undulate, usually ciliate; base cuneate; apex obtuse. Inflorescence dense, spike-like, to c. 20 cm high, with numerous short lateral branches. Longer bracteoles 4–5 mm long, lanceolate-subulate with green keel; shorter bracteoles similar. Tepals 4–5, 2–2.7–(3) mm long, oblong; keel green; apex ± truncate to rounded and cuspidate. Fruit broadly ellipsoid, circumscissile, with rounded apex, included within persistent perianth except for stigma apices. Seed 1–1.3 mm diameter, suborbicular or broadly ovoid, dark brown.

In redroot amaranth the short side branches of the flower spike are densely arranged up the main spike; in redroot they are usually all towards its base, though this is not of much use for stunted plants in very poor soil. Both have stems red towards the base and both are called redroot, so the red colour does not tell them apart. Both are eaten, with the same nitrate caution.

summary.text:
Redroot amaranth is a hairy, upright annual weed of the amaranth family (Amaranthaceae), from tropical America and introduced to New Zealand.
It was first recorded wild here in 1869, and is widespread in the South Island; in the North Island it has been collected wild at Te Kuiti, Lake Wairarapa and Lower Hutt and photographed in a Whanganui railyard. It is related to redroot (Amaranthus powellii), which shares its common name, and the two are often confused. It is recorded as poisonous to stock: it has killed cattle in New Zealand and pigs overseas through kidney damage, and it is high in oxalate and can build up nitrate. Its young leaves and seeds are eaten.

warnings: It has killed cattle in New Zealand and pigs overseas through kidney damage. It is high in oxalate and builds up nitrate, so eat it only in moderation and do not pick it from fertilised ground.

It is often confused with redroot (Amaranthus powellii), which is eaten the same way and carries the same nitrate caution. Tell them apart by the tips of the female flowers' tepals (see the lookalikes).

identification.text: Forms mats of finely and repeatedly branched stalks 2–6 cm tall with a distinctly cobwebby surface. The branching is mostly in threes, and the joints where the branches part have a clear hole. The branch tips gather into rounded, distinct heads, greenish to greenish-yellow. Fruiting bodies, when present, are dark brown convex knobs at the tips. The only other reindeer lichen in New Zealand, Cladonia mitis, branches unequally and grows in subalpine to alpine grassland and shrubland, and the two also differ in their chemistry.

summary.text: A native reindeer lichen — a lichen, not a moss — that forms pale, finely branched mats on the ground. It is very widely distributed in New Zealand, from the Three Kings Islands to Campbell Island, and also grows in south-eastern Australia, Tasmania, Africa, Madagascar and Central and South America. It is assessed Not Threatened.

warnings: Not known as a food: no source records this lichen being eaten. The reindeer lichen eaten overseas after soaking out its bitterness (Cladonia rangiferina) is a different species and is not recorded in New Zealand. This one contains usnic acid.

identification.text: A robust evergreen herb with short rhizomes up to 3 cm across and fleshy roots; the leaf bases are fibrous. Leaves 20–100 cm long and 3–5 cm wide, narrow, smooth, fleshy and green, spreading, with a pointed tip and smooth edges; the base narrows into a channelled stalk up to 20 mm wide, and the midrib is raised on the underside. The branched flower stem is up to 1 m long and rises above the leaves, with a leafy bract under each side branch. Flowers sit singly or in clusters of 2–4, each above a small bract 6–8 mm long and 2–4.5 mm wide that is undivided with a pointed tip and curls back or recoils; these bracts are green to red-purple and turn papery in fruit. Flower stalks 20–24 mm long and jointed, white above the joint and often flushed red-purple. The six tepals are free and white: the outer three narrow and pointed, 13–19 mm long and often flushed red-purple on the back; the inner three broader, 17–18 mm long, blunt, with finely toothed edges. Filaments white; the hairy stamen appendages are 5.5–9 mm long, mauve or purple where they are joined to the filament, with a yellow, curled free end. Capsule (8–)12–14 mm long and 5.5–9.5 mm wide, cylindrical to egg-shaped, green and sometimes flushed red, splitting when ripe. Seeds 1.3–2.5 mm across, black and finely bumpy.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the small bract under each flower: Arthropodium bifurcatum's are two-forked (rarely with 1 or 3–4 lobes), 4.0–5.9 mm wide, and only slightly recurved, never recoiled; rengarenga's are undivided with a single pointed tip (an occasional bract has a small notch on one side), 2.0–4.5 mm wide, and recoil when the flower opens. Where the hairy stamen appendages are joined to the filament they are white, or rarely pale lavender, in Arthropodium bifurcatum, and mauve or purple in rengarenga; the free, curled ends are yellow in both. Arthropodium bifurcatum's leaves are thicker, fleshy and upright, often bluish-grey when young, with a prominent white, fleshy midrib, and are 40–120 cm long and 4–11 cm wide; rengarenga's spread from the base and are floppy or slightly limp, with a slender midrib, and are 20–100 cm long and 3–5 cm wide. Leaf size overlaps and varies with growing conditions, and the difference in leaf angle is clearest when the two grow side by side and on young plants, so go by the bracts and stamens. Capsules overlap too: usually (10–)12–15 mm long in Arthropodium bifurcatum and 8–12 mm (sometimes 14 mm) in rengarenga. Both are robust evergreen herbs of northern coastal rocks and cliffs with white flowers, and they grow together at a number of places. No record of Arthropodium bifurcatum as food was found; see its page.

summary.text: Rengarenga (Arthropodium cirratum), also called renga lily, rock lily or māikaika, is an evergreen perennial herb of the asparagus family (Asparagaceae), endemic to New Zealand. It grows on the North and South Islands north of about latitude 42° 30′ S, primarily on the coast; its natural range is thought to lie north of about 38° S, and the populations further south, often near Māori archaeological sites, are thought to come from translocation. Māori brought it into cultivation within the last 700–800 years for its fleshy, edible roots, and it is very widely grown in gardens today. Garden clumps can be divided in spring. Its seeds are spread by wind. Its national conservation status (2023) is Not Threatened. Arthropodium bifurcatum, a separate species of northern coasts and offshore islands that grows alongside rengarenga at a number of places, was split from it in 2004; it is At Risk – Declining and is sold in nurseries under A. cirratum cultivar names. In gardens A. bifurcatum has partly taken rengarenga's place, as slugs and snails damage it less.

warnings: Eat the roots cooked: the food records are for roots cooked in an earth oven or roasted, and none covers eating them raw.

habitat.text: Blechnum chambersii is a terrestrial fern found under kauri, podocarp, broadleaved or beech forest, under mānuka, kānuka and coastal scrub, and under Salix species in swampy areas. It grows in rock crevices, under overhangs, on damp rock walls, near waterfalls, on rocky banks and roadside banks, on the forest floor, on stream banks in wet gullies, and rarely as a low epiphyte, usually favouring shaded habitats.

identification.text: Rhizomes erect, up to 70 mm long (in herbarium material), bearing scales. Rhizome scales linear to narrowly ovate, 5–12 mm long, 0.4–0.7 mm wide, dark brown, concolorous. Fronds strongly dimorphic; sterile fronds 120–700 mm long, forming a prostrate to suberect rosette; fertile fronds on same plant usually a little shorter, 85–620 mm long, positioned centrally, held erect. Sterile fronds. Stipes 10–140 mm long, red-brown, bearing a few scales proximally. Rachises yellow-brown, grooved adaxially, glabrous. Laminae 80–600 mm long, 15–115 mm wide, or very rarely to 125 mm wide, deeply pinnatifid to pinnatisect, narrowly elliptic to narrowly obovate, with a short apical segment, similar colour on both surfaces, red-tinged when young, herbaceous to coriaceous, glabrous. Pinnae in 7–54 pairs, closely spaced, narrowly oblong or narrowly triangular or triangular, straight or falcate, gradually reducing to short, rounded flanges at the lamina base; the longest pinnae at or above the middle, 14–60 mm long, or very rarely only 8 mm long or up to 68 mm long, 6–15 mm wide, or rarely only 4 mm wide, apices usually acute or rarely obtuse, margins shallowly crenate, bases adnate; the basal pinnae sub-opposite or alternate. Veins free. Fertile fronds. Stipes 20–250 mm long. Laminae 40–530 mm long, 10–70 mm wide. Pinnae in 15–52 pairs, linear, straight or falcate, 5–40 mm long, 1–3 mm wide, reducing to tiny sterile flanges at the lamina base. Sori and indusia in one row either side of costa, continuous along the length of the pinna.

summary.text:
Rereti (lance fern, nini) is a tufted ground fern whose sterile fronds form a flat to slightly raised rosette, with the narrower fertile fronds held upright in the centre; young fronds are red-tinged. It is Blechnum chambersii in the Flora of New Zealand and Austroblechnum lanceolatum in the New Zealand Threat Classification System.
It grows in lowland and montane areas throughout the North Island and the South Island, except the drier parts of Otago and south Canterbury, from near sea level to 1100 m, and on the Chatham and Stewart Islands; also in south-eastern Australia. It is especially luxuriant in limestone country, often at cave entrances and under overhangs. It is the host species for the New Zealand endemic moth Batrachedra litterata. It is easily grown from fresh spores in deep, moist soil in shade, and responds well to regular applications of lime. Not Threatened (2023).

warnings: Only about seven of New Zealand's roughly 200 ferns are edible. Eat only young fronds you are sure are rereti.

harvestEthics.text:
Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.
It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. In the Auckland region it must not be bred, distributed, released, sold or planted, and Auckland Council controls it on Aotea / Great Barrier Island, where you should report it to pestfree@aucklandcouncil.govt.nz. It is also under sustained control in Northland. In Northland no one may sell, propagate or spread it, and land occupiers must destroy it where it is the source of wild seedlings, or within 5 m of a neighbour's home when that person's health is affected and they make a complaint with a medical certificate. Removing it is risky: Northland Regional Council recommends herbicide stem injection over pulling it out, and Auckland Council says trees over 4 m should be removed by a qualified arborist. If you do remove one, dig it out without letting any part touch your skin, take every part to green waste or landfill, don't burn it, and clean your tools afterwards.

identification.text: A deciduous, sometimes suckering small tree up to 8 m tall, male and female flowers on separate trees. Its sap is poisonous. Leaves alternate, pinnate, hairless, 20–40 cm long (longest on saplings), with 4–6 (rarely 7) pairs of leaflets and usually one at the end. Leaflets glossy, curved back to drooping, 6–8 × 1.5–2.5 (rarely 3) cm, narrowly oval to lance-shaped with a lopsided base and a long, drawn-out tip, dark green to grey-green above and often flushed red, often whitish beneath; untoothed on adult trees, but strongly toothed on seedlings. Leaf stalks, the central axis, the veins and the leaf undersides are often pink. The leaves turn orange, red or scarlet in autumn. Flowers minute, yellowish-green, in branched clusters 10–20 cm long that grow from the leaf angles. Fruit a fleshy, smooth, pale shiny brown, rounded and slightly flattened berry 7–10 mm across, in hanging clusters that stay on the tree through autumn and winter and fall in spring.

lookalikes.howToTell: Rhus tree is almost hairless, with glossy leaflets; staghorn sumac is very hairy, its young branches and leaf stalks covered in soft hairs, purple when young. Rhus tree's fruits are smooth, pale shiny brown berries 7–10 mm across, in hanging clusters from the angles of the leaves; staghorn sumac's stand upright at the ends of the branches as dense, cone-like heads up to about 20 cm long, of tiny fruits about 3 mm across covered in long crimson hairs. Adult rhus tree leaflets are untoothed and glossy, but seedlings' are strongly toothed; staghorn sumac's are toothed and dull. Rhus tree leaves have 4–6 (rarely 7) pairs of leaflets and usually one at the end; mature staghorn sumac leaves have 19–23. Both turn orange to red in autumn. If in doubt, don't touch it: rhus tree sap causes a severe rash.
lookalikes.name: Staghorn sumac

lookalikes.howToTell: Rhus tree is a smaller tree, to 8 m, with smaller, hairless leaves 20–40 cm long, often pink along the stalk and veins; Japanese walnut grows to about 15 m and its leaves reach about 60 cm, the stalk and central axis densely covered in sticky glandular hairs. Adult rhus tree leaflets are glossy and untoothed (seedlings' are strongly toothed); Japanese walnut's are finely toothed, though the teeth are often sparse. Leaflet counts overlap, so don't count. Rhus tree's fruits are smooth, pale shiny brown berries 7–10 mm across; Japanese walnut's are 2.5–4 cm long, sticky, rusty-hairy and beaked, 10–22 together in long strings, each holding a hard nut. If in doubt, don't touch it: rhus tree sap causes a severe rash.
lookalikes.name: Japanese walnut

summary.text:
Rhus tree (Toxicodendron succedaneum), also called Japanese wax tree, wax tree or varnish tree, is a small deciduous tree of the cashew family (Anacardiaceae) from the Himalaya to Japan, formerly named Rhus succedanea. It was brought into New Zealand as an ornamental, grown for its brilliant autumn leaves, and has been naturalised since 1984.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): commonly planted in warmer parts of the country, and collected wild in open coastal forest on Middle Island (Mercury Group, Coromandel), as a garden weed in Auckland and on waste ground in Havelock North. It has since been collected wild at Te Puke, and in Northland it is scattered through gardens and appears to be naturalising, with seedlings and young trees along roadsides between Haruru Falls and Opua, at Russell, and from Riverside to Onerahi in Whangārei. Birds spread its seed, which stays viable for many years and also travels in moved soil, and it suckers.
Its sap causes a severe allergic skin rash in many people, and it has poisoned a number of people in New Zealand. It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds and is a pest under the Auckland and Northland regional pest management plans.

warnings: Do not eat it, and don't touch it with bare skin. Its sap can cause a severe allergic rash with blistering and intense itching, usually within 24 hours but sometimes up to a week later, lasting 10–14 days; some people have needed hospital care, while others are not affected. Some people react just from standing under or near a tree. Reactions can get stronger with each exposure. If a severe reaction develops, get medical attention.
Dead and fallen branches and leaves stay dangerous, and the resin can stay active on shoes, tools and clothes for up to a year. Never burn any part of it: the smoke causes the same reactions.
Some people in New Zealand call it 'sumac', and staghorn sumac and Japanese walnut grow in the same places. See Lookalikes.

habitat.text:
D. cupressinum's seedlings will not establish themselves where there is moderate to severe root competition and a moderately dense canopy because of low light intensities. The tree prefers sites with partial shade.
Lowland and montane forest, on Stewart Island ascending to subalpine scrub. Rimu usually favours better drained sites than kahikatea, but does grow in poorly drained soils in Westland.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

identification.text:
Rimu is a conifer usually 35 m tall, sometimes up to 60 m, with male and female cones on separate trees. The stout trunk is 1.5–2 m across and, on adult trees, bare of branches for about three-quarters of its length. The bark is dark brown and falls off in large, thick flakes, leaving a wavy pattern of raised ridges like the contour lines on a map; the wood is dark red. Young trees are pyramid-shaped, with many slender branches and hanging branchlets; adults have few, spreading branches with slender, drooping branchlets, and the crown becomes domed.
The leaves overlap along the branchlets and are dark green, bronze-green, red-green or orange. On juveniles they are 4–7 mm long (sometimes to 10 mm) and 0.5–1 mm wide, keeled, narrow, pointed and slightly sickle-shaped; on subadults they are ascending and incurved, 4–6 mm long; on adults they are pressed against the branchlet, rigid, three-sided and only 2–3 mm long, so the foliage feels firm and spiky.
Cones first appear on subadult trees, which often bear fruit before they reach the adult form. Male cones are oblong, 5–10 mm long, single or paired at the branch tips, with yellow pollen. Each female ovule sits alone at the tip of an up-curved branchlet; when ripe it becomes a fleshy red or deep-orange cup 1–2 mm long holding the seed. The seed is oblong, flattened, 3–4 mm long, semi-glossy and dark brown. The fruit takes a year or more to ripen, so ripe fruit and young female cones are often on the tree together.
Rimu is very distinctive and is not confused with any other native conifer. Only very young seedlings look a little like seedlings of silver pine (Manoao colensoi), whose leaves are coarser, fewer and glossy rather than fine, numerous and dull red-green.
Rimu usually lives 600–800 years and can reach 1000.

preparation.text: Eat the receptacles raw. For spruce beer, small branches of rimu and mānuka were boiled in water for two to four hours, until the bark stripped off easily; the branches were taken out, molasses or sugar added, the brew brought back to the boil, an equal quantity of cold water added, and yeast added once it was lukewarm, then left for a few days.

recipes.method: Written for rimu, from the beer James Cook's crew brewed at Dusky Sound, Fiordland, in March 1773, scaled down from their 10 gallons of molasses to 240 gallons of brew (1 part molasses to 24 parts brew). Boil small branches of rimu and mānuka in water for two to four hours, until the bark strips off the branches easily, to make a strong brew. Take the branches out. Stir in 100 ml molasses for every 2.4 litres of brew (sugar can be used instead; the record gives no amount for it) and bring it back to the boil. Pour it into a clean fermenting vessel with an equal volume of cold water. When the whole is lukewarm, add yeast and leave it for a few days.
recipes.title: Rimu spruce beer

summary.text:
Dacrydium cupressinum, commonly known as rimu, is a species of conifer in the family Podocarpaceae, native to New Zealand.
It is endemic, found on the North Island from North Cape south, the South Island and Stewart Island, but is uncommon in large parts of the eastern South Island; on Banks Peninsula one natural tree is all that remains. Other name: red pine.
It is assessed Not Threatened, but rimu forest has been greatly reduced by widespread logging, and very few intact rimu-dominated forests remain in the North Island. It is commonly sold by nurseries and is a popular garden tree.
The first published mention of the species, by Georg Forster in 1786, described it only for its use in beer making.
Dacrydium cupressinum is known for exhibiting mast seeding, which is the synchronised periodicity of seed production. In the Pureora Forest and the Wanganui Forest, in the North Island and the South Island, respectively, seedfall data show clear yearly fluctuations in seed production in studied specimens. A 1988 study proposes that a combination of low seed production and cool temperatures two years before, followed by warm temperatures during seedfall are necessary, but not solely responsible for triggering a mast year in the tree. The relationship between seed production in one year and conditions from two years earlier also plays an important role. Canham et al. 2014 analysed D. cupressinum specimens growing in less fertile marine terrace sites had a higher seed production rate in comparison to specimens that grew on more fertile alluvial soils. Researchers suggested that the tree has adapted to seed production in less fertile soils rather than being displaced by other species.
Rimu has a diploid chromosome count of 20.
In terms of chemical composition, the foliage of D. cupressinum contains various sesquiterpenes, with their levels showing significant variation between specimens, which is similar to the differences observed in diterpene levels. There are twelve known sesquiterpenes in the tree that have been identified by a 1985 study, but none of which show any structural similarity to lauren-1-ene. The distinctive diterpene lauren-1-ene was first discovered in the foliage of the tree, however, the concentration of this compound, along with other diterpenes, also shows significant variation between D. cupressinum specimens.
Dacrydium cupressinum contains high levels of the unique sesquiterpene terpene compounds of 9-epi-β-caryophyllene. The tree also has a distinctive flavonoid glycoside profile; the tree possesses flavonol-3-O-rhamnoglucosides and also, to a lesser extent, 3-0-methyl-myricetin glycoside compounds.

warnings: The fruit can be somewhat constipating.
Only the red receptacle is recorded as eaten. No record of the seed being eaten was found, so whether it is safe is not known.

associations.note: Recorded here under silver birch.
Recorded overseas with Salix babylonica, a weeping willow thought to be one of the parents of the hybrid weeping willow here.

habitat.text: It can be found in wet woodland — pond edges, boggy ground and stream banks — growing by poplars, silver birch, willows, alders or oaks. The New Zealand collections so far are under poplar, silver birch and goat willow.

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to pick this mushroom. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.

identification.text: The cap is up to 6 cm, bright blood-red, carmine, dark red or reddish brown, often fading with age to apricot or ochre, and it is often cracked. The pores are pale yellow with an olive tint. The stipe is yellow, usually with fine red granules towards the base. The flesh is pale yellow, often red at the base of the stipe, and stains blue when injured.

lookalikes.howToTell: Bluefoot bolete's cap is usually ochre to brown, grey-brown or blackish brown, though it can have a reddish tint or be entirely red; riverine bolete's is bright red, carmine, dark red or reddish brown, often fading with age to apricot or ochre with a reddish tint. Cap cracking and blueing do not separate them: both caps often crack, both stain blue, and colour and cracking tend to intergrade between species in this group. Habitat may help: about half of bluefoot's New Zealand collections are under oak, and others under cedar, lime, beech, pine and silver birch; riverine bolete grows in wet woodland, and its New Zealand collections are under poplar, goat willow and silver birch.

identification: boletales.com, 'Xerocomus ripariellus'. Copyright © boletales.com, all rights reserved — facts restated, no text reproduced. Cap to 6 cm, bright red to carmine or dark red, dry and velvety, cracking and fading to apricot or ochre; tubes and pores pale yellow with an olive tint, blueing when injured; stipe yellow with fine red granules towards the base, blueing; flesh pale yellow, often red at the stipe base, blueing on exposure; spores 11–15 × 4–5.5 µm, striate; wet woodland, presumed mycorrhizal with poplar, alder, willow or oak. Third machine-written page found for this species after PlantSnap; they are now the commonest kind of result for a fungus with no Wikipedia article, which is exactly the kind this catalogue has to fill. SEARCH EXHAUSTED — no openly licensed description of this species exists in English. Routes run and closed, so nobody runs them again: (1) Wikipedia, no article in any language except French, which the translation ruling bars. (2) The new-record-paper route, twice — the Chilean Salix babylonica inventory lists it without describing it, and Pluzhnyk A.V. & Prydiuk M.P. (2025), 'New records of agaricoid fungi from the Kholodnyi Yar National Nature Park', Ukrainian Botanical Journal 82(4): 291–305, DOI 10.15407/ukrbotj82.04.291, is CC BY 4.0 and open but published in Ukrainian and describes only the two species new to Ukraine. Its record is still a fact, and an awkward one: oak-hornbeam forest with lime and maple, on soil, 11.08.2021, the second Ukrainian record — dry upland woodland, not the riparian ground the name and every other source give. One collection, so it widens the habitat rather than replacing it. (3) GBIF's species description endpoint, empty for all ten taxon keys. (4) Mexia S., et al. (2025), 'The genus Xerocomellus (Boletales, Boletaceae) in Mexico', Phytotaxa 689(1): 1–14, DOI 10.11646/phytotaxa.689.1.1, CC BY-NC 4.0 and therefore quotable under the non-commercial ruling — but this species appears in it only twice, both times as a GenBank accession in a table. In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Forming small colonies in waste places, roadsides, pasture, and gardens.
In gardens it is grown in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil, kept out of waterlogged ground.

identification.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Sweetly aromatic, creeping, perennial herb. Stems decumbent to ascending, to about 20 cm tall, striate, moderately to densely hairy, much-branched from base. Basal and lower cauline leaves apetiolate, obovate, sparsely to moderately hairy, 3-pinnatisect, 15–50 × 5–15 mm; ultimate segments narrow-linear to subulate, entire, not all in one plane giving a feathery appearance; cauline leaves few, smaller than basal, oblong and becoming 1-pinnatisect. Involucral bracts sparsely hairy, 2–5 mm long; margins pale, membranous, often with an extended membranous flap at apex. Capitula solitary, about 8–20–(30) mm diameter; ray florets 13–20, female; ligules white; disc florets numerous, yellow. Receptacle scales elliptic-oblong, obtuse and often irregular at apex. Achenes 1.1–1.2 mm long, narrow-obovoid, narrowed to apex, brown, with 1–4 narrow ribs on inner surface.
Chamomile may be distinguished from Anthemis arvensis and A. cotula when mature achenes are not present, by the apex of the receptacle scales which is blunt and often irregular in C. nobile and acute to acuminate and entire in the 2 Anthemis species.
Although the plant is often confused with German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla), its morphology, properties and chemical composition are markedly different.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have scales between the florets, so check their tips with a hand lens: Roman chamomile's are blunt and often ragged at the tip, stinking mayweed's narrow and pointed. Crushed stinking mayweed smells strongly foetid; Roman chamomile is sweetly aromatic. Stinking mayweed's stems stand upright or rise from the base, usually 30–40 cm tall but from 5 cm to 60 cm; Roman chamomile creeps, its stems lying along the ground or rising to about 20 cm — so a small stinking mayweed can be as short. Stinking mayweed's stems range from almost hairless to moderately hairy and Roman chamomile's from moderately to densely hairy, so hairiness does not separate them; both have white rays around a yellow disc and feathery leaves. Stinking mayweed is not eaten in this guide: its acrid juice can blister skin and it has been reported as toxic.
lookalikes.name: Stinking mayweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Pineappleweed has no white rays — its heads are a dome of dull yellow to greenish-yellow florets, 4–10 mm across; Roman chamomile has 13–20 white rays around a yellow disc. Pineappleweed has no scales on its receptacle; Roman chamomile does. Pineappleweed's stems stand upright or rise from the base and are hairless or carry a few hairs below the heads; Roman chamomile's creep and are moderately to densely hairy. Pineappleweed's leaf segments lie more or less in one plane; Roman chamomile's do not, which makes its leaves look feathery. Crushed pineappleweed smells of pineapple, Roman chamomile sweetly aromatic. Pineappleweed's flower heads and leaves are eaten and made into tea.
lookalikes.name: Pineappleweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Common lawn daisy's leaves all grow in a basal rosette and are spoon-shaped to oval with a few rounded teeth and one main vein; Roman chamomile's leaves are divided three times into narrow, feathery segments. Lawn daisy's flower heads sit singly on hairy, leafless stalks from the rosette; Roman chamomile's stems are leafy, though the stem leaves are few and smaller than the basal ones. Lawn daisy's white rays are often tinged pink to reddish purple underneath or at the tip; Roman chamomile's are white — but a pure white head can still be a lawn daisy. Both grow in lawns and pasture, and their flower heads overlap in size (lawn daisy 15–25 mm, Roman chamomile 8–20 mm, up to 30), so place and size do not separate them. Common lawn daisy is eaten — its young leaves, flower buds and petals (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Common lawn daisy

lookalikes.howToTell: Yarrow carries many small flower heads, 5–10 mm across (as small as 3.5 mm), packed into a flat-topped or slightly domed cluster up to about 15 cm across, each head with only 4–7 rays, and its central florets are usually white as well; Roman chamomile carries its heads singly, 8–20 mm across (up to 30), with 13–20 white rays around a yellow disc. Yarrow's flowers can also be pink to deep red or purple. Yarrow's basal leaves are 6–15 cm long (up to 44), with 18–30 pairs of primary leaflets; Roman chamomile's are 15–50 mm. Yarrow's flowering stems are usually upright, up to about 80 cm; Roman chamomile's lie along the ground or rise to about 20 cm. Both have scales on the receptacle, feathery leaves and a scent, and both grow in lawns, so these do not separate them. Yarrow's young leaves are eaten in small amounts, and its leaves and flowers are made into tea (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Yarrow

lookalikes.howToTell: Roman chamomile is a low, creeping, sweetly aromatic, hairy perennial up to about 20 cm; scentless chamomile is an almost scentless, usually hairless annual or biennial with erect or ascending stems 15–100 cm tall. Roman chamomile has small, blunt scales among its florets; scentless chamomile has none. Roman chamomile's heads are about 8–20 mm across (up to 30 mm), scentless chamomile's about 30–50 mm. What does not separate them: leaves cut three times into narrow, feathery segments, and white rays around a yellow disc. There is no record of scentless chamomile being eaten or used for tea.
lookalikes.name: Scentless chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: Ox-eye daisy's flowering stems stand erect, up to about 1 m; Roman chamomile is a low, creeping, sweetly aromatic perennial whose hairy stems lie along the ground or rise to about 20 cm. Ox-eye's leaves are coarsely toothed, scalloped or shallowly lobed, the basal ones up to 12 cm long (rarely 18 cm); Roman chamomile's are cut three times into narrow segments with a feathery look, 15–50 mm long. Ox-eye's receptacle has no scales among the florets; Roman chamomile's carries small, blunt scales. Heads: ox-eye's are usually 30–60 mm across (25–65 mm at the extremes), Roman chamomile's about 8–20 mm (up to 30 mm), so they meet only between 25 and 30 mm. What does not separate them: white rays around a yellow disc, and place — both grow on roadsides, waste places and pasture. Ox-eye daisy is eaten — its young leaves and shoots, flower buds and flower heads (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Ox-eye daisy

preparation.text: Gather the flower heads when fully open and dry them; keep them no longer than 12 months. Make the tea in a covered vessel so the essential oil is not lost. For tea, 1–4 g of dried flower heads is infused in 100–150 ml of boiling water; adults take it 3 times a day between meals.

summary.text:
Chamaemelum nobile — chamomile, also called garden chamomile, perennial chamomile or Roman chamomile — is a low, creeping, sweetly aromatic perennial herb. It is exotic in New Zealand and grows wild here.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: scattered localities, commonest in Auckland and Northland; South Island: Nelson, Westland, one early collection from Bluff. (Western Europe, North Africa, Azores; first recorded 1867.) Chamomile has been previously recorded in New Zealand as Anthemis nobilis and A. mixta. C. nobile is widely cultivated as a lawn plant, and the florets are also used to make chamomile tea - it is sometimes known as perennial chamomile or as Roman chamomile.
New Zealand herbarium specimens come from North Auckland, South Auckland, Taranaki, Wellington, Nelson, Westland and Canterbury, so it has also been collected in Canterbury, outside the range the Flora gives.
New Zealand nurseries sell it for chamomile lawns, for planting between paving stones and for herb and cottage gardens; it can replace a lawn where foot traffic is light.

warnings: Do not use it if you are allergic to plants of the daisy family (Asteraceae). Allergic reactions to chamomile are commonly reported, including anaphylaxis after chamomile tea, and people allergic to ragweed, asters or chrysanthemums can cross-react.
Use in pregnancy and breastfeeding is not recommended: its safety has not been established.
Large doses of the single-flowered form can damage the lining of the stomach and bowels, and large amounts of the dried flower heads are reported to cause vomiting.

edibleParts.text: Flowers - raw. Added to salads. The leaves are rose-scented and are used as a flavouring in desserts, jellies, vinegars etc. As a flavoring, the flowers and leaves are used in cakes, jams, jellies, ice creams, sorbets, salads, sugars, and teas.

identification.text:
Soft-wooded subshrub up to about 75 cm tall, strongly aromatic, densely hairy. Stems with hairs deflexed. Stipules about 1 cm long, ovate, acuminate. Petioles of lower leaves to longer than 8 cm long. Lamina to about 7 × 10 cm on flowering plants, more or less triangular, deeply divided into 3 lobes; lobes toothed and sinuate, rough above; 2 side lobes to about 2 cm across, each with a secondary lobe near base; terminal lobe to about 2.5 cm across, with a pair of secondary lobes. Umbels about 10-flowered, densely covered in glandular hairs; peduncles 2–6 cm long; pedicels 1–6 mm long. Sepals 8–12 mm long, elliptic-lanceolate, green, densely hairy; calyx spur about 3 mm long. Corolla pink; upper 2 petals 1–1.6 × 0.5–0.8 cm, with more or less prominent purple markings and white central patch, and claw well developed; lower 3 petals 0.9–1.4 × 0.25–0.5 cm, with purple median line in lower 1/2, and claw not well differentiated. Style and stigmas becoming rose. Mericarps not seen.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Its parents are P. graveolens Aiton, which has a soft leaf indumentum and broader leaf lobes, and P. radens H. Moore (often known as P. radula) which has finely dissected leaves with linear lobes.

lookalikes.howToTell: Peppermint geranium is a subshrub to about 75 cm that smells strongly of peppermint, with more or less velvety white hairs and broad leaves up to 12 × 15 cm, rather shallowly three-lobed, the lobes reaching a quarter to half way to the midrib; its flowers are white or pinkish, 5–8 to an umbel, on stalks 2–3.5 cm long that generally radiate widely, with a calyx spur about 2 mm long. Rose geranium (P. ×asperum) is a strongly aromatic, densely hairy subshrub to about 75 cm, with more or less triangular leaves up to about 7 × 10 cm that are deeply divided into 3 toothed lobes, lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib and rough above; its pink flowers, the upper 2 petals with more or less prominent purple markings and a white central patch, sit about 10 to an umbel on stalks 1–6 mm long, with a calyx spur about 3 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates rose geranium by its leaves (lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib; a quarter to half way in peppermint geranium), and the two descriptions also differ in the flower stalks (1–6 mm against 2–3.5 cm). Peppermint geranium's flowers are white or pinkish, rose geranium's pink, so a pink flower does not separate them. A crushed leaf of peppermint geranium smells strongly of peppermint; Flora of New Zealand calls rose geranium only "strongly aromatic". The leaf test works without flowers.
lookalikes.name: Peppermint geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Rose-scented geranium is a sprawling plant whose leaves are strongly undulate and velvety, generally lobed more than half way to the midrib, with more or less oblong lobes; its pink flowers, the larger upper pair of petals marked purple, sit in dense heads on almost no stalks, with a calyx spur 4–5 mm long. Rose geranium (P. ×asperum) is a strongly aromatic, densely hairy subshrub to about 75 cm, with more or less triangular leaves up to about 7 × 10 cm that are deeply divided into 3 toothed lobes, lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib and rough above; its pink flowers, the upper 2 petals with more or less prominent purple markings and a white central patch, sit about 10 to an umbel on stalks 1–6 mm long, with a calyx spur about 3 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates rose geranium first, by leaves lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib; rose-scented geranium's lobes reach at least half way, and the key's other branch says "lobed to < 1/2 way", so a leaf cut between half and three-quarters is not decided by lobing alone. The calyx spur is a little longer in rose-scented geranium (4–5 mm against about 3 mm). Both have short-stalked heads of pink flowers with purple-marked upper petals, so the flowers do not separate them; rose geranium's leaves are described as rough above, rose-scented geranium's as velvety. Smell does not separate them: rose geranium is strongly aromatic and rose-scented geranium's scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. Flora of New Zealand notes that P. ×asperum is a hybrid of P. graveolens and P. radens; Wikipedia says P. capitatum hybridises readily, so in-between plants are possible and this card may not decide them.
lookalikes.name: Rose-scented geranium

preparation.text: The fresh leaves are brewed into a tea. The leaves are mostly used to scent food and then taken out: a leaf added to apple jelly as it boils, or a green sprig dropped into a syrup, custard or jelly and lifted out as soon as it thickens, before the leaves break up; leaves can also be layered in sugar or flour to flavour baking. Finely chopped leaves can be flecked through cakes, biscuits and puddings — 15–30 ml (1–2 tablespoons) of chopped leaves is enough for most dishes that serve six. Use them sparingly so they do not overwhelm a dish.

recipes.method: 250 ml water; 200 g sugar; 10–12 rose geranium leaves. Put 250 ml water, 200 g sugar and 10–12 rose geranium leaves in a small saucepan, bruising the leaves against the side of the pan with a spoon. Bring to the boil over moderate heat, cover, take off the heat and leave to stand for at least 30 minutes. Lift out the leaves and squeeze them into the syrup. Keeps in the fridge for up to a month, or frozen for up to a year. The source uses it in a chocolate dessert.
recipes.title: Rose geranium syrup

recipes.method: About 125 ml fresh rose geranium leaves and tender stems, firmly packed; 750 ml apple juice; one packet of powdered fruit pectin; 1.2 kg sugar. Firmly pack about 125 ml of fresh rose geranium leaves and tender stems. Bring them to the boil with part of 750 ml apple juice, take off the heat and steep for at least 15–20 minutes. Strain, add the rest of the juice and top up to 750 ml if needed. Put the juice in a heavy, large saucepan over high heat, add one packet of powdered fruit pectin and bring to a full rolling boil that cannot be stirred down. Add 1.2 kg sugar, keep stirring and bring back to a full rolling boil; boil hard for 1 minute, stirring all the time. Take off the heat, skim off the foam quickly and pour at once into sterilised jars — a whole leaf can be pressed into each jar. Seal and process for 5 minutes in a hot water bath, following the jar maker's instructions. Makes about eight 250 ml jars. Use it to fill or glaze cakes, as a sauce for fresh fruit, or with poultry. The source's ingredient list also has 30 ml lemon juice, but its method does not say when it goes in.
recipes.title: Apple and rose geranium jelly

recipes.method: 1 litre pineapple juice; 10 rose geranium leaves; 400 g sugar; 125 ml lime juice; scented geranium leaves and flowers, to garnish. Warm 1 litre pineapple juice slightly, add 10 rose geranium leaves and bruise them gently against the side of the container with a spoon. Cover and steep for 30 minutes, then take out the leaves. Stir in 400 g sugar and 125 ml lime juice until dissolved (warm it a little to speed this up). Cool, then freeze in an ice-cream maker, or pour into a shallow tray in the freezer and stir with a fork every 30–45 minutes until frozen. Garnish with scented geranium leaves and flowers.
recipes.title: Pineapple and rose geranium ice

recipes.method: 300 ml fresh cream; 4 tablespoons caster sugar; 4–6 rose geranium leaves; 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed); 250 g sour cream (or cream cheese). Heat 300 ml fresh cream, 4 tablespoons caster sugar and 4–6 rose geranium leaves in a pot, stirring often, until just short of boiling; do not let it boil. Take off the heat and cool. Mash 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed) to a purée. Beat 250 g sour cream (or cream cheese) until smooth, then beat in the purée. Strain the leaves out of the cream and fold the cream gently into the berry mixture with a spoon. Cover and chill for several hours or overnight. Serve on fresh berries or fruit salad instead of cream or yoghurt.
recipes.title: Rose geranium cream

recipes.method: Fruit: 6–8 rose geranium leaves; the juice and grated rind of two oranges; about 190 ml more orange juice; 10–12 trimmed rhubarb stalks; about 150 g brown sugar; 2 tablespoons cornflour. Topping: about 150 g brown sugar; about 90 g whole rolled oats; about 90 g fine rolled oats; about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds); 2 tablespoons soft butter. Roughly chop 6–8 rose geranium leaves and warm them gently with the juice of two oranges plus about 190 ml more orange juice; bring almost to the boil, take off the heat and leave to infuse as it cools. Cut 10–12 trimmed rhubarb stalks into 1 cm pieces — enough to fill, not overfill, the baking dish. In a large bowl mix about 150 g brown sugar, 2 tablespoons cornflour and the grated rind of the two oranges, tip in the rhubarb and mix well. Grease the dish and spread the rhubarb mixture back into it. Strain the juice over it. For the topping, mix about 150 g brown sugar, about 90 g whole rolled oats, about 90 g fine rolled oats and about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds), then rub in 2 tablespoons soft butter. Press the topping firmly over the rhubarb and around the edges. Bake at 180 °C for 45 minutes.
recipes.title: Rose geranium rhubarb crumble

recipes.method: Fill a dry glass jar with alternate layers of rose geranium leaves and caster sugar. Cover tightly and leave somewhere warm for a week or more, shaking it now and then. Sieve out the leaves before use, and sprinkle the sugar on custards, biscuits or sponge cakes.
recipes.title: Rose geranium sugar

recipes.method: 250 ml water; 200 g sugar; 10 clean rose geranium leaves; 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice; chilled water and ice, to serve; a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals, to garnish. Boil 250 ml water with 200 g sugar in a small pot. Take off the heat, add 10 clean rose geranium leaves and leave until cold, overnight if you can. Squeeze the leaves out well (repeat with fresh leaves for a stronger flavour). Add 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice, bottle and refrigerate; it keeps for up to two weeks. To serve, stir 1 tablespoon of the concentrate into each cup of chilled water and pour over ice, garnished with a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals.
recipes.title: Rose geranium lemonade

recipes.method: Makes 8 wedges. About 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter; about 60 g icing sugar; about 190 g plain flour; ¼ teaspoon salt; 1 teaspoon rose water; 8 large rose geranium leaves, washed and dried; 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar); fresh rose geranium leaves, to serve. Cream about 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter with about 60 g icing sugar until light and fluffy. Mix about 190 g plain flour with ¼ teaspoon salt, add it to the butter, then mix in 1 teaspoon rose water. Gather into a ball, wrap and refrigerate for 4–6 hours. Let it soften a little. Butter and flour the base of a 20 cm round tin. On baking paper, pat the dough out to the size of the tin. Press 8 large, washed and dried rose geranium leaves into the dough in a circle about 2.5 cm in from the edge, lay the dough in the tin leaf side down and pat it out to the edges. Score it lightly into 8 wedges, sprinkle with 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar) and chill for 45 minutes. Bake at 160 °C for about 20 minutes, until it just starts to colour. Cool in the tin, turn out, peel the baked leaves off the base, cut along the marks and serve with fresh rose geranium leaves.
recipes.title: Rose geranium shortbread

recipes.method: Written for scented geranium leaves, "preferably with a lemon scent"; no species named. 2–3 scented geranium leaves; about 250 g sifted icing sugar; a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese; 2 teaspoons softened butter; 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind; lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel, to decorate (optional). Tear 2–3 scented geranium leaves into small pieces and mix them with about 250 g sifted icing sugar in a small bowl. Leave somewhere warm overnight so the sugar takes up the scent, then pick out and discard the leaf pieces. Beat a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese, 2 teaspoons softened butter and 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind, gradually adding the scented icing sugar, until smooth. Spread over a cooled carrot cake and decorate, if you like, with lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel.
recipes.title: Scented geranium and lemon icing

IV (Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), 'Pelargonium ×asperum', https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/54414bb3-a4f0-405b-84d3-2de4eebebabe, retrieved 21/10/2026 (Webb's stray space in "P. radula )" closed); Wikipedia contributors, 'Pelargonium graveolens', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia, CC BY-SA 4.0, revision 1361378169, retrieved 21/10/2026, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelargonium_graveolens.

Name: "Rose geranium" — NZ Flora Online and NZPCN give no vernacular ("Pelargonium hybrid"); Wikipedia 'Pelargonium graveolens': "Both the true species and the cultivated plant may be called rose geranium", and its cultivated rose-scented P. 'Graveolens' is "possibly a hybrid between P. graveolens and P. radens or P. capitatum" — Webb's parents for P. ×asperum are P. graveolens × P. radens. That the cultivated rose geranium and Webb's P. ×asperum are the same plant is my reading, not a source's. iNaturalist calls it "Rose Storksbill". Close to "Rose-scented geranium" (P. capitatum), whose summary already says several species are called rose geranium.

Omitted on purpose: Webb's "It apparently spreads vegetatively - ripe mericarps have not been observed." — Colin Ogle's 2022 iNaturalist note on obs 231378051 (Whanganui) says "Commonly self-establishing from seed - becoming a weed in this garden!", and its photos show seedlings; a 1988 negative left out rather than contradicted.

Edibility, DECIDED 21/10/2026 (owner: "there are no edible parts and recipies") — option (1) of the earlier lead taken. Bridge: the Herb Society of America guide (2006) puts "P. graveolens and members of the P. 'Graveolens' cultivar group" among the culinary rose-scenteds, and says of that group "Members of this group were once classified as P. xasperum" — so the guide itself ties the culinary rose geranium to this name. Edible parts: Useful Temperate Plants 'Pelargonium graveolens' (Ken Fern, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Pelargonium+graveolens, retrieved 21/10/2026; cites Facciola, Cornucopia, and Bown; Known Hazards "None known") verbatim, citation markers dropped; Wikipedia 'Pelargonium graveolens' (CC BY-SA 4.0, revision 1361378169) Uses sentence verbatim. Both are written for P. graveolens / cultivated rose geranium, not for P. ×asperum by name. Preparation: UTP tea sentence verbatim; the rest restated from the HSA guide's Culinary Uses section (Madalene Hill and Gwen Barclay's kitchen tips, Susan Belsinger's "sparingly so that they don't overwhelm"), https://www.herbsociety.org/file_download/inline/2b2f9fc8-e827-446c-99da-1c1e8b6559d0. Recipes (all from the HSA guide above, © the named authors / HSA, all rights reserved — methods paraphrased, not quoted; written for "rose geranium" / "rose-scented geranium" leaves, which the guide does not tie to one species — that they suit this plant rests on the bridge above): 'Rose geranium syrup' — Susan Belsinger, the syrup in "Chocolate rose-scented soufflé", excerpted from Not Just Desserts (2005); 'Apple and rose geranium jelly' — Madalene Hill and Gwen Barclay, "Apple rose geranium jelly", The Flavour Connection (frozen apple juice "diluted according to directions" or bottled juice; the source lists 2 tablespoons lemon juice but never uses it in the method — said so on the page); 'Pineapple and rose geranium ice' — Ann Wilson, "Pineapple rose freeze". Conversions: 1 cup = 250 ml, 1 cup sugar ≈ 200 g, ½ pint jar ≈ 250 ml, 2 tbsp = 30 ml. Not used: the guide's other recipes (liqueur and wine: alcohol; couscous, lime curd and cooler: rose geranium is one herb among many).
Months: empty = year-round. The leaves and flowers are the parts used; Webb 1988 gives flowering Jan–Dec (FL Jan–Dec), so both are there through the year.

Origin checked 21/10/2026: NZ Organisms Register 'Pelargonium ×asperum' (https://data.nzor.org.nz/names/search?query=Pelargonium%20asperum): no biostatus record returned; NZPCN 'Pelargonium x asperum' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/pelargonium-xasperum/): Biostatus Exotic, year naturalised 1869; NZ Flora Online: Exotic. Origin 'introduced'. Kept introduced, not pest: not on DOC's List of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024 (McAlpine & Howell, Science for Conservation 340, https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/sfc340.pdf; no Pelargonium in the text), and not in Wildland Consultants' table of weed taxa in every regional pest management plan (2021, Contract Report 5396 for the PCE, Appendix 2 p. 75, read by eye: Passiflora apetala is followed by Persicaria chinensis; https://pce.parliament.nz/media/fx4pjock/hutchison-et-al-review-of-weed-management-programmes-pdf-6mb.pdf).

Lookalike cards (rose-scented geranium, peppermint geranium and rose geranium, all three pairs both ways; written by the assistant on the owner's instruction, owner, 21/10/2026: "find what you can and fill in according to the rules for Pelargonium"): every test restates Webb, C.J.; Sykes, W.R.; Garnock-Jones, P.J. 1988, Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) — the species descriptions and notes and the Pelargonium key (couplet 4: P. ×asperum "Lamina lobed to > 3/4 way to midrib"; couplet 6: P. tomentosum "Umbels diffuse; fls on long pedicels; calyx spur c. 2 mm long" against "Umbels dense; fls subsessile; calyx spur 4-5 mm long"; couplet 7: P. capitatum "Habit sprawling; lvs strongly undulate, with ± oblong lobes extending at least 1/2 way to the centre of the lamina"), https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/b8f32527-4c30-4f9b-bab4-9155d157a597, retrieved 21/10/2026; plus Wikipedia 'Pelargonium capitatum' (CC BY-SA 4.0, revision 1195218505) for that species' scent and flower-colour range. Webb gives P. capitatum no full description, only a note and its key couplets, so its side of every card rests on those. Webb's key is inconsistent for P. capitatum (couplet 4 sends it down "Lf blade not lobed or lobed to < 1/2 way to midrib", couplet 7 says its lobes extend "at least 1/2 way") — the cards say lobing does not settle rose geranium against rose-scented geranium for that reason. Card risks: `edible` into all three — peppermint geranium from the start; rose geranium and rose-scented geranium since 21/10/2026, when their pages gained edible parts (a card is not more certain than its page). Not carded, no entry: P. vitifolium (Webb: "very closely-related" to P. capitatum and "often confused"; 0 wild iNaturalist NZ records 21/10/2026), the native kopata P. inodorum, P. ×fragrans. These cards clear `warnings` on all three pages with no warning text added. Corrected 21/10/2026 (owner: "check and double check all Pelargoniums"): the peppermint geranium ↔ rose geranium cards said the key separates them by leaves and flower stalks; couplet 4 uses the leaves only, so the stalk lengths are now credited to the species descriptions.

Owner's links, 21/10/2026, read and not used for page text: NZPCN 'Pelargonium xasperum' ("Pelargonium hybrid", Exotic, naturalised 1869, origin South Africa; its similar-taxa line "lamina lobed to > 3/4 way to midrib" is Webb's key couplet, already on the cards); NZ Flora Online 'Pelargonium ×asperum' (Webb's description, already used); PlantSnap 'Pelargonium asperum' (care-app page, no sources; its "small and white with pink markings" flowers contradict Webb's "Corolla pink" — not trusted); Jade Shutes, 'Pelargonium graveolens or Pelargonium x asperum', School of Aromatic Studies (ARR) — about commercial geranium oil, no food use; it quotes Kew and PROTA treating "Pelargonium asperum Ehrh. ex Willd." as a synonym of P. graveolens. Checked 21/10/2026: Catalogue of Life lists "Pelargonium asperum Ehrh. ex Spreng." as a synonym of P. graveolens, while GBIF's backbone accepts "Pelargonium × asperum Willd." (Webb's name) as its own taxon — two names sharing an epithet, so this does not show that Webb's hybrid is P. graveolens and does not settle the edibility LEAD above.

summary.text:
This hybrid is very commonly cultivated and is the commonest of the scented-leaved geraniums to occur wild. In New Zealand it grows wild in coastal areas and on offshore islands of the North Island, and in the South Island at Nelson City, Gore Bay (North Canterbury) and Banks Peninsula; it was first recorded growing wild here in 1869. Most plants grown in N.Z. as P. graveolens are hybrids or represent other spp.
Many plants are cultivated under the species name "Pelargonium graveolens" but differ from wild specimens as they are of hybrid origin (probably a cross between P. graveolens, P. capitatum and/or P. radens). Both the true species and the cultivated plant may be called rose geranium – pelargoniums are often called geraniums, as they fall within the plant family Geraniaceae, and were previously classified in the same genus.

habitat.text: Its habitat is usually beach sand or other well-drained sandy soils. Its preferred habitat is on sand dunes, but it is a fast grower on any reasonable base, including hard clayey soil, so it readily colonises disturbed habitat.

identification.text:
Pelargonium capitatum is a low shrub up to about 100 cm in height and 1.5 m across. The stems are soft and coated in green, glandular hairs. Brushing against a bush releases a copious scent of the essential oil from damaged hairs. The scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. The flowers range from white through various shades of pink to purple.
P. capitatum differs from P. vitifolium in its sprawling habit, more undulate and velvety leaves, generally lobed more than 1/2 way to the midrib, and the typically more compact inflorescence. The flowers are very similar to those of P. vitifolium with the corolla irregular and the petals oblanceolate and pink with the larger upper pair marked purple.
Flora of New Zealand key: "Umbels dense; flowers subsessile; calyx spur 4-5 mm long"; "Habit sprawling; leaves strongly undulate, with more or less oblong lobes extending at least 1/2 way to the centre of the lamina".
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Peppermint geranium is a subshrub to about 75 cm that smells strongly of peppermint, with more or less velvety white hairs and broad leaves up to 12 × 15 cm, rather shallowly three-lobed, the lobes reaching a quarter to half way to the midrib; its flowers are white or pinkish, 5–8 to an umbel, on stalks 2–3.5 cm long that generally radiate widely, with a calyx spur about 2 mm long. Rose-scented geranium is a sprawling plant whose leaves are strongly undulate and velvety, generally lobed more than half way to the midrib, with more or less oblong lobes; its pink flowers, the larger upper pair of petals marked purple, sit in dense heads on almost no stalks, with a calyx spur 4–5 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them by the umbels (diffuse, with long flower stalks, in peppermint geranium; dense, with almost stalkless flowers, in rose-scented geranium) and the calyx spur (about 2 mm against 4–5 mm). Leaf lobing meets at about half way, so it does not settle a plant on its own. Both plants are hairy, and flower colour does not separate them (Wikipedia gives rose-scented geranium white through pink to purple flowers). A crushed leaf of peppermint geranium smells strongly of peppermint; rose-scented geranium's scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. Most of these tests need flowers.
lookalikes.name: Peppermint geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Rose geranium (P. ×asperum) is a strongly aromatic, densely hairy subshrub to about 75 cm, with more or less triangular leaves up to about 7 × 10 cm that are deeply divided into 3 toothed lobes, lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib and rough above; its pink flowers, the upper 2 petals with more or less prominent purple markings and a white central patch, sit about 10 to an umbel on stalks 1–6 mm long, with a calyx spur about 3 mm long. Rose-scented geranium is a sprawling plant whose leaves are strongly undulate and velvety, generally lobed more than half way to the midrib, with more or less oblong lobes; its pink flowers, the larger upper pair of petals marked purple, sit in dense heads on almost no stalks, with a calyx spur 4–5 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates rose geranium first, by leaves lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib; rose-scented geranium's lobes reach at least half way, and the key's other branch says "lobed to < 1/2 way", so a leaf cut between half and three-quarters is not decided by lobing alone. The calyx spur is a little longer in rose-scented geranium (4–5 mm against about 3 mm). Both have short-stalked heads of pink flowers with purple-marked upper petals, so the flowers do not separate them; rose geranium's leaves are described as rough above, rose-scented geranium's as velvety. Smell does not separate them: rose geranium is strongly aromatic and rose-scented geranium's scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. Flora of New Zealand notes that P. ×asperum is a hybrid of P. graveolens and P. radens; Wikipedia says P. capitatum hybridises readily, so in-between plants are possible and this card may not decide them.

preparation.text: No source gives a method written for this species. For rose-scented pelargoniums in general: steep the leaves in the syrup, jelly, custard or drink and lift them out before the leaves break up, and use them sparingly so they do not overwhelm the dish.

recipes.method: Written for "rose-scented geranium" leaves without naming a species. 1 litre pineapple juice; 10 rose-scented geranium leaves; 400 g sugar; 125 ml lime juice; scented geranium leaves and flowers, to garnish. Warm 1 litre pineapple juice slightly, add 10 rose-scented geranium leaves and bruise them gently against the side of the container with a spoon. Cover and steep for 30 minutes, then take out the leaves. Stir in 400 g sugar and 125 ml lime juice until dissolved (warm it a little to speed this up). Cool, then freeze in an ice-cream maker, or pour into a shallow tray in the freezer and stir with a fork every 30–45 minutes until frozen. Garnish with scented geranium leaves and flowers.
recipes.title: Pineapple and rose geranium ice

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. 300 ml fresh cream; 4 tablespoons caster sugar; 4–6 rose-scented geranium leaves; 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed); 250 g sour cream (or cream cheese). Heat 300 ml fresh cream, 4 tablespoons caster sugar and 4–6 rose-scented geranium leaves in a pot, stirring often, until just short of boiling; do not let it boil. Take off the heat and cool. Mash 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed) to a purée. Beat 250 g sour cream (or cream cheese) until smooth, then beat in the purée. Strain the leaves out of the cream and fold the cream gently into the berry mixture with a spoon. Cover and chill for several hours or overnight. Serve on fresh berries or fruit salad instead of cream or yoghurt.
recipes.title: Rose geranium cream

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. Fruit: 6–8 rose-scented geranium leaves; the juice and grated rind of two oranges; about 190 ml more orange juice; 10–12 trimmed rhubarb stalks; about 150 g brown sugar; 2 tablespoons cornflour. Topping: about 150 g brown sugar; about 90 g whole rolled oats; about 90 g fine rolled oats; about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds); 2 tablespoons soft butter. Roughly chop 6–8 rose-scented geranium leaves and warm them gently with the juice of two oranges plus about 190 ml more orange juice; bring almost to the boil, take off the heat and leave to infuse as it cools. Cut 10–12 trimmed rhubarb stalks into 1 cm pieces — enough to fill, not overfill, the baking dish. In a large bowl mix about 150 g brown sugar, 2 tablespoons cornflour and the grated rind of the two oranges, tip in the rhubarb and mix well. Grease the dish and spread the rhubarb mixture back into it. Strain the juice over it. For the topping, mix about 150 g brown sugar, about 90 g whole rolled oats, about 90 g fine rolled oats and about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds), then rub in 2 tablespoons soft butter. Press the topping firmly over the rhubarb and around the edges. Bake at 180 °C for 45 minutes.
recipes.title: Rose geranium rhubarb crumble

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. Fill a dry glass jar with alternate layers of rose-scented geranium leaves and caster sugar. Cover tightly and leave somewhere warm for a week or more, shaking it now and then. Sieve out the leaves before use, and sprinkle the sugar on custards, biscuits or sponge cakes.
recipes.title: Rose geranium sugar

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. 250 ml water; 200 g sugar; 10 clean rose-scented geranium leaves; 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice; chilled water and ice, to serve; a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals, to garnish. Boil 250 ml water with 200 g sugar in a small pot. Take off the heat, add 10 clean rose-scented geranium leaves and leave until cold, overnight if you can. Squeeze the leaves out well (repeat with fresh leaves for a stronger flavour). Add 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice, bottle and refrigerate; it keeps for up to two weeks. To serve, stir 1 tablespoon of the concentrate into each cup of chilled water and pour over ice, garnished with a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals.
recipes.title: Rose geranium lemonade

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. Makes 8 wedges. About 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter; about 60 g icing sugar; about 190 g plain flour; ¼ teaspoon salt; 1 teaspoon rose water; 8 large rose-scented geranium leaves, washed and dried; 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar); fresh rose-scented geranium leaves, to serve. Cream about 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter with about 60 g icing sugar until light and fluffy. Mix about 190 g plain flour with ¼ teaspoon salt, add it to the butter, then mix in 1 teaspoon rose water. Gather into a ball, wrap and refrigerate for 4–6 hours. Let it soften a little. Butter and flour the base of a 20 cm round tin. On baking paper, pat the dough out to the size of the tin. Press 8 large, washed and dried rose-scented geranium leaves into the dough in a circle about 2.5 cm in from the edge, lay the dough in the tin leaf side down and pat it out to the edges. Score it lightly into 8 wedges, sprinkle with 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar) and chill for 45 minutes. Bake at 160 °C for about 20 minutes, until it just starts to colour. Cool in the tin, turn out, peel the baked leaves off the base, cut along the marks and serve with fresh rose-scented geranium leaves.
recipes.title: Rose geranium shortbread

recipes.method: Written for scented geranium leaves, "preferably with a lemon scent"; no species named. 2–3 scented geranium leaves; about 250 g sifted icing sugar; a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese; 2 teaspoons softened butter; 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind; lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel, to decorate (optional). Tear 2–3 scented geranium leaves into small pieces and mix them with about 250 g sifted icing sugar in a small bowl. Leave somewhere warm overnight so the sugar takes up the scent, then pick out and discard the leaf pieces. Beat a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese, 2 teaspoons softened butter and 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind, gradually adding the scented icing sugar, until smooth. Spread over a cooled carrot cake and decorate, if you like, with lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel.
recipes.title: Scented geranium and lemon icing

summary.text:
Pelargonium capitatum is one of several species (including Pelargonium graveolens) known as rose geranium or rose-scented pelargonium in English.
It is found in fynbos along the coast of South Africa, from Lamberts Bay in the Western Cape east to Kwazulu-Natal.
It is a popular and convenient ornamental plant and it also is one of the species of Pelargonium cultivated as a source of essential oils.
Pelargonium capitatum is one of a number of related plants that have become a major problem in coastal regions of southwest Western Australia, where it invades banksia woodland and coastal heathland.
P. capitatum, rose-scented geranium, is occasionally wild in the Hokianga area of N. Auckland, as well as there being unconfirmed reports from Nuhaka, Poverty Bay and Napier. It seems to be less common in cultivation than the very closely-related P. vitifolium and the 2 spp. are often confused. P. capitatum is the main sp. used for the production of oil of geranium.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Tussock grasslands, open, well-drained sites on roadsides, river flats, banks and terraces, stabilised scree, steep open slopes, lakesides and streamsides; sea level to c. 1000 m.
Dry hill country, riverbeds and farmland.
It is often the dominant woody plant where it grows, but nearly always where other woody plants are sparse or absent (Flora of New Zealand, restated); it grows in tussock grassland and poor pastures where stony ground and light rain limit competing growth (Massey University, restated).

identification.text:
Thorny, rather erect shrub with compound leaves that smell of apples when crushed. Pink single flowers, followed by red or orange-red, oval to round hips.
Deciduous, rather erect, sometimes dense shrub 1–3–(5) m high, often with suckers; armature of few to numerous, unequal, flattened, moderately curved to strongly falcate prickles and pricklets. Leaves with 2–3–(4) pairs of leaflets; leaflets 12–40–(50) × 8–28–(35) mm, with numerous pale glands beneath; margins ± 2-serrate, with glandular hairs. Flowers 1–3–(6), single, (20)–25–40 mm diameter; petals pink or deep pink (especially in bud) except for whitish base. Fruit (10)–12–22–(28) × (8)–10–18–(20) mm, broadly ovoid to globose, red or orange-red, usually glabrous except at base, sometimes with dark red hispid glands.
From other wild roses except the rare R. micrantha it is immediately recognisable by the abundance of glands and the strong smell of apples (Flora of New Zealand).

preparation.text: Top, tail, halve and scrape out every seed and hair, or cook whole and strain through fine cloth. Into syrup, jelly or tea. The hips are mostly seed with a thin layer of flesh, so cooking them whole and straining is usually easier: simmer, mash and drain overnight through a teatowel or jelly bag, then strain the liquid again through four layers of muslin to catch the fine hairs. The taste is best after a frost.

recipes.method: Ingredients, keeping this ratio for as many hips as you have: 250 ml (1 cup) rosehips to 625 ml (2½ cups) water; then 350 g sugar for every 500 ml of strained juice. Pulse each cup of hips with its 2½ cups of water in a food processor or blender until well chopped. Bring to the boil in a heavy pot and simmer for 20 minutes. Strain through a double layer of muslin, leaving the pulp to drain for half an hour with a weight on top. Wash the muslin, fold it to make four layers and strain the juice again — this takes out the irritating hairs from inside the hips. Measure the juice back into the pot, add 350 g sugar for every 500 ml and heat gently, stirring, until it dissolves, then boil for 5 minutes. Pour into bottles sterilised in a 160 °C oven for 15 minutes and seal. Keeps about four months; refrigerate once opened. For a less sweet syrup use 200 g sugar per 500 ml and freeze it in ice-cube trays.

summary.text:
Autumn fruit of a weedy wild rose, most abundant in the drier east.
Sweet briar (Rosa rubiginosa), also called sweet brier or eglantine, is a wild rose native to Europe and North Africa and by far the commonest naturalised rose in New Zealand. Its leaves smell strongly of apples.
In New Zealand it grows in nearly all districts but is often scattered and uncommon in wetter areas in the west of the South Island, and is especially abundant in drier eastern areas from Hawke's Bay south (Flora of New Zealand, restated); it is a major scrub weed in Central Otago and inland Canterbury (Massey University, restated). Introduced as an ornamental, it had become wild by the 1860s (naturalised 1867) and by 1900 was common enough to be regarded as a noxious weed (Flora of New Zealand, restated). It is named on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.
Marlborough, Canterbury and Central Otago are where it is especially common (Knox).

warnings: There is a layer of hairs around the seeds just beneath the flesh of the hip. They irritate the mouth and digestive tract if swallowed, and are used as itching powder: remove or strain them out completely.
