identification.text: Bulb 2 × 1.5 cm, tunic scarious, outermost layer with prominent round pits, whitish-grey with stipitate offset bulbs. Leaves 2–4, about 35 × 1 cm, flat shorter than scape, light green to more or less glaucous; sheaths reddish-purple. Scape 30–60 cm high, cylindrical, sheathed by leaves at base. Umbels 5–8 cm diameter, more or less lax, with flowers and bulbils; pedicels 4–6 times length of flowers, or longer; spathe-valve 1, persistent. Flowers 10–12 mm long, about 12 mm diameter, pale pink, with deeper pink central nerves; segments more or less oblong, obtuse, margins slightly dentate. Stamens about ⅔ length of perianth; filaments entire, without appendages. Bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, shining. Capsule not seen.

lookalikes.howToTell: Onion weed's flowers are white with a green stripe down the centre of each segment; rosy garlic's are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves. Onion weed's flower stalk is sharply three-angled; rosy garlic's is round in section. Onion weed's umbel has no bulbils; rosy garlic often carries bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among its flowers, though plants without bulbils also occur, so no bulbils does not rule rosy garlic out. Onion weed's leaves are strongly channelled; rosy garlic's are flat. The onion-garlic smell, a flower stalk of similar height (20–60 cm against 30–60 cm) and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Onion weed

lookalikes.howToTell: Naples garlic's flowers are pure white; rosy garlic's are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves, often with bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among them (plants without bulbils also occur). Naples garlic's flower stalk has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one; rosy garlic's is round in section. Flat leaves, the garlic smell, an umbel 5–8 cm across and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Naples garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild garlic's leaves are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical; rosy garlic's are flat. Wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils, its few flowers about 5 mm long; rosy garlic carries a loose umbel 5–8 cm across of pale pink flowers 10–12 mm long. Both can carry bulbils in the flower head and both smell of garlic, so bulbils and smell do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Wild garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: False garlic has none of rosy garlic's garlic smell, or only a faint one. False garlic's flowers are dull white, each segment with a greenish base and a reddish midvein; rosy garlic's are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves, often with bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among them (plants without bulbils also occur). False garlic has two bracts below the head, joined at the base and tinged red; rosy garlic has a single one that stays on. Dug up, false garlic's offset bulbs are stalkless and its bulb skin is smooth and white; rosy garlic's offset bulbs sit on short stalks and the outer bulb skin has prominent round pits. A round flower stalk, flat leaves and spring flowering do not separate them. If a plant does not smell of garlic or onion when crushed, leave it. False garlic has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: False garlic

summary.text:
Allium roseum, commonly called rosy garlic, is an edible, Old World species of wild garlic.
It is native to the Mediterranean region and nearby areas, with a natural range extending from Portugal and Morocco to Turkey and the Palestine region. It is cultivated widely, and has become naturalised in scattered locations in other regions outside its natural range.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) the plant recorded is subsp. bulbiferum, which carries bulbils among its flowers: N. Auckland City; Gisborne - Tahunga. S Canterbury - Christchurch. Of the other subspecies (Useful Temperate Plants): The sub-species Allium roseum roseum does not produce bulbils.

warnings: Although no individual reports regarding this species have been seen, there have been cases of poisoning caused by the consumption, in large quantities and by some mammals, of certain members of this genus. Dogs seem to be particularly susceptible.

edibleParts.text: The young, unripe fruits (seed capsules), about 1 cm long, filled with small sweet seeds. In South Africa, where the plant is native, they are a wild snack called froetang or knikkertjies, eaten especially by children. The small corms, about 1 cm across, can also be eaten raw once the brown outer skin is peeled away; the white flesh tastes like a concentrated water chestnut, with a bitter aftertaste.

identification.text:
Slender tufts. Corm about 1 cm diameter, globose, rounded at base where smooth brown tunic splits into acuminate teeth bent to one side. Leaves 10–30 cm × 1–2 mm, rush-like, compressed-cylindrical, narrowly grooved, dark shining green. Scapes hidden by sheathing leaf-bases, 2–4–(10) from each corm, 5–15 cm long, stouter than leaves, semiterete, arched over after flowering; spathe-valves 2, long-persistent, outer longer, greenish with fine brown veins, inner with membranous reddish-brown flecked margins. Flowers lilac-pink, rosy-cerise or magenta, with yellow centre and violet-blue band at throat, 1.5–2 cm long, to 3 cm diameter; tube very short; outer lobes greener on back than inner. Capsules about 1cm long, short-cylindrical, scapes straightening when capsules mature. Seeds 2 mm long, reddish-brown, globose-triangular.
[From: Healy and Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]

summary.text: Rosy sandcrocus, also called onion grass, is a small grass-like corm plant in the iris family (Iridaceae), native to South Africa. In New Zealand it is a garden escape, first collected in North Auckland in 1940, now established and increasing; it is recorded from North Auckland, Auckland (Auckland City, Wairoa, Tauranga, Mount Maunganui) and Wellington (near Masterton), and is almost certainly more widespread and abundant in North Auckland, Bay of Plenty and Poverty Bay than is known at present. Herbarium specimens also record it wild in the South Island, at Nelson, beside the Ōpaoa River at Blenheim and on the Port Hills of Banks Peninsula. It is more common in the North Island. New Zealand plants match Romulea rosea var. australis, the form naturalised in Australia. It is unpalatable to livestock, and it is not listed as an environmental weed or in any regional pest management plan in New Zealand.

warnings: In Australia, stock grazing pasture dominated by this plant have formed fibre balls in the stomach and gut (horses, cattle and sheep), and sheep have suffered infertility, abortion and a paralysis known as onion grass staggers; the toxin responsible is unknown. These records are for grazing livestock, not people.

identification.text:
Plant to about 80 cm tall, very scabrid. Roots becoming very thick. Basal leaves with lamina very large, ovate to oblong; upper side especially densely covered with rigid, bulbous-based hairs; base cuneate to subcordate; cauline leaves similar but smaller, with the narrowly winged petiole not decurrent on stem; uppermost leaves subsessile or with short petiole. Cymes densely hispid. Calyx about 5 mm long at anthesis; lobes accrescent, extending nearly to base, lanceolate, usually subacute, rarely obtuse. Corolla 12 - 17 mm long, light purple or purplish blue at first, becoming blue, especially when dried; lobes about 1 mm long, rounded; scales narrowtriangular. Filament width usually less than anther width except at base; anthers equal to or shortly projecting beyond scales. Nutlets 3–5 mm long, finely rugose or granular.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Told from common comfrey (Symphytum officinale): rough comfrey's leaves are very scabrid, the upper side densely covered with rigid, bulbous-based hairs, and its stem leaves are not decurrent on the stem; common comfrey's leaves are densely hispid above and below but not harshly scabrid, with bulbous-based hairs never predominant, and its stem leaves run down the stem to the internode below, with the petiole broadly winged. Rough comfrey's corolla is light purple or purplish blue at first, becoming blue; common comfrey's is usually pale pink in the upper half, occasionally creamy white. Rough comfrey's nutlets are finely rugose or granular; common comfrey's are smooth. Plants of the hybrid Russian comfrey show various combinations of these characters, and it is usually difficult to find plants that can be attributed with confidence to either parent.

lookalikes.howToTell: Rough comfrey's leaves are very scabrid, the upper side densely covered with rigid, bulbous-based hairs; foxglove's leaves are hairy (sometimes almost hairless) above and grey-felted beneath with crisped hairs. The description of rough comfrey gives no underside character, and the thick leaves of comfrey and foxglove are very difficult to tell apart in spring, so the leaves alone do not separate them. The flowers do: rough comfrey's are in clusters (cymes), 12–17 mm long, light purple or purplish blue at first, becoming blue; foxglove's hang in a raceme to about 60 cm long, the corolla mostly 3.5–5 cm long, usually pinkish purple with dark white-ringed spots, sometimes pure white.

summary.text:
Rough comfrey (Symphytum asperum), also called prickly comfrey, is a hairy perennial herb of the borage family, Boraginaceae, from south-west Asia.
First recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1944. It is uncommon here, in scattered localities from Opotiki (East Bay of Plenty) to Invercargill, and most common in the Hutt Valley and parts of Southland; it has also been collected on waste ground by the railway at Ellerslie, Auckland (1987). Unlike common comfrey and Russian comfrey, it fruits prolifically here. It flowers from November to March.
Russian comfrey (Symphytum ×uplandicum), the hybrid between rough comfrey and common comfrey, is now commoner in New Zealand than either parent, and is the comfrey most used here in herbal teas and medicines. Comfrey, including this species, is a prohibited plant under the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code. This entry is here so you can recognise it.

warnings: Comfrey, including this species (listed as prickly comfrey), is a prohibited plant under the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code, so it cannot be sold as food.

Comfreys, rough comfrey among them, contain chemicals that are toxic to the liver (pyrrolizidine alkaloids) and should not be taken internally; comfrey has been linked to hepatic veno-occlusive disease and, in some cases, deaths.

Comfrey leaves have been mistaken for foxglove leaves, and foxglove is deadly: a woman who brewed foxglove leaves as comfrey tea had an irregular heartbeat and raised digoxin and needed an antidote, and in spring the thick leaves of the two are very difficult to tell apart.

identification.text:
Tree up to 8–(12) m high, usually with an erect trunk and spreading branches; young shoots pilose, sometimes densely so, but soon becoming glabrate. Buds large; outer scales glabrous, purplish, inner scales densely covered with white hairs towards apex. Leaves imparipinnate with up to 8 pairs of leaflets; petiole 20–35–(45) mm long, green or brown to purplish, pilose, but hairs deciduous, sometimes with stalked glands; leaflets (excluding smaller ones near base) narrowly oblong or oblong-elliptic, sometimes lanceolate-elliptic, (20)–30–50–(60) × 8–20–(25) mm, obtuse to acute, more or less sessile, deep green and glabrous or finely hairy above, paler and finely to densely pilose below, serrate along whole length or sometimes in upper ⅔ only; leaflets of juvenile plants and suckering shoots narrowly elliptic to elliptic-ovate, deeply and jaggedly toothed; stipules more or less deciduous, small, acuminate. Inflorescence drooping, up to about 120 mm across; pedicels and branchlets white-villous, becoming glabrate by fruiting. Sepal lobes broadly triangular, 0.6–1.3 mm long, obtuse, white-villous, at least at base, sometimes glabrous in upper part; margin with several short glandular teeth. Petals 3–4.5 mm diameter, more or less orbicular with abbreviated claw, white. Fruit depressed-globose, sometimes more or less oblong-obovoid, 5–10 mm diameter, deep orange to scarlet, sometimes crimson, glossy. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Seedlings are very common in the vicinity of parents and have more deeply and jaggedly toothed leaflets.
The sepals persist as a black, five-pointed star on the ripe fruit.
Bark smooth, shiny and grey. The flowers come in October–November and have an unpleasant smell; the berries ripen from green through yellow to orange-red.

lookalikes.howToTell: Elder's leaves grow in opposite pairs and have (3)–5–7 leaflets, toothed except near the base; rowan's leaves are alternate, with up to 8 pairs of leaflets plus one at the tip, toothed along their whole length or the upper two-thirds. Ripe elder berries are round, 4–8.5 mm across and usually shining black, in drooping clusters; rowan's are 5–10 mm, deep orange to scarlet and glossy, with the sepals left as a small dark star on the tip. Elder flowers in large flat-topped clusters mostly 10–20 cm across; rowan's flower clusters are up to about 12 cm across. Elder often grows as many stems from the base rather than one trunk. Raw elder berries, leaves, bark and stems contain cyanogenic glycosides: cook the berries and strip them from their stalks.

preparation.text: Cut whole clusters, knock them to shake out insects, wash, and pick the berries off the stalks. Cooking, freezing or drying breaks down the parasorbic acid that makes the raw berries bitter; berries picked after frosts are less bitter, and berries picked before any frost can be frozen overnight to the same effect. Discard any berries that look old, dark or fermented. For jelly, simmer the berries until soft and broken down and drip the juice through muslin, which also leaves the seeds behind; rowan jelly sets best with a pectin source such as crab apples or Bramley apple cores. The berries are also made into jam, compote, syrup, chutney, juice, wine and liqueur, or dried and ground into flour.

recipes.method: Written for rowan buds; they contain a cyanogenic glycoside (see Warnings), so treat this as a flavouring in small amounts. Young rowan flower buds and very young leaf buds; cold water; 100 g sugar per 100 ml of water, or up to twice that; 10% vodka (optional). Put young rowan flower buds and very young leaf buds in a pan and cover them with cold water, measuring the water. Add 100 g sugar per 100 ml of water, or up to twice that for a thicker syrup that keeps better. Heat, stirring to dissolve the sugar, and hold it at about 70 °C for a few minutes; the author simmers for no more than 5 minutes, as the almond flavour fades fast with heat. Leave to cool and strain into sterilised bottles, keeping the syrupy buds for the liqueur. Add 10% vodka to help it keep, or store it in the fridge, or freeze it in plastic bottles.
recipes.title: Rowan bud syrup

recipes.method: Written for rowan buds; they contain a cyanogenic glycoside (see Warnings), so treat this as a flavouring in small amounts. The syrup-coated buds left from the rowan bud syrup; cheap vodka; rowan bud syrup, to taste. Put the syrup-coated buds left from the rowan bud syrup in a jar, cover with cheap vodka and leave for about 4 weeks, shaking now and then. Strain, then sweeten to taste with the rowan bud syrup — the author aims for about 20–25% alcohol. Adding more fresh buds to the vodka strengthens the almond flavour, but also extracts more of the cyanogenic glycoside; the author says to drink correspondingly less.
recipes.title: Rowan bud liqueur

recipes.method: Written for rowan buds; they contain a cyanogenic glycoside (see Warnings), so treat this as a flavouring in small amounts. 20 ml rowan bud liqueur; 60 ml whisky (Scotch, or bourbon); ice; a rowan bud. Stir 20 ml rowan bud liqueur and 60 ml whisky (Scotch, or bourbon) over ice. Bruise a rowan bud and float it on top for its aroma.
recipes.title: The Godfather of Soil

recipes.method: Written for rowan buds; they contain a cyanogenic glycoside (see Warnings), so treat this as a flavouring in small amounts. 30 ml whisky (bourbon is best here); 30 ml rowan bud liqueur; 30 ml lemon juice; 10 ml rowan bud syrup (or to taste); 1 egg white; ice. Shake 30 ml whisky (bourbon is best here), 30 ml rowan bud liqueur, 30 ml lemon juice, 10 ml rowan bud syrup (or to taste) and 1 egg white with ice. Strain out the ice and shake again (a reverse dry shake, which makes the egg white creamy; leave it out if you prefer), then fine-strain into a glass.
recipes.title: The Godfather of Sour

recipes.method: 1.5 kg rowan berries; 1.5 kg crab apples (or Bramley apple cores); white sugar, 450 g for every 600 ml of strained juice; juice of 1 lemon. Chop the crab apples without peeling or coring and put them in a large heavy pan with the rowan berries. Just cover with water, bring to the boil, then simmer for about 20 minutes until the fruit is very soft and broken down. Tip the pulp and liquid into a muslin or clean cotton cloth over a large bowl, tie it up and let it drip for at least 4 hours or overnight; do not squeeze it or the jelly will be cloudy. Measure the juice into a pan, add 450 g sugar for every 600 ml, add the lemon juice and bring to the boil. Boil hard for about 10 minutes, then test: spoon a little onto a fridge-cold plate, leave a minute and push it with a finger — if the surface wrinkles it is set; if not, boil a few minutes more and test again. Take off the heat, pour into clean sterilised jars and seal. Serve with cheese, game or lamb.
recipes.title: Rowan and crab apple jelly

recipes.method: Ingredients: 2 cups (500 ml) fresh or frozen rowan berries (freeze fresh ones overnight first); 1/3 cup (80 ml) water; 125 g butter; 6 egg yolks; juice of 1 large orange (1/2 cup, 125 ml); 2/3 cup (160 ml) sugar. Bring the berries and water to the boil in a small pan, then simmer for 10 minutes, pressing the berries now and then to break the skins. Take off the heat and push the berries through a sieve, keeping the juice and pulp and discarding the skins and seeds; you need 2/3 cup (160 ml), topped up with the cooking liquid if short. Mix it with the orange juice. Melt the butter in a heavy pan over medium heat, add the juice, sugar and egg yolks, and cook, whisking often, until thick, 10–15 minutes. Cool completely; blend it if you want it extra smooth.
recipes.title: Rowan and orange curd

recipes.method: Juice: 140 g rowan berries, frozen then thawed; 500 ml water. Turkish delight: 1 tsp butter; 450 g sugar; 300 ml rowan juice; 1 tsp lemon juice; 25 g gelatine; 1/2 tsp vanilla essence; 1 tbsp rose water; 1 tbsp pistachios, crushed; 30 g arrowroot or cornflour. For the juice, bring the berries and water to the boil, crush the berries with a potato masher, then cover and simmer for about 45 minutes. Mash again and strain overnight through muslin in a sieve; you should have about 400 ml — make it up to 500 ml with water. Butter a 15 cm square tin. Boil the sugar, 300 ml rowan juice and lemon juice until a drop forms a hard ball in cold water, then take off the heat and leave 10 minutes. Dissolve the gelatine in 120 ml just-boiled water, add the vanilla, stir it well into the rowan syrup, and pour half into the tin. Scatter over the pistachios, stir the rose water into the rest and pour it on top. Cool, then refrigerate overnight. Turn out, cut into cubes and roll each in arrowroot or cornflour. Makes 20–30 pieces.
recipes.title: Rowan Turkish delight

summary.text:
Rowan, Sorbus aucuparia, also called mountain ash and quickbeam, is a deciduous tree up to 8–(12) m tall of the rose family (Rosaceae), native to Eurasia.
Rowan is widely grown in gardens for both its attractive foliage and fruits and is particularly common in colder areas. Most New Zealand specimens have relatively short petioles, short and obtuse leaflets, and hairy sepals and can be referred to subsp. aucuparia. The species has been known in New Zealand as Pyrus aucuparia.
In New Zealand it was introduced as an ornamental and first recorded in the wild in 1904. Birds spread its plentiful, readily germinating seeds; it smothers and outcompetes native plants and is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds. It is not legally declared a pest, but is an organism of interest under the Canterbury, Otago, Southland and Tasman–Nelson pest plans (site-led in Tasman–Nelson), and Environment Canterbury suggests removing it from gardens.

warnings: The young leaves and buds contain a cyanogenic glycoside, which releases hydrogen cyanide as it is digested; their almond taste comes from it. Toxic in high doses — keep the amounts small.

Raw berries contain parasorbic acid, which irritates the stomach lining; in large amounts it causes indigestion and can affect the kidneys, and large quantities of raw fruit can cause vomiting, especially in people not used to it. Heating or freezing turns it into non-toxic sorbic acid — cook, freeze or dry the berries before eating.
The seeds contain the cyanogenic glycoside prunasin, which can release hydrogen cyanide; strain the seeds out when making jelly, juice or syrup rather than eating them.
Little is known about its safety in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, so avoid it then.

Also recorded under contorta pine.
Also a root partner of mountain pine.
Also recorded with loblolly pine.

identification.text: Cap up to 8 cm across, convex at first and often with a small central bump (umbo), becoming flat and eventually with a shallow central depression; dark brick, bay or red-brown, dry and matt. Gills slightly decurrent, cream, later taking on the cap's colour but paler. Stem 3–5 cm long and 5–15 mm thick, cylindrical, the cap's colour or paler. Milk watery white, mild at first, gradually becoming very hot and acrid after a minute or so. No smell. The flesh tastes the same as the milk. Spore print creamy white with a slight salmon tinge.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. This one's milk is white and abundant. Its cap is dark brick, bay or red-brown, dry and matt, often with a small central boss. Both grow under pine, so habitat does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Saffron milk cap / Pine mushroom

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a little flesh and smell it. Rufous milkcap has no smell; oakbug milkcap has a strong oily smell likened to bedbugs or wet laundry. Rufous milkcap's cap often has a small central boss, and its milk is watery white; oakbug milkcap's milk is white or cream. In New Zealand rufous milkcap is reported only with pines, and oakbug milkcap is known from a single site, with oak. Cap colour does not separate them: both are matt reddish brown.

The 'late spring to late autumn' of the description is the northern season, not this one. Checked 06/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/taxa/118223

First Nature, 'Lactarius rufus' (rufous milkcap) — © First Nature / Pat O'Reilly, all rights reserved, so facts only and nothing quoted beyond the short phrases marked. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/lactarius-rufus.php Cap 4–10 cm, dark reddish brown, dry and finely matt and slightly sticky when wet, convex then funnel-shaped, often with a small central umbo; gills pale reddish cream, weakly decurrent, crowded, going blotchy with age; stem 4–9 cm by 5–20 mm, no ring; latex watery white; spores 6.5–9 × 5.5–6.5 µm; spore print pale cream with a slight salmon-pink tinge; no distinctive smell; taste mild at first, then extremely hot and acrid. Coniferous woodland on acid soil, typically under pines and occasionally under birch. Inedible in most western sources; dried and powdered after thorough cooking as a seasoning in Scandinavia and Russia. Lactarius subdulcis is similar but smaller and grows under beech.

Why this one shares saffron milk cap's ground, and the test that still separates them. First Nature puts it in coniferous woodland 'typically under pines' on acid soil — the same plantation floor saffron milk cap is gathered from, so place cannot be used to rule it out the way it can for the beech and oak milk caps. The latex does: watery white and unchanging, then extremely hot, against saffron milk cap's carrot-orange bleed. Checked 06/10/2026.

habitat.text: Only under pines (Pinus), above all radiata pine in plantation forest. Never in native bush.

harvestEthics.text: Cut rather than pull, and leave the smallest and the largest.

identification.text: Orange cap with darker concentric rings, often depressed in the centre. Orange gills that bruise dull green. The confirming test: cut the flesh and it bleeds bright carrot-orange latex, and the cut surface slowly stains green. Brittle, not fibrous, flesh. Test every cap for latex rather than reading the cap: other milk caps are zoned the same way, so the cap alone tells you nothing, and a spore print will not separate them either — the prints run white to ochre across the genus, this one's cream included.

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Coconut milk cap's milk is white, rather watery and unchanging, its cap is greyish lilac, pale greyish brown or brownish grey with leaden tints rather than orange, and it smells of coconut - faintly, in the New Zealand description. It grows under silver birch; saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine.
lookalikes.name: Coconut milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Downy milk cap's milk is white and does not change colour or stain the flesh. Downy milk cap's cap margin is rolled in and bearded with coarse white hairs when young, and the cap is white to cream, reddening at the centre with age. Saffron milk cap's cap is orange to salmon, with an incurved margin. In New Zealand and Australia, downy milk cap grows with birch, saffron milk cap only with pine. Downy milk cap's milk and flesh taste acrid, and some authors consider it toxic.
lookalikes.name: Downy milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. This one's milk is white, does not change, and dries pale cream, though its cut flesh slowly runs from white through pink, salmon and orange-red to wine red. Its cap is dark brown to almost black and unzoned, often with dull salmon patches near the centre. It is endemic, and recorded under beech.
lookalikes.name: New Zealand milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Oakbug milkcap's milk is white or cream. Its cap is dull, matt reddish brown with a cinnamon tint and stays dry, not sticky, when moist, and it has a strong oily smell likened to bedbugs or wet laundry. In Europe it grows only with oak; in New Zealand and Australia, saffron milk cap grows only with pine. Both can show concentric zones on the cap, so zoning is not the difference.
lookalikes.name: Oakbug milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. This one's milk is white and abundant. Its cap is dark brick, bay or red-brown, dry and matt, often with a small central boss, which can sit in a shallow depression on older caps. Both grow under pine, so habitat does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Rufous milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Slimy milkcap's milk is white and plentiful and dries grey, and its cut gills turn grey-buff. Its cap is drab greenish-grey or olive-grey with rings of darker blotches, and slimy in wet weather. In Europe it grows with beech, very occasionally oak; in New Zealand and Australia, saffron milk cap grows only with pine. Its taste is bitter and hot.
lookalikes.name: Slimy milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. This one's milk is white, sticky and unchanging, drying cream. Both species have zoned caps, so zoning does not separate them. Tawai's cap is a dull orange-brown or drab ochre with purplish-grey to reddish-brown bands. It is endemic, and recorded under beech.
lookalikes.name: Tawai milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Ugly milkcap's milk is white or creamy white, and old milk leaves its dirty-white gills stained olive-brown. Its cap is olive brown or yellow-green, often sticky or slimy in the middle, darkening to blackish with age. In New Zealand and Australia it grows with birch; saffron milk cap only with pine. Its milk tastes acrid, and it is reported to contain carcinogenic compounds.
lookalikes.name: Ugly milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. This one's milk is white and unchanging, drying cream. Its cap is small, 1-3.5 cm across. Saffron milk cap's is 4-12 cm in the Australasian description and from 3 cm overseas, so a small saffron cap can come close. It is a dull salmon, greyish orange or pale orange-brown, and unzoned. It is an endemic of beech forest.
lookalikes.name: Umere milkcap

preparation.text: Dry-fry or roast hard — they release a lot of water and go slimy if cooked gently. Do not eat raw.

recipes.method: 12 medium caps, 15 ml olive oil, salt and pepper. Brush the caps clean — rinse only if they are really dirty — and pat them dry. Cut them to size, or leave the small ones whole. Get the oil hot in a skillet over medium-high, add the mushrooms, season, and stir now and then for about 5 minutes until they have shrunk down and cooked through. Serve hot alongside something else.
recipes.title: Sautéed saffron milk caps

recipes.method: 250 g caps, cleaned and sliced, 200 ml sherry or red wine vinegar, 200 ml water, 100 g sugar, 50 ml olive oil, 1 tsp salt, 5 black peppercorns, 3 cloves garlic, 3 juniper berries, 2 bay leaves, a sprig each of rosemary and thyme. To clean them first, soak them in 1.4 litres of water with 120 ml white vinegar. Bring everything but the mushrooms to the boil, add them, and simmer one minute. Off the heat, let it cool, then pack into a sterilised jar with the liquid above the mushrooms. Keeps up to 6 months in the fridge as long as they stay covered.
recipes.title: Pickled saffron milk caps

recipes.method: 400 g caps sliced, 4 cloves garlic chopped, oil, 80 ml white wine, 125 g cream cheese, 3 tbsp sour cream, 2 sage leaves, 2 sprigs thyme, salt and pepper, 1 sheet butter puff pastry, 1 egg yolk beaten with 1 tsp water. Fry the garlic a minute in oil over medium heat, add the mushrooms and cook 5 minutes, adding oil as they take it. Stir in the wine, cream cheese, sour cream, sage and thyme and cook until creamy and tender, then season and cool completely — this can be done a day ahead. Heap the filling down the centre of the pastry sheet, seal the edges with the egg wash, press the ends with a fork, and bake at 220 °C for 30 minutes until golden.
recipes.title: Saffron milk cap, sage and thyme strudel

recipes.method: An onion and 2 cloves garlic, finely diced, oil, 50 g butter, 3 tbsp flour, 200 g sliced caps, 3 tsp paprika, 600–700 ml chicken stock, 60 ml sour cream, parsley. Fry the onion and garlic in oil a few minutes until translucent, melt the butter into them, then stir in the flour. Add the mushrooms, paprika and stock and simmer about 10 minutes until the mushrooms are done. Serve with a spoonful of sour cream and parsley.
recipes.title: Hungarian mushroom soup

recipes.method: 125 ml olive oil; 2 tbsp butter; 300 g caps with the stems off and thinly sliced; 3 sprigs thyme; an onion; 105 g arborio rice; 1 litre chicken stock; a pinch of saffron; 165 ml dry white wine; 125 ml cream; 25 g blue cheese; chopped chives or parsley, to serve. Sauté the mushrooms in half the oil with the butter over medium-high until coated, season, and set aside. Soften the diced onion in the rest of the oil over medium heat for 5–8 minutes without browning, while the stock warms with the saffron in another pan. Stir the rice through the onion, then add the hot stock a ladle at a time, letting each one absorb, for 15–20 minutes until the rice is cooked. Stir in the wine, blue cheese and cream, fold through half the mushrooms, and season. Plate it with the remaining mushrooms on top and chopped chives or parsley.
recipes.title: Saffron milk cap risotto

recipes.method: Pastry: 480 ml plain flour, 150 g cold cubed butter, 240 ml finely grated parmesan, 2.5 ml fine salt, 1 egg, 120–160 ml ice water. Filling: 5 caps, 4 cloves garlic sliced, olive oil, 150 g ash brie sliced, 3 eggs, 240 ml cream, 240 ml parmesan, 2 sprigs thyme. Clean the mushrooms in 1.4 litres of water with 120 ml white vinegar. Pulse the flour, butter, cheese and salt in a food processor, add the egg and 120 ml water and run it until it starts to come together, then knead on a floured bench with more water if it needs it and rest it 30 minutes at room temperature. Line an oiled 31 × 21 cm loose-bottomed tart tin, trim, and chill 45 minutes or freeze 15. Meanwhile fry the garlic then the mushrooms — whole if small, sliced if not — in oil over medium heat only until they keep their bright orange, then season and cool a little. Blind bake at 200 °C under oiled foil and weights for 20 minutes, then 10–15 minutes uncovered. Drop the oven to 150 °C, whisk the eggs, cream and parmesan, pour it into the case, arrange the mushrooms and brie on top with the thyme, and bake 30–35 minutes until just set. Serve warm.
recipes.title: Saffron milk cap and ash brie tart

recipes.method: 500 g desiree potatoes, 125 g Italian 00 flour plus extra for the bench, 40 g chestnut flour (or just more 00), 2 tbsp oil, an onion sliced, 2 cloves garlic sliced thinly, 250 g caps with the stalks off and sliced, 150 g bacon or prosciutto (optional), 100 g roasted and peeled chestnuts, 100 g butter, salt and pepper. Boil the potatoes in their skins until tender, rice them, and cool completely before working the flours in. Roll the dough into logs, cut it into pieces, and shape each one against a fork. Boil them and lift them out as they float. Fry the onion and garlic until fragrant, add the mushrooms until the edges crisp, then the bacon, chestnuts and butter. Add the drained gnocchi and fry until golden all over, then season.
recipes.title: Saffron milk cap and chestnut gnocchi

Season. Plant & Food Research gives a January-to-May season for Lactarius deliciosus under Pinus radiata here; iNaturalist NZ holds only 11 research-grade records and they run March to July, peaking in May. March to June is where the two overlap, and is what this entry lists. Checked 06/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/taxa/155197

Which other New Zealand milk caps have zoned caps: Lactarius quietus ('darker concentric bands or spots'), L. blennius ('blotches of darker colouration in concentric bands') and the endemic L. tawai ('distinctly or indistinctly concentrically zonate'). The first two from Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0; the third from McNabb (1971) via the Virtual Mycota, restated. Checked 06/10/2026.

The eleven Lactarius taxa on record in New Zealand: Lactarius rufus, L. pubescens, L. turpis, L. glyciosmus, L. tawai, L. novae-zelandiae, L. umerensis, L. deliciosus, L. blennius, L. quietus, and the undescribed Lactarius sp. 'Hauroko' (6 records, no published name). All ten named species have entries here. Checked 06/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/observations?taxon_id=54597&place_id=6803&view=species

Downy milk cap belongs on the list of zoned caps too, which is why that count went from three to four. First Nature describes Lactarius pubescens with 'faint pinkish concentric bands and pinkish-brown centre zone' — fainter than this species' banding, but present, and it is a do-not-eat entry. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/lactarius-pubescens.php

lookalikes.howToTell: the three endemic milk cap cards (tawai-milkcap, new-zealand-milkcap, umere-milkcap) said those species had never been described in print. That is wrong — McNabb, R.F.R. (1971), 'The Russulaceae of New Zealand. 1. Lactarius', New Zealand Journal of Botany 9(1): 46–66 describes all three, and the Virtual Mycota reproduces it; what does not exist is an openly licensed description. All three were corrected to say that. The tawai-milkcap card was also rewritten to carry the two real separators — host tree (pine against beech, from the Hidden Forest and NZOR facts on that entry) and the point that both species have zoned caps, so zoning does not separate them, which is the limit this entry's own zonate-cap source already records. In copyright, so facts restated, no text reproduced. Written by the assistant on the owner's instruction, 08/10/2026; flagged here so it is greppable and reversible.

lookalikes.howToTell: the tawai-milkcap card was rewritten again on 08/10/2026 once the full McNabb description was read off the Virtual Mycota page (pk=5190) — the endemic's latex is white, viscid and unchanging, which is a real separator and better than the earlier card's admission that no latex character was available. Cap colour added as dull orange-brown to dingy ochre. In copyright, so facts restated, no text reproduced. Written by the assistant on the owner's instruction; flagged here so it is greppable and reversible.

lookalikes.howToTell: the umere-milkcap and new-zealand-milkcap cards were rewritten 08/10/2026 once the full McNabb descriptions were read off the Virtual Mycota (pk=5192, pk=5184), in the same way as the tawai-milkcap card. Both endemics have white unchanging latex, which is a real separator from this species' carrot-orange; added with it are size (1–3.5 cm for umere), cap colour, the absence of zoning, and for L. novae-zelandiae the flesh running white to wine red on cutting. All three cards previously said no description was available, which was true only of openly licensed ones. In copyright, facts restated, no text reproduced. Written by the assistant on the owner's instruction; flagged here so it is greppable and reversible.

lookalikes.howToTell: two corrections to the cards written earlier on 08/10/2026, found by re-reading them against the sources. FIRST, the umere-milkcap card compared cap sizes as '1–3.5 cm against 4–15 cm'. THE 4–15 cm WAS NOT FROM ANY SOURCE — no source on this entry gives a cap size for Lactarius deliciosus at all — so the figure is removed and only the endemic's sourced measurement is given. SECOND, three cards said the endemics are 'never found under pine'. The sources record them under Nothofagus; they do not record an absence under pine, and that is a different claim. Reworded to 'recorded only from beech forest'. Corrected by the assistant, 08/10/2026.

summary.text: A popular edible mushroom of pine forests, deliberately introduced to New Zealand. Cut it and it bleeds bright carrot-orange milk.

warnings: At least eleven Lactarius species are on record in New Zealand and this is one of them; others are undescribed or unnamed, and related milk-bleeding genera grow here too. Any milk cap bleeding white, cream or watery latex is a different species — some are considered toxic, and ugly milk cap contains a mutagen that boiling does not remove.

Brown roll rim (Paxillus) has been confused with saffron milk cap: its gills also run down the stem and its cap is blotchy. Its cap edge is tightly rolled under and its cut surfaces quickly turn rusty brown. It can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, kidney failure and death, even in people who have eaten it before without harm.
Only harvest from pine. A mushroom that looks similar in native forest is not this species.
Many plantation forests are private land or actively logged — get permission and check for harvesting operations.
Some plantations are aerially sprayed. Check with the forest manager.

edibleParts.text: Young leaves and shoots, raw or cooked: in salads, as a garnish, in dressings, sauces, soups and cold drinks, and to flavour vinegar, butter and cream cheese. It goes into herb vinegars and the traditional European green sauce, can stand in for basil or, in some recipes, mint, and chopped leaves stirred into yoghurt make a dressing. The leaves taste mildly of cucumber. The flowers can go into salads as a garnish; they have little flavour. Young seedlings are boiled and eaten, and a herb tea is made from the dried leaves.

identification.text:
Herb with branching rhizomes; stems more or less erect, up to 35–(70) cm tall at flowering, glabrous to sparingly pilose, sparingly branched, greenish yellow to purplish, grooved. Lower leaves in basal rosettes; petiole short; blade oblong to narrowly oblanceolate, up to 150–(300) × 45 mm, imparipinnate; leaflets in (5)–7–10–(12) pairs, shortly petiolulate or subsessile, narrowly obovate to elliptic or orbicular, 5–12–(30) mm long, glabrous above, sparsely finely puberulent and often with a few longer hairs on veins beneath, deeply serrate, sometimes purplish especially towards margins or pale to more or less glaucous below. Cauline leaves few, similar to basal leaves but with fewer and narrower leaflets. Inflorescence a dense globose head, elongating somewhat at fruiting. Sepals ovate-oblong, (2)–3–4 mm long, free, more or less emarginate with a small cusp, green; margins whitish or pink to purple. Stamens numerous. Hypanthium usually broadly ellipsoid, rarely ellipsoid at fruiting, glabrous, almost glabrous or pubescent, (2)–4–5 mm long, usually sharply angled and winged, rarely obscurely winged; faces usually reticulate and the ridges with small projections, rarely faintly reticulate. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Crushed leaves smell of cucumber (Hands in the Dirt; Herb Federation of New Zealand).
The leaflets, up to 12 pairs, sit along the leaf stalk a little like the rungs of a ladder. The tiny green flowers are packed into small round heads at the stem tips, with red styles sticking out and longer yellow anthers hanging below (Totally Wild UK, restated).

preparation.text: Use the youngest leaves and new shoots; older leaves turn bitter and tough, and mature leaves are better added to soups. The leaves sometimes become bitter in hot dry summers (above about 25 °C) and are usually milder in winter, when it is one of the few salad herbs still green; plants on acid soil can taste distinctly bitter. Sources differ on timing: best before the plant flowers, or when it is just starting to flower. Cutting the foliage back as flower buds form, or removing the flower heads before they set seed, keeps new leaves coming; cutting off older leaves helps too. The cucumber flavour is best fresh and weakens when the leaves are dried or cooked at high temperatures. Cooked leaves taste more bitter, so salad burnet is best eaten raw. Sources differ on keeping: the leaves are best fresh and may not store, dry or freeze well, though chopped leaves can also be frozen and keep their flavour for up to a year, and leaves dried slowly keep their aroma for tea. Small leaflets make it a fiddly harvest.

recipes.method: Ingredients: 75 g butter; 1½ tablespoons chopped salad burnet; 1 tablespoon chopped spearmint; salt, black pepper and lemon juice to taste. Mix the chopped herbs. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the herbs and simmer on a very low heat for 10 minutes. Season with salt, pepper and lemon juice, and pour over grilled fish.
recipes.title: Salad burnet butter

recipes.method: Makes 2 sandwiches, about 10 minutes. Ingredients: 4 slices wholegrain bread (or wholegrain crackers); softened butter for spreading; 1 tablespoon whole fresh salad burnet leaves; 125 ml (½ cup) softened cream cheese; salt and black pepper. Butter each slice of bread. In a small bowl mix the whole leaves into the cream cheese (the leaves are too delicate to need mincing) and season with salt and pepper. Spread the mixture on two slices, top with the other two and cut into halves or quarters.
recipes.title: Cream cheese tea sandwiches with salad burnet

recipes.method: Serves 4 to 6. Ingredients: 1 wholegrain French baguette; a handful of salad burnet leaves; about 190 ml (¾ cup) chopped walnuts; good olive oil (the source gives no amount). Heat the oven to 190 °C (375 °F). Slice the baguette without cutting all the way through. Wash and chop the salad burnet, crush the walnuts into pieces, and divide both among the cuts. Drizzle olive oil into the cuts and over the top, bake 10 minutes and serve straight away.
recipes.title: French bread with walnuts and salad burnet

recipes.method: Ingredients: about 30 g each of cress, parsley, chives, salad burnet, sorrel, young borage leaves and chervil; 2 hard-boiled egg yolks; ¾ teaspoon prepared mustard; 125 ml (½ cup) sour cream (or yoghurt or crème fraîche). Whizz the herbs in a food processor until finely chopped, add the other ingredients and blend until smooth. Serve, or refrigerate and use within 2 days. Serve with fish (especially oily fish), chicken, hot new potatoes, asparagus or salads.

summary.text:
Sanguisorba minor, the salad burnet, garden burnet, small burnet, burnet (also used for Sanguisorba generally), pimpernelle, Toper's plant, and burnet-bloodwort, is an edible perennial herbaceous plant in the family Rosaceae.
It is evergreen to semi-evergreen; in warmer climates grows all year around, and in cold climates it stays green until heavy snow cover occurs.
It has also naturalized in most of North America, in South America, Australia, and New Zealand.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): S. minor is a very variable species interpreted in a broad sense to include several subspecies sometimes treated as separate species. Two subspecies are found in New Zealand; the fruiting hypanthium provides principal distinguishing characters. S. minor may have entered New Zealand as a seed contaminant. Most records of Sanguisorba or Poterium naturalised in New Zealand are based on plants of S. minor subsp. muricata (sheep's burnet), native of South Europe, North Africa and South-West Asia and first recorded in New Zealand in 1877: North Island: Wellington (Marton, Martinborough, Wairarapa coast, Wellington City area); South Island: Nelson (Takaka, Nelson City), Marlborough (Blenheim, Fairhall, Renwick, Wither Hills), lowland Canterbury and inland North and South Canterbury, Otago (Benmore, Luggate). Subsp. lasiocarpa is known from one collection only, Delta Station, Wairau Valley, Marlborough, 1947. Records of subsp. minor, salad burnet, are not substantiated by specimens although this subspecies is cultivated in New Zealand as a culinary herb. It is distinguished from subsp. muricata by the angles of the hypanthium having short and obscure wings and the faces being merely reticulate.
The New Zealand Plant Conservation Network lists sheep's burnet as Sanguisorba minor subsp. balearica, with subsp. muricata as a synonym: native of southern Europe, North Africa and south-west Asia, naturalised in New Zealand in 1877.

warnings: The safety record for this species is thin: none of the sources checked records a hazard specific to salad burnet, which is not evidence that it is safe. For the related great burnet (Sanguisorba officinalis), people taking quinolone antibiotics are advised to avoid the plant.

Wild burnet in New Zealand is mostly the subspecies muricata (sheep's burnet; the New Zealand Plant Conservation Network now lists it as subsp. balearica). The culinary subspecies minor is grown in gardens, and records of it growing wild are not backed by specimens. Most of the food sources describe Sanguisorba minor as a whole; Eatweeds names its plant as the culinary subspecies minor. None separates the subspecies for eating.

Sprouted seeds in salads or sandwiches; this use rests on a single source.

identification.text:
Biennial with cylindric rootstock. Stems erect, weakly ribbed, glabrous or sometimes with sparse cobwebby tomentum above, 30–100 cm tall. Leaves linear- to lanceolate-subulate, entire, acuminate, 5–30–(40) × 0.5–1.5–(2) cm; base sheathing; margins undulate or flat. Capitula solitary; peduncles swollen beneath capitula ( longer than 5 mm thick at fruiting). Involucre glabrous at base; involucral bracts 6–8, lanceolate-acuminate, 3.5–6 × 0.5–1 cm at fruiting, glabrous, or tomentose near apex. Corolla mauve to purple, shorter than involucre. Achenes fusiform, ribbed, the outer coarsely muricate, the inner becoming smooth; body 8–13–(15) mm long; beak shorter than or up to 2× length of body, barely clavate at apex. Pappus sordid, 1.5–2 cm long, plumose, in 2 rows, seated on a distinct tomentose annulus. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It exudes a milky juice from the stems. The taproots can become 15–30 cm long and 2–5 cm thick.

preparation.text: Collect roots and leaves before the flower stalk appears: after flowering the root quickly turns fibrous, stringy and inedible. Wild plants often grow in compacted soil, so a garden fork or spade is needed to lift the long root. A broken root discolours and spoils quickly, and roots lose flavour soon after digging, so use them promptly. Scrape off the outer layers and dip the root in cold water to keep its colour; roots that are too tough can be boiled with a pinch of baking soda and a change of water. Boiling the roots for 15 minutes before frying softens them. Roots can be roasted with other root vegetables, made into a purée to go with fish, or added to soups, stews and stir-fries. The root's flavour is mild and sweet, likened to oysters or asparagus. The thin skin can be eaten, so brushing the roots clean is often enough and avoids the milky sap. If you peel them, do it under running water and put the roots straight into lemon water; the sap browns in air and stains the hands. Whole or cut roots boil in lightly salted water in about 15 minutes.

recipes.method: Ingredients: salsify roots, white wine, butter and garlic; the source gives no amounts. Steps: dig the roots (a spade helps in compacted soil) and clean them. Boil them for 15 minutes so they are not tough, then sauté them in white wine, butter and garlic. The source gives no frying time.
recipes.title: Sautéed salsify roots

recipes.method: Serves 4. Ingredients: 4 salsify roots, 30 ml olive oil, 15 ml maple syrup, 45 ml chopped walnuts, 5 ml finely chopped parsley, salt and pepper. Steps: scrub the roots, peel them and cut into lengths of about 7 cm. Steam for about 10 minutes until a knife tip slides in easily, then drain and pat dry. Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat and fry the pieces on all sides until golden. Add the walnuts and maple syrup, toss quickly to coat, then scatter with the parsley and season. Serve as a side dish or on a bed of bitter leaves such as chicory.
recipes.title: Braised salsify with maple walnuts

recipes.method: Ingredients: 800 g salsify roots, 1 kg onions, 6 bay leaves, 5 ml caraway seeds, 2 cloves, 60 g butter, 300 ml red wine, 800 ml vegetable stock, 30 ml sweet paprika, 200 ml cream, 1 bunch chives, a little marjoram, pepper and salt. Steps: peel and chop the onions and warm them gently with the bay leaves, cloves, caraway and butter, covered, for 30 minutes. Pour in the wine and stock, season with the paprika, pepper and salt, and add a few marjoram leaves. Brush the salsify clean (the thin skin can stay on; if you peel it, do so under running water and drop the roots into lemon water), cut into pieces, add to the pot and simmer a few minutes. Stir in the cream and chopped chives and simmer a few minutes more. Serve alone or with boiled potatoes.
recipes.title: Salsify and red wine soup

recipes.method: Serves 4. Confit: 10 shallots, 60 g butter (half for the confit, half for the roots), 22 ml brown sugar, 200 ml port, 60 ml orange juice, 30 ml dark balsamic vinegar. Roots: 800 g salsify, 150 ml vegetable stock, salt, pepper and 1 spring onion (or 30 ml chopped chives). Steps: peel and finely chop the shallots, soften them in 30 g melted butter, sprinkle with the sugar and let it caramelise, then add the port and orange juice and braise gently for about 20 minutes. Season the confit with the balsamic vinegar, salt and pepper. Peel and wash the salsify and cut into 2 cm pieces; soften them in the remaining melted butter, add the stock, cover and steam for 8 to 10 minutes until tender, adding a little more stock if needed. Season lightly, scatter with the sliced spring onion and serve with the confit.
recipes.title: Salsify with shallot confit

summary.text:
Tragopogon porrifolius is a species of plant commonly known as purple or common salsify, oyster plant, vegetable oyster, Jerusalem star, Jack go to bed, goatsbeard, or simply salsify.
A biennial from the Mediterranean, first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1870 (NZPCN, restated).
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Northland, Auckland, Bay of Plenty, Gisborne, Hawke's Bay, Manawatu; S.: Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago. Salsify is occasionally cultivated for its edible root.
Two yellow-flowered relatives are also naturalised in New Zealand, but are rare: Tragopogon dubius around Cromwell in Central Otago, and goatsbeard, T. pratensis, in Canterbury. Salsify is the one with mauve to purple florets (Flora of New Zealand, restated).

warnings: Out of flower salsify looks like grass, and its leaves resemble onion leaves. Cut or broken leaves, stems and fresh roots bleed a white, milky sap.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand it is common throughout in salt marsh or on coastal rock platforms and rock crevices.
It grows in intertidal places – estuaries, sandy and muddy shores, and rocks – where it can form a dense mat. It can grow on bare mud, but its roots are shallow, so it does not grow where water currents are strong. It also grows inland in Otago, where erosion leaves the soils salty when rain is scarce.
Planted, it grows best in full sun on free-draining sandy or rocky soil; once established it tolerates drought and salt spray.
On New Zealand's national wetland plant list it is rated facultative wetland: usually a wetland plant, occasionally found on dry ground.

identification.text:
A perennial subshrub with prostrate woody stems about 3–4 mm in diameter, up to 30 cm or more long; branches numerous, the plant forming extensive patches up to 60 cm or more in diameter. Branchlets mainly opposite, usually crowded, erect or ascending, completely invested by leaves, which are long-persistent in withered state. Leaves opposite, more or less translucent, succulent, green or flushed with red; the pairs completely fused to form a terete "joint" 5–6–(15) × 3–7 mm; apex free, forming a "collar" with 2 minute lobes. Flowers axillary, in upper portion of branchlets, forming a "spike" with shorter, thicker "joints"; the flowers sunk in axils, 5–10–(15) in a ring. Perianth fleshy, thickened, more or less urceolate, with 3–5 minute teeth; stamens 1–2; style branches 2, stigmatic portion linear, minutely papillose. Fruit more or less ovoid; seeds about 2 mm in diameter, with coriaceous testa clad in minute hooked hairs.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1, as Salicornia australis.]
Its small flowers are green and yellow and open in summer.

preparation.text:
Pick the tender new growth; the young stems are at their freshest in spring and summer. Each stem has a fibrous woody core, which makes the plant much less appealing as a vegetable or a pickle. It is used mainly as a pickle.
For glassworts (Salicornia) in general: use only the green, tender tips, and cut the hard, woody lower part off thicker stems, as with asparagus. Older stems can have a woody core partway up; serve those whole and nibble the soft flesh off by hand. Glasswort is very salty, so cook it without added salt. Soaking it in fresh water and boiling it in unsalted water draws out some of the salt; steaming draws out less. Very fresh, tender tips can go raw into salads; otherwise steam them and dress with oil and lemon, or boil until just tender and then sauté with oil, garlic and chilli. To freeze, blanch for 1–2 minutes, cool, dry and freeze.

recipes.method: The author's greens, picked from roadsides around Whangaroa Harbour, were nasturtium, kawakawa, fennel, samphire, fat hen, wild mustard, cleavers and clover; the author calls it marsh samphire, picked around the Whangaroa area. The author warns that New Zealand roadsides are still sprayed with glyphosate, so pick with care. 1 garlic clove (or 4 peeled onion weed bulbs); 60 ml (¼ cup) macadamia nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) grated parmesan, dairy or plant-based (or 125 ml (½ cup) macadamias and no parmesan); 750 ml (3 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml extra-virgin olive oil; and salt and pepper. Makes about 350 g. Blend in a food processor to the texture you like. Serve on crackers or toast, as a side, or stirred through soup, pasta or rice.
recipes.title: Wild Whangaroa pesto

recipes.method: Written for glassworts (Salicornia) in general; the page names no species. Serves 4. 140 g glasswort, 2 tablespoons (28 g) butter and 2 tablespoons (30 ml) freshly squeezed lemon juice. Rinse the glasswort well. Bring about 5 cm of unsalted water to the boil in a medium pot, add the glasswort and boil for 2 minutes, then drain in a colander. For a brighter green and a crisper bite, plunge it into iced water and drain again. Melt the butter and stir in the lemon juice. Toss tender glasswort in the lemon butter and serve it as a side; if the stems have a woody core, serve the lemon butter on the side as a dip and eat them by hand. Good with fish, shellfish and eggs. Cooked glasswort keeps up to a day in a sealed container in the fridge and can be eaten at room temperature or chilled; make the lemon butter just before serving.
recipes.title: Glasswort with lemon butter

recipes.method: Written for glassworts (Salicornia) in general; the page names no species. Trim the woody ends off thicker stems. Soak the glasswort in fresh water, then boil it for 3 minutes in unsalted water and drain. Sauté it in olive oil for 2 minutes. Serve it as a side with fish, such as a whole trout, or use it in a quiche or an omelette.
recipes.title: Boiled and sautéed glasswort

summary.text:
Salicornia quinqueflora, synonym Sarcocornia quinqueflora, commonly known as beaded samphire, bead weed, beaded glasswort or glasswort, is a species of succulent halophytic coastal shrub. Its Māori name is ureure. It belongs to the amaranth family, Amaranthaceae, and is indigenous to New Zealand but not endemic: it also grows in Australia.
In New Zealand it grows on the North, South and Chatham Islands. Nationally it is assessed Not Threatened (2023), with the qualifier Secure Overseas; the Wellington region ranks it Regionally Naturally Uncommon.
Allan's Flora of New Zealand (1961) treated it as Salicornia australis. Scott (1978) moved New Zealand plants to a new genus, as Sarcocornia quinqueflora subsp. quinqueflora; Flora of New Zealand Online now lists it again under Salicornia.
Nurseries sell it for coastal gardens, wetland margins, rock gardens and restoration plantings.

identification.text:
Low-growing, with slender flexible, sprawling to prostrate, interlacing branches and branchlets, forming a more or less cushion-like mass up to about 2 m in diameter, occasionally up to 2 m tall. Branchlets numerous, with yellowish brown bark, pubescent when young. Leaves in opposite pairs or fascicles, on yellowish petioles. Stipules rounded-obtuse to broadly triangular, more or less pubescent, ciliolate. Lamina coriaceous, yellowish green, linear, obtuse, 7–12 × 1–1.5–(2) mm. Midrib alone evident. Flowers solitary, terminal on short branchlets. Male flowers with calyx absent or vestigial; corolla funnelform, lobes ovate-oblong, subacute, about equal to the tube. Female flowers with acute, narrow-triangular calyx-teeth; corolla funnelform, lobes narrow-oblong, obtuse. Drupe translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, globose, about 7 mm in diameter.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Kanono's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Karamū's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Shining karamū's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Hybrids between taupata and sand coprosma are common (Coprosma ×kirkii), so plants in between exist; if a plant fits neither description, do not use this card. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Those figures fit the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa; the North Island's wild subsp. minor has thinner, papery leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) on stalks about 10–18 mm long, and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Large-seeded coprosma's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Hūpiro's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. The Flora's key separates them by the leaf veins: mingimingi shows the midrib and the net of veins, sand coprosma the midrib alone. Sand coprosma's leaves are yellowish green, mingimingi's dark green. Both have pale blue fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

habitat.text:
Gardens, paths, waste ground, dry banks and dunes.
In New Zealand: Common to abundant in cultivated land, waste places and most other open disturbed sites, especially stony and sandy areas, depleted and open pastures, coastal cliffs, dry river beds.

identification.text: Sprawling stems that are square in cross-section, with paired oval leaves — similar in size and shape to chickweed's. The flowers give it away: five salmon-orange petals (blue-flowered plants are blue pimpernel, now treated as a separate species), open in sunshine and closed in dull weather. Chickweed's flowers are white and its stem is round.

lookalikes.howToTell: Roll the stem: chickweed's is round with a single line of hairs, pimpernel's is four-angled and hairless. Any orange or orange-red flower means pimpernel — chickweed's petals are white, divided almost to the base, and rarely absent. Pimpernel carries its flowers singly in the leaf axils, chickweed in usually loose clusters at the stem tips. Pimpernel's leaves are stalkless and often indistinctly black-dotted underneath; chickweed's lower leaves are stalked. Leaf size and the sprawling habit do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Chickweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the petals: bird's-eye speedwell's flowers have four lobes, 8–12 mm across, usually sky-blue (rarely white) with dark stripes; scarlet pimpernel's have five, (2–)6–15 mm across, orange or orange-red. Bird's-eye speedwell's leaves have a short stalk and 3–8 pairs of coarse teeth; pimpernel's have no stalk, smooth edges and often faint black dots underneath. Speedwell's stem is round and hairy; pimpernel's is square and hairless. Both sprawl across the ground, carry their flowers singly on long, slender stalks, have leaves of overlapping size, flower all year and grow in gardens and crops, so none of these tells them apart. Bird's-eye speedwell's young leaves and shoots are eaten, but its record as food is thin.
lookalikes.name: Bird's-eye speedwell

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysimachia_arvensis Corroborates the saponins and the contact dermatitis, and gives the dose picture the entry's warning summarises: the herb and its seed contain saponins, and fresh material is strongly haemolytic; the root also yields cyclamin, a highly toxic triterpenoid glycoside. Experimental doses taken by mouth caused twenty-four hours of intense nausea, headache and bodily pain, and some people get dermatitis from handling the leaf. It grows through chickweed mats — pick chickweed stem by stem, not by the handful.

identification.text:
Almost scentless, annual or biennial herb sometimes regrowing from old rootstock. Stems erect or ascending, 15–100 cm tall, ribbed, usually glabrous, sometimes sparsely hairy, branched only above to form inflorescence or sometimes also much-branched from base. Basal and lower cauline leaves appearing shortly petiolate, but usually with very reduced leaflets along sheath, usually narrow-obovate, sometimes ovate, glabrous, mostly 3-pinnatisect, 15–150 × 10–60 mm; ultimate segments filiform, entire, not all in one plane giving a feathery appearance; cauline leaves similar to basal, but apetiolate and above becoming smaller and with fewer segments. Corymb diffuse, of few to many capitula. Involucral bracts glabrous or with a few scattered hairs, 4–7 mm long; margins pale or dark brown, membranous. Capitula about 30–50 mm diameter; ray florets 12-numerous; ligules white; disc florets numerous, yellow. Achenes 1.7–2.5 mm long, brown, narrow-obpyramidal to cylindric; inner surface with 3 thick ribs; outer surface rugose, with 2, more or less globose or slightly elongated glands at apex; corona crenulate, about 0.1 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The achenes distinguish Tripleurospermum inodorum from all other naturalised New Zealand Anthemideae: they have 3 distinct ribs on the inner face and usually 2 conspicuous glands at the top of the outer face, and the receptacle is conical, especially in fruit, with no scales among the florets (Flora of New Zealand, restated).
The yellow disc grows from button-shaped to dome-shaped to nearly round as it matures, and the white rays droop as it expands until they point straight down. Cut a head in half: the disc is solid at the core (Minnesota Wildflowers, restated).
Seedlings form small, dense rosettes of very finely divided leaves rather like fern fronds, and are very hard to tell by eye from the seedlings of stinking mayweed and pineappleweed. Crush the foliage: pineappleweed smells of pineapple, stinking chamomile stinks, and scentless chamomile smells of almost nothing (PGG Wrightson, restated). Next to stinking mayweed (stinking chamomile) its flowers are slightly larger and its leaflets slightly finer (Massey University, restated).
Corn chamomile (Anthemis arvensis), also naturalised in New Zealand and also almost scentless, has scales on its receptacle — elliptic-lanceolate and long-pointed — and square achenes broadest at the top (Flora of New Zealand key, restated); in Washington State scentless chamomile spreads unnoticed because it looks so like corn chamomile.

lookalikes.howToTell: Leaves separate them best: scentless chamomile's are cut about three times into thread-like segments that do not lie in one plane, giving a feathery look; ox-eye daisy's basal leaves are long-stalked and coarsely toothed, scalloped or at most shallowly lobed, and its upper stem leaves are narrow, stalkless and clasp the stem. Cut a head in half: scentless chamomile's receptacle is conical, rising to a dome as it matures; ox-eye's is flat or slightly domed. Scentless chamomile is an annual or biennial with a taproot; ox-eye daisy is a perennial whose stems root towards the base and spread by short rhizomes. What does not separate them: smell — both are almost scentless; head size — scentless chamomile's about 30–50 mm across, ox-eye's usually 30–60 mm (25–65 mm at the extremes); white rays around a yellow disc; and place — both grow on roadsides and in waste places and pasture. Ox-eye daisy's young leaves and flower buds are eaten (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Ox-eye daisy

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: stinking mayweed smells strongly foetid; scentless chamomile is almost scentless. Look inside the head: stinking mayweed has narrow, pointed scales among the inner florets; scentless chamomile has none. Stinking mayweed's heads are about 15–30 mm across (up to 35 mm) with 8–21 rays; scentless chamomile's are about 30–50 mm with 12 to many rays, and its leaflets are slightly finer. What does not separate them: both have leaves cut three times into fine, feathery segments, white rays around a yellow disc, and both grow on roadsides, waste places and pasture; heads of 30–35 mm fall in both ranges. Stinking mayweed is generally the commoner of the two in the North Island, scentless chamomile in Canterbury and much of the South Island. Stinking mayweed is not a food plant: its acrid juice can blister skin and it is reported as toxic (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Stinking mayweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Roman chamomile is a low, creeping, sweetly aromatic perennial whose moderately to densely hairy stems lie along the ground or rise to about 20 cm; scentless chamomile is an almost scentless, usually hairless annual or biennial with erect or ascending stems 15–100 cm tall. Look inside the head: Roman chamomile has small, blunt scales among the florets; scentless chamomile has none. Roman chamomile's heads are about 8–20 mm across (up to 30 mm), scentless chamomile's about 30–50 mm. What does not separate them: both have leaves cut three times into narrow segments with a feathery look, and white rays around a yellow disc. Roman chamomile's flowers are used for herb tea (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Roman chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: In flower they are easy: pineappleweed's heads have no white rays — they are small greenish-yellow domes 4–10 mm across — while scentless chamomile's are 30–50 mm with white rays. Before flowering, crush a leaf: pineappleweed is aromatic and smells of pineapple, scentless chamomile is almost scentless. Pineappleweed's leaf segments lie more or less in one plane; scentless chamomile's do not, so its leaves look more feathery. Pineappleweed is usually 5–20 cm tall (up to 40 cm). What does not separate them: both have finely divided leaves and grow on roadsides and in waste places. Pineappleweed's flower heads are eaten and made into tea (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Pineappleweed

summary.text:
Tripleurospermum inodorum, common names scentless false mayweed, scentless mayweed, scentless chamomile, and Baldr's brow, is the type species of Tripleurospermum. It is an annual, or in some situations a short-lived perennial, found all over New Zealand and especially in Canterbury; in New Zealand it is also called false chamomile. Seeds germinate at any time of year when the soil is moist, lit and above 3 °C, mostly in spring and autumn, and one plant can set 10,000 to 200,000 seeds (PGG Wrightson, restated). Pollen is collected by solitary bees.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Auckland City, Wellington City, Hutt Valley; South Island: mainly dry eastern areas from Marlborough to Central Otago and Southland. Native range Mediterranean to Western Asia and southern Russia; first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1870.
Scentless mayweed, or scentless chamomile as it is sometimes called, is often abundant on roadsides and in waste places. It has previously been known in New Zealand as T. maritimum, Matricaria perforata, M. inodora, and Chrysanthemum inodorum.
In New Zealand stinking mayweed is generally the commoner of the two in the North Island, while scentless chamomile is the more common in Canterbury and several other parts of the South Island (Massey University, restated).

warnings: There is no record of scentless chamomile being eaten, and it is not one of the chamomiles used for tea. It looks very like them — check the receptacle and the smell (see the lookalikes).
It is not known to be toxic, but stock will not eat it and hens avoid it, and eaten in large amounts it can blister the muzzles of livestock.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand: waste places, scrubland, riverbeds, coastal areas.
In New Zealand it grows in lowland and montane places of low to high fertility, usually where rainfall is high, on acid soils but never on chalk: shrubland, tall and short tussockland, cliffs, bluffs and riverbeds, and disturbed ground such as pasture, waste ground and poorly grazed areas. It does not tolerate poor drainage.
