identification.text:
Much-branched deciduous shrub up to 2–(2.5) m high; twigs glabrous, but sericeous when young, green, more or less 5-angled. Leaves variable, usually more or less glabrous above and sericeous below, and 3-foliolate and petiolate when mature or on older twigs; leaves of younger twigs often 1–2-foliolate and subsessile; young leaves often sericeous above and below but sometimes glabrous; leaflets apetiolulate, elliptic to obovate, usually acute, sometimes emarginate, 4–16–(20) mm long; terminal leaflet > lateral leaflets. Flowers usually solitary, rarely paired, axillary; pedicels (3)–5–13 mm long. Calyx glabrous, bilabiate, about 1/4 length of corolla; upper and lower lips more or less entire or shallowly toothed. Corolla usually golden yellow, rarely partly red or tinged mauve, 16–25 mm long. Pod black, oblong, many-seeded, 15–60 mm long, with hairy margins; seeds brown or greenish brown, ellipsoid, compressed, about 3 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Cultivated forms with a partly red standard, and also sometimes the keel and wings tinged red to reddish brown, are occasionally naturalised; the name C. scoparius f. andreanus is sometimes applied to these plants.
It flowers from September to April. The pods turn black as they ripen and burst explosively on warm days, scattering the seed and leaving the empty pod halves hanging in coils on the plant.

lookalikes.howToTell: French (Montpellier) broom's twigs are round and ribbed, it is usually evergreen, and its flowers are 9–13 mm long in clusters of 4–7 at the ends of short side branches, with a densely hairy calyx; its pods are densely hairy all over, about 18–20 mm long. Scotch broom's twigs are green and more or less five-angled, it loses its leaves, and its flowers are single or paired in the leaf angles, 16–25 mm long, with a hairless calyx; its pods are black, 15–60 mm long, hairy only along the edges.
lookalikes.name: French broom

lookalikes.howToTell: Sweet broom's twigs are rounded and ribbed, it is evergreen, and its flowers are 10–30 or more together in elongated racemes at the ends of the shoots, with a densely hairy calyx; its pods are densely hairy all over, 20–40 mm long. Scotch broom's twigs are green and more or less five-angled, it loses its leaves, and its flowers are single or paired in the leaf angles, with a hairless calyx; its pods are black, 15–60 mm long, hairy only along the edges. Flower length overlaps (sweet broom 13–18 mm, Scotch broom 16–25 mm) and does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Sweet broom

lookalikes.howToTell: Gorse is sharply spiny, and on a grown plant its leaves are reduced to spines, the main ones rigid, furrowed and 15–30 mm long. Scotch broom has no spines; its green twigs are more or less five-angled, and its leaves have three leaflets on older twigs, often one or two on young twigs. Gorse seedlings have leaves of three hairy leaflets, so a seedling's leaves do not separate it from broom. Both have yellow pea flowers, usually single, and their length overlaps (gorse 13–20 mm, Scotch broom 16–25 mm), so flowers do not separate them. Gorse's pods are hairy all over and 13–25 mm long; Scotch broom's are 15–60 mm long and hairy only along the edges.
lookalikes.name: Gorse

lookalikes.howToTell: Spanish broom's twigs are stout, rounded and finely grooved, and on adult plants are usually almost leafless; its leaves are simple, 15–25 mm long on mature branches. Scotch broom's twigs are more or less five-angled, and its leaves have three leaflets on older twigs but often only one or two on young twigs, so a single leaf on a young twig does not separate them. Spanish broom's calyx is one-lipped, split above, with five short teeth on one side, a shape that sets it apart from every other wild legume in New Zealand; Scotch broom's calyx is two-lipped. Spanish broom's flowers are fragrant and usually many together in racemes at the ends of the shoots; Scotch broom's are usually single, rarely paired, in the leaf angles. Spanish broom's pods become hairless and are 50–90 mm long; Scotch broom's are black, 15–60 mm long and hairy along the edges. Flower length overlaps (Spanish broom 22–28 mm, Scotch broom 16–25 mm) and does not separate them. Spanish broom flowers from December to May, Scotch broom from September to April.
lookalikes.name: Spanish broom

summary.text:
Scotch broom (Cytisus scoparius) is a much-branched, often almost leafless, deciduous shrub of the pea family, with flexible, ridged green stems and golden-yellow pea flowers.
In New Zealand: throughout the North and South Islands; on Stewart Island at Halfmoon Bay and the mouth of the Lords River; on the Chatham Islands and Campbell Island. It comes from Europe, Asia Minor and Russia and was first recorded wild here in 1872. Broom is a widespread and troublesome weed in many areas of New Zealand, particularly in less intensively farmed hill country and riverbeds. Broom has been known in New Zealand as Sarothamnus scoparius and Spartium scoparium. In New Zealand it is also called broom, English broom and wild broom.
It was brought here as an ornamental. Plants do not flower until at least two years old and are thought to live for 10–15 years. The pods burst on hot days and throw the seed, which is also carried by gravel, mud, animals, machinery, people, roads and water; seed buried deeper survives longer in the soil.
It copes with cold better than gorse, so it is the more troublesome of the two above 300 metres and in some southern districts, and it is one of the most troublesome weeds of plantation forests, where soil under pines has held up to 36,000 seeds per square metre.
As a legume it fixes nitrogen, changing which plants can grow where it has been and opening the way for other weeds; it forms pure stands that keep native seedlings from establishing in low-canopy habitats, and the extra nitrogen on gumlands and other poor soils harms specialised plants such as orchids, ferns and kauri. On braided riverbeds it binds the gravel, so the river forms fast-flowing channels that wading birds cannot feed in, and it covers the open ground riverbed birds nest on while giving cover to cats and stoats. It needs light, so where native seedlings are present taller native species eventually shade it out, though not in kauri or tānekaha forest; in a trial on a braided-river terrace on the Canterbury Plains, native trees and shrubs sown or planted under living broom germinated and survived better than where the broom had been mulched, root-raked or crushed.

method.text: The flowers give an acid yellow on alum-mordanted wool, but only after the simmered dye bath has stood for some days and gone musty, almost mouldy; simmering the fresh flowers alone gave no dye.

sources: Snapdragon Life, 'Scotch broom as a dye plant' (https://www.snapdragonlife.com/news/blog/scotch-broom-as-a-dye-plant/, retrieved 26/11/2026) — restated

recipes.method: 400 g broom flowers; 3 litres tap water; 100 g wool, mordanted with alum. Simmer the flowers in the water for 1 hour, then leave them to steep for 4 days until the bath smells musty. Strain, squeezing out the flowers. Add the mordanted wool and keep the bath just below a simmer for 40 minutes, then leave the wool to steep for 18 hours. Drain, wash and dry the wool.
recipes.title: Acid-yellow wool dye

warnings: The seeds are poisonous, especially if chewed or crushed before swallowing.

The pods are toxic, and the plant, flowers included, contains toxic alkaloids, chiefly sparteine and cytisine, that depress the heart and nervous system; only the flower buds and flowers are eaten. In large doses sparteine causes vomiting and purging, weakens the heart and lowers blood pressure, and in extreme cases it kills by impairing breathing.

The flower buds may be toxic to some people. Large doses of broom upset the stomach and bowels, and more than 30 g of it can poison, causing dizziness, headache, changes in heartbeat, weak legs, sweating, sleepiness and widened pupils.

Broom should not be eaten by pregnant women, as it might cause a miscarriage, or by breastfeeding women, or by people with high blood pressure, heart disease or kidney disease; it contains tyramine, which can raise or lower blood pressure.
Do not eat broom while taking MAOI antidepressants, which stop the body breaking down its tyramine and can lead to dangerously high blood pressure, or while taking lithium, haloperidol or quinidine.
Spanish broom, which is often confused with Scotch broom, is poisonous in all its parts, flowers included (see the lookalikes).

It is a pest plant in New Zealand: it is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and the regional pest management plans of Northland, Auckland, Waikato, Gisborne, Hawke's Bay, Manawatū-Whanganui, Taranaki, Tasman-Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, the West Coast, Otago, Southland and the Chatham Islands name it.

identification.text:
A medium-sized to large pine whose crown flattens with age. The bark is grey and fissured low on the trunk and turns reddish or orange-brown and flaky higher up, though the red upper trunk and flat crown only show on quite large trees. The needles come in pairs, short (2.5–7 cm), fairly stiff, twisted, and nearly always bluish or grey-green, so the foliage can look silvery. The cones are small, 3–6 cm, light brownish grey, on a short stalk that curves back; they hang down, have no prickles, and fall whole each year. Short, twisted, blue-green needles in pairs with small, unarmed, stalked cones set it apart. Dwarf mountain pine and mountain pine are similar, but their cones have no stalk.
Shoots light yellow, yellowish brown or light brown, hairless. Buds cylindrical-egg-shaped, reddish brown, not or slightly resinous, the scales free at the tips. Needles 2 per bundle, 2.5–7 cm × 1–1.5 mm; resin canals near the edge; the sheath soon very short. Male cones about 5 mm long, more or less cylindrical. Young female cones stalked, the scales with a short point. Mature cones more or less hanging, 3–6 × 1.5–3 cm when closed, cylindrical-oblong or cylindrical-egg-shaped, symmetrical or slightly lopsided; the scale ends rather elongated and tending to curve towards the base, with no prickle. Seed wing lopsided, under 1 cm long. Planted trees vary: some have greener, only slightly curved needles.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have short needles in pairs and small cones of the same size; look at the cones. Contorta pine's cones are almost stalkless, have a short slender prickle on each scale, and stay closed on the tree for years; its needles are 3.5–6.5 cm, generally yellowish green. Scots pine's needles are 2.5–7 cm, twisted and bluish or grey-green, often looking silvery; its cones are small, 3–6 cm, on a short stalk that curves back, with no prickles, and fall whole each year; high on the trunk the bark turns orange-brown and flaky. Contorta pine's seeds and spring inner bark are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Contorta pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have needles in pairs and cones that fall each year. Corsican pine's needles are much longer, 6–16 cm, light green, flexible and scarcely twisted; its cones are 4–9 cm, stalkless, with at most a tiny prickle. Scots pine's needles are 2.5–7 cm, twisted and bluish or grey-green, often looking silvery; its cones are small, 3–6 cm, on a short stalk that curves back, with no prickles, and fall whole each year; high on the trunk the bark turns orange-brown and flaky. Corsican pine's seeds, needles and young cones are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Corsican pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have stiff needles in pairs and cones that fall each year. Austrian pine's needles are much longer, up to 16 cm, dark green, scarcely twisted and sharp; its cones are 4–9 cm and stalkless; its bark is dark all the way up. Scots pine's needles are 2.5–7 cm, twisted and bluish or grey-green, often looking silvery; its cones are small, 3–6 cm, on a short stalk that curves back, with no prickles, and fall whole each year; high on the trunk the bark turns orange-brown and flaky. Austrian pine's seeds, needles and young cones are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Austrian pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the needles in a bundle. Radiata pine has needles in threes, 6–15 cm, deep or dark green; its cones are 6–13 cm, stalkless, lopsided and stay on the tree for years. Scots pine has needles in pairs, 2.5–7 cm, twisted and bluish or grey-green; its cones are 3–6 cm, on a short curved-back stalk, and fall whole each year. Radiata pine's seeds and young male cones are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Monterey pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have needles in pairs; look at the cones. Bishop pine's cones are 6–9 cm, lopsided, stalkless, with stout rigid prickles, mostly in clusters of 4–5, and stay closed on the tree for many years; its needles are 7–15 cm, stiff and sharp. Scots pine's needles are 2.5–7 cm, twisted and bluish or grey-green, often looking silvery; its cones are small, 3–6 cm, on a short stalk that curves back, with no prickles, and fall whole each year; high on the trunk the bark turns orange-brown and flaky. Bishop pine's young green cones are used for syrup (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Bishop pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have short needles in pairs and small cones without prickles; look at the needles and the cone stalk. Dwarf mountain pine is usually a dense shrub or small tree; its cones are 2.5–5.5 cm, symmetrical, upright, almost stalkless, with no prickles; its needles are 3–7 cm, dark green, curved but not twisted. Scots pine's needles are 2.5–7 cm, twisted and bluish or grey-green; its cones are 3–6 cm, symmetrical, and hang on a short stalk that curves back; high on the trunk the bark turns orange-brown and flaky. Dwarf mountain pine's young cones are made into syrup (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mountain pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both can be trees with short needles in pairs; look at the cones. Mountain pine usually grows as a tree; its cones are lopsided, with the lower scales on the upper side drawn out downwards into hooks, sometimes with a blunt prickle. Scots pine's needles are 2.5–7 cm, twisted and bluish or grey-green; its cones are 3–6 cm, symmetrical, and hang on a short stalk that curves back; high on the trunk the bark turns orange-brown and flaky. Mountain pine's young cones are made into syrup (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mountain pine

preparation.text: Pick needles and shoot tips in spring: the needles toughen a lot as they age and give up little flavour after spring. Rub and smell them first; chop, pound or blend them to release the flavour. Use them chopped as a seasoning, pound them with sugar, or steep them in hot water for tea, sweetened with honey if you like. Crush and taste a young male cone before you gather more; steep them in vinegar or a neutral spirit such as vodka for a couple of weeks, or coat them in sugar for a syrup. For the famine flour, the inner bark was dried, ground to a powder and baked into bread, often mixed with oatmeal.

Months [] 23/11/2026: no New Zealand source dates the young needles, shoots or male cones of Scots pine. summary.text:
Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) is an evergreen pine of the pine family (Pinaceae) from Europe and western and northern Asia. Its young needles and shoots and its young male cones are used as a flavouring, its small seeds are eaten, and its dried inner bark was ground into a famine flour.
In New Zealand: It was first recorded wild in 1919, after being introduced for forestry. It is grown in the cooler parts of the country, especially in the east of the South Island, but is generally uncommon. The Flora (1988) found it an occasional escape, properly naturalised only at and near Glynn Wye on slopes and terraces above the Waiau River in North Canterbury, and also wild in Kaweka Forest Park in Hawke's Bay. Herbarium sheets since then record it naturalised at Golden Downs in Tasman, in Karioi Forest near Ruapehu, above Lake Chalice in Marlborough and by the Oreti River near the Mavora Lakes in Southland. Its seed is spread by the wind.
It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds and in regional pest plans from Northland to Southland and the Chatham Islands, most of them for progressive containment.

method.text: Needles: simmered, not boiled, in a covered pot of water until the water has coloured, then lifted out; wet fabric is kept in the bath at a gentle heat for about an hour, longer for a stronger colour. Scoured hemp with no mordant, dyed in an aluminium pot, came out a soft mauve-clay, and one bath coloured several pieces. The needles are also listed as giving a tan or green dye. Cones: soaked in water for a day to soften, cut into pieces, boiled for up to four hours (a lower heat loses less dye) and strained through muslin; cotton dyed for an hour and left to cool in the bath came out beige to light brown, mordanted or not, and the bath was used again the next day. On cotton and silk, cone tannins give beiges with orange and pink hues.

recipes.method: A box of pine needles about 30 × 20 cm; a 20-litre aluminium pot of cool water; a piece of hemp fabric about 1 × 1.5 m. Scour the fabric in a 40 °C wash with fragrance-free powder and about 250 ml (a cup) of baking soda, no fabric softener, then soak it in water for about an hour. Put the needles in the pot of water, cover, and bring to a simmer without boiling; turn the heat down a little and keep it there until the water has the colour you want. Lift out the needles with a fine sieve (straining through muslin gives a more even colour). Add the wet fabric, push out the air bubbles with a wooden spoon so it is all under, and keep it at a gentle heat for about an hour, stirring now and then; leave it longer for a stronger colour. Wring it out, wash and rinse it with fragrance-free powder and no softener, and dry it out of direct sun. The same bath dyes several pieces in turn.

method.text: Tinder: needles left to dry for a season, or dry ones from the forest floor, catch fire easily, more so with a little pitch. Fatwood, the dense amber wood soaked with resin in the stumps and lower branches of dead pines, is shaved into thin slivers and lit with a spark or flame, and still lights when damp. Glue: resin that has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground is gathered rather than cut from the tree, melted (on a hot rock beside a fire, for example), mixed with finely ground ash or powdered charcoal and left to cool; it is reheated to use. A little water softens old pitch into a soft glue, and pine shavings or sawdust worked into it make a wood filler. Oil or strong alcohol takes pitch off your hands. Incense: needles tied into a bundle with natural twine and dried for about two weeks. Cleaner: chopped needles covered with vinegar in a glass jar, with baking paper under the lid so it does not corrode, left for two weeks and strained; the vinegar is mixed with baking soda and castile soap for cleaning.

method.text: Resin is gathered from what has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground rather than cut from the tree, at any time of year. It sticks to everything, so keep a knife and jar just for it; oil, then soap, takes it off your hands, and rubbing alcohol off clothes. Large lumps melt faster if frozen and broken up with a hammer inside a thick paper bag. Warmed with an equal amount of beeswax, mixed and left to set in its container, it makes a simple balm; melted into an oil, strained and firmed with beeswax it makes a balm for dry or cracked skin, lips and hands.

recipes.method: 60 ml (¼ cup) pine resin; 125 ml (½ cup) oil such as olive or almond; 15–30 g grated beeswax. Melt the resin in the oil in a double boiler over a low heat. Strain through a coffee filter or a strainer, return to the double boiler, add the beeswax and heat gently until it has melted. Pour into tins or jars and store somewhere cool and dark.
recipes.title: Pine resin balm

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) pine resin; 250 ml (1 cup) olive oil, or another oil safe for skin; 125–190 ml (½–¾ cup) grated beeswax; 35 drops rosemary essential oil. Put the resin and oil in a glass jar in the top of a double boiler and simmer, stirring, until the resin melts; this can take several hours. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine sieve and return it to the double boiler. For every 250 ml of resin and oil add 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) grated beeswax (more gives a firmer balm) and heat gently until it melts. Pour into jars or tins, stir 5 drops of the essential oil into each, and put the lids on straight away so the scent stays in. Leave to cool and set, and store somewhere cool and dark. Use it on dry or cracked skin, as a lip or hand balm, or overnight on the face.
recipes.title: Pine resin and olive oil balm

habitat.text:
Isolated populations grow in coastal scrub and around forest margins. It also grows in other shrubland and sometimes among rocks in the open, from sea level to 750 m.
Fuchsia perscandens's preferred habitats are river terraces and remnants of white pine swamp forest, but the species has also been found in limestone, for example in the Wairarapa or in Marlborough.
Lowland forest, especially in clearings, around margins and in remnant stands.
In gardens it is grown in partial shade or full sun, in fertile, free-draining soil kept moist but not waterlogged.

identification.text:
Gynodioecious, deciduous liane with stout main stems to about 5 m long and 5 cm diameter, sparingly branched, sprawling when lacking support; bark pale brownish orange, more or less flaking; branchlets hairy at first. Petioles 10–20 mm long, very slender. Lamina (10)–25–30 × (10)–20–25–(30) mm, broad-ovate to suborbicular, sinuate, membranous, remotely and obscurely dentate, green or dark green above, glaucescent below, glabrous except on veins and margins; base subcordate to truncate; apex subacute. Flowers solitary or occasionally 2–3 together; pedicels very slender, about 10 mm long. Floral tube 7–15 mm long. Sepals 6–10 mm long, narrow-ovate, green or nearly so, patent to reflexed. Petals dark purple, 1–5 mm long, narrow-oblong. Stamens of ☿ flowers exserted; filaments 10–15 mm long, purple. Stigma capitate. Berry 5–10 mm long, more or less broad-cylindric, dark purple.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stems: tree fuchsia is a tree or shrub to about 12 m with a distinct trunk to 60 cm thick, and keeps its trunked form even when it is much reduced in exposed places; scrambling fuchsia is a liane, with stout main stems to about 5 m long and 5 cm thick that sprawl when they lack support, and in the open it can form a ball-like shrub of interlacing branchlets. Look at the leaf shape: tree fuchsia's leaves are usually lance-shaped to narrowly egg-shaped or oblong, with a pointed to drawn-out tip and a rounded or wedge-shaped base; scrambling fuchsia's are broadly egg-shaped to almost round, with a slightly heart-shaped to squared-off base and a slightly pointed tip. Leaf size overlaps (tree fuchsia's 2–14 cm long, sometimes 1.5 cm; scrambling fuchsia's 25–30 mm, sometimes 10 mm), and tree fuchsia has smaller leaves in exposed places, so go by shape, not size. The flowers are alike, scrambling fuchsia's smaller, but the floral tube (tree fuchsia 7–20 mm, scrambling fuchsia 7–15 mm), the sepals (5–16 mm against 6–10 mm) and the dark purple berries (about 10 mm against 5–10 mm) overlap, so flowers and fruit do not separate them. Plants intermediate in size and habit between the two, Fuchsia ×colensoi, probably their hybrid though this is not confirmed, often grow with both. Tree fuchsia's ripe berries are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Tree fuchsia

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the main stems: scrambling fuchsia is a liane whose stout main stems, to about 5 m long and 5 cm thick, sprawl when they lack support; Fuchsia ×colensoi is usually a shrub or small tree whose branches may be slender and scrambling but not its main stems, though some plants are lianoid. Without support, both can form a somewhat similar ball-like shrub of interlacing branchlets. Look at the leaves: scrambling fuchsia's are broadly egg-shaped to almost round, usually 25–30 mm long, with a slightly heart-shaped to squared-off base; Fuchsia ×colensoi's are usually egg-shaped to broadly egg-shaped or oblong-egg-shaped, less often almost round, usually 3–8 cm long, with the base usually broadly wedge-shaped, squared-off or rounded, occasionally slightly heart-shaped. Leaf size overlaps (scrambling fuchsia 25–30 mm, sometimes 10 mm; Fuchsia ×colensoi 3–8 cm, sometimes 2 cm or 10 cm), so a plant with small, round leaves may be either. Flowers and berries do not separate them: the floral tube (scrambling fuchsia 7–15 mm, Fuchsia ×colensoi 8–20 mm), the sepals (6–10 mm against 6–14 mm) and the dark purple berries (5–10 mm against about 10 mm) overlap. Fuchsia ×colensoi is intermediate in size and habit between scrambling fuchsia and tree fuchsia, probably their hybrid though this is not confirmed, and in many areas grows with both. Fuchsia ×colensoi's food record is thin (see its page).

summary.text:
Scrambling fuchsia, Fuchsia perscandens, is a deciduous liane of the willowherb family (Onagraceae), endemic to New Zealand.
It grows on the North and South Islands, from near Pipiwai in Northland to Southland, and is often uncommon over large parts of its range; in Otago, Southland and Fiordland it becomes increasingly rare and local southwards. It is assessed Not Threatened (2023).
New Zealand nurseries sell it for native and woodland gardens and for banks, where it spreads through the plants around it.

warnings: No record of people eating this species' berries was found. That they are harmless rests on a general record for all New Zealand's native fuchsias, not on a record for this one. Its berries are fewer than tree fuchsia's.

In New Zealand it grows in salt marshes and on rocky and gravelly coasts within range of high tide, throughout, more or less local.
On New Zealand's national wetland plant list it is rated facultative: it commonly grows either in wetlands or on dry ground.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In the Wellington region (Regionally Critical), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it. In Northland (Regionally Naturally Uncommon) and the Auckland region (Regionally Declining), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text:
Perennial much-branched subshrub; stems woody, bearing persistent leaf-bases, more or less ascending, up to 30 cm or more long; branchlets grooved when dry. Leaves sessile, opposite, alternate, or fascicled (on same plant), approximate, patent; lamina fleshy, linear to narrow-oblong (occasionally narrow-obovate), more or less apiculate, 4–12 × 1–2 mm. Flowers axillary, (1)–3–(4) together, each subtended by 2 bracteoles. Perianth 5-lobed; lobes ovate, erect; stigmas 2–3; seeds horizontal, red-brown, glossy.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]
The New Zealand species has the flowers in the axils of undifferentiated foliage leaves (usually 1 large, between 2 small).
The flowers are green or white.

summary.text:
Sea blite (Suaeda novae-zelandiae) is a succulent, much-branched subshrub of salt marshes and rocky coasts, in the amaranth family, Amaranthaceae, and endemic to New Zealand.
It grows on the North and South Islands. Nationally it is assessed Not Threatened (2023); regionally it is ranked Regionally Critical in Wellington, Regionally Naturally Uncommon in Northland and Regionally Declining in Auckland, and Regionally Not Threatened in Otago.
It is related to S. maritima and S. australis. Before Allan named it in 1961, New Zealand plants were misidentified as S. maritima.
It is not sold by nurseries.

habitat.text: Coastal stony waste land and roadsides. In New Zealand it grows behind beaches on rock platforms with a thin layer of soil, where it can be abundant. New Zealand herbarium specimens also record it on beach gravel just above the spray zone (Palmer Bay and Tarakena Bay, Wellington), just above the high-tide mark on crumbling mudstone (Kāwhia Harbour), on a coastal gravel beach (Waituna, Southland), and inland on a dry gravel roadside cutting near Hamilton, roadside banks and the base of a street wall in Wellington.

identification.text:
Stems glabrous, 10–30 cm tall; some shoots leafy during winter. Leaves glabrous, often with scabrid margin, mostly oblanceolate to lanceolate, 1.5–3 × 0.5–1 cm. Inflorescence 1–(3)-flowered; bracts green. Calyx wide at mouth. Capsule wide-mouthed; teeth recurved. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4. as Silene vulgaris subsp. maritima (With.) Á.Löve & D.Löve]
In New Zealand it forms flat, prostrate mats with glaucescent leaves; the calyx is purple-veined and whitish, more or less inflated, and the petals are white.

lookalikes.howToTell: Bladder campion is the taller plant of waste land, roadsides, arable land and railway yards: its stems are 30–80 cm tall, all its shoots die back in winter, and its leaves are usually 3–10 × 1–2 cm (from 1.5 × 0.5 cm); sea campion's stems are 10–30 cm, some of its shoots stay leafy through winter, and its leaves are 1.5–3 × 0.5–1 cm. Count the flowers on a stem: bladder campion usually has 6–30 (3 to 40); sea campion has 1, sometimes up to 3, so a 3-flowered stem does not tell them apart. Bladder campion's bracts are papery (scarious) and its calyx is narrowed at the mouth; sea campion's bracts are green and its calyx is wide at the mouth. In fruit, bladder campion's capsule is narrow-mouthed with erect to spreading teeth; sea campion's is wide-mouthed with its teeth curled back.
lookalikes.name: Bladder campion

lookalikes.howToTell: White campion is softly hairy: its stems, leaves and calyx have soft hairs, with glandular hairs as well higher up; sea campion's stems, leaves and calyx have no hairs apart from tiny hairs on the calyx teeth (the leaf edges are often rough). White campion's stems are usually 30–60 cm tall (15 to 130 cm) and its leaves usually 4–8 × 1–2 cm (from 2 × 0.5 cm); sea campion's stems are 10–30 cm tall and its leaves 1.5–3 × 0.5–1 cm. Count the flowers on a stem: white campion usually has 7–10 (3 to 20); sea campion has 1, sometimes up to 3, so a 3-flowered stem does not tell them apart. White campion has separate male plants (flowers with 10 stamens) and female plants (flowers with 5 styles), and its capsule has usually 10 teeth (8 to 12), erect or spreading; every sea campion flower has both stamens and 3 styles, and its capsule is wide-mouthed with 6 teeth curled back.
lookalikes.name: White campion

summary.text: Sea campion (Silene uniflora, formerly S. maritima and S. vulgaris subsp. maritima) is a low perennial of the pink or carnation family (Caryophyllaceae), native to western Europe, usually on coasts. In New Zealand it is naturalised; the Flora of New Zealand (1988) records it from New Plymouth and Wellington. Herbarium specimens also come from Kāwhia Harbour and Hamilton in the Waikato and from Waituna in Southland. Most wild records are from the south coast of Wellington, with scattered records elsewhere in both islands. It is not listed as an environmental weed or a regional pest plant.

warnings: The leaves contain saponins. These are toxic but poorly absorbed, so they mostly pass through the body without causing harm; eat only a few leaves raw, or cook them.

habitat.text: Coasts and lowlands throughout the country, very rarely in the mountains. Common on rock ledges, boulder falls and cliff faces, on damp seepages in petrel scrub, in peaty turf and saltmarsh, on estuary mud banks and around brackish ponds and lagoons. It also grows beside lakes, tarns, streams and rivers and in wet hollows, sometimes well inland and at quite high elevations.

identification.text:
Procumbent to ascending, terrestrial perennial, not rooting at nodes. Leaves pinnately 3-foliolate to 1–2-pinnate; ultimate segments broadly or narrowly ovate to deltate, usually lobed and crenate, about 5–30 mm long; upper stem leaves similar to lower and basal leaves, but often reduced and 3-foliolate or simple. Umbels compound, usually sessile or subsessile, leaf-opposed; rays 2–10–(15); bracts and bracteoles 0. Flowers numerous, white. Fruit broadly ovoid, 1.5–2.5 mm long; ribs broad and spongy. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The sprawling stems are 0.3–1.2 m long and often climb up through the plants around them. The leaves are dark green to yellow-green and smell of celery when crushed; the petals are off-white to cream. A single bract sometimes sits under an umbel, but it usually falls early. Plants vary a great deal: some, mostly on muddy ground in saltmarshes and brackish ponds, have very slender leaves and purplish leaf stalks.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand; all parts are poisonous if eaten. Look under the umbels: hemlock has about 4–8 narrow, pointed, down-turned bracts beneath each umbel and 3–6 bracteoles on the outer side of each small umbel; sea celery usually has none, occasionally a single bract that falls early. Hemlock is erect, up to 2–(3) m, with hollow stems usually spotted or blotched purple; sea celery is prostrate to ascending, its sprawling stems 0.3–1.2 m long. Hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided and sea celery's three-parted to 1–2 times divided with lobed, toothed segments that are narrow in some plants, so leaf shape alone does not separate them. Hemlock smells foetid or musty when crushed and sea celery has a celery-like aroma, but no source here treats smell as a reliable test on its own. Sea celery is mostly coastal but also grows beside lakes and streams inland, and hemlock grows in damp waste ground and riverbeds, so place does not rule hemlock out. Both have white flowers in compound umbels, though sea celery's petals can be off-white to cream.
lookalikes.name: Hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: Look under the small umbels: water celery always has 4–8 small bracteoles there, and sea celery has none. Water celery's stems root at the lower nodes; sea celery's sprawling stems do not root. Water celery's leaves are once-pinnate, with 2–8 pairs of toothed leaflets 1–8 cm long (up to 12); sea celery's are three-parted to 1–2-pinnate, with lobed segments about 5–30 mm long. Water celery grows in fresh water — drains and the margins of rivers, streams, lakes and ponds — but sea celery also grows beside lakes and streams inland, so place does not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Water celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Garden celery is occasionally found wild. It is an erect biennial up to 80–100 cm tall with hollow, grooved stems; sea celery is prostrate to ascending, its stems sprawling 0.3–1.2 m long. Sea celery usually has no bracts or bracteoles under its umbels (at most a single bract that soon falls), and celery has none, so that check does not separate them. Celery's flowers are greenish white, about 1 mm across. The surest difference is the ripe fruit: celery's are dark brown with thread-thin ribs, sea celery's have broad, spongy ribs. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Celery

preparation.text:
Use it as you would parsley or celery: in salads, soups, stocks, stews and quiches, in dressings, flavoured butter and white sauces, and with seafood. It is a strong herb, so use it sparingly so that it blends in rather than taking over. Dried leaves go into spice mixes.
It goes well with carrots and onion, as in a mirepoix.

recipes.method: Written for sea celery grown in a home garden in Perth, Western Australia; the page does not give the scientific name. Serves 2 with pasta. 60 g roasted macadamias; 40 g basil; 30 ml (2 Tbsp) extra virgin olive oil; 30 g pecorino; 1 large garlic clove; 3 large sprigs sea celery; 2 large sprigs seablite; 4–5 native mint leaves; 1 mountain pepper leaf. Chop the leafy ingredients finely first if you want a greener pesto. Pound everything in a mortar and pestle until mostly smooth but still a little chunky. Toss it through freshly cooked pasta, loosening it with a splash of the pasta water if needed. The authors serve it on their own wattleseed and peppermint gum malloreddus and warn to go easy on the mountain pepper. The authors' note allows extra basil or parsley in place of the fresh native herbs.
recipes.title: Sea celery and macadamia pesto

recipes.method: Written for dried sea parsley (Apium prostratum var. prostratum) sold by a Western Australian native-plant nursery. Serves 4 as a side. 45 ml (3 Tbsp) dried sea parsley; 1 whole cauliflower, broken into florets; 60 ml (4 Tbsp) wholegrain Dijon mustard; 30 ml (2 Tbsp) crushed garlic; 45 ml (3 Tbsp) lemon juice; olive oil; vegetable oil; salt and pepper; aioli, to serve. Heat the oven to 200 °C and line a baking tray with baking paper. Toss the cauliflower with the mustard, garlic, lemon juice and sea parsley, pour over plenty of olive oil, season with salt and pepper and toss again to coat. Spread it on the tray and bake for 25 minutes, turning once, until crisp and golden. Serve with spoonfuls of aioli. The author does not say how to dry the leaves, or what the vegetable oil is for.
recipes.title: Sea parsley baked cauliflower

recipes.method: Written for sea parsley (Apium prostratum var. prostratum) sold by a Western Australian native-plant nursery; the recipe is by RiverMint Dining. Serves 2. 350 g skin-on snapper fillets, scaled (keep the bones); 100 g warrigal greens; 200 ml vegetable purée, such as turnip, potato or pea; 150 g cold butter, cubed; 2 sticks celery; half an onion, roughly chopped; 3 lemons; 20 sprigs dried native lemongrass; 3 sprigs sea parsley; salt and pepper; olive oil. Season and dry the fillets and fry them skin side down in hot olive oil for 2 minutes, pressing down so they don't shrink; turn and cook 2 minutes more. Add a squeeze of lemon and 15 ml (1 Tbsp) butter to the pan, baste, then keep the fish warm in a low oven. For the sauce, put the juice of a lemon, 10 lemongrass sprigs, the snapper bones, onion and celery in a pan, cover with water, bring to the boil and simmer 15 minutes, skimming. Strain out the bones, return to the pan and reduce by half, adding more lemongrass to taste; season and strain again. Over medium heat, whisk in the cold butter a few cubes at a time until the sauce thickens. Bash the warrigal greens with a rolling pin, boil them for 2 minutes to remove oxalic acid, then drain and squeeze dry. Blanch the sea parsley on its stems for 15 seconds so it keeps its crunch, refresh in iced water, then pick and dry the leaves and season them. Sauté the sea parsley and warrigal greens in hot butter. Spread the purée on the plates, top with the greens and the snapper, crisp skin up, drizzle with the lemongrass sauce and garnish with the sea parsley. Warrigal greens are New Zealand spinach, which is At Risk in the wild in New Zealand; use cultivated ones.
recipes.title: Pan-fried snapper with sautéed sea parsley and warrigal greens

summary.text:
Apium prostratum, commonly known as sea celery, is a variable herb native to coastal Australia and New Zealand.
Commonly eaten by Māori in New Zealand, for whom it is known as tūtae kōau, sea celery was also an important vegetable for early explorers and colonists in Australia and New Zealand. Captain Cook ate sea celery at Botany Bay and gathered it in bulk along with Lepidium oleraceum at Poverty Bay in New Zealand in October 1769 to protect his crew from scurvy.
In New Zealand it grows on the Kermadec, Three Kings, North, South, Stewart, Chatham and Antipodes Islands, and it is also native to eastern and southern Australia and Tasmania. Three forms are recorded here. The common native form (subsp. prostratum var. filiforme) is Not Threatened (2023). Chatham Island celery (subsp. denticulatum) is endemic to the Chatham and Antipodes Islands; it is abundant there, but is listed At Risk – Naturally Uncommon (2023) because its range is so small. The Australian form (var. prostratum) is listed as exotic.

warnings: Hemlock, one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand, also has white flowers in compound umbels and grows in damp places. Before you pick, check under the umbels and along the stems as described in Lookalikes; the celery smell of a crushed leaf is not enough on its own.

On the Chatham and Antipodes Islands the plant is Chatham Island celery, which is at risk: if you harvest it there, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Never pull seaweed off by its base: trim it with scissors and leave enough on the rock for it to regrow.
Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.

summary.text:
Sea emeralds (Chaetomorpha coliformis), also called mermaid's necklace, is a native green seaweed that also grows in southern Australia and South America.
It is assessed as Not Threatened.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Never pull seaweed off by its base: trim it with scissors and leave enough on the rock for it to regrow.
Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.
Two introduced seaweeds, known together as exotic caulerpa, are unwanted organisms that spread from small pieces carried on boats and gear. Legal rules apply in MPI's controlled areas at Aotea Great Barrier Island, Ahuahu Great Mercury Island, Hauturu Little Barrier Island, Waiheke Island and Te Rawhiti Inlet in the Bay of Islands; report suspected exotic caulerpa to MPI on 0800 80 99 66.

identification.text: Glossy little branchlets, swollen like tiny grapes, grow from short upright stems, and the stems rise from creeping runners (stolons) that form a spreading network over the rock. Bladders full of seawater surround the main stem, which keeps the plant from drying out at low tide, and its runner has several holdfasts, so a patch can look like a green carpet. Bunches can be bright green or dark khaki. They are smaller than the tropical sea grapes, Caulerpa racemosa. Native caulerpas, this one included, are sometimes mistaken for exotic caulerpa, an introduced pest whose fronds are flat, oar-shaped blades rather than bunches of beads.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fronds. Sea grapes has glossy branchlets swollen like tiny grapes, in bunches on short upright stems over creeping runners; exotic caulerpa has flat, bright green blades shaped like oars, up to 10 cm long, rising from long runners, and can form dense mats on the seabed. Native caulerpas are sometimes mistaken for exotic caulerpa, including when washed up after storms. Caulerpa brachypus looks identical to Caulerpa parvifolia (only genetic analysis separates them) and is an unwanted organism: don't take or move it — note the place, take a photo and report it to MPI on 0800 80 99 66.
lookalikes.name: Caulerpa brachypus (exotic caulerpa)

preparation.text: Rinse them in fresh water and eat them raw: they are crunchy and salty, with a fresh, cucumber-like or peppery, cress-like taste. Use them in salads or as a garnish. Don't cook them — heat softens the grapes and they melt — and don't keep them in the fridge.

summary.text:
Sea grapes (Caulerpa geminata), also called grapelets, is a native green seaweed that also grows in Australia.
In New Zealand it grows all around the North Island and in the northern South Island, preferring some shelter and warm water. Caulerpa seaweeds here are mainly warm-water species, and all but one reach south only to about the Marlborough Sounds.
It is assessed as Not Threatened.
Two introduced species, Caulerpa brachypus and Caulerpa parvifolia, look identical to each other and are known together as exotic caulerpa: green, oar-shaped fronds up to 10 cm long on long runners, forming dense mats from below the tide line to 46 m deep. They are unwanted organisms that smother native seagrass and seafloor animals.

warnings: Harvest only from clean water — never near stormwater drains or sewage or industrial outfalls, in harbours, or where there is heavy boat traffic.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Never pull seaweed off by its base: trim it with scissors and leave enough on the rock for it to regrow.
Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.
Two introduced seaweeds, known together as exotic caulerpa, are unwanted organisms that spread from small pieces carried on boats and gear. Legal rules apply in MPI's controlled areas at Aotea Great Barrier Island, Ahuahu Great Mercury Island, Hauturu Little Barrier Island, Waiheke Island and Te Rawhiti Inlet in the Bay of Islands; report suspected exotic caulerpa to MPI on 0800 80 99 66.

summary.text:
Sea rimu (Caulerpa brownii) is a native green seaweed. Māori use the word 'rimu', from 'limu', a word used across the Pacific, for seaweeds, and gave the name to the tall native rimu tree because its branches of fine scale leaves closely resemble this seaweed. Unlike New Zealand's other Caulerpa, which reach south only to about the Marlborough Sounds, it grows from the lower North Island southwards.
This species can be found along the southern North Island, the South Island, Chatham Island, Stewart Island, Snares Island of New Zealand. It is also found along the coast in a large area extending from near Karratha in the northern Pilbara region to east of Esperance in the Goldfields-Esperance region of Western Australia.
It is assessed as Not Threatened.

warnings: Harvest only from clean water — never near stormwater drains or sewage or industrial outfalls, in harbours, or where there is heavy boat traffic.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Sandy beaches, near high water mark.

New Zealand herbarium sheets record it in sand above the high tide mark, on foredunes and low sand dunes, in shingle at the back of beaches, on dune gravels and at the edges of estuaries (herbarium sheets, restated).

identification.text:
Stems 10–30 cm tall, much-branched from base, stout, glabrous, sprawling to suberect, forking, not flexuous. Rosette leaves fleshy, narrow-oblong to ovate, shallowly crenate to pinnatifid, petiolate, 4–6 × 1–2 cm; margins entire, rarely crenate or sinuate; stem leaves smaller, crenate to pinnatifid, oblong to linear to linear-spathulate. Inflorescence axis straight, thickening and elongating at fruiting. Pedicels suberect to spreading, 1–3 mm long. Flowers about 1 cm in diameter, clustered. Petals 7–9 × 1–2 mm. Silique erect, (11)–13–16–(18) × 4–7 mm; upper segment mitre-shaped, tapering to a conic beak, acute, 4-angled, (8)–10–15 mm long; lower segment obconic, terete, 3–6 mm long, with 2 spreading to deflexed lateral horns at distal end.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Check the ripening fruit. In sea rocket the lower fruit segment has 2 spreading to deflexed horns at its tip and the upper segment is mitre-shaped, acute and 4-angled; in American sea rocket the lower segment has no horns and the upper segment is ovate, acuminate, notched at the tip, 4-angled or 8-ribbed, somewhat flattened, with a narrow winged beak. The flowering stem is straight in sea rocket and flexuous in American sea rocket, whose main stem is also often flexuous. Petals are 7–9 mm long in sea rocket against 4–6 mm, flowers c. 1 cm across against 6–8 mm, and rosette leaf margins are entire, rarely crenate or sinuate, against serrate. Sea rocket stems are 10–30 cm tall, American sea rocket's 30–60 cm. Fruit length and leaf lobing do not separate them: the fruit lengths overlap, and sea rocket plants can have entire or pinnatifid leaves. American sea rocket's leaves, young stems and pods are eaten in the same way.

preparation.text: Use very young leaves and stems raw in salads. Older leaves are more bitter: mix them with milder leaves as a potherb or use them in soups. Fresh flowers go into salads, and immature pods can be eaten raw. Sources disagree on cooking: the leaves are best cooked and eaten only in small quantities, yet cooking is also found to make them very bitter. Cook them only lightly: long frying or boiling makes them lose their flavour and fall apart. For the root flour, dry and grind the root and mix it with cereal flour.

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1 large handful young sea rocket leaves and tender pods; 1 handful other coastal greens, such as sea celery leaves or New Zealand spinach (warrigal greens); 40 ml olive oil; 20 ml lemon juice; 5 ml agave or maple syrup; salt and pepper; 40 ml toasted sunflower seeds. Rinse the sea rocket well in cold water and dry it. If using New Zealand spinach, blanch it in boiling water for 1 minute, cool it in cold water and squeeze it dry. Toss the greens together in a bowl. Whisk the oil, lemon juice, syrup, salt and pepper into a dressing, toss the salad gently in it, and scatter the sunflower seeds over to serve.
recipes.title: Sea rocket salad with coastal greens

recipes.method: Ingredients: about 250 ml young sea rocket leaves, loosely packed; a splash of white vinegar; salt and pepper. Rinse the leaves and blend them with the vinegar and a little salt and pepper to a paste, tasting as you go. Serve it as you would mustard or wasabi.
recipes.title: Sea rocket mustard

recipes.method: Ingredients: 10 eggs; 50 g butter; 45 ml plain flour; 500 ml whole milk; 20 ml coarse-grain mustard; lemon juice to taste; dill aquavit to taste (optional); 100 g chopped fresh herbs, such as chives, parsley and dill; salt and pepper; young sea rocket leaves and flowers to taste. Boil the eggs for 6 minutes, so the yolks are barely set. Meanwhile melt the butter in a saucepan without letting it brown, take the pan off the heat and stir in the flour. Return it to a medium heat, whisk in 200 ml of the milk until smooth, then add the rest while stirring. Keep stirring for 5 to 6 minutes, until the sauce coats the back of a spoon, and take it off the heat. Stir in the mustard, lemon juice, salt, pepper and the aquavit if using, then the herbs. Peel the warm eggs, lay them on a platter, pour the sauce over and scatter with sea rocket and coarse pepper.
recipes.title: Soft eggs in herb sauce with sea rocket

summary.text:
Sea rocket, Cakile maritima, is an annual, hairless beach plant of the mustard family (Brassicaceae), much branched from the base, with fleshy leaves, stems 10–30 cm tall and white to violet flowers. Its segmented fruits are about 13–16 mm long (11–18 mm at the extremes).

In New Zealand it is naturalised from western Europe and the Mediterranean, first recorded as naturalised in 1940, and New Zealand plants belong to subsp. maritima; the Flora records it from Northland, Auckland, Bay of Plenty, East Cape, Gisborne and Hawke's Bay, and from the Kermadec Islands (Flora of New Zealand, restated). It was first collected in New Zealand in 1937, had spread to the northern tip of the North Island by 1973 and to its southernmost point by 2010; where it and American sea rocket have both grown, American sea rocket is now rarely found, which the authors read as one species displacing a close relative (Cousens & Cousens 2011, restated). They knew it only from the North Island, but herbarium sheets record it wild in the South Island on Outer Island near Riwaka (2006) and at Whites Bay near Rārangi (2007, noted as a possible first South Island record), and on the Pencarrow coast near Wellington (2010). Since 2016, research-grade iNaturalist records have come from Marlborough, Tasman and Christchurch beaches, and one from near Dunedin.

warnings: Eat the leaves only in small quantities.

Do not use the seeds or ripe fruit as food or for oil: the seed oil is high in erucic acid, which can damage heart muscle in several animal species, and caution is urged before using sea rocket seed oil for people or animals.

Evidence on oxalic acid in the leaves is mixed: one analysis found it particularly high compared with other edible wild halophytes, while a study of Italian plants found oxalate below detectable levels.
Do not gather near sewage outlets or other shoreline pollution.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Usually wet or rather damp pastures and lawns, forest margins and clearings, dry banks and riverbeds, particularly when modified and open, less common in other habitats.
It grows on roadsides, gardens, waste-places, and woodland edges, and usually in basic and neutral soils.
In New Zealand lawns it is typical of moist to wet ground but also tolerates dryness.
Wetland status (NZPCN, from the national wetland plant list, Clarkson et al. 2021): facultative upland — occasionally in wetlands, but usually on dry ground.

identification.text:
Perennial herb. Rhizome short; aerial stems long and decumbent, becoming erect and then often purplish. Petiole often equal to lamina in lower leaves, becoming short in leaves below inflorescence. Lamina 1.7–6 × 0.7–2.3 cm, ovate or ovate-oblong, hairy, especially on veins below, usually entire or shallowly toothed, or rarely upper leaves with narrow lobes (hybrids); base cuneate to rounded. Bracts 2–10 cm long, broad-ovate to broad-reniform, acuminate, the uppermost often acute, with prominent white cilia and often purple-tinged. Calyx 7–9 mm long, purplish; upper lip shallowly 3-toothed and mucronate; lower lobe of 2 lanceolate, acuminate teeth. Corolla 10–15 mm long, usually violet, rarely pink or white. Stamen appendages more or less straight. Nutlets 1.5–2 mm long, ellipsoid or ellipsoid-obovoid, shining brown.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Cut-leaved selfheal (Prunella laciniata) has been collected from a roadside at Ngaruawahia in the Waikato. It differs from P. vulgaris in that most or all leaves are pinnately and narrowly lobed, the plants are much hairier, the lower calyx teeth are linear-lanceolate, and the corolla is cream or pink. A few specimens with some pinnately lobed leaves are probably the hybrid P. × hybrida (P. laciniata × P. vulgaris).
The leaves are puckered and covered with short, coarse hairs, and seen from above each pair is set at right angles to the pair below.
The crushed leaves have no minty smell. Once flowering is over, self-heal's head turns brown. Mown, it stays low; left unmown in waste places it grows to about 30 cm.

lookalikes.howToTell: Ground-ivy's leaves are round to kidney-shaped, 1–4.5 cm wide, with scalloped edges and a heart-shaped base, each on a slender stalk, and its blue or blue-violet flowers sit in twos or threes in the joints of ordinary leaves. Self-heal's leaves are ovate, 1.7–6 cm long and 0.7–2.3 cm wide, usually untoothed or only shallowly toothed, with a wedge-shaped to rounded base, and its flowers, usually violet, rarely pink or white, form a dense spike at the stem tip among broad bracts fringed with white hairs and often tinged purple. Flower colour does not reliably separate them, both creep, and both grow in lawns and under trees at woodland edges. Ground-ivy's young leaves are eaten, but it is advised against in pregnancy and when breast-feeding and contains pulegone.
lookalikes.name: Ground-ivy

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: pennyroyal smells strongly of mint; self-heal has no minty smell. Pennyroyal's flowers are mauve to purplish-blue, 4–6 mm long, packed in spaced rings in the joints of the leaves along the stem; self-heal's are usually violet, 10–15 mm long, in a dense head at the stem tip among broad bracts fringed with white hairs. Pennyroyal's leaves are smaller, usually 0.6–2 cm long, not puckered and dotted with glands; self-heal's are 1.7–6 cm long, puckered and coarsely hairy. Both creep, root along the stems and form mats in damp lawns and pasture, so check every plant in a mixed patch. Pennyroyal is poisonous to the liver; do not eat it.

preparation.text: Add the leaves raw to salads, or cook them in soups and stews or as a potherb. The flavour is similar to romaine lettuce, but the leaves are somewhat bitter from tannin, which washing them can remove. The leaves are a little rough, so chop them very finely before mixing them with other salad greens or putting them in a sandwich. In China the young plants have long been eaten soaked to draw out the bitterness, then dressed with oil and salt. The flowers go into salads, and the leaves into pesto. A cold-water infusion of the freshly chopped, or dried and powdered, leaves makes a refreshing drink. Leaves and flower heads can be picked through summer; picking the heads and pinching out the centre stems keeps the plant bushy, with two new heads growing in place of each one taken. For tea, wash dried seed heads well in several changes of water to remove grit, and simmer rather than boil hard: the longer it brews, the more bitter it gets.

recipes.method: Written for self-heal with galinsoga. A bunch of galinsoga and a bunch of self-heal leaves; 2 garlic cloves; 125 ml (½ cup) cashew nuts; 45 ml (3 tbsp) lemon juice; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper, optional. Blitz the garlic and cashews in a food processor or blender, add everything else and process until well combined. Adjust the seasoning, and loosen it with a little water or more lemon juice if it is too thick.
recipes.title: Self-heal and galinsoga pesto

recipes.method: Made with dried self-heal seed heads (sold as xia ku cao in Chinese herb shops). 30 g dried self-heal; 2.5 litres water; 30 g sweetened winter melon (candied, from Asian supermarkets); 100 g carrot. Wash the self-heal in a bowl of cold water, squeezing out handfuls into a colander. Change the water and wash it twice more, and keep going until the water stays clear of grit. Peel the carrot and cut it into 2 cm chunks. Put the water, self-heal and carrot in a pot, bring to the boil, then simmer on medium heat for 30 minutes. Add the winter melon and boil for 5 minutes more. Turn off the heat and strain into a teapot. Serve hot, or chill in the fridge for a few hours. Keep it at a simmer rather than a hard boil. If it is too bitter, dilute it with water or sweeten it a little at a time; honey goes in after cooking.
recipes.title: Chinese herbal tea (liang cha)

summary.text:
Prunella vulgaris, the common self-heal, heal-all, woundwort, heart-of-the-earth, carpenter's herb, brownwort or blue curls, is an herbaceous flowering plant in the mint family (Lamiaceae).
Prunella vulgaris is a perennial herb native in Europe, Asia, Africa, and North America, and is common in most temperate climates.
Prunella vulgaris can spread aggressively through creeping stolons and roots, forming dense mats that can displace other plants. Because of its ability to outcompete other desirable vegetation, it can become weedy in lawns and damp shady locations.The conspicuous flowers are a favourite of bumblebees and butterflies. 
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands: common throughout. Naturalised from the northern temperate zone, first recorded in 1867.
Other names in New Zealand (Herb Federation of New Zealand, Massey University): selfheal, hookheal, sicklewort. It was brought to New Zealand as a garden plant (NZPCN) and is now a common weed of lawns throughout the country.

warnings: Self-heal is on the NZ Plant Conservation Network's list of plants known to be poisonous in New Zealand. The list gives no reason, toxin or part, and its source (Connor and Fountain, Plants that Poison, 2009) could not be checked. No poisoning from eating it has been found recorded. Large amounts can cause diarrhoea and stomach pain.

Allergic reactions to self-heal have been reported, including a case of contact dermatitis, though such reports are rare. Seek medical advice before using it in pregnancy, when breast-feeding or if you are prone to allergies.
Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed, and self-heal often regrows after lawn weedkillers, so a healthy-looking patch is no proof the ground was not sprayed. Pick from ground you know.

identification.text:
A tall, white mushroom like a lawyer's wig. The young cap is a cylinder or narrow egg, usually 5–15 cm tall (up to 20 cm) and up to about 8 cm wide, wrapped down over most of the stem. It is white, with a smooth pale ochre to brown patch on top, and the rest breaks up into broad, shaggy, upturned white to buff scales; rain flattens them. The cap then opens into a bell, and from its lower edge upward it turns grey, then black, and melts into a black inky liquid, until only the stem is left with a small black disc on top.
The gills are free or almost free and very crowded. They are white at first, then pink, then black, and dissolve from the cap edge upward. The spore print is black.
The stem is 10–30 cm tall and 1–2.5 cm thick, white, smooth, brittle and hollow. Its base may be slightly swollen but has no sac (volva). A thin, loose ring sits on the stem; it slides up and down, is stained black by spores, and often slips to the base or falls off.
The flesh is white, thin and soft, and the taste mild. It always grows from the ground, never on wood.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are inkcaps that melt into black ink, and both come up in grass. Common inkcap is grey to grey-brown, its cap furrowed and mostly smooth, with at most a few small flat scales in the centre; it has no ring, and it grows in tight clumps from buried wood or around stumps. It contains coprine: with alcohol drunk within about three days of eating it, it is poisonous. Shaggy inkcap is white and covered in large, upturned shaggy scales, has a loose ring on its stem, grows singly or in groups from soil, and contains no coprine.

preparation.text:
Pick only as many as you can cook the same day, and cook them within a few hours: they begin to dissolve soon after picking, and even in the fridge they last only a day or two. Carry them in a wide, shallow basket, not piled on top of each other, because crushed or bruised ones break down fastest. Cut off the dirty stem base, then brush off any dirt or wipe them with a damp cloth; don't soak them.
Always cook them; raw they are bitter. They are mild and delicate and release a lot of water, so don't cut them small. Cook them gently, covered for about 5 minutes to draw out the liquid, then uncovered until it has evaporated and the butter starts to brown, or pour the liquid off and keep it for stock. Fry them in butter with onion or garlic and serve on toast, or use them in omelettes, soups, sauces, pasta, quiche and with chicken; very young, tight caps can be crumbed and fried.
To keep them, sauté them for 3–5 minutes, or blanch them in boiling water for 15–20 seconds and cool them in cold water, then freeze. Dried, they break up and never regain their texture, so use dried ones in soups, sauces and seasoning powder.

recipes.method: Serves 4. 900 g shaggy inkcaps; 1 tbsp extra virgin olive oil; 1 tbsp unsalted butter; 1 large onion, diced; 2 celery sticks, diced; ½ tsp fine sea salt, plus more to taste; 5 garlic cloves, minced; 3 sprigs fresh thyme; 1 litre low-salt chicken or vegetable stock; 250 ml full-fat coconut cream; freshly ground black pepper. Wipe the mushrooms clean with a damp cloth or paper towel rather than rinsing them. Cut each in half, then roughly chop into 2.5 cm chunks. Heat the oil and butter in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat until the butter melts and foams. Add the onion, celery and ½ tsp salt and sweat for 7–8 minutes, until the onion is soft and translucent. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds, until fragrant. Add the mushrooms and thyme and cook, stirring now and then, for about 10 minutes, until the mushrooms have released all their liquid. Pour in the stock, bring to a low boil, then cover and simmer on low for 30 minutes. Take out the thyme sprigs and purée the soup smooth with a stick blender, or carefully in a blender. Stir in the coconut cream and cook for about 5 minutes, until slightly thickened and hot through. Season with salt and pepper.
recipes.title: Shaggy inkcap soup

recipes.method: Serves 2. 400 g shaggy inkcaps; 50 g butter; salt; pepper; ½ tsp chopped parsley (optional); buttered bread, to serve. Cut away every dark, and also reddish, part of the mushrooms, generously, and clean them dry rather than washing them. Cut them lengthwise into halves or quarters. Melt the butter, add the mushrooms with salt and pepper, cover and cook for about 5 minutes, stirring several times, to draw out their water. Uncover and keep cooking until the liquid has evaporated and the butter starts to brown. Sprinkle with the parsley and eat at once, on buttered bread.
recipes.title: Fried shaggy inkcaps on buttered bread

recipes.method: Serves 6 as a first course. Shortcrust pastry for a 23 cm pie dish; 5–6 bacon rashers, cut into 2.5 cm pieces; 225–450 g shaggy inkcaps, sliced; 4 shallots or spring onions, minced; ½ cup (about 50 g) freshly grated provolone; ⅛ tsp ground nutmeg; ¼ tsp salt; a pinch of cayenne; 4 eggs, well beaten; 500 ml half-and-half (equal parts milk and cream). Roll the pastry out to a 25 cm round, line a 23 cm pie dish with it and crimp the edges. Fry the bacon until crisp, lift it out with a slotted spoon and drain it on paper towels. Pour off all but 2 tbsp of the fat and sauté the mushrooms and shallots in it until the shallots are translucent and most of the mushroom liquid has evaporated. Spread the bacon over the pastry, then the cheese, then the mushrooms and shallots. Beat the nutmeg, salt and cayenne into the eggs, add the half-and-half and pour the custard slowly over the filling. Bake in an oven preheated to 180 °C for about 35 minutes, until the custard is set and the top is brown.
recipes.title: Shaggy inkcap quiche

recipes.method: Serves 8 as a main course (16 crêpes). For the crêpes: 1 cup (125 g) plain flour; 3 eggs, beaten; ½ tsp salt; 500–625 ml milk; oil. For the filling: 700 g shaggy inkcaps, sliced; 60 g butter; 1 tbsp minced fresh basil; salt and pepper. For the sauce: 1 medium onion, minced; 1 tbsp butter; 250 ml chicken stock; 60 ml dry white wine; 250 ml half-and-half (equal parts milk and cream); salt and pepper. Stir the eggs into the flour, add the salt and enough milk to make a batter as thick as cream, and leave it to stand for at least an hour. Brush a crêpe pan or frying pan lightly with oil and heat it until a few drops of water sizzle in it. Pour in just enough batter to coat the base, tilt the pan to spread it thinly, and cook over moderate heat until the edges curl away from the pan; turn the crêpe out onto a tea towel. Repeat to make 16. For the filling, melt the butter and cook the mushrooms for 5 minutes, then add the basil, salt and pepper. Roll a spoonful or two of filling in each crêpe, fasten it with a toothpick and keep the crêpes warm in the oven. For the sauce, sauté the onion in the butter until translucent, add the stock, wine and half-and-half and boil hard until reduced by half; season. Pour the sauce over the crêpes and serve at once, with crisp steamed strips of carrot garnished with watercress.
recipes.title: Crêpes forestière

recipes.method: Serves 4–6 as a main course. 450 g shaggy inkcaps, halved; 60 g butter; 450 g cooked chicken or turkey; 1½ tbsp flour; 500 ml chicken stock; 250 ml half-and-half (equal parts milk and cream); ⅛ tsp ground nutmeg; salt and pepper; 60 ml dry sherry; 225 g vermicelli; ¼ cup (about 25 g) freshly grated Parmesan. Sauté the mushrooms in half the butter for 5–10 minutes, until browned; lift them out with a slotted spoon and mix with the chicken. Add the rest of the butter and the flour to the pan and cook, stirring, for 2–3 minutes. Whisk in the stock and keep whisking until the sauce is thick, then add the half-and-half, nutmeg, salt, pepper and sherry and cook until well blended. Take off the heat. Cook the vermicelli in plenty of boiling salted water until al dente and drain. Mix half the sauce with the chicken and mushrooms and the other half with the vermicelli. Layer the vermicelli and the chicken mixture in a buttered baking dish, sprinkle with the Parmesan and bake in an oven preheated to 180 °C for 20–30 minutes, until bubbling and brown.
recipes.title: Shaggy inkcap chicken tetrazzini

recipes.method: Very young shaggy inkcaps, caps still tight around the stem; flour; beaten egg; seasoned breadcrumbs. Clean the mushrooms, then roll them in flour, dip them in egg and coat them in seasoned breadcrumbs. Air-fry at 175 °C for 7 minutes, without preheating, until light, golden and crisp. Older, opened caps are too fragile for this.
recipes.title: Crumbed air-fried shaggy inkcaps

summary.text:
Coprinus comatus, the shaggy inkcap or lawyer's wig, is a large, distinctive inkcap of lawns, roadsides and disturbed ground.
It is introduced in New Zealand, probably with grass seed, soil or dung, and long established: Massee described it from the North Island in 1899. Massee called it 'one of the best and safest of edible fungi'. Biota of New Zealand notes that it is a species complex. It is now found throughout the country, with 969 research-grade iNaturalist records. It is the type species of Coprinus; most of the other inkcaps have since been moved to Coprinopsis, Coprinellus and Parasola. It lives on dead organic matter in the soil, and its threads can also trap and digest tiny nematode worms. Within hours of picking, or of shedding its spores, the cap digests itself into black ink, which was once used for writing; that is why it is never sold in shops. It is cultivated as food in China, and in New Zealand spawn is sold to start a patch in a lawn or garden bed. The name comatus means hairy, for the shaggy scales.

warnings: The common inkcap (Coprinopsis atramentaria) also grows in New Zealand, in grass, parks and gardens and on verges, and also melts into black ink. It contains coprine: eaten within about three days before or after drinking even a little alcohol, it causes flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, a racing or pounding heart and tingling in the limbs, starting within minutes of the drink. It is grey to grey-brown, not white; its cap is smooth and furrowed, with at most a few small flat scales in the centre and none of the shaggy scales; its stem has no ring; and it grows in tight clumps from stumps or buried wood. A shaggy inkcap is white and shaggy all over, has a loose ring on its stem and grows from soil. Shaggy inkcap itself contains no coprine.

The magpie inkcap (Coprinopsis picacea), recorded a few times in New Zealand, is poisonous and looks very like a young shaggy inkcap. It is covered in tiny white scales rather than large upturned shaggy ones, and as its cap opens and turns grey to dark brown the white scales stand out in separate patches, like a magpie's plumage.

Shaggy inkcaps take up mercury, cadmium and other toxic metals from the soil, and the more there is in the soil the more they hold. Don't pick them from busy roadsides, industrial or mining land, or lawns and parks that may be sprayed.

habitat.text: Rich soil with plenty of dead organic matter, often where it has been disturbed: compost heaps, woodchip and garden beds, garden debris, leaf and needle litter, parks, path edges and forest edges, usually in some shade near trees rather than in open pasture. It always grows from the ground, never from wood, singly, in troops or in fairy rings. In New Zealand it has been collected on the ground and in litter under radiata pine, macrocarpa, plum, rowan, kōwhai and Tecoma, and in sand under Metrosideros.

identification.text:
A large, stocky mushroom. The button is round, egg- or drumstick-shaped, with a smooth brown skin. As the cap opens, to a dome and then almost flat, 5–20 cm across, the skin breaks into coarse, shaggy brown scales on a white to cream, fibrous background, leaving a smooth brown patch in the centre; the edge is ragged and shaggy.
The gills are free of the stem, crowded and broad, white, becoming cream or pale brownish with age and often brown-edged. They never turn green. The spore print is white.
The stem is 6–20 cm tall and 1–3.5 cm thick, smooth, with no snakeskin pattern, whitish above the ring and brownish below, bruising orange-brown. It is tough and fibrous and swells into a bulb at the base. The ring sits high on the stem; it is thick, persistent, white above and brownish beneath, often double-edged, and can usually be slid up and down.
The flesh is white and thick. Cut or scratched, it turns saffron-orange to red within moments, most strongly in the stem and near its top, and then slowly darkens to wine-red or brown.
Cleland's parasol (Macrolepiota clelandii), a native parasol of grassland, open forest and bush edges, is recorded far more often in New Zealand (913 research-grade iNaturalist records). It is more slender, its stem has a snakeskin pattern of brown fibres, and its flesh does not change colour when cut. The green-spored Chlorophyllum molybdites, a frequent cause of poisoning overseas, is not known from New Zealand; a white spore print rules it out.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have free white gills, a ring, a swollen stem base and a white spore print, so a spore print does not separate them. Death cap's base sits in a ragged, white, sac-like volva, often hidden in leaf litter, and its cap is smooth, usually greenish, yellowish or bronze, with none of the coarse, shaggy brown scales of a shaggy parasol. Its buttons are white eggs inside a veil; shaggy parasol buttons are round, with a smooth brown skin. A shaggy parasol's base is a bulb with no sac (in C. brunneum it can be abruptly swollen with a rim on top), and its flesh turns orange to red within moments when cut. Dig up the whole base of every mushroom and check it.
