'Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel' from Chosen Weeds Farm, 'Cooking With Wood Sorrel', 15/03/2017 (https://thechosenweeds.com/cooking-with-wood-sorrel/) — written for the purple-leaf wood sorrel that grows in the author's south-east Texas garden; 400 °F given as 200 °C, 1 lb as about 450 g; 'Several cups' of sorrel kept because the page gives no closer amount; the page says only 'Combine mixture with the egg' after forking out the squash, and the method keeps that wording rather than saying where the squash goes. Not used from the recipe pages (15/10/2026): the casserole page's 'If you are short on time you can skip the oven step', because skipping the final bake would leave the stirred-in egg uncooked; Feral Foraging's statements that all species of wood sorrel are edible and can be used in similar ways (genus-level claims), its estimate that about 30 g a day, several times a week, is safe and its view that oxalate warnings are overblown (it contradicts every other page read here and is not a trusted source for a safety amount), and its cold-infusion and dried-leaf variants; Green Deane's statements that cooking reportedly renders oxalic acid harmless, particularly with calcium, that eating a lot raw can leach calcium from the bones, and that the juice curdles milk for cheese, and that all parts including the root bulb are edible (said of the Florida species as a group); the casserole page's medicinal and vitamin claims; the reader comment on Eat The Weeds suggesting more sorrel for a sharper cooler. Two of the owner's links have no recipe: Rachel Lambert, 'Wild Food: Wood Sorrel family', Wild Walks Southwest, 07/05/2021 (https://wildwalks-southwest.co.uk/wild-food-wood-sorrel-family/), and Diego Bonetto, 'How to identify and eat wood Sorrel', 10/08/2021 (https://www.diegobonetto.com/blog/wood-sorrel-id-forage-edible-weed) — both name O. corniculata among the species they describe. Lambert says all of them have a lemony, tart flavour and uses them in salads, in soups and as an edible decoration; Bonetto says the stalks, flowers and leaves are eaten raw or cooked, in salads and as a garnish; recorded here for edibleParts and preparation, which were empty on creeping-wood-sorrel when this was written (15/10/2026). Gratin and potato salad, as recorded on pale-pink-wood-sorrel: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (all rights reserved; retrieved 16/10/2026; supplied by the owner): Johanna Knox, 'Wood sorrel (Oxalis incarnata)', Wild Picnic, 16/07/2009, https://wildpicnic.blogspot.com/2009/07/wood-sorrel-oxalis-acetosella.html — the gratin and the potato salad. The post was first written as O. acetosella; a commenter (AJB, 26/11/2009) identified the plant pictured as 'the South African Ox. incarnata', which the author accepted, and the title now names O. incarnata. The blog covers Wellington and the Wairarapa; the post does not say where the plant grew. Not used as recipes: adding it to apple, peach or pear pie and a jelly (suggestions, not made by the author); its use to curdle milk for cheese (the author had not got it to work).

Edible parts, preparation and warning: Useful Temperate Plants (Ken Fern), 'Oxalis magellanica', https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Oxalis+magellanica, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, retrieved 16/10/2026 — Edible Uses 'Leaves - raw or cooked' (cited there to Crowe, Native Edible Plants of New Zealand, 1990, and Kunkel, Plants for Human Consumption, 1984), 'A pleasant acid flavour, but the leaves are rather small and they are also a bit chewy' and 'Use in moderation', 'Flowers - raw', 'A pleasant and decorative addition to the salad bowl' (the tasting notes are Ken Fern's own); General Information 'The plant is harvested from the wild for local use as a food.' Known Hazards (cited to Bown, Encyclopaedia of Herbs and their Uses) is word for word the text on Useful Tropical Plants 'Oxalis corniculata' (compared 16/10/2026), so the warning is the same sentence as on creeping-wood-sorrel and shamrock-wood-sorrel: oxalic acid, all right in small quantities but not in large amounts since it can bind the body's calcium, less after cooking, especial caution for rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity. Not used: its habitat 'Walls and stony places' (cited to the RHS Dictionary of Plants, a garden source, and not what NZPCN describes); the Chilean use of Oxalis juice to remove fruit stains (said of 'various species'); propagation. PFAF (https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Oxalis+magellanica, all rights reserved) is the same database. With edible parts now sourced for this species, the nine wood sorrel recipes copied here on the owner's word stay.

Habitat, paraphrased 16/10/2026 from the owner's link: NZPCN, 'Oxalis magellanica' factsheet (P.J. de Lange 2005; all rights reserved, facts only), https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/oxalis-magellanica/, retrieved 16/10/2026 — 'Coastal to montane where it is mainly confined to indigenous forested habitats, though sometimes extending into the alpine zone. A species of riparian habitats, usually found within the flood zone of streams and rivers, and around the plunge pools of waterfalls. Provided its habitat is permanently moist it may be found growing in full sun but it is more usually seen in semi-shaded situations.' and, under propagation, 'It does not cope with drying out.' Nelson Natives (owner's link, https://www.nelsonnatives.co.nz/oxalis-magellanica-white-oxalis) gives the same habitat text word for word, so it is not a second source. summary.text:
Oxalis magellanica or snowdrop wood-sorrel is an Oxalis species found in Chile, Argentina, New Zealand, and Tasmania.
In New Zealand it grows on the North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands; it is also native to Australia and South America.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

edibleParts.text: None.

habitat.text: Damp ground: stream banks, drains, old gardens and the shade under trees, often with onion weed nearby.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Clumps of strap-shaped leaves and a hollow, somewhat flattened flower stalk with several nodding white bells, each petal tipped with a green spot. Crush a leaf: no onion smell at all. Onion weed has a triangular stalk, a green stripe down the whole petal, and smells strongly of onion.
Bulb ovoid, about 2.5 cm diameter. Leaves 3–6, about equal to scape, 8–15 mm wide, linear-lorate, bright green. Scape 30–60 cm high, hollow, more or less compressed. Flowers (1–2)–3–7, 1.5–2 cm long, less than 1.5 cm diameter, campanulate, white with green-tipped segments; spathe 3–5 cm long, green at apex. Capsule almost globose. Seeds black.
[From: Healy and Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Smell first: crushed onion weed smells strongly of garlic or onion; snowflake does not. Onion weed's flower stalk is three-angled; snowflake's is hollow and somewhat flattened with winged edges. Onion weed's white bells have a green stripe down the centre of each segment; snowflake's segments are green-tipped. Strap-shaped leaves, nodding white bells, damp ground and season do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Onion weed

lookalikes.howToTell: Crushed Naples garlic smells of garlic; snowflake does not. Naples garlic carries a many-flowered, roughly flat-topped umbel 5–8 cm across of white flowers 8–10 mm long on stiff stalks; snowflake carries 3–7 flowers (sometimes 1–2), 1.5–2 cm long, with green-tipped segments. Naples garlic's flower stalk has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one; snowflake's is hollow and somewhat flattened. Flat leaves of similar width, a similar flower-stalk height, white bells and season do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Naples garlic

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leucojum_aestivum The toxicity is a whole-genus property, and there are two alkaloids, not one: 'All species of Leucojum are poisonous, as they produce the alkaloids lycorine and galantamine.' summary.text:
A garden bulb that has gone wild along streams, with strap leaves and white bells much like onion weed's — but no onion smell, and a poisonous bulb.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): native to middle and southern Europe; first collected in 1953 in grass on a roadside north of Feilding, and recorded from Auckland, the Coromandel, Gisborne–Ōpōtiki, Feilding, Palmerston North, the Hutt Valley, Little Wanganui (Nelson) and Christchurch and Little River (Canterbury).

warnings: All snowflakes (Leucojum) are poisonous: they contain the alkaloids lycorine and galantamine, and in this species both are found in the bulbs and the leaves. Cases of poisoning in people are known for snowflakes and their relatives, daffodils and snowdrops. Symptoms of lycorine poisoning vary but include vomiting, diarrhoea and convulsions.

habitat.text:
Open lowland places, mostly near the coast in natural and partially modified grasslands, very occasionally in waste places.
In New Zealand: from the coast up into the montane zone (sea level to 600 m); it was once widespread in short tussock grassland, on lava fields and clay pans, and on rocky headlands by the sea (NZPCN, restated).

harvestEthics.text: This species is at risk. If you harvest it, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In Northland (Regionally Critical), the Auckland region (Regionally Vulnerable) and the Wellington region (Regionally Endangered), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it.

identification.text:
Perennial herb with napiform or cylindric taproot to about 2.5 cm diameter; caulorrhiza short and thick, bearing long weakly ascending flowering stems. Hairs variable; longer hairs straight to slightly curved; glandular hairs short and inconspicuous. Basal leaves: petiole to 30 cm long, with fine, straight or curved long hairs and shorter straight and crisped retrorse hairs; lamina to about 7 cm diameter, reniform to orbicular, lobed to 3/4-⅞ way to midrib, glabrous or densely hairy above; lobes (5)–7, obovate; larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; median and larger lateral teeth more or less oblong, usually obtuse. Cauline leaves similar to basal but smaller, usually 3–5-lobed; teeth usually 3–5 per lobe. Peduncle and pedicels with hairs as on petioles; bracteoles lanceolate or narrow-triangular; flowers usually in pairs, occasionally solitary. Sepals ovate or elliptic-ovate; outer sepals about 5.5 × 3.5 mm excluding mucro; inner sepals slightly narrower; hairs straight or slightly curved, antrorse and ascending. Petals to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm, obovate, rose-pink. Mericarp hairy; beak to about 15 mm long. Seed about 2 × 1.6 mm diameter, subglobular to oblong, dark reddish brown or almost black; dorsal alveolae deep, usually 4–6-sided, isodiametric or longer than wide.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
'Large petals' form (Flora of New Zealand vol. IV): Taproot napiform; lamina of leaf glabrous above except for margin and base; hairs of petioles and pedicels straight, to about 1.5 mm long, perpendicular to surface; petals usually longer than 7 × 4 mm; alveolae of seed mostly 5-6-sided, isodiametric.

lookalikes.howToTell: Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped or cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. They are separated on the hairs of the leaf and flower stalks: in turnip-rooted geranium they are sharply bent near the base, point backward and lie pressed flat; in Solander's geranium they are straight to curved, stand out or point backward, but never lie flat. Two further differences are the leaf lobes (usually linear-obovate in turnip-rooted geranium, obovate in Solander's geranium) and the seed: pits about 0.1 mm across against usually more than 0.1 mm. The root is often turnip-shaped in turnip-rooted geranium and more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot in Solander's geranium, but Solander's geranium can have a turnip-shaped root too, so the root alone does not settle it. Flower colour does not separate them: both can have pink petals, and both have petals up to about 8–9 mm long. No source read records turnip-rooted geranium as food, and it is Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable. The names do not separate them: turnip-rooted geranium, Matua-kūmara and pukupuku have each been given to both plants, so a record under any of them may mean either plant.
lookalikes.name: Turnip-rooted geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped or cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Three characters separate Australasian cranesbill from Solander's geranium: the middle teeth of its leaf lobes are about as long as broad (mostly longer than broad in Solander's geranium); the pale, see-through border of its inner sepals is mostly more than 0.3 mm wide near the tip (mostly less than 0.3 mm); and its seeds are red-brown with rather shallow rectangular pits (red-brown to dark brown, with rather deep rectangular to polygonal pits). Its sepals are mostly elliptic to obovate, against ovate. The lobing does not separate them (both are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way), and both have paired flowers. Australasian cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food.
lookalikes.name: Australasian cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped or cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Cinquefoil geranium and Solander's geranium are separated on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in Solander's geranium, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in Solander's geranium. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of Solander's geranium overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Cinquefoil geranium's root is recorded as food.
lookalikes.name: Cinquefoil geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped or cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. The first difference is the life form: cut-leaved cranesbill is an annual, usually with a thin fibrous taproot and glandular hairs prominent in the flower clusters, while Solander's geranium is a perennial with a rather stout to tuberous rootstock and no, very few, or short and inconspicuous glandular hairs on the flower clusters. Cut-leaved cranesbill's leaves are cut almost to the leaf stalk into linear segments; Solander's geranium's are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into broader lobes. Both have pink petals. Older floras placed Solander's geranium under Geranium dissectum (its synonyms include Geranium dissectum var. pilosum Hook.f. and var. australe Benth.), so older records may use that name. Cut-leaved cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food.
lookalikes.name: Cut-leaved cranesbill

"large petals" among the synonyms of Geranium solanderi, and Gardner (1984, quoted there) says that form 'matches exactly the type'; NZPCN's Geranium gardneri page says gardneri 'Has been treated in New Zealand as Geranium solanderi “coarse hairs”'. Retrieved 23/10/2026. https://www.anbg.gov.au/apu/plants/gerasola.html — it quotes Cribb & Cribb 1987 p. 169 ('boiled and eaten the slender, carroty taproot was well packed with starch but not particularly palatable with a slight bitter flavour'), Flood 1980 p. 95 ('Large fleshy roots were roasted'; 'Available summer-autumn') and Zola & Gott 1992 p. 47 ('Plants with tough roots - need to be pounded; contain nutritious starch and can be eaten after cooking; some contain tannin - unpalatable'). summary.text:
Geranium solanderi (common names - native geranium, Australian cranesbill, Austral cranesbill, Cut-leaf cranesbill, native carrot, and hairy geranium) is a species of plant in the family Geraniaceae. It is native to Australia (New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia, and Tasmania), and to New Zealand.
In New Zealand, in both 2004 and 2009 it was declared "Not threatened", but in 2012, under the New Zealand Threat Classification System it was declared "At Risk - Declining", with the qualifiers SO (safe overseas) and DP (data poor), and this status was reaffirmed in 2017.
Gardner, R. O., New Zealand J. Bot. 22: 131-134 (1984), stated that most N.Z. material of G. solanderi belongs to 1 or other of 2 forms. He did not give them taxonomic recognition because their distinctness is lost in Australia.
Its 2023 national assessment is At Risk – Declining. Regional assessments rate it Regionally Threatened – Regionally Critical in Northland (2026), Regionally Threatened – Regionally Endangered in Wellington (2025) and Regionally Threatened – Regionally Vulnerable in Auckland (2025), and Regionally Data Deficient in Otago (2025). Rabbit browsing and the spread of taller, faster-growing weeds have caused it to decline across large parts of its former range (NZPCN, restated).

edibleParts.text: The fruit and the leaves. The fruit is eaten raw when fully ripe, dried, or made into jam; it has very little flesh, its seeds sit in a sticky, sweet, jelly-like mucilage, and it tastes strongly astringent, salty and sour. Unripe fruit is very astringent. The fruit is also cooked in savoury dishes such as chilli, curry and chutney. The leaves are eaten raw or cooked, or pickled; raw, they are harshly astringent, mucilaginous and barely edible.

In New Zealand it grows on cliffs and sand dunes, on the coast and inland on railway and roadside cuttings.
It favours hot, dry coastal places, and tolerates drought, wind, salt spray and sandy soils.

harvestEthics.text: It is a declared pest — an unwanted organism on the National Pest Plant Accord — under sustained control across the Auckland region and progressive containment on the Chatham Islands. It smothers native vegetation and hybridises with the native ice plant. Harvest as much as you like, and spread no stem fragments: they grow into new plants.

identification.text:
Mat-forming trailing perennial herb. Stems to 6 m long, glabrous, 2-angled, subwoody at base. Leaves smooth, sharply 3-angled, linear, acute, scarcely tapered to connate base, 70–120 × 12–17 mm, 4–7× as long as wide; keel denticulate, at least near apex. Flowers 8–10 cm diameter. Calyx glabrous; longest sepals 40–55 mm long. Petals spreading, pale yellow, turning pinkish orange with age, 30–40 mm long. Stamens about 10 mm long; filaments yellow, hairy at base; anthers yellow. Stigmas (8)–10–12. Seeds brown, obovoid, 1–1.3 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Carpobrotus edulis (L.) L.Bolus]
Leaves bitter-tasting. Fruit indehiscent, fleshy, mucilaginous; locules as many as stigmas. [Genus description, from: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Fruit 2–3 cm across, turning yellowish to reddish-purple as it ripens.
Very similar to Chilean sea fig, but told from it when flowering by the yellow petals, which fade to dull pink; Chilean sea fig has smaller, purple flowers.
Hybrids with the native ice plant have weakly 2-angled stems, leaves 2–6 cm long and flowers 4.5–6 cm across, with petals either orange-pink or yellow to whitish, turning pink with a yellow base; their pollen is mostly sterile and they form no fruit.

lookalikes.howToTell: Best told apart in flower. Chilean sea fig has purple petals, paler near the base, on flowers 6.5–8 cm across; this plant's petals are pale yellow, turning pinkish orange or dull pink with age, on flowers 8–10 cm across. Its leaves are 35–90 × 5–12 mm, against 70–120 × 12–17 mm here, but the ranges overlap, so do not rely on leaves out of flower.

preparation.text: Pick the fruit when it has turned yellowish, wrinkled and leathery; it is best eaten dry and wrinkled. Bite off the base and suck out the jelly of seeds and pulp, or peel off the skin and the dried flower parts on top and eat the fruit raw or cook it. For jam, soak the fruit overnight in salted cold water, drain and peel it, then simmer it in a sugar syrup until thick and dark red. Blanching the leaves and soaking them in salted water before pickling takes out their astringency.

recipes.method: 1 kg sour figs; 1 teaspoon salt; 2 cups (about 500 ml) sugar; a few cinnamon sticks; 1 cup (about 250 ml) water. Cover the sour figs with cold water, add the salt and soak them overnight, then drain and peel them. Add the sugar and cinnamon to the water and boil until sticky. Add the sour figs and simmer until thick and the fruit is dark red. Bottle in sterilised glass jars.
recipes.title: Sour fig jam

recipes.method: 250 g leaves; table salt; 250 g white wine vinegar; 100 g honey; 100 g caster sugar; a pinch of chilli flakes; 2 cloves; 1 teaspoon caraway seeds. Put the leaves into a pan of boiling water for 2 minutes and strain. Toss them in a bowl with a few pinches of table salt, cover with cold water and leave for 6 hours. Repeat the boiling and salting once more and strain off any excess water. Bring all the other ingredients to the boil and pour the hot pickling liquor over the leaves. Put them into airtight containers or jars.
recipes.title: Ice plant gherkins

recipes.method: Written for the Hottentot fig, which the author names Carpobrotus edulis. About 425 ml sour fig seeds and juice (the inside of roughly 150 ripe fruit; 5–10 fruit make a small single dressing); 3 tablespoons sweet apple juice; 1 tablespoon sea buckthorn juice; 140 ml staghorn sumac extract (sumac berries mashed in 570 ml spring water); 1–2 wild garlic bulbs, crushed; 1–2 teaspoons crushed hot mustard-family seeds, such as charlock or black mustard; sea salt; a little extra-virgin rapeseed or olive oil if you like. Cut open the fruit and squeeze the insides into a bowl. Pull the sumac berries off their clusters, mash them in the spring water and strain off 140 ml. Mix everything together, bottle, refrigerate and use within a week; boiled briefly and poured hot over the garlic and mustard seed in the bottle, it keeps longer. For a quick version, mix the fruit insides with a pinch of salt, a little garlic and a squeeze of lemon.
recipes.title: Sour fig salad dressing

recipes.method: Written for ice plants (Carpobrotus) in general: the author, in New Zealand, picks this species and the Chilean sea fig. 2–3 very ripe bananas, mashed; 3 large eggs; ½ teaspoon vanilla extract; 60 ml ice plant fruit paste, plus a little for the tops; 1¾ cups (440 ml) ground almonds; 1 teaspoon ground ginger; 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon; ½ teaspoon gluten-free baking powder. For the paste, cut very ripe red fruit off their stalks with a knife, halve them and squeeze or scrape out the brown, seedy pulp. Mix the banana with the eggs, vanilla and paste, then stir in everything else. Spoon into greased muffin tins and bake at 170 °C for 35–45 minutes, depending on tin size; test after 30 minutes and cook until a knife comes out clean. Spread a little more paste on top if you like.
recipes.title: Ice plant fruit and banana muffins

summary.text:
Carpobrotus edulis, the South African ice plant, sour fig or Hottentot fig, is a mat-forming succulent in the ice plant family Aizoaceae, native to South Africa and naturalised in New Zealand since 1883.
The sour fig grows on coastal and inland slopes in South Africa from Namaqualand in the Northern Cape through the Western Cape to the Eastern Cape. It is often seen as a pioneer on disturbed sites.
In New Zealand it is recorded from Northland, Auckland, Bay of Plenty, Wellington and Wairarapa, from Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago and Southland, and from Stewart Island and the Chatham Islands. It was brought in as a garden ornamental and planted for its hardiness in beach gardens. It spreads by seed, carried by animals that eat the fruit, and by creeping stems that root where they touch the ground; the stems travel in moved soil and dumped garden waste, and broken pieces grow into new plants. It is a declared pest: an unwanted organism on the National Pest Plant Accord, which bans breeding, distributing, releasing or selling it anywhere in New Zealand, and it may not be planted in the Auckland region; it is under sustained control across the Auckland region and progressive containment on the Chatham Islands, and is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. It smothers native vegetation, changes soil chemistry, and hybridises with the native ice plant, Disphyma australe; that hybrid is named ×Carpophyma mutabilis.
Carpobrotus species hybridise easily and are difficult to tell apart: a 2023 genetic study that sampled populations in New Zealand and six other countries found no clear features to identify the taxa by their form.

warnings: A syrup made from the fruit is said to be laxative, and eating the fruit is an old South African remedy for constipation.
It is a pest plant controlled with herbicide sprays such as triclopyr. Pick only where you know it has not been sprayed.

identification.text: Evergreen tree to 37 m tall, usually with a single trunk; bark grey, rough and thick. Twigs and buds densely red- or white-hairy. Leaves alternate, thick and leathery, narrowly to broadly elliptic, usually 13–20 × 6–10 cm, glossy bright green and hairless above, hairless to densely red-brown felted beneath, with smooth margins. Flowers at the tips of the twigs, 15–30 cm across, strongly lemon-scented, with creamy white, waxy tepals and many stamens with purple filaments. Fruit a cylindrical to somewhat egg-shaped cone of follicles, 7–10 × 3.5–5 cm, the follicles opening to show seeds with a red aril. A New Zealand herbarium specimen had white flowers up to 32 cm across with 9 cupped petals, and leaves shiny green above and rusty-felted beneath.

preparation.text: The flavour is strong, so the petals are not usually eaten raw. They are pickled, best in a sweet-sour pickle, and a petal is diced and used sparingly as a flavouring in salads; the flowers are also used as a spice and condiment. Flowers are best picked as they begin to open, before the petals turn brown. The leaves are used like bay leaf to flavour soups, cut into smaller pieces because they are large.

recipes.method: Written for magnolias in general; the page names no species, and the author's tree flowers in early spring before its leaves come, so it is a different magnolia. Makes 1 jar. Magnolia petals, enough to fill the jar once chopped; 1 cup (250 ml) rice wine vinegar or apple cider vinegar; ¼ cup (about 50 g) white sugar; a pinch of salt. Pull the petals off the centre of each flower, which is bitter, and throw the centre away. Leave the petals out for half an hour so any insects can crawl off, then rinse them in cold water. Chop or shred the petals and pack them into a clean jar. Warm the vinegar with the sugar and salt over low heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, pour it over the petals and press them down until covered. Let the jar cool to room temperature, then keep it in the fridge — this is a quick pickle, not a ferment. Taste after a few days. Use like pickled ginger, with sushi, in stir-fries or in sandwiches.
recipes.title: Pickled magnolia petals

recipes.method: Written for magnolias in general; the page names no species, and the author's tree flowers in early spring before its leaves come, so it is a different magnolia. 2 cups (500 ml) water; 2 cups magnolia petals, more for a stronger taste; 1 cup (about 200 g) sugar. Pull the petals off the bitter centre of each flower, leave them out for half an hour for insects to leave, and rinse in cold water. Dissolve the sugar in the water over low heat, stirring often, then bring it to the boil, add the petals and simmer on low for about 20 minutes. Lift out the petals and keep simmering the syrup until it is as thick as you want. Mix with cold water for a drink, or pour over pancakes or ice cream.
recipes.title: Magnolia syrup

recipes.method: Written for magnolias in general; the page names no species, and the author's tree flowers in early spring before its leaves come, so it is a different magnolia. Magnolia petals and a vinegar of your choice. Pull the petals off the bitter centre of each flower, leave them out for half an hour for insects to leave, and rinse in cold water. Chop the petals, pack them into a jar and cover with unheated vinegar. Leave at room temperature for a couple of weeks, then strain out the petals and keep the vinegar in the fridge between uses. Use in salad dressings and marinades. Infuse petals in vinegar, never in oil: fresh plant material in oil can grow the bacteria that cause botulism.
recipes.title: Magnolia vinegar

recipes.method: Written for southern magnolia. 500–750 ml (2–3 cups) magnolia petals; 125 ml rice vinegar; 30 ml (2 tablespoons) cane sugar; a pinch of salt. Pick petals that are almost ready to fall from the tree and pack them into a jar. Warm the vinegar, sugar and salt in a small saucepan, stirring until the sugar dissolves, until it steams and the first small bubbles appear. Pour it over the petals and leave to cool before putting the lid on. Leave for a week before using. The pickle tastes something like pickled ginger; serve it in salads or alongside sushi.
recipes.title: Pickled southern magnolia petals

recipes.method: Written for southern magnolia. 3–4 fresh magnolia petals, clean and unsprayed; 240 ml boiling water. Put the petals in a teapot, pour over the boiling water and leave to steep for about 10 minutes. Makes one cup.
recipes.title: Southern magnolia petal tea

summary.text: Southern magnolia or bull bay (Magnolia grandiflora), also called laurel magnolia or evergreen magnolia, is a large evergreen tree in the magnolia family (Magnoliaceae), native to the south-eastern United States from North Carolina to Florida and Texas, where it grows in lowland woods, on wooded dunes and in river bottoms. It is widely cultivated in warmer areas around the world. In New Zealand it is planted in gardens, parks and streets and occasionally comes up self-sown from seed spread by birds; the New Zealand Organisms Register lists it as an exotic sometimes present in the wild, Biota of New Zealand records it as a casual exotic, and it is not listed as a pest plant.

warnings: Cut or crushed leaves can cause allergic skin rashes (contact dermatitis), especially in people already sensitive to daisy-family plants; the leaves contain parthenolide, a likely allergen. Damaging the leaf releases the allergen, and a dyer who boiled the leaves developed dermatitis of the hands and face.

identification.text:
Urtica australis (southern nettle) is a stout, dense, bushy, shrub that reaches 1 by 1 metre in diameter. The base can be somewhat woody. The plant can also be semideciduous. The petioles are up to 50 mm long.
Leaves are dark green, 100–150 mm long and 80–140 mm wide, with a heart-shaped base. The margins are usually coarsely toothed, sometimes nearly smooth, and rarely completely smooth. The stinging hairs or trichomes are mainly found along the leaf edges and veins on the underside, and may be sparse or absent. Flowering occurs from December to January. Fruits form from December to March. The achenes are 1.5–2 mm long, and pale brown.
It is told from all other New Zealand nettles by its big, broad, dark green leaves, 10–20 cm long, on a stout, bushy, partly deciduous plant whose branches lie down and root before turning upright. The leaf stalk often carries a pair of small leaflets near its base.

lookalikes.howToTell: Ongaonga is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m, with numerous long-stalked white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long and pale green, triangular to ovate-triangular leaves usually 7–12 cm long (4–18 cm, overlapping southern nettle's). Southern nettle is a stout herb up to about 1 m, somewhat woody only at the base, with few short-stalked stinging hairs and broad, dark green leaves 10–20 cm long with a heart-shaped base. Both grow on Stewart Island. Its sting has killed: in 1961 a young man died of paralysis and breathing problems several hours after walking through tree nettles. If it is a woody shrub with long white stinging hairs, walk away.
lookalikes.name: Ongaonga

lookalikes.howToTell: Stinging nettle spreads by long underground rhizomes and has broadly lanceolate or ovate leaves; southern nettle's branches lie down and root at the base before turning upright, and its leaves are broadly ovate to nearly round, dark green and 10–20 cm long. Stinging nettle is rare in southern nettle's range: on Stewart Island it is recorded only at Port Pegasus.
lookalikes.name: Stinging nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush nettle is a slender, erect herb 15–60 cm tall that spreads by rhizomes, with light green, triangular to triangular-ovate leaves (2–6 cm long, sometimes up to 12 cm). Southern nettle is stout and bushy, up to about 1 m, its branches lying down and rooting before turning upright, with broadly ovate, dark green leaves 10–20 cm long, the leaf stalk often carrying a pair of small leaflets near its base. Both grow on Stewart Island. Young bush nettle leaves are eaten cooked.
lookalikes.name: Bush nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf nettle is a branched annual up to 60 cm with a short taproot and ovate or elliptic leaves 2–8 cm long (rarely 1–10 cm), and its short flower clusters, up to 3 cm, carry male and female flowers together. Southern nettle is a stout, bushy plant up to about 1 m whose branches lie down and root before turning upright, with broadly ovate, dark green leaves 10–20 cm long; most of its flower clusters are one sex, female above male. Both grow on the Chatham Islands. Young dwarf nettle leaves are eaten cooked.

summary.text:
Urtica australis, commonly known as southern nettle and onga, is a species of nettle endemic to New Zealand's southern and subantarctic islands.
Urtica australis is endemic to New Zealand. The species is found in the south-western coast of Fiordland (in the South Island). It is also found on Chatham, Stewart, and other main subantarctic islands. The 2023 assessment of U. australis in the New Zealand Threat Classification System was "At Risk – Declining".
Its specific epithet, australis, means 'southern'. It is also called Chatham Island nettle.
U. australis plays host to the Chatham Island red admiral (Vanessa gonerilla ida). It is the only known host plant of that endemic butterfly.
It also grows on islands in Foveaux Strait. It is uncommon on Stewart Island but weedy on the Chatham Islands, where it thrives on disturbance and large browsing animals hardly touch it.
It is common in damaged forest on the main Chatham Island (NZPCN, restated).

warnings: No record of southern nettle as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
Its sting is milder than ongaonga's but still painful. The stinging hairs sit mostly along the leaf edges and on the veins under the leaf, and can be sparse.

identification.text:
Deciduous shrub up to 3 m high; twigs sparsely to moderately clothed in appressed hairs, becoming more or less glabrous, rounded, striate and glaucous-green to dark green. Mature branches with few leaves; leaves glabrous or sparsely to densely hairy, simple, entire, elliptic to oblong or more or less linear on mature branches, acute to obtuse, (8)–15–25 mm long, up to 45 mm long in shaded shoots or seedlings; petioles 1–2 mm long. Inflorescence with usually numerous fragrant flowers; pedicels 2–5 mm long; bract subtending pedicel narrowly triangular, 2–4 mm long; bracteole subtending calyx linear, about 2 mm long. Calyx more or less glabrous, unilabiate. Corolla 22–28 mm long. Pod becoming glabrous, oblong and flattened, 50–90 mm long; seeds smooth, dark brown.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The flowers are fragrant, and the unusually shaped calyx with 5 reduced teeth on one side distinguishes Spanish broom from all other wild New Zealand legumes. The stout, rounded green twigs are usually almost leafless in adult plants.
It flowers from December to May. The flowers are golden and grow in racemes at the ends of the shoots.

lookalikes.howToTell: Scotch broom's twigs are more or less five-angled, and its leaves have three leaflets on older twigs, often one or two on young twigs. Spanish broom's twigs are stout, rounded and finely grooved, usually almost leafless on adult plants, and its leaves are simple, 15–25 mm long on mature branches; a one- or two-leaflet leaf on a young Scotch broom twig can look like it. Scotch broom's calyx is two-lipped; Spanish broom's is one-lipped, split above, with five short teeth on one side, which sets it apart from every other wild legume in New Zealand. Scotch broom's flowers are usually single, rarely paired, in the leaf angles; Spanish broom's are fragrant and usually many together in racemes at the ends of the shoots. Scotch broom's pods are black, 15–60 mm long and hairy along the edges; Spanish broom's become hairless and are 50–90 mm long. Flower length overlaps (Scotch broom 16–25 mm, Spanish broom 22–28 mm) and does not separate them. Scotch broom flowers from September to April, Spanish broom from December to May.

summary.text:
Spartium junceum, known as Spanish broom, rush broom, or weaver's broom, is a species of flowering plant in the family Fabaceae and the sole species in the genus Spartium. It is native to the Mediterranean.
In New Zealand: North Island — Auckland City, locally common in Hawke's Bay, locally common to abundant in Wellington Province; South Island — Nelson City, Coverham (Marlborough), Port Hills and Christchurch, Otago Peninsula. It was first recorded wild here in 1940. Spanish broom is often cultivated as an ornamental in gardens and is used in plantings around cities.
It was brought here as an ornamental and reproduces by seed, of which it produces many. It is commonly grown in some areas but has not naturalised as widely as Scotch broom.
Its seeds are spread by gravity and by moving soil. It forms dense stands that reduce native plant cover, and as a nitrogen fixer it may change which plants grow there and help other exotic plants invade.
Since 1 September 2021 Auckland Council's rules ban breeding, distributing, selling or planting it anywhere in the Auckland region. The council controls it wherever it is known on Aotea / Great Barrier Island and asks that any seen there be reported.

warnings: All parts of Spanish broom are toxic. Every part contains the alkaloids cytisine and sparteine, which act on the nervous system; sparteine can affect heart rhythm.

Eating the flowers has poisoned people: three adults who ate rice cooked with Spanish broom flowers fell ill at once with abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea and tremors, and needed hospital treatment.

The seeds poison children, more severely the more are eaten: in one report a child who ate one or two seeds had no symptoms, one who ate four or five had digestive upset, and one who ate seven or eight had digestive and nervous-system symptoms.
In severe poisoning, symptoms can progress to seizures, muscle paralysis and respiratory failure, which can kill.
The seeds are probably poisonous, like those of Scotch broom.

It is a pest plant in New Zealand: it is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and the regional pest management plans of Auckland, Manawatū-Whanganui and Canterbury name it.

identification.text:
An upright evergreen shrub up to about 2 m, with brittle woody stems densely hairy when young. Fragrant, needle-like leaves 3–7 mm long in whorls of 3–4, the edges rolled under and meeting so the underside is hidden. Masses of small white bell flowers, 3–5 mm long and pink-flushed in bud, hang from tiny stalks in dense clusters along the upper stems, March to December; the stigma is pink to crimson. A hairless capsule about 3 mm long follows.
Erect shrub to about 2 m, occasionally with a trunk over 15 cm across. Shoots densely covered with short simple hairs of varying lengths, especially when young. Leaves in whorls of 3–4, almost stalkless, (2–)3–7 mm long; margins rolled under and touching, hiding the undersurface; otherwise hairless. Flowers in side racemes, usually so crowded they look like one large terminal panicle; flower stalks about 2 mm, curved back. Calyx 1–1.5 mm, white. Corolla 3–5 mm long, tubular-bell-shaped, white except for a rose or pink flush outside in bud; lobes very short. Stamens inside the corolla. Style slightly protruding. Capsule about 3 mm, broadly ellipsoid, hairless. Tree heath (E. arborea) is similar but its young shoots carry branched (bristly) hairs and its stigma is white to pale green.

lookalikes.howToTell: Spanish heath grows to about 2 m and is white in flower: masses of small white bells, pink only in bud, from March to December. Its leaves are needle-like, 3–7 mm, in whorls of 3–4 with the edges rolled under. Heather stays low, usually under 50 cm (up to about 90 cm), flowers pink to pale purple from December to April, and has tiny 1.5–3.5 mm leaves in opposite pairs overlapping in four rows. Heather's flowering tips are made into tea (see its page).

summary.text:
Spanish heath (Erica lusitanica) is an upright heath-family shrub (Ericaceae) from south-west Europe, white with tiny bell flowers for much of the year.
In New Zealand: First recorded naturalised in 1926, it is abundant and widespread in many parts of the North and South Islands, from the Whangaroa area in Northland to Bluff, especially where rainfall is moderate to fairly high. It is a major weed in many areas and is also grown in gardens, sometimes as the very free-flowering 'Pyramidalis'. Tree heath (E. arborea) has sometimes been mistaken for it.
It spreads only by seed: each capsule holds 60–100 seeds, a bush carries millions of capsules, and soil seed banks reach about 480,000 seeds per square metre. Seed travels on wind, water and soil, and on people and animals (in wool and on feet). Plants live 40–50 years at most and resprout from the base when damaged. It forms dense stands on disturbed and bare sites that stop native seedlings establishing; in tall vegetation native plants usually replace it, but in shorter vegetation it lasts. It is an environmental weed, under sustained control in Auckland and site-led control in Southland, and an organism of interest in Canterbury, Otago, Southland, Tasman-Nelson and the Chatham Islands.

warnings: No reliable record of Spanish heath as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

identification.text:
Much-branched, prostrate, spreading to suberect, more or less farinose annual monoecious herb. Stems more or less slender; ribs and nodes often purplish or dark red. Petiole of lower leaves usually 1–2.5 cm long, slender; lamina of lower leaves 1–9 × 0.75–8 cm, mostly narrowly to broadly triangular-hastate, sometimes more or less ovate or rhombic-ovate, green, glaucous or sometimes reddish, sparsely to prominently and deeply dentate above basal lobes; base usually truncate, sometimes broad- cuneate or sagittate; apex acute or subacute. Inflorescence leaves smaller and more often ovate to lanceolate. Inflorescence of long reddish or brownish spikes; flowers in glomerules. male flowers: perianth 0.5–0.8 mm long with margins hyaline. female flowers: bracteoles 1–2 mm long at anthesis, sessile, triangular-hastate, broad-ovate or rhombic-ovate, usually dentate, less commonly entire, generally with appendages. Fruiting bracteoles to 9 × 6.5 mm, sometimes unequal, almost free or shortly united. Fruit enclosed by bracteoles, 1–2.5 mm long, more or less circular, laterally flattened; pericarp easily removed; larger-fruited plants with bracteoles often larger and lacking appendages. Testa shining black or deep brown, smooth. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is very variable in habit, colour, leaf shape and bracteoles. Plants exposed to sun, salt-laden wind and drought are often quite prostrate and somewhat succulent; in waste places, on roadsides and in similar modified places near the coast, plants are generally larger and green rather than glaucous. The lowermost leaves are opposite; the upper ones are alternate.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers and fruit. Spear-leaved orache's female flowers usually have no sepals or petals: each fruit is held between two bracteoles that grow with it, reaching up to 9 × 6.5 mm, usually toothed and generally with small outgrowths. Fat hen's flowers are mostly bisexual and its fruit is wrapped in small sepals, 0.5–3 mm long, with no bracteoles. The leaves do not separate them: both plants are mealy and very variable, and fat hen's leaves, usually wedge-based, can also be triangular with a squared-off base.
lookalikes.name: Fat hen

lookalikes.howToTell: Compare the leaves below the main flower spikes, at flowering. Spear-leaved orache's middle and lower leaves are mostly triangular to arrow-shaped with a squared-off base, though the base varies from broadly wedge-shaped to arrow-shaped; common orache's are mostly narrowly lance-shaped to lance-shaped with a wedge-shaped base, sometimes ovate and then often arrow-shaped. In fruit, spear-leaved orache's two bracteoles are almost free or joined only at the base; common orache's are joined in their lower part. Where common orache's leaves have basal lobes, these often point forward. The bracteoles of both are extremely variable in New Zealand, so check more than one character.
lookalikes.name: Common orache

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the habit and the fruit. Garden orache is erect, usually over 75 cm tall, with a stout, rigid, angled main stem; its lower leaves are 5–30 cm long on stalks up to 5 cm. Spear-leaved orache is prostrate or spreading to nearly erect, with more or less slender stems; its lower leaves are 1–9 cm long on slender stalks 1–2.5 cm long, mostly triangular-arrow-shaped and toothed above the basal lobes. In fruit, most of garden orache's female flowers sit between two free, round, untoothed bracteoles with no bumps or appendages, 6–15 mm across; spear-leaved orache's are triangular-arrow-shaped to ovate, usually toothed and generally with appendages, up to 9 mm long. Large-fruited spear-leaved orache can have bigger bracteoles without appendages, so check the habit and leaves too.
lookalikes.name: Garden orache

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaf bases, the stems and the fruit. Spear-leaved orache's lower leaves are mostly triangular-arrow-shaped and toothed above the basal lobes, with a base usually squared off (sometimes broadly wedge-shaped or arrow-shaped), on slender stalks 1–2.5 cm long; Australian orache's leaves have a broadly wedge-shaped base and blunt, forward-pointing lobes, on stout, fleshy stalks up to 20 mm long. Spear-leaved orache's stems are more or less slender; Australian orache has stout main stems up to 15 mm thick and woody at the base. In fruit, spear-leaved orache's bracteoles reach 9 mm, are usually toothed and generally have small outgrowths; Australian orache's are 3–4 mm long, entire or with one or two teeth, very fleshy, turning black and much thickened with age. Spear-leaved orache's bracteoles are extremely variable in New Zealand, so check more than one character. Both grow around the Chatham Islands lagoon, and in New Zealand Australian orache is abundant only on the Chatham Islands. No record of Australian orache as food was found (see its page).

preparation.text: Add young leaves to salads and cook older ones like spinach; mature leaves are good wilted with butter. Strip the leaves from the tougher stems. Mix them with stronger-tasting leaves if they seem bland, and go easy on the salt, as they are salty already. Grind the seed into a powder to thicken soups, or add it to wheat flour for bread or muffins; it is small and very fiddly to collect. Young, soft seeds can be sprinkled over food; take only a few so the plant can regenerate.

recipes.method: Written for spear-leaved orache, this plant. Serves 4. 2 kg mussels, cleaned and de-bearded (foraged ones need thorough cleaning and checking); a basket of very dry pine needles; malted barley, enough to cover the tray; a splash of whisky (the source uses Bowmore 12 Years Old); 1 garlic clove; 2 handfuls of orache leaves; a knob of butter; 15 ml (1 tbsp) olive oil; salt and pepper. Outside, scatter a layer of malted barley over a large metal tray, about 40–50 cm across. Lay the mussels hinge side up, side by side, in a big circle, and pile pine needles about 20 cm high over them. Light the needles in several places, upwind of the tray, and blow on them to get them going; the fire is dramatic, so choose the spot with care. When the needles have burnt down, after 5–10 minutes, pick the mussels out of their shells, carefully, as the shells can be hot. Heat the butter, olive oil and garlic in a pan over a medium heat for 1 minute, add the orache, cover and cook for 2–3 minutes. Add the mussels, season with salt and pepper and heat through. Mussels must be properly cooked: if in any doubt, bring them to a simmer and cook for 2 minutes. Serve in clean oyster shells. The source lists the whisky but its method never says where it goes, and it uses the malted barley without listing it.
recipes.title: Pine-fired mussels with orache

summary.text:
Atriplex prostrata, called the spear-leaved orache, hastate orache, thin-leaf orache and triangle orache, is a widespread species of flowering plant in the saltbush genus Atriplex, native to Europe, Macaronesia, northern Africa, Ethiopia, the Middle East, western Siberia, and Central Asia, and introduced to temperate North America, South America, Australia, New Zealand, Korea, Japan, and Primorsky Krai in far eastern Russia.
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North and South Islands and on Stewart Island. It was first recorded wild here in 1878, and it was plentiful in places by the late nineteenth century. New Zealand plants were once named as a native species, Atriplex novae-zelandiae, but no character separates them from A. prostrata elsewhere, and the species is probably introduced, since early botanists apparently did not collect it. It has also been known in New Zealand as A. hastata and A. triangularis. It is a facultative halophyte: it can grow on salty ground but does not need it.
In Australia, where creeping saltbush is one of its common names (one it shares there with the native berry saltbush, A. semibaccata), it is an environmental weed of wet, somewhat saline ground such as creek margins, estuaries and the edges of inland salt lakes.
Its name comes from an ancient Latin plant name of uncertain origin, possibly from the Greek a- 'without' and traphein 'nourishment', because many saltbushes grow in arid desert soils; prostrata means prostrate.

warnings: Plants grown on fertilised ground can concentrate harmful amounts of nitrate in their leaves.
The seeds have emetic and purgative properties.

Native saltbushes grow on the same coasts and saline ground, and all of them are Threatened or At Risk: do not pick them. Atriplex buchananii (Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable) and grey saltbush, A. cinerea (Threatened – Nationally Critical, one natural population left), are perennials with small, entire, silvery-grey or whitish leaves, round to broadly oval in A. buchananii and narrow in grey saltbush. On the Chatham Islands, A. billardierei (Threatened – Nationally Endangered) grows on sandy beaches; its fleshy leaves are densely covered in small bladder-like swellings. Holloway's crystalwort, A. hollowayi (Threatened – Nationally Critical), survives naturally only on two beaches at Te Paki in Northland. On the Chatham Islands, Atriplex australasica (At Risk – Relict), strictly coastal, grows on beaches, clay banks and cliff faces; it has wide, often deeply toothed or lobed leaves, though young plants often have entire leaves.

identification.text:
A pouch fungus around 20 by 60 mm that never opens out into gills; old New Zealand descriptions give pouches from 2–3 cm up to 8 cm tall. The cap is powder blue, purplish-blue, sage-green or sea-green, smooth and shining or pitted and furrowed. The stem is stout and solid, whitish to yellowish, often brighter yellow towards the base, widening where it meets the pouch.
Cut lengthways, the gleba inside is brown, reddish-brown or rusty orange, held in regular cell-like chambers behind a purple-brown sack-like wall. It does not bruise blue.

lookalikes.howToTell: Colour and shape do not separate them reliably. Spindle pouch is powder blue, purplish blue or greenish, usually elongated and tapering towards the tip. Weraroa is light brown when young, becoming french-grey or pale blue-grey (sometimes pale green), and can be roundish, egg-shaped or elongated. The stem is the better field check. Spindle pouch's is stout, solid, smooth and slippery, off-white to yellow and yellower towards the base, and widens towards the pouch. Weraroa's is slender, the same width throughout, fibrous and hollow, whitish to french-grey with a yellowish-brown base. Weraroa slowly bruises blue or greenish where injured, on both pouch and stem. Spindle pouch is naturally blue but does not blue when damaged. Cut one lengthways. Spindle pouch's gleba is brown to reddish-brown, rarely orange, in regular cell-like chambers inside a purple-brown sack-like layer. Weraroa's is sepia to chocolate-brown in contorted, gill-like chambers, with no sack.

The test that separates it from weraroa, which is the whole reason this page exists. Clavogaster virescens is *naturally* blue to greenish blue and has **no bluing reaction**, and contains no psilocybin; Psilocybe weraroa is a bluing Psilocybe containing psilocin and psilocybine. Because a secotioid cap never opens to show gills, the identification needs a cut through the fruitbody: in C. virescens the gleba is a reddish brown or orange chambered mass inside a sack-like structure within the peridium, and the stem is stout, smooth and slippery rather than fibrous, off-white to yellow, swollen at the top where it runs smoothly into the pouch and tapering to a yellower base. The taxonomy is why the two are tangled: the genus Weraroa was erected in 1958 for W. novae-zelandiae and this species was moved into it, and only in 2015 did it become Clavogaster virescens (Massee) J.A. Cooper again while W. novae-zelandiae became Psilocybe weraroa. Clavogaster holds two endemic species — this one and Clavogaster sp. 'whakapapa'. iNaturalist, 'Blue Pouch Fungus (Clavogaster virescens)', and Manaaki Whenua Biota of New Zealand. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/467870-Clavogaster-virescens

summary.text:
A blue-green pouch fungus of native bush with a bright yellow stem, also called the blue pouch fungus. Inedible, and often mistaken for weraroa by foragers.
Recorded on both main islands and commoner in the North Island, particularly around Wellington and Auckland. The early New Zealand collections came from Dannevirke, the Ōtaki Forks and Bluff.

identification.text:
Deciduous shrub or small tree to about 8 m high, often suckering extensively. Branchlets villous. Leaves pinnate, with 19–23 leaflets in mature plants, up to about 30 cm long; petiole and rachis villous or densely hairy, the hairs purple when young. Leaflets sessile, 4–12 × 0.8–2.5 cm, oblong-lanceolate (terminal leaflet more or less ovate), glabrate except for densely hairy midrib below, glaucous below, dull green above, serrate, acuminate at apex, becoming orange to crimson in autumn. Inflorescence terminal, villous, dense and conelike, to about 20 × 5 cm. Flowers greenish. Calyx segments lanceolate, long-ciliate. Petals 2–2.5 mm long. Fruit about 3 mm wide, broader than long, villous with long rose to crimson hairs. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Rhus tree's sap causes a severe skin rash, so tell them apart before you touch. Staghorn sumac is very hairy: its young branches and leaf stalks are covered in soft hairs, purple when young; rhus tree is almost hairless, with glossy leaflets. Staghorn sumac's fruit heads stand upright at the ends of the branches as dense, cone-like heads up to about 20 cm long, made of tiny fruits about 3 mm across covered in long crimson hairs; rhus tree's fruits are smooth, pale shiny brown berries 7–10 mm across, in hanging clusters that grow from the angles of the leaves. Staghorn sumac's leaflets are toothed and dull; adult rhus tree's are untoothed and glossy, but its seedlings' leaflets are strongly toothed, so don't rely on teeth on a young plant. Mature staghorn sumac leaves have 19–23 leaflets; rhus tree's have 4–6 (rarely 7) pairs and usually one at the end. Both turn orange to red in autumn, so autumn colour doesn't separate them.
lookalikes.name: Rhus tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree of heaven is not food. Staghorn sumac's young branches and leaf stalks are covered in soft hairs; tree of heaven's leaflets are hairless and its leaf stalk hairless or finely hairy. Staghorn sumac's leaflets are toothed all along the edge; tree of heaven's are smooth-edged apart from 1–3 coarse teeth or small lobes near the base, each tipped with a gland. Tree of heaven's leaves are much longer, 40–60 (up to 70) cm with 11–25 leaflets, and crushed leaves smell strongly, like peanuts or cashews; staghorn sumac's leaves are up to about 30 cm with 19–23 leaflets. Staghorn sumac's fruit heads are upright cones of tiny crimson-hairy fruits; tree of heaven's seeds sit in flat, twisted, papery wings 3–5 cm long, reddish brown or pinkish red. Staghorn sumac flowers in October–November, tree of heaven in December–January.
lookalikes.name: Tree of heaven

preparation.text: Pick whole fruit heads that taste strongly sour: touch a head and lick your finger. Rain washes the sour coating off, so old, faded heads have little flavour. Pull a head apart and check inside for insects. For the drink, steep the heads, or the fruits stripped off the stalks, in water for anywhere from 10 minutes to a day; cold water gives the least astringent drink, and boiling releases tannins and makes it harsh. Strain through a fine sieve or cloth, then sweeten. For a spice, dry the heads and crush the fruits.

recipes.method: 5 staghorn sumac fruit heads; 1 litre warm water; honey to taste. Put the fruit heads in a 1-litre jug, pour over the warm water and weigh the heads down so they stay under. Leave for a couple of hours or overnight. Strain, sweeten with honey and serve chilled. It turns pink and tastes sharp, like lemonade.
recipes.title: Staghorn sumac lemonade

recipes.method: 3.8 litres cold water; 1.25 litres (about 175–200 g) fresh staghorn sumac fruits stripped from the stalks, or whole heads cut up; 3 sprigs fresh mint or anise hyssop; 250–500 ml maple syrup or honey; juice of 2 large lemons (about 125 ml), plus slices to serve; ice. Whisk the fruits into the water in a large container. Crush the herb sprigs in your hand, push them under the floating fruits and stir. Leave at room temperature or in the fridge overnight, stirring hard whenever you remember. Next day taste it: if it isn't sour enough, add more fruits and leave longer. Strain through a double layer of muslin, stir in the syrup and lemon juice to taste, and chill. Serve over ice with fresh herbs. Keeps a week in the fridge; don't leave it out once sweetened, or it starts to ferment.
recipes.title: Staghorn sumac lemonade with herbs

recipes.method: 15 ml ground dried staghorn sumac; 15 ml toasted sesame seeds; 5 ml dried parsley; 5 ml dried oregano; 5 ml dried thyme; 1.25 ml salt. For the sumac, dry the fruit heads, rub the fruits off the stalks and grind them. Mix everything together. Roll a log of goat cheese in it to serve with crackers, or drizzle naan with a little olive oil, sprinkle with za'atar and warm in a 120 °C oven for 5 minutes.
recipes.title: Sumac za'atar

recipes.method: Fill a jar with staghorn sumac fruits, cover them with apple cider vinegar and leave to steep for a few weeks, then strain and bottle. For the dressing: 2 tbsp berry jam; 2 tbsp sumac vinegar; 1 tbsp olive oil. Stir together and drizzle over salad greens, cucumber, tomato, red onion or feta.
recipes.title: Sumac vinegar and berry dressing

recipes.method: Serves 4–5. For the sumac spice: about 8 large fruit heads make about 2 cups (500 ml). Break the heads apart and pull out the woody core, rinse the fruits quickly in a sieve under cold water (not for long, or the flavour and colour wash away), drain and blot dry on paper towels. Spread them in one layer on a baking-paper-lined tray and dry in the oven on its lowest setting (about 65 °C) for about 3 hours, until dry. Grind in a spice grinder, sift out any twigs and seeds, and store airtight. For the chicken: 60 ml sumac spice; 1 whole chicken, cut into 8 pieces; 15 ml sea salt and 15 ml freshly ground black pepper, plus more to season; about 1 litre buttermilk (or plain yoghurt); 750 ml (about 450 g) plain flour; 15 ml dried thyme; canola or grapeseed oil for frying. Season the chicken well with salt, pepper and 30 ml of the sumac spice, then soak it in the buttermilk for at least 20 minutes, better overnight. Mix the flour with the remaining 30 ml sumac spice, the thyme and the 15 ml each of salt and pepper, and coat each piece well. Heat 2.5 cm of oil in a large cast-iron pan to 175 °C. Fry a few pieces at a time for 6–8 minutes, turn them, cover the pan and cook about 6 minutes more, until the thickest part reaches 74 °C. Drain on paper towels and season with more salt if needed.
recipes.title: Sumac fried chicken

recipes.method: Serves 4. For the chicken: 1 large lemon; 15 ml ground dried staghorn sumac; 10 ml flaky salt; 7.5 ml black pepper; 2.5 ml cinnamon; 2.5 ml allspice; 15 ml finely chopped fresh thyme; 30 ml olive oil; 2 garlic cloves, grated; chicken thighs and breasts for 4; thyme sprigs to serve. For the plums: 450 g plums, halved, or quartered if large; 2 shallots, sliced into 5 mm rounds; 15 ml honey; 7.5 ml olive oil; 1.25 ml salt; 1.25 ml cinnamon; a pinch (0.6 ml) of allspice; half a bay leaf. Zest the lemon into a small bowl and keep the lemon. Stir in the sumac, salt, pepper, cinnamon, allspice and thyme, then 22.5 ml of the oil and the garlic, to a wet-sand texture. Rub it over the chicken and leave uncovered in the fridge for 1 to 24 hours. Take the chicken out 30 minutes before cooking and heat the oven to 230 °C. Heat 15 ml of the oil in an ovenproof pan and brown the chicken quickly over high heat, then lift it out. Lower the heat, toss the plums, shallots, honey, oil, salt, cinnamon, allspice and bay leaf in the pan, set the chicken on top and roast 15–20 minutes. Mix 15 ml juice from the lemon with the last 7.5 ml oil, drizzle it over the chicken and roast another 15–20 minutes, until the skin is golden and the chicken cooked through. Rest 10 minutes under loose foil and serve with the plums and thyme sprigs.
recipes.title: Roast chicken with sumac and plums

recipes.method: Serves 4. A sweet fruit soup, served hot or cold, or thinned as a drink. 500 ml chopped rhubarb stalks; 1 cinnamon stick; 250 ml water; 80 ml (about 70 g) sugar; 15 ml cornflour mixed with 30 ml water; 250 ml sumac juice. For the juice, soak whole fruit heads in cold water for a few hours; for a stronger juice, lift them out and soak fresh heads in the same water until it is as strong as you like, then strain through a fine sieve or cloth. Simmer the rhubarb, sugar, cinnamon and water until the rhubarb is very soft, strain and return the liquid to the pan. Stir in the cornflour mix and simmer a few minutes more, then add the sumac juice.
recipes.title: Sumac and rhubarb soup

summary.text:
Staghorn sumac (Rhus typhina), also called sumac, stag's horn sumac, velvet sumac or Virginian sumac, is a deciduous shrub or small tree of the cashew family (Anacardiaceae) from eastern North America, naturalised in New Zealand since 1958.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Hutt Valley; South Island: Christchurch area. It is commonly planted, particularly in the South Island, for its crimson, cone-like fruit heads and its coloured autumn leaves, and spreads by suckering; its vigorous suckering makes it unsuitable for small gardens. A 2002 herbarium specimen records it growing wild along a roadside near Cromwell, Central Otago.

warnings: The sap can cause a skin rash in some people.
Rhus tree, whose sap causes a severe rash, is sometimes called sumac and grows in the same places; tree of heaven is also similar. See Lookalikes.

identification.text:
Annual, with all branches reproductive. Stems erect or ascending, (5)–10–30–(50) cm tall, with spreading eglandular and shorter glandular hairs. Leaves elliptic to broadly obovate-spathulate, (5)–10–25–(30) × (2)–5–10–(15) mm, the lower narrowed gradually to base; hairs eglandular. Inflorescence compact; peduncles elongating at fruiting but pedicels always equal to or shorter than calyx; peduncles and pedicels densely hairy with long eglandular and shorter glandular hairs. Bracts elliptic to obovate, always herbaceous, with dense glandular and eglandular hairs. Sepals (3.5)–4–5–(6) mm long, with narrow scarious margins, and glandular and long eglandular hairs overtopping apex. Petals slightly longer than or equal to sepals. Styles 0.5–0.8 mm long. Capsule cylindric, 2× length of calyx. Seeds 0.3–0.5 mm long, tuberculate.
Mouse-ear chickweeds (Cerastium) in Flora of New Zealand: petals 5, white, emarginate or 2-fid up to ⅓ way, rarely 0; styles (3)–5–(6); fruit a cylindric capsule, often curved, dehiscing by twice as many short apical teeth as the styles.
Annual mouse-ear chickweed can be distinguished from the other small-flowered Cerastium species by all the bracts, even the uppermost, having green margins, pedicels equal to or shorter than calyx and sepal hairs overtopping the sepal apex.

lookalikes.howToTell: Chickweed's stem has a single line of hairs, and its leaves are hairy only on the lower edges and the midrib above; sticky mouse-ear chickweed's stems have spreading hairs mixed with shorter glandular (gland-tipped) hairs, and its leaves are hairy. Chickweed's white petals are divided almost to the base, where sticky mouse-ear chickweed's are notched or divided only up to a third of the way. Chickweed has 3 styles and a narrow egg-shaped capsule as long as or slightly longer than the calyx, opening by 6 teeth; sticky mouse-ear chickweed's capsule is cylindric and twice the length of the calyx, with usually 5 styles and twice as many teeth as styles. Chickweed's flower stalks are usually 10–40 mm long; sticky mouse-ear chickweed's are no longer than the calyx, which is usually 4–5 mm long. Chickweed is eaten too.
lookalikes.name: Chickweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mouse-ear chickweed is a perennial, often with short tufted non-flowering side branches; sticky mouse-ear chickweed is an annual whose branches all flower. Common mouse-ear chickweed has no glandular (gland-tipped) hairs on its sepals, and its sepal hairs do not reach past the sepal tip; sticky mouse-ear chickweed has shorter glandular hairs among the long ones on its stems, flower stalks, bracts and sepals, and its sepal hairs reach past the tip. In fruit, common mouse-ear chickweed's flower stalks are usually longer than the sepals; sticky mouse-ear chickweed's are no longer than the calyx. Common mouse-ear chickweed's upper bracts have papery (scarious) margins; sticky mouse-ear chickweed's bracts are all green, even the uppermost. Both are eaten.

IV (Webb, Sykes & Garnock-Jones 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA): 'Cerastium fontanum' (https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/7efd4653-c35e-46a4-be56-cf9282ffd12c) — 'Perennial, often with short tufted non-flowering axillary branches', 'fruiting pedicels usually > sepals', 'the upper [bracts] with scarious margins', 'the absence of glandular hairs on the sepals, the sepal hairs not overtopping the sepal apex'; 'Cerastium glomeratum' (https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/35a9aa44-c4e4-4174-8a6d-b7f42773993b) — 'Annual, with all branches reproductive', 'spreading eglandular and shorter glandular hairs', 'pedicels always = or < calyx', peduncles and pedicels with 'shorter glandular hairs', bracts 'always herbaceous, with dense glandular and eglandular hairs', sepal hairs 'overtopping apex', 'all the bracts, even the uppermost, having green margins'. Both throughout New Zealand. Risk 'edible' (both careRequired).

summary.text:
Sticky mouse-ear chickweed (Cerastium glomeratum), also called annual mouse-ear chickweed, is an annual herb in the family Caryophyllaceae, naturalised in New Zealand from the northern temperate zone.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands and on the Kermadec, Chatham and Auckland Islands; naturalised from the northern temperate zone, first recorded wild in 1846. It has also been referred to in New Zealand as C. viscosum.

warnings: Food records for this species are few and brief: they name the leaves and young shoots but give no amounts or other details.

identification.text:
Opposite, coarsely toothed, heart-shaped leaves on a square stem, covered in stinging hairs. Small green tassel-like flower clusters at the leaf joints.
A perennial up to 1.5 m tall that spreads by creeping underground stems (rhizomes), often into large patches that come back year after year; the stems seldom branch, and the plant dies down in winter. Leaves are 5–25 cm long, the end tooth longer than the teeth beside it. Male and female flowers are in separate clusters up to 9 cm long, usually on separate plants.
Dwarf nettle (Urtica urens), the commoner nettle in New Zealand, is a branched annual up to 60 cm with a short taproot and no rhizomes. Its leaves are 2–8 cm, the end tooth about as long as its neighbours, and its short flower clusters, up to 3 cm, usually carry male and female flowers together.

lookalikes.howToTell: Ongaonga (tree nettle) is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m tall; common nettles are herbs — Urtica urens an annual to 60 cm, Urtica dioica a perennial to 1.5 m — so height alone will not separate a tall Urtica dioica from a small ongaonga. Ongaonga's leaves are pale green, triangular to ovate-triangular and coarsely toothed, and it carries white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long on the leaf teeth, young stalks and leaf veins; ongaonga's stinging hairs are long-stalked and common nettles' short-stalked. Ongaonga has 2 stipules at each node, common nettles 4. Its sting has killed: in 1961 a young man died of paralysis and breathing problems several hours after walking through tree nettles, and stung dogs and horses have developed convulsions and breathing distress within minutes, often dying within hours. Young ongaonga can be confused with other native nettles, so do not touch a stinging plant unless you are sure it is not woody.
lookalikes.name: Ongaonga

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf nettle is a branched annual up to 60 cm with a short taproot; stinging nettle is a perennial up to 1.5 m that spreads by rhizomes into patches and seldom branches. Dwarf nettle's leaves are 2–8 cm and rounder, the end tooth about as long as the teeth beside it; stinging nettle's are 5–25 cm, the end tooth longer. Dwarf nettle's flower clusters, up to 3 cm long, usually carry male and female flowers together; stinging nettle's clusters, up to 9 cm, are one sex, usually on separate plants. Both sting, and both are eaten young and cooked.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf stinging nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush nettle is a native herb 15–60 cm tall with light green, triangular leaves 2–6 cm long (sometimes up to 12 cm); stinging nettle grows to 1.5 m with leaves 5–25 cm long. Bush nettle carries male and female flowers on the same plant, the lowest clusters all male and the upper all female; stinging nettle's male and female flowers are usually on separate plants. Bush nettle grows in forest, forest margins and shaded places; stinging nettle in waste places, cultivated land and grassland.
lookalikes.name: Bush nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Southern nettle is a stout, bushy native up to about 1 m whose branches lie down and root before turning upright, with broadly ovate, dark green leaves 10–20 cm long, the leaf stalk often carrying a pair of small leaflets near its base; its stinging hairs are mainly on the leaf edges and the veins underneath, and are often few or none. Stinging nettle spreads by long underground rhizomes into patches, and its male and female flowers are usually on separate plants; southern nettle carries both, female clusters above male. Leaf size does not separate them: stinging nettle's are 5–25 cm. Southern nettle grows only in Fiordland, the islets of Foveaux Strait, Stewart Island and the Chatham and subantarctic islands, where stinging nettle is rare (on Stewart Island it is recorded only at Port Pegasus). No record of southern nettle being eaten has been found, and it is At Risk – Declining.
lookalikes.name: Southern nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Hedge woundwort does not sting, smells strongly foetid when its leaves are crushed, and has reddish-purple two-lipped flowers 12–16 mm long, with white markings on the lower lip, in whorls up a spike; nettle stings, and its flowers are tiny, green and tassel-like at the leaf joints. Both spread by rhizomes and have opposite, toothed, heart-based leaves; hedge woundwort grows along forest margins, in scrub and around hedges. It is eaten too.
lookalikes.name: Hedge woundwort
