identification.text:
Stout biennial up to 2–(3) m high, usually with a single main stem. Stems moderately to densely clothed in stellate hairs when young, becoming more or less glabrous and woody at base when older. Leaves densely clothed in stellate hairs, velvety to touch, suborbicular, cordate at base, shortly 5–7-palmately lobed and crenulate, up to 20 cm diameter, rarely variegated; petioles 3–30 cm long; stipules narrow- to ovate-triangular, 4–8 mm long. Flowers in axillary and terminal clusters of 2–7–(10) or rarely in irregular racemes; fruiting pedicels 5–20–(30) mm long; epicalyx segments broadly ovate to suborbicular, united for lower ?-1/2, longer than calyx, distinctly enlarged and spreading at fruiting; calyx shallowly campanulate; calyx teeth more or less equal to tube, triangular, acute to acuminate, densely clothed in stellate hairs, usually more or less connivent at fruiting; petals lilac or deep pink with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long. Mericarps 6–8–(9) per fruit, usually glabrous, sometimes densely clothed in fine hairs, finely transversely ribbed on back; edges sharply angled.
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Lavatera arborea L.]
This robust species is most easily distinguished by the fused, enlarged, spreading fruiting calyx.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Both have round, palmately 5–7-lobed, round-toothed leaves, so the leaves do not separate them; use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. The flowers overlap: both are pink to purple with darker veins or markings, and tree mallow's 15–20 mm petals sit inside common mallow's 12–30 mm range. Use the epicalyx, which is longer than the calyx and enlarged in fruit in tree mallow but shorter than the calyx in common mallow (whose epicalyx segments may be somewhat joined at the base, so joining alone is not a test), and the fruit, ribbed crosswise against net-veined. Both have lobed leaves that can reach 20 cm across. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Both have round, palmately 5–7-lobed, round-toothed leaves, so the leaves do not separate them; use the petal length, the epicalyx and the fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. They differ in the epicalyx (longer than the calyx and enlarged in fruit in tree mallow, shorter and barely changed in island mallow), the fruit segments, the calyx (shallowly bell-shaped in tree mallow, long and tube-shaped in island mallow) and the petals (15–20 mm against 30–40 mm). Both are tall, both grow at coastal sites, and both have lobed leaves up to 20 cm across and pink to purple flowers with darker veins, so the leaves and flower colour do not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

preparation.text: Young leaves raw or cooked, cut very thinly or as part of a chopped mixed salad. In Andratx, Mallorca, it has been used to make omelettes and mallow salads dressed with oil and vinegar. Steam the leaves for longer than the 15–20 minutes a common-mallow recipe gives, or they stay furry, and chop them finely; they are not very slimy compared with other mallows. The young, green seed heads can be eaten fresh, when they taste a bit like raw peanuts, or fried for a few minutes, when they taste like fried sweetcorn.

recipes.method: Written for tree mallow (Lavatera arborea), on an Irish foraging blog. Young, green tree mallow seed heads; salt; ground cayenne pepper. Pick young, green seed heads (their texture is better). Take off the three leaf-like parts around each head before cooking, or while eating. Fry them for a few minutes, then season with salt and ground cayenne pepper. The author also toasts them in a popcorn maker.
recipes.title: Fried tree mallow seed heads

recipes.method: Written for tree mallow (Malva arborea), improvised by the author on molokhia, the Egyptian soup of jute mallow sometimes made with common mallow; the page gives no quantities. Tree mallow leaves, finely chopped; water; chopped onion; oil; garlic cloves; coriander seeds; salt and pepper; vegetable stock; lemon juice. Purée finely chopped raw tree mallow leaves in a blender with some water. Fry chopped onion in oil until soft. Crush garlic cloves, coriander seeds, salt and pepper in a mortar and add them with some vegetable stock and lemon juice, then add the puréed leaves. Simmer gently for a while, and purée again if it is not smooth enough. The author found tree mallow not very slimy, though the lemon is meant to offset the mucilage; one of the two tasters was not keen, possibly because of too much lemon.
recipes.title: Tree mallow and lemon soup (molokhia style)

summary.text:
Tree mallow, Malva arborea (formerly Lavatera arborea), is a stout biennial of the mallow family (Malvaceae), native to western and southern Europe and North Africa, and was brought to New Zealand as an ornamental.
It forms tall, dense clumps that can crowd out native perennials. The stands have no understorey and die back in summer, leaving coastal soil open to erosion by sea winds and to annual weeds, and can make the ground less suitable for nesting bird colonies.
In New Zealand it is local throughout the North Island (not recorded from Taranaki) and throughout the South Island, and on Ruapuke Island and the Chatham Islands. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1870.

harvestEthics.text:
Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.
An Unwanted Organism and National Pest Plant Accord species: it must not be bred, distributed, released or sold anywhere in New Zealand, and in the Auckland region it must not be planted. Auckland Council controls it on Aotea / Great Barrier Island, where you should report it to pestfree@aucklandcouncil.govt.nz rather than control it yourself. Cut stumps and root pieces send up new suckers, so pull or dig seedlings out with every piece of root; Bay of Plenty Regional Council says to put them in the general waste at a refuse transfer station. Environment Canterbury advises leaving trees over 4 m to a qualified arborist.

identification.text: A deciduous tree to about 25 m high, with smooth, pale-striped grey bark, often sending up suckers from its roots; in New Zealand male and female flowers are usually or always on separate trees. Leaves very large, 40–60 (up to 70) cm long, with 11–25 leaflets; the end leaflet is often small or missing. Leaflets 7–15 (up to 17) × 3–6 (up to 7.5) cm, narrowly to broadly oval with a long-pointed tip, hairless or hairy towards the base of the midrib underneath, bluish-green underneath; near the base each has 1–3 coarse teeth or small lobes tipped with a prominent gland. All parts have a strong smell, likened to peanuts or cashews, and the flowers smell foul. Flowers small, yellow-green, in clusters; petals 2.5–4 mm long. Seeds in flat, twisted, papery wings (samaras) 3–5 cm long, light reddish brown or pinkish red, tapering at each end, which can stay on the tree a long time.

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree of heaven's leaflets are hairless, smooth-edged apart from 1–3 coarse teeth or small lobes near the base, each tipped with a gland, and its crushed leaves smell strongly, like peanuts or cashews; staghorn sumac's leaflets are toothed all along the edge, and its young branches and leaf stalks are covered in soft hairs. Tree of heaven's leaves are 40–60 (up to 70) cm long with 11–25 leaflets; staghorn sumac's are up to about 30 cm with 19–23. Tree of heaven's seeds sit in flat, twisted, papery wings 3–5 cm long; staghorn sumac's fruit heads are upright cones of tiny crimson-hairy fruits. Tree of heaven flowers in December–January, staghorn sumac in October–November.
lookalikes.name: Staghorn sumac

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree of heaven's leaflets have 1–3 coarse teeth or small lobes at the base, each tipped with a gland, and are otherwise smooth-edged; Japanese walnut's are finely toothed along the edge, though the teeth are often sparse, with no gland pads. Tree of heaven usually has more leaflets (11–25 against 9–17; the ranges overlap). Japanese walnut's leaf stalk and central axis are densely covered in sticky glandular hairs; tree of heaven's are hairless or finely hairy, and its crushed leaves smell strongly, like peanuts or cashews. Japanese walnut's fruits are 2.5–4 cm, sticky, rusty-hairy and beaked, in long strings, each holding a hard nut; tree of heaven's seeds sit in flat, twisted, papery wings 3–5 cm long.
lookalikes.name: Japanese walnut

lookalikes.howToTell: Black walnut's nuts are edible; tree of heaven is not food. Look at the edge of a leaflet: tree of heaven's is smooth apart from 1–3 coarse teeth or small lobes near the base, each tipped with a gland; black walnut's is toothed all the way along. Crush a leaf: tree of heaven's smells strongly, likened to peanuts or cashews; black walnut's has a pungent, spicy smell of its own. Tree of heaven's seeds sit in flat, twisted, papery wings 3–5 cm long; black walnut's fruit is a round nut 3–4 cm across in a brownish-green husk. The leaflet counts overlap (tree of heaven 11–25, black walnut 15–23) and both often lack an end leaflet, so don't use either.
lookalikes.name: Black walnut

summary.text:
Tree of heaven (Ailanthus altissima), also called Chinese sumac or stinking shumac, is a fast-growing deciduous tree of the quassia family (Simaroubaceae) from China, brought into New Zealand as an ornamental and naturalised since 1983.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Auckland, Masterton; South Island: North Canterbury (Parnassus), Christchurch, South Canterbury (Holme Station). Wild herbarium specimens add Whanganui, the Rangitīkei (Turakina), Nelson and Mid Canterbury (Greendale), and Bay of Plenty Regional Council records it at small isolated sites in the Bay of Plenty, where a self-sown tree has been collected at Tauranga. It is widely planted in plantations, shrubberies and windbreaks, and escapes by suckers that form thickets, sometimes many metres from the parent tree and especially after it dies or is cut down. The Flora (1988) found it seldom came up from seed here, but wild seedlings were collected near Auckland trees in the 1980s, and regional councils now list seed as well as suckers.
Its suckers form dense thickets that crowd out native plants, a toxin from its bark and leaves builds up in the soil and stops other plants establishing, and its roots can damage drains. It is an Unwanted Organism and a National Pest Plant Accord species, and on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.

warnings: Do not eat it. It may be poisonous, and its leaves and flowers smell foul.
Its sap can cause skin rashes; people felling or clearing it have had them. Wear gloves and long sleeves if you remove it.
Rhus tree, whose sap causes a severe rash, is sometimes mistaken for it; staghorn sumac and Japanese walnut also have similar long leaves. See Lookalikes.

habitat.text:
Naturalised extensively in waste places, margins of remnant forest stands, coastal cliffs, and gardens.
In the Auckland region it grows in hedgerows, lowland and coastal forest, shrubland, disturbed sites, roadsides, wasteland and wetlands. It can invade most coastal and lowland forest types, intact or disturbed, as well as shrubland, fernland, cliffs and coastline, and it tolerates shade, frost, damp or drought, salt and wind.

harvestEthics.text:
Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.
An Unwanted Organism and National Pest Plant Accord species: it must not be bred, distributed, released or sold anywhere in New Zealand. Birds spread its seed. If you remove it, put the seed in green waste or landfill. Pulled seedlings can be left on site to rot; a cut stump regrows unless it is treated.

identification.text:
Glabrous, small or medium-sized, evergreen tree to c. 10 m high (taller in cultivation), sometimes a dense shrub. Shoots glabrous. Petioles mostly 1–2 cm long. Lamina 5–13 × 3–6 cm, ovate to elliptic-ovate, glossy above; base broad-cuneate to rounded; apex usually abruptly short-acuminate, sometimes acute. Panicles up to 25 × 20 cm, dense, broadly pyramidal; branches angular; pedicels very short. Bracts oblong or oblong-lanceolate; bracteoles much smaller, caducous. Flowers fragrant. Calyx 1–2 mm long; lobes indistinct. Corolla white; tube c. 1.5 mm long; lobes 2–2.5 mm long, oblong-elliptic, reflexed, with ± involute margins, acute. Stamens c. 4 mm long, exserted; anthers yellow. Style included. Fruit to 6 × 5 mm, ellipsoid-oblong, bluish or purplish black, ± pruinose. Seed c. 5 mm long, ± broadly ellipsoid, ribbed on back.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Shoots ± terete, prominently lenticellate. Leaves opposite, simple, entire. Inflorescence a terminal panicle of small, bisexual, usually scented flowers. Stamens 2, included or exserted, epipetalous; filaments short. [From the genus Ligustrum in Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The stems carry distinctive lumpy warts, the leaves are in opposite pairs, and the berries are coated with a powdery bloom. The fruit ripens in autumn. Chinese privet is a much shorter tree with smaller, more rounded leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: lilly pilly's is pinkish mauve or white, usually 1–1.7 cm across (up to 3 cm), with a hollow at the tip and one large seed; tree privet's berries are bluish or purplish black with a powdery bloom, no more than 6 mm long, each with a ribbed seed about 5 mm long. Lilly pilly's new leaves are reddish, unlike tree privet's. Look at the flowers: tree privet's are small and tubular, with a white tube about 1.5 mm long, four reflexed lobes 2–2.5 mm long and only two stamens, in dense clusters up to 25 × 20 cm; lilly pilly's four tiny petals, about 2 mm long, are joined into a small cap that falls, and it has numerous stamens. Lilly pilly's leaves are very aromatic when crushed and dotted with glands underneath, on stalks usually about 5 mm long; tree privet's are not described as aromatic or gland-dotted, and their stalks are mostly 1–2 cm long. Tree privet's shoots are more or less round, with prominent lumpy warts; lilly pilly's twigs are often four-angled or shortly four-winged. Both are evergreen trees with glossy, opposite leaves of overlapping size (lilly pilly usually 4–12 cm long, tree privet 5–13 cm), and both grow in scrub and on waste ground, so leaf shape and place do not separate them. Lilly pilly's fruit is eaten.
lookalikes.name: Lilly pilly

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: brush cherry's is crimson to crimson-purple and glossy, oblong to obovoid, usually 1–2 cm long (up to 2.5 cm), with its calyx lobes still on the tip and one or a few large seeds; tree privet's berries are bluish or purplish black with a powdery bloom, no more than 6 mm long, each with a ribbed seed about 5 mm long. Brush cherry's new leaves are reddish, unlike tree privet's. Brush cherry's flowers have free, round white petals about 4 mm across and numerous white stamens up to about 13 mm long, in clusters of 3–25; tree privet's are small and tubular, with four reflexed white lobes 2–2.5 mm long and only two stamens, in dense clusters up to 25 × 20 cm. Brush cherry's leaves are aromatic when crushed, mostly 1–3.5 cm wide (up to 4 cm), on stalks under 10 mm; tree privet's are not described as aromatic, are 3–6 cm wide, so the widths overlap a little, and sit on stalks mostly 1–2 cm long. Brush cherry's strong young shoots are more or less four-winged; tree privet's shoots are more or less round, with prominent lumpy warts. Both are evergreen trees with glossy, opposite leaves of overlapping length (brush cherry mostly 4–10 cm, up to 13 cm; tree privet 5–13 cm), and both grow on roadsides, in scrub and at forest margins. Brush cherry's fruit is eaten.

summary.text:
Tree privet, also called broadleaf privet, is an evergreen tree in the olive family (Oleaceae), originally from China and Korea. Chinese privet is a different species, Ligustrum sinense.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island, in North Auckland, Auckland and coastal Bay of Plenty. Naturalised from China, first recorded in 1958. This is the largest species in New Zealand and is commonly used to form a tall hedge in warmer parts of the country; unclipped trees become widespreading and reach about 14 m high.
Bay of Plenty Regional Council describes it as widespread throughout the Bay of Plenty, particularly near the coast. Wild herbarium specimens also come from a podocarp forest margin near Tikokino in Hawke's Bay (2024) and a vegetated sand dune at Pōhara Beach, Golden Bay (2009).
It is an Unwanted Organism and a National Pest Plant Accord species, and is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. Birds spread its seed, and it forms dense stands that displace native plants and stop native seedlings establishing.

warnings: Do not eat any part of tree privet. Its leaves and berries are poisonous; the black, blue-black or dark purplish berries of every privet are poisonous, and children may be tempted to eat them. The young shoots have been cooked as a famine food, but they contain a glycoside and are probably toxic.
Lilly pilly and brush cherry, which have edible fruit, can look similar and grow in the same places. Check every tree before picking (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Wetlands in open turf and grassy places, pasture and lawns (usually damp), flushes and bogs. Recorded elevations range from 0 to 1281 m.
A weed of lawns that also grows in pasture, very common in New Zealand and best in moist places (Massey).
New Zealand's national wetland plant list rates it facultative: it is common both in wetlands and on dry ground (NZPCN).

identification.text:
Perennial herb to 0.25 m tall. Stems decumbent and rooting at nodes below, ascending to erect above, eglandular-hairy; hairs uniform, antrorse. Leaf bud indistinct; leaves separating while very small, opposite-decussate, erecto-patent to spreading; lamina thin, broadly ovate to broadly elliptic, to orbicular, 5–17 mm long, 4–15 mm wide, dull green above, paler beneath; midrib and 2–4 lateral veins evident; surfaces glabrous or sparsely minutely eglandular-puberulent; margin glabrous or sparsely ciliolate, shallowly crenate or crenate-serrate, rarely entire with marginal hydathodes, teeth in 3–8 pairs; apex and base more or less rounded; petiole 0.5–5.0 mm long. Inflorescence a terminal raceme, 20–60 (rarely to 110) mm long; flowers crowded at first, becoming distant, 3–12 (rarely to 60), all bisexual; bracts alternate or rarely the lowermost opposite, oblanceolate to elliptic, overtopping pedicels, the lowest leaf-like, becoming smaller above; pedicels erecto-patent, 1–3 mm long, shortly eglandular-puberulent all around. Calyx lobes 4, obtuse, more or less equal, 2–3 mm long, glabrous or sparsely eglandular-puberulent especially at base. Corolla 3–5 mm diameter, tube white and yellow, less than 1 mm long, shorter than calyx, hairy at throat; lobes 4, pale blue fading to whitish, or rarely white or blue, darker inside and on posterior lobe, sub-erect to erecto-patent, unequal, broadly ovate to orbicular, 2–3 mm long, obtuse to rounded, nectar guides dark blue or purple, on posterior and lateral lobes. Stamen filaments white, 1.5–2.0 mm long; anthers blue. Style blue, 1.7–2.0 mm long. Capsules angustiseptate, emarginate to obcordate, sparsely glandular ciliate on margins, 3.0–3.5 mm long, 3.5–4.0 mm wide at widest point. Seeds, ellipsoid, flattened, smooth, pale brown, 0.5–0.7 mm long.
Veronica serpyllifolia plants are distinctive among New Zealand species of Veronica. Characteristic features for their identification include the perennial habit with basal part of the stem decumbent and rooting at the nodes, short, antrorse stem hairs, almost glabrous dull green leaves, small, usually very pale blue corolla with a short anterior lobe, and rounded, emarginate capsule with marginal glandular cilia.
Veronica peregrina plants have a similar growth form, but differ in being annuals, completely glabrous, their flowers are almost sessile (pedicels less than 0.5 mm long), the corolla is pure white without nectar guides, the styles less than 0.2 mm long, and the capsules are a little smaller and more rounded.
Among the speedwells common in New Zealand lawns it is the only one with white flowers streaked blue; the others are blue streaked white. Its leaves are hairless, unlike the other lawn speedwells. Out of flower it looks very like pennyroyal, with a similar leaf shape and creeping stems; crush a leaf, as pennyroyal smells strongly of mint and turf speedwell does not (Massey).
Its flowers grow only in spikes at the ends of the stems, never in spikes from the leaf bases (NatureSpot).

lookalikes.howToTell: Bird's-eye speedwell's flowers are sky-blue, 8–12 mm across, each alone on a long, slender stalk; turf speedwell's are pale blue fading to whitish, 3–5 mm across, on short stalks (1–3 mm) up a spike at the stem tips. Bird's-eye speedwell's leaves are hairy, 6–35 mm long and coarsely toothed; turf speedwell's are almost hairless, 5–17 mm long, with shallow, rounded teeth. Bird's-eye speedwell is seldom in mown turf and is commoner in gardens and crops; turf speedwell is a perennial that stays below the mower in lawns and damp pasture. Both creep and can root at the joints, and both have paired leaves and dark-striped flowers, so neither tells them apart. The older Flora (1988) gives turf speedwell's flowers as c. 8 mm across on stalks 2–6 mm long, which overlaps bird's-eye speedwell's at the edges, so go by colour and layout: turf speedwell's are white or very pale blue and sit in a long spike at the stem tips, bird's-eye speedwell's are bright blue and sit singly in the leaf joints. Bird's-eye speedwell's young leaves and shoots are eaten, but its record as food is thin.
lookalikes.name: Bird's-eye speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: pennyroyal smells strongly of mint, turf speedwell does not. In flower, pennyroyal's mauve flowers, 4–6 mm long, crowd in rings around the stem at the leaf bases; turf speedwell's are pale blue fading to whitish, flat with four lobes, 3–5 mm across, up a spike at the stem tips. Out of flower they look very alike: both creep and root along the ground, have small paired leaves of much the same shape and size, and grow in damp lawns and pasture. Do not eat pennyroyal: it damages the liver.
lookalikes.name: Pennyroyal

lookalikes.howToTell: Field speedwell's leaves are hairy on both faces, at least on the veins, and its stems carry two kinds of hairs; turf speedwell's leaves are almost hairless. Field speedwell is an annual with no creeping stems; turf speedwell is a perennial whose lower stems creep and root at the joints. Field speedwell's flowers are bright blue, 2–3 mm across, almost stalkless; turf speedwell's are pale blue fading to whitish, 3–5 mm across, on stalks 1–3 mm long. Both grow low in lawns throughout New Zealand, with small paired, toothed leaves and four-lobed flowers in a spike at the stem tips, so habitat and leaf shape do not separate them. No record of field speedwell being eaten has been found.
lookalikes.name: Field speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping speedwell's leaves are hairy on both faces and edges; turf speedwell's are almost hairless. Creeping speedwell's flowers are blue, 8–10 mm across, each alone on a thread-like stalk 15–40 mm long; turf speedwell's are pale blue fading to whitish, 3–5 mm across, on short stalks (1–3 mm) up a spike at the stem tips. Creeping speedwell's stems lie flat, sometimes rising at the tips; turf speedwell's creep and root only at the base, then rise to flower. Creeping speedwell sets no fruit in New Zealand; turf speedwell sets small notched capsules. Both are perennials that creep, root at the joints and form mats in lawns, and their leaves overlap in size (creeping speedwell 3–8 mm long, turf speedwell 5–17 mm), so habit and leaf size do not separate them. No food use of creeping speedwell has been confirmed; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Creeping speedwell

summary.text:
Veronica serpyllifolia, the thyme-leaved speedwell or thymeleaf speedwell, is a perennial flowering plant in the plantain family.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: throughout. South Island: throughout. Stewart Island, Chatham Islands, Campbell Island. First recorded by Kirk in 1864.
It survives many common lawn weedkillers, so it often stands out after a lawn has been sprayed with the wrong one (Massey).
It is native to temperate Eurasia and was naturalised in New Zealand by 1864 (NZPCN). The name serpyllifolia means thyme-leaved, from the Latin serpyllum, thyme, and folium, leaf (Biota of New Zealand).

warnings: Its record as food is thin: one foraging page (leaves, flowers and stems raw in salads) and a database listing of food use with no part or method given, so it is not given as food here.
It survives many common lawn weedkillers, so a healthy-looking patch may still have been sprayed.

habitat.text: On dead wood — fallen logs, stumps and dead branches — of both native and introduced trees, in native forest and in towns and gardens. New Zealand collections are from beech, tawa and kauri as well as peach and other fruit trees, wattles, willows and poplars; few are from conifers. Usually in groups of overlapping brackets.

identification.text: Thin, leathery brackets 2–7 cm wide and 2–5 mm thick, fan- or spoon-shaped and attached at the side with no stalk, usually overlapping in groups and sometimes forming rosettes. The upper surface is furrowed and banded in concentric zones of stiff hairs in shades of brown, grey, black, yellow and blue, with a paler, scalloped edge. The underside is white to cream and covered in tiny pores, 3–5 to the millimetre, with a pore-free rim 1–5 mm wide. Flesh white, 1–2 mm thick, with a thin black line under the hairy top when cut. Spore print whitish.

preparation.text: Pick young, firm brackets with bright banding and a clean white underside; old, faded ones riddled with insect larvae are past using. Scrub off grit with an old toothbrush and trim away any wood, then dry them — 2–3 days somewhere warm and airy, or in a dehydrator. Break them up as small as you can or slice them thinly, then simmer in water for at least 20–40 minutes and strain out the pieces — they stay tough however long they cook. Dried brackets keep for months in sealed jars somewhere cool and dark.

recipes.method: Written for turkey tail with artist's bracket (Ganoderma applanatum) and shiitake. 2 onions with their skins, roughly chopped; 1 leek; 1 bulb of garlic, halved across; 2 celery sticks (ends and tops too); 2 carrots; 1 beetroot (optional); an 8 cm piece of fresh ginger, sliced; an 8 cm piece of fresh turmeric, sliced (or 30 ml/2 tbsp powder); 50 g dried or fresh mushrooms — turkey tail, artist's bracket pieces and shiitake; 8 g dried seaweed (kelp, kombu or wakame); 2.5 ml (½ tsp) crushed black peppercorns; 1 large stick of rosemary or 6 thyme sprigs; 4 bay leaves; 4 litres water; 5–10 ml (1–2 tsp) salt. Makes 2.5 litres. Put everything in a stockpot, bring to the boil uncovered and simmer gently for 1–1½ hours. Strain out the solids, keeping the mushrooms to slice and return to the liquid. Bring it back to the boil and bottle it into jars sterilised in a 150 °C oven; the lids pop as they seal. Store sealed jars in the pantry and opened ones in the fridge. Drink it as it is, or use it as a base for miso soup or with cooked noodles or rice.
recipes.title: Turkey tail mushroom broth

recipes.method: 15–30 ml (1–2 tbsp) dried turkey tail, cleaned and crumbled; 1 litre (4 cups) water; honey, lemon or ginger to taste (optional). Put the mushroom pieces and water in a saucepan, bring to the boil, then lower to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered for 30–45 minutes, watching that the pan doesn't boil dry. Strain through a fine sieve, using a finer filter if bits remain, and throw away the tough pieces. Serve warm, sweetened or sharpened to taste. Refrigerate leftovers promptly and use within 3–4 days.
recipes.title: Turkey tail tea

recipes.method: 750 ml (3 cups) cloudy apple juice — the unfiltered, non-alcoholic 'apple cider' of North America; 30 ml (2 tbsp) dried, chopped turkey tail; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) dried astragalus root pieces; a 5 mm sliver of fresh ginger; 2 cinnamon sticks, broken; 1 whole clove; honey to serve. Put everything except the honey in a small saucepan and bring it to a simmer. Cover and keep it at a gentle simmer for about an hour — no longer, or it can turn bitter. Strain, pour into mugs and sweeten each with honey to taste. Keep leftovers in the fridge for up to about a week and warm them gently in a pan to drink.

summary.text: A common native bracket fungus of dead wood, also called rainbow bracket: thin, leathery and banded in many colours, with tiny pores underneath. It is the most common Trametes in towns. It is too tough to eat, and is used to make tea and broth.

warnings: Check the underside before using it: turkey tail has a white to cream underside covered in tiny pores. False turkey tail (Stereum ostrea) and the other Stereum crusts, common on dead wood here, have a smooth underside with no pores.
Some people react badly even to edible mushrooms, so try only a small amount the first time.

habitat.text:
Widely distributed in open habitats, especially in lowland grassland and scrub, on cliffs, often in modified communities of herbs.
In New Zealand: from the coast up into the lower montane zone (sea level to 400 m); it was once widespread in short tussock grassland, on lava fields and clay pans, and on rocky headlands by the sea (NZPCN, restated).

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to pick this plant. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.

identification.text:
Perennial herb with napiform taproot about 3 cm diameter; caulorrhiza short, bearing a number of flowering stems. Hairs variable, the longer mostly curved or bent near base. Basal leaves with petioles to about 25 cm long with retrorse hairs. Lamina to 5 cm diameter, suborbicular to orbicular, lobed to about ⅞ way to midrib; lobes 5–7, linear, inconspicuously but uniformly hairy on both sides; larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; median and larger lateral teeth usually oblong, occasionally obovate to clavate, obtuse, subacute or mucronate. Cauline leaves smaller, with fewer lobes. Flowering stems with dense retrorse hairs or occasionally glabrescent; bracteoles linear to narrowly triangular; flowers usually in pairs, occasionally solitary. Sepals about 5 × 3 mm excluding awn, ovate or elliptic-ovate; awn to 1 mm long; hairs mostly short, appressed, longer on margins. Petals about 6 × 4 mm, obovate, white to pink. Mericarps hairy; beak to 14 mm long. Seed about 2 × 1.4 mm, oblong, dark; dorsal alveolae usually deep, 4–6-sided, more or less isodiametric.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped or cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. They are separated on the hairs of the leaf and flower stalks: in turnip-rooted geranium they are sharply bent near the base, point backward and lie pressed flat; in Solander's geranium they are straight to curved, stand out or point backward, but never lie flat. The leaf lobes (usually linear-obovate in turnip-rooted geranium, obovate in Solander's geranium) and the seed also differ: pits about 0.1 mm across against usually more than 0.1 mm. The root is often turnip-shaped in turnip-rooted geranium and more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot in Solander's geranium, but Solander's geranium can have a turnip-shaped root too, so the root alone does not settle it. Flower colour does not separate them: both can have pink petals, and both can have petals up to 8–9 mm long. Solander's geranium's root is recorded as food. The names do not separate them: Biota of New Zealand gives Solander's geranium the names turnip-rooted geranium, Matua-kūmara and pukupuku, and Flora of New Zealand Online gives the same three to turnip-rooted geranium, so a record under any of them may mean either plant.
lookalikes.name: Solander's geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Australasian cranesbill and turnip-rooted geranium are separated on three characters: the middle teeth of its leaf lobes are about as long as broad (mostly longer than broad in turnip-rooted geranium); the pale, see-through border of its inner sepals is mostly more than 0.3 mm wide near the tip (mostly less than 0.3 mm); and its seeds are red-brown with rather shallow rectangular pits (red-brown to dark brown, with rather deep rectangular to polygonal pits). Its sepals are mostly elliptic to obovate, against ovate. The lobing does not separate them (both are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way), and both have paired flowers. Australasian cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food.
lookalikes.name: Australasian cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Cinquefoil geranium and turnip-rooted geranium are separated on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in turnip-rooted geranium, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in turnip-rooted geranium. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of turnip-rooted geranium overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Cinquefoil geranium's root is recorded as food.

summary.text:
Geranium retrorsum is a species of Geranium known by the common name New Zealand geranium in the United States and common cranesbill in Australia. It is native to Australia and New Zealand but can be found on other continents as an introduced species which is often a noxious weed as well.
In New Zealand this species has been classified by the Department of Conservation as Threatened - Nationally Vulnerable.
Plants treated here as G. retrorsum were treated by Allan (1961) within his concept of G. pilosum.
Its 2023 national assessment is Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable (it was Not Threatened in 2004). Regional assessments rate it Regionally Threatened – Regionally Critical in Northland (2026), Wellington (2025) and Otago (2025), and Regionally Threatened – Regionally Vulnerable in Auckland (2025). It has become very uncommon over most of its North Island range, where it now grows mainly on northern offshore islands, but is still common in parts of the eastern South Island. Rabbits threaten it by digging the plants up for their roots, and taller exotic weeds now dominate the open places it favours. Besides the typical form, two other races grow in New Zealand: one on weedy sites around Canterbury, and one so far known only around Oakley Creek, Auckland, perhaps also at Tawa, Wellington; both are treated as indigenous for now (NZPCN, restated).
In Victoria (VicFlora): Most Victorian plants differ from the type form of Geranium retrorsum from New Zealand as circumscribed by Gardner (1984). Further assessment of this species may result in Victorian (?and Australian) material being reclassified at an infraspecific level.

identification.text:
Plant usually of several leafy fans together, but lateral rhizomes sometimes carrying young shoots 10 cm or more from the parent. Stem more or less woody, about 5 mm diameter, lower internodes usually very short, occasionally to 15 cm long. Leaves distichous, equitant, (15)–25–60–(100) × 1–1.5 cm; sheath often reddish, open at base, narrowed above into a strongly keeled region where the two halves are almost completely fused; lamina of tough texture but not rigid, glossy above, the abaxial surface dull and showing numerous fine veins; margins revolute on drying and, like the keel, minutely and more or less caducously scabrid, especially towards the tip. Peduncle more or less flattened, usually with 2 long basal internodes, bracts more or less sheath-like. Panicle usually overtopping leaves, broad and very open, the branchlets diverging at narrow angles and all but the lowest bracts very small. Pedicels 1.5–4 cm long, 3–4 in a group, filiform, not strongly curved. Flowers greenish white and inconspicuous; outer tepals about 3.2–4.5 × 1.5–1.7 mm, the veins, usually 5, occupying most of the width, tip cucullate; inner tepals wider, the veins 3, occasionally 5, close together and flanked by wide translucent white margins, tip emarginate. Staminal filaments about 3 mm long, the upper ½–⅓ swollen into a more or less globose, yellow, papillose struma; anther dehiscing by a slit. Ovary about 1.5 × 1 mm, sessile; ovules 2 per locule, attached towards top of cavity. Fruit about 6.5–17 × 6.5–10 mm, globose to oblong, grey-white and dull to strong violet-blue and glossy, the pericarp spongy. Seeds usually fewer than 6, more or less quadrate to elliptic in outline with hardened funicle, black, very glossy and smooth.
New Zealand plants vary greatly in size of leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds, in length of internodes, leafiness of peduncle, shape of struma and colour of fruit. Consistent features of New Zealand plants are: extensive fusion of leaf-sheath; minute hooked teeth on upper leaf-margin and keel (tending to rub off in old leaves); lax panicle and long, slender, gently curved pedicels.
[From: Flora of New Zealand vol. II (Moore & Edgar 1970), via the Flora of New Zealand Online factsheet.]
The leaves are uniformly green to dark green, with distinct dark bands 2–4 mm wide along the margins, and the leaf sheaths light to dark green with a reddish margin. The flowers nod, are 9–11 mm across, open early in the morning and collapse by late afternoon, with the tepals strongly recurved. The berries are 8–20 × 7–10 mm.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaves and how they sit. Tūrutu grows as several leafy fans together, its leaves in two rows, each folded around the next at the base; the leaf sheath is often reddish and narrows above into a strongly keeled part where the two halves are almost completely fused, the blade is tough, glossy above and dull underneath with many fine veins, and the leaves are green to dark green with dark bands 2–4 mm wide along the edges. Its side rhizomes sometimes carry young shoots 10 cm or more from the parent. Dwarf cabbage tree's leaves are crowded in a tuft, yellow-green to green (sometimes red-spotted), more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base and the margin slightly recurved. Leaf size does not separate them: tūrutu's are (15)–25–60–(100) cm long and 1–1.5 cm (to 1.8 cm) wide, dwarf cabbage tree's 30–60–(100) cm long and 1–2 cm wide. In flower and fruit they differ more: tūrutu's flowers are greenish white and nod on thread-like stalks 1.5–4 cm long, and its berries are 6.5–17 mm long, grey-white and dull to glossy violet-blue, with spongy flesh; dwarf cabbage tree's flowers are small and widely spaced on very short stalks, whitish or pink outside, in a very open panicle up to about 60 cm long, and its berries are round, 4–5 mm across, bluish or flecked with blue. Both grow in forest and gumland scrub in the northern North Island, and both can carry berries from March to May. Two other native Dianella species, D. latissima and D. haematica, look much like tūrutu. Dwarf cabbage tree's root was eaten (see its page).

summary.text:
Dianella nigra, tūrutu, also called New Zealand blueberry or inkberry, is an evergreen perennial herb in the family Asphodelaceae, endemic to New Zealand.
It grows on the Three Kings Islands and in the North and South Islands. Its fleshy berries are dispersed by fruit-eating animals. It is assessed Not Threatened nationally (2023), and Regionally Naturally Uncommon in Otago (2025). Two related species, D. haematica and D. latissima, were described from New Zealand in 2007.
In gardens it is grown from fresh seed or by dividing whole plants, and does best in semi-shade and moist soil, though it tolerates full sun and dry ground once established. One form sold in garden centres as D. intermedia is not that species, nor it seems D. nigra in the strict sense.

warnings: The berries are reported as poisonous. They were suspected of poisoning a 21-month-old child in the late 1800s and have been called very poisonous, though by 1977 no other report suggested the plant is poisonous.
No record of tūrutu as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
When it is not in flower it is often mistaken for dwarf cabbage tree, whose root was eaten. Check the leaves before digging (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text: Riverbeds, slips, forest margins, regenerating scrub. Extremely common nationwide.

harvestEthics.text: Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.

identification.text: Shrub or small tree with arching stems and glossy, strongly veined opposite leaves. Long drooping strings of small flowers followed by shiny purple-black fruit, each holding several small seeds. The fleshy purple 'petals' surround the seeds.

lookalikes.howToTell: Tutu is highly poisonous, and eating its fruit has been linked with deaths of children in New Zealand. Both have opposite leaves (tutu occasionally in whorls of three), so arrangement does not separate them. Elder's leaves are compound, of (3)–5–7 leaflets toothed except near the base, and its tiny white flowers are in large flat-topped clusters mostly 10–20 cm across, followed by berries 4–8.5 mm across, usually shining black. Tutu's leaves are simple, with flat or slightly wavy edges, and its flowers hang in slender drooping strings 10–30 cm long, followed by fruit of dark purple fleshy petals around the seeds. Season does not separate them: elder flowers November to January, tutu flowers October to March and fruits November to April. Elderflowers and cooked elderberries are eaten; raw elderberries can cause stomach upsets, and elder leaves and stems are poisonous. If you are unsure which you are looking at, harvest neither.
lookalikes.name: Elder (flowers & berries)

lookalikes.howToTell: Kareao (supplejack) shoots are eaten as 'bush asparagus', and young tutu shoots have been mistaken for them: in 2014 a tramper in the Waitākere Ranges boiled a tutu shoot he took for supplejack and had a seizure within hours, though he ate none of it. In spring tutu sends up long, unbranched shoots like oversized asparagus, which only later grow leafy side branches, so a shoot without leaves can still be tutu. Tutu is a shrub, not a climber; its branchlets are green at first and roughly four-angled, with leaves in opposite pairs, occasionally in threes, on very short stalks 1–3 mm long. Kareao's shoots are the soft tips of twining climbing stems that are almost black and finely hairy, with thickened joints 10–20 cm apart, each wrapped at first by a papery, almost black scale leaf 1–3 cm long. Both grow in and around forest, so where it grows does not separate them. Tutu is deadly poisonous. Only eat a shoot you can follow back to a twining, almost black kareao vine with papery scale leaves at its joints; if you cannot, do not eat it.

Wikipedia contributors. 'Coriaria arborea', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriaria_arborea Corroborates the toxin and the single exception: endemic to New Zealand, growing to 7 m, and every part except the juice of the fruits contains tutin, 'which is highly poisonous to humans and livestock'. Poisoning can cause brain paralysis, convulsions, exhaustion, memory loss or death. It also records how Māori used it despite that: the petals were juiced after the poisonous seeds were filtered out through toetoe (Austroderia sp.) flower heads, making waitutu, drunk in quantity and used as a laxative, and fermented into a wine that European settlers took to as well. Leaves and young shoots treated wounds, sprains, strains and broken bones; stems of larger plants were made into flutes. Further recorded names: tāweku, tūpākihi, tāwehu, pūhou, pukou, puho, tuturakau. **The filtering is not a method to copy** — it is the context for why the warning on this page is absolute.

The honey regulation, which the warning now states precisely. New Zealand Food Safety: passion vine hoppers feeding on tutu excrete honeydew containing tutin; the resulting honey is 'chemically similar to floral honey and cannot be distinguished by taste, sight or smell' from safe honey; tutin is harmless to bees and toxic to mammals. The main risk period is January to April, over most of the North Island and the top third of the South Island. The Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code sets the maximum for tutin in honey and honeycomb at 0.7 mg/kg, and for the purposes of the Standard 'tutu' means Coriaria arborea and Coriaria sarmentosa. One compliance route is honey taken off hives by 31 December — which is where this entry's earlier 'December to April' came from, and it had the window wrong. The rules followed hospitalisations, including a family poisoned by their own honey in 2008. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.mpi.govt.nz/food-business/honey-bee-products-processing-requirements/managing-tutin-contamination-in-honey

summary.text: The most dangerous plant a New Zealand forager can meet. Learn it, then never touch it.

warnings: Every part of this plant except the fleshy petal is lethally toxic.
Contains tutin. Tutu has killed people, and it has killed circus elephants. Seeds, leaves and shoots are all lethal.

Toxic honey: bees do not visit tutu, but passionvine hoppers feed on it and excrete honeydew that bees collect. This produces genuinely poisonous honey and is the reason NZ regulates honey harvesting in tutu regions between December and April.
Never make a wine, cordial or jam from any purple-black wild berry in NZ unless you have positively identified the plant.

identification.text:
Annual or short-lived perennial herb, glabrous or glabrate; stems prostrate or decumbent, rooting at the lower nodes, sparingly branched; roots rather slender. Leaves on main stems and branches similar; petioles short or leaves subsessile. Lamina to 15 × 4 cm, lanceolate, often with dark markings above, entire or minutely serrulate, glabrous or sometimes with appressed hairs on midrib above and below, copiously dotted with glands below; margins appressed-ciliate; base cuneate to rounded; apex acuminate. Ochreae about 1.5 cm long, green or pinkish, obliquely truncate, not flared towards apex, long-ciliate. Flowers 1–4 in whorls forming simple or few-branched, terminal or axillary racemes; racemes erect or slightly curved, 1.5–8 cm long, sometimes very slender and whorls distant, sometimes wider, cylindric, and densely flowered; peduncles slender, longer than upper leaves; pedicels enveloped or slightly exserted from bracts; bracts truncate, ciliate or glabrous. Perianth 2–2.5 mm long, deep pink to whitish, eglandular, accrescent; segments more or less elliptic, imbricate. Nut 1.7–2.5 mm long, biconvex to almost plano-convex, blackish, more or less glossy. Flowers November–April.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Polygonum salicifolium, via the Flora of New Zealand Online factsheet.]
Stems up to 60 cm long, prostrate and rooting in the basal part, then ascending. The ochrea mouth is fringed with hairs (1)–2–(5) mm long.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers: water pepper's are prominently dotted with glands; tūtunawai's have none. Flower colour does not separate them: water pepper's are usually pink or rose, rarely white, tūtunawai's deep pink to whitish. Water pepper's flower spikes are slender, up to about 7 cm long, and at least partly curve downwards, with the lower flowers often spaced apart; tūtunawai's are erect or slightly curved, 1.5–8 cm long. Look at the sheath where the leaf meets the stem: water pepper's is up to 2 cm long, reddish brown, cut straight across, with none to a few fringing bristles, and more or less flared at the upper nodes; tūtunawai's is about 1.5 cm long, green or pinkish, cut obliquely, not flared, and fringed with long hairs, (1)–2–(5) mm. Water pepper's stems stand erect or nearly so, up to about 75 cm tall and often reddish; tūtunawai's lie along the ground or curve up from it, rooting at the lower nodes. Tūtunawai's leaves, up to 15 × 4 cm, often have dark markings above; water pepper's are 1–12 × 0.3–2 cm, bright or deep green. Ripe nuts: water pepper's are 2.5–3 mm long, finely granular and dull to moderately shining; tūtunawai's 1.7–2.5 mm, blackish and more or less glossy. Do not go by taste: tūtunawai is described both as lacking water pepper's peppery flavour and as having pungent-tasting leaves. Both grow in swamps, at lake edges and along streams in the North and South Islands, so place does not separate them. Water pepper's leaves are eaten as a peppery herb (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Water pepper

lookalikes.howToTell: Flower colour and leaf markings do not separate them: both have flowers without glands, pink to whitish, and leaves often marked dark above. Look at how it grows: tūtunawai's stems lie along the ground or curve up from it and root at the lower nodes, and it grows in swamps and at the edges of still or slow-moving water; willow weed is a taprooted annual with stems erect to spreading, usually on drier ground in gardens, crops, waste places, roadside banks and riverbeds. Habit and place do not settle it: willow weed also grows beside streams and lakes, it can sprawl over bare ground, and overseas its stems often root at the lowest nodes. Look at the flower spikes: tūtunawai's are usually more than 3 cm long (1.5–8 cm), generally very slender with the flowers scarcely overlapping, and sometimes branched, though a northern form has shorter, stouter, densely flowered spikes; willow weed's are usually less than 4 cm long, dense and cylindric, and only rarely slender. Both have a leaf sheath fringed with long hairs, green or pinkish, so the sheath does not separate them. Ripe nuts overlap too: tūtunawai's 1.7–2.5 mm, blackish and more or less glossy; willow weed's 2–2.5 mm, brownish black and shining. Plants that are hard to place may be hybrids: tūtunawai may be a parent of the probable willow weed hybrids. Both grow in the North and South Islands. Willow weed's leaves are eaten raw or cooked (see its page).

summary.text:
Persicaria decipiens (synonyms Polygonum decipiens and Polygonum salicifolium), tūtunawai or swamp willow weed, is a glabrous annual or short-lived perennial herb in the dock family Polygonaceae, native to New Zealand and also indigenous to Australia and Norfolk Island.
It grows in the North and South Islands from near North Cape to Southland, and on the Chatham Islands. New Zealand has two main forms: the commonest and most widespread has very slender flower spikes with at least the lower flowers spaced apart; the other, restricted to northerly areas, has densely arranged flowers on a shorter, stouter spike. It is assessed Not Threatened nationally (2023), and Regionally Naturally Uncommon in the Wellington region (2025).

warnings: It is recorded as possibly poisonous.
Its leaves are recorded as food only in Africa, where they are cooked and eaten mainly as a famine food. With no New Zealand or Māori food use on record, it is not given as food here.
It grows in the same wet places as water pepper, whose leaves are eaten as a peppery herb. Check the flowers and leaf sheaths before picking (see the lookalikes).

edibleParts.text: Leaves, raw or cooked, eaten as a vegetable — they have a strong, hot, cress- or mustard-like and sometimes salty flavour. Leaves and stems, boiled or stewed together with other greens. The roots can be cooked, or ground and mixed with vinegar as a horseradish-like relish; the root use rests on a single source, and another source records only the leaves as used.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Waste land, roadsides, cultivated land, coastal shingly land.
In New Zealand it is more typically found in crops and gardens, wherever there is bare soil for seedlings to establish; on dairy farms it turns up mainly in young pastures and in open parts of paddocks such as around water troughs and gateways, and it is seldom found in dense, older pastures (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated). In lawns it takes hold in bare patches, compacted soil and areas damaged by drought or foot traffic (New Zealand Lawn Addicts, restated).
Waste places, roadsides, cultivated fields, frequently mown lawns etc. Roadsides, waste areas, lawns, pastures, fields, gardens, disturbed areas; at elevations up to 1,000 metres.

identification.text:
Foetid annual or biennial with short-lived rosette and procumbent to ascending glabrous or sparsely hairy stems to 40 cm long. Leaves 1–2-pinnatifid, narrow-oblong to ovate, glabrous except for sparse spreading hairs on petioles of some basal leaves; rosette leaves petiolate, 6-10 × 1.5-2 cm; stem leaves smaller, usually pinnatifid, rarely 2-pinnatifid, 1-4 × 0.5-1.5 cm. Racemes (1)-3-5 cm; rachis with sparse spreading hairs; pedicels spreading, 2.5-4 mm long. Sepals about 0.5 mm long. Petals white, shorter than the sepals, or absent. Stamens usually 2, rarely 4. Silicle broader than long, emarginate, about 1.5 × 2-2.5 mm; valves finely warty or ridged, separating at maturity; stigma minute, almost sessile in apical notch of silicle. Seed comma-shaped, light brown, about 1 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Flora of New Zealand key to the two naturalised species: Silicles about 1.5 mm long, emarginate; pedicel longer than the silicle — twin cress (didymus). Silicles more than 2 mm long, apiculate; pedicel shorter than the silicle — wart cress (squamatus).
It begins as a flat rosette with its growing point at ground level; each leaf is made of several leaflets, and each leaflet has several lobes, usually more on one side than the other, so the leaflets are lopsided — unusual among weeds. As it matures it sends out stems along the ground that can form extensive mats, which from a distance look like wireweed. The flowers are tiny; the characteristic double pods confirm the identification, and the crushed foliage has a distinctive smell. The closely related wart cress (Lepidium squamatum) has pods that look like warts rather than twin pods (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Both begin as small rosettes on bare cultivated soil. Shepherd's purse sends up an erect flowering stem, (2–)15–30(–80) cm tall, and its leaves are not divided into separate lopsided leaflets; twin cress sends out stems that lie along the ground and can form mats, and smells foetid when crushed. The pods differ clearly: shepherd's purse has flat heart-shaped pods 5–10 mm long, twin cress tiny paired warty pods only about 1.5 mm long. Petals do not separate them, as both can have tiny white petals or none. Shepherd's purse leaves are eaten raw or cooked; avoid it in medicinal amounts when pregnant — see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Shepherd's purse

lookalikes.howToTell: Both form flat rosettes of narrow, deeply cut leaves on open ground, including near the sea, and twin cress can be mistaken for buck's-horn plantain. Buck's-horn plantain leaves all grow from the base, are linear with 1–4 pairs of narrow lobes or teeth, are hairy at least on the margins and have a silky tuft of hairs at the base; it flowers in dense cylindrical spikes on leafless stalks 3–45 cm long, with protruding stamens. Twin cress is hairless or nearly so, smells foetid when crushed, sends out leafy stems along the ground, and bears tiny white (or petal-less) flowers in short clusters followed by paired pods about 1.5 mm long. Buck's-horn plantain young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Buck's-horn plantain

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are low weeds of roadsides, waste places and cultivated land with finely divided leaves, and twin cress can be mistaken for pineappleweed. Crush a leaf: pineappleweed smells of pineapple, twin cress smells foetid. Pineappleweed stems are erect or ascending, 5–20(–40) cm tall, its leaves are 2–3 times divided into narrow-linear segments, and it bears rayless, cone-shaped, dull yellow to greenish-yellow flower heads 4–10 mm across. Twin cress stems usually lie along the ground, its leaves are 1–2 times divided, and it has tiny white or petal-less flowers followed by paired pods about 1.5 mm long. Leaf division alone does not separate them, since both can have twice-divided leaves. Pineappleweed flower heads and leaves are eaten raw or cooked; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Pineappleweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Yarrow and twin cress can both form low mats of divided leaves in pasture, lawns and waste places. Yarrow is strongly scented (aromatic rather than foetid) and hairy, its leaves are feathery — twice divided with the segments divided again, in 18–30(–37) pairs of leaflets, not all in one plane — and it spreads by rhizomes, sending up erect flowering stems to about 80 cm with flat-topped clusters of small white (sometimes pink) daisy-like heads. Twin cress is hairless or nearly so, smells foetid, has lopsided leaflets, stems lying along the ground, tiny white or petal-less flowers and paired pods about 1.5 mm long. Yarrow young leaves are eaten in small amounts but are bitter, and yarrow is not for use in pregnancy or by people allergic to the daisy family; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Yarrow

lookalikes.howToTell: Some farmers wrongly call twin cress 'land cress', but the plants are easy to tell apart. Land cress is an erect biennial (20–)40–60(–90) cm tall, with often glossy, deeply lyre-shaped rosette leaves that have an end lobe and (4–)5–8 or more pairs of side lobes, yellow petals 6–8 mm long, and long thin pods (30–)40–70 mm long. Twin cress lies along the ground, smells foetid when crushed, has tiny white petals shorter than the sepals (or none) and tiny paired pods about 1.5 mm long. Land cress young leaves are eaten raw or cooked for their hot, watercress-like flavour; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Land cress

lookalikes.howToTell: Both start as flat rosettes whose leaves, each made of a row of leaflets, radiate from a growing point at ground level, later send stems along the ground, and come up on bare soil on roadsides, in waste places and on cultivated ground. Crush a leaf: twin cress smells foetid; musky storksbill usually smells of musk, though not always strongly. Twin cress is hairless or nearly so; musky storksbill is densely covered in glandular hairs and feels sticky. Twin cress's leaflets are lopsided, with more lobes on one side than the other; musky storksbill's leaflets are stalkless, with more or less ovate, toothed lobes. In flower they differ clearly: twin cress has tiny white petals shorter than its 0.5 mm sepals, or none, and paired pods about 1.5 mm long; musky storksbill has clusters of about 12 pink or mauve-pink flowers, petals 4.5–8 mm long, followed by fruits with a beak 3–3.5 cm long. Musky storksbill's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked, but its record as food is thin; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Musky storksbill

preparation.text: Eat the leaves raw as a nibble or in salads, or cook them as a pot herb. The crushed plant smells foetid and opinions on its taste are mixed: many people boil the leaves and stems in several changes of water, while others eat it raw and never cook it. It can be used to stuff other foods such as fish. If grinding the root with vinegar as a relish, taste it before adding any salt.

summary.text:
Twin cress, Lepidium didymum, is a foetid annual or biennial of the mustard family (Brassicaceae).
Flora of New Zealand gives its region of origin as Europe and its first wild record in New Zealand as 1855; it is recorded from the North, South and Stewart Islands and the Kermadec, Chatham, Auckland and Campbell Islands. In New Zealand it has also been called Senebiera didyma and Coronopus didymus. Biota of New Zealand also lists Senebiera pinnatifida DC. as a former name and 'lesser swinecress' as an English name. The NZ Plant Conservation Network notes that the genus name Lepidium means scale-shaped, after the pods.
In New Zealand it can germinate at any time of year, but it establishes mainly in spring and autumn, starting as a rosette before it scrambles. In lawns its rosettes crowd out new grass seedlings and survive low mowing, and it looks most weedy over winter and early spring, when lawn grasses slow down.
Te Papa holds 32 specimens, the most recent collected by Leon Perrie on 29/12/2025 (SP129844). Manaaki Whenua's herbarium has about 89 databased New Zealand records: North Auckland 21, Wellington 21, Canterbury 17, Nelson 9, South Auckland 5, Southland 5, Gisborne 4, and two or fewer each from Hawke's Bay, Taranaki, Westland and Otago.
Although small and inconspicuous, it can cause major problems on dairy farms: milk from lactating cows that eat it develops a distinctive taint that processing companies do not want, and a company that detects it may refuse further milk from that farm until the problem is managed. Some farmers incorrectly call it land cress (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated).
The plant is harvested from the wild for local use as a food and a medicine. The dried plant material is sold for medicinal purposes in S. America. The plant also has potential for use in soil remediation projects.

warnings: Twin cress takes up lead from contaminated soil and stores it in its roots and, to a lesser extent, its leaves, and it often grows in unsavoury places — gather it only from clean ground.
In young pastures it is controlled with herbicides such as MCPB, MCPA and flumetsulam, and in lawns with MCPA, dicamba, picloram or triclopyr. Pick it only where you know none has been used.
The seeds contain erucic acid and glucosinolates; the recorded food parts are the leaves, stems and roots, not the seeds.
Its food use is thinly documented — a few foraging and plant-database sources and a single Spanish folk record — and none gives a safe quantity.
Confirm the identity by the tiny paired (twin) seed pods before eating: the young rosette resembles other rosette weeds such as musky storksbill, and from a distance its mats look like wireweed.

identification.text: A large, stout milkcap. Cap 7–23 cm across, convex when young and sunken in the centre at maturity, sticky in wet weather and otherwise dry, without zones; finely felted when young, later almost smooth or with a few fine flattened scales. Its colour is a drab olive-brown to dark brownish black with olive-brown tints, paler towards the edge, which is ochre, tightly rolled under and coarsely woolly when young. Gills joined to the stem or running a little down it, crowded, cream with ochre tints when young, later cream with dull brownish edges and marked with dull brown spots and stains. Milk plentiful, sticky and creamy white; it does not change colour in the air and dries a dull creamy white. Stem 3–7 cm long and 2–3.5 cm thick, even and stout, solid, almost smooth, about the cap's colour or slightly paler, often greenish at the top. Flesh white, thick and firm, browning slightly after long exposure to air. Little smell. The gills taste extremely acrid, the flesh slightly acrid. Spore print ochre-buff. A drop of potassium hydroxide or ammonia turns the cap surface deep purple.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Ugly milkcap's milk is white or creamy white, and old milk leaves its dirty-white gills stained olive-brown. Its cap is olive brown or yellow-green, often sticky or slimy in the middle, darkening to blackish with age. In New Zealand and Australia it grows with birch; saffron milk cap only with pine.

The July–November the description gives is North American, not this one. Checked 06/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/taxa/382886

Manaaki Whenua Landcare Research, Virtual Mycota, 'Lactarius turpis' — the New Zealand record, with the description attributed to McNabb, R.F.R. (1971), 'The Russulaceae of New Zealand. 1. Lactarius', New Zealand Journal of Botany 9(1): 46–66. McNabb's text is in copyright, so the facts below are restated and nothing is quoted. Checked 06/10/2026. https://virtualmycota.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/vM_Species_Details.aspx?pk=5191 Biostatus 'Present in region - Exotic', and the entry's only New Zealand habitat statement: commonly associated with Betula pendula throughout the South Island. On New Zealand material: cap 7–23 cm, drab olive brown or dark brownish black with olive tints, paling towards an ochraceous, strongly inrolled and coarsely woolly margin; gills pale cream with dull brown edges at maturity, spotted and stained dull brown; latex copious, viscid, creamy white, unchanging; stem 3–7 cm by 2–3.5 cm, stout, often with greenish tints at the apex; spore print ochraceous buff; gills extremely acrid and flesh slightly acrid. KOH and ammonia turn the cap rapidly deep purple, which McNabb gives as characteristic. On edibility he reports it considered poisonous by European mycologists, and Pilát (1961) that it is poisonous raw or poorly cooked and edible though not recommended once the latex is soaked out.

First Nature, 'Lactarius turpis' (ugly milkcap) — © First Nature / Pat O'Reilly, all rights reserved, so facts only and nothing quoted beyond the short phrases marked. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/lactarius-turpis.php Cap dark olive brown with a paler margin, slimy when wet, 7–18 cm, convex then slightly depressed; gills cream to pale buff turning sepia-tinged when bruised, decurrent, narrow and crowded, releasing abundant white latex that dries olivaceous; stem 4–7 cm by 1–2.5 cm, no ring; spores 6.5–7.5 × 5.5–6 µm; spore print creamy white; no significant odour; taste hot and acrid. Mycorrhizal with birch in wet woodland on acid soils. Considered poisonous for its potential carcinogenic properties; the northern European practice of boiling it and using it as a seasoning is now discouraged. Lactarius blennius is the lookalike — lighter, smaller, and without the sepia-tinged gill patches.

The spore print, and why the disagreement is worth keeping. Wikipedia gives cream, First Nature creamy white, and McNabb — on New Zealand material — ochraceous buff. The spread is the point: saffron milk cap's page says a spore print cannot separate this genus because the prints run white to ochre across it, and this species runs the width of that range on its own. Checked 06/10/2026.

Which name is correct, because both are in use. McNabb sets out the dispute: Bulliard's 1791 Agaricus necator was redescribed by Persoon (1801) and revalidated by Fries (1821) against Persoon's rather than Bulliard's fungus, so most recent workers reject Bulliard's name for A. turpis Weinm., while Singer (1962) read the misinterpretation the other way and cited the species as Lactarius necator. This entry's summary already lists both, plus L. plumbeus. Checked 06/10/2026.

summary.text: A large, drab olive-brown to blackish introduced milkcap of birch, with an extremely acrid taste. It is widely distributed in New Zealand and also found in south-eastern Australia. The same fungus has also been called Lactarius plumbeus and L. necator.

warnings: Contains the mutagenic compound necatorin. Boiling reduces it but does not eliminate it, so this is not a mushroom to eat however it is cooked — despite its use, after boiling, as a spice in northern and eastern Europe and Siberia, and for pickling in Russia.

The absence of zoning is an inference, not a statement on the page: McNabb describes no zoning for this species, and his note on Lactarius tawai calls that one 'the only species found in New Zealand with a zonate pileus' — which covers the native species he described. The wording here says no zoning is recorded rather than that there is none. Checked 08/10/2026.
identification.text: A small milk cap. Cap 1–3.5 cm across, convex when young, flattening or sinking in the centre with age, dry except in wet weather and finely powdered to the lens. Its colour is a muted salmon, sometimes closer to a grey-tinged orange or a washed-out orange-brown, and no concentric zoning is recorded on it. Gills pallid, crowded, moderately thick, up to 3 mm deep, attached to slightly or occasionally fully running down the stem. Stem 1–3 cm long and 4–7 mm thick, more or less even, coloured like the cap, solid at first and becoming chambered or hollow with age. Flesh pallid greyish orange and unchanging. The milk is white and does not change colour in the air. Gills and flesh both taste mild, and there is no distinctive smell. Found under beech.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. This one's milk is white and does not change, drying cream. Its cap is 1-3.5 cm across. Saffron milk cap's is 4-12 cm in the Australasian description and from 3 cm overseas, so a small saffron cap can come close. This one is dull salmon, greyish orange or pale orange-brown, and unzoned; saffron milk cap is pale orange to salmon and its zoning can be faint, so judge the milk. It grows under beech; saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine.

edibleParts.text: Young leaves, raw or cooked, once the spines are cut off; the peeled leaf stalks and midribs of tender leaves, raw or cooked. Young stems, peeled, raw or cooked. Flower buds before the flowers open, cooked like small globe artichokes; the receptacle (the fleshy base of the flower head) is the part eaten. Roots, raw or cooked. Seeds, roasted as a coffee substitute, or pressed for oil; ground, they go into seasoning salts.
