habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Roadsides, pastures, gardens, waste land.
In New Zealand it grows on alluvial flats, in stockyards and sheep camps and on other ground high in nitrogen, and invades pasture where summers are dry and winters moist and mild (Bay of Plenty Regional Council, restated).
Silybum marianum establishes itself in sunny, warm ruderal meadows in regularly disturbed places such as rubble deposits, at the foot of south-exposed walls or villages and on urban fallow land or on cattle pastures. However, it does not prefer dry, stony soils.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Annual or biennial. Stems branched above, ridged, with sparse mealy hairs at least above, 0.5–2 m tall, not winged. Leaves elliptic to lanceolate, lyrate-pinnatifid to pinnate, sinuate, coarsely dentate, green with conspicuous white markings along veins, (10)–20–60 × (5)–10–30 cm, with sparse short mealy hairs on lamina, and sparse long tangled multicellular hairs on midrib; base amplexicaul, auriculate, with very spinous margins; prickles marginal, yellowish, spreading, 5–12 mm long. Capitula ovoid, erect, 4–6 × 5–7 cm, solitary, terminal and pedunculate, and also sessile in axils of uppermost leaves; peduncles with appressed cobwebby tomentum. Involucral bracts sparsely covered with short mealy hairs; margins with sparse cobwebby hairs. Outer bracts leaflike, obovate with spinous apex and margins. Middle bracts oblong; appendage ovate, subulate, with spinous margins and a long spreading to recurved apical spine. Inner bracts lanceolate; appendage becoming linear-lanceolate, entire. Corolla reddish purple, 20–28 mm long; lobes unequal, 4–6 mm long. Anther filaments joined at margins into a tube which encloses the basal appendages of the anthers. Style exserted 1–2 mm beyond corolla lobes. Achenes brown or black-streaked, obovoid, weakly transversely flattened, smooth, about 6 × 3 mm; outer pappus bristles scabrid, about 15 mm long; inner hairs very fine. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

preparation.text: Gather leaves and stems before the plant flowers. Cut off the very sharp leaf spines first, which is fiddly. To peel a tender leaf, hold the base of its stalk in one hand and pull the other hand quickly and firmly from there to the tip; the peeled stalk and midrib can be eaten raw or cooked like cardoons. Young leaves are thick and mild and suit mixed salads, but can turn bitter in hot, dry weather; cooked, they stand in for spinach. Leaves and stems can be boiled with salt or added to stews. Peel the stems, and soak them to reduce their bitterness, then use them like asparagus or rhubarb or add them to salads. Use the buds before the flowers open: the flavour is mild, but they are small and more fiddly than globe artichokes. Boiled, the roots have a mild flavour and a somewhat mucilaginous texture.

recipes.method: Serves 2. Ingredients: 50 g milk thistle leaves, 1 egg (about 52 g in the shell), a pinch of fine salt, 60 g plain flour, 60 ml lightly sparkling water, peanut oil for frying. Steps: pick fairly large leaves just before the plant sends up its flower stalk, wearing thick gloves, and snip the spines off all around the edges with scissors. Wash the leaves and pat them dry on a cotton cloth. Beat the egg with the salt and flour, then add the water a little at a time until the batter is creamy. Cut the leaves into palm-sized pieces, dip them in the batter and fry in hot oil for a few minutes until cooked. Drain on kitchen paper and eat hot.
recipes.title: Milk thistle leaves in batter

recipes.method: Makes about 48 servings of a quarter teaspoon. Ingredients: 15 ml (1 tbsp) whole milk thistle seeds, 15 ml dulse flakes, 15 ml dried nettle leaves, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) whole celery seed, 5 ml garlic powder, 5 ml onion powder, 7.5 ml finely chopped calendula petals (optional), 75 ml (5 tbsp) unrefined sea salt. Steps: grind the milk thistle seeds, dulse, nettle, celery seed and calendula in a spice or coffee grinder as fine as you like. Tip into a clean jar, stir in the garlic and onion powder, then add the salt and mix again. Sprinkle on roast meat and potatoes, or add to soups.
recipes.title: Milk thistle seasoning salt

recipes.method: Ingredients: 225 g sesame seeds, 30 g milk thistle seeds, 20 g dulse flakes (or kelp), 2 g calendula flowers, 4 g nettle leaf, 20 g sea salt. Steps: toast the sesame seeds gently over a low to medium heat until fragrant. Grind everything together in a spice grinder, food processor or mortar and pestle. Bottle it and sprinkle a teaspoon at a time on food, in place of salt.
recipes.title: Milk thistle gomasio

recipes.method: Ingredients: 750 ml (3 cups) coarse sea salt, 30 ml (6 tsp) milk thistle seed powder, 30 ml (6 tsp) ground ginger, 15 ml (3 tsp) ground turmeric. Steps: for the powder, grind milk thistle seeds very fine in a coffee grinder or high-speed blender and sift out any large pieces through a fine sieve. Mix the salt, milk thistle powder, ginger and turmeric well in a large bowl. Keep in a glass jar in a cool, dry place for up to 6 months. Use in salad dressings and marinades, or as a finishing salt (fine salt can replace the coarse).
recipes.title: Milk thistle, ginger and turmeric salt

summary.text:
Silybum marianum is a species of thistle.
It comes from the Mediterranean and south-west Europe and was first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1869 (Flora of New Zealand).
Milk thistle has been potentially observed to modify fire regimes in its invasive range. Its invasion into new habitats may also be encouraged by fire.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Northland, Auckland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty, East Cape, Volcanic Plateau, Wellington; S.: Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago, Southland; Chatham Islands. S. marianum has also been referred to in New Zealand as Carduus marianus.
A biennial or annual, it dies off after setting seed in summer. Most seed blows no more than about 10 m from the plant, but seed is also spread in hay, by water, in mud, in produce and grain, and on machinery and animals (NZPCN, restated).
It is a pest plant under regional pest management plans: eradication in Waikato; progressive containment in Bay of Plenty (where it is not common), Manawatū-Whanganui and Tasman-Nelson; sustained control in Auckland, Hawke's Bay (with a boundary rule) and Taranaki; both progressive containment and sustained control in Gisborne; and an organism of interest in Canterbury. It is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds (DOC weeds database and regional council pages, restated).

warnings: Variegated thistle is recorded as poisonous. Its leaves can hold large amounts of nitrate, especially when heavy rain follows a long drought, after heavy fertiliser or after the plant has been sprayed with herbicide; in the gut nitrate is turned to nitrite, which stops the blood carrying oxygen. It grows especially on ground high in nitrogen, such as stockyards and sheep camps. Its leaves have poisoned cattle and sheep, and cattle that gorge on wilted plants (cut or sprayed) can die within 2 hours.

It may cause allergic reactions, particularly in people allergic to related plants such as ragweed, chrysanthemum, marigold and daisy, and in people allergic to artichokes. Medicinal preparations of the seed are not to be used by anyone hypersensitive to the daisy family; their reported side effects include dry mouth, nausea, upset stomach, diarrhoea, headache and allergic reactions, from skin rash and hives to asthma and anaphylaxis.
Safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and medicinal seed preparations are not recommended then.
The leaf margins carry stiff yellowish spines 5–12 mm long, and the flower-head bracts end in long spines.

identification.text:
It grows in tufts and clusters on wood, many caps rising from one base; now and then singly or in twos and threes. The cap is 1–8 cm across, rounded at first, then almost flat, sometimes with a slight bump in the centre. It is smooth and sticky to slimy, bright yellow to orange-brown with a darker, tawny centre, or yellowish brown all over. The flesh is thick at the centre and very thin at the edge, tinged yellow.
The gills are attached to the stem but notched just before it, broad, and white to pale yellow. The stem is 5–10 cm long and 6–8 mm thick, tough and rubbery, springing back when squeezed. It is yellowish at the top, orange-brown below and darker towards the base, which narrows into the wood, and it is finely velvety. It has no ring. The smell is mild and fresh, sometimes slightly fruity. The spore print is white.
The sticky yellow-orange cap with the dark velvety stem is the classic combination. On pine the caps are often dwarfed, though still in dense clusters.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small orange-brown mushrooms on rotting wood, so place and cap colour do not separate them. Wood nipple fungus belongs to the group of the deadly Galerina marginata and probably carries the same toxins. Look at the stem: velvet shank's is velvety and dark brown towards the base, with no ring. The Galerina's is slender, 2–4 mm thick, pale tan to rusty orange, with a thin ring high up that can soon fall away. Look at the gills: white to pale yellow in velvet shank, rusty orange to cinnamon in the Galerina. Velvet shank's cap is sticky, 1–8 cm across, and it grows in dense tufts from one base. The Galerina's cap is 1–2.5 cm across, often with a pointed bump in the centre, and it grows singly or in loose groups, rarely in tight clumps. A spore print settles it: white for velvet shank, cinnamon-brown for the Galerina.

preparation.text:
Never eat it raw: always cook it thoroughly. Cut off the dark lower half of the stems. Wipe the sticky caps with a damp cloth, and rinse them quickly only if they are dirty; peeling the skin off the cap before cooking is recommended. After frost, use only firm mushrooms, and throw away any that are soft, slimy or discoloured.
The sticky coating melts away in cooking and thickens broths. Velvet shanks keep a slight crunch after cooking and turn slippery in broth. They suit soups, noodle soups, ramen and hot pots, stir-fries with garlic, soy sauce and sesame, sauces, and risotto.
They dry well. Dried caps can be ground into a seasoning, and the tough stems can be dried and powdered.

recipes.method: Written for wild velvet shank. Serves 2. 200 g velvet shanks; 40 g cornflour; 40 g plain flour; 100 ml ice-cold water; 1 tsp salt; ½ tsp smoked paprika; vegetable oil for frying. Clean the mushrooms, cut off and discard the dark lower half of the stems and keep the caps and tender upper stems. Rinse briefly only if very dirty, then pat completely dry: dry mushrooms give a crisp shell. Whisk the cornflour, flour, salt and paprika, then whisk in the water a little at a time to a smooth, thin batter. Heat about 2.5 cm of oil in a deep frying pan or pot to 170 °C. Dip the mushrooms in the batter, let the excess drip off, and fry for 2–3 minutes a side until golden and crisp. Drain on a rack or paper towels and serve at once, with garlic aioli, spicy mayonnaise or sea salt, or on top of a winter soup.
recipes.title: Crispy fried velvet shank

recipes.method: Written for wild velvet shank. Serves 3. 200 g velvet shanks; 250 g very thinly sliced beef (ribeye, sirloin or flank); 2 tbsp soy sauce; 2 tbsp mirin; 1 tbsp sake or dry sherry; 1 tbsp sugar; 1 tbsp vegetable oil; sesame seeds. Clean the mushrooms and cut away the dark lower stems; halve or quarter large caps. Lay a slice of beef flat, put a few mushroom pieces at one end with the caps poking out, and roll it up tightly. Mix the soy sauce, mirin, sake and sugar until the sugar dissolves. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat and brown the rolls, seam side down first, turning them for 2–3 minutes. Pour in the sauce, lower the heat and let it bubble and thicken, rolling the bundles until glossy. Serve with the pan sauce, sesame seeds, steamed rice and pickled vegetables.
recipes.title: Velvet shank beef rolls

recipes.method: Written for wild velvet shank. Serves 4. 150 g velvet shanks; 800 ml dashi; 3 tbsp white or mixed miso; 150 g silken tofu; 1 tbsp dried wakame; 2 spring onions. Soak the wakame in cold water for 5 minutes and drain. Clean the mushrooms, discarding the tough lower stems; leave small caps whole and halve large ones. Cube the tofu and slice the spring onions. Bring the dashi to a gentle simmer, add the mushrooms and cook 3–4 minutes until tender and slippery. Add the tofu and wakame, simmer 1 minute, then turn off the heat. Dissolve the miso in a ladle of the hot broth and stir it in; do not boil the soup once the miso is in. Serve topped with the spring onions.
recipes.title: Velvet shank miso soup

recipes.method: Written for wild velvet shank. Serves 2–3. 150 g velvet shanks; 2 large eggs; 30 g carrot; 2 spring onions; ½ tsp salt; a pinch of black pepper; 2 tbsp vegetable oil. Clean the mushrooms, remove the tough lower stems, and chop the caps and upper stems into 1 cm pieces. Dice the carrot very small and slice the spring onions thinly. Beat the eggs, stir in the vegetables and mushrooms, and season. Heat the oil in a large non-stick frying pan over medium-low heat, spoon in small rounds 5–7 cm across and press them flat. Cook 2–3 minutes until golden, turn and cook 2 minutes more. Drain on paper towels and serve warm with a dipping sauce of 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp rice vinegar, a pinch of sugar and a few drops of sesame oil.
recipes.title: Velvet shank pancakes (jeon)

recipes.method: Written for wild velvet shank. Serves 2. 200 g velvet shanks; 20 g butter; 1 tbsp soy sauce; 1 garlic clove; 1 tbsp sake or white wine (optional); black pepper; 1 spring onion. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Clean the mushrooms, trimming off the tough velvety stem bases, and pile them in the centre of a 30 cm square of heavy foil (or a double layer). Scatter over the finely chopped garlic, dot with the butter, drizzle with the soy sauce and sake, and add pepper. Fold the edges together several times to seal the parcel tightly. Bake on a tray for 15 minutes, or cook on a barbecue over medium heat for 12–15 minutes. Open carefully (hot steam) and serve with the buttery juices and sliced spring onion.
recipes.title: Foil-baked velvet shank

recipes.method: Written for wild velvet shank. Serves 2. 450 g velvet shanks, cleaned and sliced; 2 large onions, sliced; 2 garlic cloves, crushed; 2 tbsp olive oil; salt and pepper; 1 cup (250 ml) quinoa; 500 ml water or chicken or vegetable stock; 125 ml (½ cup) chopped cherry tomatoes; 60 ml (¼ cup) chopped parsley; 2 tbsp balsamic vinegar; 1 tsp honey; 1 tbsp lemon juice. Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat and cook the onions about 10 minutes until soft and caramelised. Add the garlic for a minute, then the mushrooms; season and cook until tender, 5–7 minutes. Meanwhile rinse the quinoa, bring it to the boil in the water or stock, cover and cook on low about 20 minutes until tender and the liquid is absorbed. Mix the quinoa with the tomatoes, parsley, vinegar, honey and lemon juice and season. Serve the mushrooms and onions over the salad.
recipes.title: Velvet shank with caramelised onions and quinoa salad

recipes.method: Written for a mix of wild mushrooms; the author lists velvet shank (enokitake) among those that suit it. Serves 4. 1.5 litres mushroom or chicken stock; 170 g carrot in 2.5 cm matchsticks; 115 g spring onions in 2.5 cm pieces; one 5 mm slice of fresh ginger; 225 g fresh wild mushrooms in bite-sized pieces; 125 ml soy sauce, or to taste; a tiny pinch of chilli flakes; 115 g shredded spinach or other tender greens; salt. To serve: 570 g cooked soba noodles (about 140 g a person); toasted sesame oil; chopped coriander. Cook the soba ahead in lightly salted water, rinse in cool water and toss in a little sesame oil. Simmer the stock, carrot, spring onions, ginger, mushrooms, soy sauce and chilli in a 4-litre pot for 20 minutes, until the vegetables are tender. Add the greens and cook a minute more, then taste and add salt if needed. Warm the noodles in bowls, ladle the very hot soup over, and finish with sesame oil and coriander.
recipes.title: Wild mushroom soup with soba noodles

summary.text:
Flammulina velutipes, the velvet shank, also called velvet foot or winter mushroom, is a gilled mushroom (family Physalacriaceae) that grows in clusters on wood.
Flammulina means 'little flame', for its colour. It is a winter mushroom: one of the few that fruit in really cold weather, often through frost.
In New Zealand it is naturalised and found over much of the country, less often in warm areas such as Northland; there are 1,547 research-grade iNaturalist records. It was recorded at Dannevirke in 1899. Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic: DNA sequences from New Zealand urban and natural habitats point to an old introduction from Europe that has naturalised in native broadleaf–podocarp forest. Horak (1971) had hesitated to call it introduced and treated the New Zealand form as a distinct variety.
The white, long-stemmed enoki sold in shops is a different species, Flammulina filiformis, from Asia. The two were long treated as one, until DNA showed they are distinct. F. filiformis is not found wild in New Zealand. Grown in the dark with high carbon dioxide, it has long pale stems and tiny caps.
New Zealand also has an endemic Flammulina, F. stratosa, ranked Data Deficient; it has no iNaturalist records here.

warnings: Never eat velvet shank raw; always cook it thoroughly.

Rustgills (Gymnopilus) also grow in orange clusters on stumps and logs, and have brown spore prints. The spectacular rustgill (G. junonius), common in New Zealand, is inedible and contains neurotoxins. It is bright yellow-orange, ageing orange-brown or reddish brown, and its spore print is rusty brown. The common rustgill (G. penetrans), also recorded here, has crowded thin gills that get rusty spots as they age, a cap that is usually dry, and rusty spores. Velvet shank has a sticky cap, a dark velvety stem with no ring, white to pale yellow gills and a white spore print: check the print before eating any.

identification.text: Greyish, velvety-hairy (tomentose), unarmed perennial herb or subshrub to about 1.5 m tall; mature stems with 2 ridges. Leaf stalks to 3 cm long. Leaf blade (1.5–)2.5–11 × (0.5–)1–6 cm, ovate or lance-ovate, hairy above and below, entire or nearly so; base narrowing gradually; apex pointed to long-pointed. Flower clusters umbrella-like; flower stalks very variable in length, becoming strongly turned downward in fruit. Calyx 2–3 mm long, its lobes very small. Corolla 8–13 mm across, white; lobes lance-shaped or narrowly triangular, densely hairy outside, soon bending back. Anthers 1.5–3 mm long. Berry 5–7 mm across, round, dull purplish black or purple; stone cells none. Seeds 1–1.5 mm long, roughly round.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaves and shoots: velvety nightshade is greyish and velvety-hairy (a dense soft felt of hairs) above and below, so the leaves feel like velvet; black nightshade's hairs are usually scattered, short and simple, and the plant is sometimes nearly hairless. Look at the berries: velvety nightshade's are 5–7 mm across and dull purplish black or purple, black nightshade's are 7–10 mm across and usually rather dull black, sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow, so size and colour overlap and neither settles it alone. Velvety nightshade is a perennial herb or subshrub recorded to about 1.5 m, with mature stems that have 2 ridges; black nightshade is an annual or short-lived perennial herb recorded to about 75 cm. Flowers, leaf size and place do not separate them: both have white flowers 8–13 mm (velvety) or 10–13 mm (black) across, leaf blades of overlapping size (2.5–11 cm against 2–12 cm long), and both grow in gardens and orchards. Black nightshade's green berries and leaves are poisonous (see its page); velvety nightshade is not food here either.

summary.text:
An introduced grey, velvety-hairy nightshade, a close relative of black nightshade, with dull purplish-black berries and no recorded food use.
Velvety nightshade (Solanum chenopodioides, Solanaceae) comes from south-eastern South America and was naturalised in New Zealand by 1958. The Flora of New Zealand says it was apparently first collected at Greymouth in 1941 and had greatly increased in many parts of the country, recording it in the North Island from the Aupouri Peninsula and Parengarenga to Auckland, the Rangitikei River, Manawatu and the Wellington area, and in the South Island particularly on the west side, where it was common in many places. Manaaki Whenua's Biota register also lists New Zealand specimens from the Canterbury, Otago and Marlborough land districts, east of that range. The Department of Conservation's weeds database does not classify it as a weed. The Flora of New Zealand notes that the name 'deadly nightshade', which belongs to a different and far more toxic plant, is often wrongly given to the black nightshade group, which includes this species.

warnings: Plants in the genus Solanum all contain poisonous compounds to some extent, particularly in the green parts, and there is no New Zealand record of this species' berries or leaves being safe to eat.

The true deadly nightshade (Atropa bella-donna) is a different plant and one of the most dangerous in New Zealand; its name is often wrongly given to the black nightshade group, which includes this species.

habitat.text:
Low intertidal to subtidal, on almost any hard surface: rock reefs and rock pools, wharf piles, seawalls, moorings, ropes, buoys and boat hulls.
In New Zealand it grows from about mid-low-water-neap level down to 15 m, occasionally 18 m. It is commonest in sheltered harbours and ports, but it also grows on wave-exposed coasts, including in native kelp forests, and it also grows attached to native seaweeds such as Carpophyllum flexuosum and Cystophora scalaris.

harvestEthics.text:
Wakame is an unwanted organism under the Biosecurity Act 1993 and on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. Unless MPI permits it, it is an offence to knowingly spread or release it, to sell it or offer it for sale, or to propagate or breed it. Commercial harvest needs MPI permission, and plants growing on natural surfaces such as reefs may be harvested commercially only as part of a programme to control it.
Take it only from where it already grows. Carry no live plants or pieces to another place, never put any back in the sea elsewhere, and clean your gear, boat and anchor before you move on. On reefs take only the wakame: disturbing or removing the native seaweeds around it can help it spread.
Regional pest plans add their own rules. In Northland no one may knowingly transport material that may harbour it unless it has been removed or made non-viable; in Gisborne it may be disposed of only at a legal landfill or an authorised green-waste site; Auckland bans breeding, distributing, releasing or selling it live. Otago Regional Council asks for sightings to be reported, and in Fiordland MPI, DOC and Environment Southland are working to eliminate it from Te Puaitaha/Breaksea Sound; every vessel entering the Fiordland Marine Area must hold a Fiordland Clean Vessel Pass.
Some mātaitai reserves that ban taking seaweed exempt it: the Lyttelton Harbour/Whakaraupō and Rāpaki mātaitai reserves ban all seaweed other than Undaria, and the Makaawhio mātaitai reserves in South Westland all seaweed other than karengo and Undaria. Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.

identification.text:
A kelp usually up to about 1 m long, sometimes 2 m, with one large, thin blade that is often deeply divided into lobes. A well-defined midrib runs up the middle of the blade and continues into the stalk. The holdfast is a clump of forked, finger-like branches. Colour ranges from pale golden brown to dark brown; mature plants look brown, green and yellow, and crinkly. Mature plants carry a reproductive structure, the sporophyll, at the base of the stalk: thicker and often darker than the blade, deeply folded and, when large, seeming to spiral around the stalk. Young plants do not have it yet.
Told from common kelp (Ecklonia radiata) by its midrib, more prominent than anything on Ecklonia's blade, by the folded sporophyll at the base of the stalk on mature plants, and by its thinner, membranous, slimy blade.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look for a midrib: wakame's blade has a well-defined midrib that runs up the middle and continues into the stalk, more prominent than anything on common kelp's blade. Mature wakame also has a reproductive structure at the base of the stalk, thicker and often darker than the blade, deeply folded and, when large, seeming to spiral around the stalk; common kelp's stalk is cylindrical and unbranched, and its reproductive structures show as darker patches on the blade lobes. Young wakame does not have the folded structure yet, so rely on the midrib. Wakame's blade is also thinner, membranous and slimy. Size, shape and colour do not separate them: both grow to about 1 m, both have a large blade deeply divided into lobes and a holdfast of finger-like branches, both can look wrinkled, and both are golden brown, wakame ranging to dark brown. Both grow from the low intertidal into the subtidal on hard surfaces, and their ranges overlap around the North and South Islands, Stewart and the Snares; common kelp is absent from the Chatham Islands, where wakame is found.

preparation.text: Rinse well. For salads, cut out the central stalk. Drop the blades into boiling water for about 30 seconds, until they turn from khaki to bright green, then shred and dress as a salad, or add to soups such as miso soup and Korean miyeok-guk. The stalks are chewy and a little crunchy: blanch them for 10 to 20 seconds and stir-fry them. Dried wakame is soaked in cold water before use.

recipes.method: Fresh wakame, choosing thin, tender blades; sesame oil; rice vinegar; tamari; mirin; cucumber. Cut out and discard the central stalks. Boil the blades until they change from khaki to emerald green, which takes only about 30 seconds. Shred them and dress them Japanese-style with sesame oil, rice vinegar, tamari and mirin. Serve with cucumber as a salad.
recipes.title: Wakame salad

recipes.method: Written for dried miyeok (wakame). Serves 2 to 3. 16 g dried miyeok, soaked in cold water for 30 minutes; 1.9 litres (8 US cups) water; 450 g beef brisket or skirt steak, cut into thin, small pieces; 4 garlic cloves, minced; 25 ml (1 tbsp plus 2 tsp) fish sauce, or salt and soy sauce to taste; 10 ml (2 tsp) toasted sesame oil. Rinse and drain the soaked miyeok, squeeze out the excess water and cut it a few times into bite-size pieces. Put it in a large, heavy pot with the water, cover and boil for about 10 to 12 minutes. Turn the heat down to medium, add the beef, cover and cook for 40 minutes. Stir in the garlic and fish sauce and cook another 10 minutes, until the beef is tender and the broth savoury. Stir in the sesame oil. Serve with rice and side dishes such as kimchi. It keeps in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 4 days.
recipes.title: Miyeok-guk (seaweed soup with beef)

recipes.method: Written for dried wakame. 60 ml (4 tbsp) unseasoned rice vinegar; 30 ml (2 tbsp) sugar; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) kosher salt, or half that of table salt, for the dressing; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) soy sauce; 15 ml (1 tbsp) dried wakame; 2–3 Japanese cucumbers; 5 ml (1 tsp) kosher salt, or half that of table salt, for the cucumbers; 7.5 ml (½ tbsp) toasted white sesame seeds. Warm the vinegar, sugar, salt and soy sauce in a saucepan over medium heat, whisking, until the sugar dissolves; take it off the heat and let it cool. Soak the wakame in a bowl of water for 5 minutes to rehydrate. Peel the cucumbers in alternate stripes and slice them thinly into rounds. Massage the salt into the cucumber and leave for 5 minutes. Squeeze the water out of the wakame and put it in a bowl; squeeze the liquid from the cucumber and add it. Add the sesame seeds, pour over the dressing, toss and serve.
recipes.title: Sunomono (cucumber and wakame salad)

recipes.method: Written for dried wakame. Dried wakame; 15 to 30 ml (1 to 2 tbsp) sesame or olive oil; 15 ml (1 tbsp) sesame seeds (optional). Cut the dried wakame into bite-size pieces. Warm the oil in a frying pan, add the wakame and stir-fry over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, tossing, until it turns green and crisp. Drain on paper towels and sprinkle with roasted sesame seeds to serve.
recipes.title: Seaweed chips

recipes.method: Written for dried wakame. Dried wakame; sesame seeds; parsley or coriander; spring onion; rice vinegar; soy sauce; sesame oil; 5 ml (1 tsp) sugar. Soak the wakame in warm water for about 30 minutes, longer if it is not yet soft. Meanwhile stir a splash each of rice vinegar, sesame oil and soy sauce with the sugar until it dissolves. Chop the spring onion and parsley or coriander finely. Drain the wakame, chop it to the size you like and return it to the bowl. Add the dressing, the greens and the sesame seeds and mix until everything is evenly coated.
recipes.title: Wakame sesame salad

recipes.method: Written for salted, packaged wakame stalks (miyeok julgi). Serves 8. 280 g salted wakame stalks; 5 ml (1 tsp) vegetable oil; 5 ml (1 tsp) sesame oil; 10 ml (2 tsp) chopped garlic; 15 ml (1 tbsp) cooking sake or mirin; about 1.5 ml (1/3 tsp) sea salt; about 1 ml (1/4 tsp) sugar; sesame seeds. Rinse the stalks in three changes of water to wash off the salt, then soak them in fresh water for 30 to 40 minutes, until they no longer taste salty, and drain. Heat both oils in a large frying pan over medium-high heat and sauté the stalks for 1 to 2 minutes until coated. Turn the heat to medium, add the garlic and sake and sauté about 1 minute. Add half the salt, taste and add more if needed, then the sugar, and turn off the heat. Do not cook too long or at too low a heat, or the stalks turn slimy. Sprinkle with sesame seeds and serve at room temperature or cold. It keeps in the fridge for up to a week.
recipes.title: Stir-fried wakame stalks (miyeok julgi bokkeum)

summary.text:
Wakame (Undaria pinnatifida), or Asian kelp, is an introduced kelp from north-east Asia, eaten there as wakame and in Korea as miyeok, and an unwanted organism in New Zealand.
It is native to Japan, Korea and China, and has also been introduced to the Mediterranean, the north-east Atlantic, Tasmania and Argentina. It was first found in Wellington Harbour in 1987 and has spread, largely on boat hulls, to many ports, harbours and coasts; it is now found around the North Island, South Island, Stewart, Chatham and Snares Islands. Often called 'the gorse of the sea', it can form dense underwater forests that displace native seaweeds and change native marine communities. It is an unwanted organism under the Biosecurity Act 1993 and on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and MPI runs programmes to remove it from Fiordland and the Chatham Islands.
Each plant lives about six months. Plants grow fast from winter to spring and break down in late summer and autumn, but in New Zealand some are present all year. At two months old a plant can release millions of spores.

warnings: Wakame grows readily in ports, marinas and harbours, on wharf piles and moorings. Harvest only from clean water, away from harbours and heavy boat traffic, and never near stormwater or wastewater outfalls.
Seaweed can carry contaminants from the water it grows in: lead where the shore takes industrial, sewage and drainage waste, and norovirus where wastewater flows into the sea.

Wakame is a brown seaweed, and brown seaweed can contain very high levels of iodine. High levels of iodine can cause thyroid problems, so eating it more than every once in a while may be unsafe, especially when pregnant or breastfeeding.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Forest and scrub, forest margins, roadsides, stream beds, pasture, lakeshores, almost always in shaded sites.
It grows in woodland, beech woodland in particular, and on lime-rich soils and substrates: wall mortar, the crack where a wall meets the pavement, and cemeteries. It avoids strong light and favours the shaded side of a wall.
On the national wetland plant list it is rated facultative upland: occasionally in wetlands, usually not.

identification.text:
Glabrous perennial. Stem usually single, erect, not branched or branching above, finely grooved, (20)–50–100 cm tall. Rosette and lower stem leaves petiolate, 7–20 × 3–10 cm, lyrate-pinnatifid with a large triangular or reniform ternatifid coarsely toothed terminal lobe and 1–3 pairs of small ovate-hastate coarsely toothed lateral lobes; hydathodes prominent at tips of teeth; lamina thin, bright green above, pale and glaucous beneath. Upper leaves similar, with petiole becoming broadly winged and amplexicaul-auriculate at base; uppermost leaves not divided, linear to oblong, amplexicaul. Inflorescence diffusely paniculate. Capitula numerous, narrowly cylindric. Outer involucral bracts 2–4, very short, ovate to lanceolate, 1/10-? length of inner bracts. Inner involucral bracts linear, strictly erect, often purplish, 5–7 mm long; margins scarious. Receptacle areoles with raised glabrous margins. Florets 1½× length of involucre; corolla pale yellow. Achenes usually 5 or fewer, dark brown to black, 10-ribbed, fusiform, flattened, very finely scabrid, shortly beaked, 3–4.5 mm long. Pappus bristles in 2 more or less unequal rows, fine, white.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Each head usually has five florets, which look like five petals, with five anthers sticking out of them; a stem carries a few hundred heads. The plant often shows red pigment.

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the florets in a head: wall lettuce has 5 or fewer, prickly lettuce usually more (12–20). Under the head, wall lettuce's bracts are in two distinct rows, a few very short outer ones and a row of linear inner ones; prickly lettuce's are in more than two rows of gradually changing length. Wall lettuce is hairless, its lower leaves stalked and lyre-shaped with a large triangular or kidney-shaped, three-lobed end lobe and 1–3 pairs of small side lobes; prickly lettuce's lower leaves taper to the base and carry stiff hairs and spiny bristles on the veins beneath, especially the midrib. Wall lettuce's achene is shortly beaked; prickly lettuce's beak is about as long as its body. Both have milky sap and small yellow heads in a loose, branched spray. Prickly lettuce's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they are bitter (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Prickly lettuce

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the florets in a head: wall lettuce has 5 or fewer, wild lettuce usually more. Under the head, wall lettuce's bracts are in two distinct rows, a few very short outer ones and a row of linear inner ones 5–7 mm long; wild lettuce's are in more than two rows of gradually changing length, the involucre (11)–13–15 mm long. Wall lettuce is hairless, its lower leaves stalked and lyre-shaped with a large triangular or kidney-shaped, three-lobed end lobe; wild lettuce's lower leaves taper to the base, carry spiny bristles under the midrib, and its stem has pale spines up to 4 mm long, especially low down. Wall lettuce's achene is shortly beaked; wild lettuce's beak is about as long as its body. Both have milky sap and yellow heads in a loose, branched spray. Wild lettuce is not one to eat: eight people in Iran were taken to hospital after eating it (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Wild lettuce

lookalikes.howToTell: Wall lettuce is hairless all over; nipplewort's stems carry fine crinkled hairs, especially low down, and its leaf margins are fringed with hairs, though the leaf surfaces range from hairless to densely hairy. Count the florets: wall lettuce's heads have usually 5, nipplewort's 8 to 15. Wall lettuce's leaf end-lobe is large, triangular or kidney-shaped and itself three-lobed, coarsely toothed with prominent water pores (hydathodes) at the tooth tips; nipplewort's is broadly ovate to triangular to round, bluntly toothed and not three-lobed. Under the head, nipplewort's bracts are strongly veined or keeled; wall lettuce's inner bracts are linear, strictly erect and often purplish, with 2–4 very short outer ones. In seed, wall lettuce's achenes are dark brown to black, shortly beaked and topped with a white pappus; nipplewort's are pale, without beak or pappus. Both have milky sap, lyre-shaped lower leaves with a large end lobe, small yellow heads in a loose branched spray, and grow at forest margins and roadsides. Nipplewort's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Nipplewort

lookalikes.howToTell: Break a stem or leaf: wall lettuce's sap is milky, mountain fireweed's is watery. Wall lettuce's heads have usually 5 or fewer strap-shaped, pale yellow florets; mountain fireweed has no strap-shaped florets, only a yellow disc 2–3 mm across of tiny tubular florets of two kinds. Wall lettuce's leaves are thin, coarsely toothed, with prominent water pores (hydathodes) at the tooth tips; mountain fireweed's are thicker, with more rounded teeth. In seed, wall lettuce's achenes are dark brown to black; mountain fireweed's are paler and sparsely papillate. Both are hairless or nearly so, have lobed leaves that clasp the stem higher up and achenes topped with fine white pappus hairs, and both grow at forest margins and by streams. Mountain fireweed is a native plant with no food record, and its genus, Senecio, is known for liver-damaging pyrrolizidine alkaloids (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mountain fireweed

preparation.text: Use the leaves raw in mixed salads, or cook them. In Sicily, where it is called cardedda di muru, the leaves are commonly gathered and eaten both raw and cooked.

recipes.method: The author's greens were the leaves of Indian, alpine (woodland) and garden strawberries, red deadnettle, wall lettuce, herb Robert and nasturtium. A handful of mixed strawberry leaves, stems removed (they are tough); a handful of beetroot leaves and stems; several stems of red deadnettle with their flowers; 5 wall lettuce leaves; 5 herb Robert leaves; red nasturtium flowers and several leaves; a few celery and small kale leaves, optional. Blend the leaves and flowers with 500–750 ml (2–3 cups) water, then add 1 punnet of strawberries, 1 red apple, 2 kiwifruit and 2 bananas and blend again.
recipes.title: Wild and tame strawberry smoothie

summary.text:
Lactuca muralis, the wall lettuce, is a perennial flowering plant in the tribe Cichorieae within the family Asteraceae.
Lactuca muralis is a native of Europe but has invaded shady roadsides, paths and logged areas of the Pacific Northwest and New England.
The specific Latin epithet muralis is interpreted as 'growing on walls'.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Coromandel southwards; S.: throughout; St. Naturalised from Europe, Asia Minor and North Africa, first recorded in 1899. M. muralis has also been referred to in N.Z. as Lactuca muralis.
Older floras placed it in Lactuca with the other lettuces. It is kept apart as Mycelis on a small difference in the seed hairs (in Mycelis the inner row is longer than the outer), and Stace (2019) has suggested returning it to Lactuca. Prenanthes muralis is its original name.
It overwinters with only a few green leaves and puts up new ones in late spring (Scotland). Its seeds fly on a pappus, but most seedlings come up within about 2 m of the parent.
Most of Landcare Research's databased herbarium specimens come from the South Island: Canterbury 14, Marlborough 9, Nelson 4, Otago 3, Westland 2 and Southland 1, against Wellington 4 and South Auckland 1. Auckland Museum holds one collected in the Rotorua Ecological District on 24/01/2016.

warnings: Its food record is thin: one plant database and one Sicilian field survey name the leaves, and no source gives a safe amount. The same database's other edition lists the raw root, not the leaves, as the edible part.

habitat.text: In New Zealand it grows on rock walls and rock faces, often shaded, including bluffs under forest, and among rocks on a shore. Observers record it as locally abundant on shaded rock faces in broadleaved and sycamore forest in Dunedin, as a common weed of rock walls in Christchurch, and among rocks on an estuary shore at Redcliffs. In Newtown, Wellington, several hundred plants grow in the open on a rocky road cutting above a footpath. In gardens it seeds itself into rock gardens, pots and dry walls. In its homeland it grows on shady walls and in damp rock crevices, and sometimes at the base of old trees.

identification.text:
A fleshy perennial that grows from a rounded underground tuber; the leafy parts die back each year. The basal leaves are round, shining or dull green and up to about 8 cm across, with the stalk joined under the middle of the blade, which is dimpled there like a navel; the edge is scalloped. They grow in rosettes and may turn reddish in strong sun or drought. The flowering stem is upright, usually unbranched, often reddish or purplish lower down, and up to about 50 cm tall; flowers cover most of its length, and its leaves quickly shrink to small bracts. The flowers are narrow bells 7–9 mm long, pale green and sometimes red-dotted outside, with five short lobes about as broad as long, and they hang down or angle downwards on short stalks. New Zealand specimens and observations show it flowering in November and December.
In plain terms: look for a rosette of round, fleshy leaves with a dimple in the middle, growing out of a crack in a wall or rock face. The dimple is the quickest check. Horizontal navelwort (Umbilicus horizontalis), which grows in some of the same places, has flowers only on about the upper half of the stem, held sideways on almost no stalk; wall pennywort's flowers cover most of the stem and mostly hang down.

preparation.text: Wash the leaves and eat them raw. They are succulent and crunchy, a little like cucumber, and go well in salads or sandwiches (for instance with chives or sorrel). They taste mildest in winter and early spring and stronger in summer, and leaves from some walls and rocks can be very bitter. Cooked leaves go slimy, so they are mostly used raw. Snip a couple of leaves from each rosette, only where the plant is plentiful; the roots are shallow and tear away easily, so avoid pulling the plant out.

recipes.method: 100 g wall pennywort leaves; 50 g spring onions (the author also uses onion weed, Allium triquetrum — see its entry before picking it); juice and zest of 1 lime; 3 tbsp sesame or peanut oil; 1 tsp miso; 1 green chilli, finely chopped; 2 garlic cloves, finely chopped; 100 g roasted peanuts, roughly ground. Serves 2 as a starter or side. Put the leaves in a mortar. Finely chop the spring onions, garlic and chilli and add them with the peanuts and lime zest. Whisk the oil and miso together in a bowl. Bash the salad with the pestle until roughly broken up, not puréed. Spoon into bowls and dress with the oil and miso. The author lists the lime juice but does not say where it goes.

summary.text:
Wall pennywort (Umbilicus rupestris), also called navelwort, hipwort or penny-pies, is a fleshy perennial in the stonecrop family (Crassulaceae). The common and Latin names (Umbilicus means navel) come from the navel-like dimple in the middle of each leaf. It is native to Britain, southern and western Europe, North Africa and Macaronesia.
In New Zealand it is an exotic plant that the Flora of New Zealand lists as 'Pennywort' (biostatus Exotic) and Biota of New Zealand records as casual (Heenan et al. 2008). Herbarium specimens of plants growing wild come from Newtown, Wellington, where Te Papa botanists collected it in 2022 and 2024 from a rocky road cutting with several hundred plants. Older specimens are from gardens where it spread on its own from seed: a rock garden at Orton Bradley Park on Banks Peninsula (2000, 2002), pots in St Albans, Christchurch (2002), and a Dunedin wall where it had been planted (2001); one came from a Pukekohe nursery shade house (1992). Recent iNaturalist NZ records of wild plants (30 research-grade) are from Wellington (Newtown, Hataitai, Thorndon, Ōwhiro Bay), Dunedin, and Canterbury (Christchurch, Diamond Harbour, Governors Bay). It is not on DOC's environmental weed list or in any regional pest plan (checked 28/10/2026).
A second navelwort, Umbilicus horizontalis, also grows wild in New Zealand, in some of the same places (Ōwhiro Bay in Wellington, Beckenham in Christchurch, and Dunedin); a Christchurch specimen first named wall pennywort was later re-identified as it.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Series vol. IV, Webb, C.J.; Sykes, W.R.; Garnock-Jones, P.J. 1988, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) — 'Juglans regia', abbreviations spelled out, hyphens between numbers set as en dashes
identification.text:
Large tree with compound leaves of five to nine leaflets, aromatic when crushed. Round green husks 3.5–5 cm long that split and blacken to release the familiar wrinkled shell.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Large tree to over 20 m high, with broad spreading crown. Shoots glabrous, stout, dark, with prominent, Y-shaped leaf scars; buds grey, more or less finely puberulent. Leaves to about 55 cm long; petiole and rachis to about 30 cm long on adult branches. Leaflets 5–9, densely glandular-puberulent when young, becoming glabrous except for axillary hair tufts on undersurface, entire; base cuneate to rounded; apex rounded to acute or cuspidate; lowest pair of leaflets much smaller; terminal leaflet largest. Lamina of terminal leaflet mostly 10–20 × 5–11 cm (sometimes larger on strong vegetative shoots), broad-elliptic or elliptic-obovate. Male catkins 5–11 cm long, puberulent. Female flowers in clusters of 1–3, sessile or subsessile, densely glandular-puberulent; stigmas to 3 mm long, pale green. Fruit 3.5–5 cm long, subglobose, glabrous but gland-dotted, green, not beaked. Shell thick or thin, rugose; sutures thick and easily dividing in half at maturity. Seed very convoluted. Wild or self-sown trees tend to have thick-shelled nuts.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both edible; this is about which you have. Count and feel the leaflets: walnut has 5–9 with smooth (untoothed) edges, the end leaflet the largest and the lowest pair much smaller; Japanese walnut has 9–17, finely toothed though the teeth are often sparse, the end leaflet about the size of the side ones. Seedling walnuts can have toothed leaflets, so check an adult tree. Walnut's fruits sit in clusters of 1–3 close on the twig; Japanese walnut's hang 10–22 together in long strings. Walnut's fruit is 3.5–5 cm, nearly round, smooth and green with gland dots, not beaked; Japanese walnut's is 2.5–4 cm, egg-shaped, beaked, sticky and rusty-hairy. Walnut's shell splits easily in half along its seams when ripe; Japanese walnut's thick shell has raised seams that split with difficulty and an often sharp tip.
lookalikes.name: Japanese walnut

lookalikes.howToTell: Both edible; this is about which you have. Count and feel the leaflets: walnut has 5–9 with smooth (untoothed) edges, the end leaflet the largest and the lowest pair much smaller; black walnut has 15–23, toothed, the largest in the middle of the leaf and the end leaflet usually missing or small. Seedling walnuts can have toothed leaflets, so check an adult tree. Walnut's fruit is 3.5–5 cm, smooth and green with gland dots; black walnut's is 3–4 cm with a brownish-green husk. Crack one: walnut's shell splits easily in half along its seams when ripe; black walnut's is very hard and sharply ridged, and the kernel is hard to get out.

preparation.text: Gather fallen nuts promptly, husk them (wear gloves — the husk stains skin brown and the stain is very hard to remove), then dry for several weeks before storing.

recipes.method: Written for walnuts by New Zealand growers; the page does not name the species. 1 kg fresh green walnuts; 250 g salt; 2 litres boiling water, in two lots; 1 litre malt vinegar; 400 g brown sugar; 1 tsp salt; 1 tsp pickling spice; 1 tsp black peppercorns; ½ tsp whole cloves. Pick the nuts early, around Christmas, while they are green and before the shell forms: push a sturdy needle through each and throw out any that will not pierce easily. Wear gloves, as the juice stains skin and is very hard to remove. Prick the walnuts all over with a fork and put them in a large bowl. Dissolve half the salt in 1 litre of boiling water, pour it over to cover and leave in a cool place for a week. Drain, cover with a second brine made the same way and leave another week. Drain and spread the nuts in one layer on a tray, and set them outside in a sunny spot for 3–4 days, bringing them in at night, until black and dry. Bring the vinegar, sugar, teaspoon of salt and spices to the boil and simmer about 5 minutes to dissolve the sugar, then cool and strain out the spices. Bring the liquid back to the boil, pack the walnuts into clean jars and pour it over so every nut is covered. Cover and keep somewhere dark for at least a month before eating; the growers find them better after 4 months. Use vinegar-proof lids, or put a layer of cling film between lid and liquid, as vinegar corrodes metal lids and taints the walnuts.
recipes.title: Pickled green walnuts

recipes.method: Written for walnuts; the page does not name the species. 500 ml (2 cups) walnuts; ½ tsp salt. Heat the oven to 150 °C, or 140 °C if your oven runs hot. Spread the walnuts on a baking tray and toast for 12–15 minutes, watching that they do not burn, until toasted and fragrant. Let them cool. Process with the salt in a food processor until they turn into a smooth, runny butter.
recipes.title: Walnut butter

recipes.method: Written for walnuts; the page does not name the species. Makes about 375 ml (1½ cups). 250 ml (1 cup) toasted walnuts, roughly chopped; 250 ml (1 cup) parsley; 1 garlic clove; 250 ml (1 cup) grated parmesan; 1 tsp lemon zest and 2 tbsp lemon juice; ¼ tsp salt, and pepper; 125 ml (½ cup) olive oil; 4 slices bruschetta and some blue cheese, to serve. Blitz the walnuts, parsley, garlic, parmesan, lemon zest and juice, salt and pepper in a food processor until combined. Add the oil and blend again. Keep in a jar and use as needed. To serve it the author's way, heat the oven to 170 °C, spread the pesto thickly on the bruschetta, scatter with crumbled blue cheese and bake for 4 minutes to just melt the cheese; serve warm.
recipes.title: Walnut pesto

recipes.method: Written for walnuts by New Zealand growers; the page does not name the species. 150 g sausage mince; 150 g beef mince; ½ onion, grated; 10 ml salt; 2.5 ml pepper; 5 ml turmeric; 15 ml Worcestershire sauce; 375 ml water; 5 ml Vegemite; 15 ml tomato paste; 2.5 ml ground saffron dissolved in 45 ml hot water; 500 ml ground walnuts; 250 ml pomegranate molasses; 15 ml sugar; salt and pepper to taste. Mix both minces with the onion, salt, pepper and turmeric and roll into about 20 small balls. Brown them all over in a pan over medium heat, move them to a large pot and sprinkle with the Worcestershire sauce. Stir the Vegemite and tomato paste into the water with the saffron water, pour it over the meatballs, cover and bring back to the boil. Mix the ground walnuts, pomegranate molasses and sugar, stir them into the liquid, bring to the boil, then cover and simmer gently for 1 hour, stirring now and then. Season and serve with basmati rice. Chicken, venison or eggplant can replace the beef.
recipes.title: Fesenjoon (walnut and pomegranate stew)

recipes.method: Written for walnuts by New Zealand growers; the page does not name the species. An Azerbaijani dish, badymdjan dolmasy. 3–4 small eggplants; 250 g walnuts, coarsely ground; 300 g onions, finely chopped; 100 g butter; salt and pepper; 500 ml hot vegetable stock. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Cut the stem ends off the eggplants, put them in a pot of cold salted water and bring to the boil, then lift them out, halve them lengthwise and scoop out the seeds. Lay the halves in a baking dish just big enough to hold them and season. Cook the onions in the butter until soft, stir in the walnuts and cook briefly, then fill the eggplant halves. Pour the hot stock around them and bake uncovered for 30–40 minutes. Serve hot or cold.
recipes.title: Walnut-stuffed eggplant

recipes.method: Written for walnuts by New Zealand growers; the page does not name the species. 250 ml finely ground walnuts; 185 ml sugar; 3 egg whites. Heat the oven to 210 °C and line two baking trays with baking paper. Beat the egg whites, adding the sugar gradually, to stiff peaks, then gently fold in the walnuts. Pipe meringues onto the trays with a fluted nozzle, put them in the oven, turn the oven off at once and leave them inside for 1 hour. Keep airtight.
recipes.title: Walnut meringues

recipes.method: Written for walnuts by New Zealand growers; the page does not name the species. 120 g rolled oats; 75 g walnuts; 120 ml hot water; 15 ml butter; 2.5 ml honey; 1.25 ml salt; 1.25 ml baking soda; 5 ml dried thyme. Heat the oven to 160 °C. Blitz the walnuts and oats in a food processor to a very fine crumb. Melt the butter and honey in the hot water, add it with the salt, baking soda and thyme, and blitz to a smooth dough. Knead on the bench and roll out about 3 mm thick, cut into shapes and lay on baking-paper-lined trays, pricking each a few times. Bake about 12–15 minutes, until golden at the edges. Good with blue cheese and relish.
recipes.title: Walnut oat crackers

recipes.method: Written for walnuts by New Zealand growers; the page does not name the species. 500 ml chopped walnuts; 1 litre chopped flat-leaf parsley; 500 ml chopped mint; 3 spring onions, finely chopped; 2 large tomatoes, seeded and chopped; 125 ml lemon juice; 125 ml walnut oil; salt to taste. Toss the walnuts, parsley, mint, spring onions and tomatoes in a bowl. Whisk the lemon juice, walnut oil and salt, pour over and toss again.
recipes.title: Walnut tabbouli

recipes.method: Written for walnuts by Geoff Scott for Tuapeka Honey (Otago); the page does not name the species. Makes a 20 cm loaf. 20 g active dried yeast; 100 ml water; 100 ml milk; 120 g honey; 55 g butter, melted; 200 g flour; 280 g wholemeal flour; 15 g salt; 130 g walnuts. Whisk the yeast with the water, milk, honey and butter. Add both flours, mix to a dough and knead 5 minutes, then add the salt and knead 5 minutes more. Cover and leave to rise 2–3 hours, until doubled. Roll out on a lightly floured bench to about 20 × 30 cm, scatter the walnuts over and press them in. Roll up from a short end into a spiral, pressing out air as you go, and put it in a greased 20 cm loaf tin. Cover and leave to rise again 2–3 hours, until doubled. Bake at 200 °C for 15 minutes, then at 150 °C for 30 minutes more. Turn out to cool on a rack, then wrap and keep in the fridge. Serve thin slices toasted, with blue cheese and honeycomb.
recipes.title: Honey and walnut bread

recipes.method: Written for walnuts by Domenica Houlihan for RNZ; the page does not name the species. Thin, crisp slices like biscotti. 3 large eggs; 60 ml sugar; 250 ml flour; 125 g walnuts. Heat the oven to 160 °C and line a loaf tin of about 20 × 10 cm with baking paper. Whisk the eggs and sugar until well mixed, then fold in the flour and walnuts without over-mixing. Spread in the tin and bake 45 minutes, until lightly coloured. Cool on a rack, wrap in foil and refrigerate overnight. Heat the oven to 150 °C, slice the loaf very thinly (about 2–3 mm) with a sharp knife and lay the slices on two baking-paper-lined trays. Bake 20–25 minutes until browned, watching closely at the end as they burn easily. Cool on a rack and keep airtight.

summary.text:
Old farm and roadside trees drop far more than anyone collects.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands, sporadic throughout. Naturalised from south-east Europe east to the temperate Himalaya and China. Walnuts were amongst the first nut plants introduced to New Zealand by early settlers from Europe.

warnings: Nuts left lying damp on the ground develop moulds. Discard any kernel that is shrivelled, discoloured or smells rancid.
Walnuts are tree nuts, one of the commonest causes of food allergy in New Zealand, and can cause life-threatening allergic reactions in some people.

identification.text:
Procumbent to ascending, aquatic or amphibious perennial, rooting at lower nodes. Stems hollow, grooved, striate, up to 180 cm long. Basal leaves 1-pinnate, with a leaf stalk; leaflets in 2–8 pairs, ovate to lanceolate, serrate, sometimes lobed, particularly the end leaflet, 1–8–(12) cm long, without stalks; stem leaves similar to basal, but the uppermost often reduced to 3–5 leaflets. Umbel 2–4 cm in diameter, compound, almost without a stalk or shortly stalked, opposite a leaf; rays 4–14; bracts 0–2, linear to lanceolate; bracteoles 4–8, ovate-triangular. Flowers numerous, white, 1–2 mm in diameter. Fruit ovoid, dark brown, 1.5–2.5 mm long; ribs light brown, slender or slightly thickened. Flowers November–February.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Apium nodiflorum.]
A sprawling water plant up to a metre tall, with glossy, bright green leaves of paired, toothed leaflets and white flowers close to the leaf bases. Crushed, it smells of raw carrot; watercress smells of cress. Watercress also has rounded leaflets, a peppery taste, and four-petalled white flowers in spikes, not umbels; see Lookalikes.

lookalikes.howToTell: Watercress belongs to the cabbage family: its small white flowers have 4 petals and grow in stalked spikes (racemes) that lengthen into narrow, curved pods 8–18 mm long, and its leaves have a hot, mustardy taste. Water celery is an umbellifer: its tiny white flowers, 1–2 mm across with 5 petals, sit in small compound umbels 2–4 cm across on short stalks opposite the leaves. Watercress's leaflets are rounded with smooth or wavy edges; water celery's are toothed, and its crushed leaves smell of carrot. Water celery grows in shallow ponds, drains and the margins of slow streams and can be mistaken for watercress, so habitat does not separate them. Watercress from water draining grazed land can carry liver fluke and should be cooked.
lookalikes.name: Watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Look under the small umbels: water celery always has 4–8 small bracteoles there, and celery has none. Water celery lies along the ground or rises from it and roots at its lower nodes; celery stands erect, up to 80–(100) cm, and does not root at the nodes. Water celery's leaves are once-pinnate, with 2–8 pairs of toothed leaflets 1–8 cm long (up to 12); celery's are 1–2-pinnate, with lobed segments 2–4 cm long. Both grow in wet ground, so place does not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Narrow-fruited watercress's leaflets are rounded, with smooth or wavy edges, and smell peppery when crushed; water celery's are toothed, in 2–8 pairs. In flower, narrow-fruited watercress has white four-petalled flowers in spikes, followed by narrow curved pods; water celery has small compound umbels of tiny white flowers on short stalks opposite the leaves, with 4–8 small bracteoles under each small umbel. Both grow in streams and drains, so place does not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Narrow-fruited watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Look under the small umbels: water celery always has 4–8 small bracteoles there, and sea celery has none. Water celery's stems root at the lower nodes; sea celery's sprawling stems do not root. Water celery's leaves are once-pinnate, with 2–8 pairs of toothed leaflets 1–8 cm long (up to 12); sea celery's are three-parted to 1–2-pinnate, with lobed segments about 5–30 mm long. Sea celery is mostly coastal but also grows beside lakes and streams inland, so place does not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Sea celery

summary.text:
Fool's watercress. A streamside umbellifer that smells of raw carrot when crushed and is mistaken for watercress and grows in the same wet ground as hemlock. Eaten in Europe.
Helosciadium nodiflorum (synonym Apium nodiflorum) is not poisonous to humans, and it has traditionally been gathered and eaten in Spain, Italy, Portugal and Morocco. Native to Britain, central and southern Europe, south-western Asia to Persia and North Africa, it was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1947, possibly arriving as a seed contaminant or with ornamental pond plants. Flora of New Zealand (1988) gives it as established locally throughout the North Island except Taranaki and collected once in eastern coastal Southland; NZPCN now gives a scattered distribution from Northland to Wellington, abundant in many areas, and established in the north and west of the South Island.
It regrows from broken-off shoots, which root readily, and from seed. It can be mistaken for watercress and collected and passed on as such. It is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds and is a sustained control pest across the whole Tasman-Nelson region.

warnings: Pull watercress stem by stem and smell each one. Anything that smells of carrot, celery or parsley rather than cress is not watercress.
Hemlock, a deadly relative, also lacks the pepper smell.
Liver fluke risk: water plants growing where sheep, goats or cattle graze can carry Fasciola hepatica, caught by eating them raw. Do not eat it raw from water draining grazed land.

habitat.text:
Lakesides, ponds, ditches, drains, riverbeds and wet, poorly drained pastures and waste land, in lowland areas. [From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4]
It also grows at the edges of river banks and in marshy areas, and submerged in clear, moderately flowing streams. In pasture it comes up each spring, especially along streams and in wet patches where pugging has set the grass back, and sometimes in damp waste areas and crops. Grown in a garden, it does best in sun in soil that stays wet, and does not like shade; in drier soil it survives but grows less.

identification.text:
Almost glabrous annual herb; stems erect or suberect, to about 75 cm tall, often reddish; roots rather slender. Leaves on main stem similar to those on branches, subsessile or shortly petiolate. Lamina 1–12 × 0.3–2 cm, lanceolate or linear-lanceolate, bright or deep green, with small translucent glandular dots; margins ciliolate and more or less undulate; base cuneate to attenuate; apex obtuse to acuminate. Ochreae to 2 cm long, reddish brown, truncate, with 0-few fringing bristles, more or less flared at upper nodes. Racemes slender, spike-like, to about 7 cm long, at least partly curving downwards, the lower flowers often distant; pedicels short, enclosed by bracts at anthesis, later protruding. Perianth 1.5–3 mm long, prominently dotted with brownish glands, usually pink or rose, rarely white, accrescent; segments more or less broad-elliptic, strongly imbricate. Nut 2.5–3 mm long, trigonous or biconvex, dark brown or black, finely granular and appearing dull to moderately shining. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Polygonum hydropiper L.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers: water pepper's are prominently dotted with glands; tūtunawai's have none. Flower colour does not separate them: water pepper's are usually pink or rose, rarely white, tūtunawai's deep pink to whitish. Tūtunawai's flower spikes are erect or slightly curved, 1.5–8 cm long; water pepper's are slender, up to about 7 cm long, and at least partly curve downwards, with the lower flowers often spaced apart. Look at the sheath where the leaf meets the stem: tūtunawai's is about 1.5 cm long, green or pinkish, cut obliquely, not flared, and fringed with long hairs, (1)–2–(5) mm; water pepper's is up to 2 cm long, reddish brown, cut straight across, with none to a few fringing bristles, and more or less flared at the upper nodes. Tūtunawai's stems lie along the ground or curve up from it, rooting at the lower nodes; water pepper's stand erect or nearly so, up to about 75 cm tall and often reddish. Tūtunawai's leaves, up to 15 × 4 cm, often have dark markings above; water pepper's are 1–12 × 0.3–2 cm, bright or deep green. Ripe nuts: tūtunawai's are 1.7–2.5 mm long, blackish and more or less glossy; water pepper's 2.5–3 mm, finely granular and dull to moderately shining. Do not go by taste: tūtunawai is described both as lacking water pepper's peppery flavour and as having pungent-tasting leaves. Both grow in swamps, at lake edges and along streams in the North and South Islands, so place does not separate them. Tūtunawai is recorded as possibly poisonous and is not given as food (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Tūtunawai

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers: water pepper's are prominently dotted with brownish glands; willow weed's have none. Flower colour does not separate them: water pepper's are usually pink or rose, rarely white, willow weed's usually pale to deep pink, occasionally white. Water pepper's flower spikes are slender, up to about 7 cm long, and at least partly curve downwards, with the lower flowers often spaced apart; willow weed's stand erect and are dense and cylindric, usually unbroken at the base, up to 4 cm long (rarely 5), though some plants have a slender, rather open spike 3–5 cm long. Look at the sheath where the leaf meets the stem: willow weed's is up to about 1.5 cm long, green or pinkish, and fringed with long hairs; water pepper's is up to 2 cm long, reddish brown, with none to a few fringing bristles, and more or less flared at the upper nodes. Willow weed's leaves usually have a dark blotch in the centre, though not always, and are 1.2–4 cm wide; water pepper's are described as bright or deep green and are 0.3–2 cm wide, so a leaf wider than 2 cm is not water pepper's, but a narrower one does not tell them apart. Ripe nuts: willow weed's are 2–2.5 mm long and shining; water pepper's 2.5–3 mm, finely granular and dull to moderately shining. Plants with glandular flowers on a very slender spike may be hybrids between the two, which are fairly common locally around Auckland and in Waikato. Both grow on riverbeds, waste land and wet ground in the North and South Islands, so place does not separate them. Willow weed's leaves are eaten raw or cooked (see its page).

preparation.text: Use it sparingly: every part has an acrid, peppery taste, and the wild plant is far more pungent than the cultivated forms grown as a vegetable in Japan. The leaves can be made into an acid, peppery condiment. The heat fades the more it is mixed with other ingredients: a raw leaf burns like a fresh chilli, while a small handful stirred through a finished rice dish gives only a gentle tingle. In Japan the leaves are blended with vinegar into a sauce, tade-su, eaten with raw or cooked fish.

recipes.method: 30 g fresh water pepper leaves and tips; 90 ml (6 tbsp) mirin; 90 ml (6 tbsp) Japanese rice vinegar. Blend everything until very smooth. Drizzle it over avocado or white fish.
recipes.title: Water pepper tade-su

recipes.method: 40 g water pepper leaves and seeds (about ½ packed cup); 60 ml (¼ cup) rice wine vinegar or cider vinegar — not white vinegar, which is too strong; 30 ml (2 tbsp) water; 30 ml (2 tbsp) maple syrup (optional); 60 ml (¼ cup) toasted sesame oil or a nut oil such as walnut (the author uses hickory nut oil); 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt. Purée everything in a high-speed blender until smooth and keep it in the fridge. Makes about 180 ml of a slightly sweet-and-sour sauce that tastes like horseradish or wasabi. Serve it with sushi or with baked or poached fish.

summary.text:
Water pepper (Persicaria hydropiper, synonym Polygonum hydropiper) is an almost hairless annual herb in the dock family Polygonaceae, native to temperate Eurasia and North Africa.
It was first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1906, possibly arriving as a seed contaminant, and is now abundant in lowland areas throughout the North and South Islands. It spreads by seed carried by water or waterfowl. Its leaves have a very strong, burning, peppery taste, and it is not usually grazed by livestock, especially cattle. It is not controlled in New Zealand. It can be grown from seed sown in spring, which germinates readily, or from cuttings, which root easily.

warnings: Water pepper is recorded as possibly poisonous in New Zealand, and it has been found toxic to pigs and sheep.
The oily exudate from glands on the plant can irritate the skin, and repeated handling of the leaves and stems can blister it.
The root has been used in traditional medicine to end pregnancy, and root extracts have antifertility and oestrogen-like effects in rats.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): In muddy ponds, ditches, swamps and slow-flowing waters; abundant in some places but absent in others.
It grows standing in, or at the edge of, farm drains, roadside ditches, swamps, ponds, dams, water races, slow streams and rivers, estuaries and marshy pasture, in humus-rich soil. It grows in both nutrient-poor and nutrient-rich water and tolerates some brackish water. In shaded drains and other sheltered water some plants keep submerged leaves through winter.
It copes with water levels that rise and fall and with ponds that dry out in summer, grows in the open or in light shade, and does poorly among taller plants.
On New Zealand's national wetland plant list it is rated obligate wetland: it almost always grows in wetlands.

identification.text:
Stems stout, erect, to 1 m high; rootstock short, stout. Leaves all basal, erect; laminae 8–20 × 3–10 cm, ovate, subacute, rounded or subcordate at base; petiole long. Inflorescence a large, much-branched panicle; branches whorled, more or less straight, usually ascending, basally bracteate. Flowers usually pale lilac, about 1 cm diameter, pedicels slender, bracteate; sepals oblong; petals rounded. Achenes about 20, about 2.5 mm long, rounded, compressed, in a dense circular head; persistent style from below middle of inner edge of achene, more or less straight; stigmatic portion occupying 1/8–1/5 of style-length.
[From: Healy and Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]
A hairless plant of pond and ditch edges, 0.5–1.8 m tall. Its broad, oval leaves, 8–23 cm long and 3–10 cm wide with a pointed tip and a rounded or heart-shaped base, stand upright in a rosette on long stalks that are D-shaped in cross-section; rarely, the leaves float or grow under water. The leaves above water die back over winter. From November to February it sends up a pyramid-shaped flower stalk up to about 1 m tall, with whorls of branches and many three-petalled flowers up to 1 cm across, pale lilac, pale pink or white with a yellow spot at the base of each petal. Each flower opens for only part of a day, in the afternoon. They are followed by rings of about 20 flat seeds which, seen from above, leave a gap in the middle.
Lance-leaved water plantain (Alisma lanceolatum), scattered from Gisborne to Wellington and in Canterbury and Otago, is very similar. Its leaves are lance-shaped or narrowly elliptic and taper gradually into the stalk; its petals are usually pale pink, often with pointed tips; and the seeds in its fruiting head touch and overlap in the middle, leaving no gap. Young plants without flowers can be hard to tell apart.

lookalikes.howToTell: Greater plantain's tiny flowers are packed into a dense, unbranched spike on a leafless stalk, and its leaves usually have fine hairs on the veins underneath, though some plants are hairless. Water plantain is hairless, its upright oval leaves sit on long, D-shaped stalks and die back over winter, and from November to February it carries a branched flower stalk up to about 1 m tall with whorls of pale lilac or white, three-petalled flowers up to 1 cm across. Greater plantain also grows in moist places and drains, so where it grows does not separate them.

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp plantain's tiny flowers are packed into a dense, unbranched spike, usually over 10 cm long, on a round stalk densely hairy near the top; its leaves are lance-shaped to broadly elliptic, hairy on the raised veins underneath, tapering into an often purple stalk. Water plantain is hairless, its upright oval leaves sit on long, D-shaped stalks and die back over winter, and from November to February it carries a branched flower stalk up to about 1 m tall with whorls of pale lilac or white, three-petalled flowers. Both grow in swamps and wet ground, so where it grows does not separate them.

summary.text:
Water plantain, also called mad-dog weed, is a hairless perennial water plant that grows rooted at the edges of ponds, ditches and slow water, its leaves standing up out of the water.
It is native to Europe, western Asia, northern and central Africa and Australia. In New Zealand it was first collected in the Waikato in 1929, perhaps escaping from ornamental ponds or arriving as a seed or soil contaminant. It is scattered and locally common from Northland to northern Southland, but absent from large parts of the southern and eastern North Island and the eastern South Island. It spreads by seed, carried by water and waterfowl, and by side shoots from the rhizome; the seeds can lie dormant, and in Scotland have been found to stay viable for ten years. In moving water it can be a nuisance, slowing the flow and trapping debris and silt. Despite the name it is not a plantain: it is a monocot in the water-plantain family, Alismataceae, named for its plantain-like leaves. The name mad-dog weed comes from its old use against rabies, and it was among the medicinal plants of Gerard's Herbal of 1597.
The starchy rootstock has been eaten after drying or long cooking, and the leaves and stalks after long boiling: heat or thorough drying destroys the poison in the fresh plant. Missouri's conservation department, writing of water plantains generally, says they can be dangerous to people and cattle and does not recommend eating them.
Like many water plants it takes up heavy metals from polluted water and stores them in its roots, and it has been suggested for cleaning stormwater and industrial wastewater.

warnings: Do not eat it. The fresh leaves and roots are poisonous, and its plantain-like rosette can be mistaken for a plantain, which is eaten raw.
The fresh leaves can irritate the skin.

identification.text: Hairless compound leaves of rounded leaflets with smooth or wavy edges, the end leaflet larger than the rest. Hollow stems that trail, float or sprawl over mud and root at the leaf nodes. Small four-petalled white flowers, from spring through summer, followed by narrow, curved pods about 12–15 mm long with the seeds in two rows. Sharp peppery taste. Narrow-fruited watercress is almost identical: see Lookalikes.

lookalikes.howToTell: Water celery's leaflets are toothed, in 2–8 pairs, and its crushed leaves smell of carrot; watercress's leaflets are rounded with smooth or wavy edges and have a hot, mustardy taste. In flower, water celery has small compound umbels of tiny 5-petalled white flowers on short stalks opposite the leaves; watercress has 4-petalled white flowers in racemes followed by narrow curved pods. Water celery grows in shallow ponds, drains and the margins of slow streams, and it can be mistaken for watercress and collected and passed on as such. Water celery's young leaves and shoots are eaten in Mediterranean countries, but it is an umbellifer, and deadly hemlock — another umbellifer — also grows on damp ground in New Zealand, so be certain of the identification.
lookalikes.name: Water celery

lookalikes.howToTell: The two are very alike and the leaves do not separate them. The surest test is the ripe seeds: watercress has them in two distinct rows in each half of the pod, each seed with 20–50 coarse pits per face; narrow-fruited watercress has them in a single row, with 100–150 small pits. Watercress also tends to have smaller flowers (petals 4–6 mm long against 5–6 mm), shorter flower stalks (10–15 mm against 12–20 mm) and wider pods (2–2.5 mm against about 1.5 mm). Narrow-fruited watercress's leaves turn brown or purple in autumn and winter. Both grow in the same streams and drains. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Narrow-fruited watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Bog yellow cress has yellow petals only about as long as the sepals (1.5–2.5 mm), usually stands upright from a taproot, and its leaves are deeply lobed with toothed edges. Watercress has white petals, about twice as long as the sepals, and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, with rounded leaflets with smooth or wavy edges. Bog yellow cress's pods are short and plump, 2–7 mm long; watercress's are narrow, 8–18 mm. Both grow at the edges of streams and other wet places, so place does not separate them. Bog yellow cress's young leaves and stems are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Bog yellow cress

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping yellowcress has yellow flowers on upright stems and spreads by creeping underground parts; its upper leaves are cut into narrow, toothed or untoothed lobes. Watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, with rounded leaflets with smooth or wavy edges. Both grow in wet ground and both have petals about twice as long as the sepals, so place and petal length do not separate them. Creeping yellowcress has no reliable food record.
lookalikes.name: Creeping yellowcress

lookalikes.howToTell: Land cress has yellow flowers on upright stems from a stout taproot, and grows on river banks, roadsides and waste land; watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, and grows in streams, ditches and drains. Land cress's pods are 30–70 mm long; watercress's are 8–18 mm. Both have lobed leaves and a hot, cress-like taste, so taste does not separate them. Land cress's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Land cress
