preparation.text: Pick young leaves; they are slightly less bitter. The long leaves at the base of plants, away from the flowering stems, give the best yield. The bitterness stays whatever you do, so use a leaf or two: chop finely and mix with milder soft herbs such as parsley, chervil or tarragon. High heat destroys the flavour — add it at the end of cooking, off the heat, just to warm through. Simmering whole plants in stock gives a bitter broth. Young leaves are best picked before the plant flowers; pick flowers while it is in bloom, in the morning once the dew has dried. For tea, infuse the flowers and leaves. The flowers, fresh or dried, can be steeped hot or cold to flavour drinks, ice cream and custards such as crème brûlée; dried flowers make it possible out of season.

recipes.method: Serves 4. About 225 g dried penne; 4 tablespoons finely chopped fresh garlic; kosher salt; 3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil; 3 tablespoons grapeseed or canola oil; 1 teaspoon crushed red pepper flakes, or more to taste; a large handful of yarrow leaves, picked from the stem and chopped to give 2 teaspoons; ¼ cup (about 60 ml) dry white wine; 4 anchovy fillets in oil, rinsed and chopped (optional); Parmesan to serve. Pile the chopped yarrow and the chilli flakes together and mince them finely. Bring a pot of water to the boil, salt it until it tastes like the sea, and cook the penne until al dente. Meanwhile, warm the garlic with both oils and the anchovy in a 25 cm sauté pan over low heat until fragrant and lightly browned; do not let the garlic burn. Take the pan off the heat, swirl it for a minute to cool, then add the wine. Drain the pasta, add it to the pan and toss to coat; cook for a minute to drive off the raw wine flavour. Add the yarrow and chilli mixture and toss just to heat through. Divide among 4 bowls, top with Parmesan and a little more olive oil if you like, and serve at once with a big green salad.
recipes.title: Penne aglio olio with yarrow

recipes.method: Makes about 85 g of tea blend. 28 g (1 oz) yarrow flowers; 28 g (1 oz) German chamomile flowers; 28 g (1 oz) peppermint leaves. Blend the herbs together and store them in an airtight container. For each cup (about 240 ml) of tea, use 1 teaspoon of the blend.
recipes.title: Yarrow, chamomile and peppermint tea

recipes.method: 4 anchovy fillets; 1 tbsp (15 ml) capers, finely chopped; 1 garlic clove, finely chopped; zest and juice of ½ lemon; 90 ml olive oil; 3 tbsp (45 ml) finely chopped yarrow leaves; salt and pepper. Pound the anchovies, capers and garlic in a mortar (or in a sturdy bowl with the end of a rolling pin) until broken down, then tip into a bowl. Add the lemon zest and juice, whisk in the olive oil in a steady stream, then stir in the yarrow and season with salt and pepper. Spoon over cooked chicken or fish, potatoes, pizza or salads. Leave out the anchovies for a vegetarian version.
recipes.title: Yarrow salsa verde

summary.text:
Achillea millefolium, commonly known as yarrow or common yarrow, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae.
Yarrow is native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, being found in Europe, Asia, and North America.
In North America, both native and introduced genotypes, and both diploid and polyploid plants are found.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.; S.: throughout, but more common in drier South Id areas; St.: local; K., Ch., A., C. Naturalised from Europe, Caucasia, Iran, Siberia and the Himalaya, first recorded in 1867.
It was once sown in New Zealand pastures for its tolerance of dry summers and its mineral content, and is still sold in pasture mixtures for organic farming; it becomes a problem weed when a paddock is cultivated and cropped, because its rhizomes survive cultivation (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated).
Other English names recorded in New Zealand include milfoil, nosebleed, sanguinary and thousand seal (Biota of New Zealand); it is also known as woundwort, staunch weed and carpenter's weed (Herbal Academy) — not to be confused with the woundworts (Stachys).
It is common throughout New Zealand and the offshore islands, especially in drier areas, and is readily grazed by stock (Common Weeds of New Zealand, restated).
The genus is named after Achilles, said to have treated his soldiers' wounds with it at Troy; millefolium is Latin for 'thousand-leaved' (NZPCN).

warnings: Do not eat or drink it if you are allergic to plants of the daisy family (Asteraceae), such as chamomile, arnica or marigold.

Skin reactions occur: touching the flowers can, in rare cases, cause an allergic rash with reddening and small blisters, and extended use, as medicine or food, can cause allergic skin rashes or sensitivity to sunlight in some people. (A tested extract of dried leaves and stalks was not phototoxic.)
Not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding: its safety has not been established, and it has a reputation as an abortifacient.

Keep to small, occasional amounts. The essential oil holds a trace of thujone — too little at medicinal doses of the flowers to be judged a risk — but large or frequent doses over a long period may be harmful.
Medicinal use in children under 12 has not been established.
Deadly hemlock is listed as a similar species, and mistaking one for the other can kill. Check the stem and flower heads on every plant — see the lookalike cards.

identification.text:
Tufted or scrambling, prostrate annual; stem more or less glabrous. Leaves sparsely hairy; tendrils simple or branched; leaflets in (3)–4–7–(8) pairs, sometimes alternate, elliptic-oblong, 3–20 mm long; stipules entire or with 1–3, adaxial, basal lobes. Inflorescence much shorter than leaves, 1–(2)-flowered. Peduncle much shorter than flowers. Pedicel 1–2 mm long. Calyx somewhat gibbous at base; calyx teeth unequal; lower teeth more or less equal to tube; upper teeth much shorter than tube. Corolla pale yellow, sometimes tinged purple, 15–30 mm long; limb of standard more or less equal to claw. Pod moderately hairy, brown to black, 3–6-seeded, 25–40 mm long; seeds light brown with dark brown and black blotches.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Flowers or seeds are needed to identify vetches. Yellow vetch is very similar to common vetch (Vicia sativa) but has a yellow corolla and unequal calyx teeth.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers and pods. Yellow vetch's corolla is pale yellow, sometimes tinged purple, and its calyx teeth are unequal: the lower teeth about as long as the calyx tube, the upper ones much shorter. Common vetch's corolla is usually purple, reddish purple or rose, sometimes white or pink, and its calyx teeth are more or less equal. Yellow vetch's pods are moderately hairy and hold 3–6 seeds; common vetch's are more or less hairless or finely downy and hold 5–12. The leaves do not separate them: both have tendrils and several pairs of leaflets, and leaflet sizes overlap, so flowers or seeds are needed. Both grow on Banks Peninsula, the only place yellow vetch is established. Common vetch is eaten (see its page).

summary.text: Yellow vetch (Vicia lutea) is a tufted or scrambling annual of the pea family, Fabaceae, introduced to New Zealand from southern and western Europe to the Caucasus and North Africa and first recorded here in 1904. In New Zealand it is established at several places on Banks Peninsula only. It is very similar to common vetch, and flowers or seeds are needed to tell them apart. It flowers in November and December. It is not a listed pest plant.

warnings: Its only food records are for the seeds: in Spain the unripe seeds were eaten raw as a snack, and the ripe seeds were milled with wheat flour for bread in times of shortage. No study of the seeds' chemistry was found, and vetch seeds can be toxic, so it is not given as food here.

The vetches grown as fodder are generally toxic to people and other animals with a simple stomach, at least if eaten in quantity. Common vetch and broad bean, and probably other vetches, contain compounds that can cause favism in people with G6PD deficiency.
It is very similar to common vetch, which is eaten. Check the flower colour and the calyx teeth before picking any vetch on Banks Peninsula (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
Small tree to about 10 m high (larger in cultivation). Bark peeling in thin scaly strips, dark reddish brown. Trunk often short with main branches arising near the ground and tending to form a dense crown. Shoots green, ribbed. Leaves with short yellowish green petiole, radial on erect shoots, more or less 2-ranked on horizontal shoots. Lamina 1.2–2.5 cm × 1.5–2 mm, sometimes smaller in first leaves of season, dark green, more or less shining above, with 2 broad pale green stomatal bands beneath, revolute; midrib raised on both sides; apex acute or mucronate. Fruit (with aril) 10–15 × 8–11 mm, oblong, crimson; flesh viscid. Seed 5.5–7 mm long, ovoid-ellipsoid, angled, greenish brown.
The seed cones are modified, each cone containing a single seed almost surrounded by a fleshy scale which develops into a soft, bright red berry-like aril. The aril is open at the end. The arils mature 6 to 9 months after pollination.
The aril is gelatinous and very sweet tasting. The male cones are globose, 3–6 mm in diameter, and shed their pollen in early spring. Yews are mostly dioecious with male and female cones on separate trees, but occasional individuals can be variably monoecious, or change sex with time.

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a few needles: yew's have no real scent; Douglas fir's smell of oranges. Turn a shoot over: yew's needles have two broad pale green bands beneath, never silver; Douglas fir's have two whitish, silvery bands. Yew's shoots are green and ribbed; Douglas fir's are light to dark brown with short hairs and end in long, narrow, sharply pointed, shining purplish-brown buds up to 1 cm long. Female yews carry soft crimson berry-like arils 10–15 mm long around a single seed, and yew has no woody cones; Douglas fir carries woody cones 4–10 cm long that hang down, with three-pointed bracts sticking out between the scales. Most yews are male or female trees, so a tree without red arils can still be yew. Needle size and arrangement do not separate them: yew's are 1.2–2.5 cm long and Douglas fir's 1.5–3.8 cm, and both can lie in two flat rows. Douglas fir's needles are used for tea and flavouring (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Douglas fir

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at how the seed sits. On tōtara, the seed (one, sometimes two) sits on top of the swollen, usually red receptacle, which is made of 2–4 scales, acute and free at the tips. On yew, the single seed sits inside a red, fleshy cup (the aril) that almost surrounds it and is open at the end. Look at where each leaf joins the shoot: tōtara's leaves are stalkless, joined by a narrow base; yew's leaves have a short yellowish-green stalk, and its shoots are green and ribbed. Adult tōtara leaves are 3–4 mm wide and yew's 1.5–2 mm, but tōtara's juvenile leaves are only 1–2 mm wide, so width separates only adult foliage. Mature tōtara has thick, stringy, furrowed bark; yew's bark is thin and peels in scaly, dark reddish-brown strips. Both have red, fleshy 'berries' and needle-like leaves of similar length (yew 1.2–2.5 cm, adult tōtara 1.5–3 cm), so colour and leaf length do not separate them. Tōtara's red receptacle is eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Tōtara

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at how the seed sits. On snow tōtara, the seed (one, sometimes two, green when fresh) sits on a receptacle of two acute, red, swollen bracts. On yew, the single seed sits inside a red, fleshy cup (the aril) that almost surrounds it and is open at the end. Look at where each leaf joins the shoot: snow tōtara's leaves are close-set and spirally arranged, rigid, with distinctly thickened margins; yew's leaves have a short yellowish-green stalk, lie more or less in two rows on horizontal shoots, and have two broad pale green bands beneath. Snow tōtara's leaves are 0.5–1.5 cm long and yew's 1.2–2.5 cm, so short leaves point to snow tōtara, but the ranges overlap. Snow tōtara is a prostrate or spreading shrub, sometimes suberect to 3 m, whose branches root where they touch the ground; yew is a small tree to about 10 m, but a young yew can be small. Snow tōtara grows mostly in subalpine scrub, tussock grassland and rock, and yew in modified lowland sites, but snow tōtara also grows in lowland forest in Westland, so where it grows does not prove it. Snow tōtara's receptacle is eaten, on thin evidence (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Snow tōtara

lookalikes.howToTell: Young miro and young yew look alike. Look at where each leaf joins the shoot: miro's leaves are stalkless or nearly so, each leaf blade running straight into the stem; yew's leaves have a short yellowish-green stalk. Miro's shoots are yellow; yew's are green and ribbed. Look at the fruit: miro's is a plum-like drupe up to 20 mm long, red to pink-red or purplish with a waxy bloom, with a single large stone 11–17 mm long enclosed in the flesh; yew's is a red, fleshy cup 10–15 mm long that almost surrounds the seed and is open at the end. Leaf size does not separate them: miro's adult leaves are 1.5–2.5 cm long and 2–3 mm wide, yew's 1.2–2.5 cm long and 1.5–2 mm wide. Miro's fruit flesh is eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Miro

lookalikes.howToTell: Turn a shoot over: yew's needles have two broad pale green bands beneath, never white or silver; grand fir's have two white bands. Yew's shoots are green and ribbed; grand fir's are brownish, with resinous winter buds. Female yews carry soft crimson berry-like arils 10–15 mm long around a single seed, and yew has no woody cones; grand fir carries upright cones that break up on the tree, leaving a bare spike. Most yews are male or female trees, so a tree without red arils can still be yew. Both have flat needles lying in two rows. Grand fir's tips and needles are used for tea and flavouring (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Grand fir

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have short flat needles lying in two rows along the shoot, and their lengths overlap (yew's 12–25 mm, western hemlock's about 8–20 mm). Turn a shoot over: yew's needles have two broad pale green bands, never white or silver; western hemlock's have two conspicuous white bands. Yew's needles end in a point, sometimes a tiny one; western hemlock's are blunt. Yew's shoots are green and ribbed; western hemlock's twigs are hairy and yellowish green, with a small peg where each needle has fallen, and its top and branch tips droop. Female yews carry a soft crimson berry-like aril 10–15 mm long around a single seed, and yew has no woody cones; western hemlock carries small woody cones about 2 cm long that hang down. Most yews are male or female trees, so a tree without red arils can still be yew. Western hemlock's spring tips and inner bark are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Western hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: Pick a needle and look. Yew's needles are flat, 1.2–2.5 cm, dark green above with two broad pale green bands beneath, and often lie in two rows; its shoots are green and ribbed. Norway spruce's needles are stiff and sharp, roughly four-sided so they roll between your fingers, spread all round the shoot and leave a rough woody peg when they fall; its cones are cylindric, usually over 10 cm and hang down. Female yews carry soft crimson arils 10–15 mm long around a single seed, and yew has no woody cones. Norway spruce's young spring tips are used for tea and syrup (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Norway spruce

lookalikes.howToTell: Turn a shoot over: yew's needles have two broad pale green bands beneath, never white or silver; Greek fir's have two conspicuous pale bands. Yew's shoots are green and ribbed; Greek fir's young shoots are pale cream and shiny, with red-brown, very resinous winter buds. Female yews carry soft crimson arils 10–15 mm long around a single seed, and yew has no woody cones; Greek fir carries large upright cones that break up on the tree. Both can have flat needles lying in two rows. Greek fir's tips and needles are used for tea and flavouring (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Greek fir

preparation.text: Eat raw, or cook into jam, jelly or fruit leather. Pull the flesh off each seed by hand, or with the blunt side of a fork, and throw the seed away before the flesh goes near your mouth or the pot. Do not put a whole fruit in your mouth to spit the seed out. Never crush, blend, juice or boil whole fruit to separate the seeds; take every seed out first.

recipes.method: Written for yew. 400 g yew aril flesh, seeds taken out; 1 sweet-sour apple; 1 vanilla pod; 200 g 2:1 jam-setting sugar. Rinse the fruit and pull the flesh off every seed by hand before anything is cooked. Peel, core and chop the apple. Cook the aril flesh with the apple and the vanilla pod for about 20 minutes. Take out the vanilla pod and purée. Stir in the jam-setting sugar, bring to the boil and boil hard for about 4 minutes, then pour hot into sterilised jars.
recipes.title: Yew aril and apple jam

recipes.method: Written for yew. Separate every aril from its seed by hand, using the blunt side of a fork; do not try to boil the seeds out. Put the seeded flesh in a pan with just enough water to cover, bring to the boil and simmer until it reaches a jam-like consistency, which comes quickly because the flesh is very gloopy. Mashed crab apple can be added to help it set, though it dulls the pink colour. If it is too sweet, add lemon juice to taste and simmer again to jam consistency. Spoon into a sterilised jar, lay a circle of greaseproof paper on top and screw on the lid. Eat on sourdough with something sour such as goat’s cheese, or freeze in ice cubes for drinks.
recipes.title: Yew aril jam

recipes.method: Written for wild fruit, yew included. Take the seed out of every yew aril before cooking. Cook the seeded flesh, alone or with other fruit such as chopped crab apples, in a large pan on low heat with just enough water to stop it sticking, until it is thoroughly mushy. Pass it through a fine sieve and add sugar or honey to taste. Spread the purée no more than 3 mm thick on lined baking trays and dry it overnight in a very low oven, no hotter than 50 °C, with the fan on or the door slightly open. Roll the leathers in cling film or cut them up into a sealed tub; they keep a month or two in the fridge.
recipes.title: Yew aril fruit leather

recipes.method: Written for yew. Makes two 10 cm tarts. Before you start: arum (Arum maculatum) is poisonous raw and edible only as flour from well-roasted root; cherry plum kernels contain cyanogenic glycosides (see cherry plum's page); the author himself calls yew berries and cherry plum kernels toxicologically ambiguous foods and the tart 'somewhat extreme and absurd'. Pastry: 150 g arum flour; 50 g sweet chestnut flour; 50 g wild oat flour; 50 g mixed wild grass seed flour; 100 g walnut oil or animal fat, or a mix; 15 ml (1 tbsp) yew aril juice concentrated three times, made from seeded flesh; 15 ml (1 tbsp) verjuice or staghorn sumac extract; a little cold water if needed. Sift the flours into a bowl, rub in the fat or oil with your fingertips until it looks like crumbs, make a well, pour in the verjuice or sumac and the yew syrup, and mix to a smooth dough without overworking it, adding a little cold water if needed. Wrap and chill for a couple of hours. Crème pâtissière: 570 ml cherry plum kernel milk; 1.8 litres water; a large handful of dried, sun-bleached carrageen seaweed; 100 g wild pear juice concentrated five times; 60 g arum flour. Boil the seaweed in the water for 30 minutes, cool slightly, strain through muslin, and simmer the liquid gently until about 280 ml is left; set aside to cool. For the kernel milk, grind two large handfuls of washed, dried cherry plum stones, stir into about 1.1 litres of hot water for a minute, leave 15 minutes, strain, boil the liquid down by half, mix in the pear concentrate and cool. Whisk the cooled kernel milk into the seaweed extract and chill. Topping: 300 g fully ripe yew arils; 5 sweet wild apples; 250 ml (1 cup) wild apple juice; 1 heaped teaspoon of jam and 15 ml (1 tablespoon) water for the glaze. To finish: roll each half of the pastry about 2 mm thick on a work surface dusted with arum flour and line two greased 10 cm loose-bottomed flan tins about 2.5 cm deep, leaving a 0.5 cm overlap that you crimp between finger and thumb. Rest the cases an hour in the fridge or freezer, prick the bases with a fork and bake 15 minutes at 180 °C until barely coloured. Juice three apples; peel, core and thinly slice the other two and stew the slices in the juice for a couple of minutes, then cool. Re-whisk the chilled crème and spread it in the cases, leaving room for the fruit. Take the seed out of each yew aril with tweezers without damaging the seed, and set the arils on the crème in shrinking circles from the edge, leaving a 4 cm circle of crème in the middle. Fan the apple slices over that. Heat the jam with the water until it thickens and brush or drip it over the tops.

summary.text:
Taxus baccata, English yew, is a conifer in the yew family, Taxaceae. It is native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia east to the Himalaya.
In New Zealand it grows wild in the North and South Islands, widespread but often scattered and rarely common, and was first recorded naturalised in 1968. Yew is a very common species in cultivation throughout New Zealand and persists in old gardens long after they have been allowed to revert to scrub or forest. The conspicuous crimson fruits are often eaten and dispersed by birds. All the mature wild plants recorded in the Flora were spreading or bushy small trees; none was the commonly grown Irish yew ('Fastigiata'), a female clone that fruits heavily and whose seeds germinate freely.
A notable Irish yew at Caccia Birch House, Palmerston North, planted about 1920, measured 14.5 m tall in 2012.

warnings: Eat only the red flesh. The seed inside is highly poisonous: chewing or crushing even a few seeds can cause severe heart poisoning, and there is no specific antidote.
A seed swallowed whole is not reliably harmless; it can be broken down in the gut and release the poison.
Never crush, blend, juice or boil whole fruit to separate the seeds. Drying and cooking do not destroy the poison.
The red flesh is not free of yew toxins: it contains small amounts of other yew taxanes, and no safe amount has been measured.
Every other part of the tree is poisonous. The poison acts on the heart, and the lethal dose for an adult is reported to be 50 g of needles. Eating the berries together with leaves has killed people.
Fresh or wilted yew foliage has caused many stock deaths in New Zealand. Dried yew material stays poisonous for several months, so fallen needles and clippings are poisonous too.
Children have died after eating whole yew berries with the seeds chewed. Keep children away from yew.

Symptoms start 1 to 5 hours after eating: vomiting, diarrhoea and stomach cramps, then heart rhythm problems, seizures and collapse. If a seed was chewed or swallowed, or leaves were eaten, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766 immediately.

Young yew can be mistaken for young miro, whose fruit is eaten, and its red fleshy fruit can be mistaken for the edible red receptacles of tōtara and snow tōtara. Check the leaf base and how the seed sits (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
A small to medium-sized tree, up to about 20 m in cultivation, with wide-spreading branches and a fairly dense crown. The bark is thick and fissured, grey on the lower trunk and dark reddish brown or reddish higher up, where it peels readily to show bright orange-brown beneath. The needles come in threes, 13–28 cm long (sometimes 33 cm), very slender and flexible, grass-green, hanging down below the branches. The buds are shining brown, not resinous, and stand prominently upright, often at right angles to the shoot. Mature cones are 6–9 × 3–4 cm when closed, egg-shaped to oblong, light brown, usually curved and lopsided at the base, stalkless or nearly so, several to a cluster and pointing backwards; they stay closed on the tree for several years. The very slender, drooping, grass-green needles and the upright buds set it apart from every other wild pine in New Zealand with needles in twos or threes.
Shoots bluish-white (glaucous) for at least a season, hairless, rough with old leaf bases. Bud scales spreading in the upper part. Needle sheaths persistent, usually 1.5–2.5 cm long on mature needles; resin canals in the middle. Male cones to 1 cm, cylindrical to egg-shaped, crowded around the upturned shoot tips. Young cones stalked, changing from pink to brown as they mature. Cone-scale ends flat apart from a sunken centre with a very small prickle that often falls. Seed small, its wing to about 1.5 cm, broad and lopsided. Both varieties grow here: var. patula has nearly stalkless cones, var. longipedunculata long-stalked ones.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have long needles in threes and lopsided cones that stay closed on the tree; look at how the needles hang. Radiata pine has needles in threes, 6–15 cm, deep or dark green; its cones are lopsided, 6–13 cm, and stay on the tree for years. Mexican weeping pine has very slender, flexible, grass-green needles in threes, 13–28 cm, hanging down below the branches, and shining brown buds standing upright, often at right angles to the shoot; its cones, 6–9 cm, curved and lopsided, point backwards in clusters and stay closed on the tree for years. Radiata pine's seeds and young male cones are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Monterey pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have long needles in threes; look at the needles and the cones. Ponderosa pine has needles in threes, 10–23 cm, stout, rigid and dull green; its stalkless cones open and fall but leave a ring of basal scales on the branch, and the tree is more open. Mexican weeping pine has very slender, flexible, grass-green needles in threes, 13–28 cm, hanging down below the branches, and shining brown buds standing upright, often at right angles to the shoot; its cones, 6–9 cm, curved and lopsided, point backwards in clusters and stay closed on the tree for years. Ponderosa pine's seeds and inner bark are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Ponderosa pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have long, slender needles in threes and grow wild in Rotoehu Forest; look at the needles and the cones. Loblolly pine has needles in threes, 13–21 cm, slender, semi-rigid and bright green; its cones are 7–12 cm, stalkless, with a recurved spine on each scale, and fall whole after opening; its bark is grey on the surface and pinkish beneath. Mexican weeping pine has very slender, flexible, grass-green needles in threes, 13–28 cm, hanging down below the branches, and shining brown buds standing upright, often at right angles to the shoot; its cones, 6–9 cm, curved and lopsided, point backwards in clusters and stay closed on the tree for years. Loblolly pine's inner bark is an emergency food (see its page).

preparation.text: Pick cones while they are still green and soft enough to cut through with a knife; brown, woody or opened cones will not do. Green cones ooze sticky resin, so wear gloves. Look the cones over and throw out any with holes or insects. Smaller cones give a stronger flavour; large ones can be cut up so more fit in the jar.

recipes.method: Pack 225 g (about 500 ml) young green Mexican weeping pine cones and 450 g brown sugar into a 1 litre jar. Leave in a warm, sunny place for 30 days, shaking it now and then. For the first few weeks open the jar occasionally to let out gas, as the mixture may ferment. Scrape the cones and sugar slush into a pot, add 30 ml water, and bring to a brisk simmer for 5–10 minutes, just until the sugar melts (reducing it further makes it crystallise as it cools). Strain, discard the cones and bottle the hot syrup. It keeps best in the fridge once opened. Use it like maple syrup: on pancakes, fresh fruit or soft cheese, or a little in desserts and dressings.
recipes.title: Mugolio (young pine cone syrup)

recipes.method: Put 10 young green Mexican weeping pine cones in a jar and top up with 500 g brown sugar, shaking so the sugar settles round the cones. Close the jar and leave it for about 2 weeks, until all the sugar has turned to syrup. Pass it through a sieve and bottle. Add it to marinades or pour it over pancakes.
recipes.title: No-cook green pine cone syrup

summary.text:
Mexican weeping pine, or patula pine (Pinus patula), is an evergreen pine of the pine family (Pinaceae) from southern Mexico, named for its long, drooping needles. Like other pines, its young green cones can be steeped in sugar for a syrup.
In New Zealand: It was introduced for forestry and first recorded wild in 1957. It is grown for timber in several state forests and has become popular in parks and gardens. Around Rotoehu Forest in the Bay of Plenty and Golden Downs in Nelson it regenerates freely where the canopy is open and has spread into nearby land, and at Rotoehu it has colonised many sites; it is also wild along roads at Rai Saddle, between Nelson and Marlborough, and in the upper Wairau valley in Marlborough. Both of its varieties are naturalised here. Its seed is spread by the wind.
It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds and in the Northland, Greater Wellington, Tasman-Nelson and Marlborough regional pest plans.

method.text: Needles: simmered, not boiled, in a covered pot of water until the water has coloured, then lifted out; wet fabric is kept in the bath at a gentle heat for about an hour, longer for a stronger colour. Scoured hemp with no mordant, dyed in an aluminium pot, came out a soft mauve-clay, and one bath coloured several pieces. The needles are also listed as giving a tan or green dye. Cones: soaked in water for a day to soften, cut into pieces, boiled for up to four hours (a lower heat loses less dye) and strained through muslin; cotton dyed for an hour and left to cool in the bath came out beige to light brown, mordanted or not, and the bath was used again the next day. On cotton and silk, cone tannins give beiges with orange and pink hues.

recipes.method: A box of pine needles about 30 × 20 cm; a 20-litre aluminium pot of cool water; a piece of hemp fabric about 1 × 1.5 m. Scour the fabric in a 40 °C wash with fragrance-free powder and about 250 ml (a cup) of baking soda, no fabric softener, then soak it in water for about an hour. Put the needles in the pot of water, cover, and bring to a simmer without boiling; turn the heat down a little and keep it there until the water has the colour you want. Lift out the needles with a fine sieve (straining through muslin gives a more even colour). Add the wet fabric, push out the air bubbles with a wooden spoon so it is all under, and keep it at a gentle heat for about an hour, stirring now and then; leave it longer for a stronger colour. Wring it out, wash and rinse it with fragrance-free powder and no softener, and dry it out of direct sun. The same bath dyes several pieces in turn.

method.text: Tinder: needles left to dry for a season, or dry ones from the forest floor, catch fire easily, more so with a little pitch. Fatwood, the dense amber wood soaked with resin in the stumps and lower branches of dead pines, is shaved into thin slivers and lit with a spark or flame, and still lights when damp. Glue: resin that has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground is gathered rather than cut from the tree, melted (on a hot rock beside a fire, for example), mixed with finely ground ash or powdered charcoal and left to cool; it is reheated to use. A little water softens old pitch into a soft glue, and pine shavings or sawdust worked into it make a wood filler. Oil or strong alcohol takes pitch off your hands. Incense: needles tied into a bundle with natural twine and dried for about two weeks. Cleaner: chopped needles covered with vinegar in a glass jar, with baking paper under the lid so it does not corrode, left for two weeks and strained; the vinegar is mixed with baking soda and castile soap for cleaning.

method.text: Resin is gathered from what has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground rather than cut from the tree, at any time of year. It sticks to everything, so keep a knife and jar just for it; oil, then soap, takes it off your hands, and rubbing alcohol off clothes. Large lumps melt faster if frozen and broken up with a hammer inside a thick paper bag. Warmed with an equal amount of beeswax, mixed and left to set in its container, it makes a simple balm; melted into an oil, strained and firmed with beeswax it makes a balm for dry or cracked skin, lips and hands.

recipes.method: 60 ml (¼ cup) pine resin; 125 ml (½ cup) oil such as olive or almond; 15–30 g grated beeswax. Melt the resin in the oil in a double boiler over a low heat. Strain through a coffee filter or a strainer, return to the double boiler, add the beeswax and heat gently until it has melted. Pour into tins or jars and store somewhere cool and dark.
recipes.title: Pine resin balm

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) pine resin; 250 ml (1 cup) olive oil, or another oil safe for skin; 125–190 ml (½–¾ cup) grated beeswax; 35 drops rosemary essential oil. Put the resin and oil in a glass jar in the top of a double boiler and simmer, stirring, until the resin melts; this can take several hours. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine sieve and return it to the double boiler. For every 250 ml of resin and oil add 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) grated beeswax (more gives a firmer balm) and heat gently until it melts. Pour into jars or tins, stir 5 drops of the essential oil into each, and put the lids on straight away so the scent stays in. Leave to cool and set, and store somewhere cool and dark. Use it on dry or cracked skin, as a lip or hand balm, or overnight on the face.
recipes.title: Pine resin and olive oil balm

habitat.text: Scrub and modified forest, often among native scrub on ridges, banks and in geothermal valleys near plantations, where it escapes now and then from cultivation. It grows best in light, well-drained sandy or gravelly soil, will grow in poor soil, needs full light, tolerates drought but not air pollution, and dislikes poorly drained ground.

identification.text:
A small to large tree, up to about 50 m, pyramidal until well after maturity, the crown becoming irregular later. The bark stays smooth and greyish green until the tree is fully grown, then roughens towards the base; on old trees it is fissured into long, rectangular plates. The needles come in fives, 4–13 cm long and very slender, soft and tending to droop, green above and bluish below, in dense masses towards the branch ends. Mature cones hang singly on curved stalks up to 2 cm long; they are 7–16 cm long and 3–5 cm wide when open, cylindrical, often curved, tapering towards the tip, yellowish brown and very resinous, with thin, flexible, round-ended scales. They shed their seeds and then fall whole. The mainly smooth trunk and the soft needles in fives, green above and bluish below, set it apart from every other wild pine in New Zealand, all of which have needles in twos or threes.
Shoots brown or greenish brown, finely hairy at first, later hairless except for a tuft of hairs below each needle bundle. Buds narrow egg-shaped, greenish, not resinous, their scales with free, finely pointed tips. Needle sheaths fall by midsummer; needles broadly triangular in cross-section, with resin canals at the edges. Male cones under 1 cm, narrowly cylindrical. Young cones stalked and cylindrical. Cone-scale ends rounded, without a prickle. Seeds 5–6 mm, with a narrow wing to about 1.5 cm. Bhutan pine (Pinus wallichiana), common in parks and domains but not known to run wild, is very similar but has hairless shoots and longer needles and cones.

preparation.text: Use fresh needles for tea or a soda; for a flavoured sugar or salt, let them dry on a towel for a few hours first. Pick male cones while they are still firm and unopened; they taste sweet and not resinous, and were boiled as a flavouring or stewed with meat. The seeds are only about 6 mm long and fiddly to gather, and are mostly used as a flavouring; the cones shed them soon after opening. The soft white inner bark was separated from the hard, dark outer bark and eaten fresh, or dried and pounded into a flour to thicken soups or stretch other flour. For syrup, pick cones while they are still green and soft enough to cut through with a knife; brown, woody or opened cones will not do. Green cones ooze sticky resin, so wear gloves. Throw out any with holes or insects.

recipes.method: Rinse fresh eastern white pine needles gently under cool, unchlorinated water (chlorinated tap water kills the wild yeast). Pack them into a 1 litre jar, about 500–750 ml of needles, and add an equal volume of unchlorinated water with 15 g sugar for every 250 ml of water (white or brown sugar or honey; artificial sweeteners will not ferment). Cap the jar, leaving a little headspace, shake gently to dissolve the sugar and leave it somewhere warm. Bubbles should appear after a day. After 3–4 days strain off the needles and drink it over ice straight away, as the fizz does not last.
recipes.title: White pine needle soda

recipes.method: Spread 60 ml fresh eastern white pine needles on a towel for a few hours until dry, or the sugar will clump. Snip them roughly with scissors, then pulse with 100 g white sugar in a clean coffee or spice grinder until the needles are a fine green dust and the sugar turns bright green. Sift out any woody bits if you want it fine for baking. Use it in place of a quarter of the sugar in shortbread, to rim a glass, or sprinkled over coffee.
recipes.title: White pine sugar

recipes.method: Dry and snip 60 ml fresh eastern white pine needles as for pine sugar, then pulse with 125 ml coarse sea salt just until the needles are broken down and coat the salt crystals, like green sand; do not powder the salt. Sprinkle it over roast vegetables once they come out of the oven, on fried eggs, or on creamy soups just before serving.
recipes.title: White pine salt

recipes.method: Chop 125 ml fresh eastern white pine needles very finely in a food processor or spice grinder and pick out any long fibres or whole needles. Beat them with 225 g softened unsalted butter, 100 g sugar, 10 ml grated orange zest and a pinch of salt until creamy. Work in 250 g plain flour a little at a time to make a dough. Divide it between two sheets of baking paper and roll each into a log about 4 cm across; wrap and freeze for 15 minutes. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Cut the logs into 6 mm slices, lay them 2.5 cm apart on lined trays and bake for about 10 minutes, until the edges are golden. Cool on a rack. Makes about 48.
recipes.title: White pine shortbread

recipes.method: Pack 225 g (about 500 ml) young green eastern white pine cones and 450 g brown sugar into a 1 litre jar. Leave in a warm, sunny place for 30 days, shaking it now and then. For the first few weeks open the jar occasionally to let out gas, as the mixture may ferment. Scrape the cones and sugar slush into a pot, add 30 ml water, and bring to a brisk simmer for 5–10 minutes, just until the sugar melts (reducing it further makes it crystallise as it cools). Strain, discard the cones and bottle the hot syrup. It keeps best in the fridge once opened. Use it like maple syrup: on pancakes, fresh fruit or soft cheese, or a little in desserts and dressings.
recipes.title: Mugolio (young pine cone syrup)

recipes.method: Put 10 young green eastern white pine cones in a jar and top up with 500 g brown sugar, shaking so the sugar settles round the cones. Close the jar and leave it for about 2 weeks, until all the sugar has turned to syrup. Pass it through a sieve and bottle. Add it to marinades or pour it over pancakes.
recipes.title: No-cook green pine cone syrup

summary.text:
Eastern white pine, also called strobus pine or Weymouth pine (Pinus strobus), is an evergreen pine of the pine family (Pinaceae) from eastern North America, the only wild pine here with soft needles in fives. Its fresh needles make a tea or soda, its unopened male cones and small seeds are eaten, its inner bark was a famine flour, and like other pines its young green cones can be steeped in sugar for a syrup.
In New Zealand: It was introduced for forestry and first recorded wild in 1957. It is grown mostly in state forests, especially around Rotorua, and is an occasional escape from them: it runs wild among scrub in the Waimangu Valley, on Rainbow Mountain and around Waiotapu, near Stanley Brook in Nelson, around Hanmer in North Canterbury, and at Makahu Saddle in the Kaweka Range, where seedlings and saplings are abundant. Its seed is spread by the wind.
It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds and in the Northland and Greater Wellington regional pest plans.

method.text: Needles: simmered, not boiled, in a covered pot of water until the water has coloured, then lifted out; wet fabric is kept in the bath at a gentle heat for about an hour, longer for a stronger colour. Scoured hemp with no mordant, dyed in an aluminium pot, came out a soft mauve-clay, and one bath coloured several pieces. The needles are also listed as giving a tan or green dye. Cones: soaked in water for a day to soften, cut into pieces, boiled for up to four hours (a lower heat loses less dye) and strained through muslin; cotton dyed for an hour and left to cool in the bath came out beige to light brown, mordanted or not, and the bath was used again the next day. On cotton and silk, cone tannins give beiges with orange and pink hues.

recipes.method: A box of pine needles about 30 × 20 cm; a 20-litre aluminium pot of cool water; a piece of hemp fabric about 1 × 1.5 m. Scour the fabric in a 40 °C wash with fragrance-free powder and about 250 ml (a cup) of baking soda, no fabric softener, then soak it in water for about an hour. Put the needles in the pot of water, cover, and bring to a simmer without boiling; turn the heat down a little and keep it there until the water has the colour you want. Lift out the needles with a fine sieve (straining through muslin gives a more even colour). Add the wet fabric, push out the air bubbles with a wooden spoon so it is all under, and keep it at a gentle heat for about an hour, stirring now and then; leave it longer for a stronger colour. Wring it out, wash and rinse it with fragrance-free powder and no softener, and dry it out of direct sun. The same bath dyes several pieces in turn.

method.text: Tinder: needles left to dry for a season, or dry ones from the forest floor, catch fire easily, more so with a little pitch. Fatwood, the dense amber wood soaked with resin in the stumps and lower branches of dead pines, is shaved into thin slivers and lit with a spark or flame, and still lights when damp. Glue: resin that has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground is gathered rather than cut from the tree, melted (on a hot rock beside a fire, for example), mixed with finely ground ash or powdered charcoal and left to cool; it is reheated to use. A little water softens old pitch into a soft glue, and pine shavings or sawdust worked into it make a wood filler. Oil or strong alcohol takes pitch off your hands. Incense: needles tied into a bundle with natural twine and dried for about two weeks. Cleaner: chopped needles covered with vinegar in a glass jar, with baking paper under the lid so it does not corrode, left for two weeks and strained; the vinegar is mixed with baking soda and castile soap for cleaning.

method.text: Resin is gathered from what has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground rather than cut from the tree, at any time of year. It sticks to everything, so keep a knife and jar just for it; oil, then soap, takes it off your hands, and rubbing alcohol off clothes. Large lumps melt faster if frozen and broken up with a hammer inside a thick paper bag. Warmed with an equal amount of beeswax, mixed and left to set in its container, it makes a simple balm; melted into an oil, strained and firmed with beeswax it makes a balm for dry or cracked skin, lips and hands.

recipes.method: 60 ml (¼ cup) pine resin; 125 ml (½ cup) oil such as olive or almond; 15–30 g grated beeswax. Melt the resin in the oil in a double boiler over a low heat. Strain through a coffee filter or a strainer, return to the double boiler, add the beeswax and heat gently until it has melted. Pour into tins or jars and store somewhere cool and dark.
recipes.title: Pine resin balm

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) pine resin; 250 ml (1 cup) olive oil, or another oil safe for skin; 125–190 ml (½–¾ cup) grated beeswax; 35 drops rosemary essential oil. Put the resin and oil in a glass jar in the top of a double boiler and simmer, stirring, until the resin melts; this can take several hours. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine sieve and return it to the double boiler. For every 250 ml of resin and oil add 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) grated beeswax (more gives a firmer balm) and heat gently until it melts. Pour into jars or tins, stir 5 drops of the essential oil into each, and put the lids on straight away so the scent stays in. Leave to cool and set, and store somewhere cool and dark. Use it on dry or cracked skin, as a lip or hand balm, or overnight on the face.
recipes.title: Pine resin and olive oil balm

identification.text:
A small to medium-sized tree, up to about 15 m (taller in cultivation), often lopsided, with an open crown of rather slender, wide-spreading grey branches. The bark on mature trunks is fissured, grey outside and reddish brown beneath. The needles come in pairs, mostly 4–12 cm long (2–17 cm) and about 1 mm wide, rather flexible and greyish green. The buds are not resinous, with dark reddish-brown scales curled back and fringed with white. The cones are the surest sign: 6.5–11 × 3.5–4.5 cm when closed, cone-shaped, nearly symmetrical and brown, each on a stout stalk 1–3 cm long bent back so the cone points back along the branch; they stay closed on the tree for several years.
Shoots brownish grey or bluish-grey, hairless, staying smooth for some years. Needle sheaths short on mature needles. Male cones 5–8 mm, broadly cylindrical to nearly round, sometimes crimson. Young cones stalked, with blunt or rounded scales, crimson when young on Banks Peninsula trees. Cone-scale ends flat or with a raised, keeled centre, without a prickle. Seed wing large and broad, 1.5–3 cm. Its trees vary a good deal in New Zealand, but the cones on their stout, bent-back stalks pick it out.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have long needles in pairs and buds with reddish scales curled back and fringed with white, and both keep their cones on the tree for years; look at the needles, bark and cone stalk. Maritime pine has stiff, sharp needles about 2 mm wide, dull green, 6–17 cm long; mature bark deeply fissured into smooth, shining reddish-brown plates; and large cones, 7–15 cm, stalkless or nearly so, with a prickle on each scale. Aleppo pine has slender, flexible needles about 1 mm wide, greyish green, mostly 4–12 cm long; rough, fissured grey bark; and cones 6.5–11 cm on a stout stalk 1–3 cm long, bent back along the branch, with no prickle on the scales. Maritime pine's seeds and young green cones are eaten (see its page).

preparation.text:
Seeds: the ripe cones stay closed on the tree for years, so the seeds must be freed with heat. In Tunisia closed cones are cut from the tree and heated (in earth ovens, for two days) until they turn brown and their scales open, then struck and the seeds sifted out. The seeds are small and dark grey to almost black. Clean them of grit and husk, dry them, then grind them, wet or dry, and work them through a very fine sieve or cloth with cold water, pressing hard, until the water runs clear; the dark liquid carries the flavour and the pulp is thrown away. The recipe here cooks the strained liquid straight away.
Young cones: pick them while still green and soft enough to cut through with a knife; brown, woody or opened cones will not do. Green cones ooze sticky resin, so wear gloves, and throw out any with holes or insects.

recipes.method: Makes 8 cups. Whisk 250 g ground Aleppo pine seeds into 1 litre cold water for 2 minutes, then pour through a very fine sieve (or one lined with a clean cloth) into a heavy pan, pressing the pulp hard with a ladle. Return the pulp to the bowl with another 500 ml water, stir and strain again; throw the pulp away. Whisk 100 g flour and 150 g sugar into the cold liquid until smooth, then cook over medium heat for about 30 minutes, stirring all the time and scraping the bottom, until it is as thick as a soft purée, comes away from the pan and small drops of oil shine on top. Fill 8 cups two-thirds full and leave to set for about 20 minutes. For the custard, whisk 2 egg yolks with 60 g sugar, 8 g vanilla sugar and 30 g cornflour, loosen with a little of 500 ml cold milk, then heat the rest of the milk almost to the boil, whisk it in, and thicken over low heat for 1 minute. Cool it to lukewarm and pour it gently over the back of a spoon onto the cream, about 1 cm deep. Chill for at least 2 hours. Just before serving, toast 40 g almonds and 30 g hazelnuts in a dry pan for 5 minutes, chop them with 30 g unsalted pistachios and scatter over.
recipes.title: Assidat zgougou (Aleppo pine seed cream)

recipes.method: Pack 225 g (about 500 ml) young green Aleppo pine cones and 450 g brown sugar into a 1 litre jar. Leave in a warm, sunny place for 30 days, shaking it now and then. For the first few weeks open the jar occasionally to let out gas, as the mixture may ferment. Scrape the cones and sugar slush into a pot, add 30 ml water, and bring to a brisk simmer for 5–10 minutes, just until the sugar melts (reducing it further makes it crystallise as it cools). Strain, discard the cones and bottle the hot syrup. It keeps best in the fridge once opened. Use it like maple syrup: on pancakes, fresh fruit or soft cheese, or a little in desserts and dressings.
recipes.title: Mugolio (young pine cone syrup)

recipes.method: Put 10 young green Aleppo pine cones in a jar and top up with 500 g brown sugar, shaking so the sugar settles round the cones. Close the jar and leave it for about 2 weeks, until all the sugar has turned to syrup. Pass it through a sieve and bottle. Add it to marinades or pour it over pancakes.

No human poison or toxic claim for Pinus halepensis was found (searched 23/11/2026): PFAF's Known Hazards is the genus-wide dermatitis line plus its own single-source allergy, asthma and stomach line; Massey University's isocupressic acid table (https://poisonousplants.massey.ac.nz/plantToxins/isocupr.html, retrieved 23/11/2026) does not list it; a web search for human or livestock toxicity found plant-care pages calling it non-toxic and a mouse and rat study of cold-pressed seed oil reporting no deaths or toxic signs at up to 5000 mg/kg (PubMed 35613671, known from a search summary only, not read). Safety point not made a warning: Minervini et al. 2020 say the traditional method rests the ground seeds in water for 24 h at room temperature, where they ferment of their own accord, and that zgougou 'hides health risks due to eventual pathogenic microorganisms and derived toxins' (they found coliform Enterobacter dominant); a single research paper, not a regulator, and the recipe here strains and cooks the liquid straight away, without the rest. The resin is not given as an edible part: chewing it is PFAF's alone.

summary.text:
Aleppo pine, or Jerusalem pine (Pinus halepensis), is an evergreen pine of the pine family (Pinaceae) from the Mediterranean. In Tunisia its small dark seeds are ground and strained for assidat zgougou, a pudding first made in the famine of the 1860s and now eaten for the Prophet's birthday, and its resin flavours the Greek wine retsina. Like other pines, its young green cones can be steeped in sugar for a syrup.
In New Zealand: The name was mentioned by a Christchurch gardener in 1865, and the tree has been planted in many places from Northland southwards, above all in parks, domains and cemeteries. Most of New Zealand's Anzac pines, planted to remember the Gallipoli campaign, are Aleppo pines, some grown from seed brought back from the Gallipoli area after the First World War; the true Lone Pine was a Turkish red pine. It was first recorded wild in 1925 and is locally common on open, sunny coastal slopes and sea cliffs, from Mangonui south to Auckland and the inner Hauraki Gulf islands, and at Diamond Harbour on Banks Peninsula. Its seed is spread by the wind.
It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds and in the Northland and Greater Wellington regional pest plans.

method.text: Needles: simmered, not boiled, in a covered pot of water until the water has coloured, then lifted out; wet fabric is kept in the bath at a gentle heat for about an hour, longer for a stronger colour. Scoured hemp with no mordant, dyed in an aluminium pot, came out a soft mauve-clay, and one bath coloured several pieces. The needles are also listed as giving a tan or green dye. Cones: soaked in water for a day to soften, cut into pieces, boiled for up to four hours (a lower heat loses less dye) and strained through muslin; cotton dyed for an hour and left to cool in the bath came out beige to light brown, mordanted or not, and the bath was used again the next day. On cotton and silk, cone tannins give beiges with orange and pink hues. Bark: in Marche, Italy, a decoction of the bark dyed fishermen's nets reddish until the Second World War.

recipes.method: A box of pine needles about 30 × 20 cm; a 20-litre aluminium pot of cool water; a piece of hemp fabric about 1 × 1.5 m. Scour the fabric in a 40 °C wash with fragrance-free powder and about 250 ml (a cup) of baking soda, no fabric softener, then soak it in water for about an hour. Put the needles in the pot of water, cover, and bring to a simmer without boiling; turn the heat down a little and keep it there until the water has the colour you want. Lift out the needles with a fine sieve (straining through muslin gives a more even colour). Add the wet fabric, push out the air bubbles with a wooden spoon so it is all under, and keep it at a gentle heat for about an hour, stirring now and then; leave it longer for a stronger colour. Wring it out, wash and rinse it with fragrance-free powder and no softener, and dry it out of direct sun. The same bath dyes several pieces in turn.

method.text: Tinder: needles left to dry for a season, or dry ones from the forest floor, catch fire easily, more so with a little pitch. Fatwood, the dense amber wood soaked with resin in the stumps and lower branches of dead pines, is shaved into thin slivers and lit with a spark or flame, and still lights when damp. Glue: resin that has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground is gathered rather than cut from the tree, melted (on a hot rock beside a fire, for example), mixed with finely ground ash or powdered charcoal and left to cool; it is reheated to use. A little water softens old pitch into a soft glue, and pine shavings or sawdust worked into it make a wood filler. Oil or strong alcohol takes pitch off your hands. Incense: needles tied into a bundle with natural twine and dried for about two weeks. Cleaner: chopped needles covered with vinegar in a glass jar, with baking paper under the lid so it does not corrode, left for two weeks and strained; the vinegar is mixed with baking soda and castile soap for cleaning.

method.text: Resin is gathered from what has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground rather than cut from the tree, at any time of year. It sticks to everything, so keep a knife and jar just for it; oil, then soap, takes it off your hands, and rubbing alcohol off clothes. Large lumps melt faster if frozen and broken up with a hammer inside a thick paper bag. Warmed with an equal amount of beeswax, mixed and left to set in its container, it makes a simple balm; melted into an oil, strained and firmed with beeswax it makes a balm for dry or cracked skin, lips and hands.

recipes.method: 60 ml (¼ cup) pine resin; 125 ml (½ cup) oil such as olive or almond; 15–30 g grated beeswax. Melt the resin in the oil in a double boiler over a low heat. Strain through a coffee filter or a strainer, return to the double boiler, add the beeswax and heat gently until it has melted. Pour into tins or jars and store somewhere cool and dark.
recipes.title: Pine resin balm

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) pine resin; 250 ml (1 cup) olive oil, or another oil safe for skin; 125–190 ml (½–¾ cup) grated beeswax; 35 drops rosemary essential oil. Put the resin and oil in a glass jar in the top of a double boiler and simmer, stirring, until the resin melts; this can take several hours. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine sieve and return it to the double boiler. For every 250 ml of resin and oil add 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) grated beeswax (more gives a firmer balm) and heat gently until it melts. Pour into jars or tins, stir 5 drops of the essential oil into each, and put the lids on straight away so the scent stays in. Leave to cool and set, and store somewhere cool and dark. Use it on dry or cracked skin, as a lip or hand balm, or overnight on the face.

identification.text:
A medium-sized to large tree with a rather open crown, the stout trunk bare of branches for most of its length. The bark on mature trees is thick and deeply fissured into small irregular plates with smooth, shining, dark red or reddish-brown faces; this is not obvious until the tree is fully mature. The needles come in pairs, 6–17 cm long (up to 26 cm) and about 2 mm wide (looking narrower because the edges curl in), dull green, stiff and sharp-pointed. The buds are large, sometimes over 4 cm, not resinous, with dark reddish scales curled back and strongly fringed with white. The mature cones are large, 7–15 × 4–6 cm when closed, cylindrical-egg-shaped, nearly symmetrical and shining brown, stalkless or nearly so, with a prickle on each scale; they often stay on the tree for several years.
Shoots deep brown, somewhat shining, hairless, rough with old leaf bases. Needle sheaths 5–10 mm on older needles; resin canals in the middle. Young and juvenile needles strongly bluish-white (glaucous) and finely toothed. Male cones under 1.5 cm, egg-shaped. Young cones stalkless, prominent and broadly egg-shaped, purple on young Auckland trees. Cone-scale ends diamond-shaped and keeled. Seed wing lopsided, to 2.5 cm (3 cm). Trees here vary a good deal in needle length and cone size.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have long needles in pairs and buds with reddish scales curled back and fringed with white, and both keep their cones on the tree for years; look at the needles, bark and cone stalk. Aleppo pine has slender, flexible needles about 1 mm wide, greyish green, mostly 4–12 cm long; rough, fissured grey bark; and cones 6.5–11 cm on a stout stalk 1–3 cm long, bent back along the branch, with no prickle on the scales. Maritime pine has stiff, sharp needles about 2 mm wide, dull green, 6–17 cm long; mature bark deeply fissured into smooth, shining reddish-brown plates; and large cones, 7–15 cm, stalkless or nearly so, with a prickle on each scale. Aleppo pine's seeds and young green cones are eaten (see its page).

preparation.text:
Seeds: the ripe cones often stay on the tree for several years. The seeds are about 1 cm long, rich in oil and taste of resin, and can be eaten raw or cooked.
Young cones: pick them while still green and soft enough to cut through with a knife; brown, woody or opened cones will not do. Green cones ooze sticky resin, so wear gloves, and throw out any with holes or insects.

recipes.method: Pack 225 g (about 500 ml) young green maritime pine cones and 450 g brown sugar into a 1 litre jar. Leave in a warm, sunny place for 30 days, shaking it now and then. For the first few weeks open the jar occasionally to let out gas, as the mixture may ferment. Scrape the cones and sugar slush into a pot, add 30 ml water, and bring to a brisk simmer for 5–10 minutes, just until the sugar melts (reducing it further makes it crystallise as it cools). Strain, discard the cones and bottle the hot syrup. It keeps best in the fridge once opened. Use it like maple syrup: on pancakes, fresh fruit or soft cheese, or a little in desserts and dressings.
recipes.title: Mugolio (young pine cone syrup)

recipes.method: Put 10 young green maritime pine cones in a jar and top up with 500 g brown sugar, shaking so the sugar settles round the cones. Close the jar and leave it for about 2 weeks, until all the sugar has turned to syrup. Pass it through a sieve and bottle. Add it to marinades or pour it over pancakes.
recipes.title: No-cook green pine cone syrup

Caution careRequired 23/11/2026: seeds on two records naming this species — Plants For A Future, 'Pinus pinaster' (https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Pinus+pinaster, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026 ('Seed - raw or cooked. Rich in oil, it has a resinous flavour. The seed is about 1cm long[200]') and The Agroforestry Research Trust, 'Pinus pinaster – Maritime Pine' (seed listing, https://www.agroforestry.co.uk/product/pinus-pinaster/), retrieved 23/11/2026 ('Bears edible seeds, 10 mm (0.4") long'); Useful Temperate Plants (Ken Fern), 'Pinus pinaster' (https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Pinus+pinaster), retrieved 23/11/2026 repeats PFAF and is the same source. The Agroforestry Research Trust's line may rest on the same reference as PFAF's (the 10 mm figure matches), so it is the weaker of the two. Pages saying the seeds are not eaten (a supplement shop and a French tree list, known from a search summary only, not read) mean that commercial pine nuts come from stone pine; they make no toxic claim. Young green cones for syrup on three genus-wide records, which count for every pine without a toxic claim of its own (owner 23/11/2026: 'yes, unless there is a poison or toxic claim for that species') — Alan Bergo, Forager Chef, 'Mugolio: Pine Cone Syrup' (published 23/10/2020, modified 31/03/2026), https://foragerchef.com/mugolio-pine-cone-syrup/ (live page behind a bot check; read from the Wayback Machine copy), restated, retrieved 23/11/2026; Ellen Zachos, Backyard Forager, 'Mugolio' (18/11/2023), https://backyardforager.com/mugolio/, restated, retrieved 23/11/2026; James, Totally Wild UK, 'Mugolio Recipe: Green Pine Cone Syrup' (18/07/2022), https://totallywilduk.co.uk/2022/07/18/green-pine-cone-syrup-recipe/, restated, retrieved 23/11/2026. No human poison or toxic claim for Pinus pinaster was found (searched 23/11/2026): PFAF's Known Hazards is the genus-wide dermatitis line plus its own single-source allergy, asthma and stomach line (not a warning, as on eastern-white-pine); Massey University's isocupressic acid table (https://poisonousplants.massey.ac.nz/plantToxins/isocupr.html, retrieved 23/11/2026) does not name it; a web search for toxicity and the cattle-abortion toxin found nothing naming it.

Months [] 23/11/2026: no New Zealand source dates either part. PFAF's 'seeds ripen in April' and Forager Chef's 'spring or early summer' for young cones are northern-hemisphere seasons, not shifted; and the Flora says the mature cones often stay on the tree for several years.

IV (Webb, Sykes & Garnock-Jones 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY-NC-SA), 'Pinus pinaster Aiton' (https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/8c49e8a6-d761-4ba1-b1c2-3493e8346a9f), retrieved 23/11/2026 — abbreviations spelled out, restated; NZ Plant Conservation Network, 'Pinus pinaster' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/pinus-pinaster/, all rights reserved, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026; Department of Conservation, Weeds database 'Pinus pinaster' (https://weeds.doc.govt.nz/species/pinus-pinaster, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026; Herbarium sheets (GBIF New Zealand preserved specimens, 175 records, retrieved 23/11/2026; filtered for wild notes, the extra places opened on scd.landcareresearch.co.nz): CHR 644143 (Te Mamaku / Ruby Bay, Nelson, 11/01/2018: 'Naturalised at roadside'), NZFRI 33135 (Wainui Conservation Area near Works Road, northern Bay of Plenty, 02/04/2021: 'Occasional seedling in road edge short scrub'), CHR 418858 (Waikumete Cemetery, Glen Eden, Auckland, 31/10/1984: 'Scrub with groves of regenerating eucalypts & pines on old kauri gumland', 'Spontaneous tree'; 'Young female cone purple'), NZFRI 18478 (Rotorua lakefront, 1989: 'Scrubland on lakeshore ... Adventive'), NZFRI 11247 (Broadlands, 1981: 'Adventive - invading scrub around thermal area'), and the Hanmer-area sheets CHR 455663, 455730, 455731 and 439917 (1987–1988: roadside banks and Waiau terrace scrub, 'Adventive'). All lie in regions the Flora already names; Ruby Bay and Wainui add places, not regions. The rest are plantations, parks, shelterbelts, gardens and arboretums.. The Flora's range is Northland, Auckland, Coromandel Peninsula and Rotorua in the North Island, and north-west Nelson, north Canterbury (Hanmer area) and Port Levy (Banks Peninsula) in the South; habitat 'Scrub, open places such as grassy slopes, cliff faces'; cultivated in most parts of the country in plantations, parks, domains, shelterbelts and gardens; long naturalised and probably the first conifer brought to New Zealand (P. novazaelandica Don, described in 1830, was based on maritime pine); probably wild in more places than those listed, as it escapes readily; in warmer parts of the North Island, especially Auckland and the Waiotapu area near Rotorua, fairly large areas of open scrub are dominated by it, an aggressive coloniser that thrives on poor soils and regenerates very prolifically after fire. NZPCN (Timmins & MacKenzie 1995; Atkinson 1997): coastal and lowland, low-fertility sites; shrubland, tussockland, cliff, bluff and coastal communities; tolerant of drought, partial shade and frost, not of poor drainage or dense shade; regenerates after fire near a seed source.

Warnings 23/11/2026: the four conifer warnings on monterey-pine apply and are carried over — pregnancy and allergy (Mark Williams, Galloway Wild Foods, 'Forager's Guide to Conifers' (15/02/2021), https://gallowaywildfoods.com/foragers-guide-to-conifers/ (as cited on scots-pine, retrieved 23/11/2026)), dermatitis (Plants For A Future, 'Pinus pinaster' (https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Pinus+pinaster, restated), retrieved 23/11/2026, Known Hazards: 'The wood, sawdust and resins from various species of pine can cause dermatitis in sensitive people[222]') and sprayed trees (Wilding Pines (National Wilding Conifer Control Programme), 'Controlling wilding pines', https://www.wildingpines.nz/controlling-wilding-pines, retrieved 05/11/2026 (cited on monterey-pine)).

summary.text:
Maritime pine, or cluster pine (Pinus pinaster), is an evergreen pine of the pine family (Pinaceae) from the western Mediterranean and south-western Europe, with handsome bark of small shining reddish-brown plates. Its oily seeds can be eaten, though they taste of resin, and like other pines its young green cones can be steeped in sugar for a syrup.
In New Zealand: It was probably the first conifer brought here, and was already growing well by 1830. It has been planted in most parts of the country, in plantations, parks, domains, shelterbelts and gardens, and escapes readily. It grows wild in Northland, Auckland, the Coromandel Peninsula, around Rotorua and in the northern Bay of Plenty, and in the South Island around Nelson, near Hanmer and at Port Levy on Banks Peninsula. In warmer parts of the North Island, especially around Auckland and Waiotapu near Rotorua, it dominates large areas of open scrub on poor soils and comes back thickly after fire. Its seed is spread by the wind.
It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds and in the regional pest plans of most of the country, from Northland to Southland.

method.text: Needles: simmered, not boiled, in a covered pot of water until the water has coloured, then lifted out; wet fabric is kept in the bath at a gentle heat for about an hour, longer for a stronger colour. Scoured hemp with no mordant, dyed in an aluminium pot, came out a soft mauve-clay, and one bath coloured several pieces. The needles are also listed as giving a tan or green dye. Cones: soaked in water for a day to soften, cut into pieces, boiled for up to four hours (a lower heat loses less dye) and strained through muslin; cotton dyed for an hour and left to cool in the bath came out beige to light brown, mordanted or not, and the bath was used again the next day. On cotton and silk, cone tannins give beiges with orange and pink hues. Bark: in Corsica this pine was used to dye fishing nets, as Aleppo pine bark was in Italy.

recipes.method: A box of pine needles about 30 × 20 cm; a 20-litre aluminium pot of cool water; a piece of hemp fabric about 1 × 1.5 m. Scour the fabric in a 40 °C wash with fragrance-free powder and about 250 ml (a cup) of baking soda, no fabric softener, then soak it in water for about an hour. Put the needles in the pot of water, cover, and bring to a simmer without boiling; turn the heat down a little and keep it there until the water has the colour you want. Lift out the needles with a fine sieve (straining through muslin gives a more even colour). Add the wet fabric, push out the air bubbles with a wooden spoon so it is all under, and keep it at a gentle heat for about an hour, stirring now and then; leave it longer for a stronger colour. Wring it out, wash and rinse it with fragrance-free powder and no softener, and dry it out of direct sun. The same bath dyes several pieces in turn.

method.text: Tinder: needles left to dry for a season, or dry ones from the forest floor, catch fire easily, more so with a little pitch. Fatwood, the dense amber wood soaked with resin in the stumps and lower branches of dead pines, is shaved into thin slivers and lit with a spark or flame, and still lights when damp. Glue: resin that has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground is gathered rather than cut from the tree, melted (on a hot rock beside a fire, for example), mixed with finely ground ash or powdered charcoal and left to cool; it is reheated to use. A little water softens old pitch into a soft glue, and pine shavings or sawdust worked into it make a wood filler. Oil or strong alcohol takes pitch off your hands. Incense: needles tied into a bundle with natural twine and dried for about two weeks. Cleaner: chopped needles covered with vinegar in a glass jar, with baking paper under the lid so it does not corrode, left for two weeks and strained; the vinegar is mixed with baking soda and castile soap for cleaning.

method.text: Resin is gathered from what has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground rather than cut from the tree, at any time of year. It sticks to everything, so keep a knife and jar just for it; oil, then soap, takes it off your hands, and rubbing alcohol off clothes. Large lumps melt faster if frozen and broken up with a hammer inside a thick paper bag. Warmed with an equal amount of beeswax, mixed and left to set in its container, it makes a simple balm; melted into an oil, strained and firmed with beeswax it makes a balm for dry or cracked skin, lips and hands.

recipes.method: 60 ml (¼ cup) pine resin; 125 ml (½ cup) oil such as olive or almond; 15–30 g grated beeswax. Melt the resin in the oil in a double boiler over a low heat. Strain through a coffee filter or a strainer, return to the double boiler, add the beeswax and heat gently until it has melted. Pour into tins or jars and store somewhere cool and dark.
recipes.title: Pine resin balm

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) pine resin; 250 ml (1 cup) olive oil, or another oil safe for skin; 125–190 ml (½–¾ cup) grated beeswax; 35 drops rosemary essential oil. Put the resin and oil in a glass jar in the top of a double boiler and simmer, stirring, until the resin melts; this can take several hours. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine sieve and return it to the double boiler. For every 250 ml of resin and oil add 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) grated beeswax (more gives a firmer balm) and heat gently until it melts. Pour into jars or tins, stir 5 drops of the essential oil into each, and put the lids on straight away so the scent stays in. Leave to cool and set, and store somewhere cool and dark. Use it on dry or cracked skin, as a lip or hand balm, or overnight on the face.
recipes.title: Pine resin and olive oil balm

identification.text:
A small, spreading, open tree up to 10 m (to about 16 m when planted), its branches very irregular and often curved. The bark is rough, grey on the surface and reddish brown beneath, flaking in thick scales. The needles come in pairs, short (1–5 cm), curved or twisted, deep green, stiff and sharp-tipped, lying at different angles to the shoot. The cones are 2.5–5.5 cm, stalkless and smooth, with no prickle on the scales; they are narrow, pale or yellowish brown, and usually curve towards the tapering tip so they look lopsided. They point forward or out along the branch and usually stay closed on the tree for many years, sometimes covering the twisted branches down to the trunk. Strongly twisted shoots and needles and smooth, sharply bent cones set it apart from contorta pine and dwarf mountain pine.
Shoots greenish to brown or dark brown, hairless. Buds cylindrical or cylindrical-egg-shaped, very resinous, brown with whitish resin; scales pressed tight. Needles 2 per bundle, 1–5 cm × 1.5–2 mm; resin canals near the edge; the sheath soon very short. Male cones about 1 cm long, broadly cylindrical to almost round. Young female cones stalkless, the scales with a short point. Mature cones taking two years to ripen, 2.5–5.5 × 1.7–2.5 cm, narrowly conical to almost oblong when closed; scale ends flat or sometimes convex, the central boss unarmed. Seed wing broadly lopsided, 0.5–1 cm long.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have short needles in pairs and cones that stay closed on the tree for years, and they grow wild together and can cross; look at the shoots and cones. Contorta pine's shoots and needles are not or only slightly twisted, the needles 3.5–6.5 cm and generally yellowish green; its cones are 3–6 cm, broadly egg-shaped and lopsided at the base, usually point down or back along the branch, and have a short slender prickle on each scale. Jack pine's shoots and needles are strongly twisted, the needles 1–5 cm and deep green; its cones are narrow, smooth with no prickles, point forward or out, and curve sharply towards the tapering tip. Contorta pine's seeds and spring inner bark are eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Contorta pine

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small pines with short needles in pairs; look at the shoots and cones. Dwarf mountain pine is usually a dense shrub; its needles are 3–7 cm, dark green, curved but not twisted; its cones are 2.5–5.5 cm, symmetrical, egg-shaped, more or less upright, dark brown, and do not stay long on the tree after ripening. Jack pine's shoots and needles are strongly twisted, the needles 1–5 cm and deep green; its cones are narrow, curved sharply towards the tapering tip so they look lopsided, pale or yellowish brown, and stay closed on the tree for many years. Dwarf mountain pine's young cones are made into syrup (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mountain pine

preparation.text:
Eat the inner bark fresh, raw or cooked, or dry it and grind it to a powder to thicken soups or mix with cereal flour for bread.
For syrup, pick cones while they are still green and soft enough to cut through with a knife; brown, woody or opened cones will not do, and jack pine's ripe cones stay shut on the tree for years. Green cones ooze sticky resin, so wear gloves. Throw out any with holes or insects. Smaller cones give a stronger flavour; large ones can be cut up so more fit in the jar.

recipes.method: Pack 225 g (about 500 ml) young green jack pine cones and 450 g brown sugar into a 1 litre jar. Leave in a warm, sunny place for 30 days, shaking it now and then. For the first few weeks open the jar occasionally to let out gas, as the mixture may ferment. Scrape the cones and sugar slush into a pot, add 30 ml water, and bring to a brisk simmer for 5–10 minutes, just until the sugar melts (reducing it further makes it crystallise as it cools). Strain, discard the cones and bottle the hot syrup. It keeps best in the fridge once opened. Use it like maple syrup: on pancakes, fresh fruit or soft cheese, or a little in desserts and dressings.
recipes.title: Mugolio (young pine cone syrup)

recipes.method: Put 10 young green jack pine cones in a jar and top up with 500 g brown sugar, shaking so the sugar settles round the cones. Close the jar and leave it for about 2 weeks, until all the sugar has turned to syrup. Pass it through a sieve and bottle. Add it to marinades or pour it over pancakes.

summary.text:
Jack pine (Pinus banksiana) is an evergreen pine of the pine family (Pinaceae) from northern North America. Its inner bark and young green cones are edible.
In New Zealand: It was introduced for forestry and first recorded wild in 1957. It was planted mainly in Kaingaroa Forest south of Rotorua and in some inland parts of Canterbury, Otago and Southland, and has regenerated prolifically around Kaingaroa Forest and in several places in Canterbury, such as near Lake Tekapo. Herbarium sheets record it wild in the Tasman Valley at Mount Cook Station and naturalising along a firebreak in Naseby Forest, Central Otago, among contorta pine, which it can hybridise with; putative hybrids have also been collected in Karioi Forest. DOC records an infestation at Denniston on the West Coast, and a wild tree has been collected at Totara Park, Manurewa. It has occasionally been called P. divaricata here.
It is listed on DOC's Weeds database and in the Northland and Greater Wellington regional pest plans. It is named after Sir Joseph Banks (1743–1820), the English naturalist and botanist.

method.text: Needles: simmered, not boiled, in a covered pot of water until the water has coloured, then lifted out; wet fabric is kept in the bath at a gentle heat for about an hour, longer for a stronger colour. Scoured hemp with no mordant, dyed in an aluminium pot, came out a soft mauve-clay, and one bath coloured several pieces. The needles are also listed as giving a tan or green dye. Cones: soaked in water for a day to soften, cut into pieces, boiled for up to four hours (a lower heat loses less dye) and strained through muslin; cotton dyed for an hour and left to cool in the bath came out beige to light brown, mordanted or not, and the bath was used again the next day.
