recipes.method: A box of pine needles about 30 × 20 cm; a 20-litre aluminium pot of cool water; a piece of hemp fabric about 1 × 1.5 m. Scour the fabric in a 40 °C wash with fragrance-free powder and about 250 ml (a cup) of baking soda, no fabric softener, then soak it in water for about an hour. Put the needles in the pot of water, cover, and bring to a simmer without boiling; turn the heat down a little and keep it there until the water has the colour you want. Lift out the needles with a fine sieve (straining through muslin gives a more even colour). Add the wet fabric, push out the air bubbles with a wooden spoon so it is all under, and keep it at a gentle heat for about an hour, stirring now and then; leave it longer for a stronger colour. Wring it out, wash and rinse it with fragrance-free powder and no softener, and dry it out of direct sun. The same bath dyes several pieces in turn.

method.text: Tinder: needles left to dry for a season, or dry ones from the forest floor, catch fire easily, more so with a little pitch. Fatwood, the dense amber wood soaked with resin in the stumps and lower branches of dead pines, is shaved into thin slivers and lit with a spark or flame, and still lights when damp. Glue: resin that has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground is gathered rather than cut from the tree, melted (on a hot rock beside a fire, for example), mixed with finely ground ash or powdered charcoal and left to cool; it is reheated to use. A little water softens old pitch into a soft glue, and pine shavings or sawdust worked into it make a wood filler. Oil or strong alcohol takes pitch off your hands. Incense: needles tied into a bundle with natural twine and dried for about two weeks. Cleaner: chopped needles covered with vinegar in a glass jar, with baking paper under the lid so it does not corrode, left for two weeks and strained; the vinegar is mixed with baking soda and castile soap for cleaning.

method.text: Resin is gathered from what has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground rather than cut from the tree, at any time of year. It sticks to everything, so keep a knife and jar just for it; oil, then soap, takes it off your hands, and rubbing alcohol off clothes. Large lumps melt faster if frozen and broken up with a hammer inside a thick paper bag. Warmed with an equal amount of beeswax, mixed and left to set in its container, it makes a simple balm; melted into an oil, strained and firmed with beeswax it makes a balm for dry or cracked skin, lips and hands.

recipes.method: 60 ml (¼ cup) pine resin; 125 ml (½ cup) oil such as olive or almond; 15–30 g grated beeswax. Melt the resin in the oil in a double boiler over a low heat. Strain through a coffee filter or a strainer, return to the double boiler, add the beeswax and heat gently until it has melted. Pour into tins or jars and store somewhere cool and dark.
recipes.title: Pine resin balm

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) pine resin; 250 ml (1 cup) olive oil, or another oil safe for skin; 125–190 ml (½–¾ cup) grated beeswax; 35 drops rosemary essential oil. Put the resin and oil in a glass jar in the top of a double boiler and simmer, stirring, until the resin melts; this can take several hours. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine sieve and return it to the double boiler. For every 250 ml of resin and oil add 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) grated beeswax (more gives a firmer balm) and heat gently until it melts. Pour into jars or tins, stir 5 drops of the essential oil into each, and put the lids on straight away so the scent stays in. Leave to cool and set, and store somewhere cool and dark. Use it on dry or cracked skin, as a lip or hand balm, or overnight on the face.
recipes.title: Pine resin and olive oil balm

identification.text:
A tall evergreen conifer, conical when young, with whorled branches and smooth bark. The needles are flat and lie in two flat rows either side of the shoot (except on very young plants), glossy dark green above with two white bands beneath, and very aromatic when bruised. Each needle leaves a flat round scar when it falls, so older shoots are smooth. The shoots are brownish and the winter buds resinous. The cones stand upright on the branches and break up on the tree, leaving a bare central spike; their bract scales are hidden.
Other firs grown in New Zealand differ: white fir (A. concolor) and noble fir (A. procera) have grey-blue needles, and noble fir's bract scales stick out of the cone; Spanish fir (A. pinsapo) has needles spreading all round the shoot. Caucasian fir (A. nordmanniana), the fir most often found wild, has needles that crowd forward over the top of the shoot, and buds that are not resinous.

lookalikes.howToTell: Turn a shoot over: grand fir's needles have two white bands beneath; yew's have two broad pale green bands, never white or silver. Grand fir's shoots are brownish, with resinous winter buds; yew's shoots are green and ribbed. Grand fir carries upright cones that break up on the tree, leaving a bare spike; female yews carry soft crimson berry-like arils 10–15 mm long around a single seed, and yew has no woody cones. Most yews are male or female trees, so a tree without red arils can still be yew. Both have flat needles lying in two rows, so the arrangement does not separate them. Every part of yew except the red flesh of the aril is deadly.
lookalikes.name: Yew

lookalikes.howToTell: Young Douglas firs have flat needles in two rows like grand fir's, and both are aromatic, so don't go by scent; look at the buds and cones. Douglas fir's buds are long, narrow, sharp-pointed and shining purplish brown, like a beech bud; grand fir's winter buds are blunter and resinous. Douglas fir's cones hang down, 4–10 cm long, with three-pointed bracts sticking out between the scales, and fall whole; grand fir's cones stand upright on the branches, hide their bracts and break up on the tree, leaving a bare spike. Douglas fir's tips and needles are also used for tea and flavouring (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Douglas fir

lookalikes.howToTell: Both grow wild at Hanmer Springs and both have tips used for tea; look at the needles and cones. Grand fir's needles are flat, lie in two rows either side of the shoot, are glossy green above with two white bands beneath, and leave a flat round scar so old shoots feel smooth; its cones stand upright and break up on the tree, leaving a bare spike. Norway spruce's needles are stiff, sharp and roughly four-sided, spread all round the shoot and leave a rough woody peg when they fall; its cones hang down, usually over 10 cm, and stay whole. Norway spruce's young tips are also used for tea and syrup (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Norway spruce

preparation.text: Pick the light green new spring tips; older growth is more resinous and astringent. Take them from side branches, never the top of a young tree. Steep tips or needles in hot water for tea, blitz needles with sugar for baking, chop them into marinades and dressings, or infuse them in syrup or spirits. Needles can be dried in a low oven and kept in an airtight jar.

recipes.method: 60 ml (4 tbsp) fresh green grand fir needles; 80 g caster sugar; 140 g butter, softened; 200 g plain flour. Heat the oven to 150 °C and line a large baking tray. Blitz the needles with the sugar in a food processor until the needles are very fine, and set aside 2 tablespoons of the scented sugar. Add the butter and blitz until pale, then add the flour and pulse until it clumps into a dough. Roll it out about 5 mm thick between sheets of baking paper, cut out shapes and bake 25–30 minutes, until lightly browned at the edges. While still warm, move to a rack and sprinkle with the reserved fir sugar. Makes about 24.
recipes.title: Grand fir shortbread

recipes.method: 30 g fresh green grand fir needles; 1 unwaxed orange; 10 g root ginger; 1 cinnamon stick; 15 ml (1 tbsp) green cardamom pods; 15 ml (1 tbsp) star anise, roughly broken; maple syrup or honey to sweeten. Heat the oven to 75 °C. Spread the needles in a lined roasting tin; pare the orange zest in thin strips and slice the ginger thinly onto a lined tray. Dry the zest 30 minutes and the ginger 1 hour, then turn the oven off and leave the needles in it overnight. Crush the cardamom, star anise and cinnamon and mix everything together. Keep in an airtight jar, cool and dark, for up to 6 months; makes one 350 ml jar. For a mug, infuse a heaped tablespoon for 8 minutes, strain and sweeten.
recipes.title: Grand fir spiced tea

recipes.method: 15 ml (1 tbsp) grand fir needles, finely chopped; 5 ml (1 tsp) wholegrain mustard; 30 ml (2 tbsp) white wine vinegar; 5 ml (1 tsp) water or oyster juice; 30 ml (2 tbsp) grapeseed oil; 1 spring onion, finely chopped; 12 freshly shucked oysters. Whisk the needles, mustard, vinegar and water in a small bowl, then whisk in the oil in a slow stream. Stir in the spring onion and season lightly with salt and pepper. Spoon over the oysters.
recipes.title: Grand fir vinaigrette for oysters

recipes.method: 1 kg side of salmon; 30 ml (2 tbsp) honey; 30 ml (2 tbsp) sea salt; 15 ml (1 tbsp) cracked black pepper; 60 ml (¼ cup) chopped fresh grand fir needles. Remove the pin bones and skin, and cut the salmon into strips about 5 cm wide. Mix the salmon with the honey, salt, pepper and needles in a glass or stainless steel dish, cover and leave at least 30 minutes. Hot-smoke over soaked wood chips for at least 30 minutes, or cook on a soaked cedar plank on a hot covered barbecue for at least 20 minutes, until the fish just begins to flake. Serve warm. Serves 6–8.
recipes.title: Smoked salmon with honey and grand fir needles

recipes.method: For the infused gin: 100 g grand fir tips; a 750 ml bottle of gin. For one cocktail: 45 ml grand fir gin; 30 ml unfiltered apple cider; 15 ml lime juice; 7.5 ml apricot liqueur; 7.5 ml honey syrup (two parts honey to one part water, simmered until dissolved and cooled). Blend the tips with the gin on medium speed for 30 seconds, leave in the fridge for 24 hours, then strain; the gin thickens slightly and turns green. Shake the cocktail ingredients with ice and double-strain into a coupe.
recipes.title: Grand fir gin cocktail

recipes.method: Written for fir or spruce tips. 500 ml (2 cups) water; 500 ml (2 cups) sugar; 500 ml (2 cups) fir tips; 15–30 ml (1–2 tbsp) lemon juice (optional). Bring the water and sugar to the boil in a lidded pot, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Turn off the heat, stir in the tips, cover and leave to cool; leave overnight for a stronger flavour. Strain through muslin, add lemon juice to taste and bottle. Keeps about 4 months in the fridge; it does not freeze well. Makes about 500 ml.
recipes.title: Fir tip syrup

summary.text:
Grand fir (Abies grandis), also called giant fir, is a tall evergreen fir of the pine family (Pinaceae) from western North America. Its young shoot tips and needles are used for tea and flavouring.
In New Zealand: It was introduced for forestry and is grown in gardens, arboreta and plantations from Rotorua to Southland. It was first recorded wild in 1990, when saplings of various sizes were collected in scrub around Conical Hill at Hanmer Springs, beside a planted tree. Self-sown seedlings have also been recorded under planted trees at Marton and Bulls and in plantation understoreys in Canterbury, and wild seedlings and saplings near Te Anau. The 1988 Flora of New Zealand did not yet count it among the naturalised firs. DOC records it on its Weeds database but does not class it as a weed.

warnings: Yew, a deadly poisonous conifer, has flat needles in two rows like grand fir's. Check every tree before you pick (see the lookalikes).
Take extra care in pregnancy: many sources recommend against eating or drinking any conifer, including conifer-needle teas, while pregnant.
Try only a little the first time: allergic reactions to conifers are not common, but are more likely than with most foods.
Do not pick from trees that may have been sprayed. Wilding conifers are controlled with herbicide.

associations.note: Poisonous. Fly agaric has been recorded with black cottonwood overseas.

identification.text:
A large tree, almost pyramid-shaped when young, that suckers moderately. The bark is grey and fissured, peeling when young. The shoots are somewhat angled and brown. The buds and very young shoots are very sticky and smell of balsam, and are hairless. The leaf stalks are up to about 9 cm long, round and hairless. The leaves are up to 13 (sometimes 18) × 10 cm, usually triangular-egg-shaped or egg-shaped, sometimes narrower, greenish white beneath and hairless apart from a finely fringed edge, more or less green when very young, with green veins above and finely round-toothed edges; the base broadly wedge-shaped, square or slightly heart-shaped, the tip pointed. The catkins are male, hanging, up to about 10 cm long, with crimson anthers. All wild New Zealand trees are male and one clone, so there is no cotton or seed.
Balm of Gilead (P. × gileadensis), also sticky and balsam-scented, is a female clone that suckers much more and has hairy leaf stalks and leaf veins and round young shoots. P. yunnanensis has reddish purple or yellowish brown year-old shoots, leaves reddish brown as they unfold and pink veins above.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are big poplars of riverbanks and roadsides with very sticky, balsam-scented buds and young leaves that are whitish beneath, so scent and buds do not separate them; look at the leaf stalks, shoots and suckering. Balm of Gilead's leaf stalks are 3.5–7 cm, roughly round, sticky and covered in spreading hairs, and its leaf veins are hairy above and beneath; its young shoots are roughly round; it suckers very freely, forming stands over large areas from one or a few trees; and the trees here are all female, with catkins 13–19 cm long that give white silky cotton. Black cottonwood's leaf stalks are up to about 9 cm, round and hairless, its veins are hairless and green above, its young shoots are somewhat angled and brown, it suckers only moderately, and the wild trees here are all male, so there is no cotton. Balm of Gilead is not given as food on its page.
lookalikes.name: Balm of Gilead poplar

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are big, moderately suckering balsam poplars of riverbanks with very sticky, balsam-scented buds, hairless leaf stalks, so look at the colour of the shoots and the unfolding leaves. Yunnan poplar's year-old shoots are reddish purple or yellowish brown, its leaves are reddish brown as they unfold, and its veins are pink above, with a very glossy upper surface; its leaves are to 18 × 13.5 cm with a base that is slightly to deeply heart-shaped, and its catkins reach about 16 cm. Black cottonwood's year-old shoots are brown, its leaves are green as they unfold, its veins are green above, its leaves are to 13 (sometimes 18) × 10 cm with a base broadly wedge-shaped, square or only slightly heart-shaped, and its catkins reach about 10 cm. Yunnan poplar is not given as food on its page.

preparation.text: The inner bark is only good while the sap runs and the leaves are expanding, when it is thick, sweet and juicy; peel a test strip first to see if it is ready. Remove the outer bark and scrape the white, soft inner layer off the wood in long ribbon-like strips, or scrape it from the inside of the peeled bark. It tastes mildly sweet with a slight bitterness. Eat it fresh, on the spot or soon after, sometimes with oil; it spoils and ferments quickly, so it cannot be dried and kept for winter. It can be chopped finely to make it easier to chew.

summary.text:
Black cottonwood (Populus trichocarpa), also called western balsam poplar or cottonwood, is a large poplar of the willow family (Salicaceae) from western North America. Its spring inner bark and sap are edible.
In New Zealand: It has been planted in a number of places in both main islands. Its suckers come up some distance from the parent and can look wild, especially after the original tree dies. All wild plants here are male and belong to one clone, so it spreads only by suckers, never by seed. The Flora of New Zealand records it wild on riverbanks in Christchurch (Hagley Park, by the Avon River); herbarium sheets also record vigorous plants on the Wai-iti River bank at Wakefield, Nelson, and big trees on the Waingawa River flats in Wairarapa, and iNaturalist records saplings on the shore of Lake Manapōuri. Like other poplars here, it often looks naturalised where it was planted beside rivers and lakes. DOC records it on its Weeds database but does not class it as a weed.

warnings: Eat the inner bark fresh, the day you strip it: it spoils and ferments quickly.

identification.text:
A large deciduous tree, to about 25 m tall in cultivation, with rough, fissured bark. Shoots dark reddish brown or brown, hairless, with prominent raised pores. Leaf stalk up to 6 cm long. Leaves on adult shoots mostly 11–20 × 7–15 cm, egg-shaped or oblong, with 3–5 pairs of lobes cut a third to two-thirds of the way to the midrib, each lobe ending in a bristle tip and usually with 1–4 bristle-tipped teeth; slightly shiny above, usually hairless, sometimes with a few brownish hairs in the vein angles beneath; turning deep red before they fall; base wedge-shaped. Male catkins up to about 8 cm long. Acorns take two years to ripen, 1–2 on a stalk 1–1.5 cm long. Cup 1.5–2 cm across, shallow, with flat-lying, hairless or minutely hairy scales. Acorn 2–2.5 cm long, egg-shaped, about a quarter enclosed by the cup.
Two other American oaks are often confused with it. Scarlet oak (Q. coccinea) has more deeply lobed leaves, very shiny above, that colour even more brightly in autumn; its acorns are very like red oak's. Pin oak (Q. palustris), the commonest of the three here, generally has smaller leaves with lobes cut more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib on fruiting shoots, more conspicuous tufts of hair in the vein angles, and a smaller, even shallower cup.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are big deciduous oaks whose acorns are eaten once leached; look at the leaves and acorns. English oak's leaves have 3–7 pairs of rounded lobes with no bristles, and small ear-like lobes at the base that almost hide the leaf stalk, usually under 2 mm long; its acorns ripen in their first year, are 2–4 cm long and oblong, a quarter to a third in the cup, on a fruiting stalk 3–13 cm long. Red oak's leaves are larger, with 3–5 pairs of pointed, bristle-tipped lobes, a wedge-shaped base and a leaf stalk up to 6 cm long; its acorns take two years to ripen, are 2–2.5 cm and egg-shaped, about a quarter in a shallow cup, on a stalk 1–1.5 cm long. Red oak's acorns are more bitter and need longer leaching (see its page).
lookalikes.name: English oak

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are American oaks of the red oak group, often confused with each other, and both have acorns that are eaten once leached for a long time; look at the leaves and the acorn cup. Red oak's leaves are larger, mostly 11–20 cm, with 3–5 pairs of lobes cut only a third to two-thirds of the way to the midrib and at most a few brownish hairs in the vein angles; its acorns are 2–2.5 cm and egg-shaped, about a quarter enclosed by a cup 1.5–2 cm across. Pin oak's leaves are generally smaller (about 5–16 cm long), with five or seven lobes cut more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib on fruiting shoots, so the sinuses are deep and U-shaped, and conspicuous tufts of hair where the veins meet beneath; its acorns are about 1–1.6 cm and rounded, in a thin, very shallow cup, smaller than red oak's.

preparation.text: Gather acorns once they are ripe and brown, leaving any that are discoloured, soft or holed. Red oak's kernel is very bitter, high in tannin and oil, so it needs much longer leaching than English oak. The papery skin sticks to the nut and is bitter and darkens the flour; freezing fresh acorns for a week or two before cracking makes it easier to remove. Chop or grind the shelled nuts small, cover with about three times their volume of cold water, and pour it off and add fresh every day: red oak usually takes one to two weeks, sometimes longer. Keep tasting: it is done when it tastes bland, not bitter, even if the water stays tinted. Cold leaching keeps the starch that binds baking. For a quicker leach, boil the pieces and change the water every 20–30 minutes; red oak takes two to three hours, and the starch is lost. Dry the meal and grind it to flour; it is oily, so keep it in the fridge or freezer.

recipes.method: Written for red oak acorns. Use leached acorn flour (see preparation). 250 ml (1 cup) acorn flour; 250 ml (1 cup) plain, wholemeal or gluten-free flour; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 10 ml (2 tsp) baking powder; 2 eggs; 60 ml (¼ cup) oil or melted butter; 500 ml (2 cups) milk; 80 ml (⅓ cup) maple syrup, honey or sugar. Mix the dry ingredients, then stir in the wet ones slowly to a smooth batter that pours; add milk if it is too thick or flour if too runny. Oil a hot griddle or pan, pour in 125 ml (½ cup) of batter at a time and cook 2–3 minutes, until bubbles rise, then flip and cook 1–2 minutes more. Serve with butter, jam or maple syrup. Makes about 12; leftovers freeze.
recipes.title: Acorn pancakes

recipes.method: Written for red oak acorns. Use leached acorn flour (see preparation). 250 ml (1 cup) acorn flour; 250 ml (1 cup) bread, plain, wholemeal or gluten-free flour; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 22 ml (1½ tbsp) baking powder; 1 egg; 250 ml (1 cup) milk; 45 ml (3 tbsp) maple syrup, honey or sugar; 45 ml (3 tbsp) oil or melted butter. Heat the oven to 200 °C and grease a loaf tin. Mix the dry and wet ingredients separately, then stir them together just until combined; a thick, lumpy batter is fine. Bake 30–40 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean, then turn out and cool 10–15 minutes. Makes one loaf; keeps a week in the fridge, or freeze it.
recipes.title: Acorn quick bread

recipes.method: Written for red oak acorns. Use leached acorn flour (see preparation). 500 ml (2 cups) acorn flour; 250 ml (1 cup) oat flour; 30 ml (2 tbsp) sunflower oil or lard; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; water. Mix the flours, fat and salt, and add water to make a moist but not runny batter. Shape into biscuits and bake at 190 °C for 15–20 minutes.
recipes.title: Acorn and oat biscuits

recipes.method: Written for red oak acorns. Use leached acorn meal (see preparation). 236 ml (1 cup) acorn meal; 236 ml (1 cup) cornmeal or fine maize flour; 59 ml (¼ cup) honey; 14 ml (1 tbsp) melted butter or oil; a pinch of salt; warm water. Mix everything in a large bowl with enough warm water to make a moist but not sticky dough. Divide into 12 equal balls, cover and rest 10 minutes. With wet hands, pat each into a thick round. Cook in an ungreased cast-iron pan over medium-high heat until the edges dry and the underside browns, then flip and brown the other side. Serve warm. Makes 12.
recipes.title: Acorn and cornmeal cakes

recipes.method: Written for any acorn flour, best cold-leached (see preparation). 125 ml (½ cup) wholemeal or plain flour; 125 ml (½ cup) finely ground cold-leached acorn flour; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt; a few scrapes of nutmeg; 2 eggs; 125 ml (½ cup) milk, water or the nut milk left from leaching. Mix everything to a smooth batter with no lumps. Bring a pot of salted water to a simmer and press the batter through the holes of a colander in batches; cook about 30 seconds, then lift out, drain and toss with a little oil. Reheat in butter with chopped chives and parsley. Serves 4 as a side.
recipes.title: Acorn flour spaetzle

recipes.method: Written for leached acorn meal from any oak; red oak meal needs its longer leach first (see preparation). 1.5 litres (6 cups) leached acorn meal; 1.5 litres (6 cups) spelt or other bread flour; 7.5 ml (½ tbsp) salt; fresh yeast; water; sesame, poppy or sunflower seeds. Mix the acorn meal, flour and salt in a large bowl. Dissolve the yeast in 125 ml (½ cup) lukewarm water and stir it in, then knead well, adding water or flour until the dough is neither stiff nor sticky. Cover with a cloth and leave to rise overnight. Knead again and shape into two loaves; score the tops, brush with water and sprinkle with seeds. Bake at 200 °C for 45 minutes. Makes two large loaves.
recipes.title: Acorn and spelt bread

recipes.method: Written for acorns generally. Ripe acorns, shelled and leached in hot water until no longer bitter (see preparation); salt. Spread the damp, leached chunks on a baking tray, sprinkle with salt and toast on a high heat for 15–20 minutes, until the colour starts to darken. Cool before eating, or add them to a winter stew.
recipes.title: Roasted acorns

recipes.method: Written for acorns generally. Ripe acorns, shelled and leached in hot water until no longer bitter (see preparation). Lay them in an ovenproof dish and roast on a low heat for 1½–2 hours to dry them slowly, moving them around often so they don't catch. They brown as they dry: take them out when they reach a light or dark roast, as you prefer. Cool, grind and brew like coffee. It has no caffeine and tastes unlike ordinary coffee.
recipes.title: Acorn coffee

Caution careRequired 24/11/2026: food records for red oak acorns — Moerman, D., Native American Ethnobotany Database (BRIT), http://naeb.brit.org/ 'Quercus rubra' (http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Quercus+rubra), retrieved 24/11/2026: Ojibwa (Smith 1932, p. 402: 'Acorns leached with lye and used as of the most important starchy foods'), Potawatomi (Smith 1933: 'Dried, ground acorns used as a flour to make gruel', soaked in lye from hardwood ashes 'to swell them and remove the tannic acid'), Omaha, Pawnee, Ponca and Dakota (Gilmore 1919, p. 75: 'Acorns leached with basswood ashes to remove the bitter taste and used for food'), Iroquois (Waugh 1916, p. 123: 'Acorns used for food') — several independent fieldworkers; Plants For A Future, 'Quercus rubra' (PFAF = Temperate Plants Database, one source; all rights reserved, facts restated), https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Quercus+rubra, retrieved 24/11/2026 ('Seed - cooked', 'A staple food for several native North American Indian tribes', tannins leached in running water, roasted seed a coffee substitute; PFAF's reference 257 is Moerman's book, so not independent of NAEB); Wikipedia contributors, 'Quercus rubra' (CC BY-SA 4.0), https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Quercus_rubra&action=raw, retrieved 24/11/2026 ('The acorns can be collected in autumn, shelled, tied up in a cloth, and leached to remove bitterness. They can then be eaten whole or ground into meal', citing Elias & Dykeman, Edible Wild Plants, 2009, p. 233; 'Its kernel is white and very bitter'; 'Northern red oak kernels have highly concentrated amounts of bitter-tasting tannin'). careRequired as on english-oak: raw acorns must be leached. Lye leaching (Ojibwa, Potawatomi) not given as a method — no safety source for home lye use.

Cards 24/11/2026: red oak ↔ English oak — both grow wild in New Zealand near parks and plantations and both are acorn entries; every test from the Flora of New Zealand vol. IV accounts of Quercus rubra (https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/b66924f3-ef16-4528-ab20-5c512b787ecf: lamina 11–20 cm, 3–5 pairs of lobes with 'aristate apex', petiole to 6 cm, base cuneate, fruiting peduncle 1–1.5 cm, 'frs reaching maturity in second year', cup shallow, acorn 2–2.5 cm 'c. 1/4 enclosed') and Quercus robur (as on english-oak: 3–7 pairs of rounded lobes, ear-like base hiding the petiole under 2 mm, acorn 2–4 cm oblong, peduncle 3–13 cm). Not a named confusion in an NZ source, but the two most common wild oaks here share the same food use and preparation; risk 'edible' both ways (both careRequired acorn entries).

Cards 24/11/2026: pin oak ↔ red oak — named confusion: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb, Sykes & Garnock-Jones 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY-NC-SA), 'Quercus rubra' account, its note on pin oak (https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/b66924f3-ef16-4528-ab20-5c512b787ecf), retrieved 24/11/2026 — abbreviations spelled out, restated; the Flora has no account of pin oak itself ('It is often confused with 2 other American oaks of subgen. Erythrobalanus'; pin oak 'generally has smaller lvs than the other 2 spp., the lf lobes extend > 3/4 of the distance to the midrib on reproductive shoots, the axillary hair tufts are more conspicuous and the cup is smaller and even shallower than in Q. rubra'). Red oak's tests are from the same Flora account (lamina 11–20 cm, 3–5 pairs of lobes cut a third to two-thirds of the way, a few brownish hairs in the vein angles, cup 1.5–2 cm, acorn 2–2.5 cm ovoid, about 1/4 enclosed); pin oak's leaf length, five or seven lobes, deep U-shaped sinuses and acorn size and cup are from the overseas descriptions (NC State; Wikipedia citing the Flora of North America) because the NZ Flora gives only the comparisons. Both are NZ plants (red oak naturalised 1988; pin oak casual). Risk 'edible' both ways (both careRequired acorn entries).

summary.text:
Red oak (Quercus rubra), also known in New Zealand as Q. borealis, is a large deciduous oak of the beech family (Fagaceae) from eastern North America. Its acorns are edible once leached.
In New Zealand: It is widely planted in parks, domains and larger gardens in many towns and cities, and its leaves turn deep red in autumn. Cultivated trees fruit freely, and young self-sown trees occasionally come up near them, particularly in untended or ungrazed ground around parks and plantations; it was recorded naturalised in 1988, in the North Island and in the South Island south to South Canterbury. Self-sown seedlings have been recorded around planted trees in Christchurch, Richmond, Kurow and Rotorua. DOC records it on its Weeds database but does not class it as a weed.

warnings: Raw acorns are bitter with tannins, which can be toxic: always leach them first.
Eating too many acorns can cause digestive upsets.

associations.note: Poisonous. Fly agaric has been recorded with western hemlock overseas.

identification.text: A large evergreen tree with a narrow crown and a drooping top and branch tips, especially when young. The bark is thick and deeply furrowed on mature trees. The needles are borne singly, spiral round the shoot but twist to lie in flat layers either side of it, giving the branches a flattened, lacy look. They are unequal in length, about 8–20 mm, flat and blunt, dark green above with two conspicuous white bands beneath. The twigs are hairy and yellowish green, with a small peg where each needle has fallen (the leaf base stays on). The cones are numerous, hanging and small, about 2 cm long, with rounded scales, purplish green when unripe and light brown when ripe. The wild trees at Castle Hill were recorded in 2003 as up to about 6 m tall, with horizontally spreading branches, bright yellow-green leaves and hairy shoots and young stems.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have short flat needles lying in two rows along the shoot, so shape and arrangement do not separate them, and length does not either (western hemlock's are about 8–20 mm, yew's 12–25 mm). Turn a shoot over: western hemlock's needles have two conspicuous white bands beneath; yew's have two broad pale green bands, never white or silver. Western hemlock's needles are blunt at the tip; yew's end in a point, sometimes a tiny one. Western hemlock's twigs are hairy and yellowish green, with a small peg where each needle has fallen; yew's shoots are green and ribbed. Western hemlock's top and branch tips droop and it carries small woody cones about 2 cm long that hang down; yew has no woody cones, and female yews carry a soft crimson berry-like aril 10–15 mm long around a single seed. Most yews are male or female trees, so a tree without red arils can still be yew. Crushed hemlock needles smell citrusy and yew's hardly smell at all, but do not rely on smell alone. Every part of yew except the red flesh of the aril is deadly.
lookalikes.name: Yew

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have flat needles in two rows on shaded shoots; look at the needles, the twig and the cones. Western hemlock's needles are short, about 8–20 mm, blunt, with two conspicuous white bands beneath, and each leaves a small peg on the twig when it falls (the leaf base stays on); its top and branch tips droop. Douglas fir's needles are 15–38 mm, whitish beneath, and leave no persistent leaf base, so the twig is ridged but not pegged; its winter buds are long, narrow, sharp and shining purplish brown. Western hemlock's cones are small, about 2 cm long, with rounded scales; Douglas fir's are 5–10 cm long and papery, hang down, and have three-pointed bracts sticking out between the scales. Douglas fir's tips and needles are used for tea and flavouring too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Douglas fir

lookalikes.howToTell: Only the name is shared; the plants look nothing alike. Western hemlock is a large evergreen conifer tree with needles, hairy twigs and small woody cones that hang down. Hemlock (poison hemlock) is an erect annual or biennial herb up to 2–3 m high with hollow stems that are usually spotted or blotched purple, finely divided fern-like leaves, white flowers in umbels, and a foetid or musty smell when crushed. Every part of poison hemlock is deadly if eaten. Never eat a plant just because it is called hemlock.

preparation.text:
Shoot tips: pick the light green new growth in spring. Eat it raw, add it to salads, sauces or baking, use it to flavour meat as it cooks, or steep it in hot water for tea.
Inner bark: take it only in spring, before the bark sticks to the wood and turns tough, and taste a strip first to check it is sweet. Peel off the outer bark and scrape the soft inner layer from the wood or from the inside of the bark. Eat it fresh or cook it, then press it into cakes and dry them. Dried inner bark can be ground to a powder to thicken soups or be mixed into flour for bread.

recipes.method: Written for conifer tips generally (fir, Douglas fir, spruce, pine or hemlock). 500 ml (2 cups) conifer tips; 500 ml (2 cups) water; 250 ml (1 cup) raw honey. Fill a jar of about 500 ml with the tips. Boil the water, pour it over the tips and leave it to steep for several hours until completely cool. Strain out the tips and measure 250 ml (1 cup) of the tea (you can also use all of it and adjust the honey to taste); stir in the honey until combined. Keep it in the fridge for 3–4 weeks, or freeze it in ice-cube trays for longer. Drizzle it over soft cheese, use it as a glaze for meat, or stir it into lemonade, sparkling water, cocktails or dressings.

summary.text:
Western hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla) is a large evergreen conifer of the pine family (Pinaceae), native to the Pacific north-west of North America. Its spring shoot tips and inner bark are edible.
In New Zealand: It was planted for timber, shelter and as an ornamental. It is self-establishing at Castle Hill in Canterbury, where trees planted in gaps that snow damage opened in mountain beech forest have produced many seedlings and saplings and adult trees reach the beech canopy. Seedlings have also been recorded spreading from an old plantation in Craigieburn Forest Park and as a wilding among other wilding conifers at Te Anau. Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and casual, NZPCN gives 2010 as the year it was recorded naturalised, and it is not on DOC's weed list.
The name 'hemlock' was given to the conifer because its crushed foliage smells a little like poison hemlock (Conium maculatum), but the two are unrelated: western hemlock is not poisonous, and poison hemlock is a deadly herb of the carrot family.

warnings: Western hemlock is a conifer tree. Do not confuse it with poison hemlock (Conium maculatum), the deadly herb of the carrot family that shares part of its name (see the lookalikes). Never eat a plant just because it is called hemlock.
Yew, a deadly poisonous conifer, has flat needles in two rows like western hemlock's. Check every tree before you pick (see the lookalikes).
Take extra care in pregnancy: many sources recommend against eating or drinking any conifer, including conifer-needle teas, while pregnant.
Try only a little the first time: allergic reactions to conifers are not common, but are more likely than with most foods.
Do not pick from trees that may have been sprayed. Wilding conifers are controlled with herbicide.

associations.note: Larch bolete has been recorded with Japanese larch.

identification.text: A deciduous conifer, commonly 20–40 m tall in forestry (the Hanmer trees recorded in 1998 were 8–9 m high, with widespreading, more or less horizontal branches). The needles are 2–5 cm long, light green, borne in clusters on short woody shoots, and turn bright yellow before they fall in autumn, leaving the shoots bare until spring. The young female cones are greenish. The cones are mostly 1.5–3.5 cm long (some Hanmer trees had cones to 3–4 × 2–2.5 cm, broad and oblong or barrel-shaped), and the margins of their scales curve outwards, giving the ripe cone an almost rosetted look. The bark is smooth and red-brown when young, becoming scaly, fissured and grey with age; the Hanmer trees had rough bark with small scales, pinkish below. Its needle clusters are less dense and more regular than European larch's. Japanese larch crosses with European larch, and the hybrid (Larix × eurolepis) is sterile; some wild trees may be hybrids and look in between.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are deciduous conifers with soft needles in tufts on short woody shoots, and they are planted in the same places and cross, so some trees are hybrids that look in between; look at the cones and the needle clusters. Japanese larch's young female cones are greenish and the scale margins of its ripe cones curve outwards, giving an almost rosetted look; its needles are 2–5 cm and light green, in clusters that are less dense and more regular. European larch's young female cones are crimson, with prominent crimson bract scales; its ripe cones are 1.5–3.5 cm, with scales that are not prominently recurved; its needles are 1.5–4 cm and grass-green, with 40–65 in a dense, irregular cluster. European larch's young needles are eaten the same way (see its page).

preparation.text: Steep the young needles in hot water for tea, or make a cordial (see the recipe). Use them on the day you pick them, as their aroma fades quickly. They can also be chopped into salads and pesto.

recipes.method: Written for larch (Larix spp) generally. The author makes it by his nettle cordial method, with young larch needles in place of the nettle. Equal parts water and white sugar (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar); at least a cupful (about 250 ml) of young larch needles, pressed down; a little citric acid or lemon juice, or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar. Pick the young needles in spring, while they are bright, almost luminous green and taste sharp, like sorrel. Make a syrup of equal parts water and white sugar (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar), heating gently and stirring until the sugar dissolves. Add at least a cupful (about 250 ml) of needles, pressed down, or more. Keep it on the heat until steaming hot, but don't let it boil. Strain out the needles. Stir in a little citric acid or lemon juice, or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar, until it tastes slightly sharp. It keeps for several weeks in the fridge.
recipes.title: Larch needle cordial

Tests: European larch from the Flora of New Zealand vol. IV account (needles 1.5–4 cm, 40–65 per fascicle, grass-green, very soft; female cones with prominent crimson bract scales; mature cone 1.5–3.5 × 1.7–2.5 cm with ovuliferous scales 'not prominently recurved') and NZPCN; Japanese larch from the same Flora note, the guide (needles 2–5 cm, light green) and NZFRI 25852 (scales 'pale green before maturity, curving outwards'). summary.text:
Japanese larch (Larix kaempferi) is a deciduous conifer of the pine family (Pinaceae), native to the mountains of central Japan. Its young needles are used for tea and cordial.
In New Zealand: It is planted for timber and as an ornamental in parks and gardens, and is a pioneering tree that tends to spread in open country if it is not grazed. The Flora of New Zealand (1988) reported it wild near planted stands at Hanmer, unconfirmed. Since then herbarium sheets have recorded numerous seedlings established on a roadside beneath plantings on the Clarence Valley Road near Hanmer Springs (2017), seedlings on a roadside bank near a plantation in Canterbury (1998) and a seedling at Golden Downs in Nelson (2018), and iNaturalist records a few naturalised among planted trees in Mount Richmond Forest Park (2018). All the wild records are beside plantations. Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and casual, and the wilding conifer quick ID guide rates its spreading vigour as high.
It is not on DOC's weed list. The Canterbury regional pest plan names only European larch among the larches, and covers other introduced conifers as wilding conifers and pest agent conifers. Hybrid larch, the cross with European larch, is sterile and does not spread as wildings.

warnings: Take extra care in pregnancy: many sources recommend against eating or drinking any conifer while pregnant.
Try only a little the first time: allergic reactions to conifers are not common, but are more likely than with most foods.
Do not pick from trees that may have been sprayed: wilding conifers are controlled with herbicide.

associations.note: Saffron milk cap has been recorded with Canary Island pine overseas.

identification.text:
A large pine with purplish to red-brown bark that is thick and scaly and breaks into large irregular plates divided by deep fissures. The needles are in bundles of three, yellow-green, very long (15–30 cm) and slender (about 1 mm wide), drooping, with finely toothed edges; the sheath at the base of each bundle stays on, 14–21 mm long. The young branchlets are stout, brownish and hairless. The winter buds are not resinous, with orange to red-brown scales that curve back. The cones are brown or red-brown, point backwards along the branch on a short stout stalk, open readily when ripe in their second year, and have no prickle on the scales; the seeds are shiny brown to black, 11–15 mm long, with a wing 15–25 mm long. Its very long, fine, slightly drooping needles, symmetrical brown cones and orange-brown, curved-back bud scales set it apart from other pines grown here.
Radiata pine, also three-needled, has shorter (10–18 cm), thicker (1.2–2 mm), dark green needles that do not droop, and its cones are strongly lopsided and stay closed on the tree, sometimes for years.

preparation.text: Pick cones while they are still green and soft enough to cut through with a knife; brown, woody or opened cones will not do. Green cones ooze sticky resin, so wear gloves. Look the cones over and throw out any with holes or insects. Smaller cones give a stronger flavour; large ones can be cut up so more fit in the jar.

recipes.method: Pack 225 g (about 500 ml) young green Canary Island pine cones and 450 g brown sugar into a 1 litre jar. Leave in a warm, sunny place for 30 days, shaking it now and then. For the first few weeks open the jar occasionally to let out gas, as the mixture may ferment. Scrape the cones and sugar slush into a pot, add 30 ml water, and bring to a brisk simmer for 5–10 minutes, just until the sugar melts (reducing it further makes it crystallise as it cools). Strain, discard the cones and bottle the hot syrup. It keeps best in the fridge once opened. Use it like maple syrup: on pancakes, fresh fruit or soft cheese, or a little in desserts and dressings.
recipes.title: Mugolio (young pine cone syrup)

recipes.method: Put 10 young green Canary Island pine cones in a jar and top up with 500 g brown sugar, shaking so the sugar settles round the cones. Close the jar and leave it for about 2 weeks, until all the sugar has turned to syrup. Pass it through a sieve and bottle. Add it to marinades or pour it over pancakes.

summary.text:
Canary Island pine (Pinus canariensis), also called Canary pine, is a large evergreen pine of the pine family (Pinaceae) from the Canary Islands. Its young green cones can be made into syrup.
In New Zealand: It is widely planted in parks, gardens and old homesteads, from Auckland and Great Barrier Island to Canterbury and Gisborne. Self-sown plants have been collected beside Whangaparapara Road on Great Barrier Island (2000) and on the slopes of Mount Wellington in Auckland (1986), and saplings have been photographed on Aotea / Great Barrier Island (2019, 2026), one under kānuka. Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and casual.
It is listed on DOC's Weeds database and in the Northland regional pest plan (sustained control) and the Greater Wellington regional pest plan (progressive containment).

method.text: Needles: simmered, not boiled, in a covered pot of water until the water has coloured, then lifted out; wet fabric is kept in the bath at a gentle heat for about an hour, longer for a stronger colour. Scoured hemp with no mordant, dyed in an aluminium pot, came out a soft mauve-clay, and one bath coloured several pieces. Cones: soaked in water for a day to soften, cut into pieces, boiled for up to four hours (a lower heat loses less dye) and strained through muslin; cotton dyed for an hour and left to cool in the bath came out beige to light brown, mordanted or not, and the bath was used again the next day. On cotton and silk, cone tannins give beiges with orange and pink hues.

recipes.method: A box of pine needles about 30 × 20 cm; a 20-litre aluminium pot of cool water; a piece of hemp fabric about 1 × 1.5 m. Scour the fabric in a 40 °C wash with fragrance-free powder and about 250 ml (a cup) of baking soda, no fabric softener, then soak it in water for about an hour. Put the needles in the pot of water, cover, and bring to a simmer without boiling; turn the heat down a little and keep it there until the water has the colour you want. Lift out the needles with a fine sieve (straining through muslin gives a more even colour). Add the wet fabric, push out the air bubbles with a wooden spoon so it is all under, and keep it at a gentle heat for about an hour, stirring now and then; leave it longer for a stronger colour. Wring it out, wash and rinse it with fragrance-free powder and no softener, and dry it out of direct sun. The same bath dyes several pieces in turn.

method.text: Tinder: needles left to dry for a season, or dry ones from the forest floor, catch fire easily, more so with a little pitch. Fatwood, the dense amber wood soaked with resin in the stumps and lower branches of dead pines, is shaved into thin slivers and lit with a spark or flame, and still lights when damp. Glue: resin that has run down the trunk or fallen to the ground is gathered rather than cut from the tree, melted (on a hot rock beside a fire, for example), mixed with finely ground ash or powdered charcoal and left to cool; it is reheated to use. A little water softens old pitch into a soft glue, and pine shavings or sawdust worked into it make a wood filler. Oil or strong alcohol takes pitch off your hands. Incense: needles tied into a bundle with natural twine and dried for about two weeks. Cleaner: chopped needles covered with vinegar in a glass jar, with baking paper under the lid so it does not corrode, left for two weeks and strained; the vinegar is mixed with baking soda and castile soap for cleaning.

recipes.method: 60 ml (¼ cup) pine resin; 125 ml (½ cup) oil such as olive or almond; 15–30 g grated beeswax. Melt the resin in the oil in a double boiler over a low heat. Strain through a coffee filter or a strainer, return to the double boiler, add the beeswax and heat gently until it has melted. Pour into tins or jars and store somewhere cool and dark.
recipes.title: Pine resin balm

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) pine resin; 250 ml (1 cup) olive oil, or another oil safe for skin; 125–190 ml (½–¾ cup) grated beeswax; 35 drops rosemary essential oil. Put the resin and oil in a glass jar in the top of a double boiler and simmer, stirring, until the resin melts; this can take several hours. Strain through cheesecloth or a fine sieve and return it to the double boiler. For every 250 ml of resin and oil add 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) grated beeswax (more gives a firmer balm) and heat gently until it melts. Pour into jars or tins, stir 5 drops of the essential oil into each, and put the lids on straight away so the scent stays in. Leave to cool and set, and store somewhere cool and dark. Use it on dry or cracked skin, as a lip or hand balm, or overnight on the face.
recipes.title: Pine resin and olive oil balm

identification.text:
A tall evergreen, cone-shaped tree with thin scaly bark and whorled branches that droop towards their tips; the young shoots turn chestnut brown. The needles are single, stiff and sharp-pointed, spread all round the shoot and curve upwards, shining deep green, roughly four-sided in section rather than flat, with rows of pale stomatal lines on every side, and smell resinous when crushed. Each needle sits on a short woody peg that stays on the shoot when it falls, so older shoots feel rough. The cones hang down, are cylindric, usually over 10 cm long (to about 11 cm on a New Zealand sheet), with thin flexible scales; they ripen in their first year and stay whole on the tree.
Sitka spruce, the other spruce found wild here, has strongly flattened, pungent-pointed, sweetly scented needles and cones only 3.5–5.5 cm long. Firs have flat needles that leave a smooth round scar and upright cones that break up on the tree. Yew has flat needles with two pale green bands beneath and green, ribbed shoots (see the lookalikes).

lookalikes.howToTell: Pick a needle and look. Norway spruce's needles are stiff and sharp, roughly four-sided in section so they roll between your fingers, and spread all round the shoot with pale lines on every side; they leave a rough woody peg when they fall. Yew's needles are flat, 1.2–2.5 cm, dark green above with two broad pale green bands beneath and none on top, and often lie in two rows on side shoots; its shoots are green and ribbed. Norway spruce carries cylindric cones usually over 10 cm long that hang from the branches; female yews carry soft crimson berry-like arils 10–15 mm long around a single seed, and yew has no woody cones. Most yews are male or female trees, so a tree without red arils can still be yew. Every part of yew except the red flesh of the aril is deadly.
lookalikes.name: Yew

lookalikes.howToTell: Young Douglas firs are named in the Flora as looking like young spruces, and both grow in plantations. Look at the needles, buds and cones. Norway spruce's needles are stiff, sharp-pointed and roughly four-sided, with pale lines on every side, and leave rough pegs on the shoot; its buds are rounded and not resinous, and its cones, usually over 10 cm, have thin flexible scales and no bracts showing. Douglas fir's needles are flat, 1.5–3.8 cm and blunt-tipped, with two pale bands beneath, and smell of oranges when crushed (Norway spruce smells resinous); its buds are long, narrow, sharp and shining purplish brown like a beech bud, and its hanging cones, 4–10 cm, have three-pointed bracts sticking out between the scales. Douglas fir's tips and needles are also used for tea and flavouring (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Douglas fir

lookalikes.howToTell: Both grow wild at Hanmer Springs and both have tips used for tea; look at the needles and cones. Norway spruce's needles are stiff, sharp and roughly four-sided, spread all round the shoot and leave a rough woody peg when they fall, so old shoots feel rough; its cones hang down, usually over 10 cm, and stay whole. Grand fir's needles are flat, lie in two rows either side of the shoot, are glossy green above with two white bands beneath, and leave a flat round scar so old shoots feel smooth; its cones stand upright and break up on the tree, leaving a bare spike. Grand fir's tips and needles are also used for tea and flavouring (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Grand fir

preparation.text: Pick the soft, bright green new growth in spring, once it has pushed out of its rust-coloured papery covering; older shoots turn resinous and tough. Take a few tips from side branches spread over the tree, never the leader of a young tree, and rub off any brown papery scales. Taste one first, as the flavour varies from tree to tree. Eat the earliest tips raw, steep them in hot water for about 10 minutes for tea, simmer them in a syrup, grind them with salt or sugar and dry the mix in a low oven, or infuse them in cream or spirits.

recipes.method: Written for spruce or fir tips. 500 ml water; 500 ml sugar; 500 ml spruce tips; 15–30 ml (1–2 tbsp) lemon juice (optional). Bring the water and sugar to the boil in a lidded pot, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Turn off the heat, stir in the tips and lemon juice, cover and leave to cool; leave overnight for a stronger flavour. Strain through muslin and bottle. Keeps about 4 months in the fridge. Makes about 500 ml.
recipes.title: Spruce or fir tip syrup

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 loosely filled cup) young Norway spruce tips, brown papery scales removed; 250 ml water; 250 g sugar; zest of 1 lemon in thin strips; juice of ½ lemon (15–30 ml). Rinse the tips, simmer them covered in the water for 15 minutes, add the zest and leave to infuse for 1 hour. Strain, topping up to 250 ml with water if needed. Return to the pan with the sugar, heat until dissolved and simmer gently 3–5 minutes, then stir in the lemon juice. Cool quickly, bottle and refrigerate within 2 hours at 4 °C or below; use within 48 hours, or freeze small portions. Makes 350–400 ml.
recipes.title: Norway spruce tip citrus syrup

recipes.method: Written for Picea abies. 2 handfuls young spruce tips; 500 ml water; 500 g brown sugar. Bring the tips and water to the boil, leave to steep for half an hour, then strain through a fine cloth. Boil the liquid with the sugar and reduce until it is a thick syrup. Pour into bottles and label them. The page gives no keeping time.
recipes.title: Spruce shoot syrup

recipes.method: Written for Picea abies. 60 g young light green shoots, chopped coarsely then whizzed in a food processor; 300 g coarse sea salt. Mix the two, spread on a baking tray lined with baking paper and dry at 50 °C (fan) with the oven door open for 3–4 hours. Crumble the dried salt and keep it airtight.
recipes.title: Spruce needle salt

recipes.method: Written for spruce tips (Picea species). 500 ml spruce tips, chopped or crushed; 625 ml boiling water; 250 ml more tips; 80 ml cornstarch; 250 ml sugar; a pinch of salt; 5 egg yolks; 15 ml (1 tbsp) lime juice; 15 ml (1 tbsp) butter; 30 ml (2 tbsp) finely minced tips. Pour the boiling water over the first 500 ml of tips, cover and infuse 15–30 minutes, then strain. Blend the infusion with the extra 250 ml tips for 15 seconds and strain again; you need 500 ml of milky infusion. Whisk the cornstarch, sugar and salt in a pan, add the infusion, yolks and lime juice, and cook over medium-low heat, scraping the pan, 5–8 minutes until thick; once it bubbles slowly cook 1 more minute. Stir in the butter, cool covered with film on the surface for about 15 minutes, stir in the minced tips and chill. Makes about 750 ml.
recipes.title: Spruce tip curd

recipes.method: Written for spruce tips. 125 ml spruce tips, lightly chopped; 500 ml heavy cream; 250 ml whole milk; 125 ml sugar; a dash of sea salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) vodka (optional, keeps it from freezing rock hard). Mix the tips with the cream and milk and infuse in the fridge for 8–12 hours. Strain, stir in the sugar, salt and vodka until the sugar dissolves, keeping it cold, and churn in an ice cream maker for 20–25 minutes.
recipes.title: Spruce tip ice cream

Norway Spruce') and My Amazing Finds, 'Spruce Tip Citrus Syrup with Lemon' (undated), https://myamazingfinds.com/spruce-tip-citrus-syrup/, retrieved 24/11/2026 (a syrup 'made with young Norway spruce tips'), plus Plants For A Future, 'Picea abies' (PFAF = Temperate Plants Database, one source; all rights reserved, restated), https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Picea+abies, retrieved 24/11/2026 ('A refreshing tea, rich in vitamin C, can be made from the young shoot tips'; PFAF reference 172, Schofield, 183, Facciola; one source). No human toxic claim found for Norway spruce (PFAF Known Hazards 'None known'); a livestock-only note (Galloway: 'Many conifers are toxic to ruminants') is not a warning. careRequired because yew is a deadly conifer. Not used: inner bark, male catkins, seed and immature cones (PFAF only here; cone syrups on Norway spruce exist but no preparation source was checked); mature needles (one source, Galloway).

Months [9, 10, 11] 24/11/2026: no New Zealand source dates the tips. Every source says 'spring' (Galloway: 'usually April to June in the UK'; Wildkräuterwerkstatt: 'April/Mai bis Anfang Juni'), so the northern spring is mapped to New Zealand spring, September to November; the northern calendar months are not shifted. PFAF's 'in flower from May to June, seeds ripen October to November' is a northern calendar for flowers and seed, not a food part here.

summary.text:
Norway spruce (Picea abies) is a tall evergreen of the pine family (Pinaceae) from northern and central Europe. Its soft new spring tips are used for tea, syrups, salt and desserts.
In New Zealand: It is commonly planted and several forms are grown, doing better in the colder parts of both main islands. It has been collected wild on White Horse Hill in Mount Cook National Park, where it had spread only to a very limited extent from planted trees, and saplings grow in exotic forest at Hanmer Springs. Most records are of planted trees. DOC records it on its Weeds database but does not class it as a weed.

warnings: Yew, a deadly poisonous conifer, can be mistaken for a conifer you want to eat. Check every tree before you pick (see the lookalikes).
Take extra care in pregnancy: many sources recommend against eating or drinking any conifer, including conifer-needle teas, while pregnant.
Try only a little the first time: allergic reactions to conifers are not common, but are more likely than with most foods.
Do not pick from trees that may have been sprayed. Wilding conifers are controlled with herbicide.

associations.note: Poisonous. Fly agaric has been recorded with Atlas cedar in New Zealand.
Bluefoot bolete has been recorded under Atlas cedar in New Zealand.
Porcini has been recorded with Atlas cedar in New Zealand.

identification.text: A large evergreen, broadly pyramidal tree with more or less horizontal branches. The needles are 1–3 cm long and glaucous (blue-grey; the blue cultivar 'Glauca' is very common in New Zealand gardens); on the long shoots they are single and alternate, and on the short spur-like shoots they grow in tufts. The male cones stand upright at the shoot tips; the female cones are upright too, 5–7 (to 8) cm long and 4–5 (to 6) cm wide, barrel-shaped, and break up at or soon after ripening. Deodar and Lebanon cedar are often confused with it: their mature cones are often nearly twice as large, their needles longer, and the deodar's long shoots droop. Larch also carries its needles in tufts, but sheds them in autumn; Atlas cedar is evergreen.

summary.text:
Atlas cedar (Cedrus atlantica), also called Atlantic cedar, is a large evergreen tree of the pine family (Pinaceae) from the Atlas Mountains of Algeria and Morocco. No record of it as food was found.
In New Zealand: It is widely grown, and the blue cultivar 'Glauca' is very common. The 1988 Flora of New Zealand found it wild at Riccarton, Christchurch, where a small population of young plants had come up in gravel beside the railway lines. Seedlings have since been collected under planted trees in Canterbury and recorded at Ashburton, Wigram and Livingstone. Biota of New Zealand lists it as both cultivated and casual. DOC records it on its Weeds database but does not class it as a weed.

warnings: No record of Atlas cedar as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

identification.text:
A tall evergreen fir, pyramidal, with grey-brown bark that is rough and platy near the base. The needles are flat and dark green and shining above, with two conspicuous pale bands beneath, and on most New Zealand specimens spread all round the shoot and point forwards. The winter buds are red-brown and very resinous. Young shoots are pale cream and shiny, later nearly white. The cones stand upright and break up on the tree, as in all firs; they are large (one sheet gives 16 cm by 4 cm) with the tips of the bract scales showing and pointing outwards.
Other firs grown here differ: grand fir has long, flat needles in two rows, green above and white-banded below, with bract scales hidden; white fir and noble fir have grey-blue needles; Spanish fir also has needles spreading all round the shoot. Firs are hard to separate, and the one wild record rests on a few identifiers.

lookalikes.howToTell: Turn a shoot over: Greek fir's needles have two conspicuous pale bands beneath; yew's have two broad pale green bands, never white or silver. Greek fir's young shoots are pale cream and shiny and its winter buds red-brown and very resinous; yew's shoots are green and ribbed. Greek fir carries large upright cones that break up on the tree, leaving a bare spike; female yews carry soft crimson berry-like arils 10–15 mm long around a single seed, and yew has no woody cones. Most yews are male or female trees, so a tree without red arils can still be yew. Both can have flat needles lying in two rows, so the arrangement does not separate them. Every part of yew except the red flesh of the aril is deadly.

preparation.text: Pick the light-coloured new spring tips; older growth is more resinous. Take them from side branches spread over the tree, never the top of a young tree. Steep tips or needles in hot water for tea, simmer tips in a syrup, chop needles into marinades or use them as you would rosemary on roasts, or infuse them in spirits.

recipes.method: Written for fir or spruce tips. 500 ml water; 500 ml sugar; 500 ml fir tips; 15–30 ml (1–2 tbsp) lemon juice (optional). Bring the water and sugar to the boil in a lidded pot, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Turn off the heat, stir in the tips and lemon juice, cover and leave to cool; leave overnight for a stronger flavour. Strain through muslin and bottle. Keeps about 4 months in the fridge; it does not freeze well. Makes about 500 ml.
recipes.title: Fir tip syrup

recipes.method: Written for any fir, spruce or hemlock tips. 250 ml spring fir tips; 250 ml water; 250 ml sugar (white, demerara or turbinado). Put the tips in a jar, cover with the water, close the lid and leave somewhere warm, preferably in the sun. Strain the liquid into a small pan, add the sugar and stir over medium heat until dissolved. Pour into a clean jar and keep it in the fridge, where it lasts several weeks.

summary.text:
Greek fir (Abies cephalonica), also called Grecian fir, is a tall evergreen fir of the pine family (Pinaceae) from the mountains of southern Greece. Firs' young tips and needles are used for tea and flavouring.
In New Zealand: It is grown in botanic gardens, arboreta and pinetums, such as Christchurch, Whaka and Eastwoodhill. Biota of New Zealand lists it as cultivated only. One wild record comes from Kelburn in Wellington, where young firs of many sizes were growing in deep shade beneath planted trees. DOC records it on its Weeds database but does not class it as a weed.

warnings: Yew, a deadly poisonous conifer, has flat needles in two rows like some firs'. Check every tree before you pick (see the lookalikes).
Take extra care in pregnancy: many sources recommend against eating or drinking any conifer, including conifer-needle teas, while pregnant.
Try only a little the first time: allergic reactions to conifers are not common, but are more likely than with most foods.
Do not pick from trees that may have been sprayed. Wilding conifers are controlled with herbicide.

associations.note: Poisonous. Fly agaric has been recorded with Tasmanian blue gum overseas.

identification.text: A large to very large tree. The bark is rough towards the base but peels in long strips, leaving a mottled grey and whitish upper trunk and branches; young stems are square in cross-section, winged and waxy grey-white. Young leaves are in opposite pairs for many pairs, stalkless, grey-waxy, egg-shaped and clasp the stem with a heart-shaped base, up to about 20 × 10 cm (the Flora allows 40 × 16 cm). Adult leaves are alternate on a stout stalk up to about 4 cm long, 11–25 × 2–4.5 cm, lance-shaped and strongly sickle-curved, thick and leathery, bluish green and the same colour on both sides, with a clear vein 1–3 mm in from the edge. A single large, warty, waxy grey-white flower bud (very rarely three together) sits in each leaf axil with no stalk, up to about 2.8 × 2.5 cm, with a ribbed, funnel-shaped base and a flat cap with a central knob. The woody fruit are rounded to funnel-shaped, 10–21 mm long and 14–27 mm wide, ribbed, warty and waxy grey-white. It flowers from August to November. The leaves are often pimply from the feeding of small chalcid insects, which the Flora calls characteristic. Shining gum (Eucalyptus nitens) has very similar bark and leaves but small buds in clusters of seven (see Lookalikes).

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are tall eucalypts with very similar bark and leaves, so look at the buds and fruit. Tasmanian blue gum's flower buds are single (very rarely in threes), large, stalkless and waxy grey-white with a warty surface, up to about 25 mm long and 20 mm wide, with a ribbed, funnel-shaped base and a flat cap with a central knob; its woody fruit are 10–21 mm long and 14–27 mm wide, ribbed, with the disc raised above the rim. Shining gum's flower buds are small, stubby and stalkless, up to about 7 mm long and 4 mm wide, in clusters of seven; its fruit are cup- or barrel-shaped, only 4–7 mm long and wide, with the disc sunk below the rim. Tasmanian blue gum keeps slabs of rough bark on its lower trunk and flowers mainly from August to November; shining gum has smooth bark with at most a thin stocking of rough grey bark on the lowest metre and flowers from summer to early autumn. Neither tree is eaten.

summary.text:
Tasmanian blue gum (Eucalyptus globulus), called blue gum in the colder parts of New Zealand, is a large eucalypt of the myrtle family (Myrtaceae) from Tasmania. No part of it is recorded as a food for foragers; its leaf oil, which is poisonous if swallowed, is a commercial product.
In New Zealand: It has been widely planted for timber since early settlement, particularly in the lowlands of the South Island such as Canterbury, and NZPCN dates its naturalisation to 1880. The Flora calls it the first eucalypt recorded wild here and still the species most likely to naturalise in many cooler parts of the country. Seedlings and saplings are recorded near planted trees from Southland and Otago to Auckland and the Chatham Islands, along roadsides, on coastal banks and lakeshores, in regenerating scrub and on burnt ground. Trees here belong to subspecies globulus. It is not on DOC's weed list. It is here as a root partner of the fungi that grow with it.

warnings: Do not eat any part of Tasmanian blue gum. Its leaf oil is distilled commercially as a flavouring, but no part of the tree is recorded as food for foragers.

Eucalyptus oil, distilled from the leaves of any eucalypt, is poisonous if swallowed: a few drops can poison an infant. Keep it away from children. If anyone swallows it, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766 (0800 POISON).

associations.note: Poisonous. Fly agaric has been recorded with shining gum overseas.

identification.text: A tree to about 70 m tall with mostly smooth bark, pale grey to greenish grey with patches of white, cream or pale brown, sometimes with a thin stocking of rough grey bark on the lowest metre; ribbons of shed bark often hang in the crown. Young stems are square in cross-section and prominently winged, and may be waxy grey-white. Adult leaves are alternate, glossy green and the same colour on both sides, up to 300 × 40 mm, with the vein along the edge running parallel to and well in from the margin. Young leaves are usually blue-green or waxy grey-white, opposite and stalkless for many pairs until the sapling stage, egg-shaped to lance-shaped, up to 180 × 95 mm, clasping the stem, with a pointed tip; shoots from a cut stump keep these young leaves and are conspicuous. Flowers are in clusters of seven in the leaf axils on an angular, flattened stalk up to 15 mm long; the buds are stubby, stalkless, oblong to egg-shaped, up to 7 × 4 mm, green and pink with a conical cap, and the flowers are white. The woody fruit are stalkless, cup- to barrel-shaped, up to 7 × 7 mm, with the disc sunk below the rim. It flowers from summer to early autumn. Tasmanian blue gum has very similar bark and leaves but large single buds and fruit over 1 cm (see Lookalikes).

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are tall eucalypts with very similar bark and leaves, so look at the buds and fruit. Shining gum's flower buds are small, stubby and stalkless, up to about 7 mm long and 4 mm wide, in clusters of seven; its fruit are cup- or barrel-shaped, only 4–7 mm long and wide, with the disc sunk below the rim, and it flowers from summer to early autumn; its smooth bark has at most a thin stocking of rough grey bark on the lowest metre. Tasmanian blue gum's flower buds are single (very rarely in threes), large, stalkless and waxy grey-white with a warty surface, up to about 25 mm long and 20 mm wide, with a ribbed, funnel-shaped base and a flat cap with a central knob; its woody fruit are 10–21 mm long and 14–27 mm wide, with the disc raised above the rim; it keeps slabs of rough bark on its lower trunk and flowers mainly from August to November. Neither tree is eaten.

summary.text:
Shining gum (Eucalyptus nitens), also called silvertop, is a tall eucalypt of the myrtle family (Myrtaceae) from the high country of New South Wales and north-eastern Victoria. No part of it is recorded as food.
In New Zealand: It is widely planted for forestry, shelter and in parks and gardens, and the NZ Myrtaceae Key says it is occasionally naturalised from nearby planted trees; NZPCN dates its naturalisation to 1988. Seedlings are recorded near planted trees and firewood plantations at Papatowai in the Catlins, St Arnaud, the Aniseed Valley, Rabbit Island, Glentunnel, Linton Park, Hobsonville and Waiouru, and a sapling grew after the 2024 fires at Craigieburn. Observers sometimes cannot tell young shining gum from Tasmanian blue gum. It is not on DOC's weed list. It is here as a root partner of the fungi that grow with it.

warnings: No record of shining gum as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

Eucalyptus oil, distilled from the leaves of any eucalypt, is poisonous if swallowed: a few drops can poison an infant. Keep it away from children. If anyone swallows it, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766 (0800 POISON).

identification.text: A deciduous tree to about 15 m (to about 20 m in cultivation). The bark is dark brown and strongly fissured. The young shoots are hairless but sticky with glands, and the winter buds are short-stalked and purplish. The leaves are 4–10 × 2.5–10 cm on stalks 7–15 mm long (often purplish), broadly oblong to egg-shaped, folded like a fan in bud, finely to coarsely toothed, with 6–7 prominent raised vein pairs, a wedge-shaped base and a rounded or notched tip; they are hairy on the veins beneath at first, soon hairless apart from tufts in the vein angles. Male catkins hang in groups of 3–8 behind the shoot tips, 2.5–7 cm long, opening in spring before the leaves, with purplish bracts and yellow anthers; the small female catkins sit in groups of 3–7 and ripen into woody cones 1.3–1.7 cm long that stay on the tree. The nutlet is about 3 mm long with a wing narrower than the nut. In winter alders are easy to spot by the many developing catkins and the persistent woody cones. NZPCN gives 'No similar tree in that habitat'. Green alder (Alnus viridis), also naturalised here, is a multi-stemmed shrub of 0.75–2 m with stalkless dark buds that enclose the female catkins in winter; black alder is a tree with short-stalked buds that do not.

summary.text:
Black alder (Alnus glutinosa), also called common alder, European alder or alder, is a deciduous tree of the birch family (Betulaceae) from Europe, Asia and North Africa. Nitrogen-fixing root nodules let it grow on poor soils. No part of it is recorded as food.
In New Zealand: It was brought in for shelter, erosion control and as an ornamental, and has been widely planted in both islands, especially in colder areas. It was first recorded wild in 1914, and the Flora lists it as naturalised from the Waikato and Rotorua to Otago; NZPCN calls it especially common in the Waikato and Wairarapa, where it can be a problem weed. It spreads by wind- and water-borne seed and by suckers, along riversides and lake edges. DOC lists it as an environmental weed (2024 list), under sustained control in the Auckland regional pest plan and site-led control in the Waikato plan. It is here as a root partner of the fungi that grow with it.

warnings: No record of black alder as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

identification.text:
A tree up to about 25 m, usually spreading, that suckers profusely. The bark is grey, rather smooth to shallowly fissured. The shoots are round and covered in white felt, and the buds are white with pressed-down felt and not sticky. Young leaves are not aromatic. The leaf stalks are 1.5–5 cm long, white-felted and slightly flattened. On vigorous shoots the leaves are 3–10 × 2–9.5 cm, roughly triangular, with 3–5 toothed or lobed main lobes; on older shoots they are smaller, oval to almost round, lobed or strongly toothed, with no translucent border. The leaves are always white and woolly beneath, woolly at first on top, then smooth and shining green. The catkins are female, hanging, 2–8 cm long, and about October the capsules split and shed so much white cotton that it looks like a snowstorm. All naturalised trees here are female and belong to one clone.
Grey poplar (P. × canescens), a hybrid of white poplar and aspen, looks very like it and is told apart only by its leaves, which become smooth beneath as they mature; white poplar's stay white and woolly. Aspen's leaves are also smooth and blue-green beneath, on strongly flattened stalks.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are suckering poplars with non-sticky buds and unscented young leaves, so look at the underside of the leaf and the leaf stalk. White poplar's leaves stay densely white and woolly beneath, the shoots and buds are white-felted, its leaf stalk is only slightly flattened, and the leaves on vigorous shoots have 3–5 toothed or lobed main lobes. Aspen's leaves are hairy only when very young, soon smooth, green above and blue-green (glaucous) beneath; its shoots are dark and its buds hairless; its leaf stalk, 2–7 cm long, is strongly flattened, which makes the leaves tremble in the slightest breeze; and the leaves are broad-egg-shaped to almost round with coarse curved teeth. The trees here are usually female for white poplar and male for aspen. Aspen is not given as food on its page.

summary.text:
White poplar (Populus alba), also called silver poplar, silver-leaf poplar or abele, is a tall poplar of the willow family (Salicaceae) from southern and central Europe, western Asia and north Africa. Its inner bark is a famine food.
In New Zealand: It has been planted in many places but is generally regarded as undesirable because it suckers so strongly, which has produced large stands in coastal eastern South Island. It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds: it forms huge stands that keep native plants out, and its roots can clog watercourses. It spreads by suckers, which move with soil, planting and dumped garden waste; all the naturalised trees here are female and belong to one clone. The Flora of New Zealand records it as naturalised in both islands, especially in eastern areas.

associations.note: Poisonous. Fly agaric has been recorded with aspen overseas.

identification.text:
A tree up to about 16 m, widespreading and almost hairless, that often suckers profusely. The bark is greenish or yellowish green and rather smooth except near the base. The shoots are dark, slightly hairy at first and slightly angular when young. The buds are hairless and not sticky, and the young leaves are not aromatic. The leaves are hairy at first and soon smooth, on strongly flattened stalks 2–7 cm long, which is what makes them tremble in the slightest breeze. The leaf blade is 2.5–12 × 3–12 cm, broad-egg-shaped to almost round, sometimes broader than long, green above and blue-green (glaucous) beneath, with coarse, often curved teeth and no translucent border. The catkins are male, hanging, up to 10 cm long, with purple anthers; female trees are rare and seen only in cultivation.
White poplar's leaves stay white and woolly beneath, and grey poplar (P. × canescens) is the hybrid between the two. American aspen (P. tremuloides), planted in a number of places, has pale yellowish bark when young and finely toothed leaves that are hairy when young.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are suckering poplars with non-sticky buds and unscented young leaves, so look at the underside of the leaf and the leaf stalk. Aspen's leaves are hairy only when very young, soon smooth, green above and blue-green (glaucous) beneath; its shoots are dark and its buds hairless; its leaf stalk, 2–7 cm long, is strongly flattened, which makes the leaves tremble in the slightest breeze; and the leaves are broad-egg-shaped to almost round with coarse curved teeth. White poplar's leaves stay densely white and woolly beneath, the shoots and buds are white-felted, its leaf stalk is only slightly flattened, and the leaves on vigorous shoots have 3–5 toothed or lobed main lobes. The trees here are usually male for aspen and female for white poplar. White poplar's inner bark is a famine food (see its page).

summary.text:
Aspen (Populus tremula), also called European aspen, is a poplar of the willow family (Salicaceae) from temperate Eurasia, named for its leaves that tremble in the slightest breeze. 'Quaking aspen' is also the usual name of an American species, P. tremuloides.
In New Zealand: It is planted occasionally, particularly in the South Island and the colder parts of the North Island. The Flora of New Zealand records it forming dense stands in a few places in Canterbury, in pastures beside old plantations and shrubberies; most of this is suckers from planted trees, and the wild trees are almost all male, because female trees are rare and seen only in cultivation. DOC records it on its Weeds database but does not class it as a weed.

warnings: Too little evidence of aspen as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
