identification.text:
A very large, spreading tree that suckers extensively. The bark is grey and fissured. The shoots are roughly round and hairless except when very young. The buds are very sticky and hairless, and the young leaves are very aromatic, with a balsam scent. The leaf stalks are 3.5–7 cm long, roughly round when fresh, sticky, with spreading hairs. The leaves are 6–23 × 5.5–20 cm, broad-egg-shaped, hairy on the veins above and beneath, green above and greenish white beneath, with a fringed edge, round teeth tipped with glands and no translucent border; the base is heart-shaped or slightly so, sometimes rounded, with two glands (sometimes faint), and the tip is drawn out to a point. The catkins are female, hanging, 13–19 cm long, and the capsules are full of long white silky hairs. It is known only as a female clone.
Black cottonwood, also sticky and balsam-scented, suckers only moderately and has hairless leaf stalks and veins, angled brown shoots and male trees here. Yunnan poplar has pink leaf veins, very glossy upper leaves and reddish purple or yellowish brown year-old shoots.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are big poplars of riverbanks and roadsides with very sticky, balsam-scented buds and young leaves that are whitish beneath, so scent and buds do not separate them; look at the leaf stalks, shoots and suckering. Black cottonwood's leaf stalks are up to about 9 cm, round and hairless, its veins are hairless and green above, its young shoots are somewhat angled and brown, it suckers only moderately, and the wild trees here are all male, so there is no cotton. Balm of Gilead's leaf stalks are 3.5–7 cm, roughly round, sticky and covered in spreading hairs, its leaf veins are hairy above and beneath, its young shoots are roughly round, it suckers very freely, and the trees here are all female, with long catkins that give white silky cotton. Black cottonwood's inner bark is eaten fresh in spring (see its page).

summary.text:
Balm of Gilead poplar is a hybrid poplar of the willow family (Salicaceae), known only as a female clone, whose buds and young leaves are very sticky and smell strongly of balsam. The Flora of New Zealand thinks its parents are probably the North American balsam poplar and eastern cottonwood. iNaturalist files it as Populus × ontariensis; the Flora of New Zealand and NZPCN call it P. × gileadensis, and Biota and DOC call it P. × jackii.
In New Zealand: It has been widely planted and, because it suckers so strongly, sometimes forms stands covering large areas from one or a few trees, in rough pastures, along roadsides and near farm boundaries. The Flora records it in Hawke's Bay and Wairarapa in the North Island and the Christchurch area, Albury, Jollie Gorge, Mt Cook Station, the Liebig Range and Central Otago in the South Island. DOC records it on its Weeds database but does not class it as a weed.

warnings: No record of balm of Gilead poplar as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

identification.text:
A large, widespreading tree that suckers moderately. The bark is grey and fissured. The shoots are somewhat angled when young, almost winged on strong vegetative shoots, and reddish purple to yellowish brown. The buds are very sticky and hairless, and the young shoots are strongly sticky and smell of balsam. The leaf stalks are up to about 10 cm long, almost round and hairless. The leaves are up to 18 × 13.5 cm, broad-egg-shaped, hairless apart from a finely fringed edge, greenish white beneath and glossy green above, reddish brown as they unfold, with the midrib and veins pink above; the edge is finely round-toothed with no translucent border, the base slightly to deeply heart-shaped and without glands, the tip long-pointed. The catkins are male, hanging, up to about 16 cm long, with anthers crimson towards the tip. Until recently all New Zealand trees were male, probably one clone, but female clones have since been brought in for planting.
Black cottonwood has brown year-old shoots, leaves that are green as they unfold and green veins above. Balm of Gilead poplar is a female clone with hairy leaf stalks and veins that suckers much more.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are big, moderately suckering balsam poplars of riverbanks with very sticky, balsam-scented buds, hairless leaf stalks, so look at the colour of the shoots and the unfolding leaves. Black cottonwood's year-old shoots are brown, its leaves are green as they unfold, its veins are green above, its leaves are to 13 (sometimes 18) × 10 cm with a base broadly wedge-shaped, square or only slightly heart-shaped, and its catkins reach about 10 cm. Yunnan poplar's year-old shoots are reddish purple or yellowish brown, its leaves are reddish brown as they unfold, its veins are pink above, with a very glossy upper surface, its leaves are to 18 × 13.5 cm with a base slightly to deeply heart-shaped, and its catkins reach about 16 cm. Black cottonwood's inner bark is eaten fresh in spring (see its page).

summary.text:
Yunnan poplar (Populus yunnanensis), also called Chinese poplar, is a large balsam poplar of the willow family (Salicaceae) from south-west China, with sticky, balsam-scented buds and young shoots.
In New Zealand: It has been very commonly planted for amenity, erosion control and windbreaks, especially in the North Island, partly because possums leave its foliage alone. The Flora of New Zealand says it is now often impossible to tell whether trees on riverbanks or by shelter belts were planted, and that it is apparently the balsam poplar most likely to grow wild, although it does not sucker as extensively as balm of Gilead poplar. It has hybridised spontaneously with a black poplar (Populus deltoides) at Waipukurau and Waitotara. DOC records it on its Weeds database but does not class it as a weed.

warnings: No record of Yunnan poplar as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

identification.text:
A tree up to about 15 m, with grey-brown fissured bark and long drooping branchlets, often more than 1 m unbranched at the tips, that hang to the ground or the water; over flowing water they twist together into 'ropes'. The leaves are very narrow, 105–173 mm long and 15–35 mm wide, with fine, even teeth and flat edges, smooth and glossy above and distinctly waxy blue-grey (glaucous) beneath, and on the hanging branchlets they lie in a herringbone pattern. There are two forms, the only weeping willows in New Zealand: weeping willow (f. pendulina) has greyish yellow-green to olive year-old branchlets, only female catkins, mottled leaves that turn brittle in late summer and get leaf rust; golden weeping willow (f. salamonii) has uniformly yellow year-old branchlets, catkins of mixed sex, and leaf galls.
Without long drooping branches, f. pendulina can be hard to tell from the female crack willow (Salix × fragilis), which has plenty of leaf galls and evenly dense pores (stomata) on the upper leaf surface.

summary.text:
Weeping willow (Salix × pendulina) is a hybrid weeping willow of the willow family (Salicaceae); the Flora of New Zealand now places both of New Zealand's weeping willows, weeping willow and golden weeping willow, under this name, where older books used Salix babylonica or S. × sepulcralis (kemp willow).
In New Zealand: It is a very common cultivated tree on river and stream banks, in parks and along trails. The Flora records only two definite cases of it becoming wild, so most trees are planted. DOC lists it as a weed (125 records), and the Otago regional pest plan lists it as an organism of interest.

warnings: No record of weeping willow as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

associations.note: Poisonous. Fly agaric has been recorded with pin oak overseas.

identification.text:
A medium to large deciduous oak. It is one of three American oaks of the red oak group (the Flora's Erythrobalanus) planted in New Zealand that are often confused with one another, the others being red oak (Q. rubra) and scarlet oak (Q. coccinea). Compared with them, pin oak generally has smaller leaves, with lobes cut more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib on fruiting shoots, more conspicuous tufts of hair in the vein angles beneath, and a smaller, even shallower acorn cup than red oak's.
Overseas descriptions (no New Zealand account covers these): leaves about 5–16 cm long, dark green on both sides, with five or seven lobes ending in bristle-tipped teeth and deep, U-shaped sinuses, with small tufts of tan hair where the veins meet beneath. Bark smooth and grey on young trees, rougher on old ones. The branching is distinctive: the upper branches rise, the middle ones are held out level and the lowest droop. Young trees and the lower branches of older ones keep their dead leaves through winter. Acorns take two years to ripen and are rounded, about 1–1.6 cm long, in a thin, shallow cup that covers a quarter to a third of the nut.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are American oaks of the red oak group, often confused with each other, and both have acorns that are eaten once leached for a long time; look at the leaves and the acorn cup. Pin oak's leaves are generally smaller (about 5–16 cm long), with five or seven lobes cut more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib on fruiting shoots, so the sinuses are deep and U-shaped, and conspicuous tufts of hair where the veins meet beneath; its acorns are small, about 1–1.6 cm and rounded, in a thin, very shallow cup. Red oak's leaves are larger, mostly 11–20 cm, with 3–5 pairs of lobes cut only a third to two-thirds of the way to the midrib and at most a few brownish hairs in the vein angles; its acorns are 2–2.5 cm and egg-shaped, about a quarter enclosed by a larger cup 1.5–2 cm across. Scarlet oak, the third lookalike, has more deeply lobed, very glossy leaves (see red oak).
lookalikes.name: Red oak

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are big deciduous oaks whose acorns are eaten once leached; look at the leaves and acorns. Pin oak's leaves (about 5–16 cm) have five or seven lobes ending in bristle-tipped teeth, with deep sinuses and tufts of hair where the veins meet beneath; its acorns take two years to ripen and are small, about 1–1.6 cm and rounded, in a thin, shallow cup. English oak's leaves have 3–7 pairs of blunt, rounded lobes with no bristles, and small ear-like lobes at the base that almost hide the leaf stalk, usually under 2 mm long; its acorns ripen in their first year, are 2–4 cm long and oblong, a quarter to a third in the cup, on a fruiting stalk 3–13 cm long. Pin oak's acorns are more bitter and need much longer leaching than English oak's (see its page).
lookalikes.name: English oak

preparation.text: Gather acorns once they are ripe and brown, leaving any that are discoloured, soft or holed. Pin oak belongs to the red oak group, whose acorns carry more tannin than white oak group acorns and need much longer leaching than English oak's. The papery skin sticks to the nut, is bitter and darkens the flour; freezing fresh acorns for a week or two before cracking makes the skin come off more easily. Chop or grind the shelled nuts small, cover with about three times their volume of cold water, and pour it off and add fresh every day: red-group acorns usually take one to two weeks, sometimes longer. Keep tasting: it is done when it tastes bland, not bitter, even if the water stays tinted. Cold leaching keeps the starch that binds baking. For a quicker leach, boil the pieces and change the water every 20–30 minutes; red-group acorns take two to three hours, and the starch is lost. Dry the meal and grind it to flour; it is oily, so keep it in the fridge or freezer.

recipes.method: Written for acorns generally; red-group acorns need the long leach first (see preparation). 1 egg; 5 ml (1 tsp) oil; 5 ml (1 tsp) honey or sugar; 125 ml (½ cup) ground, leached acorns; 125 ml (½ cup) cornmeal; 125 ml (½ cup) wholemeal or plain flour; 10 ml (2 tsp) baking powder; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 125 ml (½ cup) milk. Break the egg into a bowl, add everything else and beat together; if the batter is too thick to pour, thin it with milk. Pour onto a hot, greased griddle and cook slowly until brown on both sides. Serve with butter and syrup or blackberry jam.
recipes.title: Acorn and cornmeal pancakes

recipes.method: Written for any acorn flour, best cold-leached (see preparation). 125 ml (½ cup) wholemeal or plain flour; 125 ml (½ cup) finely ground cold-leached acorn flour; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt; a few scrapes of nutmeg; 2 eggs; 125 ml (½ cup) milk, water or the nut milk left from leaching. Mix everything to a smooth batter with no lumps. Bring a pot of salted water to a simmer and press the batter through the holes of a colander in batches; cook about 30 seconds, then lift out, drain and toss with a little oil. Reheat in butter with chopped chives and parsley. Serves 4 as a side.
recipes.title: Acorn flour spaetzle

recipes.method: Written for leached acorn meal from any oak; pin oak meal needs the longer red-group leach first (see preparation). 1.5 litres (6 cups) leached acorn meal; 1.5 litres (6 cups) spelt or other bread flour; 7.5 ml (½ tbsp) salt; fresh yeast; water; sesame, poppy or sunflower seeds. Mix the acorn meal, flour and salt in a large bowl. Dissolve the yeast in 125 ml (½ cup) lukewarm water and stir it in, then knead well, adding water or flour until the dough is neither stiff nor sticky. Cover with a cloth and leave to rise overnight. Knead again and shape into two loaves; score the tops, brush with water and sprinkle with seeds. Bake at 200 °C for 45 minutes. Makes two large loaves.
recipes.title: Acorn and spelt bread

recipes.method: Written for acorns generally. Ripe acorns, shelled and leached in hot water until no longer bitter (see preparation); salt. Spread the damp, leached chunks on a baking tray, sprinkle with salt and toast on a high heat for 15–20 minutes, until the colour starts to darken. Cool before eating, or add them to a winter stew.
recipes.title: Roasted acorns

recipes.method: Written for acorns generally. Ripe acorns, shelled and leached in hot water until no longer bitter (see preparation). Lay them in an ovenproof dish and roast on a low heat for 1½–2 hours to dry them slowly, moving them around often so they don't catch. They brown as they dry: take them out when they reach a light or dark roast, as you prefer. Cool, grind and brew like coffee. It has no caffeine and tastes unlike ordinary coffee.
recipes.title: Acorn coffee

summary.text:
Pin oak (Quercus palustris), also called Spanish oak, is a deciduous oak of the beech family (Fagaceae) from the north-east and centre of North America. Its acorns are edible once leached.
In New Zealand: It is widely planted in parks, streets and gardens, and is easily the commonest of the three American red-group oaks grown here (with red oak and scarlet oak). Biota of New Zealand lists it as casual: self-sown seedlings are recorded under or beside planted trees in Auckland, Tauranga, Feilding and Kaingaroa Forest, but no stand independent of planted trees is recorded, and the Flora notes that of the three, pin oak trees are the least likely to have self-sown seedlings near them. DOC records it on its Weeds database but does not class it as a weed.

warnings: Raw acorns are bitter with tannins, which can be toxic: always leach them first.
Eating too many acorns can cause digestive upsets.

identification.text: A very large deciduous tree, with a straight trunk. No NZ account describes it (it is not in the Flora's account of naturalised plants), so this is from overseas descriptions. Leaves alternate, simple, about 10–15 cm long and as wide, with four lobes and a flat, shallowly notched tip, so the top of the leaf looks cut off square; long slender stalks; bright green and shining above, paler beneath, turning clear yellow in autumn. Flowers solitary, upright, cup-shaped and tulip-like, about 5–6 cm long, greenish yellow with an orange band at the base of each petal, held high in the tree. Fruit an upright, narrow, cone-like cluster of winged seeds, about 5–8 cm long, which breaks up and leaves a bare spike on the tree through winter. Bark brown, furrowed, aromatic and bitter.

summary.text:
Tulip tree (Liriodendron tulipifera), also called tulip poplar, is a very large deciduous tree of the magnolia family (Magnoliaceae) from eastern North America, known for its tulip-shaped flowers and square-tipped leaves. Its flowers hold sweet nectar.
In New Zealand: It is planted in parks, gardens and arboreta. Biota of New Zealand lists it as casual: self-sown seedlings are recorded near planted trees at Rotorua, Selwyn, Whanganui, Nelson, Palmerston North and Whangārei, though no stand independent of planted trees is recorded. DOC records it on its Weeds database, as tulip poplar, but does not class it as a weed. Biota also records New Zealand's green mistletoe, Ileostylus micranthus, growing on it.

identification.text: A deciduous shrub to medium-sized tree, 3–20 m high, with a short, straight trunk or several stems and a spreading crown. Young twigs grooved, grey to red-brown or dark red, with white hairs. Leaves 6–30 × 6–20 mm, broadly egg-shaped, thin, glossy green above and paler beneath with hairs along the veins, the veins distinct and no fringed pits (domatia) where they meet; the margin wavy to lobed, irregularly double-toothed with blunt teeth and finely fringed with hairs; the tip blunt and the base lopsided; leaf stalk 1–6 mm long and hairy. Bark smooth, grey or purplish brown with prominent horizontal white lenticels on young trees, rough, fissured and grey on old ones. Fruit a small cupule 5–6 mm long that splits into four resinous, hairy valves, holding nuts 3.5–4.5 mm long. It is told from every New Zealand beech by being deciduous, by its young leaves being folded in the bud (plicate), and by the smooth purple-grey bark with white lenticels on young trunks.

summary.text:
Antarctic beech (Nothofagus antarctica), known as ñire in its native Chile and Argentina, is a deciduous beech of the southern beech family (Nothofagaceae) from southern South America (the Flora's type specimen is from Tierra del Fuego).
In New Zealand: It is planted in arboreta, and Biota of New Zealand lists it as casual. The Flora records seedlings and saplings establishing from cultivated plantings at two inland montane sites in Canterbury, on a river terrace in the Havelock River and in a hill planting of exotic trees in the Broken River catchment of the Craigieburn Range; its first record is a Canterbury herbarium sheet from May 1998. DOC records it on its Weeds database but does not class it as a weed.

warnings: No record of Antarctic beech as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

identification.text:
A deciduous birch. No Flora account describes it, but the Flora notes that it is grown in New Zealand, that its leaves and young shoots are hairy and its bark brownish or grey, and that it may sometimes have been planted by mistake for silver birch, whose leaves and shoots are hairless, shoots resinous and warty, and bark silvery-white and papery, usually becoming dark grey and rough at least on the lower trunk.
Overseas descriptions (no NZ account covers these): a tree 10–20 m tall, rarely to 27 m, more upright than silver birch, with a slender crown. Bark smooth but dull grey-white, becoming browner, finely marked with dark horizontal lenticels and with obvious horizontal grooves, and never papery like silver birch's. Twigs grey-brown and finely downy, not warty. Leaf stalks downy. Leaves egg-shaped to triangular, 2–5 cm long and 1.5–4.5 cm wide, with a pointed tip, more rounded at the base than silver birch's, and a finely toothed margin where silver birch's is coarsely double-toothed.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are birches whose sap is tapped in spring, and the Flora says downy birch may sometimes have been planted by mistake for silver birch; look at the shoots, leaf stalks and bark. Downy birch's young shoots, leaves and leaf stalks are hairy or downy, its bark is brownish or grey, browner than silver birch's, with obvious horizontal grooves and not papery, and its leaf margin is finely toothed. Silver birch's shoots and leaves are hairless, its shoots are sticky with resin and dotted with warts, its bark is silvery-white and papery, usually turning dark grey and rough on the lower trunk, and its leaf margin is coarsely double-toothed. Both saps are used the same way (see their pages).

preparation.text: Collect the sap in early spring, while it is rising and before the leaves open. Drill a small hole about 1 cm wide and about 5 cm deep into the trunk, push in a length of plastic tubing and run it into a container, sealing any gaps where the tube enters. Drink the sap fresh, ferment it, or boil off the water to concentrate it into a syrup. Between 4 and 7 litres can be drawn from a mature tree in a day without killing it, as long as the hole is filled afterwards; prolonged or heavy tapping will kill the tree.

summary.text:
Downy birch (Betula pubescens), also called white birch, is a deciduous tree of the birch family (Betulaceae), native to most of Europe and east to western Siberia and central Asia. Its sap can be tapped in spring.
In New Zealand: It is grown in gardens and parks and may sometimes have been planted by mistake for silver birch. Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and cultivated; a few iNaturalist records report saplings or seedlings near adult trees, in the Bay of Plenty, at Upper Moutere and at Rotorua, but no established wild stand is recorded. DOC records it on its Weeds database but does not class it as a weed. The introduced fungi that grow with silver birch here, among them birch bolete and fly agaric, are recorded with downy birch overseas.

associations.note: Poisonous. Fly agaric has been recorded with snow gum in New Zealand.

identification.text: A tree up to about 30 m tall, or a many-stemmed shrub, with smooth bark over the whole trunk, shed in irregular patches to leave white, cream and grey with yellow patches; the young branches may be waxy grey-white. Adult leaves are alternate and stalked (8–33 mm), slightly sickle-shaped to lance-shaped or elliptic, 60–200 × 12–50 mm, glossy green and the same colour on both sides, with parallel side veins and the vein along the edge running well in from the margin. Young leaves are dull blue-green or waxy grey-white, opposite and stalkless or short-stalked for two to five pairs, then alternate and stalked, up to 170 × 85 mm. The flowers are in stalked clusters of 9 to 15 or more in the leaf axils; the buds are usually stalked (stalk to 6 mm), broadly club-shaped, 4–8 × 3–5 mm, and the flowers are white. The woody fruit are cup-shaped, funnel-shaped or rounded, 5–11 (up to 13) mm long and 5–11 mm wide, with three (sometimes four) valves level with the rim or enclosed. It flowers in spring and summer, with some flowering from late winter. The NZ Myrtaceae Key groups it with the blue-leaved ash eucalypts and separates it from the others by its smooth bark over the whole trunk and the parallel side veins of its adult leaves.

summary.text:
Snow gum (Eucalyptus pauciflora), also called cabbage gum or white sally, is a eucalypt of the myrtle family (Myrtaceae) from the higher country of south-eastern Australia, including Tasmania. The trees grown here belong to subspecies pauciflora. No part of it is recorded as food.
In New Zealand: It is grown in parks, tree collections and forestry trials. The NZ Myrtaceae Key does not record it as naturalised, and Biota lists it as Exotic, Cultivated (Wilcox 2012); DOC does not classify it as a weed. Observers have recorded young trees coming up on their own: wildings at Pukaki, self-seeded trees at Jacks Point, plants recruiting after a fire at Lake Pearson, and others at Twizel and in Craigieburn Forest Park, and a herbarium sheet records an adventive sapling at Rotorua. An observer in Fiordland National Park ring-barked one as an introduced species. It is here as a root partner of the fungi that grow with it.

warnings: No record of snow gum as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

Eucalyptus oil, distilled from the leaves of any eucalypt, is poisonous if swallowed: a few drops can poison an infant. Keep it away from children. If anyone swallows it, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766 (0800 POISON).
